What makes a married woman more likely to be in the labour force, and by how much? The data are 753 married women in 1975; 568 in every thousand were working. The outcome \(y_i\) is 1 if the woman works, and the model for the probability is The Bayesian version adds a prior on \(\beta\) and reports its posterior distribution. The engine uses an independent normal prior on each slope, \(\beta_j \sim N(0, s^2)\) per one-standard-deviation change in \(x_j\) (Gelman et al. 2008), so a single number \(s\) is meaningful whatever the units of the variables; the default \(s = 2.5\) is weakly informative: a one-s.d. change in a regressor is unlikely to move the log odds by more than about 5. The constant has an \(N(0, 10^2)\) prior.

Link Sampler Properties Probit Albert-Chib (1993) Gibbs sampler: draw a latent normal variable for each observation, then the coefficients Exact conditional distributions: no tuning, no rejection Logit Independence Metropolis-Hastings with a Student- \(t\) proposal centred at the posterior mode Acceptance rate is reported; draws are correlated Both link functions give almost the same probabilities; the logit coefficients are about 1.6 to 1.9 times the probit ones, and the logit has odds ratios. The engine runs several chains from different starting points and reports the R-hat statistic. Why Bayesian? Three reasons. (1) The marginal effect on the probability is a nonlinear function of the coefficients and the data; with draws you get its full posterior, with an interval that means what people think it means, and no delta method. (2) A prior can include earlier evidence. (3) With a rare outcome, a small sample or separation (a regressor that predicts the outcome perfectly), maximum likelihood either fails or produces estimates that are infinite; a prior keeps the problem well posed (Step 8).

How to write it: the model We estimate the probability of labour force participation by Bayesian logit (Polson et al. 2013 and Gelman et al. 2008 for the prior). Each slope has an independent normal prior with standard deviation 2.5 per one-standard-deviation change in its regressor, and the constant a normal prior with standard deviation 10. The posterior is sampled by independence Metropolis-Hastings with a Student- \(t\) proposal at the posterior mode, in two chains of 2,000 draws after 1,000 burn-in draws. We report posterior means, 95% credible intervals, odds ratios and average marginal effects computed draw by draw.

How to read it Of 753 women, 57% were in the labour force. Working women are better educated (12.7 years against 11.8), have much more experience (13.0 years against 7.5), are slightly younger (42.0 against 43.3) and have far fewer small children (0.14 against 0.37 children under six on average), and live in households with a somewhat lower income from other sources ($18,900 against $21,700). nwifeinc is the husband's and other household income in thousands of dollars, so it is the income a woman has if she does not work. kidslt6 counts children under six and kidsge6 children aged six to eighteen.

How to read it Each row is a posterior distribution for a coefficient in the log odds. An extra year of education raises the log odds of working by 0.229 (posterior standard deviation 0.044; 95% credible interval 0.146 to 0.316), and a year of experience by 0.121. Age lowers it by 0.092 a year, and each child under six by 1.46, a large effect. Household income from others lowers it by 0.020 per thousand dollars, with a posterior probability of 0.994 that the effect is negative. Children aged six or older have a coefficient of 0.058, with a posterior probability of being positive of only 0.775: the data cannot tell the sign.

The second table sets the maximum likelihood estimates against the posterior means and standard deviations. They agree to within 0.12 standard errors for every coefficient (education 0.227 against 0.229; children under six \(-1.439\) against \(-1.456\) ). With 753 observations and a weak prior this is the expected result: the Bayesian logit reports the same answer with a better interpretation.

The coefficient is not the effect on the probability. The odds ratio \(e^{\beta}\) is the factor by which a one-unit change multiplies the odds of working. The average marginal effect is the change in the probability, averaged over the women in the sample; for a dummy variable it is the change from 0 to 1. Both are computed for each posterior draw, so they come with credible intervals. How to read it A year of education multiplies the odds of working by 1.26 (95% interval 1.16 to 1.37); each child under six multiplies them by 0.24 (0.15 to 0.35), so the odds fall by about three-quarters. In probability terms, the average woman's probability of working rises by 4.2 percentage points per year of education (95% interval 2.7 to 5.5), by 2.2 points per year of experience, and falls by 1.6 points per year of age and by 25.7 points per child under six (interval \(-31.6\) to \(-19.5\) ). An extra thousand dollars of other household income lowers it by 0.4 points ( \(-0.6\) to \(-0.1\) ). The effect of children over six, 1.1 points, has an interval from \(-1.7\) to 3.8 points that includes zero. State effects on the probability in the paper, because readers cannot interpret log odds, and report the interval.

How to read it R-hat compares the variance between the two chains with the variance within each; values near one, as here (at most 1.002), mean the chains have found the same distribution. The effective sample size is the number of independent draws the 4,000 correlated draws are worth: between 1,810 and 2,341 for every parameter, which is plenty for means and intervals. The Metropolis-Hastings acceptance rate, in the note under the table, is 0.73: the proposal fits the posterior closely, so most proposed draws are accepted. The trace plot shows the draws of experience, the best-determined coefficient, wandering around a stable level, and the histogram is the posterior density.
If R-hat is above 1.05 or the effective sample size is a few dozen, do not report the results: run longer, drop highly collinear regressors or tighten the prior. Step 8 shows that case.

How to read it A posterior predictive check simulates new data from the fitted model and asks whether they look like the real data. The model predicts that 57.1% of women work, with a 95% range from 53.0% to 61.1% across posterior draws, and the sample share (56.8%) lies inside it. This is a weak check, since a logit with a constant reproduces the share by construction, but it confirms that nothing is wrong with the constant. Discrimination is moderate. The model classifies 74.0% of women correctly at a 0.5 cut-off, against 56.8% by always predicting that a woman works, and the area under the ROC curve is 0.797 (0.5 is chance, 1 is perfect). The Brier score is 0.181; always predicting the sample share would give 0.245. Participation depends on much that the model does not observe, which is why 26% are still misclassified.
Robustness: the prior and the link

How to read it Each row of the first table is a separate run with a different prior standard deviation, from 0.5 (tight) to 100 (almost flat). The slopes for \(s \ge 2.5\) are within 0.005 of each other, and the maximum likelihood row is within about 0.01 of them. The tight prior pulls the large coefficients towards zero: children under six \(-1.35\) at \(s = 0.5\) against \(-1.44\) , and education 0.218 against 0.227. No conclusion changes: the signs and sizes are the same under every prior. The second table compares the average marginal effects under the two links: they differ by less than 0.01 for every variable (education 0.0415 and 0.0404; children under six \(-0.257\) and \(-0.266\) ). Logit and probit coefficients differ by a scale factor; marginal effects are the same quantities and are the sensible thing to compare.

Women with three or more children under six are rare: three women, none of whom works. A dummy for them predicts the outcome perfectly. Maximum likelihood cannot estimate its coefficient. How to read it The likelihood keeps rising as the coefficient falls, so the maximum does not exist: the fitting routine stops at \(-18.7\) with a standard error of 5,566, which means nothing. A Bayesian estimate exists, because the prior stops the posterior from running off to \(-\infty\) , but it is the prior's answer, not the data's . The posterior mean of the coefficient moves from \(-7.8\) to \(-140\) as the prior standard deviation goes from 0.5 to 10 per standard deviation of the dummy (which is only 0.063, so a prior s.d. of 2.5 is a coefficient s.d. of about 40), and the diagnostics sound the alarm: the final run (prior s.d. 10) has an effective sample size of about 60 for the dummy and an R-hat of 1.44. Do not report the coefficient.

What the data do identify is the effect on the probability . The average marginal effect is stable: \(-0.53\) at \(s = 0.5\) , \(-0.55\) , \(-0.57\) and \(-0.57\) at \(s = 10\) , with an interval whose upper end is \(-0.26\) at the tightest prior and between \(-0.35\) and \(-0.53\) at the others. Having three small children lowers the probability of working by 53 to 57 points, which is the sample's finding (none of three works); but with three women the result is a statement about those three. Say so, and either pool categories (two or more children) or treat the dummy as uninformative and drop it.

How to write it: results Table 1 reports the Bayesian logit for labour force participation among 753 married women. Education and experience raise the probability of working and age, household income from other sources and young children lower it. An extra year of schooling multiplies the odds of working by 1.26 (95% credible interval 1.16 to 1.37) and raises the probability by 4.2 percentage points (2.7 to 5.5); a child under six multiplies the odds by 0.24 (0.15 to 0.35) and lowers the probability by 25.7 points (19.5 to 31.6). Children aged six to eighteen have no clear effect (posterior probability of a positive effect 0.78). The two chains converge (R-hat at most 1.002, effective sample sizes above 1,800). The posterior means are within 0.12 standard errors of maximum likelihood, and the conclusions are the same under priors with standard deviation from 0.5 to 100 per standard deviation of the regressor, and under a probit link (average marginal effects within 0.01). The model classifies 74% of women correctly (area under the ROC curve 0.80), against 57% for always predicting participation.

Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

How much does an extra year of education raise wages, once experience, tenure, ability and demographics are held fixed? This is the Mincer wage regression. The model is with \(x_i\) containing education, experience, tenure, IQ and dummies for marriage, race, region and city. OLS gives one number per coefficient and a standard error. A Bayesian regression gives a whole posterior distribution for each coefficient: you can read off the probability that the return to schooling exceeds 5%, combine the data with the results of earlier studies, and compare specifications without a p-value threshold. The OES engine uses a conjugate Normal-inverse-gamma prior. Everything is exact: no simulation, no convergence to check, and the log marginal likelihood is available in closed form. Two priors are offered for the slopes:
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

Prior What it says When to use it Zellner's g-prior \(\beta \sim N(\beta_0, g\,\sigma^2 (X'X)^{-1})\) : the prior is as informative as \(1/g\) of an observation's worth of the sample, scaled to the regressors Default. Unit-free, so it needs no judgement about the scale of each variable. \(g = n\) is the "unit-information prior" Normal \(\beta_j \sim N(\beta_{0j}, s^2)\) , the same standard deviation for every slope When the variables are in comparable units, or when you have a prior from earlier work The constant has a flat prior and \(\sigma^2\) an inverse-gamma(0.01, 0.01) prior in both cases. A large \(g\) (or large \(s\) ) lets the data speak; a small one pulls the slopes towards the prior mean \(\beta_0\) .
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

Frequentist or Bayesian? With 663 observations and a weak prior, the two give almost the same numbers, and that is the point: a Bayesian regression is a way of reporting the answer (probabilities, intervals that mean what people think they mean) and of using extra information, not a different estimate. Use it when the sample is small, when you have genuine prior information, or when model comparison is part of the question. How to write it: the model We estimate the log-wage equation by Bayesian linear regression with a Zellner g-prior on the slopes ( \(g = n\) , the unit-information prior), a flat prior on the constant and an inverse-gamma(0.01, 0.01) prior on the error variance (Zellner 1986; Liang et al. 2008). With this conjugate prior the marginal posterior of each coefficient is a Student- \(t\) distribution, available in closed form, and we report its mean, standard deviation, 95% credible interval and the posterior probability that the coefficient is positive.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

How to read it 663 men, with log wages averaging 6.81 (about $900 a month) and a standard deviation of 0.41. Education averages 13.7 years. Nine in ten are married, 8% are Black, 32% live in the South and 72% in a city. Dummy variables like these have a standard deviation below 0.5, while IQ has 14.7: the g-prior is useful here because it scales the prior for each coefficient by the spread of its regressor, so you do not have to choose a different prior standard deviation for IQ and for a dummy.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

How to read it Each row is a posterior distribution. Take education: the posterior mean is 0.055 with a standard deviation of 0.008, so a year of schooling raises wages by about 5.5%, and there is a 95% probability that the effect lies between 3.9% and 7.1%. That is a direct statement about the parameter; a frequentist confidence interval cannot be read that way. The last column, \(P(>0)\) , is the posterior probability that the effect is positive: 1.000 for education, experience, marriage and city; 0.999 for tenure and IQ; and 0.012 and 0.019 for Black and South, whose effects are negative with high probability. Compare with OLS: coefficients agree to the third decimal place. The g-prior with \(g = n\) carries the weight of a single observation, so with 663 observations it moves nothing. This is the expected result with a weak prior and a decent sample; Step 6 shows what happens with a stronger prior.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

The log marginal likelihood is the probability of the data under the model with the coefficients integrated out. It rewards fit and automatically penalises a model for having parameters it does not need. The difference between two models is the log Bayes factor . How to read it A log Bayes factor above about 1 is "some evidence" for the full model, above 2.3 is "strong" and above 4.6 "decisive" (Jeffreys' scale). Dropping urban costs almost 17 log points: the city dummy is decisive. Dropping IQ costs 2.0 and tenure 1.3: moderate evidence for both. Dropping south or black raises the marginal likelihood by 1.1 and 0.7: the data, after the penalty for extra parameters, slightly prefer the model without them. This does not mean the coefficients are zero (both have \(P(>0)\) below 0.02); it means they are not worth their cost in predictive terms.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

Report the table if the specification is a topic in the paper, and describe the scale you use. Do not use the Bayes factor as a mechanical rule; use it with the posterior intervals and with economic reasoning.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

If earlier studies find a return to education of about 7%, you can say so. prior_mean sets the prior mean of each slope: one number for all, or a list in the order of the regressors. How to read it The posterior mean of the education coefficient barely moves (0.0551 against 0.0550), because this prior carries the weight of one observation. To let earlier work matter, use a small g or a Normal prior with a small standard deviation, and report the sensitivity table below. In a small sample the prior would matter much more, and writing it down becomes part of the paper's identification of the result.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior
Robustness: how much does the prior matter?

How to read it Each row re-estimates the slopes under a different prior. For \(g \ge 663\) and for the Normal priors with standard deviation 1 or 10, the slopes are the same as OLS: the data dominate. With \(g = 10\) the coefficients shrink by about 9% (education 0.050), and with \(g = 1\) by half (education 0.028; marriage 0.10 against 0.20). The tight Normal prior (standard deviation 0.1) pulls every slope towards zero, with the largest effect on marriage (0.075) and race ( \(-0.037\) ), which have the largest coefficients. What to say: the signs and ranking of the effects do not depend on the prior unless it is much more informative than the data. If a result flips only for a prior that acts like a handful of observations, it is not robust. The table is cheap evidence to show a referee.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior
Robustness: how much does the prior matter?

For a non-conjugate prior (a Normal prior with the same standard deviation for each slope and independent of \(\sigma^2\) ), the posterior is obtained by a Gibbs sampler, which needs a convergence check: How to read it The effective sample size equals the number of draws (3000) for every coefficient, because a Gibbs sampler for a linear model draws from two exact conditional distributions and the chain mixes immediately. Geweke's test compares the first 10% and the last 50% of the chain: a statistic with |z| above 2 would mean the chain had not settled. It is borderline for black (z = 2.0): with nine parameters one such value is expected by chance, and increasing the burn-in confirms nothing changes. Report effective sample sizes for any sampler you use.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

How to read it Residual autocorrelation is rejected by neither the portmanteau nor the Ljung-Box test, as expected in a cross-section. Residuals are not normal (Jarque-Bera rejects) and the variance is not constant (Breusch-Pagan, p = 0.003). The regression coefficients stay consistent, but the posterior standard deviations assume a constant variance and are too small if the variance is unevenly spread: the table compares the posterior standard deviations with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC3) OLS standard errors. The ratios run from 0.90 (Black) to 1.06 (South), so the robust errors are within about 10% of the posterior ones and the conclusions stand, with one qualification: with robust errors the South coefficient is borderline (t about 1.96). Report the robust errors next to the posterior as a check; the point estimates are the same.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

How to write it: results Table 1 reports posterior summaries. A year of education raises hourly wages by 5.5% (posterior standard deviation 0.8 percentage points; 95% credible interval 3.9% to 7.1%), with a posterior probability of one that the effect is positive. Experience, tenure, IQ, marriage and living in a city have positive effects (probability above 0.999), while the effects of being Black or living in the South are negative with probabilities of 0.988 and 0.981. The posterior means are almost identical to OLS because the g-prior carries the weight of one observation. The log Bayes factors indicate decisive support for the city dummy (16.8), and moderate support for IQ (2.0) and tenure (1.3); the data slightly prefer a model without the South and Black dummies, though their credible intervals exclude zero. The signs and ranking of the effects are unchanged for all priors except those that carry the weight of fewer than ten observations (Table 2). Residual diagnostics show heteroskedasticity, so we also compare with heteroskedasticity-robust OLS standard errors, which are within 10% of the posterior standard deviations; the South coefficient is then only borderline significant.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

Bayesian Shrinkage Regression (Horseshoe, Lasso, Ridge): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

How much do neighbourhood characteristics affect house prices, when you allow every regressor to enter nonlinearly and to interact with the others? The hedonic price equation of Harrison and Rubinfeld (1978) has eight regressors: air pollution ( lnox ), rooms, distance to employment centres, access to highways, the property tax rate, the pupil-teacher ratio, the share of lower-status residents ( lowstat ) and crime. Adding their squares and all 28 pairwise products gives 44 regressors . With 506 tracts OLS handles this; with 120 it does not: the model has almost as many parameters as observations, the coefficients are noisy and the predictions are worse than those of the simple model.

A shrinkage prior is a prior on the coefficients that puts most of its mass near zero. With standardised regressors, and the three priors differ in how \(\lambda_j\) (the scale of each coefficient) and \(\tau\) (the overall scale) are distributed: Prior Scales What it does Horseshoe (Carvalho et al. 2010) \(\lambda_j\) and \(\tau\) half-Cauchy Shrinks small coefficients hard and leaves large ones nearly untouched: built for a few large effects among many noise terms Bayesian lasso (Park and Casella 2008) \(\lambda_j^2\) exponential: Laplace prior on \(\beta_j\) Shrinks every coefficient by roughly the same amount towards zero Ridge \(\lambda_j = 1\) : common scale, half-Cauchy \(\tau\) Shrinks all coefficients by the same proportion: best when there are many small effects

All three are sampled by Gibbs samplers whose conditional distributions are exact (Makalic and Schmidt 2016 for the horseshoe), and the regressors are standardised so that one prior suits every variable. The engine reports for each coefficient the posterior mean and interval, the probability that the effect is non-negligible (a one-standard-deviation change in the regressor moves the outcome by more than 5% of its standard deviation; you can change the 5%) and the shrinkage factor \(\kappa_j = 1/(1 + n\tau^2\lambda_j^2)\) , which is 1 when the coefficient is pulled all the way to zero and 0 when the data are left alone (Piironen and Vehtari 2017). Shrinkage is not selection

A coefficient that is shrunk is not set to zero. The posterior reports how much is left and how uncertain it is. If you need a list of variables, use the probability of a non-negligible effect or the interval, and say which rule you used; if you need a list of variables with a stated probability of belonging, use the model-averaging guide. How to write it: the model We estimate the hedonic price equation with 44 regressors (eight characteristics, their squares and all pairwise products, each standardised) on a random sample of 120 tracts, with a horseshoe prior on the coefficients (Carvalho et al. 2010): each coefficient has a normal prior with standard deviation \(\sigma\tau\lambda_j\) , and \(\lambda_j\) and \(\tau\) have half-Cauchy priors. The error variance has the usual improper prior. We sample the posterior by Gibbs sampling with the scale-mixture representation of Makalic and Schmidt (2016), in two chains of 2,000 draws after 1,000 burn-in draws, and compare with the Bayesian lasso, a ridge prior and OLS.

How to read it The file has 506 tracts and 44 regressors already built: the eight characteristics, centred and divided by their standard deviations, their eight squares and the 28 products of pairs. In a random training sample of 120 tracts, the regressors have means near zero and standard deviations near one, as they should; log price has mean 9.92 and standard deviation 0.39. The other 386 tracts are held out to test the predictions in Step 8. Standardisation matters for shrinkage: a prior of one scale only treats all coefficients alike if the regressors have the same scale (the engine does this itself, and reports the coefficients in the original units).

How to read it The model explains 88.4% of the variance of log price in the training sample, with a residual standard deviation of 0.150 (log points) against 0.39 for log price itself. The table lists the 12 coefficients with the largest standardised posterior means. Three stand out: the share of lower-status residents ( \(-0.206\) , 95% interval \(-0.279\) to \(-0.135\) ), its interaction with the property tax ( \(-0.154\) , \(-0.257\) to \(-0.066\) ) and the number of rooms (0.109, 0.038 to 0.177). A one-standard-deviation increase in the lower-status share lowers the price by about 21 log points, other things at their means. Their shrinkage factors are 0.010, 0.019 and 0.043, so the prior left them almost untouched. The next nine have shrinkage between 0.15 and 0.31, intervals that include zero, and posterior probabilities of a non-negligible effect between 0.51 and 0.79.

The first chart shows the 20 largest standardised coefficients, posterior mean against OLS (OLS is far larger for almost all of them), and the second their shrinkage, which rises from near 0 for the three clear effects to between 0.15 and 0.35 for the rest. The "expected number of non-negligible coefficients" in the summary (20.3) is the sum of the 44 probabilities; it is large because many coefficients have probabilities near one half, which means undecided , not present .

How to read it Three of the 44 intervals exclude zero, and the same three have a probability above 0.9 of being non-negligible. Look at the eight linear terms. Rooms (0.109) and the lower-status share ( \(-0.206\) ) are clear. The other six are undecided: pollution \(-0.021\) (interval \(-0.111\) to 0.024), distance \(-0.034\) , highway access 0.024, property tax \(-0.027\) , the pupil-teacher ratio \(-0.018\) and crime \(-0.049\) , with probabilities of a non-negligible effect between 0.43 and 0.58 and shrinkage between 0.28 and 0.37. The data do not say these effects are zero; with 120 tracts they cannot tell. A paper should say "not distinguishable from zero in this sample", not "no effect". With all 506 tracts the picture would be sharper.

How to read it With 44 regressors and 120 observations, OLS is unstable. The standard errors on highway access (0.264) and the property tax (0.312) are five to eight times the posterior standard deviations (0.047 and 0.041), and the coefficients are large and erratic: crime \(-0.205\) against a posterior mean of \(-0.049\) , pollution \(-0.105\) against \(-0.021\) , distance \(-0.135\) against \(-0.034\) . The ratio column shows the share of the OLS coefficient that survives: about 0.2 to 0.27 for those four, so OLS overstates them by a factor of four or five, which is the overfitting that the prior corrects. The two clear effects are not shrunk much: the lower-status share (ratio 1.08) and rooms (1.36; the posterior is larger than OLS, because OLS splits the rooms effect over correlated interaction terms that the prior shrinks). Ignore the ratios for the property tax (7.4) and the pupil-teacher ratio ( \(-12.5\) ): the OLS coefficients are almost exactly zero ( \(-0.004\) and 0.001), so a ratio is meaningless.

How to read it The table lists the ten parameters with the smallest effective sample sizes out of 45. The worst is 280 (the interaction of rooms and highway access) out of 4,000 draws, and the largest R-hat in the whole run is 1.011, so the two chains agree. A few hundred effective draws are enough for means and standard deviations but rather few for the tails of a 95% interval: the horseshoe prior has heavy tails and mixes more slowly than a normal prior. For a paper, use 10,000 draws per chain, which takes a few seconds. If R-hat exceeded 1.05, or the effective sample size fell below about 100 for a parameter you report, increase draws and burn before trusting the intervals.

How to read it Each row re-estimates the model under a different prior, and the columns are the eight largest coefficients. The three leading terms keep their size and sign whatever the prior: the lower-status share is \(-0.204\) (horseshoe), \(-0.189\) (lasso) and \(-0.170\) (ridge), and rooms is 0.111, 0.114 and 0.118. The horseshoe leaves the large coefficient closest to its OLS value ( \(-0.191\) ), and ridge shrinks it most, as expected: ridge applies the same proportional shrinkage to everything. For the small coefficients the three priors agree and all disagree with OLS: crime is \(-0.071\) , \(-0.065\) and \(-0.066\) against \(-0.205\) in OLS, and the property-tax interaction with crime and the others are halved or more. The conclusions about which effects matter do not depend on the prior; their size depends a little.

Estimate on 120 random tracts, predict the other 386, and repeat for ten random training samples. The measure is the root mean squared error of log price. How to read it The three shrinkage priors predict about 15% better than OLS: root mean squared errors of 0.183 (horseshoe), 0.180 (lasso) and 0.180 (ridge), against 0.218 for OLS with all 44 regressors and 0.210 for OLS with only the eight linear terms. Using all 44 regressors without shrinkage is worse than using the eight (0.218 against 0.210): extra terms hurt when they are not shrunk, and help when they are. The horseshoe beats OLS in all ten samples. It does not beat the lasso or the ridge here (it wins 1 and 2 of ten): the signal in this problem is dense, with many small effects and only a few large ones, and the horseshoe's advantage is in sparse problems where nearly all coefficients are zero. Choose the prior from the structure you expect, and report the comparison.

How to write it: results Table 1 reports the posterior of the hedonic price equation with 44 regressors, estimated on 120 randomly drawn tracts with a horseshoe prior. Three terms are clearly different from zero: the share of lower-status residents (posterior mean \(-0.206\) per standard deviation, 95% credible interval \(-0.279\) to \(-0.135\) ), its interaction with the property tax ( \(-0.154\) ; \(-0.257\) to \(-0.066\) ) and the number of rooms (0.109; 0.038 to 0.177). The other 41 coefficients have intervals that include zero and posterior probabilities of a non-negligible effect between 0.4 and 0.8, so the sample cannot tell whether they are zero. OLS on the same sample gives coefficients that are four to five times larger for pollution, distance, access and crime, with standard errors up to eight times larger. The chains converge (R-hat at most 1.011, smallest effective sample size 280). The three leading effects are the same under a Bayesian lasso and a ridge prior. In ten random splits, the shrinkage priors predict log prices of the 386 held-out tracts with a root mean squared error of 0.18 against 0.22 for OLS with all regressors and 0.21 for OLS with the linear terms only.

Bayesian Local Projections: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

How does unemployment (and inflation) respond over the following four years to an unexpected rise in the policy rate? A local projection (Jordà 2005) answers it with one regression per horizon \(h=1,\dots,H\) : where \(r_t\) is the T-bill rate, \(w_t\) holds the contemporaneous inflation and unemployment (identifying the shock recursively, with the interest rate ordered last) and four lags of all three variables. \(\theta_h\) is the response of \(z\) at horizon \(h\) to a one-point policy shock. The regressions at different horizons are estimated separately, so the path \(\hat\theta_1,\dots,\hat\theta_H\) can zigzag, and the standard errors grow with \(h\) . The Bayesian version (Miranda-Agrippino and Ricco 2021; Barnichon and Brownlees 2019) adds the prior that the response moves smoothly with the horizon:

Together with the estimates \(\hat\theta_h\sim N(\theta_h,v_h)\) , the posterior of the whole path is normal and exact, with no simulation needed. The tightness \(\tau\) can be chosen by maximising the marginal likelihood (empirical Bayes). With \(\tau\to\infty\) you get the plain local projections; with \(\tau\to0\) a constant response. What the prior does and does not do The smoothness prior reduces noise by borrowing strength across horizons. It does not fix bias from a misspecified shock, from omitted variables or from a weak instrument. A smoother path can look more convincing than the data justify, so always show the unsmoothed local projection next to the Bayesian one and report how the result depends on \(\tau\) .

How to write it: the model We estimate impulse responses of unemployment and inflation to a monetary policy shock with Bayesian local projections. For each horizon from one to sixteen quarters we regress the outcome on the Treasury bill rate, controlling for contemporaneous inflation and unemployment, which identifies the shock recursively with the interest rate ordered last, and for four lags of the three variables. We place a random-walk prior on the response across horizons, with the prior standard deviation chosen by maximising the marginal likelihood of the local-projection estimates (Miranda-Agrippino and Ricco 2021), and report posterior means with 68% and 90% credible sets. Standard errors of the single-horizon estimates are Newey-West with \(h+1\) lags.
Load the data and run the local projections

How to read it The sample has 202 quarters. After a one-point policy shock, the unemployment response is slightly negative at first (−0.12 at horizon 4, within one standard error), turns positive from the seventh quarter and peaks at 0.27 points in quarter 9 (s.e. 0.09). The standard errors differ by a factor of five across horizons and the path is jagged (−0.07, 0.10, 0.22, 0.27, 0.23), which is typical of local projections. Inflation rises for the first year (a price puzzle: 0.52 in quarter 1, not significant) and then falls to about −1 point from quarter 8, but the individual estimates zigzag between −0.43 and −1.12.

How to read it The VAR gives a smoother and smaller unemployment response, which reaches 0.17 after three years and does not fall back, against a local-projection peak of 0.27 in quarter 9. The paths are correlated at 0.69 for unemployment and 0.89 for inflation, so the two methods tell the same qualitative story: a short-run dip, a rise in unemployment at 2 to 3 years and lower inflation. The differences in size and timing are the usual ones: the VAR imposes the dynamics of its lag structure at all horizons, and the local projections do not.
The smoothness prior and its tightness

How to read it The marginal likelihood prefers a smooth path (τ = 0.059 for unemployment, 0.19 for inflation) to both extremes: the log marginal likelihood is 23.5, against −18.0 with almost no smoothing and 18.3 with a constant response. Inflation needs a looser prior than unemployment because its local-projection path is more erratic. The posterior mean for unemployment follows the local projection (dip, then rise) but is smoother, peaks lower and has narrower bands; the 90% set at horizon 8 is [0.07, 0.25], against [0.07, 0.37] for the plain local projection. The posterior treats the horizon estimates as independent, so the bands understate uncertainty about the shape of the path.

How to read it The posterior probability that unemployment is higher than it would have been is 1.00 at horizon 8 and 0.99 at horizon 12, but only 0.36 at horizon 4 and 0.71 at horizon 16: the effect comes in the second and third year and then fades. The posterior mean peaks at 0.16 points, and the probability that the peak exceeds 0.1 is close to one while exceeding 0.3 has a probability of only 0.04. For inflation, the probability of a decline is 1.00 at horizons 8, 12 and 16 (posterior means of −0.60, −0.88 and −0.91), but it is not credibly negative in the first year (probability of an increase 0.58 at horizon 4).
Robustness: the tightness, the lag length and the sample

How to read it The tightness matters for the size of the response and the width of the bands. With a very smooth prior (τ = 0.02) the horizon-8 response is 0.09, against 0.15 with τ = 0.05, 0.16 at the marginal-likelihood choice, and 0.22 with no smoothing. So the sign and timing of the response do not depend on the prior but the peak is between 0.09 and 0.22, and the posterior standard deviation shrinks from 0.091 to 0.034 as the prior tightens. Changing the lags from two to six moves the horizon-8 mean between 0.14 and 0.17. In the first half of the sample (to 1984) the local projection reaches 0.40 at horizon 8, so the effect appears larger in the earlier period, which is consistent with a change in the transmission of policy (see the TVP-VAR guide).
Robustness: the tightness, the lag length and the sample

How to write it: results A one-point unexpected rise in the policy rate lowers inflation and raises unemployment with a delay. The unemployment response is close to zero in the first year, turns positive in the second and peaks at about 0.16 percentage points around quarter 9 (posterior mean; 90% credible set 0.07 to 0.25 at quarter 8), after which it fades; the posterior probability that unemployment is above its baseline is 1.00 at quarter 8 and 0.99 at quarter 12. Inflation is little changed in the first year and falls by about 0.6 points after two years and 0.9 points after three. The Bayesian local projections have a smoothness prior with the tightness chosen by the marginal likelihood; they follow the unsmoothed local projections and the VAR (correlations of 0.69 for unemployment and 0.89 for inflation), but with narrower bands. The size of the peak depends on the prior (between 0.09 and 0.22 at quarter 8), and the response is larger in the first half of the sample.
What to report in the paper

Item What to show Identification the shock and the contemporaneous controls, stated plainly Local projections the unsmoothed estimates with HAC intervals, for transparency Prior the smoothness prior, how its tightness was chosen, the marginal likelihood Posterior posterior means with credible sets, and posterior probabilities where they answer the question Benchmark a VAR response on the same figure Robustness tightness, lag length and sub-samples Common mistakes Presenting the smooth path as the data. The smoothness is the prior's work. Show the raw local projections too. Ignoring that horizon-by-horizon estimates are correlated. The posterior here treats them as independent, which understates the uncertainty about the shape of the path. Say so, or use a joint covariance.
What to report in the paper

Choosing the tightness by looking at the figure. Choose it by the marginal likelihood or a stated rule and show the sensitivity. Treating the recursive shock as truth. A price puzzle (inflation rising after a tightening) usually means that the shock is contaminated by information the central bank had. Add controls or use an external instrument. Reading credible sets as confidence intervals. They are probability statements conditional on the prior. Comparing responses with different scaling. Check that the LP and the VAR use the same shock size.
Bayesian Model Averaging: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Which of the fourteen variables that might affect wages really belong in a wage equation? The Mincer equation has education and experience, but a researcher can also add IQ, a knowledge-of-the-world test score, tenure, age, marital status, race, region, city, the number of siblings, birth order and both parents' schooling. With 14 candidates there are \(2^{14} = 16{,}384\) possible regressions. Picking one by testing and dropping variables treats the chosen model as if it were known in advance, and the standard errors then ignore the uncertainty about the choice. Bayesian model averaging (BMA) keeps all the models. For model \(M\) with regressors \(X_M\) the engine uses Zellner's g-prior on the slopes, a flat prior on the constant and \(p(\sigma^2) \propto 1/\sigma^2\) :

Under this prior the Bayes factor of \(M\) against the model with no regressors is available in closed form (Liang et al. 2008), where \(p_M\) is the number of regressors and \(R_M^2\) the model's \(R^2\) . A model is rewarded for fit and penalised for each extra regressor. The posterior probability of a model is its Bayes factor times its prior probability, divided by the sum over all models. The posterior inclusion probability (PIP) of a variable is the total probability of the models that contain it. Choice Options in the engine Default g-prior UIP: \(g = n\) ; RIC: \(g = k^2\) ; BRIC: \(g = \max(n, k^2)\) BRIC

Model prior uniform over models; binomial with a fixed expected size; random inclusion probability with a uniform prior (beta-binomial) random Search exact enumeration of all models (up to 18 regressors); MC3 sampler above that exact up to 14 The random-inclusion-probability prior does not tell the data how many regressors to expect: it gives every model size the same prior probability, which is why it is the usual default (Ley and Steel 2009). Why not just use the t-statistics? A t-statistic answers "is this coefficient zero in this one model?" and depends on which other variables are in it. A PIP answers "how likely is the variable to belong, given that the rest are uncertain?" It also separates no evidence of an effect from evidence of no effect : a variable with a PIP near zero is one the data say is not needed; a variable with a PIP of one half is one the data cannot decide about.

How to write it: the model We address model uncertainty by Bayesian model averaging over all \(2^{14}\) linear regressions that include a subset of the 14 candidate regressors and always include a constant. We use Zellner's g-prior with \(g = \max(n, k^2)\) (Fernandez, Ley and Steel 2001), a flat prior on the constant and the usual improper prior on the error variance, so that marginal likelihoods are exact (Liang et al. 2008). The prior over models is the beta-binomial prior with a uniform prior on the inclusion probability (Ley and Steel 2009). We report posterior inclusion probabilities, model-averaged coefficients and the posterior probabilities of the best models, and we study sensitivity to both priors.

How to read it 663 men with no missing values in any of the 15 variables. Log wages average 6.81 with a standard deviation of 0.41. Many of the candidates are correlated: education and the two parents' schooling, IQ and the knowledge test, age and experience. Correlated candidates are where model averaging matters most, because a single regression can pick any one of a group of substitutes and say nothing about the others. All regressors must be numeric; categorical variables must be turned into dummies first.

How to read it All 16,384 models were evaluated, so there is no simulation error. The columns are the PIP, the model-averaged posterior mean and standard deviation (a coefficient counts as zero in the models that exclude the variable), the mean and standard deviation given that the variable is in the model, and the probability that the coefficient has the sign of its mean given inclusion. Three variables are in nearly every good model: urban (PIP 1.000), educ (0.999) and married (0.998). A year of education raises wages by 4.5% (posterior standard deviation 0.011), a city location by 19.6% and marriage by 20.4%. IQ (0.931), experience (0.824) and tenure (0.799) are probably in. Mother's education is a coin flip (0.559), age is close to one half (0.466), and the other variables have PIPs between 0.07 and 0.35: black (0.351), south (0.336), the knowledge test (0.311), father's education (0.275), birth order (0.133) and number of siblings (0.065). The chart shows the same ordering. With 7 variables above one half, the expected model has 8 regressors (8.05).

The last two columns show why model-averaged and conditional coefficients differ. Black has a model-averaged coefficient of \(-0.042\) with a standard deviation of 0.066, because the variable is in only 35% of the weight and averaging shrinks the estimate. Given that it is in, the coefficient is \(-0.119\) (standard deviation 0.057). Quote the first as the best overall estimate and the second as "the effect if it matters".
The best models and the number of regressors

How to read it No model dominates: the best has a posterior probability of only 0.048, and the ten best together hold about 0.24. They all contain IQ, education, tenure, marriage and city, and differ in whether they add experience, age, mother's or father's education, race, region or the knowledge test. That is the case for averaging: a researcher who picked the best model would have been right 5% of the time, and the standard errors would not reflect that. The size table compares the prior with the posterior. The prior gives each size from 0 to 14 the same probability (0.067); the posterior puts 0.81 of its weight on models of 7 to 9 regressors and almost none (0.006) on models of 5 or fewer. The data have moved the prior a long way, so the results do not depend on the prior's information about size.

How to read it The two rankings agree about the extremes: the six variables with the highest PIP are the ones with the largest t-statistics (urban 6.2, education 4.3, marriage 4.0, IQ 3.0, tenure 2.5, experience 2.5), and the variables with the lowest PIPs have the smallest t-statistics. Where they differ, the PIP is more informative. Mother's education (t = 1.55, p = 0.12) has a PIP of 0.56, because many good models include it. Age (t = 1.37) has 0.47. Black (t = \(-1.87\) , p = 0.06) has a PIP of 0.35: a coefficient that is borderline in one regression carries only a third of the posterior weight, since models without it fit almost as well. A rule of thumb is that a PIP above 0.9 is "robust", 0.5 to 0.9 "probably in" and below 0.5 "not supported"; state the rule if you use one.

The results should not depend on the arbitrary choices of the prior. The sensitivity table re-evaluates all 16,384 models under nine combinations of g-prior and model prior. How to read it The three variables with a PIP near one stay at 0.995 to 1.000 in all nine rows. The middle group moves: experience between 0.74 and 0.88 and tenure between 0.62 and 0.88, with the lowest values under the binomial prior with expected size 3.5, which favours small models, and the highest under RIC with the random prior (9.1 regressors expected). UIP and BRIC are identical because \(n = 663\) exceeds \(k^2 = 196\) , so \(g = n\) in both. The conclusions about which variables matter are the same for all nine priors; only the borderline ones (tenure, experience) change by more than 0.1, and neither crosses 0.5. Report the range of PIPs over the priors you tried.
Check the search: the MC3 sampler

With more than about 18 regressors the models cannot all be enumerated, and the engine uses MC3, a sampler that moves between models by adding, dropping or swapping a regressor. You can also request it with 14 regressors to check it against the exact answer. How to read it With 50,000 iterations the sampler visits 850 of the 16,384 models, concentrated where the posterior mass is, and its PIPs are within 0.026 of the exact values (largest differences: age \(-0.026\) , experience 0.018, father's education \(-0.017\) , black 0.016). The ranking of the variables is the same and the same seven variables lie above 0.5. The acceptance rate is 0.26. For a problem too large to enumerate, run MC3 with two different seeds and more iterations, and check that the PIPs agree to about 0.02 before reporting them.

BMA is mainly an inference tool, but one should check that it does not forecast worse than the alternatives. Draw 200 men at random as a test sample, fit each method to the other 463 and compare the root mean squared error of the log wage; repeat for 20 random splits. How to read it All three regressions predict much better than the sample mean (RMSE 0.410 against 0.354 to 0.359), but they are close to each other: the full regression is best at 0.354, the top model at 0.355 and BMA at 0.359. BMA beats the full regression in only 2 of 20 splits. This is an honest result and an ordinary one: with 463 observations and 14 mostly useful regressors there is little to be gained from shrinking or selecting, so averaging should not be sold as a forecasting improvement here. Its value is in the inference of Steps 3 to 5, where it says which variables the data support and how sure that is. Averaging helps prediction when the number of candidates is large relative to the sample (a growth regression with 60 candidates and 90 countries), and in that case run this check on your own data.

How to write it: results Table 1 reports posterior inclusion probabilities and model-averaged coefficients for the 14 candidate determinants of log wages. Three variables are in almost every model with substantial probability: living in a city (PIP 1.00; coefficient 0.196), education (0.999; 0.045 per year) and marriage (0.998; 0.204). IQ (0.93), experience (0.82) and tenure (0.80) are probably in the model, mother's education and age are undecided (0.56 and 0.47), and race, region, the knowledge-of-the-world score, father's education, birth order and the number of siblings have inclusion probabilities of 0.35 or less. No single model dominates: the highest-probability model has a posterior probability of 0.048, and the posterior is concentrated on models with 7 to 9 regressors (81%). The inclusion probabilities of the three leading variables are at least 0.995 under nine combinations of g-prior and model prior (Table 2); experience and tenure range from 0.62 to 0.88. An MC3 sampler reproduces the exact inclusion probabilities within 0.03. In 20 random splits, model averaging predicts log wages with an RMSE of 0.359, close to the full regression (0.354); we therefore use it for inference about which variables matter, not as a forecasting device.

Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

What happens to output and inflation after an unexpected rise in the short-term interest rate? This is the classic question of the monetary VAR. The model is a VAR( \(p\) ) in three variables, quarterly GDP growth, CPI inflation and the 3-month Treasury bill rate: With \(p = 4\) lags each equation has \(1 + 3 \times 4 = 13\) coefficients, 39 in all, plus 6 in \(\Sigma\) . Fifty years of quarterly data give about 200 observations: enough to estimate the coefficients, but not to estimate them precisely . Unrestricted OLS fits the noise, impulse responses come out jagged, and forecasts are poor. A Bayesian VAR adds a prior that pulls every coefficient towards a sensible benchmark. The Minnesota prior (Litterman 1986) says that each variable behaves like its own random walk or white noise, that recent lags matter more than distant ones, and that other variables' lags matter less than a variable's own. The data then move the coefficients away from this benchmark only as far as they have evidence for.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

Term Meaning Default here \(\delta_i\) prior mean of variable \(i\) 's own first lag 1 for an I(1) series in levels, 0 for a stationary one \(\lambda_1\) overall tightness: how strongly all coefficients are pulled to the prior 0.2, then chosen by the data \(\lambda_2\) extra tightness on the lags of other variables 0.5 \(\lambda_3\) how fast the prior tightens with the lag length ( \(1/l^{\lambda_3}\) ) 1 \(\lambda_4\) tightness on the constant 100 (essentially flat) Four priors, one idea The OES engine offers the four priors of the ECB's BEAR toolbox. They share the Minnesota means and scales and differ in how they treat \(\Sigma\) : Minnesota (Litterman): \(\Sigma\) is fixed at the residual variances of univariate AR models. Exact, fast, equation by equation. Good for forecasting.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

Normal-Wishart: \(\Sigma\) is estimated with an inverse-Wishart prior, and the posterior and the marginal likelihood are analytic, so lag length and tightness can be chosen by the data. It forces \(\lambda_2 = 1\) . Independent Normal-Wishart: frees \(\lambda_2\) and allows block exogeneity; estimated by Gibbs sampling. Normal-diffuse: Minnesota prior on the coefficients, no information on \(\Sigma\) ; Gibbs sampling. Start with Normal-Wishart to choose the lags and \(\lambda_1\) , then report the prior you prefer and show the others as robustness. How to write it: the model We estimate a Bayesian VAR in real GDP growth, CPI inflation and the 3-month Treasury bill rate, \(y_t = c + \sum_{l=1}^{p} A_l y_{t-l} + u_t\) , \(u_t \sim N(0,\Sigma)\) , on quarterly U.S. data for 1959Q3–2009Q3. Following Litterman (1986) and Kadiyala and Karlsson (1997), we use a Normal-Wishart prior with Minnesota moments: the prior mean of each variable's own first lag is one for the interest rate, which is persistent, and zero for growth and inflation; all other coefficients have prior mean zero, with prior standard deviations that shrink with the lag length.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors
Load the data and test for unit roots

The prior mean of the own first lag depends on whether a series is persistent. Test first. How to read it GDP growth and inflation reject a unit root in levels (ADF p-values below 0.05) and are treated as stationary: prior mean 0 on their own first lag. The T-bill rate does not reject; it is stationary only after differencing, so it gets a random-walk prior (prior mean 1). Notice that nothing is differenced: a Bayesian VAR is estimated in levels, and the prior handles the persistence. Sims, Stock and Watson (1990) show that inference on impulse responses remains valid in levels even with unit roots or cointegration.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors
Choose the lag length and the tightness

The Normal-Wishart prior gives the marginal likelihood , the probability of the data under the model with the coefficients integrated out. It rewards fit and penalises complexity automatically, so it can choose both the number of lags and \(\lambda_1\) (Giannone, Lenza and Primiceri 2015). How to read it Lags. The marginal likelihood rises quickly up to three or four lags and then flattens: extra lags add little once the prior has shrunk them. BIC, which has no prior to shrink with, prefers fewer lags. With quarterly data four lags is the convention, and the marginal likelihood supports it; more lags would be harmless under the prior. Tightness. The marginal likelihood peaks at \(\lambda_1 = 0.2\) : looser priors overfit, tighter ones ignore the data. This is the value used below. Always report how \(\lambda_1\) was chosen; a value picked to deliver a result is a red flag for referees.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

How to read it Each row is a posterior: its mean, standard deviation, 95% credible interval and the posterior probability that the coefficient is positive. The interest-rate equation is a monetary policy rule in reduced form: the T-bill rate is highly persistent (own first lag about 0.93) and rises after strong GDP growth and higher inflation, with posterior probabilities above 0.9 for several of these lags. "Distance from OLS" in the summary shows how much the prior moved the coefficients: about half, which is typical for a VAR of this size. A credible interval is read literally: given the model and the prior, there is a 95% probability that the coefficient lies in it. Bayesian results do not need p-values, but P(> 0) close to 0 or 1 plays the same role.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors
Impulse responses: a monetary policy shock

The policy shock is identified recursively (Cholesky), with the interest rate ordered last : the Fed reacts within the quarter to output and inflation, while output and prices respond to the interest rate only with a lag. This is the standard ordering of Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (1999). How to read it After a one-standard-deviation rise in the T-bill rate, GDP growth falls, and the 68% credible band stays below zero for about two years. Inflation, however, rises before it falls back: the well-known price puzzle (Sims 1992). It usually means the VAR omits information the Fed uses to forecast inflation, such as commodity prices; the FAVAR guide shows how adding many indicators addresses it. Report the puzzle honestly rather than hiding it; it is a known limitation of small monetary VARs.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors
Impulse responses: a monetary policy shock
Bayesian VAR papers report 68% bands (16th to 84th percentiles) by convention, as here; add 90% bands if referees ask.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors
How important is the shock? Variance decomposition

How to read it Monetary policy shocks explain only a few percent of the forecast-error variance of GDP growth and inflation, even after five years. Most movements in output and inflation are due to other shocks; the interest rate itself is driven increasingly by output and inflation, as the policy rule implies. This is the standard result: policy matters for how the economy responds, but surprises in policy are a small source of fluctuations.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

How to read it Stability. Almost every posterior draw has all roots inside the unit circle, and the largest root at the posterior mean is below one: the VAR is stationary and impulse responses die out. Autocorrelation. Ljung-Box does not reject for GDP growth and inflation but does for the T-bill rate, and the joint portmanteau test rejects. A fifth or sixth lag removes most of it; check that the responses do not change (they do not, in Step 7). Normality and ARCH. Strongly rejected for inflation and the interest rate. The 1970s oil shocks and the Volcker disinflation produce large residuals, and their variance changes over time. The coefficient estimates remain valid, but bands that assume constant variance are too narrow in volatile periods. The SV-VAR guide models this directly; mention it as a limitation.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

With the Normal-Wishart prior the posterior draws are independent, so there is nothing to converge. The Gibbs samplers (Independent Normal-Wishart, Normal-diffuse) need a check: How to read it Effective sample sizes are close to the number of draws and the Geweke statistics are small: the chain mixes well and has settled. If |z| were above 2 for several parameters, increase the burn-in.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

A result that depends on the prior is not a result. Three checks: How to read it Tightness. With tight and moderate priors ( \(\lambda_1 \le 0.2\) ) the output response is negative at every horizon. With very loose priors and with OLS, the response at four quarters turns positive : without shrinkage the VAR fits noise, and the sign is not robust. This is exactly why a Bayesian VAR is used, and the table is the evidence a referee needs. Prior family. All four priors give a fall in GDP growth of similar size. Report the Normal-Wishart results and these as robustness. How to read it Recursive one- and four-quarter-ahead forecasts over the last 20% of the sample. The BVAR beats the OLS VAR for inflation at both horizons and is close for the other variables; a random walk is hard to beat for the interest rate at short horizons, as usual. In a forecasting paper, test the differences formally with the Diebold-Mariano test and report several evaluation windows.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

When some variables cannot be affected by the others, such as world variables in a model of a small open economy, the Independent Normal-Wishart and Normal-diffuse priors can impose it: the coefficients of the other variables in the block's equations get (almost) zero prior variance. Here GDP growth is (for illustration) made block-exogenous: the lags of inflation and the interest rate in its equation are pushed to zero. In a real application use it for foreign variables, oil prices or anything determined outside the economy you model.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

How to write it: results The marginal likelihood selects four lags and an overall tightness of \(\lambda_1 = 0.2\) . Figure 1 shows the responses to a one-standard-deviation monetary policy shock, identified recursively with the interest rate ordered last. GDP growth falls by about 0.1 percentage point within a year, and the 68% credible band excludes zero for two years. Inflation initially rises, the price puzzle familiar from small monetary VARs (Sims 1992), before returning to its baseline. Policy shocks account for less than 3% of the forecast-error variance of output growth at all horizons. The output response is negative under all four priors (Minnesota, Normal-Wishart, Independent Normal-Wishart and Normal-diffuse) and for any \(\lambda_1 \le 0.2\) ; with much looser priors, and with OLS, the response becomes erratic, which illustrates the value of shrinkage in a sample of this length.

Bayesian Change Points: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Did the flow of the Nile fall at some point in the twentieth century, and when? The series is the annual flow at Aswan, 1871 to 1970. Hydrologists and statisticians have studied it since Cobb (1978), because the flow seems to drop around 1898, the time of the first Aswan dam works. The question is the same in many applications: a relationship or a level shifted somewhere in the sample, you do not know where, and you want to know how sure you can be that it shifted at all, how many times, and where. The model divides the sample into regimes by unknown break dates. In each regime \(y_t = x_t'\beta_r + \varepsilon_t\) , \(\varepsilon_t \sim N(0, \sigma_r^2)\) , with its own coefficients \(\beta_r\) and variance \(\sigma_r^2\) (for the Nile, just a mean level and a variance). The priors are

on the regime parameters : a conjugate normal-inverse-gamma prior with Zellner's g-prior on the coefficients ( \(g = n\) , applied to the standardised data) and an inverse-gamma(1, 0.1) prior on the standardised variance, so that each regime's marginal likelihood is available in closed form; on the breaks : independently, between any two consecutive observations there is a break with probability \(p\) , so that the expected number of breaks is the one number you choose (default 1). Regimes must have a minimum length. With these priors the posterior over all segmentations can be computed exactly by dynamic programming (Barry and Hartigan 1993; Fearnhead 2006), so the engine reports exact probabilities for the number of breaks and for a break after each date, with no sampler to check. The cost grows with the square of the number of observations, so the limit is 700.

Output What it answers Number of breaks The posterior probability of 0, 1, 2, ... breaks, and the log Bayes factor of each against no break Break dates The posterior probability of a break after each date, and the table of the highest Regimes For the single most probable segmentation, the posterior mean, standard deviation and interval of each coefficient in each regime Sensitivity The same results under other priors on the number of breaks and on the size of the coefficients Why not just test for a break? A sup-F test (Bai and Perron) asks whether the data reject "no break" and then estimates a date with an asymptotic interval that can be wide or odd when the shift is small. The Bayesian answer gives the probability that a break occurred after each date, including the probability of no break, and the intervals are valid in small samples. The price is a prior: the expected number of breaks and the size of the shifts that the prior thinks are plausible. Step 6 shows how much the results depend on it.

How to write it: the model We search for structural breaks in the mean annual flow of the Nile by Bayesian change-point analysis. Each regime has its own mean and error variance, with a conjugate normal-inverse-gamma prior (a g-prior with \(g = n\) on the standardised series), and the prior on the break dates is an independent Bernoulli( \(p\) ) probability for every pair of consecutive years, with \(p\) set so that the expected number of breaks is one and with regimes of at least five years (Barry and Hartigan 1993). The posterior distribution over all segmentations is computed exactly by dynamic programming (Fearnhead 2006). We report the posterior probability of the number of breaks, the probability of a break after each year, and the regime means in the most probable segmentation.

How to read it The data are the annual flow, in hundreds of millions of cubic metres, for 100 years. The mean over the whole sample is 919 with a standard deviation of 169, but the two sub-sample means differ by almost a quarter: 1,098 for 1871 to 1898 and 850 for 1899 to 1970. The split date is already the answer the literature gives; here the method has not seen it. Running the analysis without the date is the point of the guide.

How to read it The posterior probability of exactly one break is 0.925, of two breaks 0.071 and of three 0.004; the probability of no break is below 0.00005, and the posterior mean number of breaks is 1.08. The last column is the log Bayes factor against no break: one break is favoured by 20.1 log points (a factor of about \(5 \times 10^8\) , far beyond "decisive" on Jeffreys' scale), two breaks by 17.5, which is less, so the data prefer one break over two by 2.6 log points. The prior puts 0.37 on no break and 0.37 on one, so the data have moved nearly all the probability to one break.

The bar chart is the probability of a break after each year. It is concentrated in one place, around 1898, and almost zero elsewhere. The second chart, drawn below, shows the series with the mean of each regime.

How to read it The probability of a break after 1898 (so that 1899 is the first year of the low regime) is 0.760. A break after 1897 has probability 0.111, after 1896 0.061 and after 1899 0.052: together these four years hold 98% of the probability, so the date is known within about three years, and no other year has more than 0.014. The table below is the most probable segmentation: a mean of 1,096 (posterior standard deviation 25) up to 1898, and 851 (15) from 1899, a fall of 245 units or 22%. The regime means are close to the sample means (1,098 and 850); the prior pulls them very slightly towards the overall mean. The residual standard deviation is 135 in the first regime and 124 in the second: the fall in mean was not accompanied by a change in variability.
State a date as a probability, not as a number: "the break occurred in 1898 with probability 0.76 and in 1895 to 1899 with probability 0.98".

How to read it The Bai-Perron procedure (Step on structural breaks in the Time-Series Guide) selects one break, dated 1899 as the first year of the new regime, the same date as the Bayesian most probable segmentation (after 1898). Its 95% confidence interval is 1895 to 1903, wide and asymmetric, against the Bayesian four-year spread; the two are different objects (a confidence interval from a limiting distribution against a posterior probability). The regime means are close (1,097.8 and 850.0 for Bai-Perron, 1,096 and 851 for the Bayesian analysis, which shrinks them slightly towards the overall mean). The two methods agree about the number and the date; the Bayesian result adds the probability of each alternative.
Robustness: the prior and the minimum regime length

How to read it The first table re-runs the exact calculation with 12 combinations of the prior expected number of breaks (0.5, 1, 2 and 4) and the prior scale of the regime means (n/10, n and 10n). The probability of at least one break is 1.0 in every row, one break is the most probable number in every row, and the posterior mean number of breaks varies from 1.02 to 1.70, the highest where the prior expects four breaks and the coefficient prior is tight. The second table varies the minimum regime length from 5 to 25 years: the result is the same, one break after 1898 with probability one. Nothing in the conclusion depends on the prior.
Diagnostics: does it raise false alarms?

A method that always finds a break is useless. Simulate 60 series of 100 independent normal observations, with no break, and see how often the posterior probability of a break is high. How to read it In none of the 60 series without a break did the posterior probability of at least one break exceed 0.5, and the largest value was 0.41; the average was 0.077. With the prior probability of 0.63 of at least one break (the prior expected number of breaks is one), the data pulled the probability down to under 0.1 on average. The method does not invent breaks in noise. The reverse check, whether it finds a break that is there, is the Nile itself, and the test suite checks both with Monte Carlo experiments.
When the relationship changes: the Phillips curve

A break can be in a relationship and not just in a mean. The data are quarterly U.S. inflation and unemployment, 1959 to 2009 (202 quarters). Each regime has its own constant, its own slope on unemployment and its own variance; regimes must last at least 24 quarters (six years). How to read it The posterior probability of exactly five breaks is 0.972 (six: 0.027): the number of breaks is well determined, with a log Bayes factor of 89 against no break. The dates are much less certain. The single most probable date, after 1973Q2, has a probability of only 0.65, the next, after 2003Q3, has 0.43, and the others (1967Q2, 1972Q4, 1984Q1, 1990Q4) between 0.23 and 0.34, because adjacent quarters trade off against each other and several segmentations are nearly as good.
When the relationship changes: the Phillips curve

The most probable segmentation shows the Phillips curve changing. The slope (in percentage points of inflation per point of unemployment) is \(-0.76\) in 1959 to 1967 and \(-0.65\) in 1967 to 1973; it triples to \(-1.78\) in 1973 to 1984 (interval \(-2.26\) to \(-1.31\) ), when the level of inflation at average unemployment was 10.5%; it falls to \(-1.11\) in 1984 to 1990; and it is flat from 1991 to 2003 (0.08, interval \(-0.16\) to 0.32) with inflation at 2.5%, and uncertain in the last, short regime ( \(-0.49\) , interval \(-1.49\) to 0.50). The residual standard deviation was highest in 1973 to 1984 (2.4) and lowest in 1991 to 2003 (0.95).
When the relationship changes: the Phillips curve

Bai-Perron on the same data also selects five breaks, at 1968Q2, 1973Q3, 1979Q1, 1984Q1 and 1993Q2 (first quarter of each new regime). The two methods agree on the count and on 1973Q3 and 1984, and on the flat curve in the last long regime ( \(-0.32\) , standard error 0.28, against the Bayesian 0.08). They disagree about the other dates, and both say those dates are poorly determined: the Bai-Perron interval for the last break runs from 1991Q2 to 1995Q2. (The Bai-Perron constants are intercepts at zero unemployment, so they cannot be compared with the Bayesian ones, which are the level at the average unemployment rate of the sample.) A caution: the model assumes independent errors, and inflation is persistent, so serial correlation can make the number of breaks appear larger than it is. Treat the number as an upper reading and check it with the HAC-robust Bai-Perron tests.

How to write it: results The Bayesian change-point analysis finds one break in the annual flow of the Nile, with posterior probability 0.925 for exactly one break and a log Bayes factor of 20.1 against none. The break occurred after 1898 with probability 0.76 and after 1896 to 1899 with probability 0.98. The mean flow fell from 1,096 (posterior standard deviation 25) to 851 (15), a fall of 22%, and the variance did not change. The result is the same for prior expected numbers of breaks from 0.5 to 4, prior scales from n/10 to 10n and minimum regime lengths of 5 to 25 years, and it agrees with the Bai-Perron estimate (1899, 95% interval 1895 to 1903). In 60 simulated series without a break, the posterior probability of a break never exceeded 0.41. For the Phillips curve, the probability of five breaks is 0.97, but the dates are uncertain (the highest, after 1973Q2, has probability 0.65); the slope of the curve is \(-1.8\) in 1973 to 1984 and statistically zero in 1991 to 2003.
