Bayesian Structural Time Series: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

What is the flow of the Nile now, behind the year-to-year noise, and how sure are we? Annual flow at Aswan jumps around from year to year because of rainfall, but there is also a slowly moving level (the drop around 1898 that the change-point guide found). A structural time-series model separates the two. The simplest, the local level model , is The level \(\mu_t\) is a random walk that is seen through noise. The ratio \(\sigma_\eta / \sigma_\varepsilon\) (the signal-to-noise ratio) decides how fast the level may move: small means that the level is nearly constant and each year's flow is mostly noise. Two components can be added: a slope : \(\mu_{t+1} = \mu_t + \delta_t + \eta_t\) , \(\delta_{t+1} = \delta_t + \zeta_t\) , the local linear trend , for a series that grows;

a seasonal pattern of period \(s\) (12 for monthly data): \(\gamma_t + \gamma_{t-1} + \dots + \gamma_{t-s+1} = \omega_t\) , so that the effects sum to about zero over a cycle and may evolve. Each component has its own variance. In the Bayesian version all the states and all the variances have a joint posterior. The engine draws all states at once from their exact Gaussian conditional distribution (the precision matrix is banded, so a banded Cholesky factorisation does it in milliseconds; Chan and Jeliazkov 2009), then draws each variance from an inverse gamma, so that there is no Kalman-filter loop and no tuning. Observations that are missing are simply left out of the likelihood and the states over the gap are drawn from the model, which interpolates. Future periods are treated the same way as missing ones, which gives forecasts.

Output What it answers Component standard deviations How much the level, slope, seasonal and noise move, next to the classical (Kalman filter) estimate States Level and slope at the last date, and the seasonal effects, with intervals Forecast Mean and 95% interval for each future period Missing values The level over a gap, with a band that widens where there is no data Why a prior on the variances matters The variance of a component that is small but not zero is weakly identified: a random-walk slope with a standard deviation of 0.003 and one of 0.000 describe the past about equally well, but they give very different forecasts two years ahead. The Bayesian answer is to put a prior on it. The engine's default guesses that each component moves by 1% of the standard deviation of the series per period (the choice of Scott and Varian 2014), with a weak inverse-gamma prior of shape 1 so that the data can overrule it. Step 7 shows how much the forecasts depend on the guess and how to test it.

How to write it: the model We model annual Nile flow as a local level plus noise, estimated by Bayesian methods. The level follows a random walk with variance \(\sigma_\eta^2\) ; observations equal the level plus independent normal noise with variance \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2\) . The prior on each variance is inverse gamma, with a prior guess of 1% of the standard deviation of the series for the level (Scott and Varian 2014) and a weak prior for the noise. We draw the whole state vector jointly from its Gaussian conditional distribution and each variance from its inverse-gamma conditional (Chan and Jeliazkov 2009), in two chains of 3,000 draws after 1,000 burn-in draws, and compare the variances with the maximum-likelihood estimates from the Kalman filter.

How to read it The 100 annual flows have a mean of 919 and a standard deviation of 169 (in hundreds of millions of cubic metres). The first differences have a standard deviation of 168, no smaller than the series itself, and a first-order autocorrelation of \(-0.4\) . That is the signature of a local level: a noisy series around a slowly moving level has differences with a negative first autocorrelation. For pure noise around a constant level it would be \(-0.5\) ; for a random walk without noise it would be 0.

How to read it The noise standard deviation is 127 (95% interval 105 to 150), close to the Kalman-filter maximum-likelihood value of 123. The level standard deviation is 29 (13 to 60) against the maximum-likelihood 38, which lies well inside the interval. The posterior is wide for this component because the level moves a little each year and the data can hardly tell a small drift from none; the maximum-likelihood point estimate hides that. The signal-to-noise ratio is 0.23: the level moves by about a fifth of the noise each year, so the level is much smoother than the series. The level at the last observation (1970) is 822 with a standard deviation of 61 and a 95% interval of 695 to 931, while the last observation itself is 740, a value that the model treats as mostly noise and pulls back towards the level of the recent years.

The first chart is the series with the posterior level and its 95% band: the level falls from about 1,100 before 1900 to about 850, the same break that the change-point guide dated to 1898, here seen as a fast but smooth descent.
Diagnostics: the sampler and the residuals

How to read it The noise variance has an R-hat of 1.014 and an effective sample size of 455 out of 6,000 draws. The level variance mixes more slowly: R-hat 1.059 and an effective sample size of 125. That is typical, since a small variance is weakly identified; the states themselves mix well because they are drawn in one block. If you report the interval for the level variance, use more draws (10,000 or more) until the R-hat is below 1.05 and the effective size is above 400; the level and forecasts are far less sensitive. The residual check finds nothing wrong: 5% of the standardised residuals are beyond \(\pm 2\) , as expected; the first autocorrelation is 0.09 and the Ljung-Box p-value is 0.15. These residuals come from the smoothed states, so they are a little too well behaved by construction; the hold-out test in Step 7 is the stronger check.

Remove the flow for 1920 to 1929 and let the model fill the gap. How to read it The summary shows that 10 values are filled in and 90 are used. Where the data are missing the level is no longer pinned down by an observation, so the band widens: 228 at 1920 against 165 with all the data, and 268 in 1925 against 173, the middle of the gap. After the gap the band returns to its normal width (182 in 1935 against 177). The level over the gap moves by at most about 20 units from the one estimated with all the data (848 against 827 in 1925), well within the band. A gap is thus filled with an estimate whose uncertainty is reported, not with a point that looks like data.
Trend, seasonality and a forecast: airline passengers

The Box and Jenkins airline series, 144 months of international passengers, in logs so that the multiplicative seasonal pattern becomes additive. The model has a local linear trend, a seasonal of period 12 and a 24-month forecast. How to read it Components. The noise standard deviation is 0.013 (maximum likelihood 0.011), the level 0.026 (0.026), the seasonal 0.0067 (0.0080) and the slope 0.0028 against a maximum-likelihood estimate of essentially zero. That is the weakly identified one: the posterior says the slope varies a little (0.0017 to 0.0049) where the point estimate says it does not vary at all, and it passes this uncertainty to the forecast. The slope at the last observation is 0.0057 a month (about 7% a year) with a posterior probability of 0.75 that it is positive; its interval, \(-0.013\) to 0.023, shows that the recent growth is not well pinned down.
Trend, seasonality and a forecast: airline passengers

Seasonality. July and August stand 0.23 and 0.22 log points above the level (about 26% and 24% in passengers), the lowest month is November, 0.22 log points below (19% fewer passengers), then February, 0.12 below (11% fewer). The intervals are about \(\pm 0.03\) wide, so the pattern is well determined. Forecast. The mean forecast for July 1961 is 6.45 in logs, about 632 passengers (95% interval 6.24 to 6.65, or 510 to 776), and for December 1962 it is 6.20, or about 495 (5.55 to 6.83, or 258 to 923). The interval widens with the horizon as the level and the slope uncertainties accumulate: a standard deviation of 0.04 one month ahead, 0.16 at a year and 0.32 at two years. The smoothed residuals have a negative autocorrelation ( \(-0.30\) ), which is a property of residuals computed from smoothed states, not a sign of misfit.
Trend, seasonality and a forecast: airline passengers
The charts show the series with the level and its band, the forecast with the predictive band and the seasonal pattern of the last year.
Test the forecast, and the prior, on held-out data

The only honest test of a forecast is to hide the end of the series, forecast it and compare. Fit to December 1958 and forecast the 24 months of 1959 and 1960, with three different guesses for how much each component moves. How to read it All 24 actual values lie inside the 95% band at every prior, so none of the bands is wrong; they differ in width and accuracy. With the tightest guess (0.1% of the standard deviation) the slope standard deviation is 0.0005, the mean absolute error of the forecast is 0.071 in logs (about 7%) and the band at two years is 0.67 wide. With the default (1%) the slope standard deviation is 0.0028, the error is 0.149 and the band 1.28. With a loose guess (5%) the slope is allowed to wander (0.0097), the error is 0.308 and the band 3.14, almost five times as wide as the first. For this series, which has a steady trend, a smaller prior is better, in agreement with the maximum-likelihood estimate of zero for the slope variance; the default is calibrated but conservative.
Test the forecast, and the prior, on held-out data

The lesson is general. The forecast depends on the prior for the slope variance, so report the prior, show a hold-out test and, if forecasts matter, choose the prior by hold-out error (an out-of-sample comparison of a few values, as here), not by the width of the band alone.

Simulate 40 series of 150 observations from a local level with known parameters (noise s.d. 1, level s.d. 0.3), run the default model and count how often the 95% interval for the last level contains the true level. How to read it The interval contains the true level in 95% of the 40 series (38 of 40), as a 95% interval should; with 40 replications the simulation standard error is about 3.5 points. The test suite repeats this with other designs, compares the Nile variances with the Kalman-filter maximum likelihood (the published values of Durbin and Koopman: 15,099 and 1,469 for the variances) and checks that a seasonal pattern and a regression coefficient are recovered and that forecasts are calibrated.

How to write it: results The annual flow of the Nile is a smooth level observed with large noise: the posterior mean of the noise standard deviation is 127 (95% interval 105 to 150) and that of the level innovations is 29 (13 to 60), so the signal-to-noise ratio is 0.23. The level at the end of the sample is 822 (95% interval 695 to 931). The variance estimates agree with the maximum-likelihood Kalman-filter values (123 and 38). The R-hat of the variances is below 1.06 and the effective sample sizes range from 125 to 455. For monthly airline passengers, a local linear trend with a seasonal of period 12 gives a seasonal peak in July 0.23 log points (about 26%) above the level and a trough in November 0.22 log points (19%) below, and a forecast of about 632 passengers in July 1961 (95% interval 510 to 776). In a hold-out test, a fit to 1958 forecast 1959 and 1960 with a mean absolute error of 0.07 in logs when the prior guess for the component variances was 0.1% of the standard deviation of the series and 0.15 at 1%, with all 24 observations inside the 95% band.

Stochastic-Volatility VAR (SV-VAR): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Were the shocks of the 1970s larger than those of the 1990s, and does it matter for inference? The model is a VAR with constant coefficients and time-varying shock variances: where \(H_t = \text{diag}(h_{1t}, h_{2t}, h_{3t})\) holds the variances of the three structural (Cholesky) shocks and \(A_0\) is a lower-triangular matrix of contemporaneous relations (Cogley and Sargent 2005). The log-variances follow random walks: volatility can rise or fall gradually, but cannot jump back. The coefficients get the Minnesota prior of the BVAR guide. The model is estimated by Gibbs sampling, drawing the log-variances with the mixture-of-normals approximation of Kim, Shephard and Chib (1998). The parameter \(s_i\) , the variance of the innovation to the log-volatility, controls how fast volatility moves.

Volatility or coefficients? Changing volatility and changing coefficients are hard to tell apart, and a model that allows only one of them will attribute all the instability to it. Sims and Zha (2006) found that most of the apparent change in U.S. monetary policy since the 1960s was a change in the size of the shocks. The TVP-VAR guide allows time-varying coefficients with constant variance; this guide allows time-varying variance with constant coefficients. Compare them, and if both matter, use a TVP-SV-VAR (not in OES). How to write it: the model We estimate a VAR with stochastic volatility (Cogley and Sargent 2005) in inflation, unemployment and the three-month Treasury bill rate, with two lags. The VAR coefficients are constant, with a Minnesota prior with overall tightness 0.1; the structural shocks, identified recursively with the interest rate ordered last, have volatilities that follow independent random walks in logs. The posterior is simulated with a Gibbs sampler in which the log-volatilities are drawn using the mixture approximation of Kim, Shephard and Chib (1998); we use 4,000 draws after 2,000 burn-in.
Load the data and test for unit roots

How to read it Inflation rejects a unit root (p = 0.03); unemployment and the T-bill rate do not (p = 0.11 and 0.28), so they get a random-walk prior on their own first lag ( delta = "0, 1, 1" ). The VAR is in levels, as in the BVAR guide.

How to read it The coefficients are constant, so the interest-rate equation is read as in the BVAR guide: the policy rate is persistent (own lags 1.03 and \(-0.10\) , sum 0.93) and responds to inflation with a positive sign (probability 0.88 for the first lag, with an interval that includes zero). The new objects are the \(s_i\) , the variances of the quarterly innovations in log volatility: 0.20 for inflation, 0.38 for unemployment and 0.23 for the interest rate, all clearly above zero (the 95% intervals start at 0.08, 0.17 and 0.11). A value of 0.2 means that the log-variance of a shock moves by about 0.45 per quarter, so its standard deviation by about 22%. Unemployment shocks have the most erratic volatility. If an \(s_i\) had been close to zero, that shock would have constant variance and the model would reduce to the ordinary BVAR for it.

How to read it The charts show the posterior median standard deviation of each structural shock. The table gives the minimum, the maximum and the last value. The interest-rate shock is largest in 1980Q3 (2.5 percentage points, the Volcker period) and smallest in 1997Q3 (0.15): a 17-fold range. Inflation shocks are smallest in 1993Q1 (0.6) and largest in 2008Q4 (5.3), the collapse of prices at the start of the financial crisis. Unemployment shocks range from 0.09 (1999Q2) to 0.93 (2009Q2). The period averages show the Great Moderation : from 1960–1983 to 1984–2006 the volatility of inflation fell by 42%, that of unemployment by 40% and that of the interest rate by 50%, and it rose again in 2007–2009 (inflation shocks 4.2, above the 1960–1983 average of 2.4). Say how you chose the break at 1984 (it is the convention, not an estimate), and note that the table shows posterior medians without bands.
Is the volatility model needed? Compare with constant variance

How to read it If the volatility model is right, the shocks divided by their estimated volatility should be white noise with no ARCH. They are: the ARCH test does not reject for any of the three standardised shocks (p = 0.72, 0.37 and 0.18), while in the constant-variance BVAR it rejects for all (p below 0.0001). The heavy tails also disappear: the Jarque-Bera statistic of the interest-rate residual falls from 1,652 to 6.3, and normality is not rejected for the inflation shock (p = 0.12). Volatility changes, not fat-tailed shocks, explain most of the non-normality. What the volatility model does not fix is serial correlation: the Ljung-Box test still rejects for the standardised inflation and unemployment shocks (statistics 59 and 46), as in the constant-variance VAR. That is a problem with the conditional mean, and the remedy is more lags (Step 8). Report both tables: the contrast is the argument for the SV-VAR.
Impulse responses in calm and volatile periods

How to read it The charts show the response of inflation and unemployment to an interest-rate shock at three dates: the volatile 1980Q3, the calm 1997Q3 and the last date. With constant coefficients the responses have the same shape at every date, and differ only in the size of a one-standard-deviation shock: after a year inflation rises by 0.87 in 1980Q3 and by 0.05 in 1997Q3, a ratio of 17, which is the ratio of the shock sizes (2.5 and 0.15). Per percentage point of policy shock, both are about 0.35. Do not read the difference as a change in monetary transmission: it is a change in the size of the shock. Report responses to a shock of fixed size (such as 25 basis points) or normalise them, as the BVAR guide does. This is the key contrast with the TVP-VAR, where the responses change shape because the coefficients change. As in the BVAR guide, inflation rises after the shock (the price puzzle).

How to read it For the VAR coefficients the effective sample sizes are above 1,400 (efficiency of 35% to 100%) and the Geweke statistics are below 2 in absolute value except one (the second T-bill lag in the interest-rate equation, \(-2.1\) ), unremarkable among many parameters. The variances \(s_i\) of the volatility innovations mix more slowly: effective sample sizes of 125 to 187 (efficiency of 3% to 5%), below the guideline of 200, though their Geweke statistics are fine (up to 1.9). For a paper, use 10,000 draws or more and check that the volatility paths do not change.
Robustness: lags, tightness and the amount of volatility drift

How to read it Each row is a variant of the model, and each number the ratio of average volatility in 1984–2006 to that in 1960–1983 (below one means the Great Moderation). With one, two or four lags the ratios are 0.56 to 0.60 for inflation, 0.58 to 0.60 for unemployment and 0.48 to 0.51 for the interest rate. A tighter prior ( \(\lambda_1 = 0.05\) ) gives 0.48 for inflation, a looser one ( \(\lambda_1 = 0.3\) ) 0.68; the interest-rate ratio is stable at about 0.5. The conclusion that volatility fell by 30% to 50% is robust; the size of the fall for inflation depends on the prior by about 20 percentage points, so report a range.

How to write it: results Constant-variance residuals show strong conditional heteroskedasticity in all three variables (ARCH test p < 0.0001) and heavy tails (Jarque-Bera 1,652 for the interest rate). Allowing the variance of each structural shock to follow a random walk removes both: the standardised shocks show no ARCH (p between 0.18 and 0.72) and are close to normal. Estimated volatility fell sharply: between 1960–1983 and 1984–2006 the average standard deviation of inflation shocks fell by 42%, that of unemployment shocks by 40% and that of interest-rate shocks by 50%, and it rose again in the financial crisis. The interest-rate shock was 17 times larger in 1980Q3, at the height of the Volcker disinflation, than in 1997Q3. The ratios hardly change with one to four lags, and the fall in volatility ranges from 30% to 53% across lag lengths and prior tightness. Because the coefficients are constant, the impulse responses at different dates differ only in the size of the shock; for time-varying propagation we refer to the TVP-VAR. Standardised inflation and unemployment shocks remain serially correlated, which is a limitation of the model's conditional mean.

Bayesian Threshold VAR: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Does monetary policy work differently when inflation is high? A threshold VAR (Tsay 1998; Koop and Potter 2006) splits the sample into two regimes according to whether a threshold variable \(z_{t-d}\) lies above a threshold \(r\) : The coefficients and the covariance matrix differ between regimes. The threshold \(r\) and the delay \(d\) are unknown. In the Bayesian version used here, each regime has a Normal-Wishart prior (Minnesota-type moments), so its marginal likelihood is available in closed form and the posterior of \((r, d)\) is exact , computed over a grid of candidate thresholds. There is nothing to simulate for the threshold, so no convergence to check; coefficients are then drawn within each regime.

Two checks before you trust a threshold model Does the data prefer two regimes? The log Bayes factor of the threshold model against the linear VAR answers this directly. A threshold VAR can always fit better than a linear VAR; the Bayes factor penalises the extra parameters. If it is negative, use the linear VAR. Is the threshold variable the right one? Different candidates give very different Bayes factors (Step 3). Choose by the Bayes factor, and say that you did: the choice is part of the model. Also check that each regime has enough observations: with two lags of three variables, a regime has 21 coefficients per equation, so a regime of 30 quarters is thin. The prior helps but results for the small regime are imprecise.

How to write it: the model We estimate a Bayesian threshold VAR (Tsay 1998; Koop and Potter 2006) in GDP growth, inflation and the three-month Treasury bill rate, with two lags. The regime is determined by whether inflation, \(d\) quarters earlier, exceeds a threshold \(r\) . Each regime has its own coefficients and covariance matrix, with a Normal-Wishart prior with Minnesota moments (overall tightness 0.2). Because the marginal likelihood is available analytically in each regime, the joint posterior of the threshold (over a 40-point grid between the 15th and 85th percentiles of the threshold variable) and the delay (one or two quarters) is computed exactly. We compare the threshold model with a linear VAR using the log Bayes factor, and report results for the posterior mode of the threshold.
Load the data and test for unit roots

How to read it Inflation and GDP growth reject a unit root; the T-bill rate does not (p = 0.28). The regimes are defined by a stationary variable, which is what a threshold model needs: a trending threshold variable would spend the whole sample in one regime. Quarterly annualised inflation is volatile (it ranges widely), so the high regime also catches quarters of temporary price spikes, not only the high-inflation years.
Do you need a threshold, and on which variable?

Run the model with each candidate threshold variable and compare the log Bayes factor against the linear VAR. How to read it A positive log Bayes factor favours the threshold model; above 4.6 is "decisive" on Jeffreys' scale. Inflation (26.4) and the T-bill rate (16.8) are strongly supported; GDP growth ( \(-4.0\) ), consumption growth ( \(-3.7\) ), unemployment ( \(-8.4\) ) and investment growth ( \(-2.9\) ) are not (the linear VAR is preferred), and money growth is at zero (1.0). So the economy's dynamics depend on the level of inflation or interest rates, not on the stage of the business cycle measured by growth. Inflation is the natural choice for the question, and its Bayes factor is the largest; we use it below. This is a model choice made on the data: report the table.
Do you need a threshold, and on which variable?

Caution: a Bayes factor in favour of a regime split can also reflect different volatility in the two regimes (the 1970s were more volatile than the 1990s). Compare with the SV-VAR guide, which allows changing volatility without splitting the coefficients.

How to read it The data choose a threshold of 6.65% annualised quarterly inflation, with a delay of two quarters (the posterior probability of a delay of one quarter is below 0.0001): the economy is in the high regime when inflation two quarters earlier exceeded 6.65%. That regime holds 30 of the 200 quarters (15%) and the low regime 170. The log Bayes factor against a single linear VAR is 26.4 , overwhelming support for two regimes (on Jeffreys' scale, above 4.6 is decisive). The posterior mean of the threshold (6.646) equals the mode (6.647): with a finer grid of 100 points, 95% of the posterior mass sits on 6.65 and 3% on 6.58. Do not over-read this precision: it arises because moving a single quarter between regimes changes the marginal likelihood a great deal when the high regime has only 30 quarters. Step 9 shows how the threshold moves when the minimum regime size changes.

How to read it Because the regime is a function of an observed variable, regime membership is known once the threshold is fixed, so every probability is 1. The 30 high-inflation quarters fall into two real episodes and eight isolated quarters. The episodes are 1974Q1–1975Q2 (the first oil shock) and 1978Q2–1982Q1 (the second oil shock and the Volcker disinflation, 16 quarters). The single quarters are 1969Q3, 1973Q3, 1975Q4, 1977Q3, 1982Q4, 1991Q1, 2006Q1 and 2008Q4: spikes in the quarterly CPI, some from energy prices, not episodes of sustained inflation. In a paper, describe the high regime as largely the oil-shock years, and note that it is close to a period dummy for the 1970s, which limits what can be inferred about "high inflation" in general.

How to read it The policy-rate equation shows what changes. In the low regime the rate follows the economy: it responds to lagged GDP growth (0.046, 95% interval 0.016 to 0.072; probability of a positive sign 1.00) and is very persistent (own lag 0.91). In the high regime the response to growth is small and imprecise (0.015, interval \(-0.10\) to 0.14), the response to inflation is 0.059 ( \(-0.11\) to 0.22), and the own lag is lower (0.71, interval 0.38 to 1.02). With only 30 quarters, the intervals are wide: the data cannot say that the rule changed, only that the low-regime rule is estimated precisely and the high-regime rule is not. Report this limitation rather than reading the point estimates as a regime-dependent policy rule.

How to read it Responses to a one-standard-deviation rise in the T-bill rate, within each regime (the chart shows posterior medians without credible bands). Output: in the low-inflation regime GDP growth does not respond (+0.01 after a year); in the high-inflation regime it falls by 0.40 percentage point after a year, 0.18 after two and 0.07 after three. Inflation: in the low regime it rises (0.15 after a year, 0.11 after two): the price puzzle of the BVAR guide; in the high regime there is no price puzzle ( \(-0.006\) after a year and \(-0.06\) after two). So the textbook sign of monetary transmission appears in the high regime, which is the regime of the oil-shock years, and the price puzzle in the low regime. Because the high regime has 30 observations, do not report these differences as significant without computing credible bands from the draws; the Bayes factor in Step 3 says that the regimes differ, not that each difference is large.

How to read it In the low regime (170 quarters) the joint portmanteau test does not reject (p = 0.10), but Ljung-Box rejects for inflation (p = 0.0001) and the interest rate (p = 0.034), normality is rejected for both, and the ARCH test rejects for GDP growth (p = 0.035). In the high regime (30 quarters) Ljung-Box rejects for inflation (p = 0.018) and nothing else does, but these tests have little power with 30 observations, so the absence of rejections says little. Remaining autocorrelation in inflation suggests more lags; Step 9 shows that the threshold and the Bayes factor survive three and four lags. Changing volatility between the regimes is not modelled beyond the regime-specific covariance matrix; if it matters to your question, see the SV-VAR guide.
Robustness: lags, trimming, grid and prior

How to read it Each row changes one thing. Lags: with one to four lags the threshold is 6.65 and the Bayes factor is 31.8, 26.4, 22.9 and 23.9. Minimum regime share: allowing 10% in each regime moves the threshold to 7.05 (29 high quarters); requiring 25% moves it to 5.0 (50 high quarters), with a Bayes factor of 16.7: the threshold is sensitive to how small the high regime may be, so report the trimming. Grid and delay: a grid of 100 points and a maximum delay of four quarters change nothing (the delay stays at two). Prior: the Bayes factor ranges from 5.4 ( \(\lambda_1 = 0.1\) ) to 45.7 ( \(\lambda_1 = 0.5\) ). Marginal likelihoods depend on the prior, so the size of the Bayes factor is not robust, but it is positive and large in every variant, so the conclusion that two regimes beat one is. Report a range, not a single number.

How to write it: results We compare a Bayesian threshold VAR with a linear VAR using the log Bayes factor, for seven candidate threshold variables. The data support inflation (log Bayes factor 26.4) and the Treasury bill rate (16.8) as threshold variables; GDP growth, consumption growth, unemployment and investment growth are not supported (log Bayes factors between \(-8.4\) and \(-2.9\) ). With inflation as the threshold variable the posterior concentrates on a delay of two quarters and a threshold of 6.65%, which defines a high-inflation regime of 30 quarters, 22 of them in the oil-shock episodes of 1974–75 and 1978–82. In the low-inflation regime, a rise in the policy rate does not reduce output and raises inflation (the price puzzle); in the high-inflation regime output falls by 0.4 percentage point after a year and inflation does not rise. These regime differences are estimated with 30 observations and are imprecise. The threshold, the delay and the sign of the Bayes factor do not change with one to four lags, the grid, or the prior tightness; the threshold moves between 5.0 and 7.05 depending on the minimum regime size (10% to 25%), and the Bayes factor ranges from 5.4 to 45.7 with the prior.

Time-Varying Parameter VAR (TVP-VAR): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Has the effect of monetary policy on inflation changed since the 1960s? The model lets all VAR coefficients drift: where \(X_t\) holds a constant and \(p\) lags of the three variables. With three variables and two lags each date has 21 coefficients; the random walk lets them move a little each quarter. How much they move is governed by \(Q\) , whose prior is set from a training sample : the first 40 observations are used only to estimate a constant-parameter VAR, whose coefficients and covariance matrix centre the prior for \(\beta_0\) and \(Q\) (Primiceri 2005). The scale \(k_Q\) says how fast coefficients may drift: small values give nearly constant coefficients, large values a flexible but noisy path.

Be sceptical of time variation A TVP-VAR can always find movement in coefficients, even when the true model is constant, because the random walk is flexible and the data are noisy. Three habits keep a paper honest: (1) test whether coefficients really moved, using the posterior probability that they changed (Step 4); (2) show that the results do not depend on \(k_Q\) and the training sample (Step 8); (3) in a macroeconomic VAR, ask whether changing volatility (the SV-VAR guide) rather than changing coefficients explains the instability: much of the apparent time variation in the 1970s and 1980s turned out to be a change in shock variances (Sims and Zha 2006).

How to write it: the model We estimate a time-varying parameter VAR with random-walk coefficients and a constant error covariance matrix, in inflation, unemployment and the three-month Treasury bill rate, with two lags (Cogley and Sargent 2005; Primiceri 2005). The prior for the initial coefficients and the covariance of their innovations is calibrated on a training sample of the first 40 quarters (1959–1969), so estimation starts in 1969Q4 with 160 observations; the prior scale of the innovation variance is \(k_Q = 0.01\) . The posterior is simulated with a Gibbs sampler, drawing the coefficient paths with the Carter-Kohn (1994) simulation smoother, using 6,000 draws after 4,000 burn-in draws. Impulse responses at a date use the coefficients of that date, identified recursively with the interest rate ordered last.
Load the data and test for unit roots

How to read it A TVP-VAR is estimated in levels without a prior on unit roots: the training sample sets the prior mean of the coefficients, and the random walk lets the persistence change. Inflation rejects a unit root at 5% (p = 0.03), unemployment and the T-bill rate do not (p = 0.11 and 0.28). If you use differences, say so. Because coefficients can drift above one, the model can produce explosive paths in short stretches; the summary line "Iterations with no stable path" counts the draws where this could not be avoided (zero here).

How to read it 160 observations are used for estimation, 1969Q4 to 2009Q3, with the first 40 quarters kept for the prior. The covariance matrix of the residuals is constant here (stochastic volatility is the subject of the SV-VAR guide): inflation shocks have a variance of about 5, shocks to unemployment about 0.06, and interest-rate and inflation shocks are positively correlated (0.81 covariance), while unemployment shocks are negatively correlated with both.

The central table compares each coefficient at the start and the end of the estimation sample, with the posterior probability that it increased. How to read it Each row shows a coefficient at the start (1969Q4) and the end (2009Q3), and the posterior probability that it increased. Only 2 of 21 coefficients have a probability below 0.05 or above 0.95, which is what chance alone would give (about 2.1). So the evidence that the conditional means moved is thin. The exception is the second lag of inflation in the inflation equation: it falls from 0.36 to \(-0.19\) (probability of an increase 0.008), and the sum of the two own lags of inflation falls from about 0.5 to about zero, in line with the finding that U.S. inflation became less persistent (Cogley and Sargent 2005); a paper would test the sum directly, from the draws.

Look at the T-bill coefficients in the inflation equation to see why single coefficients mislead: the first lag falls by 0.88 and the second rises by 0.96, with probabilities of 0.17 and 0.87, because the two lags move in opposite directions and their sum barely changes (0.24 at the start, 0.32 at the end). Always judge time variation by sums of lags and by impulse responses, not by one coefficient.

How to read it The charts show the posterior median path of the T-bill rate's own first lag and of the constant of each equation. The own lag is about 0.98 in 1969, dips to 0.91 around 1979, and rises above one after 1990, reaching 1.19 by 2009. This should not be read as an explosive process: the second lag is about \(-0.27\) at the end, so the sum of the two lags is about 0.92. The constant in the interest-rate equation falls from about 1.0 to about 0.2, as inflation and rates came down. A path of this kind is a statement about the model's best description of each period, estimated with few effective observations at each date: treat its wiggles as noise, and its broad drift as the finding.

How to read it The charts show the response of inflation and unemployment to a one-standard-deviation rise in the T-bill rate, using the coefficients of 1969Q4, 1989Q4 and 2009Q3. (The date-specific responses here are posterior medians; compute bands from the draws if the paper relies on the comparison.) Inflation rises after the shock at all three dates: the price puzzle holds in every period. The response is 0.27 after two quarters in 1969 and 0.24 in 1989, and in 2009 it is delayed (0.02 after one quarter, 0.31 after two) and then more persistent, at 0.34 after eight quarters and 0.22 after twenty, against 0.19 and 0.03 in 1969. Unemployment falls by about 0.2 point after a year in 1969 and hardly moves in 1989 (0 after four quarters, +0.10 after eight, the expected sign). In 2009 it falls by 0.45 after eight quarters, the wrong sign for a tightening.

The 2009 responses are the least reliable: the policy rate was close to zero, its own lag exceeds one, and a shock to it is a very different object from a shock to the funds rate in 1969. A common remedy is to end the sample before the crisis or to treat it separately; if your sample ends in the crisis, say that the final responses reflect the zero lower bound.

How to read it Convergence of a TVP-VAR is demanding, because there are hundreds of states. With 6,000 draws after 4,000 burn-in, the effective sample sizes of the coefficients at the last date are 235 to 336 (efficiency of 4% to 6%, above 200 but low) and those of the covariance terms 1,600 to 3,700. Two covariance parameters fail Geweke's test : \(\Sigma_{\text{inflation, T-bill}}\) (z = 3.5) and \(\Sigma_{\text{T-bill, T-bill}}\) (z = 2.4): the chain for the covariance matrix is still drifting. With the default 1,000 draws the sample size for the T-bill coefficient was 26 and the statistic \(-4.5\) . In a paper, run at least 15,000 draws with a long burn-in, and report the convergence table, or the posterior means for the covariance matrix are suspect.

Residual diagnostics: serial correlation is rejected for all three variables (Ljung-Box p = 0.014, 0.003 and below 0.001), as is normality (Jarque-Bera 1,524 for the interest rate), and so is the absence of ARCH, in all three. The constant covariance matrix is therefore wrong, and the time variation in coefficients may be absorbing changes in volatility: the SV-VAR guide models these directly, and a paper that claims changing transmission should show that it survives stochastic volatility.
Robustness: the amount of drift, the training sample and the lags

How to read it The table follows the own first lag of the T-bill rate at the start, the middle and the end of the sample. \(k_Q\) (0.003, 0.01, 0.03): the path barely changes (end value 1.20 to 1.22), so the amount of drift permitted by the prior does not drive the result. Training sample of 30 or 50 quarters: the end value is 1.23 and 1.09; it is lower with the longer training sample, as the model has less time to drift. One lag: the own lag is flat at about 0.9 throughout. The comparison with the two-lag model shows that the rise above one is a feature of the two-lag specification (offset by the second lag), while the persistence of the rate (the sum of the lags) rises from about 0.75 to about 0.92 in the two-lag model and is roughly 0.9 throughout in the one-lag model. The honest summary is that the TVP-VAR finds modest changes in the persistence of the policy rate, and that their size depends on the specification.

How to write it: results We find limited evidence of time variation in the conditional means. Of the 21 coefficients, only two changed between 1969Q4 and 2009Q3 with posterior probability above 95%, no more than would be expected by chance; the main exception is the persistence of inflation, where the sum of the two own lags falls from about 0.5 to about zero. The policy-rate equation shows a decline in the constant from about 1.0 to 0.2 and a persistence that is higher at the end of the sample than at the start, with a size that depends on the lag length. Inflation rises after a monetary tightening at all three dates studied (1969Q4, 1989Q4, 2009Q3), so the price puzzle is not a feature of one regime. The responses at the end of the sample are affected by the near-zero policy rate and should be read with caution. These results do not depend on the prior scale of the coefficient innovations ( \(k_Q\) between 0.003 and 0.03). Residual tests reject a constant covariance matrix, so we cannot rule out that changing volatility, not changing coefficients, explains part of the variation; the stochastic-volatility VAR in the next section addresses this. Convergence statistics (Table A) show adequate effective sample sizes for the coefficients but not for two covariance parameters, for which longer chains are needed.

Report What Where Model Random-walk coefficients, training sample, \(k_Q\) , draws Step 1 Evidence Coefficients at two dates with \(P(\text{change} > 0)\) ; how many pass a threshold Step 4 Results Paths of key coefficients; impulse responses at selected dates Steps 5 and 6 Diagnostics Effective sample sizes and Geweke statistics; residual tests Step 7 Robustness \(k_Q\) , training sample, lags Step 8 Alternative Constant-parameter BVAR; SV-VAR BVAR and SV-VAR guides References. Cogley and Sargent (2005), Review of Economic Dynamics ; Primiceri (2005), Review of Economic Studies ; Carter and Kohn (1994), Biometrika ; Sims and Zha (2006), American Economic Review ; Koop and Korobilis (2010), Foundations and Trends in Econometrics ; Del Negro and Primiceri (2015), Review of Economic Studies .
Shift-share (Bartik) instrumental variables: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
The question and the identification logic

A region's wage growth \(x_\ell\) is correlated with unobserved local demand shocks, so OLS of regional employment growth \(y_\ell\) on \(x_\ell\) is biased. The shift-share instrument uses only the variation that comes from national industry shocks \(g_n\) combined with each region's initial industry shares \(s_{\ell n}\) : There are two ways to justify it. Share exogeneity (Goldsmith-Pinkham, Sorkin and Swift 2020): the initial shares are uncorrelated with later unobserved shocks, and the shares are the instruments. Shock exogeneity (Borusyak, Hull and Jaravel 2022): the national shocks \(g_n\) are as good as randomly assigned across industries, and the shares are exposure weights. Say which one your paper relies on, because the diagnostics differ.
The question and the identification logic

Symbol Variable Definition \(y_\ell\) dy change in log regional employment \(x_\ell\) dx change in log regional wage \(s_{\ell n}\) share initial industry shares (60 industries) \(g_n\) shock national industry shocks \(\beta\) true effect, set to 0.5 in the simulation Before you estimate anything Decide which assumption you are making and why. For shock exogeneity you need many industries and no single industry dominating (the effective number of industries should be large). For share exogeneity you need to argue why initial industry mix is unrelated to later local shocks. Exclude regions' own contribution to the national shock (leave-one-out shocks) when regions are large. How to write it: design We instrument the change in regional wages with a shift-share instrument, the average of national industry shocks weighted by the region's initial employment shares. Identification relies on the shocks being as good as randomly assigned across industries conditional on the weights (Borusyak, Hull and Jaravel 2022). We report Rotemberg weights to show which industries drive the estimate, shock-level (exposure-robust) standard errors, and sensitivity to dropping the highest-weight industries.

How to read it Regions specialise in a few industries each, and across the 60 industries no single one is large: the biggest has 2% of the average share and the effective number of industries is 59.5. That matters for shock exogeneity, which needs many small shocks, not a few large ones. The instrument varies a lot across regions (standard deviation 0.030) and moves with regional wage growth. The data are simulated, so these numbers describe the design, not a real economy.

How to read it The first stage is strong (slope 1.03, F = 487, R² = 0.44). OLS gives 1.00, double the true value of 0.5, because the unobserved local shock raises both wages and employment. 2SLS with the shift-share instrument gives 0.503 (s.e. 0.058), with an interval of 0.39 to 0.62 that covers the truth. The reduced form divided by the first stage gives the same number, which is the Wald logic of the estimator.
Which industries drive the estimate? Rotemberg weights

How to read it The estimate is a weighted average of 60 industry-specific estimates, and no industry dominates: the top five carry 43% of the absolute weight, with 13 industries having small negative weights (−0.018 in total). The individual industry estimates range widely (for the top six, 0.19 to 0.94) because each uses only one share, so they are noisy. In a real paper, look at whether the high-weight industries are ones for which the share exogeneity assumption is credible, and whether their individual estimates agree.
Inference that respects the shock structure

How to read it The exposure-robust (industry-level) standard error is 0.075, about 1.3 times the conventional 0.058, which would widen the interval. In this simulation the local errors are independent across regions, so the conventional interval also covers well (96% over 400 draws, against 94% for the shock-level one). That is a feature of the design: with real data, regions that share industries have correlated residuals and the conventional standard errors can be far too small, so the shock-level standard error is the safe choice.
Diagnostics: pre-trend, shock balance and leave-one-out

How to read it The instrument does not predict the pre-period outcome (0.07, t = 1.2) and the shocks are unrelated to a random industry characteristic (t = −1.6). Dropping the highest-weight industries moves the estimate between 0.45 and 0.54 while the standard errors rise from 0.058 to 0.083, so no single industry drives the result. The last line shows what a violation does: when the shocks are correlated with industry-level conditions that also raise local outcomes, 2SLS rises to 0.69 against the true 0.5, and the usual diagnostics would not flag it automatically. A pre-trend test is only informative if the confounder also acts in the pre-period. How to write it: results
Diagnostics: pre-trend, shock balance and leave-one-out

Instrumenting regional wage growth with a shift-share instrument gives an effect on employment of 0.50 (s.e. 0.058; exposure-robust s.e. 0.075), against an OLS estimate of 1.00 that is biased by local demand shocks. The first stage is strong (F = 487). The Rotemberg weights are spread over many industries (the top five carry 43% of the absolute weight), the estimate stays between 0.45 and 0.54 when the highest-weight industries are dropped, and the instrument does not predict the pre-period outcome. The identifying assumption is that the national shocks are uncorrelated with local unobserved shocks, which the diagnostics cannot prove: correlation between the shocks and industry-level conditions would raise the estimate to 0.69 in our simulation. (These results use simulated data.)
What to report in the paper

Item What to show Identification share or shock exogeneity, and the argument for it Instrument how it is built, leave-one-out shocks, effective number of industries First stage the coefficient and the F statistic Rotemberg weights the top industries, and the estimates that use them Inference exposure-robust standard errors (not only region-clustered ones) Diagnostics pre-trend, shock balance, leave-one-out sensitivity Common mistakes Conventional standard errors. Regions that share industry exposure have correlated residuals, so region-robust standard errors can be much too small. Use shock-level or exposure-robust inference. No statement of which exogeneity assumption. The checks for share exogeneity (pre-trends, Rotemberg weights) and for shock exogeneity (shock balance, many shocks) differ. One industry doing all the work. Report the Rotemberg weights and test dropping the top industries.
What to report in the paper

Shocks that include the region itself. Use leave-one-out national shocks when a region is a large part of the national industry. Weak first stage or negative weights unreported. Show the F statistic and the share of negative weights. Treating the simulation as evidence. Simulated data show how a method behaves. In your own paper, the argument for exogeneity must come from the setting.
Difference-in-Differences: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Between 2005 and 2010 many U.S. states passed Castle Doctrine or “stand-your-ground” laws, which remove the duty to retreat before using lethal force in self-defence. Supporters argued they would deter crime; critics that they would escalate confrontations. Did the laws change homicide rates? This guide uses the 13 states that adopted a law in 2007 and the 29 states that never did, from the data of Cheng and Hoekstra (2013). States adopting in other years are left out, so every treated state shares one adoption date. (The staggered-DiD guide uses all of them.) The difference-in-differences estimate compares the change in homicide in adopting states with the change in non-adopting states over the same years:

Symbol Variable in the file Definition \(\ln h_{st}\) l_homicide Log homicides per 100,000 population \(D_{st}\) castle_law 1 in a treated state from the year its law took effect \(\alpha_s\) , \(\lambda_t\) — State and year fixed effects \(\tau\) — The DiD estimate: the average effect on the treated (ATT) The identifying assumption \(\tau\) is causal under parallel trends : without the laws, homicide in the adopting states would have changed by the same amount as in the non-adopting states. The levels may differ (the state effects absorb that); the changes must not. The assumption cannot be tested after 2007, but its implication for the years before 2007 can, and the event study does so.

How to write it: design We compare homicide rates in the 13 states that enacted Castle Doctrine laws in 2007 with those in states that did not enact such laws between 2000 and 2010, using a difference-in-differences design with state and year fixed effects. The identifying assumption is that, absent the laws, homicide rates in adopting and non-adopting states would have followed parallel trends.
Load the data and look at the two groups

How to read it Adopting states have higher homicide rates throughout: that difference in levels is what the state fixed effects remove. What matters is whether the two lines move in parallel before 2007 . By eye they track each other reasonably closely, with year-to-year noise. The event study turns this impression into a test.

How to read it This table is the whole idea of DiD. Each group's change from before to after removes its permanent level; the difference between the two changes removes everything common to both groups in the later years (national crime trends, the recession). What remains is attributed to the law. With one adoption date and a balanced panel, this number is exactly the two-way fixed-effects estimate in the next step.

How to read it Estimate. The laws are associated with homicide rates about 6% higher, but the confidence interval is wide and includes zero: in this subsample the effect is not statistically significant. Clustered standard errors. The treatment varies at the state level and homicide is serially correlated within states, so standard errors must be clustered by state (Bertrand, Duflo and Mullainathan 2004). With 42 clusters this is fine; with fewer than about 30, use the wild cluster bootstrap.
Event study: test the pre-trends and trace the dynamics

How to read it Each point is the difference between adopting and non-adopting states in that year, relative to 2006 (year −1). Leads (before adoption). They fluctuate around zero, and the joint test does not reject that they are all zero. There is no evidence that adopting states were already on a different path before 2007. That is the implication of parallel trends that can be checked. Lags (after adoption). The estimated effects after 2007 are small and imprecise: no clear sign of a jump in homicide among this group of states. An insignificant pre-trend test is not proof of parallel trends: the test may simply lack power. A referee may ask for a sensitivity analysis (Rambachan and Roth 2023), which shows how large a violation of parallel trends would have to be to overturn the conclusion.
Robustness: placebo date and a different comparison

How to read it Placebo date. Pretending the law took effect in 2004 and using only pre-2007 data should give no effect. It does not, which supports the comparison. Different base period. The event-study average uses only 2006 as the base year, while the TWFE estimate uses the average of all pre-treatment years. The two answers differ because individual years are noisy, but both point estimates are small relative to their uncertainty. Report both and say so.

How to write it: results Table 1 reports the difference-in-differences estimates. Homicide rates in states that enacted Castle Doctrine laws in 2007 rose by about 6 percent relative to non-adopting states, but the estimate is imprecise and not statistically different from zero (standard errors clustered by state). Event-study estimates show no differential pre-trends: the coefficients for the years before adoption are jointly insignificant, and a placebo law dated to 2004 has no effect. Common mistakes Using this two-way fixed-effects regression when units adopt at different dates. The estimate can then be badly biased; see the staggered-DiD guide. Not clustering at the level of treatment assignment. Treating insignificant leads as proof of parallel trends. Show the event-study plot, and consider a sensitivity analysis.
Controlling for variables that the policy itself affects (bad controls). Ignoring anticipation: if behaviour changes when a law is announced, the base period must precede the announcement.
Event Study and Pre-Trend Sensitivity: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

The staggered DiD guide estimates the average effect of castle doctrine laws. This guide looks at the path of the effect around adoption and at how much we can trust the "no pre-trend" claim. Our question is: does the murder rate in adopting states move differently from that in never-adopting states before adoption, and how does it change after adoption? With adoption year \(g\) for each state and event time \(\ell=t-g\) , the Sun–Abraham regression interacts cohort and event-time indicators, using never-treated states as controls and \(\ell=-1\) as the reference period: where \(\hat w_{g|\ell}\) is the share of cohort \(g\) among the treated states observed at event time \(\ell\) . The conventional alternative uses one coefficient per event time for all treated states together.

Symbol Variable in the file Definition \(y_{it}\) l_murder log murder rate per 100,000 \(D_{it}\) castle_law 1 if the state has a castle doctrine law in year \(t\) \(g\) adoption year (2006 to 2010); never-treated states have none \(\ell\) years since adoption Before you estimate anything Decide the window of event time to report (here −5 to 3), the reference period (−1) and the control group (never-treated states). Event times near the ends of the window are identified by few cohorts, so coefficients there are noisy and may describe different cohorts. State the weights, not only the plot. How to write it: design We estimate dynamic effects of castle doctrine laws with an event-study design. Adoption dates run from 2006 to 2010, and 29 states never adopt. We use the interaction-weighted estimator of Sun and Abraham (2021), with never-treated states as the control group and the year before adoption as the reference period. Standard errors come from a bootstrap that resamples states. We test pre-trends with a joint Wald test, evaluate its power, and bound the post-treatment effects under smoothness restrictions on possible violations of parallel trends.
Load the data and look at event time

How to read it There are 50 states over 2000–2010, 29 never treated and 21 adopting between 2006 and 2010. The cohort of 2007 has 13 states, the others have 4, 2, 1 and 1. Because the panel ends in 2010, the later event times rest on the earliest cohorts: at event time 3 only the 2006 and 2007 cohorts are observed (14 states), and at event time 4 only a single state. We report −5 to 3. In the figure the mean murder rate of the 2007 cohort drifts up relative to the never-treated states before adoption, which the event study will quantify.

How to read it The conventional event-study regression, with end points binned at −5 and 3, gives lead coefficients of −0.14 at five years before adoption, −0.05, −0.02 and −0.09 at two years before, and lag coefficients of 0.02 to 0.03 at event times 0 to 2 and −0.02 at event time 3. The leads are mostly negative: treated states had lower murder rates than at l = −1 earlier on, so their murder rates were rising relative to controls before the laws.
The interaction-weighted estimator of Sun and Abraham

How to read it The Sun–Abraham estimates are very close to the conventional ones (−0.134, −0.055, −0.020 and −0.094 for the leads; 0.022, 0.030, 0.042 and −0.012 for the lags), because the effects are small and the never-treated states form most of the comparison group. The difference is largest at event time 2 (0.042 against 0.022). Bootstrap standard errors are 0.04 to 0.06. Two of the four leads are individually significant (l = −5: t = −2.1, and l = −2: t = −2.3), and none of the lags is (|t| ≤ 0.7). The number of cohorts behind each point falls from five to two at l = 3, so the later lags describe fewer states.
Test the pre-trends and ask how much power the test has

How to read it The joint test of the four pre-treatment coefficients rejects zero: Wald = 11.35, p = 0.023. Parallel pre-trends are not supported. A linear trend fitted to the pre-coefficients has a slope of 0.028 per year. The power curve shows how large a linear trend the test would have caught: with 80% power it detects a slope of 0.052 per year, and a trend of that size would add 0.05 to the coefficient at l = 0 and 0.21 at l = 3. The pre-test is therefore not powerful against trends that are small in the pre-period but would be as large as the effects we are looking for in the post-period.
How sensitive is the effect to a violation of parallel trends?

How to read it Smoothness restrictions bound how much the violation can change from one period to the next. With M = 0 the violation is a linear trend, and the bound on the effect is −0.033 to 0.008 at l = 0, −0.080 to 0.002 at l = 1 and −0.123 to 0.000 at l = 2, so extrapolating the pre-trend takes the estimated effect to zero or below. Allowing the slope of the violation to change, with M equal to half of the largest second difference seen before treatment (0.167), widens the sets a lot, to −0.16 to 0.09 at l = 0 and −0.75 to 0.50 at l = 2. None of the 95% intervals excludes zero for any M, including M = 0. The sets are wide because the pre-coefficients are noisy (each has a standard error of 0.04 to 0.06) and the violation can build up over several periods. The sensitivity analysis cannot give a positive or negative effect: it shows that the data are compatible with no effect at all. The approximation (identified set widened by 1.96 standard errors, with the pre-period box taken from the 95% intervals) is conservative.
How sensitive is the effect to a violation of parallel trends?

How to write it: results The event study shows no significant effect of castle doctrine laws on the murder rate after adoption: the Sun–Abraham estimates are 0.022, 0.030, 0.042 and −0.012 at event times 0 to 3 (bootstrap standard errors 0.05 to 0.06). The conventional event-study regression gives nearly the same numbers. However, pre-trends are not parallel (joint Wald test p = 0.023): murder rates in adopting states rose relative to never-treated states before adoption. The pre-trend test has 80% power only against a linear trend of 0.052 per year, which would add 0.05 to 0.21 to the post-treatment coefficients. If the pre-trend is extrapolated linearly, the post-treatment effects are between −0.12 and 0.01. We conclude that these data cannot distinguish a small effect of the laws from the continuation of a pre-existing trend.
What to report in the paper

Item What to show Estimator Sun–Abraham (or Callaway–Sant'Anna), the control group, the reference period and the window Coverage which cohorts contribute at each event time Inference the bootstrap or clustering method, with states or units as the resampling unit Pre-trends the joint test and its power, not only "the leads are insignificant" Sensitivity how large a violation of parallel trends the result can tolerate (smoothness or relative-magnitude bounds) Comparison the conventional event study next to the robust one Common mistakes Treating insignificant leads as proof of parallel trends. The pre-test can have low power, and passing it does not remove bias (Roth 2022). Using a single set of leads and lags under staggered adoption. With heterogeneous effects the coefficients can mix cohorts and even pick up other periods' effects. Use an interaction-weighted or imputation estimator.
What to report in the paper

Binning or dropping end points without saying so. End points rest on few cohorts and states. Plotting only the point estimates. Show intervals from a bootstrap or clustered errors that account for the correlation between event times. Normalising to a noisy reference period. The whole picture shifts with the reference. Report how the result changes with another choice. Ignoring sensitivity. A small post effect next to a clear pre-trend can come from the trend. Report the bounds.
Randomised Experiments: Balance, Adjustment and Randomisation Inference
Randomised Experiments: Balance, Adjustment and Randomisation Inference: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code and more.
Randomised Experiments: Balance, Adjustment and Randomisation Inference

What is the average effect of the treatment, and how sure are we? With random assignment, the difference in mean outcomes between treated and control units is unbiased for the average treatment effect, and its Neyman variance estimate is \(s_1^2/n_1 + s_0^2/n_0\) . Pre-treatment covariates are not needed for identification, but adjusting for them can lower the variance. The estimator of Lin (2013) regresses the outcome on treatment, the demeaned covariates and their interactions with treatment, which is never asymptotically less precise than the difference in means and does not require the covariate effects to be the same in both arms. With a small sample, randomisation inference replaces the asymptotic p-value: under the sharp null that treatment has no effect on any unit, every re-assignment of the same number of treated units was equally likely, so the permutation distribution of any test statistic is exact.
Randomised Experiments: Balance, Adjustment and Randomisation Inference

Three checks before you report an experiment Did the randomisation work? Compare the covariates between arms and test them jointly. Some imbalance is expected by chance (one covariate in twenty at 5%), but a joint rejection suggests a problem with the assignment or the data. Is the standard error right for the design? Complete randomisation gives the Neyman variance. Clustered or stratified assignment needs a variance that respects it. Could the study have found an effect? Report the minimum detectable effect. A null result from an underpowered study is not evidence of no effect. How to write it: the model We analyse the National Supported Work demonstration, in which 185 of 445 disadvantaged workers were randomly assigned to a job-training programme and the rest served as controls. The outcome is earnings in 1978, in thousands of dollars. We report the difference in means with the Neyman standard error, the regression-adjusted and Lin (2013) estimates controlling for age, education, race, marital status, degree status and earnings in 1974 and 1975, and an exact randomisation test of the sharp null of no effect with 2,000 permutations. We check the balance of pre-treatment covariates and report the minimum detectable effect.
Randomised Experiments: Balance, Adjustment and Randomisation Inference
Load the data and check balance

How to read it The sample has 445 workers, 185 assigned to training and 260 to the control group, and mean earnings in 1978 are $5,300, with 31% of workers earning nothing. Most covariates are balanced: the standardised differences are at most 0.14 except for Hispanic (-0.175) and the absence of a high-school degree (-0.304, 71% of the treated against 84% of the controls, p = 0.002). The joint F test of the eight covariates predicting treatment gives F = 2.14 and p = 0.031, which rejects balance at 5%. One covariate with a p-value of 0.002 out of eight is more than chance would give, so the controls are somewhat more disadvantaged than the treated, which is a reason to report the covariate-adjusted estimate next to the unadjusted one.
Randomised Experiments: Balance, Adjustment and Randomisation Inference
The effect: difference in means, adjustment and Lin

How to read it The difference in means is 1.794 (standard error 0.671): trainees earn $1,794 more in 1978, t = 2.67 and p = 0.0075. Adjusting for covariates gives 1.676 (0.677) and the Lin estimator 1.622 (0.695), a reduction of 0.12 to 0.17, which is in the direction expected if the treated group started out slightly better off, and well within one standard error. The standard errors do not fall, because the covariates predict 1978 earnings poorly in this sample, so adjustment here is a robustness check and not a gain in precision. The randomisation test of the sharp null for the Lin statistic gives p = 0.0095. The effect is about 36% of the mean earnings of the control group (4.55).
Randomised Experiments: Balance, Adjustment and Randomisation Inference

How to read it The minimum detectable effect at 80% power and a 5% test is 1.77, almost exactly the estimated effect, and 39% of the control mean. The study was therefore only just large enough to detect an effect of this size, and smaller effects would have gone unnoticed. The exact randomisation test of the difference in means gives p = 0.004, against 0.0075 from the normal approximation, so the two agree on rejection. Earnings are skewed and a third of the workers earn nothing, which is why a test that does not rely on normality is a useful check.
Randomised Experiments: Balance, Adjustment and Randomisation Inference

How to read it The effect is 1.15 (standard error 0.75) for workers without a high-school degree and 3.19 (1.45) for those with one, and 2.03 (0.75) for black workers against 0.80 (1.38) for others. The effect is 1.69 for workers with earnings in 1975 and 1.71 for those without. None of these differences is established: degree against no degree is 2.04 with standard error 1.63 (p = 0.21) and black against non-black is 1.23 with standard error 1.57 (p = 0.44). With seven subgroup tests, 0.35 nominal rejections at 5% would occur by chance. Treat subgroup results as descriptive, and specify them in advance if you want to report them as findings.
Randomised Experiments: Balance, Adjustment and Randomisation Inference

How to write it: results Workers randomly assigned to the training programme earned $1,794 more in 1978 than the controls (Neyman standard error 0.671, p = 0.0075). Controlling for pre-treatment covariates with the interacted estimator of Lin (2013) gives $1,622 (standard error 0.695), and the exact randomisation test of the sharp null of no effect, based on 2,000 permutations, gives p = 0.0095. The treatment and control groups differ in the share without a high-school degree (71% against 84%) and the joint balance test rejects at 5% (F = 2.14, p = 0.031), so we report the adjusted estimate, which is smaller than the unadjusted one. The minimum detectable effect is $1,773 (39% of the control mean), so the study could detect an effect of this size but not a much smaller one. Differences in effect across subgroups are not statistically significant (for example degree against no degree, p = 0.21).

Generalized Synthetic Control: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
The question and why DiD fails here

The question: did stand-your-ground laws change the murder rate? The DiD guides used homicides from vital statistics; this guide uses the murder rate from police reports (FBI Uniform Crime Reports), in logs, for the same 50 states and the same laws. A second measure of the same outcome is a standard robustness check, and here it raises a problem the first measure did not. The difference-in-differences model assumes that, without treatment, every state's outcome would have moved by the same amount each year. Generalized synthetic control relaxes that: The \(f_t\) are a small number of unobserved common factors (for example, national trends in public-sector hiring or crime policy), and the loadings \(\lambda_i\) let each state respond to them differently. DiD is the special case with no factors. If treated states load more heavily on a rising factor, their outcome rises faster even without treatment, and DiD would wrongly attribute that to the law.
The question and why DiD fails here

How the method works Estimate the factors from the never-treated states, which are untouched by the policy. For each treated state, estimate its loadings from its pre-treatment years only. Predict its untreated outcome after adoption, \(\hat Y_{it}(0)\) , and take the gap \(Y_{it} - \hat Y_{it}(0)\) as the effect. Choose the number of factors by cross-validation: hold out each pre-treatment year in turn and see which number predicts it best. How to write it: design Because event-study estimates indicate that adopting and non-adopting states were on different trends before the laws took effect, we estimate the effect with the generalized synthetic control method of Xu (2017). It models untreated outcomes with state and year effects and a small number of latent factors with state-specific loadings, estimated from never-treated states, and imputes the counterfactual for each adopting state from its pre-adoption path. The number of factors is selected by cross-validation.
Load the data and test the pre-trends

How to read it The leads are not flat: the joint test rejects that they are zero at the 5% level. Before adopting a law, murder rates in the adopting states were already moving differently from those in the other states. Any DiD estimate here mixes that pre-existing difference in trends with the effect of the law, which is why the model selection tool sends this dataset to generalized synthetic control.

How to read it With zero factors the model is two-way fixed effects. Adding factors lets states follow different trends; too many factors overfit the short pre-treatment period. Cross-validation picks the number that best predicts held-out pre-treatment years of the treated states. A non-zero choice confirms that unit-specific trends matter, as the event study suggested.

How to read it Before adoption , the gaps between each treated state and its counterfactual should be close to zero: they measure how well the model fits. In the five years before adoption they stay within about ±0.07, against DiD leads of up to −0.13 in the first step: the factor has absorbed most of the difference in trends. The gaps 8 to 10 years before adoption rest on the one or two states that adopted last and are noisy; they inflate the overall pre-treatment RMSE. After adoption , the gaps are the estimated effects. The average effect on the murder rate is small and not significant. Standard errors come from bootstrapping states (both treated and control), re-estimating everything each time.

How to read it Two-way fixed effects suggests murder rose by about 9% (p ≈ 0.10). GSC and the Callaway–Sant'Anna estimator, which handle the pre-trend in different ways, both put the effect near 2% and far from significance. The TWFE estimate is the outlier: it averages over all pre-adoption years and so attributes the adopting states' different pre-trend to the law. Because the pre-trend test rejected parallel trends, the GSC estimate, whose counterfactual fits the pre-treatment years, is the one to lead with. Report all three: the comparison shows how much the conclusion depends on the treatment of trends.

How to write it: results Event-study estimates reveal differential pre-trends in murder rates between adopting and non-adopting states (joint test of pre-adoption coefficients, p = 0.02), so difference-in-differences estimates are not credible for this outcome. Using the generalized synthetic control method with one latent factor selected by cross-validation, we find no significant effect of Castle Doctrine laws on the murder rate. The pre-adoption gaps between adopting states and their estimated counterfactuals are small, indicating a good fit. Common mistakes Using GSC with very few pre-treatment periods. The loadings of each treated unit are estimated from its pre-treatment years; with fewer than about five, the counterfactual is unreliable. Using GSC with very few control units. The factors are estimated from them.

Choosing the number of factors by looking at the post-treatment results. Fix it by cross-validation on pre-treatment data only. Forgetting to show the pre-treatment fit. It is the main evidence that the counterfactual is credible. In Stata or R, use gsynth (Xu) or fect (Liu, Wang and Xu) for the full method with covariates and parametric bootstrap.

Interrupted Time Series: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

On 31 January 1983 wearing a front seatbelt became compulsory in Great Britain. How many deaths and serious injuries of car drivers did the law prevent? The law applied to the whole country at once, so there is no untreated region to compare with. This is the classic dataset of Harvey and Durbin (1986). The interrupted time series (ITS) design uses the pre-law path of the series as the counterfactual, through a segmented regression: Term Meaning \(\beta_1\) Pre-law trend per month \(D_t\) 1 from February 1983 onwards \(\delta\) Level change : the immediate effect of the law \(\gamma\) Slope change : how the trend changed after the law \(\mu_m\) Month effects: road deaths are seasonal

The identifying assumption Without the law, the series would have continued along its pre-law trend and seasonal pattern. Nothing else that affects road deaths may change at the same time. This is a strong assumption, and the credibility of an ITS study rests on arguing it: listing other events (fuel prices, speed limits, recessions) and showing they did not coincide with the intervention. How to write it: design Because the seatbelt law applied nationwide from February 1983, no contemporaneous control group exists. We estimate its effect with an interrupted time series design: a segmented regression of monthly driver casualties on a linear trend, month effects, and a level and a slope change at the date the law took effect, with Newey–West standard errors to allow for serial correlation.
Load the data and look at the series

How to read it The series has a strong seasonal pattern (more casualties in winter), a gently falling trend, and a visible drop in early 1983. There is also a fall around 1974, the time of the first oil crisis, when fuel prices jumped and a national speed limit was introduced. Keep it in mind: it is exactly the kind of event that can masquerade as, or contaminate, a policy effect.

How to read it Level change ( post ). In the month the law took effect, driver casualties fell by about 300, roughly 17% of the pre-law monthly average. The effect is large and highly significant. Slope change ( t_post ). Positive: after the immediate drop, the series fell less steeply than before. With only 23 post-law months, this slope is estimated imprecisely, and it should not be extrapolated far. Standard errors are Newey–West with a few lags, which keeps inference valid when monthly errors are serially correlated.

How to read it The dashed line extends the pre-law trend and seasonal pattern into the post-law period: what the model says would have happened without the law. The observed series lies well below it after February 1983. Summed over the post-law months, this is several thousand fewer drivers killed or seriously injured, the number a policy reader wants.

How to read it The Durbin–Watson statistic below 2 and the Ljung–Box tests show positive serial correlation in the residuals: a bad month tends to be followed by another. The Newey–West errors already allow for this. Modelling the autocorrelation directly, with AR(1) errors, is the standard robustness check. The level change remains large and significant.

How to read it A placebo date is a date when nothing happened. Estimated on pre-law data only, it should show no effect. May 1978 : no significant effect, as it should be. January 1976 : a large negative “effect” of about −150, significant at the 10% level. This is not a failure of the method: it picks up the 1974–75 oil-crisis fall in the data, which a single linear trend cannot capture. It shows that this series has other breaks , and that the trend before 1983 is not as simple as the model assumes. Report both placebos. The case for the seatbelt effect rests on the size and sharpness of the 1983 drop, which no other event matches, and Harvey and Durbin strengthened it by modelling fuel prices and traffic volume and by comparing with rear-seat passengers, who were not covered by the law. When a comparison series exists, use it.

How to write it: results The segmented regression indicates an immediate reduction of about 300 drivers killed or seriously injured per month when the seatbelt law took effect, around 17 percent of the pre-law average (Newey–West standard errors). The estimate is robust to modelling the residual autocorrelation with AR(1) errors. A placebo intervention in 1978 shows no effect; a placebo in 1976 shows a sizeable decline, significant at the 10 percent level, reflecting the fall associated with the 1974 oil crisis, which underlines that the attribution of the 1983 drop to the law rests on the absence of other changes at that date. Common mistakes Ignoring seasonality: a policy that starts in a low season looks effective.

Using conventional standard errors with autocorrelated monthly data. Extrapolating the pre-trend far beyond the intervention, or over-interpreting a slope change estimated from few post-periods. Not checking for other events at the same date. ITS has no comparison group to absorb them. When a comparison series exists (an unaffected group, region or outcome), use it: that turns the ITS into a comparative ITS or a DiD.
