The question and why OLS fails

What is the return to a year of schooling? A regression of log wages on years of education gives an answer, but not a causal one: people who study longer may also be more able or more motivated, and those traits raise wages on their own. Ability is not in the data, so OLS is biased (most likely upwards). Card (1995) proposed an instrument: whether a man grew up near a four-year college . Living near a college lowers the cost of attending, so it raises schooling; the argument is that, given region and urban residence, it affects wages only through schooling. The question and why OLS fails

educ endogenous treatment Years of schooling nearc4 instrument 1 if a four-year college was in the county at age 14 black , smsa , south , married , exper controls Race, urban residence, region, marital status, experience The three conditions Relevance: the instrument moves schooling. Testable: the first stage. Exclusion: proximity affects wages only through schooling. Not testable. Threat: families who live near colleges may differ in ways that also raise wages; that is why urban and regional controls matter. Independence: proximity is as good as random given the controls. Not testable. It must be argued. A paper's IV section stands or falls on the argument for exclusion and independence, not on the regression output.
The question and why OLS fails

How to write it: identification Because schooling is likely correlated with unobserved ability, we instrument years of education with an indicator for growing up near a four-year college, following Card (1995). Proximity lowers the cost of college attendance and so raises schooling; conditional on race, region, urban residence, marital status and experience, we assume it affects wages only through its effect on schooling.
Load the data and estimate OLS

How to read it OLS says each additional year of schooling is associated with wages about 7% higher, very precisely estimated. Precision is not the problem; bias is. The IV estimate will tell us how much of this association is causal.
The first stage: is the instrument relevant?

How to read it Men who grew up near a four-year college completed about a third of a year more schooling, holding the controls fixed. The robust F statistic is about 16.5, above the Staiger–Stock rule of thumb of 10, so the instrument is not weak in the traditional sense. It is not strong either: it explains only half a percent of the variation in schooling left after the controls. Lee, McCrary, Moreira and Porter (2022) show that conventional 2SLS t-tests have correct size only with F above about 105, which is why the Anderson–Rubin test below matters.

How to read it Reduced form. Men who grew up near a college earn about 4% more. Show this regression: it is the causal effect of the instrument itself, and if it is zero there is nothing to scale up. 2SLS. With one instrument, the 2SLS estimate is exactly the reduced form divided by the first stage: about 0.12, a return of 12% per year of schooling, larger than OLS. Precision. The 2SLS standard error is more than ten times the OLS one. The confidence interval is wide. Why would the IV estimate exceed OLS when ability bias pushes OLS up? Because the IV estimate is a local average treatment effect (LATE): the return for men whose schooling was changed by college proximity, typically from families for whom cost was a real barrier. Their return to schooling may be higher than average. Measurement error in schooling, which biases OLS towards zero, is another explanation.

How to read it The Anderson–Rubin test has the correct size however weak the instrument . It tests each candidate value of the return \(b_0\) by asking whether the instrument still predicts \(\ln w - b_0 \cdot educ\) ; the confidence set collects the values that are not rejected. Here it rejects a zero return, and the 95% set runs from about 0.03 to 0.25: wider than the conventional 2SLS interval, but excluding zero. This is the interval to report when the first stage is not overwhelmingly strong.

How to read it The test adds the first-stage residual to the OLS regression: if schooling were exogenous, the residual would add nothing. It does not reject. That does not prove schooling is exogenous: with an imprecise 2SLS estimate the test has little power, and the gap between 0.07 and 0.12 is economically large. With one instrument, the exclusion restriction cannot be tested at all (no overidentification test); Card's full dataset adds proximity to a two-year college, which allows a Hansen J test.

How to write it: results OLS estimates imply a return to schooling of about 7 percent per year. Instrumenting schooling with proximity to a four-year college, the 2SLS estimate is about 12 percent (robust standard error 0.05). The first stage is significant, with a robust F statistic of 16.5; because conventional 2SLS inference can be unreliable at this instrument strength, we also report the Anderson–Rubin 95 percent confidence set, which excludes zero. The 2SLS estimate is a local average treatment effect for men whose schooling was affected by college proximity, and its exceeding OLS is consistent with higher returns for individuals facing cost barriers to college, or with measurement error in schooling.

Common mistakes Treating the first-stage F above 10 as the end of the weak-instrument question. Report Anderson–Rubin intervals. Not reporting the first stage and the reduced form. Arguing exclusion with a statistical test. With one instrument there is none; even with several, the Hansen test only checks that instruments agree. Interpreting 2SLS as an average effect for everyone. It is local to the compliers. Computing the second stage by hand with OLS on fitted values: the standard errors are wrong. Use an IV routine.
Lee Bounds for Sample Selection and Attrition
Lee Bounds for Sample Selection and Attrition: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
Lee Bounds for Sample Selection and Attrition

What is the effect of treatment on an outcome that is seen only for some units? Let \(S\) indicate that the outcome is observed. If treatment raises \(P(S=1)\) , the treated and control units who are observed are not comparable, so the plain difference is biased even under random assignment. Lee's argument: if treatment can only move units into selection, never out ( monotonicity ), the observed treated group is a mix of units that would be selected anyway and units pulled in by treatment. The share of the second kind is Trimming the top \(p\) of the treated outcomes gives the lowest possible treated mean for the always-selected, and trimming the bottom \(p\) gives the highest. Subtracting the control mean gives a lower and an upper bound on the effect for the always-selected. The bounds are wide when \(p\) is large.
Lee Bounds for Sample Selection and Attrition

Three checks before you report Lee bounds Is treatment randomised? The method needs random assignment, or ignorability, to compare the arms at all. Is monotonicity plausible? Ask whether treatment could plausibly push some units out of selection while pulling others in. If so, the bounds are not valid. Is the effect for the always-selected the quantity you need? It is not the effect for everyone, and the always-selected cannot be identified unit by unit. How to write it: the model We ask whether job training raised the earnings of workers in the National Supported Work demonstration. Earnings are observed as a wage-like outcome only for workers with a job in 1978, and assignment to training raised employment, so the observed earnings of the two arms are not comparable. We estimate Lee (2009) trimming bounds for the effect on earnings of workers who would have a job whether or not they were trained, assuming that training can only raise the chance of employment. Confidence intervals take the 2.5th percentile of the lower bound and the 97.5th percentile of the upper bound over 500 bootstrap resamples (Imbens and Manski 2004).
Lee Bounds for Sample Selection and Attrition
Load the data and look at selection

How to read it Of 445 workers, 185 were assigned to training. In 1978, 75.7% of the trained had a job against 64.6% of the controls, so training raised the chance of observing earnings by 11 percentage points, and earnings among the employed are 8.39 for the trained against 7.05 for the controls (thousand dollars). The difference of 1.34 is not the effect of training on earnings: the trained group includes 14.6% of workers who would not have had a job without training, whose earnings may be lower or higher than those of the rest.
Lee Bounds for Sample Selection and Attrition

How to read it The share to trim is 14.6% of the treated workers with a job. After trimming the top 14.6% the lower bound on the effect is -1.14, and after trimming the bottom 14.6% the upper bound is 2.62, so the effect of training on the earnings of workers who would be employed either way lies between -1.14 and 2.62 thousand dollars. With sampling error the interval is -2.56 to 4.47. The naive difference of 1.34 sits inside the bounds, but so does zero: selection alone prevents us from saying that training raised the earnings of the employed. The result that training raised total earnings (a gain of 1.79 per worker in this sample) therefore comes from getting people into jobs and not from higher pay once employed, which the data cannot establish.
Lee Bounds for Sample Selection and Attrition
Compare with bounds that assume nothing

How to read it The worst-case bounds fill the missing outcomes with the lowest and highest possible values and make no assumption about who is selected. With the observed range of earnings (0.04 to 60.31) they run from -19.5 to 16.4, which says nothing; restricting earnings to the range 0 to 25 narrows them to -7.1 to 7.9, and the tighter the assumed range the more informative they become. The Lee bounds, from -1.14 to 2.62, are far narrower because the monotonicity assumption does the work that the range assumption does here. The price is that the bounds apply only to the always-selected.
Lee Bounds for Sample Selection and Attrition

How to read it Earnings in 1975 were fixed before assignment, so the true effect of training on them is zero. Treating positive earnings in 1975 as the selection indicator, 40.0% of the treated and 31.5% of the controls are selected, a gap of 8.5 points that arose by chance. The Lee bounds are -1.77 to 0.70 and contain zero, as they should, and the interval of -3.18 to 2.65 is wide because 21% of the treated are trimmed. A placebo that excludes zero would show that the design, not the programme, is producing the result.
Lee Bounds for Sample Selection and Attrition

How to write it: results Assignment to training raised employment in 1978 by 11 percentage points (75.7% against 64.6%), so earnings among the employed cannot be compared directly. Lee bounds for the earnings effect on workers who would be employed with or without training are -1.14 to 2.62 thousand dollars, with a 95% bootstrap interval of -2.56 to 4.47, trimming 14.6% of the treated workers. The bounds include zero and cannot rule out either a small loss or a gain of several thousand dollars. They are far narrower than worst-case bounds (-7.1 to 7.9 for earnings between 0 and 25), but they rely on monotonicity, that training does not lead any worker to give up a job they would otherwise have had. A placebo on earnings in 1975 gives bounds of -1.77 to 0.70, which contain the true effect of zero. We conclude that the gain in total earnings comes mainly from higher employment, and that the data do not identify an effect on pay for those already employed.

Matching, inverse-probability weighting and doubly robust estimation

Do men with a college degree earn more than otherwise similar men without one? The data come from Card's (1995) wage sample. The outcome is the log wage ( lwage ) and the treatment is \(D_i=1\) if the man has 16 or more years of schooling. Education is chosen, not assigned, so a raw comparison mixes the effect of college with who goes to college. Matching, weighting and doubly robust methods all rest on two assumptions: Unconfoundedness : \((Y_i(0),Y_i(1))\perp D_i\mid X_i\) . Nothing unobserved drives both selection and wages once \(X_i\) is held fixed. This cannot be tested. Overlap : \(0<e(X_i)<1\) , where \(e(x)=\Pr(D_i=1\mid X_i=x)\) is the propensity score. Treated men must have untreated counterparts and the reverse. This can be checked.
Matching, inverse-probability weighting and doubly robust estimation

Symbol Variable Definition \(Y_i\) lwage log wage \(D_i\) college 1 if educ ≥ 16 \(X_i\) black , smsa , south , married , exper race, city residence, region, marital status, experience (and its square) We leave out nearc4 (living near a four-year college), which is the instrument of the IV guide and is not a confounder to adjust for here. Before you estimate anything Write down why the covariates should be enough: which variables drive the choice of college and also wages, and which of them you do not observe (ability, family background). Never condition on variables affected by the treatment, such as occupation. Decide whether you want the effect on the treated (ATT) or on the whole population (ATE) before choosing the estimator.
Matching, inverse-probability weighting and doubly robust estimation

How to write it: design We estimate the effect of a college degree on log wages under selection on observables, conditioning on race, region, city residence, marital status and a quadratic in experience. We estimate the propensity score with a logit, check overlap and balance, and compare nearest-neighbour matching, inverse-probability weighting, regression adjustment and augmented inverse-probability weighting. Standard errors are bootstrapped with the propensity score re-estimated in every draw. We assess an omitted confounder with the robustness value of Cinelli and Hazlett (2020).
Matching, inverse-probability weighting and doubly robust estimation
Data, raw difference and the propensity score

How to read it 27% of the men have a college degree. The average propensity score is 0.50 for graduates and 0.19 for non-graduates, so the covariates predict selection strongly. The logit shows that Black men, men in the South and men with more experience are less likely to hold a degree. Experience is the strongest predictor because it is mechanically linked to schooling: men who study longer enter the labour market later. The scores run from 0.005 to 0.958.
Matching, inverse-probability weighting and doubly robust estimation

How to read it Before adjustment the groups are far apart (standardised difference −1.28 for experience, −0.47 for race). After ATT weighting every covariate is within 0.1 except experience (−0.19), so the balance is good but not perfect and you should say so. Overlap is the weak point: 16% of non-graduates have a score below the lowest graduate score, 31 graduates have scores above 0.9 and no non-graduate does. ATT weights are moderate (maximum 4.8), but the effective number of controls falls from 2,187 to 647.
Matching, inverse-probability weighting and doubly robust estimation

How to read it The raw gap is 0.23 log points. Adjusting raises the estimate, because graduates are younger and less experienced. For the ATT, IPW gives 0.22, regression adjustment 0.25, AIPW 0.25 and one-nearest-neighbour matching 0.30 (a much wider interval, ±0.11, because it uses few controls). For the ATE the estimates are 0.34 (IPW), 0.38 (regression adjustment) and 0.38 (AIPW). The doubly robust and regression estimates agree, which is reassuring, and the ATE exceeds the ATT because graduates are not a random sample: the model implies a larger gain for those who are less likely to attend. The ATT estimates are therefore not comparable with the ATE.
Matching, inverse-probability weighting and doubly robust estimation
Robustness: trimming, specification and an omitted confounder

How to read it Trimming matters for the ATE: it falls from 0.38 (AIPW, no trimming) to 0.28 once scores outside [0.1, 0.9] are dropped, which shows that the ATE leans on the extreme-score men for whom overlap is poor. The matching ATT is stable at 0.30–0.32. Controlling only for race, city and region gives an ATE of 0.18, about half, so the result depends on adjusting for experience, as expected. The robustness value is 24.9%: an omitted confounder would have to explain about a quarter of the residual variance of both college attendance and wages to wipe out the regression estimate, and none of the observed covariates explains more than 5.1% of wage variance. That is a strong requirement, but ability and family background are exactly the type of omitted variable that could matter, so it is a bound, not proof.
Matching, inverse-probability weighting and doubly robust estimation
Robustness: trimming, specification and an omitted confounder

How to write it: results Conditioning on race, region, city residence, marital status and experience, a college degree is associated with about 0.38 log points higher wages for the population (AIPW ATE; 95% CI 0.31 to 0.44) and 0.25 for graduates (ATT; 0.21 to 0.30), against a raw gap of 0.23. The ATT estimates range from 0.22 to 0.30 across IPW, regression adjustment, AIPW and matching, and the ATE falls to 0.28 when scores outside [0.1, 0.9] are trimmed, because overlap is weak at the extremes. Weighting balances all covariates within 0.1 standard deviations except experience (0.19). An omitted confounder would have to explain about 25% of the residual variance of both schooling and wages to explain away the estimate. These estimates rest on unconfoundedness and should be read as conditional associations unless that assumption is credible.

What to report in the paper

Mixing estimands. ATE and ATT differ when effects vary. Do not compare them as if they were one number. Treating matching as magic. It is a way to adjust for observed covariates, not a way to remove selection on unobservables. Use an IV or a design if unconfoundedness is not plausible.
Causal Mediation Analysis: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

How much of the effect runs through the mediator? With treatment \(T\) , mediator \(M\) , outcome \(Y\) and covariates \(X\) , estimate The average causal mediation effect is \(a\,b\) , the average direct effect is \(c'\) , and they add up to the total effect. If the effect of the mediator may depend on treatment, an interaction \(\kappa\,TM\) is added to the outcome model and the effects are reported for each treatment arm. The estimates are causal under sequential ignorability : the treatment is ignorable given \(X\) , and the mediator is ignorable given \(T\) and \(X\) . Randomising \(T\) secures the first condition but not the second, because people choose or are selected into the mediator. The sensitivity analysis asks how large the correlation \(\rho\) between \(\varepsilon_1\) and \(\varepsilon_2\) , a proxy for an omitted common cause, would have to be for the ACME to be zero.

Three checks before you report a mediation analysis Is the treatment randomised or ignorable? If not, neither the total effect nor the split is causal. Could something unmeasured drive both the mediator and the outcome? Report the sensitivity analysis, and say in words what such a variable might be. Is the mediator measured before the outcome? A mediator measured at the same time as the outcome, or a component of it, makes the indirect effect partly mechanical. How to write it: the model We ask how much of the earnings effect of the National Supported Work job-training programme works through employment. The treatment is random assignment to training, the mediator is an indicator for any employment in 1978, and the outcome is earnings in 1978, in thousands of dollars. Mediator and outcome models are linear and include age, education, race, marital status, degree status and earnings in 1974 and 1975. We report the average causal mediation effect, the average direct effect and the total effect with percentile confidence intervals from 500 bootstrap resamples, and a sensitivity analysis for violations of sequential ignorability (Imai, Keele and Yamamoto 2010).
Load the data and look at the mediator

How to read it In 1978, 75.7% of the workers assigned to training had a job, against 64.6% of the controls, an increase of 11 percentage points, and their mean earnings were 6.35 against 4.55 (thousand dollars). Workers without a job in 1978 have earnings of exactly zero, and those with a job earn 7.66 on average. Employment is therefore the extensive margin of earnings, not an independent variable measured earlier, so the mediated effect in this example is partly an accounting split of the earnings gain into getting a job and earning more once employed. The example illustrates the method, and the warning that a mediator measured at the same time as the outcome gives a partly mechanical result.

How to read it The total effect of 1.676 splits into a mediated part of 0.818 (95% bootstrap interval 0.23 to 1.47, p = 0.008) and a direct part of 0.858 (interval -0.20 to 2.01, p = 0.13), so about half of the effect runs through employment (proportion mediated 0.49), although the interval for the proportion is wide (0.15 to 1.33). The path coefficients explain the split: training raises the probability of working by 0.110, and a worker with a job earns 7.42 more (thousand dollars) than one without, holding treatment fixed, so the product is 0.82. Only the mediated part is distinguishable from zero. The direct part, the additional earnings among those employed, is positive but too imprecise to separate from zero.
Sensitivity to an unmeasured confounder of mediator and outcome

How to read it At rho = 0 the ACME is 0.818, and it falls to zero at rho = 0.519: if an unmeasured factor made the errors of the employment and earnings equations correlated at about 0.52, there would be no mediated effect. A positive correlation is what omitted motivation or ability would produce, since it raises both the chance of working and earnings, so the estimate at rho = 0 is more likely to be too large than too small, and negative values of rho (where the ACME is larger) are harder to motivate. A correlation of 0.5 is large, but it is the kind of value that a strong unobserved trait could produce, so the conclusion that employment mediates part of the effect should be stated with the sensitivity threshold alongside it.
Does the effect of the mediator depend on treatment?

How to read it With the interaction, the effect of having a job on earnings is 6.99 for the control group and 8.18 for the treated (interaction 1.19). The ACME is 0.771 in the control state and 0.902 in the treated state, and the ADE is 0.781 and 0.913. Averaged over the two, they are 0.836 and 0.847, within 0.03 of the model without an interaction, so the interaction does not change the split. The coefficient on treatment in the interaction model (0.010) is the effect of training for a worker with no job, whose earnings are zero by construction, and it should not be read as the direct effect.

How to read it The split is stable across covariate sets: the ACME is between 0.81 and 0.83, the ADE between 0.84 and 0.96, the total effect between 1.67 and 1.79, the proportion mediated between 0.46 and 0.50, and the sensitivity threshold between 0.52 and 0.53. Treatment is randomised, so the covariates matter little for the total effect, and in this sample they predict the mediator and outcome weakly, which is why the estimates hardly move. Robustness to covariates is not robustness to an unmeasured confounder of the mediator and the outcome, which only the sensitivity analysis addresses.

How to write it: results Random assignment to training raises earnings in 1978 by 1.68 thousand dollars (bootstrap 95% interval 0.48 to 3.05). We estimate that 0.82 (0.23 to 1.47) of this runs through employment and 0.86 (-0.20 to 2.01) is a direct effect, so about half of the effect (0.49, interval 0.15 to 1.33) is mediated. The result is insensitive to the covariate set and to allowing the earnings effect of employment to differ by treatment (ACME 0.84, ADE 0.85). It relies on the assumption that no unmeasured factor affects both employment and earnings given the covariates; the mediated effect would be zero if the errors of the employment and earnings equations were correlated at 0.52. Employment and earnings are measured in the same year and workers without a job have zero earnings, so the mediated effect partly reflects how earnings are defined, and we interpret the split as the contribution of the extensive margin.

Distributional Effects: Quantile Treatment Effects and KS Tests
Distributional Effects: Quantile Treatment Effects and KS Tests: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code and more.
Distributional Effects: Quantile Treatment Effects and KS Tests

Where in the distribution does the treatment act? For a binary treatment \(T\) the quantile treatment effect at quantile \(\tau\) is the difference between the \(\tau\) -th quantiles of the outcome with and without treatment. With random assignment the two quantiles are estimated from the two arms and need no covariates. A QTE of 3 at the 75th percentile means that the person at the 75th percentile of the treated outcomes earns 3 more than the person at the 75th percentile of the control outcomes. It is not the effect on the person who is at the 75th percentile without treatment unless treatment leaves everybody's rank unchanged (rank invariance). The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic \(\sup_y |F_1(y) - F_0(y)|\) tests whether the two distributions are equal, and its one-sided versions test dominance.
Distributional Effects: Quantile Treatment Effects and KS Tests

Three checks before you report quantile effects Is treatment randomised or ignorable? Without it the difference in quantiles is not causal. Does a rank-preserving reading make sense? Say whether you mean a shift of the distribution or an effect on individuals at a rank. Are many quantiles tested? Pointwise intervals do not control the error across the grid, so do not pick the quantile with the largest effect after looking. How to write it: the model We ask where in the earnings distribution job training acts. The treatment is random assignment to the National Supported Work programme and the outcome is earnings in 1978, in thousands of dollars. We estimate quantile treatment effects at the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles as differences between the quantiles of the treated and control groups, with percentile confidence intervals from 500 bootstrap resamples. We compare them with conditional quantile regressions on age, education, race, marital status, degree status and earnings in 1974 and 1975, and test equality and first-order dominance of the two distributions with Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics and permutation p-values.
Distributional Effects: Quantile Treatment Effects and KS Tests
Load the data and look at the outcome

How to read it Mean earnings are 6.35 for the trained and 4.55 for the controls, an average gain of 1.79 thousand dollars. A large part of each group has no earnings at all: 35.4% of the controls and 24.3% of the trained. The outcome is therefore a mass at zero followed by a long right tail, and the mean is driven by the tail. This is the kind of distribution where an average effect says little about who gains, and the lower quantiles cannot move if the programme does not get people out of zero earnings.
Distributional Effects: Quantile Treatment Effects and KS Tests

How to read it The effect is zero at the 10th percentile, where both groups have zero earnings. At the 25th percentile it is 0.49 (0.00 against 0.49, interval 0.00 to 1.08): the share of zeros is 35% among the controls and 24% among the trained, so the 25th percentile of the controls is still zero while that of the trained is positive. At the median the effect is 1.09 (3.14 against 4.23, interval -0.48 to 2.99), at the 75th percentile 2.35 (7.29 against 9.64, interval 0.62 to 3.85) and at the 90th percentile 3.20 (11.36 against 14.55, interval 0.07 to 6.54). The gains grow along the distribution and their intervals exclude zero only at the 75th and 90th percentiles, so the programme moves the upper part of the earnings distribution most. The average of 1.79 is the weighted total of these.
Distributional Effects: Quantile Treatment Effects and KS Tests

How to read it With the covariates the coefficient on treatment is 0.00 at the 10th and 25th percentiles, 1.07 at the median (p = 0.083), 2.65 at the 75th percentile (p = 0.0007) and 2.13 at the 90th (p = 0.060). The pattern matches the unconditional effects and the 75th percentile is now sharply estimated, because the covariates, mainly earnings in 1974 and 1975, explain much of the spread. A conditional quantile effect is the effect at a quantile of the outcome among workers with the same covariates, so it equals the unconditional QTE only if the covariates affect all quantiles alike. Here the two agree closely, which is what randomisation implies on average.
Distributional Effects: Quantile Treatment Effects and KS Tests

How to read it The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is 0.132, with a permutation p-value of 0.039, so the earnings distributions of the two groups differ at the 5% level. The one-sided test of dominance rejects that the treated outcome is not larger (p = 0.012), while the test in the other direction cannot be rejected (statistic 0.000, p = 1.0). The treated distribution lies to the right of the control distribution at every earnings level: there is no earnings level at which the trained workers are more likely than the controls to be below it. This is a stronger statement than a positive average, because it implies that every utility function that increases in earnings gives a higher value for training.
Distributional Effects: Quantile Treatment Effects and KS Tests
Robustness to the quantile grid and the bootstrap

How to read it The point estimates do not depend on the grid or the seed, because they are differences of sample quantiles, so the range across runs is zero; only the bootstrap intervals move with the seed. The effect is zero up to the 20th percentile, 0.94 at the 30th, about 1.1 to 1.5 through the middle of the distribution and rising in the upper tail and reaching 3.20 at the 90th and 3.93 at the 95th percentile. A sensible summary is the shape (zero in the bottom fifth, increasing above) and not any single quantile, and the intervals at individual quantiles should not be read as simultaneous.
Distributional Effects: Quantile Treatment Effects and KS Tests

How to write it: results Assignment to job training raises mean earnings by 1.79 thousand dollars, but the gain is not spread evenly. The quantile treatment effect is zero at the 10th percentile and 0.49 at the 25th, where a third of the controls have no earnings, 1.09 at the median (95% bootstrap interval -0.48 to 2.99), 2.35 at the 75th percentile (0.62 to 3.85) and 3.20 at the 90th (0.07 to 6.54). Conditional quantile regressions with covariates give the same pattern (2.65 at the 75th percentile, p = 0.0007). A Kolmogorov-Smirnov test rejects equality of the earnings distributions (p = 0.039) and the one-sided test rejects that the control distribution lies to the right (p = 0.012), so the treated distribution dominates the control distribution in the first-order sense. We read the effects as differences between distributions, not as effects on individuals at a given rank, which would need rank invariance, and we do not adjust the quantile intervals for the number of quantiles examined.

Regression Discontinuity: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. Treatment assigned by a cutoff.

Do voters choose policies, or only politicians? If candidates converge to the median voter, it should not matter much for how a district is represented which party narrowly wins. If they do not, a narrow Democratic win should produce a much more liberal representative than a narrow Republican win. Lee, Moretti and Butler (2004) answered this with a regression discontinuity. Whether a Democrat wins is determined by a cutoff: the Democratic vote share \(R_i\) crossing 0.5. Districts where the Democrat won 50.5% and those where she won 49.5% are, on average, alike in everything except who won. So the jump in the winner's liberal voting score at 0.5 measures the effect of electing a Democrat:

Symbol Variable in the file Definition \(Y\) score ADA score of the elected representative (0 = conservative, 100 = liberal) \(R\) demvoteshare Democratic share of the two-party vote \(D\) democrat 1 if the Democrat won (= 1 exactly when \(R \ge 0.5\) : a sharp design) — lagdemvoteshare Democratic vote share in the previous election (determined before the election) The identifying assumption The potential outcomes are continuous at the cutoff: nothing else jumps at 0.5. This fails if candidates can precisely control which side of 0.5 they land on (manipulation), which would make the winners of close races systematically different. It can be checked in two ways: the density of the running variable should not jump at the cutoff, and characteristics determined before the election should not jump either.

How to write it: design We exploit the discontinuity in party control created by the 50 percent threshold in two-party House elections. Comparing districts in which the Democratic candidate barely won with districts in which she barely lost identifies the effect of electing a Democrat on the representative's voting record, under the assumption that potential outcomes are continuous in the vote share at the threshold.
Load the data and plot the discontinuity

How to read it Always start with this plot: averages of the outcome in narrow bins of the running variable. The jump at 0.5 is unmistakable: districts that barely elect a Democrat are represented by someone with an ADA score roughly 45–50 points higher than districts that barely elect a Republican. On either side the relationship with the vote share is fairly flat. A plot like this, with the estimate overlaid, should be Figure 1 of an RD paper.
Local linear estimate with a data-driven bandwidth

How to read it The estimate fits a separate straight line on each side of the cutoff, using only elections within a vote-share distance \(h\) of 0.5 and giving more weight to those closest to it. The jump of about 47 points is the effect of a Democratic win on the winner's ADA score: party, not the median voter, determines roll-call voting. The WLS lines reproduce it exactly, which shows there is nothing hidden in the helper function. Local linear regression is the standard. Global high-order polynomials (fitting a fourth-degree curve to all the data) can produce misleading estimates and should not be used (Gelman and Imbens 2019).

How to read it The estimate barely moves between half and double the optimal bandwidth, and a local quadratic gives the same answer. That stability is what a referee wants to see. If the estimate changed sharply with the bandwidth, the effect would depend on functional-form assumptions away from the cutoff.

How to read it If candidates could precisely engineer narrow wins (through fraud or recounts, say), there would be too many elections just above 0.5 and too few just below. The histogram shows no such heaping, and the McCrary test finds no significant jump in the density. In settings like test scores or income eligibility, where people know the cutoff, this test often fails, and an RD with sorting is not credible.
Validity 2: covariate balance and placebo cutoffs

How to read it Covariate balance. The previous election's vote share was determined before this election, so it should not jump at 0.5. It shows a small jump of about 3 percentage points, statistically significant, and it does not disappear with half the bandwidth. This imbalance in close House elections is documented in the literature (Caughey and Sekhon 2011 discuss sorting in very close races). It must be reported. Re-running the main estimate with the covariate as a control leaves it essentially unchanged (47.2 against 46.7), so the imbalance does not drive the result. Placebo cutoffs. At vote shares of 0.4 and 0.6, where nothing changes, the estimated jumps are small compared with the 47-point effect at 0.5.

How to write it: results Figure 1 shows a sharp discontinuity in the ADA score of the elected representative at the 50 percent vote-share threshold. Local linear estimates with the Imbens–Kalyanaraman bandwidth imply that a Democratic victory raises the representative's ADA score by about 47 points (robust standard error 1.3). The estimate is stable across bandwidths from half to twice the optimal one and under a local quadratic specification. A McCrary test shows no discontinuity in the density of the vote share at the threshold. The previous election's Democratic vote share displays a small discontinuity of about 3 percentage points, consistent with incumbency effects; controlling for it does not change the results.

Common mistakes Using global high-order polynomials instead of local linear regression. Reporting one bandwidth only. Skipping the density test and covariate balance: they are the evidence that the design is valid. Forgetting that the RD effect is local : it applies to units at the cutoff (close elections), not to all districts. Treating a fuzzy design as sharp. If crossing the cutoff only raises the probability of treatment, divide the outcome jump by the treatment jump (a local IV estimate). For inference, the bias-corrected robust confidence intervals of Calonico, Cattaneo and Titiunik ( rdrobust ) are now standard.
Synthetic Control: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

In 1993 Texas began a massive expansion of its prison capacity, roughly doubling the number of beds within a few years. How much did the expansion increase the number of black men in Texas prisons? The example follows Cunningham's Causal Inference: The Mixtape . With one treated state, there is nothing to average over and no obvious control group. Which state, or average of states, shows what Texas would have looked like without the expansion? The synthetic control method (Abadie and Gardeazabal 2003; Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller 2010) answers this with weights: The weights are chosen so that the synthetic Texas matches the real Texas as closely as possible before 1993 . The effect in each later year is the gap between the two.

Why the weights are restricted Nonnegative weights that sum to one keep the synthetic unit inside the range of the actual donor states: an interpolation, not an extrapolation. The result is a transparent comparison: a reader can see which states make up synthetic Texas and judge whether they are plausible. How to write it: design We estimate the effect of the 1993 Texas prison expansion with the synthetic control method. The counterfactual for Texas is a weighted average of the other states, with nonnegative weights summing to one, chosen to reproduce the pre-1993 path of the outcome. Inference is based on placebo tests in which each donor state is in turn treated as if it had expanded its prisons.
Load the data and look at Texas

How to read it Texas has many more black male prisoners than the average state, even before 1993, so the simple average is a poor comparison: its level and trend differ. Any DiD against the average would rest on a parallel-trends assumption that the picture makes implausible. The synthetic control builds a better comparison.

How to read it Synthetic Texas is a combination of a few large states. The pre-treatment root mean squared prediction error (RMSPE) is small relative to the size of the series: the weighted combination tracks Texas closely before 1993. A poor pre-treatment fit would make any post-treatment gap uninterpretable, so always report this number. This guide matches on the outcome path only. The full method also matches on predictors (income, unemployment, demographics) with a second set of weights on those predictors; the synth packages in Stata and R do this.
The effect: actual against synthetic Texas

How to read it The two lines move together until 1993 and then separate sharply: by the late 1990s Texas held tens of thousands more black men in prison than synthetic Texas. The gap is the estimated effect in each year. It grows as the new capacity came into use.

How to read it Each grey line is a placebo: the same method applied to a state that did not expand its prisons, as if it had. If Texas's gap were unusual only by chance, many placebo gaps would look like it. The standard comparison uses the ratio of post- to pre-treatment RMSPE, which accounts for how well each synthetic unit fitted before 1993. The permutation p-value is Texas's rank among all states divided by the number of states. On this statistic Texas ranks 9th of 51 (p ≈ 0.18). But look at which states beat it: Pennsylvania's ratio is over 300 because its synthetic control fits its pre-1993 path almost perfectly, so even a modest later deviation is enormous relative to that fit . With only 8 pre-treatment years, the ratio is a fragile statistic.

A second statistic is the average post-1993 gap as a share of each state's own pre-1993 level. On this measure Texas's gap, more than its entire pre-1993 level, ranks second of 51 (p ≈ 0.04). Report both, and explain the difference: the effect is very large in size, and the conventional ratio-based p-value is weakened by placebo states with near-perfect pre-treatment fits. A standard refinement drops placebo states whose pre-treatment fit is much worse than Texas's (Abadie et al. 2010 use two or five times its pre-RMSPE); here the problem runs the other way, which is why a second statistic helps.
Robustness: leave-one-out and an in-time placebo

How to read it Leave-one-out. Dropping each state with a positive weight in turn and re-estimating should not change the conclusion. If it did, the result would hinge on one donor. In-time placebo. Pretending the expansion happened in 1989 and using only earlier years for the weights, there should be no gap between 1989 and 1992. A gap would mean synthetic Texas cannot track Texas even when nothing happens.

How to write it: results Synthetic Texas, a weighted combination of a few other large states, closely reproduces the number of black male prisoners in Texas before 1993. After the expansion of prison capacity, the two series diverge sharply: by the end of the decade Texas held tens of thousands more black men in prison than its synthetic counterpart. The result is robust to excluding any single donor state, and an in-time placebo shows no divergence before 1993. In placebo-in-space tests, the gap for Texas relative to its pre-1993 level is the second largest of 51 states (permutation p = 0.04); on the ratio of post- to pre-treatment prediction errors, Texas ranks ninth of 51, because several placebo states have near-perfect pre-treatment fits that inflate their ratios.

Common mistakes Including donors that were affected by the same policy, or by spillovers from the treated unit. Interpreting a gap when the pre-treatment fit is poor. Using conventional standard errors. With one treated unit, inference comes from placebo permutations. Choosing the pre-treatment period or the donor pool after looking at the results. Too short a pre-treatment period: the weights then fit noise.
Synthetic Difference-in-Differences: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

In 1993 Texas began a massive expansion of prison capacity. How many more black men were in Texas prisons after 1993 than there would have been without the expansion? This is the question of the synthetic control guide, with the same data (Cunningham, Causal Inference: The Mixtape ), so that the estimators can be compared directly. Plain difference-in-differences needs parallel trends with the average of all other states. Synthetic control builds a weighted average of states that matches Texas before 1993 and needs a good pre-treatment fit. Synthetic DiD uses both ideas. With \(\hat\omega_i\) the unit weights and \(\hat\lambda_t\) the time weights, where \(\hat\omega\) makes the weighted controls follow the treated unit's pre-treatment path up to a constant (and are regularised so that they do not concentrate on one state), and \(\hat\lambda\) makes the weighted pre-treatment periods resemble the post-treatment period for the controls. The intercept freedom is what separates it from synthetic control.

Symbol Variable in the file Definition \(Y_{it}\) bmprison black male prisoners in the state's prisons \(D_{it}\) expansion 1 for Texas from 1993 \(N_0,T_0\) 50 comparison states and 8 pre-treatment years (1985–1992) Before you estimate anything Check the three conditions behind the estimator: a long enough pre-period (here 8 years), enough comparison units whose weighted average can follow the treated unit, and no spillovers from Texas into the other states. State which weights you expect to matter before you see them. With one treated unit, inference cannot use cluster-robust standard errors, so use placebo or jackknife methods. How to write it: design We estimate the effect of the 1993 Texas prison expansion on the number of black male prisoners using synthetic difference-in-differences (Arkhangelsky et al. 2021), with the other 50 states as the comparison pool and 1985–1992 as the pre-treatment period. We compare the estimate with difference-in-differences and synthetic control. We obtain standard errors from placebo estimates in which each comparison state is assigned the treatment in turn.
Load the data and look at Texas against the other states

How to read it Texas was already far above the rest: 27,568 prisoners in 1992 against an average of 6,972 for the other states (median 3,101). The gap is a level difference, not a trend difference, which is exactly what the difference-in-differences family allows. Because a handful of large states dominate the pool, simple averages of controls are a poor comparison.
Difference-in-differences and synthetic control on the same data

How to read it Plain DiD gives about 29,800 more prisoners a year, but it compares Texas with the average state, which is much smaller and may follow a different path. Synthetic control puts its weight on Florida, New York and Illinois (about 0.37, 0.36 and 0.27) and gives about 21,000, with a pre-treatment root mean squared error of 863. The 9,000 gap between the two is a warning that the parallel-trends assumption with the average state is not credible here.

How to read it Synthetic DiD gives about 19,500 more prisoners a year, close to synthetic control and well below DiD. The unit weights go to Florida (0.33), Illinois (0.30), New York (0.23) and Ohio (0.11), an effective number of 3.8 states. The time weights put all the mass on 1992, so the estimate is effectively a comparison of the post-period with the last pre-period. The effect is about zero in 1993, is 9,000 in 1994 and reaches 22,000–27,000 from 1995, which is consistent with prison capacity being built up gradually. The pre-treatment gaps (about −1,300 to −2,800) are measured relative to 1992, so they show that Texas was growing less fast than its synthetic path before the policy rather than a fit failure; the estimator allows for the level difference but not for that drift.

How to read it Treating each of the 50 comparison states as if it had been treated gives a placebo standard error of about 1,340 for synthetic DiD, against 1,660 for synthetic control and 4,190 for DiD. No placebo effect is as large as the Texas estimate (a share of 0 out of 50, so the placebo p-value is at most 1/51 = 0.02), and the interval is about 16,900 to 22,100. The placebo mean is 108, close to zero. With one treated unit these are approximate, and the placebo states are smaller than Texas, so their spread is probably understated for a state of Texas's size.
Robustness: regularisation, an in-time placebo and the scale of the outcome

How to read it Making the unit weights more concentrated or more spread out moves the estimate between about 19,000 (effective number of states 2) and 22,400 (40 states), so the conclusion does not depend on the regularisation, but the size does. The in-time placebo, which pretends that treatment began in 1989 and uses only pre-1993 data, finds 4,100, about a fifth of the main effect. That is larger than the year-to-year noise of the controls (132), so some of the main estimate may reflect Texas's pre-existing faster growth, and it should be reported as a limit. In logs, dropping Vermont (which has zero prisoners in some years), the estimate is 0.29 (about 34% more prisoners) against 0.40 from DiD; the weights are then spread thinly over many small states, so the levels and logs answer different questions.
Robustness: regularisation, an in-time placebo and the scale of the outcome

How to write it: results The synthetic difference-in-differences estimate is that the 1993 expansion raised the number of black male prisoners in Texas by about 19,500 a year over 1993–2000 (placebo 95% interval 16,900 to 22,100), a rise of roughly 34% in logs. This is close to the synthetic control estimate (21,000) and much smaller than the difference-in-differences estimate (29,800), which compares Texas with a very different average state. The effect builds up over time, from about zero in 1993 to 27,000 in 2000. Placebo estimates from the 50 other states are never as large. An in-time placebo of 4,100 and the dependence on the regularisation (19,000 to 22,400) suggest some residual uncertainty about the exact size.
What to report in the paper

Item What to show Design treated unit(s), comparison pool, pre- and post-period lengths Weights the largest unit weights, the time weights and the effective number of units Comparison DiD and synthetic control on the same data, so that readers see what the estimator changes Fit the pre-treatment gaps of the synthetic DiD counterfactual Inference placebo or jackknife standard errors (with a single treated unit), and the number of placebos Robustness regularisation, an in-time placebo, the outcome scale Common mistakes Using DiD standard errors with one treated unit. There is nothing to average over. Use placebo or jackknife inference. Reading unit weights as causal. They are a tool to build a counterfactual, and they can be unstable. Show the effective number of units.
What to report in the paper

Forgetting that weights concentrate. Time weights often land on the last pre-period. If so, the estimate is close to a comparison with that one year, and you should say so. Ignoring scale. In levels, large units dominate. Check a log or per-capita version. Choosing the regularisation after seeing the result. Use the default rule, and show the sensitivity. Ignoring spillovers. If the treatment affects the comparison states, the counterfactual is contaminated.
Staggered Difference-in-Differences: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
The question and why timing matters

The question is the one in the DiD guide: did stand-your-ground laws change homicide rates? But now all 21 adopting states are used, and they passed their laws in different years. That is the usual situation in policy evaluation: minimum-wage increases, Medicaid expansions, carbon taxes and central-bank reforms all arrive at different dates in different places. The tempting regression is the same as before: Why the conventional regression fails Goodman-Bacon (2021) showed that \(\tau^{TWFE}\) is a weighted average of every 2×2 DiD comparison in the data. Some of those comparisons use states that adopted earlier as the control group for states that adopt later . If the effect of the law grows or changes over time, the earlier adopters' outcomes are still moving because of their own treatment, and subtracting them removes part of the effect, or even flips its sign. Some weights can be negative. The fix is to estimate the effect for each adoption cohort separately, against clean controls, and then average: the group-time ATT of Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021).
The question and why timing matters

How to write it: design States enacted Castle Doctrine laws at different dates between 2006 and 2010. Because two-way fixed-effects estimates are biased under staggered adoption when treatment effects vary over time or across cohorts (Goodman-Bacon 2021; de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille 2020), we estimate cohort-specific average treatment effects on the treated, using never-treated states as controls, and aggregate them following Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021).
Load the data and look at the cohorts

How to read it Five adoption cohorts, with most states adopting in 2007, and 29 states that never adopt. The never-treated states are the clean comparison group. Without them, the not-yet-treated states could serve instead.

How to read it The TWFE estimate is about 0.07: homicide about 7% higher after adoption, though not significant with clustered standard errors. This is the number many papers would report. Under staggered adoption it is not a well-defined average of the effects, so it has to be checked against estimators that are.
Group-time effects: one clean comparison per cohort and year

How to read it Each cell is a separate 2×2 comparison: cohort \(g\) against the never-treated states, between year \(t\) and the year before adoption, \(g-1\) . Cells before adoption are placebo comparisons and should be near zero; cells after adoption are effects. Nothing in this table uses an already-treated state as a control. The cohorts with one or two states (2006, 2009, 2010) are noisy, so the cells are aggregated next.
Aggregate: the event study and the overall ATT

How to read it Event study. The group-time effects are averaged by years since adoption, weighting cohorts by size. Standard errors come from a cluster bootstrap over states. Pre-trends. The leads are jointly insignificant at 5% (p ≈ 0.07). Not a clean pass: a sensitivity analysis is advisable. The overall ATT is about 0.02, a third of the TWFE estimate and far from significance. Look at the leads. They are all negative, around −0.04 to −0.10: relative to the never-treated states, homicide in adopting states was lower several years before adoption than in the year just before it. In other words, it was already rising. This estimator measures everything against the year before adoption, so it does not count that earlier rise as an effect of the law.
Aggregate: the event study and the overall ATT
The large estimate four years after adoption rests on the single 2006 adopter (Florida) and should not be over-interpreted.

How to read it The imputation estimator fits state and year effects only on untreated observations , predicts what each treated state-year would have been without the law, and averages the gaps. Like Callaway–Sant'Anna, it never uses treated observations as controls, so it is free of the staggered-adoption bias. It gives about 0.07, close to TWFE . So in this dataset the bias from comparing late with early adopters is small. The real divergence is between estimators that use all pre-treatment years as the baseline (TWFE, imputation: about 0.07) and the one that uses only the year before adoption (Callaway–Sant'Anna: about 0.02). The leads explain it: homicide in adopting states was already rising relative to controls before the laws, and an all-years baseline attributes part of that rise to the law.

The honest conclusion: the estimated effect depends on how the pre-trend is handled, and none of the estimates is statistically significant. Report all three, show the event study, and add a sensitivity analysis for violations of parallel trends (Rambachan and Roth 2023). (Standard errors for the imputation estimator are best obtained with the did_imputation package in Stata or a cluster bootstrap.)

How to write it: results Because states adopted Castle Doctrine laws at different dates, we report heterogeneity-robust estimators alongside the two-way fixed-effects estimate. The two-way fixed-effects and imputation estimators, which use all pre-adoption years as the baseline, both indicate an increase in homicide of about 7 percent; the Callaway–Sant'Anna estimator, which uses the year before adoption as the baseline, indicates about 2 percent. None of the estimates is statistically significant. The pre-adoption event-study coefficients are negative and jointly significant at the 10 but not the 5 percent level, suggesting that homicide was already rising in adopting states; the results are therefore sensitive to how this pre-trend is treated. Common mistakes

Reporting only the TWFE coefficient under staggered adoption. Running a conventional event-study regression with relative-time dummies under staggered adoption: it suffers from the same contamination (Sun and Abraham 2021). Use cohort-specific estimates. Not saying which controls are used: never-treated or not-yet-treated. They rest on different assumptions; report both if possible. Ignoring small cohorts. A cohort of one state drives the event-time estimates where it is alone.
Weak-Instrument-Robust IV Inference: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

What can you conclude about the coefficient when the instruments might be weak? In \(y = \beta x + w'\gamma + u\) with \(x = z'\pi + w'\delta + v\) , 2SLS is a ratio of reduced-form coefficients, and when \(\pi\) is close to zero the ratio is badly behaved: biased toward OLS, with a non-normal distribution. The weak-instrument-robust tests avoid the ratio. To test \(\beta=\beta_0\) , define the residual \(y-\beta_0 x\) and ask whether the instruments predict it. The Anderson-Rubin (AR) statistic is the Wald test of that regression and is valid for any \(\pi\) . The Lagrange multiplier (LM) statistic of Kleibergen uses one direction in instrument space and is more powerful with strong instruments. The conditional likelihood ratio (CLR) test of Moreira conditions on the part of the data that carries the information about instrument strength. The confidence set contains every \(\beta_0\) that is not rejected, and it can be wide, bounded away from 2SLS, or unbounded, which is the correct answer when the data do not identify \(\beta\) .

Three checks before you report an IV estimate How strong is the first stage? An F statistic below 10 is the usual warning. Report it, together with the robust sets if it is low. Do the 2SLS and robust sets agree? If they do, nothing is lost. If they do not, believe the robust one. Are the instruments valid? With more instruments than endogenous variables, the minimum of the AR statistic is an overidentification test. A rejection means the instruments disagree with each other. How to write it: the model We estimate the return to a year of schooling in the Card (1995) data on 2,215 men, instrumenting years of education with proximity to a two-year college and to a four-year college. The wage equation includes experience and its square and indicators for race, urban residence and the South. Because the first-stage F statistic is low, we report, in addition to 2SLS and LIML confidence intervals, the weak-instrument-robust confidence sets from the Anderson-Rubin, Lagrange multiplier and conditional likelihood ratio tests (Andrews, Moreira and Stock 2006), inverted over a grid of values of the return to schooling. The conditional likelihood ratio p-values are simulated with 1,000 draws. We also use the minimum of the Anderson-Rubin statistic as an overidentification test.
Load the data and look at the first stage

How to read it The sample has 2,215 men with complete records, mean education 13.6 years and mean log wage 6.29. Sixty-nine percent grew up near a four-year college and 44% near a two-year college. Education is correlated 0.12 with proximity to a four-year college and only 0.05 with proximity to a two-year college, against 0.47 and 0.44 with father's and mother's education. The OLS return to a year of schooling is 0.076 (standard error 0.0043). Near-college indicators are the instruments Card used, and their correlation with education is small, so weak instruments are the concern.
One instrument: all the tests give the same set

How to read it With proximity to a four-year college as the only instrument, the first-stage F statistic is 6.31 (partial R-squared 0.003), below the rule-of-thumb 10. The 2SLS return is 0.097 with standard error 0.077, a Wald interval of -0.054 to 0.248. With one instrument the Anderson-Rubin, LM and CLR tests coincide, and their set runs from -0.113 to 0.369, about 60% wider than the Wald interval. The Anderson-Rubin test does not reject a zero return (p = 0.24), and the OLS value of 0.076 is well inside the set. A single weak instrument cannot rule out a negative or a very large return.
Two weak instruments: the sets diverge

How to read it Adding proximity to a two-year college makes the first stage weaker, not stronger: F falls to 3.78 (p = 0.023). The 2SLS estimate rises to 0.170 with a Wald interval of 0.018 to 0.323, which looks significant. LIML gives 0.264 (standard error 0.138), well away from 2SLS, which is itself a sign of weak instruments. The robust sets tell a different story about precision: the Anderson-Rubin set is 0.119 to 0.948, the conditional likelihood ratio set is 0.061 to infinity, and the LM set is unbounded. The robust tests exclude a zero return (the AR test of beta = 0 has p = 0.007, and the AR and CLR sets exclude zero), but they say nothing about an upper bound: a return of 0.9 per year of schooling is not rejected. The Wald interval is about a third as wide as the Anderson-Rubin set, and the extra width is the cost of weak instruments that the Wald interval hides. The overidentification test is borderline (p = 0.053).
Strong instruments that may not be valid

How to read it Parents' education is a strong instrument: F = 126.6, and every set is close to the Wald interval (0.074 to 0.124 for AR, 0.076 to 0.124 for LM and CLR), with an overidentification p-value of 0.15, so with strong instruments the robust sets cost nothing. Strength is not validity, though, because parents' education is correlated with family background and ability and may belong in the wage equation directly. Using all four instruments, F is 64.6 and 2SLS is 0.099 (0.013), but the overidentification test rejects (minimum of the AR statistic 8.78, p = 0.032), and the Anderson-Rubin set shrinks to 0.091 to 0.111, narrower than the Wald interval. That narrow set is not precision. The AR test has power against instruments that disagree, and here the near-college and parental-education instruments imply different returns, so the narrowness reflects a misspecified set of instruments. The LM and CLR sets, which look only at the direction in which the instruments are informative, stay at 0.076 to 0.126.

How to write it: results With proximity to a four-year college as the instrument, the first-stage F statistic is 6.3, and the 2SLS return to a year of schooling is 0.097 (standard error 0.077). The 95% Anderson-Rubin confidence set, which is valid for any instrument strength, runs from -0.113 to 0.369 and does not reject a zero return (p = 0.24). Adding proximity to a two-year college lowers the first-stage F statistic to 3.8; 2SLS then gives 0.170 (Wald interval 0.018 to 0.323), but the robust sets are much wider (Anderson-Rubin 0.119 to 0.948, conditional likelihood ratio 0.061 to infinity, LM unbounded), so the data do not bound the return from above. With parental education as instruments (F = 127) the robust sets coincide with the Wald interval (0.074 to 0.124); however, a joint model with all four instruments rejects overidentifying restrictions (p = 0.032), and we do not interpret the shrinking of the Anderson-Rubin set in that case as precision. Sets assume homoskedastic errors; the conditional likelihood ratio p-values use 2,000 simulation draws.

Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model

How strongly did the Federal Reserve respond to inflation, and which shocks drove U.S. inflation? Calibration cannot answer this: it requires estimating the policy rule jointly with the rest of the economy. Bayesian estimation (Smets and Wouters 2003; An and Schorfheide 2007) combines the model's likelihood, computed with the Kalman filter, with prior information about the parameters. The model is the New Keynesian model of An and Schorfheide (2007), with a technology growth shock \(z_t\) , a demand (government spending) shock \(g_t\) and a monetary policy shock \(\varepsilon^R_t\) : and measurement equations that link the model to the data: Data and measurement are part of the model Three observables and three shocks. A linear DSGE model with fewer shocks than observables is stochastically singular : it implies an exact linear relation among the observables that the data reject. Never use more observables than shocks (or add measurement errors).
Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model

Demeaned data. Each observable has its sample mean removed, so the model is estimated in deviations and the constants (trend growth, the inflation target, the real rate) are not estimated. Estimating them requires that the model's steady state matches the data's means, which with these data would force a real interest rate near zero. Demeaning is a common, transparent choice; state it in the paper. Units. Output growth is in percent per quarter; inflation and the interest rate are annualised percentages, hence the factor 4. How to write it: data We estimate the model on three quarterly U.S. series for 1966Q1–2007Q4: the growth rate of real GDP, inflation measured by the GDP deflator (annualised), and the effective federal funds rate. The sample ends before the zero-lower-bound period. All series are demeaned prior to estimation.

varobs names the observables; their names must match the column headers of the data file. estimation first finds the posterior mode ( mode_compute = 5 , Dynare's Newton-type optimiser), then runs two independent Metropolis–Hastings chains of 10,000 draws each, discards the first half of each chain as burn-in ( mh_drop ), and reports posterior means and 90% highest-posterior-density intervals. mh_jscale scales the proposal distribution; it is tuned so that about a quarter to a third of proposals are accepted. Chains for a paper should be much longer (at least 2 × 100,000); this page uses short chains so that it can be rebuilt in minutes. The output reports, for each parameter: the prior mean, the posterior mean, the 90% HPD interval, the prior distribution and the prior standard deviation.

How to read it Acceptance ratio. Between about 0.2 and 0.4 is the target. Too high means the sampler takes tiny steps and explores slowly; too low means it rarely moves. R-hat (Gelman and Rubin 1992) compares the variance between the two chains with the variance within them. Values close to 1 (below about 1.1) indicate that the chains have converged to the same distribution. Dynare reports the related Brooks–Gelman diagnostics graphically. Trace plots. The two chains should overlap and move freely around the same region, with no trends.
Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model

How to read it Bars are the posterior, dashed lines the prior. Where the two differ, the data are informative. The policy rule. The response to inflation \(\psi_1\) is estimated just above 1, lower than its prior mean: over 1966–2007, which includes the high-inflation 1970s, the Federal Reserve on average barely satisfied the Taylor principle. Interest-rate smoothing \(\rho_R\) is high. The Phillips curve slope \(\kappa\) is estimated at about 0.15: inflation responds weakly to the output gap. Shock persistence. The demand and technology shocks are very persistent ( \(\rho_g\) , \(\rho_z\) near 0.97), a common finding in small models: persistent shocks absorb dynamics the model's frictions cannot generate. Where the posterior looks like the prior , the data say little about that parameter. The identification guide shows how to check this before estimating.

How to read it Each line is the posterior mean response to a one-standard-deviation monetary policy shock; the shaded band is the 90% HPD interval, which reflects parameter uncertainty. Unlike a VAR, the DSGE model identifies the shock through its structure: every response follows from the estimated equations.
Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model

How to read it The black line is demeaned inflation; the coloured areas show how much of it each smoothed shock accounts for in each quarter (plus the effect of initial conditions, not shown). In this small model the persistent technology growth shock accounts for almost all of it (94% of the squared contributions), including the Great Inflation of the 1970s and the disinflation of the 1980s; monetary policy shocks account for the rest. The demand shock does not move inflation at all: in this model it shifts output and its natural level together. That is a property of a three-shock model with no cost-push shock: a richer model would split inflation between more shocks, so read the decomposition as model-dependent.
Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model

How to write it: results Table 2 reports the prior and posterior distributions. The posterior mean of the response of the policy rate to inflation is about 1.2, with a 90 percent interval just above one, indicating that over 1966–2007 the Federal Reserve on average satisfied the Taylor principle only narrowly; interest rates were adjusted gradually (posterior mean of the smoothing coefficient about 0.77). The slope of the Phillips curve is estimated at about 0.15. Two Metropolis–Hastings chains were run; the Gelman–Rubin statistics are close to one for all parameters. A contractionary monetary policy shock lowers output and inflation (Figure 3). Common mistakes More observables than shocks: stochastic singularity. Data and model in different units (annualised vs quarterly, percent vs fractions, levels vs growth rates).
