Reporting estimates from chains that have not converged, or from very short chains. Running the sampler without first checking the mode ( mode_check ) and identification. Priors so tight that the posterior equals the prior, then presenting the result as an estimate. Always plot priors against posteriors.
Higher-Order Solutions and Welfare: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Dynare code, real output and sample text.
The question and why first order is not enough

How costly are business cycles, and does uncertainty change how the economy behaves on average? In a first-order solution, the mean of every variable equals its steady state, whatever the size of the shocks: households behave as if they were certain about the future (certainty equivalence). That makes first-order solutions unable to measure: precautionary behaviour : uncertainty raising saving and the capital stock; welfare : the average utility loss from fluctuations, which depends on variances, a second-order term; asymmetry : large positive and negative shocks having responses of different size. The model is the RBC model of the first guide with one extra equation, a recursive definition of lifetime utility:
The question and why first order is not enough

Pruning Higher-order perturbation solutions can explode in simulations, because the squared terms feed back on themselves. Pruning (Kim, Kim, Schaumburg and Sims 2008; Andreasen, Fernández-Villaverde and Rubio-Ramírez 2018) removes the terms of higher order than the approximation, keeping simulations stable and making theoretical moments available. Always use it at order 2 and above.

How to read it The policy functions now contain a constant correction and terms in squared states. The constant (the ghs2 term in Dynare's notation) is how risk enters: it shifts every variable away from its steady state even when no shock occurs in a given period. The theoretical moments below are computed from the pruned second-order solution.
Precautionary saving and the welfare cost of fluctuations

How to read it Precautionary saving. With uncertainty, the average capital stock is above its steady state: households save more as insurance against bad productivity draws. Output is higher on average as a result. A first-order solution would show zero difference for every variable. Welfare cost. The consumption-equivalent cost \(\lambda\) solves \(E[\mathcal W] = \mathcal W_{ss} + \ln(1-\lambda)/(1-\beta)\) : the share of consumption households would give up every period to live in the steady state instead of the fluctuating economy. Here it is negative , about −0.03%: households are slightly better off with fluctuations. That is not a bug. With elastic labour supply and capital, households can work and invest more when productivity is high and less when it is low, and that option is worth more than the utility lost to consumption volatility (Cho, Cooley and Kim 2015). Lucas (1987) found the cost of fluctuations to be tiny in an endowment economy; in this production economy it is tiny and of the opposite sign. Models with incomplete markets, unemployment risk or nominal rigidities typically produce positive and larger costs.
How the answer changes with the size of shocks

How to read it Size of shocks. Doubling the shock standard deviation multiplies the precautionary capital and the welfare effect by four, tripling it by nine: both are proportional to the variance of the shocks, the signature of a second-order effect. Third order. The model file can be solved at third order with dynare rbc2 -DORD=3 . With symmetric shocks, third-order terms leave average outcomes essentially unchanged; they matter for time-varying risk premia and models with stochastic volatility. Dynare provides theoretical moments only up to second order, so third-order results come from long pruned simulations.

How to read it With a linear solution the two lines would coincide exactly. At second order the squared terms add the same correction to positive and negative shocks, so their responses can differ in size. In this smooth RBC model the difference is virtually nil , even for a five-standard-deviation shock: the model is close to linear around its steady state. Strong asymmetries need strong nonlinearities, such as the occasionally binding constraint of the zero-lower-bound guide.

How to write it: results We solve the model with a second-order perturbation and pruning, which captures the effect of uncertainty on average outcomes. Productivity risk raises the average capital stock above its deterministic steady state, reflecting precautionary saving. The welfare effect of business-cycle fluctuations, measured as the permanent percentage of consumption that would make households indifferent between the stochastic economy and its deterministic steady state, is very small and slightly favourable: with elastic labour supply, households exploit productivity fluctuations by working and investing more in good times. Both effects scale with the variance of the shocks. Common mistakes Computing welfare from a first-order solution. The linear approximation of a utility function gets welfare comparisons wrong; use second order.

Simulating at order 2 or 3 without pruning. Comparing welfare across policies without a common starting point: conditional and unconditional welfare can rank policies differently. Reporting means from a first-order solution as “effects of uncertainty”: they equal the steady state by construction.
Identification Before Estimation: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Dynare code, real output and sample text.
The question and why it comes first

Which parameters can the data actually tell us about? In a DSGE model the observables depend on the parameters through the solution of the model, and some parameters may have no separate effect: they enter only in a combination, or their effect is indistinguishable from another parameter's. Such parameters are not identified . Estimating them anyway gives posteriors that mirror the priors, and conclusions that are really assumptions. Iskrev (2010) and Komunjer and Ng (2011) showed how to check identification from the model alone: a parameter is (locally) identified if the moments, or the spectrum, of the observables change when the parameter changes, in a way that no combination of other parameters can replicate. Dynare implements both checks in the identification command.
The question and why it comes first

Two kinds of problems Non-identification : a parameter has no effect on the observables, or two parameters enter only as a product or ratio. The Jacobian of the moments with respect to the parameters is rank-deficient. Weak identification : the parameter is identified in principle, but its effect is small or nearly collinear with another's, so the data are only weakly informative. The Jacobian is close to rank-deficient.

How to read it Dynare runs three tests, and they do not all agree: Komunjer and Ng (2011) , the test on the model's minimal state-space system, finds all parameters identified . The reduced-form test (Iskrev 2010) and the spectrum test (Qu and Tkachenko 2012) flag the policy-rule block ( \(\psi_1\) , \(\psi_2\) , \(\rho_R\) and the standard deviation of the monetary shock) as collinear with the other parameters: their effects on the observables can be closely mimicked by combinations of other parameters. This is not a quirk of the code. Cochrane (2011) argued that Taylor-rule coefficients are hard to identify in New Keynesian models precisely because, under determinacy, the equilibrium never shows the off-equilibrium responses those coefficients govern. In practice it means the data will be only weakly informative about the policy rule, and its posterior will lean on the prior: compare the prior and posterior of \(\psi_1\) in the estimation guide before interpreting it. The other parameters are cleanly identified.
A model that is not identified

How to read it The Phillips curve depends on the Calvo parameter \(\theta\) and the labour-supply parameter \(\varphi\) only through the slope \(\kappa\) . Many combinations of \(\theta\) and \(\varphi\) give the same \(\kappa\) , and therefore exactly the same predictions for output, inflation and interest rates. Now all three tests fail, including Komunjer–Ng, and each names the same culprit: [varphi, theta] are pairwise collinear . Unlike the weak identification of the policy rule, this is exact non-identification. This is a typical situation, not a contrived one. Small models usually identify the slope of the Phillips curve but not the structural parameters behind it. The remedies are: estimate the reduced-form coefficient ( \(\kappa\) ) and calibrate one of the structural parameters;
A model that is not identified

add data that the other parameter affects separately (hours or wages identify \(\varphi\) ); use informative priors from micro evidence, and say clearly that the posterior for that parameter reflects the prior.

How to write it: identification Before estimation, we verify local identification of the estimated parameters at the prior mean using the rank conditions of Iskrev (2010) and Komunjer and Ng (2011), as implemented in Dynare. The Komunjer–Ng test indicates that all estimated parameters are locally identified, although the reduced-form and spectral tests point to weak identification of the policy-rule parameters, a known feature of New Keynesian models (Cochrane 2011); we therefore interpret their posteriors with reference to the priors. In an alternative parameterisation in which the Calvo probability and the inverse Frisch elasticity are estimated separately, the two are not separately identified, because they enter the model only through the slope of the Phillips curve; we therefore estimate the slope directly.

Common mistakes Estimating first and checking identification only when a posterior looks like its prior. Taking a well-behaved posterior as evidence of identification: a tight prior produces a tight posterior even for an unidentified parameter. Checking identification at one parameter value only. Dynare can check it across draws from the prior ( prior_mc option), which reveals regions where it fails. Estimating more structural parameters than the observables can inform, instead of estimating reduced-form coefficients.

A CSV of quarterly time series, one column per series (for example real GDP, the GDP deflator and a policy rate). The tool checks each series, proposes the transformation that matches a model variable, and writes the data file and the Dynare lines for estimation. The model itself is solved and estimated in Dynare, on your own computer. Drop a CSV file here, or Trending series are turned into quarterly growth rates in percent: 100·Δlog for levels (GDP, prices), 100·Δ for series already in logs. Series without a trend (inflation, interest rates) are kept in levels. All observables are demeaned, so the model's steady state does not have to match the sample means. The file is analysed on your own device and is not uploaded anywhere.

Nine routes to a finished paper
Each guide takes one model through the Dynare file, the solution checks, the results and the text for the paper, with the .mod file, real Dynare output and figures.
Medium-Scale New Keynesian Model: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Dynare code, real output and sample text.

Which frictions and which shocks are needed to fit the joint behaviour of output, consumption, investment, inflation and interest rates? Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (2005) and Smets and Wouters (2007) showed that a New Keynesian model with a handful of real and nominal frictions can fit U.S. data about as well as a VAR. Their model is the basis of most policy models in central banks. This guide estimates a compact version: capital accumulation with investment adjustment costs , consumption habits , Calvo prices with indexation , a Taylor rule, and six shocks (technology, preference, investment-specific, government spending, price mark-up and monetary policy). Wages are flexible, which keeps the model small but, as the results show, pushes the price-rigidity parameter to absorb what wage rigidity would explain.

Equation Log-linear form (deviations from the steady state) Consumption Euler, with habits \(h\) \(c_t = \frac{h}{1+h} c_{t-1} + \frac{1}{1+h} E_t c_{t+1} - \frac{1-h}{1+h}(R_t - E_t\pi_{t+1}) + b_t\) Investment, adjustment cost \(\varphi_i\) \(i_t = \frac{1}{1+\beta} i_{t-1} + \frac{\beta}{1+\beta} E_t i_{t+1} + \frac{1}{(1+\beta)\varphi_i} q_t + \varepsilon^i_t\) Value of capital \(q_t = \beta(1-\delta) E_t q_{t+1} + (1-\beta(1-\delta)) E_t r^k_{t+1} - (R_t - E_t \pi_{t+1})\) Phillips curve, indexation \(\iota_p\) \(\pi_t = \frac{\iota_p}{1+\beta\iota_p}\pi_{t-1} + \frac{\beta}{1+\beta\iota_p}E_t\pi_{t+1} + \kappa\, mc_t + \varepsilon^p_t\) Labour supply (flexible wages) \(w_t = \sigma_l l_t + \frac{1}{1-h}(c_t - h c_{t-1})\) Five observables, six shocks The model has more shocks than observables, so it is not stochastically singular. Each observable has a natural shock: preference shocks for consumption, investment-specific shocks for investment, government spending for output, mark-up shocks for inflation and monetary shocks for the interest rate. With fewer shocks, the model would be forced to explain everything with too few sources of variation.

How to read it Two short chains of 4,000 draws are run so that the page can be rebuilt quickly; for a paper, run at least 2 × 100,000 and check convergence as in the estimation guide. Frictions. Habit persistence is very high (around 0.9): consumption responds sluggishly, as in the data. The investment adjustment cost is clearly positive, which delivers the hump-shaped response of investment. Price rigidity. The Calvo parameter is estimated near 0.96, implying that prices stay fixed for about 25 quarters (six years) on average, far longer than micro evidence suggests. This is the classic symptom of a missing friction: without sticky wages, marginal cost moves too much, and the only way to fit smooth inflation is to make prices extremely sticky. Smets and Wouters add wage rigidity for exactly this reason. Report the number and say what it means.

Policy. The inflation response is about 1.3 with strong smoothing (about 0.85), close to the small model. Persistence. Technology and government spending shocks are very persistent; the investment and preference shocks much less so.

How to read it The table gives, for each variable, the percentage of its unconditional variance due to each shock, averaged over the posterior draws (computed by the moments_varendo option). Investment is dominated by the investment-specific shock (about 70%), and through investment so is output (more than half); consumption leans on the government-spending and preference shocks; inflation is driven mainly by technology shocks, with mark-up shocks second (about 30%). Each shock has a clear role, but the investment shock explaining most of output is a familiar warning sign. Whether that is economics or a sign that the shocks are absorbing misspecification is the central debate about medium-scale models (Chari, Kehoe and McGrattan 2009). A paper should report this table and discuss it.

How to write it: results We estimate a medium-scale New Keynesian model with habit formation, investment adjustment costs and partially indexed Calvo prices on five U.S. observables. The posterior points to strong habit persistence and substantial investment adjustment costs, in line with Smets and Wouters (2007). The estimated degree of price stickiness is implausibly high relative to micro evidence, which we attribute to the absence of nominal wage rigidity in our specification. Investment-specific shocks account for most of the variance of investment and output, and technology shocks for most of the variance of inflation, with mark-up shocks second. Common mistakes Adding shocks until the model fits, then interpreting each shock as structural.

Ignoring implausible estimates (a Calvo parameter of 0.96): they are diagnostics of misspecification. Short chains in a model with twenty parameters: check convergence for every parameter. Comparing models by marginal data density without the same data and the same treatment of the means.
Three-Equation New Keynesian Model: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Dynare code, real output and sample text.

How does a monetary policy shock move output and inflation, and how should the central bank respond to shocks? The three-equation New Keynesian model is the workhorse for this question. It adds monopolistic competition and Calvo price setting to the household and firm problems of the RBC model, and replaces money with an interest-rate rule. Log-linearised around a zero-inflation steady state: with \(\kappa = \frac{(1-\theta)(1-\beta\theta)}{\theta}(\sigma + \varphi)\) . Here \(x_t\) is the output gap, \(\pi_t\) inflation, \(i_t\) the nominal rate, \(r^n_t\) the natural rate of interest (a demand shock), \(u_t\) a cost-push shock and \(v_t\) a monetary policy shock. Parameter Value Meaning \(\beta\) 0.99 Discount factor \(\sigma\) 1 Inverse intertemporal elasticity of substitution

\(\varphi\) 1 Inverse Frisch elasticity \(\theta\) 0.75 Calvo probability of not resetting prices (average price duration of 4 quarters) \(\phi_\pi\) , \(\phi_x\) 1.5, 0.125 Taylor-rule responses to inflation and the output gap \(\rho_i\) 0.8 Interest-rate smoothing Why the model is written in gaps and deviations Every variable is a deviation from a zero-inflation steady state, so the steady state is zero and no steady_state_model is needed. The economics lies in the coefficients: \(\kappa\) summarises how strongly inflation reacts to the output gap, and it falls quickly as prices become stickier.

How to read it model(linear) tells Dynare the equations are already linear, so it skips the linearisation. The check. The model has two forward-looking variables (the output gap and inflation) and two eigenvalues outside the unit circle: the Blanchard–Kahn conditions hold, and the equilibrium is unique. Variance decomposition. In this calibration demand shocks dominate both the output gap (75%) and inflation (69%); cost-push shocks explain about 14% of inflation and monetary shocks under a fifth of each. With different shock variances these shares change: they are a property of the calibration, not a finding.

How to read it Monetary policy shock. A surprise increase in the policy rate lowers the output gap and inflation on impact. Because inflation and the gap fall, the Taylor rule partly offsets the shock, so the interest rate rises by less than the shock itself. Demand shock. A rise in the natural rate raises the output gap and inflation together; the central bank raises the rate. Demand shocks move output and inflation in the same direction. Cost-push shock. Inflation rises while the output gap falls: the central bank faces a trade-off , the reason inflation targeting is hard in practice.

How to read it Doubling the response to inflation lowers the volatility of both inflation and the output gap. That is because demand shocks dominate in this calibration, and for demand shocks there is no trade-off: stabilising inflation also stabilises the gap (the “divine coincidence”). A stronger response to the output gap also lowers both, by less for inflation. The policy rate becomes more volatile in both cases. A trade-off appears only through cost-push shocks; with larger cost-push shocks, the ranking of rules depends on how society weighs the two goals, which is the subject of the optimal-policy guide.

How to read it Dynare reports one eigenvalue outside the unit circle for two forward-looking variables: “The rank condition ISN'T verified!”. With \(\phi_\pi = 0.9\) , the central bank raises the nominal rate by less than one-for-one with inflation, so the real rate falls when inflation rises. Self-fulfilling expectations of inflation are then possible, and the model has many equilibria (it is indeterminate ). This is the Taylor principle : the response to inflation must exceed one (with a small output-gap response, roughly \(\phi_\pi > 1\) ). When you see this Blanchard–Kahn error in your own model, check the policy rule before anything else.

How to write it: results Figure 1 shows the responses to monetary, demand and cost-push shocks in the calibrated model. A 25-basis-point monetary tightening lowers the output gap and annualised inflation on impact, and its effects dissipate within a few quarters. Demand shocks move output and inflation in the same direction, while cost-push shocks create a trade-off between stabilising inflation and stabilising the output gap. The model is determinate under the baseline rule; with a response to inflation below one, the equilibrium is indeterminate, as implied by the Taylor principle. Common mistakes Mixing quarterly and annual rates. Write the model in quarterly rates and annualise only when reporting. Reporting impulse responses from an indeterminate model. Dynare refuses to solve it; do not “fix” this by changing timing until it runs.

Treating the variance decomposition of a calibrated model as evidence. It reflects the assumed shock variances. Forgetting interest-rate smoothing, which makes the response of the policy rate gradual, as in the data.
Optimal Monetary Policy: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Dynare code, real output and sample text.

How should a central bank respond to shocks, and how much does commitment matter? In the New Keynesian model, a second-order approximation to household welfare gives the central bank a quadratic loss in inflation and the output gap (Woodford 2003; Galí 2015): The constraints are the IS curve and the Phillips curve of the NK guide, with a cost-push shock \(u_t\) and a natural-rate (demand) shock \(r^n_t\) . Three policies are compared: Policy Dynare command Meaning Commitment ramsey_model The central bank chooses the whole future path of policy once and sticks to it Discretion discretionary_policy It re-optimises every period, taking future policy as given Optimal simple rule osr The best Taylor rule \(i_t = \phi_\pi \pi_t + \phi_x x_t\)

Why the comparison matters Commitment is the best the central bank can do, but it requires credibility: promises about future policy must be believed. Discretion is what happens without that credibility. A simple rule is what central banks can actually communicate. The gaps between the three losses measure the value of commitment and the cost of simplicity.

How to read it Under commitment and discretion there is no policy rule in the model block: the interest rate is the planner's instrument, and Dynare derives the optimality conditions itself. That is why the model has one equation fewer than variables. planner_objective states the period loss; planner_discount its discount factor. For the simple rule, the rule is in the model and osr searches over its coefficients to minimise the weighted sum of variances given in optim_weights . The bounds keep \(\phi_\pi\) above 1 (determinacy) and within a range a central bank could announce. The output above is the commitment solution: note how the cost-push shock of the previous period still affects today's choices, a sign of the history dependence of commitment.

How to read it Commitment has the lowest loss by construction. Discretion is worse: the stabilisation bias. Without the ability to promise future restraint, the central bank must fight a cost-push shock entirely with today's output gap, while under commitment it spreads the adjustment over time by promising to keep policy tight after the shock fades. The optimised simple rule does worse than both. It hits the upper bound of \(\phi_\pi = 10\) : optimal policy fully offsets demand shocks (the divine coincidence), and a rule can only approximate that by responding ever more strongly to inflation. Even so, a rule that reacts only to current inflation and the gap cannot reproduce the history dependence of commitment, the promise to stay tight after a cost-push shock has passed. Adding the lagged interest rate or the price level to the rule is the standard way to close much of this gap.
Volatility of the interest rate is not in the loss here. Adding a term in \(i_t^2\) to the objective is the standard way to obtain smoother, more realistic optimal rules.

How to read it Under discretion , the output gap and inflation simply follow the shock: once the shock is gone, policy has no reason to do anything. Under commitment , the output gap stays negative after the shock has faded and inflation turns slightly negative: the central bank promises to undo part of the price increase. Because firms expect this, they raise prices less today. The cumulative change in the price level is close to zero under commitment, which is why optimal commitment policy resembles price-level targeting .

How to write it: results We compute optimal monetary policy under commitment and under discretion, and the Taylor rule that minimises the central bank's loss, in the calibrated New Keynesian model. Discretion raises the loss substantially relative to commitment, reflecting the stabilisation bias: under commitment, the central bank keeps policy tight after a cost-push shock has dissipated, which lowers inflation expectations and spreads the adjustment over time, so that the price level returns close to its initial path. A Taylor rule with optimised coefficients performs worse than discretion in this model, because a rule responding only to current inflation and the output gap cannot replicate the history dependence of optimal commitment policy.

Common mistakes Leaving the policy rule in the model when computing Ramsey or discretionary policy: the instrument must be free. Using an ad hoc loss function and calling the result “optimal”. Derive the weights from welfare, or state that the loss is a mandate. Optimising a simple rule without bounds: coefficients run off to extreme values that no central bank would announce. Comparing policies by one variable's volatility rather than by the loss.
Real Business Cycle Model: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Dynare code, real output and sample text.

Can productivity shocks alone generate business cycles that look like the data? That was the question of Kydland and Prescott (1982), and the real business cycle (RBC) model is still the starting point of every DSGE model: the New Keynesian models in the later guides add frictions to exactly this core. A representative household chooses consumption \(C_t\) , hours \(H_t\) and investment to maximise subject to \(C_t + I_t = Y_t\) , \(K_{t+1} = (1-\delta) K_t + I_t\) and production \(Y_t = A_t K_t^{\alpha} H_t^{1-\alpha}\) , with productivity \(\ln A_t = \rho \ln A_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t\) . The equilibrium conditions are: Condition Equation Euler equation \(\frac{1}{C_t} = \beta E_t\left[\frac{1}{C_{t+1}}\left(\alpha \frac{Y_{t+1}}{K_{t+1}} + 1 - \delta\right)\right]\)

Labour supply \(\psi H_t^{\varphi} C_t = W_t = (1-\alpha)\frac{Y_t}{H_t}\) Production \(Y_t = A_t K_t^{\alpha} H_t^{1-\alpha}\) Capital accumulation \(K_{t+1} = (1-\delta)K_t + I_t\) Resource constraint \(Y_t = C_t + I_t\) Before writing any code Write the model down completely: every agent's problem, every constraint, the first-order conditions and the market-clearing conditions. Count equations and endogenous variables: they must be equal. Most Dynare errors are mistakes in this step, not in the code.

Parameter Value Source or target \(\beta\) 0.99 Annual real interest rate of about 4% \(\alpha\) 0.33 Capital share of income \(\delta\) 0.025 Annual depreciation of about 10% \(\varphi\) 1 Frisch elasticity of labour supply of 1 \(\psi\) set in the steady state Hours equal to 1/3 of the time endowment \(\rho\) 0.95 Persistence of measured productivity (Solow residual) \(\sigma_\varepsilon\) 0.007 Volatility of the Solow residual How to write it: calibration The model is calibrated at a quarterly frequency to the U.S. economy. The discount factor of 0.99 implies an annual real interest rate of about 4 percent, the capital share is 0.33, and the depreciation rate of 0.025 corresponds to 10 percent per year. The labour-disutility parameter is chosen so that households work one third of their time in the steady state. The productivity process has persistence 0.95 and innovation standard deviation 0.007, consistent with estimates for the Solow residual.

How to read it Blocks. var declares the endogenous variables, varexo the shocks, parameters the parameters. The model block contains one equation per endogenous variable. Variables dated (+1) are expectations, (-1) lags. Capital k is the end-of-period stock, so production uses k(-1) . Logs. Writing exp(y) wherever \(Y\) appears makes y the log of output, so all results are percentage deviations from the steady state. steady_state_model . The steady state is computed analytically, which is faster and more reliable than a numerical solver. The parameter psi is set here so that hours equal 1/3: a standard way to calibrate a parameter to a target. steady and check compute the steady state and verify the Blanchard–Kahn conditions. stoch_simul solves the model by a first-order perturbation and reports moments of HP-filtered variables ( hp_filter=1600 ), comparable with HP-filtered data.
Check the steady state and the solution

How to read it Steady state. A capital–output ratio of about 9.4 (quarterly, so about 2.4 annually), an investment share of about 24% and a consumption share of about 76% are close to the long-run ratios of the U.S. economy. Check these ratios in every model before going further: a wrong steady state invalidates everything after it. Blanchard–Kahn condition. A unique stable solution exists when the number of eigenvalues outside the unit circle equals the number of forward-looking variables. Here they match, so the model is determinate. check stops with an error when they do not; the New Keynesian guide shows such a failure.
Impulse responses to a productivity shock

How to read it A one-standard-deviation productivity shock (0.7%) raises output on impact by more than the shock itself, because hours and capital respond. Investment moves far more than consumption : households smooth consumption and channel the temporary windfall into capital. Hours rise because the wage is temporarily high (intertemporal substitution). These are the qualitative predictions to compare with the data.
Compare the model with the data

How to read it This is the classic RBC table. The model is judged on second moments it was not calibrated to match. Output volatility. The model produces about 80% of the observed volatility of output (1.20% against 1.49%) with productivity shocks alone: the original RBC finding. Relative volatility. As in the data, investment is several times more volatile than output (3.3 times in the model, 4.3 in the data) and consumption less volatile. The model gets the ranking right. Comovement. Consumption and investment are strongly procyclical in both. Failures. The model's consumption is far too smooth (a relative volatility of 0.34 against 0.82 in the data) and its correlations too close to one: with a single shock, everything moves together. These failures motivate the extra shocks and frictions of the medium-scale model.

How to write it: results Figure 1 shows the responses to a one-standard-deviation productivity shock. Output rises on impact by more than productivity itself, as hours and, gradually, the capital stock increase; investment responds several times more strongly than consumption, reflecting households' desire to smooth consumption. Table 2 compares the model's business-cycle moments with HP-filtered U.S. data for 1966–2007. Productivity shocks alone account for most of the observed volatility of output and reproduce the ranking of volatilities: investment is far more volatile than output, and consumption less. The model, however, generates too little volatility in consumption and too much comovement among the aggregates. Common mistakes Timing of capital: Dynare uses end-of-period stocks, so production uses k(-1) . Getting this wrong produces Blanchard–Kahn errors.

Comparing model moments with unfiltered data, or filtering one and not the other. Calibrating a parameter to a moment and then claiming the model “explains” that moment. Solving for the steady state numerically when it has a closed form: a wrong initial value can give a wrong steady state without an error message.
Small Open-Economy New Keynesian Model: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Dynare code, real output and sample text.

Should a small open economy target domestic inflation, CPI inflation, or the exchange rate? Many emerging-market central banks face exactly this choice. Galí and Monacelli (2005) answered it in a New Keynesian model in which home and foreign goods are imperfect substitutes and the home economy is too small to affect the rest of the world. With the parameter values of Cole and Obstfeld (unit elasticities, \(\sigma = \eta = \gamma = 1\) ), the log-linear model reduces to: where \(\tilde y_t = y_t - \bar y^n_t\) is the output gap, \(\bar y^n_t = \Gamma_a a_t\) natural output driven by domestic productivity \(a_t\) , \(\bar r^n_t = -\sigma_\alpha \Gamma_a (1-\rho_a) a_t\) the natural rate, \(\alpha\) the degree of openness, and \(\kappa_\alpha = \lambda(\sigma_\alpha + \varphi)\) .

Four regimes are compared: Regime Rule DIT Strict domestic-inflation targeting: \(\pi_{H,t} = 0\) , the optimal policy in this model DITR Domestic-inflation Taylor rule: \(i_t = \phi_\pi \pi_{H,t}\) CITR CPI-inflation Taylor rule: \(i_t = \phi_\pi \pi_t\) PEG Fixed exchange rate: \(e_t = 0\) Why one model file with a switch The regimes differ in one equation. Writing four files invites inconsistencies. Dynare's macro language ( @#if , @#define ) keeps one file and selects the rule at run time: dynare soe -DRULE=2 .

How to read it The default run uses the domestic-inflation rule ( RULE = 1 ). The model is determinate. Note how the exchange rate enters: the level e appears with a lag, so it is a state variable, and under the peg it is pinned at zero.
Impulse responses under the three regimes

How to read it A domestic productivity improvement lowers home production costs and raises natural output. DIT (the optimum). Domestic inflation stays at zero and output rises one-for-one with its natural level. The interest rate falls with the natural rate and the currency depreciates: the terms of trade worsen so that foreigners buy the extra home output. The exchange rate does all the adjusting, as it would with flexible prices. DITR. The simple rule cuts the rate too little, so output rises by less than its natural level, the output gap is negative and domestic inflation falls. CITR. CPI inflation includes the rise in import prices from the depreciation, so it falls less than domestic inflation and the central bank cuts the rate even less at first. Output rises less, but the gap closes faster.
Impulse responses under the three regimes
PEG. The nominal exchange rate cannot move, so the relative price must adjust through sticky domestic prices. Domestic inflation falls and the adjustment is slow.

How to read it The table follows Table 1 of Galí and Monacelli (2005). The welfare loss is their second-order approximation to household welfare, which penalises domestic-inflation variance (price dispersion) and output-gap variance: The optimum. Strict domestic-inflation targeting has zero loss: it reproduces the flexible-price allocation. Every simple rule falls short of it. Among the simple rules , the CPI rule does best in this calibration and the domestic-inflation Taylor rule worst, with the peg close to it. The ranking of simple rules is not universal: it depends on the response coefficient, the shock process and the degree of openness. Re-run the comparison under your own calibration rather than quoting a ranking.

The exchange rate has a unit root under the floating regimes (its level drifts after every shock), so its unconditional standard deviation is infinite and Dynare reports NaN . Under the peg it is zero by construction. Caveat. These results rest on the Cole–Obstfeld assumptions, complete risk sharing and the absence of foreign-currency debt. Emerging-market models with currency mismatch or imported-input costs can change them substantially.

How to write it: results Figure 1 compares the responses to a domestic productivity shock under three monetary regimes. Under domestic-inflation targeting, the nominal exchange rate depreciates and the terms of trade adjust, leaving domestic inflation and the output gap nearly unchanged. Under an exchange-rate peg, the adjustment of relative prices must occur through sticky domestic prices, generating larger fluctuations in domestic inflation and the output gap. Strict domestic-inflation targeting replicates the flexible-price allocation and is optimal. Among simple rules, a CPI-inflation Taylor rule yields a smaller welfare loss than a domestic-inflation Taylor rule or a peg in our calibration. Common mistakes Writing the Phillips curve in CPI inflation. Firms set domestic prices; CPI inflation follows from the definition.

Forgetting that the exchange-rate level is a state variable once a peg is possible. Ranking regimes by the volatility of the variables they target. Rank them by a welfare criterion. Using the Cole–Obstfeld special case and then generalising the ranking to economies with incomplete markets or dollar debt.
The Zero Lower Bound with OccBin
The Zero Lower Bound with OccBin: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Dynare code, real output and sample text.
The Zero Lower Bound with OccBin

How much deeper is a recession when the central bank cannot cut the interest rate below zero? Between 2008 and 2015, and again in 2020, policy rates in many economies sat at or near zero, and a central question of macroeconomics became how the zero lower bound (ZLB) changes the effects of shocks. The model is the three-equation New Keynesian model of the NK guide, with one change: the interest rate follows the Taylor rule only when the rule prescribes a rate above the bound. Variables are deviations from the steady state, so the bound is \(\underline{i} = -i^*\) , minus the steady-state nominal rate. With a 2% annual real rate and a 2% inflation target, \(i^* = 4\%\) a year, 1% a quarter.
The Zero Lower Bound with OccBin

How OccBin works OccBin treats the model as two linear models, one for each regime: the Taylor rule (constraint slack) and \(i_t = \underline{i}\) (constraint binding). For a given path of shocks it guesses in which periods the constraint binds, solves the model backwards through time with the right regime in each period, checks whether the guess is consistent (the constraint binds exactly when the shadow rate is below the bound), and iterates until it is. The solution is nonlinear globally but piecewise linear, and expectations take into account that the economy will leave the ZLB later.
The Zero Lower Bound with OccBin

How to read it Two versions of the policy equation , tagged with the same name and with relax and bind , tell Dynare which equation holds in which regime. occbin_constraints states when the constraint binds and when it is relaxed, in terms of model variables. Using the shadow rate inot makes the condition transparent. shocks(surprise) defines the shock path for the simulation: an unexpected fall in the natural rate in period 1. occbin_solver computes the piecewise-linear solution and, for comparison, the linear solution that ignores the bound. The check output confirms that the model is determinate in the regime where the Taylor rule applies.
The Zero Lower Bound with OccBin
Compare the OccBin and the linear solution

How to read it The linear solution lets the interest rate fall below the bound, by about 3.6 percentage points (annualised) beyond the steady-state rate of 4%, so it implies a negative nominal rate. With the ZLB , the rate stays at the bound for a few quarters. The real interest rate rises as inflation falls, the opposite of what the economy needs, so the output gap and inflation fall much further than in the linear solution. Expectations matter. Households and firms know the rate will be stuck for a while, which lowers expected inflation and raises the expected real rate even before the bound binds: the amplification comes partly from the future.
The Zero Lower Bound with OccBin
Compare the OccBin and the linear solution
This is why the ZLB is a nonlinearity a linear model cannot approximate: the size of a recession depends on whether the constraint binds.
The Zero Lower Bound with OccBin
Policy question: does a higher inflation target help?

How to read it A higher inflation target raises the steady-state nominal rate and so gives the central bank more room to cut before reaching zero. The same shock then produces a shorter spell at the bound and a milder recession: with a 4% target instead of 2%, the trough of the output gap is about 45% shallower. This is the argument of Blanchard, Dell'Ariccia and Mauro (2010) for raising inflation targets. The model leaves out the costs of higher steady-state inflation (price dispersion, relative-price distortions), which a welfare analysis must add before drawing a policy conclusion.
The Zero Lower Bound with OccBin

How to write it: results We solve the model with the occasionally binding zero lower bound using the OccBin algorithm of Guerrieri and Iacoviello (2015), as implemented in Dynare. Following a large adverse shock to the natural rate of interest, the policy rate reaches the bound and remains there for several quarters. Relative to a linear solution that ignores the bound, the fall in the output gap is more than twice as large and the fall in inflation substantially deeper, because the real interest rate rises as inflation falls. A higher inflation target shortens the spell at the bound and attenuates the recession. Common mistakes Simulating a ZLB episode with a linear model and truncating the interest rate afterwards: expectations are then wrong.
The Zero Lower Bound with OccBin

Writing the bound in levels when the model is in deviations (or the reverse). The bound in deviations is minus the steady-state rate. Forgetting that OccBin is a perfect-foresight solution conditional on the shock path: agents do not take into account the probability of future ZLB episodes. Global methods do, at a much higher computational cost. Estimating a model on ZLB-era data with a linear filter. Dynare's OccBin also provides a piecewise Kalman filter for estimation.
Explosive Bubble Tests (SADF and GSADF): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Did prices ever grow faster than a random walk? For a series \(y_t\) the ADF regression is and a unit root ( \(\rho = 0\) ) is tested against the right-tail alternative \(\rho > 0\) : an explosive root, growth that feeds on itself. Three statistics use different windows: Statistic Windows ADF The whole sample SADF (Phillips, Wu and Yu 2011) Sup of the ADF over windows that start at the first observation and end at \(r_2\) GSADF (Phillips, Shi and Yu 2015) Sup over all windows \([r_1, r_2]\) with at least \(r_0 = T(0.01 + 1.8/\sqrt T)\) observations: it can find several bubbles The backward SADF at \(r_2\) , \(\text{BSADF}(r_2) = \sup_{r_1}\text{ADF}_{r_1}^{r_2}\) , is compared with its critical value at every date to date-stamp the episodes: an episode starts when BSADF crosses above its critical value and ends when it falls below. Critical values are simulated from random walks (with a drift that vanishes with the sample size) of the same length, so they depend on the sample and the minimum window.

A rise in the price can reflect rising fundamentals. The price-dividend ratio holds dividends fixed, so an explosive ratio is harder to attribute to fundamentals. How to write it: the model We test for explosive behaviour in the monthly price-dividend ratio of the S&P 500 with the SADF and GSADF tests of Phillips, Wu and Yu (2011) and Phillips, Shi and Yu (2015). The ADF regression has a constant and no lags, the minimum window is the rule \(T(0.01 + 1.8/\sqrt T)\) , and critical values come from 200 simulated random walks with a vanishing drift of the same length. Episodes are dated where the backward SADF exceeds its 95% critical value for at least log(T) consecutive months.

How to read it The series has 1,830 months from January 1871 to June 2023. The price-dividend ratio averages 28.8; its lowest value is 7.2 (June 1932, the bottom of the Depression) and its highest 90.2 (August 2000). It stood at 33.3 in September 1929, 38.2 in August 1987 and 77.4 in December 2021. A ratio is used because it holds dividends, the simplest measure of fundamentals, fixed.

How to read it Both tests reject a unit root against an explosive alternative with Monte Carlo p-values below 0.005 (none of the 200 random walks had a statistic as large). The SADF statistic is 3.46, against a 5% critical value of 1.66 and a 1% value of 2.25. The GSADF is 4.16, against 2.40 (5%) and 2.64 (1%). The GSADF is the more powerful test when there is more than one bubble, and the data show several. The note gives the minimum window, 95 months, from the rule \(T(0.01 + 1.8/\sqrt T)\) , and the number of simulated random walks.

How to read it The backward SADF dates seven episodes. The earliest are 1879 to 1880 (10 months) and 1917 to 1918 (8 months). The 1920s bubble runs from October 1928 to October 1929 (13 months, peak statistic 2.73): the test dates the bubble to the year before the crash. Two postwar episodes follow, 1955 to 1956 (13 months) and 1958 to 1959 (10 months), then the pre-crash run-up of January to September 1987 (9 months, 2.49). The longest and strongest episode is the dot-com bubble, October 1996 to August 2001, 59 months with a peak statistic of 4.16, which is also the GSADF statistic. The two charts show the BSADF sequence against its 95% critical value and the ratio.
Robustness: the minimum window and the price alone

How to read it Minimum window. With a minimum window of 100 months the episodes are essentially the same (1879 to 1880, 1917 to 1918, 1928 to 1929, 1955 to 1956, 1958 to 1959, 1987 and 1996 to 2001) and a short episode from June 2021 to January 2022 appears. With a window of 60 months more short episodes appear (1886 to 1887, 1945 to 1946, 2008 to 2009), and the GSADF critical values rise (5%: 2.62): a shorter minimum window makes the test pick up shorter and weaker episodes. The big three, 1929, 1987 and 1996 to 2001, are present for every choice. The price alone. For the price level the GSADF statistic is 19.8 against a 5% critical value of 2.43, and the episodes cover most of the postwar period: from 1953 to 1974 and from 1982 to 2008 and again from 2009. A price series that grows with the economy and with dividends will look explosive in any long expansion; the ratio is the better test of a bubble, because dividends grow and the ratio does not need to.

How to read it For random walks of 300 observations the GSADF rejects at the 5% level in 2 of 40 samples, which is within the sampling range for a 5% test (the standard error is about 3.5 percentage points). With an explosive episode of 40 periods (3% growth a period, starting at period 150) followed by a collapse, the test detects it in all 20 samples and the median dated start is period 152. The test suite checks the ADF window statistics against statsmodels, the detection of a simulated bubble and the rejection rate under the null.

How to write it: results We test for explosive behaviour in the monthly price-dividend ratio of the S&P 500, January 1871 to June 2023 (1,830 months). The right-tailed unit root tests reject a random walk: the SADF is 3.46 (5% critical value 1.66) and the GSADF is 4.16 (5% critical value 2.40, 1% value 2.64), with critical values from 200 simulated random walks and a minimum window of 95 months. Date-stamping with the backward SADF gives seven episodes: 1879 to 1880, 1917 to 1918, October 1928 to October 1929, 1955 to 1956, 1958 to 1959, January to September 1987 and October 1996 to August 2001 (59 months, the strongest). The three large episodes are found with minimum windows of 60 and 100 months. The price alone is explosive in most of the postwar period, which is why the ratio is used. In simulations the GSADF rejects 2 of 40 random walks at the 5% level and detects a simulated bubble in 20 of 20 samples, dating its start within about 2 periods.

Factor-Pricing Regressions and the GRS Test

Do the factors price the assets? The factor model is where \(f_t\) are excess returns of the factors (for the CAPM, the market). If the factors price the assets, every \(\alpha_i\) is zero. A t-test on one alpha says little when there are many assets, so Gibbons, Ross and Shanken (1989) test all alphas at once: where \(\hat\Sigma\) is the residual covariance, \(\hat\mu\) the mean of the factors and \(\hat\Omega\) their covariance. The denominator is the squared Sharpe ratio of the factors; the numerator measures how much the alphas would add to it. How to write it: the model We test whether the market factor prices three industry portfolios by regressing each portfolio's monthly excess return on the market excess return. The alpha of each portfolio is tested with Newey-West standard errors, and the hypothesis that all alphas are jointly zero is tested with the Gibbons, Ross and Shanken (1989) F test, which is exact for normal homoskedastic errors.
Factor-Pricing Regressions and the GRS Test

How to read it The panel has 516 months, January 1960 to December 2002. The market excess return averages 0.42% a month with a standard deviation of 4.48, a monthly Sharpe ratio of 0.093. The food portfolio has the highest mean (0.66) and the lowest volatility (4.54); durables and construction are more volatile (5.80 and 5.79). The returns are already excess returns, so no risk-free rate is subtracted.
Factor-Pricing Regressions and the GRS Test

How to read it All three portfolios load strongly on the market. The beta of food is 0.78 (Newey-West standard error 0.056): a defensive industry that moves less than the market. Durables and construction have betas of 1.11 (0.036) and 1.16 (0.038): cyclical industries that amplify it. The R-squared is 0.60 for food and 0.74 and 0.80 for the other two, so the market explains most of the variation in each. The alpha is the average monthly return the market does not explain. For food it is 0.34 percentage points a month (t = 2.42, p = 0.016), about 4% a year, which is significant on its own. For durables (0.06, t = 0.48) and construction ( \(-0.05\) , t = \(-0.43\) ) it is indistinguishable from zero. The summary shows the joint GRS test (F = 2.61, p = 0.051) and the Sharpe ratios discussed below.
Factor-Pricing Regressions and the GRS Test

How to read it The GRS test asks whether the three alphas are zero together: F(3, 512) = 2.61, p = 0.051. The chi-square form of the same test gives 7.89 (p = 0.048). The market factor does not quite price the three portfolios at the 5% level: the rejection is marginal and comes from food. The chart shows each alpha with its 95% interval; only food's interval excludes zero. The Sharpe ratio explains the size of the effect. The market alone has a monthly Sharpe ratio of 0.093; adding the three alphas would raise the best attainable ratio to 0.155. That is the gain an investor could get by trading on the pricing errors, if they were real.
Factor-Pricing Regressions and the GRS Test

How to read it The rolling 60-month beta of food is not constant. It was 1.01 in the first window (ending 1964), reached its highest value, 1.09, in December 1975, and fell to 0.29 in the last window (ending December 2002). The food industry became much less sensitive to the market over the sample, a reminder that a single full-sample beta averages over very different periods and that an alpha estimated on the whole sample partly reflects the changing beta.
Factor-Pricing Regressions and the GRS Test

How to read it Market timing. Adding the squared market return (Treynor-Mazuy) leaves the betas unchanged (food 0.78, durables 1.11, construction 1.16) and the coefficients on the squared term are tiny (7.5e-05, 0.0021 and 0.0027 per squared percentage point; the squared market return is as large as 100 to 1,000 in crisis months), so there is no sign of market timing. The food alpha stays at 0.34 (p = 0.024) and the joint test is a little weaker (F = 2.19, p = 0.088). Sub-periods. The joint test splits the sample in two: for 1960 to 1981 F = 0.44 (p = 0.72), for 1982 to 2002 F = 3.51 (p = 0.016). The mispricing is a feature of the second half, when the food beta fell from 0.92 to 0.65. This is a caution for the write-up: a rejection of the model on the whole sample can come from one period.

Diagnostics: size and power of the GRS test

How to read it In 100 simulated samples of 240 months with five assets and no alpha, the 5% GRS test rejects in 6% of the samples, so its size is right. When every asset has a true alpha of 0.35 percentage points a month, it rejects in all 100: the test has ample power at this sample size. (The sampling error on a rejection rate from 100 samples is about 2 to 4 points.) The test suite also checks the alphas and betas against statsmodels with Newey-West errors, the GRS statistic against its formula and the multi-factor case with a known alpha and betas.
Factor-Pricing Regressions and the GRS Test

How to write it: results We regress the monthly excess returns of three U.S. industry portfolios on the market excess return, January 1960 to December 2002 (516 months). The market betas are 0.78 for food, 1.11 for durables and 1.16 for construction (Newey-West standard errors 0.04 to 0.06), and the market explains 60% to 80% of the variance. The alpha is 0.34 percentage points a month for food (t = 2.42, p = 0.016) and is not significantly different from zero for durables (0.06) or construction ( \(-0.05\) ). The GRS test of zero alphas for all three portfolios gives F(3, 512) = 2.61 (p = 0.051); the alphas would raise the monthly Sharpe ratio from 0.093 to 0.155. The result is not due to market timing (the squared market return is insignificant), but it depends on the period: the test does not reject in 1960 to 1981 (p = 0.72) and rejects in 1982 to 2002 (p = 0.016), when the rolling market beta of food fell from about 1.0 to 0.3. The size and power of the test in simulation are 6% and 100%.

Dynamic Conditional Correlation (DCC-GARCH): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Is the correlation between two assets a constant? A constant correlation makes portfolio risk easy to compute, but it is unlikely to be true: diversification tends to fail when it is needed most. The DCC model of Engle (2002) has two steps. First each return follows a univariate GARCH(1,1): Second, the standardised residuals \(z_t\) have the conditional correlation matrix \(R_t\) obtained from where \(\bar S\) is the unconditional correlation of the standardised residuals. The parameter \(a\) says how much the correlation reacts to yesterday's joint shock, \(b\) how persistent it is. If \(a = b = 0\) the correlation is constant. How to write it: the model We estimate a DCC-GARCH model (Engle 2002) for the daily returns of three stocks. In the first step each return has a GARCH(1,1) model estimated by Gaussian quasi-maximum likelihood. In the second step the correlation of the standardised residuals follows the DCC recursion, estimated by maximum likelihood with the first-step estimates as given. We test constant correlation (a = b = 0) with a likelihood-ratio test, and check that the standardised residuals have no remaining ARCH.

How to read it The three stocks have daily volatilities of 1.75% (IBM), 1.37% (GE) and 1.29% (Mobil) against 0.78% for the market, over 2,528 days from January 1989 to December 1998. The unconditional correlations are moderate: 0.33 for IBM and GE, 0.30 for GE and Mobil and 0.16 for IBM and Mobil. A single number per pair is what the DCC model replaces with a path.

How to read it Step 1. Each GARCH(1,1) is highly persistent: \(\alpha + \beta\) is 0.988 for IBM, 0.982 for GE and 0.981 for Mobil, with long-run daily volatilities of 1.9%, 1.4% and 1.3%. The Ljung-Box p-values of the squared standardised residuals are 0.74, 0.16 and 0.025: there is no remaining ARCH for IBM and GE, and a slight remainder for Mobil. Step 2. The correlation recursion has \(a = 0.0093\) (standard error 0.0023, t = 4.1) and \(b = 0.9869\) (0.0034). The news term is small and significant and the persistence is very high: \(a + b = 0.996\) , so a shock to the correlation takes a long time to die out (the half-life is about \(\ln 0.5 / \ln 0.996\) , roughly 180 trading days). The standard errors treat the first-step estimates as known.

How to read it The conditional correlation of IBM and GE averages 0.31 (close to the unconditional 0.32) but ranges from 0.04 to 0.60, with 90% of days between 0.10 and 0.53. IBM and Mobil range from \(-0.07\) to 0.44 and GE and Mobil from 0.02 to 0.72. The likelihood-ratio test of a constant correlation gives 109.9 with 2 degrees of freedom (p < 0.0001); the parameters are on the boundary under the null, which makes the usual p-value conservative, so the rejection stands. The charts show the DCC correlation against the constant one.
Do correlations rise when the market is volatile?

How to read it On the 10% of days with the highest recent market volatility (the 10-day mean absolute return of the market index), the IBM-GE correlation averages 0.475; on the calmest half of the days it averages 0.268. The correlation between the market's recent volatility and the DCC correlation is 0.50. Correlations are higher when the market is turbulent, the feature that makes diversification weaker in a crisis; a constant-correlation model misses it. (The check uses every fifth day of the sample, as in the chart.)
Robustness: the pair and the sub-sample

How to read it Estimating the IBM-GE pair alone gives almost the same dynamics ( \(a = 0.009\) , \(b = 0.989\) ) and a correlation range of 0.02 to 0.63. Splitting the sample in half shows that the dynamics are not stable: in the first half \(a = 0.010\) and \(b = 0.987\) ; in the second half \(a = 0.034\) and \(b = 0.905\) , a correlation that reacts more and fades faster. The likelihood-ratio test still rejects a constant correlation in both halves (47.1 and 18.0). If you use the correlation for risk, re-estimate it on recent data and report both halves.
Diagnostics: does the estimator recover the dynamics?

How to read it In 10 simulated series of 3,000 days with true \(a = 0.05\) and \(b = 0.90\) , the mean estimates are \(a = 0.052\) and \(b = 0.873\) , with standard deviations across samples of 0.013 and 0.037. The news coefficient is recovered and the persistence is slightly underestimated, which is a known bias of the DCC estimator when the true persistence is lower than 0.98. The test suite also checks the first-step GARCH estimates against the arch package (parameters within 0.01 and log-likelihood within 1) and that a constant correlation of 0.5 is recovered.

How to write it: results We estimate a DCC-GARCH model for the daily returns of IBM, GE and Mobil, January 1989 to December 1998 (2,528 days). The univariate GARCH(1,1) models are persistent ( \(\alpha + \beta\) between 0.98 and 0.99) and leave no ARCH in the standardised residuals of IBM and GE. The correlation recursion has \(a = 0.0093\) (s.e. 0.0023) and \(b = 0.9869\) (0.0034). A likelihood-ratio test rejects a constant correlation (LR = 109.9, 2 df, p < 0.0001). The conditional correlation of IBM and GE averages 0.31 and ranges from 0.04 to 0.60; it is 0.48 on the 10% most volatile days of the market and 0.27 on the calmest half. The dynamics differ between sub-samples ( \(a = 0.010\) and 0.034 in the first and second half). In simulation the estimator recovers the news parameter (0.052 for a true 0.05) and slightly underestimates the persistence (0.873 for 0.90).

Portfolio Optimisation and Out-of-Sample Comparison: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Does optimising beat not optimising? Given mean returns \(\mu\) and a covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) , Markowitz (1952) chooses weights \(w\) with \(\sum_i w_i = 1\) : Strategy Weights Equal weights \(w_i = 1/N\) Minimum variance \(\min_w w'\Sigma w\) ; unconstrained solution \(w \propto \Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1\) Maximum Sharpe ratio \(\max_w (w'\mu - r_f)/\sqrt{w'\Sigma w}\) ; unconstrained solution \(w \propto \Sigma^{-1}(\mu - r_f)\) Risk parity each asset contributes the same share \(w_i(\Sigma w)_i/w'\Sigma w = 1/N\) The problem is that \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\) are estimated, and the optimiser puts large weights where the estimates are most favourable (and most wrong). Three remedies are standard: shrink the covariance matrix towards a structured target (Ledoit and Wolf 2004), forbid short positions , and use strategies that need no means (minimum variance, risk parity, equal weights). The test of any of them is the out-of-sample performance: estimate on a rolling window, hold the weights for a month, and compare the realised returns.

How to write it: the model We compare four strategies on the daily returns of four European stock indexes: equal weights, minimum variance, maximum Sharpe ratio and risk parity, all long-only and estimated with a Ledoit-Wolf shrunk covariance matrix. The sampling uncertainty of the weights is measured by a bootstrap that resamples the periods with replacement. The out-of-sample comparison estimates the weights on the previous 250 days, holds them for 21 days and rolls forward; the Sharpe-ratio differences from equal weights are tested with the Jobson-Korkie test with Memmel's correction.

How to read it The sample has 1,859 daily log returns for the German DAX, Swiss SMI, French CAC and British FTSE from 1991 to 1998, a period in which all four rose strongly (the DAX from 1,614 to 5,474). The SMI has the best annualised Sharpe ratio (1.4), the CAC the worst (0.63) and the FTSE the lowest volatility (0.80% a day). The markets are highly correlated (0.58 to 0.73), so diversification gains are limited.

How to read it In sample, the maximum-Sharpe portfolio puts 93% in the SMI (weights: DAX 1%, SMI 93%, CAC 0%, FTSE 5%), earns 20.1% a year with volatility 14.3% and a Sharpe ratio of 1.40; its effective number of assets is only 1.1. The minimum-variance portfolio holds the two least volatile markets (SMI 33%, FTSE 67%), with volatility 12.0% and Sharpe 1.18. Equal weights and risk parity are spread across all four assets (effective number about 4) with Sharpe ratios of 1.12 and 1.14. The maximum-Sharpe portfolio looks best because it is the one fitted to this sample.

How to read it The bootstrap shows how little the maximum-Sharpe weights are determined by the data. The SMI weight has a 95% interval from 0.24 to 1.00; the DAX and FTSE weights range from 0 to 0.60 and 0.56. The CAC weight is below 1% in 92% of the resamples and the DAX weight in 59%: the optimiser puts the money in whichever market looked best in each resample. This is the estimation-error problem: means are estimated imprecisely (a daily mean has a standard error of about 0.02 percentage points, a third of its size), and the optimiser acts on the noise. The chart plots the weights of the four strategies.
The honest test: out of sample

How to read it Out of sample, the picture is different. All four strategies earn very similar Sharpe ratios: 1.18 for equal weights, 1.20 for minimum variance, 1.19 for maximum Sharpe and 1.21 for risk parity. The in-sample Sharpe ratio of the maximum-Sharpe portfolio, 1.40, falls to 1.19 out of sample. None of the differences from equal weights is statistically significant (z between 0.05 and 1.09; p between 0.28 and 0.96). The optimised portfolios differ in how they get there: the maximum-Sharpe portfolio trades 40% of the portfolio at each monthly rebalancing (turnover 0.40), minimum variance 9% and risk parity only 1.7%, which matters if there are trading costs. Minimum variance and risk parity reduce volatility (12.0% and 13.0% against 13.3%) at a small cost in return.
Robustness: shorting, shrinkage and the window

How to read it Short positions. Allowing short positions with the sample covariance matrix wrecks the maximum-Sharpe portfolio: volatility of 140% a year, a Sharpe ratio of 0.04 and a turnover of 10 times the portfolio at each rebalancing, because the unconstrained solution takes huge leveraged positions on noisy means. Minimum variance, which needs no means, is unaffected (Sharpe 1.22). Shrinkage. With long-only positions and the sample covariance, the results are very close to those with shrinkage; with four assets and 250 days the covariance matrix is well estimated, and shrinkage matters more when the number of assets is large. Window. With a 500-day window the Sharpe ratios are 1.33 (equal weights), 1.31 (minimum variance), 1.13 (maximum Sharpe) and 1.35 (risk parity); with a 120-day window they are 1.24, 1.27, 1.00 and 1.27. The strategy that uses means is the worst in both and gets worse as the window shortens, which is what estimation error predicts. The ranking of the other three changes with the window, a sign that their differences are noise.
Diagnostics: the estimation-error problem in a simulation

How to read it In a simulation with 20 assets (best possible Sharpe ratio 2.32), the true Sharpe ratio of a portfolio estimated from 250 days of data is 1.74 for equal weights, 1.83 for minimum variance and 1.05 for the maximum-Sharpe weights, averaged over 200 samples. With many assets and a short sample, the portfolio that uses the estimated means is by far the worst, even though it is the optimal one for the sample: a result in the spirit of DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal (2009). The test suite checks the unconstrained weights against the closed forms \(\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1\) and \(\Sigma^{-1}\mu\) , the equalisation of risk contributions in risk parity and the out-of-sample equal-weight returns against a manual calculation.

How to write it: results We compare four long-only strategies on the daily returns of the DAX, SMI, CAC and FTSE, 1991 to 1998 (1,859 days), with a Ledoit-Wolf covariance matrix. In sample, the maximum-Sharpe portfolio has an annualised Sharpe ratio of 1.40, but its weights are imprecise (the SMI weight is 0.93 with a bootstrap 95% interval of 0.24 to 1.00). Estimating on a rolling 250-day window and holding for 21 days, the out-of-sample Sharpe ratios are 1.18 (equal weights), 1.20 (minimum variance), 1.19 (maximum Sharpe) and 1.21 (risk parity); none differs significantly from equal weights (Jobson-Korkie p between 0.28 and 0.96), and the maximum-Sharpe portfolio trades 40% of the portfolio a month against 2% for risk parity. Allowing short positions makes the maximum-Sharpe portfolio unusable (volatility 140%, Sharpe 0.04). In a simulation with 20 assets and 250 days of data the maximum-Sharpe weights deliver a true Sharpe ratio of 1.05 against 1.74 for equal weights.

Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall

How bad can a bad day be? The value at risk at level \(p\) is the return quantile \(\text{VaR}_t\) with \(\Pr(r_t < \text{VaR}_t \mid \mathcal F_{t-1}) = p\) , and the expected shortfall is the mean return below it: Each model forecasts the conditional distribution of tomorrow's return: Model Forecast of the distribution Historical simulation The empirical distribution of the last \(w\) returns Normal, rolling window Normal with the mean and standard deviation of the last \(w\) returns EWMA Normal with variance \(\sigma_t^2 = \lambda\sigma_{t-1}^2 + (1 - \lambda)r_{t-1}^2\) (RiskMetrics, \(\lambda = 0.94\) ) GARCH(1,1), t errors Variance from a GARCH(1,1) fitted on the first window, and a t distribution for the standardised residuals
Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall

GARCH filtered historical simulation The same variance, and the empirical quantile of the standardised residuals The forecasts are out of sample : no forecast uses data from its own day or later, and the GARCH parameters are estimated once on the first window. A forecast is violated when the return falls below it. Backtests ask three questions: Test Null hypothesis Kupiec (unconditional coverage) The violation rate equals \(p\) Christoffersen independence A violation today does not make one tomorrow more likely Conditional coverage Both together (chi-square with 2 degrees of freedom) How to write it: the model We forecast the one-day 99% value at risk and expected shortfall of the market index with five models: historical simulation on a rolling window of 500 days, a normal distribution with the rolling mean and standard deviation, the RiskMetrics EWMA with decay 0.94, a GARCH(1,1) with t errors estimated on the first 500 days and filtered forward, and a filtered historical simulation that uses the empirical quantile of the GARCH residuals. All forecasts are out of sample. We test the violation rate with Kupiec's likelihood-ratio test, the independence of the violations with Christoffersen's test, and their combination, and compare the realised losses on violation days with the expected shortfall forecast.
Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall

How to read it The sample has 2,528 trading days, 3 January 1989 to 31 December 1998. Daily returns average 0.068% with a standard deviation of 0.78%, the worst day is \(-6.59\) % and the best is +4.82%. The distribution is skewed to the left (skewness \(-0.70\) ) and has fat tails (excess kurtosis 7.66). Returns more than three standard deviations from the mean occur on 1.27% of days, almost five times the 0.27% that a normal distribution gives, and the 1% quantile of all returns is \(-2.06\) %. This is why a normal model underestimates the risk.
Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall

How to read it There are 2,028 out-of-sample days (the first 500 are the estimation window), so a correct 99% model should be violated on about 20 of them. Historical simulation is violated 29 times (1.43%), the rolling normal 48 times (2.37%) and the EWMA 47 times (2.32%): the two normal models understate the risk by more than half. The GARCH(1,1) with t errors, whose fitted t distribution has 4.7 degrees of freedom, is violated 20 times (0.99%), exactly the target. The GARCH filtered historical simulation is violated only 12 times (0.59%), so it is too conservative. The mean VaR shows why: \(-1.54\) % for the rolling normal, \(-1.81\) % for historical simulation, \(-1.98\) % for the GARCH-t and \(-2.21\) % for the filtered simulation. The mean expected shortfall follows the same order. On violation days the average return is below the expected shortfall forecast for the normal models (the ratio of realised to forecast shortfall is 1.28 and 1.26) and close to it for the other three (1.01 to 1.03). The quantile loss, which rewards a forecast of the quantile for being accurate and not only for being safe, is lowest for the GARCH-t (0.0288) and the filtered simulation (0.0292).
Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall

How to read it Kupiec's test rejects a violation rate of 1% for the rolling normal and the EWMA (p < 0.0001), does not reject it for the GARCH-t (p = 0.95), and is borderline for historical simulation (p = 0.068) and the filtered simulation (p = 0.046, too few violations). The independence test adds that the violations of historical simulation are clustered (p = 0.007), as are those of the two normal models (p = 0.03): after one violation another is more likely, because these models react slowly when volatility rises. The GARCH-t is the only model with independent violations at the 5% level and the only one passing the conditional coverage test comfortably (p = 0.43); the filtered simulation passes it too (p = 0.13).
Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall

How to read it The first chart shows the daily returns with the VaR forecasts of the rolling normal and the GARCH-t. The rolling-window line changes slowly and sits above the GARCH line most of the time; the GARCH line widens in turbulent periods and narrows in calm ones, which is why fewer returns fall below it. The second chart compares the violation rate of each method with the expected 1%: the normal models are more than double, historical simulation is in between and the two GARCH models are at or below the target.
Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall
Robustness: the tail level and the window

How to read it At the 5% level the ranking is different: all methods are close to 5% except the filtered simulation, which is too conservative (3.55%); the rolling normal (5.52%) and EWMA (5.23%) are fine because the normal distribution is accurate in the middle of the distribution. The fat tails matter only far out. At the 1% level the window matters. With a 250-day window every model is violated too often (1.54% to 2.77%): 250 days include only two or three tail observations, and the GARCH parameters estimated on 250 days are imprecise. With 1,000 days the GARCH models are at 1.51% and 1.37%, historical simulation is at 2.03% and the normal models at 2.75% to 3.21%. A long window helps the GARCH models and does not help the others, because they react to the past 1,000 days as slowly as to the past 500.
Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall

How to read it In 20 simulated series from a GARCH(1,1) with t(6) errors, 2,500 days each, the mean violation rate of the 99% VaR is 1.19% for the GARCH-t, 1.34% for historical simulation and 1.84% for the rolling normal. Kupiec's test rejects the rolling normal in 18 of 20 samples, historical simulation in 8 and the GARCH-t in 6. The GARCH-t is the true model here but is still rejected in 6 samples out of 20, more than the 1 expected: the parameters are estimated once on 600 days and an estimation error of that size makes the violation rate drift. This is the usual estimation risk of backtests with few violations (about 20 per sample), and the reason to read the tests together with the violation counts. The test suite also checks the Kupiec statistic and the violation counts against a manual calculation.
Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall

How to write it: results We forecast the one-day 99% value at risk and expected shortfall of the CRSP value-weighted market index on 2,028 out-of-sample days (24 December 1990 to 31 December 1998) with five models. The index has fat tails (excess kurtosis 7.7) and returns beyond three standard deviations occur on 1.27% of days. Out of sample, the rolling normal and the EWMA are violated on 2.37% and 2.32% of days, against the 1% target (Kupiec p < 0.0001), and their violations cluster (independence p = 0.03). Historical simulation is violated on 1.43% (p = 0.068, independence p = 0.007). A GARCH(1,1) with t errors is violated on 0.99% of days (p = 0.95) with independent violations (p = 0.19) and has the lowest quantile loss; the realised loss on violation days is 1.01 times its expected shortfall, against 1.28 for the rolling normal. At the 5% level all models except the filtered simulation are close to nominal, and at 1% the ranking holds for windows of 500 and 1,000 days but not for 250. In simulation, Kupiec's test rejects the rolling normal in 18 of 20 GARCH-t samples.
