Morgan (1996), RiskMetrics Technical Document ; Barone-Adesi, Giannopoulos and Vosper (1999), Journal of Futures Markets ; McNeil and Frey (2000), Journal of Empirical Finance ; Bollerslev (1986), Journal of Econometrics ; Acerbi and Tasche (2002), Journal of Banking and Finance .
Volatility Forecast Evaluation: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Which forecast of tomorrow's variance is best? Five forecasts of the one-day-ahead variance \(h_t\) are compared on the days after the first estimation window: Forecast Definition GARCH(1,1) \(h_t = \omega + \alpha\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta h_{t-1}\) , parameters from the first window EWMA \(h_t = \lambda h_{t-1} + (1 - \lambda)\varepsilon_{t-1}^2\) , \(\lambda = 0.94\) Rolling variance (window \(w\) and 25 days) The sample variance of the previous \(w\) (or 25) returns Constant The variance of the first window The realised variance is not observed. The squared return \(\varepsilon_t^2\) is an unbiased but very noisy proxy. Patton (2011) showed that with a noisy proxy only some losses rank forecasts correctly, among them the QLIKE loss, \(\log h_t + \varepsilon_t^2/h_t\) , and the squared error , \((\varepsilon_t^2 - h_t)^2\) ; the squared error is correct but dominated by a few extreme days. Two tests complete the comparison:

Test What it checks Mincer-Zarnowitz regression \(\varepsilon_t^2 = a + b\,h_t + u_t\) : an unbiased forecast has \(a = 0\) , \(b = 1\) Diebold-Mariano (Diebold and Mariano 1995) Whether the average loss of two forecasts differs, with a Newey-West variance for the serial correlation of the loss differences How to write it: the model We compare out-of-sample one-day variance forecasts from a GARCH(1,1) estimated on the first 500 days, the RiskMetrics EWMA with decay 0.94, rolling 500-day and 25-day sample variances and a constant. The squared demeaned return is the variance proxy. Forecasts are ranked by the QLIKE loss and the squared error, bias is tested with Mincer-Zarnowitz regressions with Newey-West standard errors, and differences from the EWMA benchmark are tested with Diebold-Mariano statistics with 10 lags.

How to read it The squared return is a very noisy proxy for the variance: its mean is \(6.06 \times 10^{-5}\) , and the largest value is 72 times the mean (the worst day of the sample, \(-6.6\) %). It is still informative: the autocorrelations of squared returns at lags 1 to 5 are 0.21, 0.15, 0.08, 0.12 and 0.20, the volatility clustering that the models exploit. There are 2,528 trading days, 2,028 of them forecast out of sample.

How to read it The EWMA has the lowest QLIKE loss ( \(-8.937\) ), followed by the GARCH(1,1) ( \(-8.888\) ), the 25-day variance ( \(-8.886\) ), the 500-day variance ( \(-8.853\) ) and the constant ( \(-8.732\) ); the summary reports the best forecast by QLIKE. The squared-error losses (MSE) of the GARCH and the EWMA are almost identical (3.315 and 3.319, in units of \(10^{-8}\) ) and the others are higher (3.42 to 3.59). The R-squared of the Mincer-Zarnowitz regression is small for every forecast (at most 0.087) because the proxy is noisy, so the ranking matters more than the level. The chart compares the volatility forecasts (annualised, in percent) with the absolute return.

How to read it An unbiased forecast has intercept 0 and slope 1 in the regression of the squared return on the forecast. The EWMA has a slope of 0.79 (standard error 0.15) and the joint test does not reject at 5% (p = 0.060). The GARCH(1,1) has a slope of 1.55 (0.20) and a negative intercept: a joint rejection (p = 0.0001), because its parameters were fixed on the first 500 days and the persistence of volatility changed afterwards. The 25-day variance has a slope of 0.64 (0.14) and is rejected (p = 0.0005): it reacts too strongly to the latest days, so its forecasts are more dispersed than the true variance. The 500-day variance has a slope of 1.42 (0.37) but a wide interval and is not rejected (p = 0.34), which is low power more than evidence of unbiasedness. The constant has no variation to regress on.

How to read it Against the EWMA, a positive statistic means a larger loss. On QLIKE the constant (3.37, p < 0.001) and the 25-day variance (4.00, p < 0.001) are clearly worse, the GARCH (1.76, p = 0.079) and the 500-day variance (1.89, p = 0.059) are worse at the 10% level only. On the squared error, which is dominated by a few days, only the 25-day variance differs significantly from the EWMA (2.40, p = 0.017). The two losses agree that the 25-day and constant forecasts are not better, and disagree about the others because the squared error has almost no power against the larger days; this is the reason to prefer QLIKE.
Robustness: the window and the benchmark

How to read it With a 250-day window the GARCH, whose parameters come from only 250 observations, is much worse (QLIKE \(-8.690\) against \(-8.883\) for the EWMA) and the 250-day variance is at \(-8.841\) ; with a 1,000-day window the EWMA is still the best ( \(-8.946\) ), followed by the GARCH ( \(-8.899\) ) and the 25-day variance ( \(-8.888\) ), and the 1,000-day variance and the constant are the worst ( \(-8.684\) and \(-8.681\) ). Taking the GARCH as the benchmark, the EWMA is better (DM \(-1.76\) , p = 0.079), the constant is worse (3.27, p = 0.001 on QLIKE; p = 0.047 on the squared error), and the 500-day and 25-day variances do not differ (p = 0.40 and 0.95). The EWMA has no parameters to estimate, which is why it is hard to beat in a sample with a structural change.
Diagnostics: does QLIKE pick the right model?

How to read it In 20 simulated series from a GARCH(1,1) with t(6) errors (3,000 days, window 600) the GARCH has the lowest QLIKE in 15 samples and the EWMA in the other 5, and no other forecast is ever the best: the loss ranks the true model first most of the time even with a squared-return proxy and a short window, but not always. With 5 samples in 20 going to the EWMA, a single sample of real data can reverse the ranking, which is why the Diebold-Mariano p-values should be read with the losses. The tests check the QLIKE and squared-error computations against a manual calculation, the Mincer-Zarnowitz slope of a correct GARCH forecast on simulated GARCH data and that the Diebold-Mariano test sides with the better forecast.

How to write it: results We compare five one-day variance forecasts of the CRSP market index on 2,028 out-of-sample days (December 1990 to December 1998), using the squared return as the proxy. The EWMA (decay 0.94) has the lowest QLIKE loss ( \(-8.937\) ); the GARCH(1,1) estimated on the first 500 days follows ( \(-8.888\) ), then the 25-day variance ( \(-8.886\) ), the 500-day variance ( \(-8.853\) ) and a constant ( \(-8.732\) ). Against the EWMA, the constant and the 25-day variance are significantly worse (Diebold-Mariano p < 0.001), the GARCH and the 500-day variance are worse at the 10% level (p = 0.079 and 0.059). Mincer-Zarnowitz regressions reject unbiasedness for the GARCH (slope 1.55, p = 0.0001) and the 25-day variance (slope 0.64, p = 0.0005) and not for the EWMA (slope 0.79, p = 0.060). The ranking is the same with a 1,000-day window; with 250 days the GARCH is much worse. In simulations from a GARCH the true model has the lowest QLIKE in 15 of 20 samples.

References. Patton (2011), Journal of Econometrics ; Diebold and Mariano (1995), Journal of Business and Economic Statistics ; Mincer and Zarnowitz (1969); Andersen and Bollerslev (1998), International Economic Review ; Hansen and Lunde (2005), Journal of Applied Econometrics ; Bollerslev (1986), Journal of Econometrics ; J.P. Morgan (1996), RiskMetrics Technical Document .
Nelson-Siegel Yield Curve: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

What is the shape of the yield curve, and how does it move? The Nelson-Siegel curve for the yield of maturity \(\tau\) is Each factor has a meaning: Factor Loading Interpretation \(\beta_0\) 1 at all maturities Level : the long-term yield \(\beta_1\) Decays from 1 to 0 Slope : the short rate minus the long rate with a negative sign (a negative \(\beta_1\) is a normal, upward-sloping curve) \(\beta_2\) Hump-shaped Curvature : the medium-term yield relative to the short and long ones The parameter \(\lambda\) fixes where the curvature loading peaks (at about \(1.79/\lambda\) months). With \(\lambda\) given, the factors are linear and are estimated by OLS at every date; \(\lambda\) is estimated here by minimising the squared fitting error over the whole sample. Diebold and Li (2006) model the factors as AR(1) processes and forecast the curve by forecasting the factors.

How to write it: the model We fit the Nelson-Siegel curve to the yields of seven maturities (1, 3, 6, 12, 36, 60 and 120 months) at every month, with the decay parameter \(\lambda\) chosen to minimise the squared fitting error over the whole sample. The level, slope and curvature factors are estimated by OLS at each date. We forecast the yields 12 months ahead by AR(1) forecasts of the factors, estimated on an expanding window, and compare them with the random walk and with AR(1) forecasts of each yield, with root mean squared errors on the last 40% of the sample.

How to read it The sample has 531 months from December 1946 to February 1991. Yields average 4.8% at 1 month and 6.2% at 10 years, an upward-sloping curve on average, with a standard deviation of about 3.2 points at every maturity: the level of rates moves much more than the slope. The 1-month yield was above the 10-year yield in 9% of months (mostly in 1973 to 1974, 1979 to 1981 and 1989).

How to read it The decay parameter that minimises the fitting error is \(\lambda = 0.138\) per month, which puts the peak of the curvature loading at about 13 months (Diebold and Li (2006) fix 0.0609, a peak at 30 months, for monthly data). The mean root mean squared error of the fit across the seven maturities is 0.108 percentage points, ranging from 0.074 at 12 months to 0.131 at 10 years. Three factors reproduce yields of seven maturities to within about a tenth of a percentage point; the mean errors by maturity are within 0.09. The chart shows the average and the last yield curve with the fitted curve.

How to read it The level factor has a mean of 6.14 and ranges from 1.66 to 14.86 with a first-order autocorrelation of 0.996 and 0.90 after 24 months: a very persistent factor that tracks the rise of the 1960s and 1970s and peaks in 1981 (the 10-year yield peaked in September 1981). The slope factor has a mean of \(-1.35\) (an upward-sloping curve), ranges from \(-5.8\) to 3.7 (a positive value is an inverted curve) and is much less persistent: 0.90 at one month, 0.35 after 12 months and 0.03 after 24. The curvature factor has a mean of 0.21, a standard deviation of 2.0 and autocorrelations of 0.80, 0.42 and 0.12. The persistence of the level and the transitory nature of the slope are the standard features that Diebold and Li found for later data.

How to read it Twelve months ahead, the random walk is the best forecast at every maturity: root mean squared errors of 2.40, 2.16 and 1.54 for the 1-month, 12-month and 10-year yields, against 2.68, 2.47 and 1.74 for AR(1) forecasts of the factors and 2.43, 2.21 and 1.64 for AR(1) forecasts of the yields. This differs from Diebold and Li, who found that AR(1) factors beat the random walk at the 12-month horizon on 1985 to 2000 data. In this sample, which includes the 1979 to 1982 shift in monetary policy, the factor AR(1) cannot predict the large changes in the level, and its slow mean reversion pulls the forecast towards a mean that the 1960s and 1970s had left behind. The result is a caution: a good in-sample fit says nothing about forecasting.
Robustness: the decay parameter and the horizon

How to read it With \(\lambda = 0.0609\) the mean fitting error rises to 0.131 and the factor forecast of the 1-month yield becomes 2.55 (still worse than 2.40 for the random walk). With \(\lambda = 0.3\) the fit is 0.125 and the forecast is 2.72. The conclusion does not depend on \(\lambda\) . At six months the random walk is also best (1.92, 1.70, 1.03 against 2.00, 1.78, 1.12 for the factors); at 24 months its lead grows (3.26, 3.07, 2.23 against 3.76, 3.55, 2.66). In this sample the random walk is the benchmark to beat at all three horizons.
Diagnostics: does the fit recover a known curve?

How to read it Fitting a known curve with the three factors and \(\lambda = 0.0609\) on 200 dates and eight maturities returns \(\lambda = 0.0609\) exactly and the factor means to three decimals (5.242, \(-1.519\) and 0.249) when there is no noise. With noise of 0.05 percentage points on each yield, the estimated \(\lambda\) is 0.0597, the mean fitting error is 0.039 and the factor means are 5.233, \(-1.512\) and 0.304: the level and slope are recovered, and the curvature is the factor that is hardest to pin down. The test suite also checks the factors against scipy least squares at a fixed \(\lambda\) .

How to write it: results We fit the Nelson-Siegel curve to the monthly yields of seven maturities, 1 to 120 months, December 1946 to February 1991 (531 months). The decay parameter, estimated by minimising the squared fitting error, is 0.138 per month; the mean root mean squared error of the fit is 0.108 percentage points. The level factor is very persistent (autocorrelation 0.996) and ranges from 1.7 to 14.9; the slope factor averages \(-1.35\) (upward-sloping curve) and is transitory (autocorrelation 0.35 after 12 months). The AR(1) forecasts of the factors do not beat the random walk at a 12-month horizon (root mean squared errors of 2.68, 2.47 and 1.74 against 2.40, 2.16 and 1.54 for the 1-month, 12-month and 10-year yields), and the result is the same for \(\lambda = 0.0609\) and \(\lambda = 0.3\) and for horizons of 6 and 24 months. In simulation the fit recovers a known curve and its decay parameter.

From Data to Decision: a free 400-page handbook on model selection for applied economic research, by Tuhin G. M. Al Mamun.

Why this handbook. Applied economists rarely lack methods; they lack a defensible way to choose among them. This handbook starts from the question, not the estimator: which test or diagnostic tells you which model to use, what to do when the evidence is mixed, and how to write the result up. Every chapter takes one real dataset through that path (tests, estimation, diagnostics, robustness, and the text of the paper) with the code and its output shown, so you can reproduce each step. The decision paths, the choice of tests and the design of the inference are based on my own learning, knowledge and implementation. Interactive versions of the guides are on the main website. The handbook is free to read and share.

Which Stimulates More? Spending and Transfers in Korea’s Wage-Rigid Economy

Read Job Market Paper ↗ This paper examines how fiscal policy transmits through government spending and direct transfers in South Korea using a Heterogeneous Agent New Keynesian (HANK) model with wage rigidity and debt-sensitive taxation. Calibrated to Korean macroeconomic data, the model captures key institutional features, including household heterogeneity, liquidity constraints, and labor market stickiness. A 1% increase in government spending generates a peak output gain of 0.5% that persists over 60 quarters, while an equivalent transfer shock yields a sharper 0.2% consumption increase that fades within 10 quarters. Tax feedback plays a critical role—spending raises labor income tax rates by up to 0.6 percentage points, compared to only 0.3 points under transfers—affecting household behavior and fiscal sustainability. Sensitivity analysis shows that fiscal multipliers decline sharply with higher steady-state bond supply, stronger tax adjustment rules, and more aggressive monetary tightening. For instance, increasing the bond supply target from 30% to 100% of GDP reduces the impact multiplier by over 46%, while a shift to aggressive monetary policy lowers it by more than 50%. These findings highlight the trade-offs between short-run stabilization and long-run fiscal discipline, offering new insights into optimal policy coordination in an unequal, wage-rigid economy.

Bayesian Markov-Switching Regression: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Can the data find the recessions without being told where they are? In a Markov-switching regression the regime \(s_t \in \{1, \dots, K\}\) is hidden and follows a first-order Markov chain with transition probabilities \(p_{ij} = \Pr(s_t = j \mid s_{t-1} = i)\) ; conditional on the regime the series is an ordinary regression: The intercept always switches; slopes and the variance may or may not. The maximum-likelihood version (the Markov-switching guides) gives point estimates and asymptotic standard errors, which are often unreliable here because the likelihood is multi-modal and the effective sample is the number of regime changes, which is small. The Bayesian version (Albert and Chib 1993; Chib 1996; Kim and Nelson 1999) samples everything jointly:

the whole regime path \(s_{1:T}\) , by forward filtering and backward sampling (Hamilton filter, then a draw for each period from the last backwards); the regression coefficients, by a normal update given the regimes; the variances, by inverse-gamma draws; each row of the transition matrix, by a Dirichlet draw from the counts of transitions. The result is a posterior for every parameter, for the duration \(1/(1 - p_{jj})\) of each regime, for the long-run share of time in each regime, and for the regime of every period. Label switching (the regimes can swap names between draws) is fixed by ordering the regimes by their intercepts (or by their variances), which the output reports.

Output What it answers Regime parameters Posterior mean, interval of the intercept, slopes and standard deviation in each regime, next to the maximum likelihood Transition probabilities Probability of moving between regimes, with intervals Durations and long-run shares How long each regime lasts and how much of the time it occupies Regime dates Runs of periods in which a regime is more likely than not, and agreement with a reference series Diagnostics R-hat and effective sample sizes, and the share of draws in which the labels had to be reordered How to write it: the model We model U.S. quarterly GNP growth as a two-regime Markov-switching regression with a regime-dependent mean and a common variance, estimated by Gibbs sampling (Albert and Chib 1993; Chib 1996). The regime path is drawn by forward filtering and backward sampling, the regime means by a normal update, the variance by an inverse-gamma update and each row of the transition matrix by a Dirichlet update. The priors are N(0, 5²) on the standardised regime means, inverse gamma(2, 1) on the standardised variance and Dirichlet(1, 1) on each row of the transition matrix. The regimes are ordered by their means to fix the labelling. We run two chains of 3,000 draws after 1,000 burn-in draws and check convergence with R-hat and effective sample sizes.

How to read it The 135 quarters of growth (in percent, annualised) have a mean of 0.74 and a standard deviation of 1.07, ranging from \(-2.39\) to 3.11. The NBER calls 27 of the quarters recessions; growth in those was \(-0.58\) on average and 1.08 in the rest. The NBER dates are not used in the estimation; they are the check against which the method's dates are judged.

How to read it The sampler is sound: R-hat is at most 1.003 and the smallest effective sample size is 481 out of 6,000 draws, and no draw needed relabelling, so the two regimes are well separated. Regime means. Regime 1, the slow regime, has a mean growth of \(-0.50\) with a posterior standard deviation of 0.36 (95% interval \(-1.32\) to 0.11); regime 2, the fast regime, has 1.11 (0.86 to 1.40). The maximum-likelihood values ( \(-0.49\) and 1.10) are close to the posterior means. The interval of the slow regime is wide because only a quarter of the quarters belong to it, and it just reaches zero: the data say that growth in the slow regime is probably negative, but not with certainty. The common standard deviation is 0.85 (0.73 to 0.98).

Persistence. The probability that the fast regime continues is 0.89 (0.74 to 0.97): an expected duration of 11 quarters (95% interval 4 to 29). The slow regime continues with probability 0.65 (0.34 to 0.86), for an expected duration of 3.3 quarters (1.5 to 7.2). These are asymmetric, as the business cycle is: expansions are long and recessions short. The long-run share of the slow regime is 25% (7% to 51%). The intervals are wide, and the maximum-likelihood standard errors would hide this; the Bayesian interval for a duration is the honest one.

How to read it The method finds eight slow-growth episodes, among them 1953Q3 to 1954Q2, 1957Q3 to 1958Q1, 1969Q4 to 1970Q2, 1974Q1 to 1975Q1 and 1981Q2 to 1982Q3. They are the recessions that the NBER dates as 1953 to 1954, 1957 to 1958, 1969 to 1970, 1973 to 1975 and 1981 to 1982. The posterior probability averages 0.86 over the first episode and 0.89 over the 1974 to 1975 one: the dating is clear for the large recessions and less so for the marginal ones (1960 at 0.62 and the single quarter 1970Q4 at 0.56). Against the NBER series, the method classifies 93.3% of the quarters in the same way. It places 81.5% of the NBER recession quarters in regime 1 and only 3.7% of the other quarters, and the correlation between the probability of regime 1 and the recession indicator is 0.83. The first chart shows the probability of each regime over time; the second the series with the regime-weighted mean.

How to read it R-hat is between 1.001 and 1.003 for every parameter and the effective sample sizes range from 481 (the mean of the slow regime) to 2,093. The staying probabilities, 952 and 660, are the quantities that mix most slowly in Markov-switching models because they depend on the sampled regime path. The last line of the note reports the share of draws in which the labels had to be reordered: 0.0% here. A high share (more than 10%) means that the regimes are barely separated and that the ordering is doing a lot of work; then reduce the number of regimes or add information.

Recessions are often more volatile as well as slower. Let each regime have its own standard deviation. How to read it The standard deviation is 0.97 in the slow regime (95% interval 0.70 to 1.27) and 0.78 in the fast one (0.58 to 0.96), the same as the maximum-likelihood values (0.97 and 0.79), but the intervals overlap heavily: the data do not say that the regimes differ in volatility. The means move too, to \(-0.21\) and 1.21. The regime dating changes in a revealing way: the share of the NBER recession quarters in regime 1 rises from 0.82 to 0.96, but the share of other quarters in regime 1 also rises from 0.04 to 0.13, so the overall agreement falls from 93% to 89%. Letting the variance switch gives the slow regime more room to absorb volatile quarters that are not recessions. The constant-variance model is the better dating device for these data.

The Dirichlet prior on each row of the transition matrix is flat by default. Because regimes are persistent you may want to add prior weight to the diagonal. How to read it Adding 2 or 5 extra prior observations of staying in a regime raises the posterior probability of staying in the slow regime from 0.65 to 0.70 and 0.74, and the expected duration from 3.4 to 6.9 and 4.5 quarters (the duration is a ratio of a small number and is noisy across runs). The fast regime hardly moves (0.886, 0.892, 0.899). With 135 quarters and about 25 in the slow regime the prior does matter for the slow regime, and it should be reported. The regime means and the dating, which depend mostly on the data, change little.

Hamilton's own model has the regime in the mean of an autoregression. Here the lag of the series enters as a regressor with a common coefficient and only the intercept switches, which is a different model. How to read it With one lag, the autoregressive coefficient is 0.34 (95% interval 0.09 to 0.57) and the regimes blur: the slow regime's level is \(-0.14\) (interval \(-1.20\) to 0.75), the agreement with the NBER falls to 79%, the share of the NBER recession quarters in regime 1 falls to 63%, and in 3.8% of the draws the labels had to be reordered. The lag soaks up the persistence that the regimes were capturing. The effective sample sizes are 239 to 1,441 after 6,000 draws. With only 135 quarters the data cannot sharply identify the regimes and an autoregression at the same time. If you need Hamilton's mean-switching autoregression, use the Markov-switching autoregression guide; if you add lags here, check the agreement, the share of reordered draws and the effective sample sizes, as in this step.

Simulate 30 series of 250 observations from a two-regime chain with known means ( \(-1\) and 2), standard deviation 1 and transition probabilities of 0.9 and 0.85. How to read it The 95% intervals of the two regime means contain the truth in 90% and 93% of the 30 samples (the standard error with 30 samples is about 4 points), and on average 97.4% of the periods are assigned to the right regime. The test suite adds a check against maximum likelihood, recovery of transition probabilities, variance switching, common and switching slopes, and that a series of pure noise does not produce two separated regimes.

The same sampler with switching slopes and variance. The relation between inflation and unemployment, 1959 to 2009; the intercept is the level of inflation at the average rate of unemployment. How to read it The model separates two eras. The low-inflation regime holds 1959Q2 to 1972Q4 and 1983Q2 to 2009Q3: inflation at average unemployment is 2.8% (95% interval 2.4% to 3.2%), its standard deviation is 1.8 and the slope on unemployment is \(-0.18\) with an interval of \(-0.57\) to 0.21: a flat Phillips curve. The high-inflation regime holds 1973Q1 to 1983Q1, the Great Inflation: the level is 9.0% (5.9% to 11.3%), the volatility 3.4 and the slope \(-1.18\) ( \(-2.18\) to 0.29), steeper but imprecise, since only 41 quarters belong to it.

Both regimes are persistent: the low-inflation regime continues with probability 0.97 and the high one with 0.93 (0.81 to 0.99). The convergence report shows R-hat up to 1.01 and effective sample sizes from 144 to 4,440 after 15,000 draws: with long regimes there are few transitions to learn from, so the variance and persistence parameters mix slowly. Use long runs for this model and report the diagnostics; the run here takes a minute or two.

How to write it: results Two regimes are identified in U.S. quarterly GNP growth. Mean growth is \(-0.50\) in the slow regime (95% interval \(-1.32\) to 0.11) and 1.11 in the fast regime (0.86 to 1.40), with a common standard deviation of 0.85. The fast regime persists with probability 0.89 (expected duration 11 quarters, 95% interval 4 to 29) and the slow regime with probability 0.65 (3.3 quarters, 1.5 to 7.2). The regimes match the NBER recessions: 93% of the quarters are classified the same way, 81.5% of the NBER recession quarters fall in the slow regime and 3.7% of the others. The sampler's R-hat is at most 1.003 and the effective sample sizes exceed 480. The posterior means are close to the maximum-likelihood estimates. Letting the variance switch, or adding an autoregressive term, blurs the regimes (agreement 89% and 79%), so the constant-variance specification is used. In simulation, the 95% intervals of the regime means covered the truth in 90% to 93% of the samples. Applied to inflation and unemployment, the model separates a low-inflation regime (2.8% at average unemployment, slope \(-0.18\) ) from the 1973 to 1983 high-inflation regime (9.0%, slope \(-1.18\) ).

Markov Chain Transition Model: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Where do people go next, and where do they end up? A Markov chain says that the state tomorrow depends on the state today and not on the earlier history: From the counts \(n_{ij}\) of moves from \(i\) to \(j\) the maximum-likelihood estimate is \(\hat p_{ij} = n_{ij}/n_{i\cdot}\) . The Bayesian version puts a Dirichlet prior on each row, \(p_{i\cdot} \sim \text{Dirichlet}(\alpha, \dots, \alpha)\) , so that the posterior is Dirichlet \((\alpha + n_{i1}, \dots, \alpha + n_{iK})\) and can be sampled directly. For each draw of the matrix the engine computes the quantities you care about: Quantity Definition Long-run share The stationary distribution \(\pi\) with \(\pi P = \pi\)

Duration \(1/(1-p_{ii})\) , the expected length of a spell in state \(i\) First-passage time The expected number of periods to reach state \(j\) from state \(i\) Mobility Shorrocks index \((K - \operatorname{tr}P)/(K-1)\) : 0 means nobody moves, 1 means no persistence Two tests check the assumptions: independence (is the first-order chain better than a chain with no memory at all?) and time homogeneity (are the probabilities the same in the first and the second half of the sample?). When there is a unit column the moves are counted within each unit in time order, and no move is counted across two units. How to write it: the model We model union membership as a first-order Markov chain on two states. The transition counts are taken within each worker across consecutive years. Each row of the transition matrix has a Dirichlet(1, 1) prior, and the posterior is sampled with 4,000 draws. For each draw we compute the stationary distribution, the expected durations, the mean first-passage times and Shorrocks' mobility index, and report posterior means and 95% intervals. We test the Markov property against independence and the stability of the matrix over time with likelihood-ratio tests.

How to read it The panel has 545 men observed in eight years, 4,360 observations and so 3,815 transitions, since the first year of each worker has no earlier state. The share of union members is about 25% in every year, between 21% and 26%. A stable share can hide a lot of movement, or none: the transition matrix says which.

How to read it Of the 2,894 transitions that start from non-membership, 2,637 end in non-membership: the probability of staying out is 0.911 (95% interval 0.900 to 0.921) and the probability of joining in a year is 0.089 (0.079 to 0.100). Of the 921 transitions that start from membership, 670 stay: the probability of staying in is 0.727 (0.697 to 0.755) and of leaving 0.273 (0.245 to 0.303). Membership is much less sticky than non-membership, and the posterior means are almost the same as the frequencies because the counts are large and the prior is worth two observations per row.

How to read it If these probabilities held for ever, the share of members would settle at 24.6% (95% interval 21.7% to 27.6%), close to the observed 24.4%, so the sample is at its long-run balance. A non-member stays out for 11.3 years on average (10.0 to 12.7), a member stays in for 3.7 years (3.3 to 4.1). The chart compares the observed shares with the long-run shares.

How to read it A non-member takes on average 11.2 years to join (10.0 to 12.7): the same as the duration, because there are only two states. A member takes 3.7 years to leave (3.3 to 4.1). The diagonal gives the mean recurrence time of each state: 1.33 years for non-membership (the state is occupied three years in four) and 4.07 for membership. The Shorrocks index is 0.36 (0.33 to 0.39): on a scale from 0 (nobody moves) to 1 (no persistence) that is moderate mobility.

How to read it The first test compares the chain with a model in which the state is drawn independently each year with the observed shares. The likelihood-ratio statistic is 1,417 with 1 degree of freedom: where you were last year is overwhelmingly informative about where you are now. The second test compares the first four transition years with the last three: the statistic is 11.3 with 2 degrees of freedom (p = 0.004), so the matrix is not perfectly stable over the period; the 1980s unions were losing ground. The change is small next to the persistence, but if the period were longer you would estimate the matrix separately for sub-periods.
Cut a continuous variable into states

A wage is not a state, but cutting it into terciles makes it one. How to read it The three states are the terciles of log wages in the pooled sample (the cut points are in the state names). The highest state is the stickiest: a worker in the top third stays there with probability 0.84 (0.82 to 0.86), for an expected 6.3 years, against 0.61 for the middle (2.6 years) and 0.68 for the bottom (3.2 years). Movement is mostly to the neighbouring state; going from the bottom to the top in one year has probability 0.05 and from the top to the bottom 0.04. The first-passage times are asymmetric: 7.9 years (7.3 to 8.7) from the bottom to the top but 15.3 (13.2 to 17.7) from the top to the bottom.
Cut a continuous variable into states

The long-run shares are 20%, 30% and 50%, compared with one third each in the sample: wages rise over time, so the chain drifts upward, and the homogeneity test rejects (statistic 38.6, 6 degrees of freedom, p < 0.0001). This is the warning that goes with every Markov chain on a trending variable: the long-run shares describe where the process would go if the matrix stayed the same, not a forecast. Cut the states by year, or use wage growth, if you want a stationary chain.

How to read it With no prior (the maximum-likelihood estimate) and with one observation per cell the joining probability is 0.089 and the leaving probability 0.273. A prior worth 20 observations per cell moves them to 0.094 and 0.282, and a prior worth 100 per cell, which is still small next to the 2,894 and 921 transitions, to 0.115 and 0.313. The prior matters when a state has few transitions, so report the weight you used and, for a rare state, show the results for more than one weight.

Simulate 30 chains of 300 periods with stay probabilities of 0.85 and 0.75. How to read it The 95% intervals contain the true probability in 90% of the samples for the first state and 97% for the second (the standard error with 30 samples is about 4 points), as they should. The test suite also checks the posterior mean against the exact Dirichlet formula, the stationary distribution and first-passage times against closed-form values for a two-state chain, a three-state chain against the eigenvector solution, the tests against chains with and without memory and with a change in the matrix, and the error messages.

How to write it: results Union membership is persistent. A non-member joins in a given year with probability 0.089 (95% interval 0.079 to 0.100); a member leaves with probability 0.273 (0.245 to 0.303). A non-member stays out for 11.3 years on average (10.0 to 12.7) and a member stays in for 3.7 years (3.3 to 4.1). The long-run share of members implied by these probabilities is 24.6% (21.7% to 27.6%), equal to the observed share, and the Shorrocks mobility index is 0.36 (0.33 to 0.39). The likelihood-ratio test rejects independence (statistic 1,417, 1 degree of freedom) and, weakly, a constant matrix across the sample (11.3, p = 0.004). With log wages cut into terciles the top state is the most persistent (0.84) and it takes 15.3 years (13.2 to 17.7) on average to fall from the top to the bottom but 7.9 (7.3 to 8.7) to climb from the bottom to the top; because wages trend upward the long-run shares (20%, 30%, 50%) differ from the sample shares. In simulation the 95% intervals covered the true probabilities in 90% to 97% of the samples.

Markov-Switching Autoregression (Hamilton): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Are there recessions in the data, and can the data find them without being told? In a Markov-switching autoregression (Hamilton 1989) the mean of the series depends on an unobserved state \(s_t\) : and the state follows a first-order Markov chain with transition probabilities \(p_{ij} = \Pr(s_t = j \mid s_{t-1} = i)\) . The model is estimated by maximum likelihood with the Hamilton filter. For each period it gives a filtered probability (using data up to \(t\) ) and a smoothed probability (using the whole sample) of being in each state. Three checks before you trust a regime model Is the series stationary? The regimes should describe shifts in the mean of a stationary series. A trending series produces "regimes" that are just the trend.

Does the data need two regimes? Compare one, two and three regimes with information criteria, and run the linearity test. A regime model fits better than a linear one by construction; the question is whether it fits enough better. Are the regimes sharply identified? A good model puts each period in one regime with high probability. The regime classification measure (RCM, Ang and Bekaert 2002) summarises this. How to write it: the model We estimate Hamilton's (1989) Markov-switching autoregression for quarterly GNP growth, with a state-dependent mean, a common variance and four autoregressive lags. The state follows a two-state first-order Markov chain. We estimate the model by maximum likelihood using the Hamilton filter and report smoothed state probabilities (Kim 1994). To compare the number of regimes we use AIC and BIC, and we test linearity with the likelihood-ratio statistic and the critical values of Garcia (1998) and the bound of Davies (1987), because the standard asymptotic distribution does not apply when parameters are unidentified under the null.
Load the data and test for unit roots

How to read it Quarterly GNP growth is stationary: the ADF tests reject a unit root and the KPSS test does not reject stationarity. That is what a regime-in-the-mean model needs. If your series is in levels and trending, difference it (growth rates) first.
How many regimes? Is the series linear?

How to read it One regime has the lowest AIC (379.3) and BIC (396.6); two regimes give 380.5 and 406.4, three give 386.4 and 426.6. The information criteria do not prefer a switching model for this sample. The linearity test agrees: the statistic is 4.8, far below the Garcia 5% critical value of about 14, and the Davies bound gives p = 0.95. So the data do not reject a linear AR model. This is an honest and well-known result for Hamilton's sample: with 131 quarters, the evidence for regimes is weak when judged by the likelihood alone. The regimes are still useful as a description, because they line up with the NBER dates (Step 5), but you should not claim that the test proves two regimes. Report this table.

How to read it Regime 1 is the high-growth state: the mean growth is 1.15% per quarter (about 4.6% a year) and it lasts 10.4 quarters on average. Regime 0 is the low-growth state: the mean is \(-0.42\) % per quarter, it lasts 4.1 quarters on average, and the state occupies 27.5% of the sample. The transition probabilities are \(p_{00} = 0.75\) and \(p_{11} = 0.90\) ; the expected duration of a regime is \(1/(1-p_{ii})\) . The low-growth mean is imprecise ( \(z = -1.4\) , p = 0.18) while the high-growth mean is very precisely estimated ( \(z = 15.6\) ): the recession state has few observations. The estimate \(p_{10} = 0.096\) is significant (p = 0.011), so a move from expansion to the low state is likely about once in ten quarters. Only the third lag of growth is significant at 5% ( \(-0.25\) ). The RCM is 21.7, below the usual threshold of 30, so the periods are assigned to regimes fairly sharply.
Regime dates and the NBER recession dates

How to read it The low-growth regime is dated 1953Q3–1954Q2, 1957Q1–1958Q1, 1960Q2–1960Q4, 1969Q3–1970Q4, 1974Q1–1975Q1, 1979Q2–1980Q3 and 1981Q2–1982Q4, mostly with an average probability above 0.9. These are the post-war US recessions. Against the NBER recession indicator, 91.6% of quarters are classified alike, 96.3% of NBER recession quarters are detected, and 9.6% of non-recession quarters are flagged as low growth (false signals). The model finds the recessions without being told where they are. The dated episodes also include 1969Q3–1970Q4 and 1979Q2–1980Q3, which overlap the NBER recessions of 1969–70 and 1980. When you write this up, say which dates you compare with and how you define "detected" and "false signal".

How to read it The residuals pass: no autocorrelation (Ljung-Box p = 0.40; Hosking portmanteau p = 0.42), no sign of non-normality (Jarque-Bera p = 0.19) and no ARCH effects (p = 0.85). The model that allows only the mean to switch is adequate for the series' dynamics. If the ARCH test rejected, you would let the variance switch too (Step 7).
Robustness: lags, switching variance, switching dynamics and regimes

How to read it The lag order matters a great deal for the dating. With four lags (Hamilton's choice) the model detects 96% of NBER recession quarters; with two lags it detects 56% and with one lag 52%, though concordance stays above 90% because most quarters are expansions. The shorter models put the low state on fewer quarters, so a claim like "the model finds the recessions" holds for the four-lag specification only. Allowing the variance to switch keeps the detection rate (96%) but raises false signals to 17% and worsens the BIC (410.1 against 406.4). Allowing the autoregressive coefficients to switch raises the log-likelihood to \(-176.3\) but the BIC is 415.9 and only 67% of recession quarters are detected. A third regime improves the log-likelihood to \(-177.0\) but the BIC is 422.3 and one of the three regimes is a single quarter. The baseline is the best on the information criteria among the switching models.

How to write it: results The two-regime model separates a high-growth state (mean 1.15% per quarter, expected duration 10.4 quarters) from a low-growth state (mean \(-0.42\) % per quarter, expected duration 4.1 quarters). The transition probabilities are 0.75 for staying in the low state and 0.90 for staying in the high state. The smoothed probabilities date seven low-growth episodes between 1953 and 1982 that correspond to the post-war US recessions: 91.6% of quarters are classified in agreement with the NBER indicator, 96.3% of NBER recession quarters are detected and 9.6% of other quarters are flagged. The regime classification measure is 21.7, which indicates a sharp classification. However, the likelihood evidence for two regimes is weak: one regime has the lowest AIC and BIC, and the linearity statistic (4.8) is below the Garcia 5% critical value (about 14; Davies p = 0.95). The regime estimates are therefore best read as a description of the cycle that agrees with the NBER dates, not as a rejection of a linear model. The dating depends on the lag order: with two or fewer lags only about half of the NBER recession quarters are detected.

Markov-Switching Panel VAR: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Did the OECD economies share a regime change in the 1970s? The panel Markov-switching VAR has the same form as the Markov-switching VAR for one economy, with one important restriction: one unobserved regime path is shared by all units , and the parameters are pooled across units, where \(i\) indexes countries, \(t\) years and \(s_t\) is the regime in year \(t\) (the same for every country). The likelihood adds up the units' contributions given the regime, so all countries inform the regime probabilities. As in the single-economy model, you choose what switches: MSI (intercepts), MSIH (intercepts and covariance matrices) or MSIAH (also the autoregressive coefficients). By default the data are demeaned by country, so that country-specific levels do not create regimes.

Three checks before you trust a panel regime model Is the shared-regime assumption plausible? The model cannot find country-specific regimes. If countries had different cycles, the estimated regime is an average. Check that the dating survives dropping each country in turn (Step 8). Are the variables stationary? Persistent series such as unemployment can create regimes out of trends. How many regimes, and how many time periods? The regime path has only \(T\) points however many countries you have. Here \(T = 24\) , so regimes of one or two years carry little information. How to write it: the model We estimate a panel Markov-switching VAR with one lag in GDP growth and the unemployment rate for 14 OECD countries, 1966–1990. A single regime path, a first-order Markov chain with two states, is shared by all countries: the regime in a given year is the same for every country. Intercepts and covariance matrices are regime-specific (MSIH), and the autoregressive coefficients are pooled and common to the regimes. The variables are demeaned by country. We estimate the model by maximum likelihood with the EM algorithm from several starting values and take standard errors from the numerical Hessian. We choose the number of regimes with AIC and BIC.
Load the data and test for unit roots

How to read it The panel is balanced: 14 countries with 25 years each (350 observations; 24 usable years per country with one lag). The unit-root tests, computed on the cross-country average, give a mixed picture. Unemployment is I(1) : the ADF test does not reject a unit root in levels (p = 0.50) but rejects it in first differences (p = 0.02), and KPSS rejects stationarity (p = 0.02). GDP growth is borderline (ADF p = 0.06, KPSS p = 0.06). So the unemployment series is persistent, and part of what the regimes capture could be its upward drift in the 1970s and 1980s. We estimate the model on demeaned levels as the default does; for a stricter treatment, use the change in unemployment and check that the dating survives.
How many regimes? Better than a linear panel VAR?

How to read it Two regimes fit much better than a linear panel VAR: the log-likelihood is \(-985.4\) against \(-1055.2\) (LR statistic 139.6, Davies p < 0.001), and AIC (2002.8 against 2128.4) and BIC (2063.9 against 2162.7) both prefer two regimes to one. Three regimes are better still on both criteria (AIC 1960.9, BIC 2056.3). We keep two regimes as the baseline, because the three-regime model has a short regime (expected duration 2.5 years, 21% of the years, in two separate spells) and because with 24 distinct regime dates any extra regime rests on very few years; but you must report that the criteria favour three and show what three regimes look like (Step 5 and Step 8).

How to read it Regime 0 is the slow-growth regime: it holds 62.5% of the years, lasts 7.3 years on average ( \(p_{00} = 0.86\) , standard error 0.09), and the implied mean is 0.7 percentage points of GDP growth below the country average and 2.3 points of unemployment above it. Regime 1 is the fast-growth regime: 37.5% of the years, 3.1 years on average ( \(p_{11} = 0.68\) , standard error 0.16), with growth 1.7 points above the country average and unemployment 2.0 points below. The regimes are in deviation from each country's own mean because the data are demeaned. The pooled dynamics are: growth depends on its own lag (0.23) and on lagged unemployment (+0.31), unemployment is persistent (0.80) and falls after faster growth ( \(-0.14\) ). The innovation covariance matrices differ less than the means: the variance of the growth innovation is 2.7 in regime 0 and 3.7 in regime 1, and that of unemployment is 0.66 and 0.32. The correlation of the two innovations is \(-0.56\) and \(-0.46\) . The RCM is 2.8, a very sharp classification, which is what a regime path shared by 14 countries should deliver. The standard errors on the transition probabilities are large, so treat the durations as rough.

How to read it The slow-growth regime covers 1974–75, 1977–78 and 1980–1990 (11 years in a row), and the fast-growth regime covers 1967–1973 (7 years), 1976 and 1979, all with average probabilities of 0.92 or above. So the model finds the break at the 1973–74 oil shock, a short rebound in 1976, a second oil shock around 1979, and a long slowdown through the 1980s. The one-year episodes (1976 and 1979) have to be reported as single years, not as regimes, because with one year the data cannot tell a regime from a shock. With three regimes (Step 8), 1974–75 and 1981–83 (the two deep slowdowns) form one regime, 1977–80 and 1984–90 a second, and 1967–73 with 1976 the third.

How to read it Impulse responses are regime-specific Cholesky responses, with GDP growth ordered first, and the shock is one standard deviation. A growth shock lowers unemployment by 0.45 on impact and by 0.59 a year later in regime 0 (0.26 and 0.47 in regime 1), and the effect disappears after about eight years. A one-standard-deviation unemployment shock raises growth by 0.21 a year later in regime 0 (0.16 in regime 1). Because the autoregressive coefficients are common, the shape is the same in both regimes and the response is larger in regime 0 only because its shocks are larger. The positive response of growth to an unemployment shock is a mean-reversion effect in demeaned data, not an economic channel: do not give it a structural interpretation. These responses have no confidence bands.

How to read it Growth residuals have no autocorrelation (Ljung-Box p = 0.21) and no ARCH (p = 0.64); unemployment residuals have autocorrelation (p = 0.003) and no ARCH (p = 0.22); both reject normality (p < 0.001). The panel portmanteau test rejects (p = 0.003). The remaining autocorrelation in unemployment suggests that one lag is not enough: with two lags the log-likelihood rises from \(-985.4\) to \(-932.8\) and the regime dating is unchanged (Step 8). The standard errors are approximate.

How to read it Specification. Intercepts only (MSI) gives 14.8 years for the slow-growth regime and agrees with the baseline in 96% of the years (23 of 24). Letting all coefficients switch (MSIAH) raises the log-likelihood by 12 and gives the same dating up to one year (96%), with a BIC of 2063.0 against 2063.9: no clear evidence that the dynamics switch. Two lags and no demeaning both agree with the baseline in 96% of the years; starting values (20 against 6) make no difference. Three regimes. The dating agrees with the baseline in only 58% of the years, and the regime shares are 21%, 46% and 33%: the third regime is not a small refinement of the two-regime result. Report it next to the baseline. Leave one country out. Dropping each of the 14 countries in turn leaves the dating almost unchanged: agreement with the baseline is 96% to 100% (23 or 24 of 24 years), and the share of years in the slow-growth regime stays between 58% and 67%. The expected duration of the slow-growth regime is 6.6 to 7.5 years for ten of the fourteen runs and 13.6 to 14.6 years when Italy, Norway, Sweden or West Germany is dropped, because the 1979 interruption then disappears (the slow-growth regime runs from 1977 to 1990). So the main result is not driven by one country, but the one-year interruption of 1979 is fragile.

How to write it: results We estimate a panel Markov-switching VAR for GDP growth and unemployment in 14 OECD countries, 1966–1990, with a single regime path shared by all countries. The data prefer two regimes to a linear panel VAR (BIC 2063.9 against 2162.7; likelihood-ratio statistic 139.6, Davies p < 0.001); the information criteria favour three regimes, which we report as a robustness check. The slow-growth regime holds 62.5% of the years, with growth 0.7 points below and unemployment 2.3 points above the country means, and an expected duration of 7.3 years; the fast-growth regime holds 37.5% of the years, with growth 1.7 points above and unemployment 2.0 points below the country means, and an expected duration of 3.1 years. The slow-growth regime is dated 1974–75, 1977–78 and 1980–1990; the fast-growth regime is dated 1967–1973, 1976 and 1979. The regime dating is robust to the specification (intercepts only, all coefficients switching, two lags, no demeaning) and to dropping any one country (agreement with the baseline of 96% to 100% of the years); the one-year interruption of 1979 is fragile, and the three-regime solution is different (58% agreement). Unemployment is I(1) in these data and has residual autocorrelation, so the regimes may partly reflect its persistence, and standard errors are approximate.

Markov-Switching Regression: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Does the Phillips curve differ between calm and turbulent regimes? In a Markov-switching regression (Goldfeld and Quandt 1973; Hamilton 1989) the coefficients and the error variance depend on an unobserved state \(s_t\) : Here \(y_t\) is inflation and \(x_t\) contains lagged inflation and lagged unemployment. You choose which parts switch: the intercept always does; the slopes and the variance can switch or be common. The model is estimated by maximum likelihood with the Hamilton filter. Three checks before you trust a regime regression Is the dependent variable stationary? Regimes in a trending series are the trend in disguise. Does the data need regimes at all? Compare the one-regime regression with two and three regimes, and use the linearity test with the Garcia critical value or the Davies bound (the usual \(\chi^2\) test is not valid).

Is each regime a real regime? A regime that contains two or three observations is not a regime but an outlier, and its variance goes to zero. Check the share and duration of every regime (Step 5). How to write it: the model We estimate a two-regime Markov-switching regression (Hamilton 1989) of quarterly inflation on its own lag and the lagged unemployment rate. The intercept, the slopes and the error variance are regime-specific, and the regime follows a first-order Markov chain. We estimate it by maximum likelihood, starting from the solution of the restricted model with common slopes and from several random starts, and keep the solution with the highest likelihood. We compare one, two and three regimes with AIC and BIC, and test linearity with the likelihood-ratio statistic, the critical values of Garcia (1998) and the bound of Davies (1987), because the standard asymptotic distribution does not hold when parameters are unidentified under the null.
Load the data and test for unit roots

How to read it Quarterly inflation rejects a unit root at 5% with a constant (p = 0.025), is borderline with a trend (p = 0.07), and the KPSS test does not reject stationarity at 5% (p = 0.077). We treat it as stationary, which is what a regime-in-the-mean model needs; the evidence is not overwhelming, so say so. If the series were clearly I(1) (as the federal funds rate is, with p = 0.29), you would model its change instead.
How many regimes? Is the relationship linear?

How to read it The log-likelihood rises from \(-466.1\) with one regime to \(-426.0\) with two, and the linearity statistic is 80.1, far above the Garcia 5% critical value of about 14 (Davies p < 0.001): the data reject a single regime . Two regimes against three is a closer call: the BIC is 905.1 for two and 905.0 for three, AIC prefers three (845.6 against 872.1). We stay with two regimes for two reasons: the BIC does not prefer three, and the three-regime solution collapses (Step 7). The three-regime row in this table comes from one default start, so treat it as indicative.

How to read it Regime 0 is the calm regime: it holds 66.5% of the quarters, lasts 29.8 quarters on average ( \(p_{00} = 0.967\) ), and inflation averages 2.9%. Regime 1 is the turbulent regime: 33.5% of the quarters, 16.7 quarters on average ( \(p_{11} = 0.94\) ), inflation averages 6.1%. The sharpest difference is the error variance : 1.6 against 13.5, more than eight times larger. The intercepts differ (1.66, p = 0.009, and 3.52, p = 0.10), but the second is imprecise. The coefficient on lagged inflation is almost the same in both regimes (0.50 and 0.56, both highly significant), and the coefficient on lagged unemployment is small and insignificant in both ( \(-0.04\) and \(-0.14\) ). So the regimes differ in the level and the volatility of inflation, not in how it responds to unemployment. The probability of leaving the turbulent regime (0.06) is only marginally significant (p = 0.08). The RCM of 15.4 shows a sharp classification. No collapse warning was raised.

How to read it The turbulent regime covers 1973Q1–1983Q1 (41 quarters, average probability 0.99, the oil shocks and the disinflation of 1979–82), short episodes in 1985–86 and 1989–90, and 2005Q2–2009Q3 (18 quarters, the energy price swings and the 2008–09 crisis). The calm regime covers 1959Q4–1972Q4 and 1991Q1–2005Q1. The short episodes (3 and 5 quarters) have lower probabilities (0.77–0.91); do not interpret them as separate events. Show the probability figure, not only the dates.

How to read it The residuals fail all three tests: autocorrelation (Ljung-Box p = 0.0003), non-normality (Jarque-Bera p < 0.001) and ARCH (p < 0.001). Quarterly inflation is noisy, has outliers (the minimum is \(-8.8\) ) and has dynamics beyond one lag, which the regime-dependent variance only partly absorbs. The standard errors are therefore approximate; report that, and note that the regime conclusion (a turbulent and a calm state) does not depend on them. If dynamics are the point, use the Markov-switching autoregression with more lags or the Markov-switching VAR.
Robustness, and what a collapsed regime looks like

How to read it Slopes: letting the slopes switch gives almost the same likelihood as common slopes ( \(-426.0\) against \(-426.2\) ), and the BIC is 10 points lower with common slopes (894.8 against 905.1), so the slopes do not need to switch. Unemployment: dropping it leaves the likelihood and BIC unchanged ( \(-426.2\) , 894.8): the Phillips-curve term adds nothing. Variance: forcing a common variance lowers the log-likelihood by 23 (to \(-449.3\) ) and raises the BIC to 946.2, and the regimes become 54% and 46%: switching variance is the essential feature. Collapse: with two lags, and with three regimes, the estimation converges to a regime that holds only 2% of the quarters, and the warning flags both. In the three-regime case one regime holds three quarters and has a variance of zero, and the log-likelihood rises to \(-350.8\) , higher than the non-degenerate solutions, which is exactly why a higher likelihood alone is not a criterion. Report the number of observations in each regime for every specification.

How to write it: results We estimate a two-regime Markov-switching regression of quarterly U.S. inflation on lagged inflation and lagged unemployment, 1959Q4–2009Q3. The data reject a single regime (likelihood-ratio statistic 80.1, against a Garcia 5% critical value of about 14). The calm regime (66.5% of quarters, expected duration 29.8 quarters) has average inflation of 2.9% and error variance 1.6; the turbulent regime (33.5% of quarters, 16.7 quarters) has average inflation of 6.1% and error variance 13.5. The turbulent regime is dated 1973Q1–1983Q1 and 2005Q2–2009Q3, with short episodes in 1985–86 and 1989–90. The slope on lagged inflation is 0.50 in the calm and 0.56 in the turbulent regime; the coefficient on unemployment is not significant in either ( \(-0.04\) and \(-0.14\) ). A specification with common slopes has a lower BIC (894.8 against 905.1), and dropping unemployment changes nothing, so the regimes differ in level and volatility, not in the response of inflation to unemployment. Allowing the variance to switch is essential (the log-likelihood falls by 23 without it). The residuals show autocorrelation and ARCH, so standard errors are approximate. Specifications with three regimes or two lags converge to a regime of fewer than five quarters, and we do not report them.

Markov Switching with Time-Varying Transition Probabilities: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code and more.
Markov Switching with Time-Varying Transition Probabilities

Does a monetary tightening raise the probability that the economy slides into the low-growth regime? Hamilton's (1989) model lets GNP growth have a different mean and variance in two hidden states, with constant transition probabilities. The time-varying version lets the probabilities depend on a variable \(z_{t-1}\) that is known when the quarter begins: The coefficients \(b_k\) say how the driver changes the probability of staying in regime \(k\) . With \(b_k=0\) the model is the constant-probability model. Here \(z_{t-1}\) is the previous quarter's change in the federal funds rate, in percentage points. Symbol Variable Definition \(y_t\) gnp_growth quarterly growth rate of real GNP, in percent \(z_{t-1}\) dff change in the federal funds rate in the previous quarter
Markov Switching with Time-Varying Transition Probabilities

\(s_t\) hidden regime: 0 = high-growth, 1 = low-growth (labelled after estimation) Before you estimate anything Choose the driver for an economic reason before looking at the fit, make sure it is predetermined (observed at \(t-1\) ), and keep the model small: each driver adds two parameters, and the likelihood of a regime-switching model has several local maxima. Use many starting values, check that the regimes are labelled consistently, and compare the regime dates with an independent dating when you have one. How to write it: the model We estimate a two-state Markov-switching model of quarterly U.S. GNP growth, 1954Q3–1984Q4, in which each state has its own mean and variance and the transition probabilities depend on the previous quarter's change in the federal funds rate through a logit (Filardo 1994). We estimate it by maximum likelihood using the Hamilton filter, from twenty random starting values, and label the state with the higher mean as the high-growth state. We compare it with the constant-probability model using a likelihood-ratio test, a permutation test (the driver is shuffled 200 times) and the information criteria, and compare the smoothed regime probabilities with the NBER recession dates.
Markov Switching with Time-Varying Transition Probabilities
Load the data and estimate the constant-probability model

How to read it The sample has 120 quarters (1955Q1–1984Q4), of which 23 (19%) are NBER recession quarters. Growth averages 1.05% outside recessions and −0.55% in recessions. The constant-probability model finds a high-growth state (mean 1.18, variance 0.60, expected duration 9.8 quarters) and a low-growth state (mean −0.07, variance 1.06, 5.0 quarters), which is the familiar Hamilton result. The driver, the change in the funds rate, has a small average difference between the quarters before a recession (0.24) and other quarters (0.04), so a link is not obvious from the raw data.
Markov Switching with Time-Varying Transition Probabilities
Estimate the model with time-varying transition probabilities

How to read it Both slopes are positive and each is significant at about the 5% level: a rise in the funds rate in the previous quarter raises the probability of staying in the low-growth state (slope 0.77, p = 0.052) and of leaving the high-growth state (slope 5.16 in the logit of moving to low growth, p = 0.031). The log-likelihood rises from −168.5 to −161.3 (LR = 14.46, p = 0.0007), and both AIC (338.6 against 349.1) and BIC (360.9 against 365.8) prefer the model with time-varying probabilities. The regime means and variances change a little (high growth 1.30 with variance 0.51, low growth 0.05 with variance 1.01). The slope for the high-growth state is large and imprecisely estimated (standard error 2.39).
Markov Switching with Time-Varying Transition Probabilities
What the driver does to the probabilities

How to read it The implied probabilities move a lot. After a quarter with no change in the funds rate, the probability of staying in high growth is 0.99 and in low growth 0.92. A one-point rise cuts the probability of staying in high growth to 0.47 and raises that of staying in low growth to 0.96; a two-point rise gives a probability of about zero of staying in high growth. These are sharp, close to a rule that a tightening of two points or more ends an expansion, which reflects the large and imprecise logit slope and the few quarters with large rate changes, so we report probabilities at stated values of the driver and not durations (which become extremely long or one quarter at the extremes). The probability of staying in high growth ranges from 0.00 to 1.00 over the sample.
Markov Switching with Time-Varying Transition Probabilities
Regime dates against the NBER dates

How to read it The time-varying model does not date the cycle better than the constant-probability model. The constant model agrees with the NBER in 88% of quarters, catches 96% of recession quarters and has 13% false alarms. The time-varying model agrees in 72%, catches 91% and has 33% false alarms: it flags 53 low-growth quarters against 35, because tightenings of the funds rate that were not followed by an NBER recession (1956, 1959, 1968, 1979) push it into the low-growth state. The smoothed probabilities of the two models are correlated at 0.90. So the driver improves the likelihood by explaining switches, but it also pulls the regimes away from the NBER definition. Whether that is a better or a worse description of the regimes depends on whether you want to date recessions or to find low-growth episodes.
Markov Switching with Time-Varying Transition Probabilities
Is the time variation real? A permutation test

How to read it The permutation test supports the link, but less strongly than the asymptotic test. The likelihood-ratio statistic with the true driver is 14.46; with a shuffled driver the 95th percentile is 10.03 and the maximum 15.64, and the permutation p-value is 0.015, against 0.0007 from the chi-square(2) distribution. The chi-square approximation is therefore too optimistic, in line with the known problems of testing in regime-switching models, but the evidence still favours time-varying probabilities.
Markov Switching with Time-Varying Transition Probabilities
Robustness: the driver, the variance and the starting values

How to read it Other versions of the driver give the same direction: the two-quarter change (LR = 21.5), the change lagged two quarters (LR = 34.2) and the level of the funds rate (LR = 9.5, p = 0.009) all improve the likelihood, with negative slopes for staying in the high-growth state; the lagged change is the strongest, which warns against reading much into one driver. The samples are slightly different (117 quarters) because of the lags. With a common variance in the two regimes the driver still adds 12.4 to the likelihood ratio, and the likelihood is lower (−163.4 against −161.3). All 12 random starting values reach the same maximum (−161.30), so the estimate is not a local optimum.
Markov Switching with Time-Varying Transition Probabilities
Robustness: the driver, the variance and the starting values

How to write it: results A two-state Markov-switching model of GNP growth, 1955Q1–1984Q4, with transition probabilities that depend on the previous quarter's change in the federal funds rate, fits better than the constant-probability model (log-likelihood −161.3 against −168.5; likelihood-ratio test p = 0.0007, permutation p = 0.015). A rise in the funds rate raises the probability of moving from high growth to low growth and of staying there: after no change the probability of staying in high growth is 0.99, after a one-point rise 0.47. The coefficient for the high-growth state is imprecisely estimated (logit slope 5.2, standard error 2.4), and the sensitivity to other versions of the driver is consistent in sign but varies in size. The time-varying model does not match the NBER recessions better than the constant-probability model (72% agreement against 88%, 33% false alarms against 13%), because it also flags tightening episodes that were not followed by recessions. We therefore interpret the low-growth state as a low-growth regime associated with tightening, not as a recession indicator.

What to report in the paper

What to report in the paper

Trusting the chi-square p-value alone. The likelihood has local maxima and regime models are hard to test; show a permutation or bootstrap p-value. One starting value. Report that different starting values reach the same maximum. Label switching. Label the regimes by their means after estimation, not by their position in the output. Reading the logit coefficient as a probability change. Report the implied probabilities and durations at stated values of the driver. Too many drivers. Markov-Switching VAR: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Do GDP growth and inflation behave differently in calm and turbulent regimes, and do shocks have different effects? A Markov-switching VAR (Krolzig 1997) lets the parameters of a VAR depend on an unobserved state \(s_t\) that follows a Markov chain: You choose what switches. MSI : only the intercepts. MSIH : intercepts and covariance matrix; the autoregressive coefficients are common to all regimes. MSIAH : everything switches. The more switches, the more parameters and the more regimes can be fitted to outliers. The model is estimated by maximum likelihood with the EM algorithm (the Hamilton filter and the Kim smoother) from several starting values; standard errors come from the numerical Hessian.

Three checks before you trust a Markov-switching VAR Are the variables stationary? Regimes should describe shifts in means and volatility of stationary variables. How many regimes, and what switches? A model that switches too much can create a regime out of a few outliers. Compare the information criteria and look at the size of every regime (Step 7). Is it better than a linear VAR? The usual \(\chi^2\) test is not valid; use the information criteria and the Davies bound. How to write it: the model We estimate a Markov-switching VAR (Krolzig 1997) with two lags in GDP growth and inflation. The regime, which is unobserved, follows a first-order Markov chain with two states. The intercepts and the covariance matrix of the innovations are regime-specific (MSIH); the autoregressive coefficients are common to both regimes. We estimate the model by maximum likelihood with the EM algorithm from several starting values, using the Hamilton filter and the Kim smoother for the regime probabilities, and take standard errors from the numerical Hessian. We choose the number of regimes with AIC and BIC and compare with a linear VAR using the likelihood-ratio statistic and its Davies bound (Davies 1987), because the standard asymptotic distribution does not hold when the transition probabilities are unidentified under the null.
Load the data and test for unit roots

How to read it GDP growth rejects a unit root at any usual level; inflation rejects it at 5% with a constant (p = 0.025), is borderline with a trend (p = 0.07), and the KPSS test does not reject stationarity at 5% (p = 0.077). Both are treated as stationary, so the VAR can be estimated in levels of these growth rates.
How many regimes? Better than a linear VAR?

How to read it The two-regime model fits much better than a linear VAR: the log-likelihood is \(-910.8\) against \(-968.8\) (LR statistic 115.9, Davies p < 0.001), and AIC (1861.7 against 1963.6) and BIC (1927.6 against 2006.5) both prefer two regimes. Two against three regimes: AIC prefers three (1853.6), BIC prefers two (1927.6 against 1949.3). We use two, because the BIC prefers it and the third regime is hard to interpret (Step 8).

How to read it Regime 0 is the turbulent regime: 39.5% of quarters, 10.4 quarters on average ( \(p_{00} = 0.90\) , standard error 0.04); implied mean GDP growth 1.9% and inflation 5.2%. Regime 1 is the calm regime: 60.5% of quarters, 16.1 quarters on average ( \(p_{11} = 0.94\) , standard error 0.03); mean GDP growth 3.8% and inflation 3.3%. The covariance matrices differ most: the standard deviation of the GDP-growth innovation is 4.2 in regime 0 and 2.2 in regime 1, and that of inflation is 3.5 against 1.0. The correlation of the two innovations is 0.18 in regime 0 and about zero in regime 1. All four intercepts are significant. The autoregressive coefficients are common: inflation is persistent (0.38 and 0.37 on its two lags), GDP growth depends on its own lags (0.20 and 0.17) and, weakly, inflation affects growth negatively ( \(-0.17\) at lag 2 but not significant). The RCM is 19.5, a fairly sharp classification.

How to read it The turbulent regime is dated 1972Q4–1983Q2 (43 quarters, average probability 0.96) and 2005Q3–2009Q3 (17 quarters, 0.94), with short episodes in 1959–61, 1966, 1970–71, 1985–86 and 1990–91. The calm regime covers 1991Q2–2005Q2 (57 quarters) and most of the 1960s. The short episodes of two to six quarters have lower and more variable probabilities (for 1966 the average is 0.65): do not read them as separate events. Present the probability figure with the table.

How to read it The shock is one standard deviation of the regime's Cholesky factor, with GDP growth ordered first (so inflation does not affect GDP growth on impact: this is an assumption, state it). In the MSIH-VAR the autoregressive coefficients are common, so the shape of the responses is the same in both regimes and the difference is the size of the shocks : a one-standard-deviation inflation shock is 3.4 percentage points in the turbulent regime and 1.0 in the calm one. A GDP-growth shock raises inflation by 0.63 on impact and 0.58 a quarter later in regime 0, against 0.03 and 0.19 in regime 1. An inflation shock lowers GDP growth by 0.52 after four quarters in regime 0 and by 0.16 in regime 1. If you want to claim that the propagation of shocks differs between regimes, you need the MSIAH model (Step 8). These responses have no confidence bands; do not claim significance for the differences.

How to read it Residuals are acceptable for GDP growth (Ljung-Box p = 0.65, ARCH p = 0.21) and not for inflation: autocorrelation (p = 0.02) and ARCH (p < 0.001). Both reject normality (p < 0.001), which reflects outliers. The multivariate portmanteau test rejects at 5% (p = 0.026). The standard errors are therefore approximate. Residual ARCH in inflation suggests that two variance regimes do not capture all the volatility change; the SV-VAR in the Bayesian section handles this.
Robustness: what switches, lags, regimes and starting values

How to read it What switches. With intercepts only (MSI), the second regime is a 1.4-quarter episode holding 6% of the periods: a collapse onto outliers, and the BIC is 1981.3. Letting all coefficients switch (MSIAH) raises the log-likelihood by only 3.4 and the BIC to 1963.2, against 1927.6 for MSIH, so there is no evidence that the dynamics switch. Lags. BIC is lowest with three lags (1912.9; four lags 1916.8, two lags 1927.6, one lag 1959.7; the sample shrinks by one quarter per extra lag, so these are close but not exact comparisons). With three lags the classification agrees with the baseline in 91% of the quarters, but the regimes no longer differ in the level of inflation (implied means 4.12 and 4.08), only in growth (1.9% and 3.8%) and volatility: the label "high-inflation regime" depends on the lag order , so describe the regimes by volatility and growth unless the result holds across lags. Regimes. Three regimes hold 27%, 28% and 44% of the periods, with expected durations of 7.1, 51.8 and 12.5 quarters. Starting values. Twenty starting values give exactly the same log-likelihood as the default, so the solution is not a local maximum.

How to write it: results We estimate a Markov-switching VAR (Krolzig 1997) with two regimes and two lags in quarterly GDP growth and inflation, 1959Q4–2009Q3, with regime-specific intercepts and covariance matrices (MSIH). It fits much better than a linear VAR (BIC 1927.6 against 2006.5; likelihood-ratio statistic 115.9, Davies p < 0.001). The turbulent regime holds 39.5% of the quarters, lasts 10.4 quarters on average, and has mean GDP growth of 1.9%, mean inflation of 5.2% and innovation standard deviations of 4.2 and 3.5; the calm regime holds 60.5% of the quarters, lasts 16.1 quarters, and has mean growth of 3.8%, mean inflation of 3.3% and innovation standard deviations of 2.2 and 1.0. The turbulent regime is dated 1972Q4–1983Q2 and 2005Q3–2009Q3. Because the autoregressive coefficients are common, impulse responses have the same shape in both regimes and differ in size, since shocks are about three times larger in the turbulent regime; allowing the coefficients to switch does not improve the BIC (1963.2). The result is robust to the starting values (20 starts give the same maximum). It is not robust to the lag order in one respect: with three lags the regimes no longer differ in mean inflation, only in growth and volatility. A model with intercepts only collapses onto a 1.4-quarter regime. Residuals for inflation show autocorrelation and ARCH, so standard errors are approximate.
