Conditional and Mixed Logit (Discrete Choice): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

How do cost and travel time affect the choice of travel mode? Traveller \(i\) chooses mode \(j\) with the highest utility where \(x_{ij}\) are attributes of the mode as the traveller faces them (cost, times), \(\alpha_j\) are mode-specific constants, \(w_i\) are traveller characteristics with mode-specific effects \(\delta_j\) (one mode is the base), and \(\varepsilon_{ij}\) is Gumbel. This gives the closed-form choice probability In the mixed logit some coefficients are random, \(\beta_i \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) , and the probability is the average of the logit formula over the distribution of \(\beta_i\) , computed by simulation. Variable Definition id , alt traveller and mode (air, train, bus, car); four rows per traveller

choice 1 for the mode the traveller chose ttme terminal (waiting) time in minutes; 0 for car invc , invt in-vehicle cost in dollars and in-vehicle time in minutes gc generalized cost (cost plus time valued at the traveller's wage) hinc , psize household income (thousand dollars) and party size (do not vary across the modes) Before you estimate anything Is the data in the right shape? One row per traveller and alternative, an identifier for the traveller, one for the alternative and a 0/1 indicator that sums to 1 within each traveller. Which variables vary across alternatives? Cost and time do, and enter with a single coefficient. Income does not, so it can only enter through coefficients that differ by mode (relative to a base mode).

Is the substitution pattern plausible? The conditional logit says that adding an alternative takes probability from all others in proportion to their shares. Test this. How to write it: model section We model each traveller's choice among air, train, bus and car as a conditional logit in which the utility of a mode depends on the terminal time, in-vehicle cost, in-vehicle time and generalized cost of that mode, plus mode-specific constants (car is the base). We compute willingness-to-pay ratios and elasticities with the delta method, test the independence of irrelevant alternatives with a Hausman-McFadden test, and estimate a mixed logit in which the coefficient on terminal time is normally distributed across travellers.
Load the data and look at the choices

How to read it The shares are balanced: train 30%, air 28%, car 28%, bus 14%. Air is the fastest in the vehicle (about 134 minutes) but the most expensive ($85) and needs the longest terminal time (about 61 minutes); car has no terminal time and is the cheapest ($21); train and bus are slow (about 10 hours in the vehicle) and cheaper than air. This variation in attributes across modes is what identifies the coefficients.

How to read it Longer terminal time, higher cost and longer in-vehicle time all lower the utility of a mode (z statistics between −4.4 and −9.5), and the signs are as expected; the coefficient on generalized cost is positive because it is highly collinear with the cost and time variables it is built from, so read it jointly with the others. The log-likelihood is −184.5. The constants say that, with everything else equal, air, bus and train are all preferred to car in this sample. The model has a McFadden R-squared of 0.37 against equal shares and 0.35 against market shares.
Step 2: Willingness to pay and elasticities

How to read it The cost coefficient converts the time coefficients into dollars. A minute of in-vehicle time is worth 16 cents, or $9.4 an hour, and a minute of terminal time is worth $1.22, or $73 an hour, about eight times as much: waiting at a terminal is much more costly than being on the move. The own-cost elasticities are −5.0 for air and −1.4 for car, so air demand is very sensitive to price and car demand is not. The cross elasticities are identical for every other mode (a feature of the conditional logit that the next step tests), and the predicted shares equal the observed shares by construction, since the constants fit them exactly.
Step 2: Willingness to pay and elasticities

How to write it: main result Travellers value a minute of in-vehicle time at 16 cents (standard error 1.6 cents), or $9.4 per hour, and a minute of terminal time at $1.22, or $73 per hour. Demand for air travel is elastic with respect to its cost (elasticity −5.0), while demand for car travel is not (−1.4). The model reproduces the observed mode shares and has a McFadden R-squared of 0.37.
Step 3: Is the independence of irrelevant alternatives plausible?

How to read it Removing air (chi-squared 34), bus (46) or train (30) changes the coefficients of the attributes far more than sampling error allows, and the test rejects the independence of irrelevant alternatives in each case. The traveller who is choosing between train and bus is not choosing in the same way when air is available as when it is not: there is a common unobserved taste for public transport. This rejects the strict substitution pattern of the conditional logit, and the results should be read as an approximation. Two remedies are a nested logit (public transport in one nest) and a mixed logit.
Step 4: Mixed logit with a random coefficient on terminal time

How to read it Allowing the terminal-time coefficient to vary across travellers improves the log-likelihood from −193 to −178 (comparing models with the same three attributes), which rejects a common coefficient at any usual level (chi-squared 29.5). The mean coefficient is −0.18 and its standard deviation 0.11, so about 4% of travellers would have a positive coefficient. Terminal time is zero for car, so its coefficient also reflects how strongly each traveller dislikes the public modes relative to car, and the random coefficient captures part of the unobserved taste for car that the independence of irrelevant alternatives test detected. Mixed logit needs a choice of distribution and draws; check that the results are stable when you increase the number of draws.
What to report in the paper

Report the number of travellers and alternatives; the coefficients, the base alternative and the constants; the log-likelihood and McFadden R-squared; willingness-to-pay ratios and elasticities; the test of independence of irrelevant alternatives; and, if you use a mixed logit, the distributions assumed, the number of draws and a likelihood-ratio test against the conditional logit. How to write it: results and robustness Table 5 reports the conditional logit. A Hausman-McFadden test rejects the independence of irrelevant alternatives (chi-squared 30 to 46, p < 0.001 when dropping any of air, bus or train), so we also estimate a mixed logit with a random coefficient on terminal time (100 Halton draws). The mixed logit fits significantly better (likelihood-ratio statistic 29.5) with a mean coefficient of −0.18 and a standard deviation of 0.11. The cost and in-vehicle-time coefficients are similar in the two models (cost −0.021 against −0.014, in-vehicle time −0.0066 against −0.0040), so the willingness-to-pay ratios in the conditional logit should be treated as approximate.

Mistakes to avoid Wrong data shape. The conditional logit needs one row per person and alternative, not one row per person. Putting a case-specific variable in with a single coefficient. Income does not vary across modes, so it cancels out; it must have a mode-specific coefficient. Reading constants as preferences without the base. Constants are relative to the base alternative. Ignoring the independence of irrelevant alternatives. Test it, and use a nested or mixed logit if it fails. Including a generalized cost variable together with its components. It is collinear with them and the signs become uninterpretable. Few draws in a mixed logit. Use at least 100 Halton draws and check stability.

Interpreting a normal random coefficient with a large spread literally. The normal puts weight on the wrong sign; consider a lognormal for cost. Computing elasticities without averaging. Own and cross elasticities differ across people; report the average over the sample.
Poisson and Negative-Binomial Regression (Counts): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

How do cost sharing and health status affect the number of doctor visits? The RAND experiment randomly assigned families to insurance plans with different coinsurance rates. In a Poisson model the expected count is A coefficient is the change in the log expected count, so \(\exp(\beta)\) is a multiplicative effect, the incidence-rate ratio. The Poisson distribution forces the variance to equal the mean. The negative binomial (NB2) allows \(\operatorname{Var}(y) = \mu + \alpha\mu^2\) , with a dispersion parameter \(\alpha \ge 0\) . Variable in the file Definition mdvis number of face-to-face doctor visits in the year lncoins log of coinsurance rate plus one (0 to 4.6) idp 1 if the plan has an individual deductible

lpi log of participation incentive payment fmde log of the maximum medical expenditure at the plan's deductible (0 if no deductible) physlm 1 if the person has a physical limitation disea chronic-disease index (number of chronic conditions, scaled) hlthg , hlthf , hlthp self-rated health good, fair, poor (excellent is the base) Before you estimate anything Is the outcome a count? Non-negative whole numbers, with no fixed upper limit. For a count out of a known number of trials use a binomial model. Is the exposure the same for everyone? If people are observed for different lengths of time (or populations differ in size), use an exposure variable so the model describes a rate.

Are there more zeros than the model can produce? If so, a zero-inflated or hurdle model may be needed (next guide). How to write it: model section The number of doctor visits is a non-negative count, so we model its conditional mean as \(\exp(x'\beta)\) and estimate it by Poisson maximum likelihood with standard errors that are robust to overdispersion. Because the variance far exceeds the mean, we also estimate a negative-binomial model with a dispersion parameter and compare the two. We report incidence-rate ratios and average marginal effects on the expected number of visits.
Load the data and look at the count

How to read it The variance is almost eight times the mean, so the Poisson assumption of equal mean and variance fails badly, and a third of the sample has no visits. The variance exceeds the mean in every group of the chronic-disease index, and the mean differs across groups, which is the relationship the regression will quantify.
Step 1: Poisson regression with robust standard errors

How to read it Each additional point of the chronic-disease index raises the log expected number of visits by 0.038, and having an individual deductible lowers it by 0.26. Poor self-rated health raises it by 0.50. The robust standard errors are about 2.5 times the model-based ones, which shows how much the Poisson formula understates uncertainty when the data are overdispersed. Poisson estimation of the mean remains consistent even then, which is why the robust version is the safe default.
Step 2: Rate ratios and marginal effects

How to read it A person with a deductible plan has 0.77 times the visits of one without (a 23% reduction, confidence interval 0.69 to 0.87), and a person in poor health has 1.65 times the visits of one in excellent health. In levels, a deductible lowers the expected count by 0.71 visits per year on average, and each point of the chronic-disease index adds 0.11. The rate ratio is the same for everybody; the marginal effect in levels is larger for people who already visit often, which is why it is averaged. How to write it: main result Individual deductibles reduce expected doctor visits by 23% (incidence-rate ratio 0.77, 95% confidence interval 0.69 to 0.87), or 0.71 visits per person per year at the sample average. Each point of the chronic-disease index raises visits by about 3.9%, and people in poor health have 65% more visits than those in excellent health.
Step 3: Is the variance equal to the mean?

How to read it Both ratios are far above 1 (6.9 and 4.4), and the Cameron-Trivedi test strongly rejects equidispersion (t = 7.9). The Poisson model predicts 8% zeros against the 32% in the data. These are symptoms of overdispersion and unobserved heterogeneity among people with the same covariates, and they motivate the negative binomial.

How to read it The dispersion parameter alpha is 1.39, far from zero, and the likelihood-ratio test rejects the Poisson model decisively; the AIC falls by about 8,400. The negative binomial predicts 33% zeros against the observed 32%. The coefficients are close to the Poisson ones (a deductible lowers visits by 24% against 23%, a point of the disease index raises them by 4.3% against 3.9%), but the negative binomial weights observations differently, and the two agree to this extent only if the mean is well specified. A large difference between the two would be a warning about the mean function.
Step 5: How well does each model reproduce the distribution?

How to read it The Poisson curve badly underpredicts zeros and long counts and overpredicts the middle; the negative binomial follows the observed distribution closely: the largest gap between observed and predicted shares over the counts 0 to 10 is 0.24 for the Poisson and 0.014 for the negative binomial. When the zeros are still too frequent after the negative binomial, consider a zero-inflated or hurdle model.
What to report in the paper

Report the mean and variance of the count; the model and why you chose it (the dispersion tests); coefficients with robust standard errors, incidence-rate ratios and average marginal effects; the comparison of Poisson and negative binomial; and any exposure variable. How to write it: results and robustness Table 2 reports Poisson and negative-binomial estimates. The variance of visits is 7.8 times its mean, a Cameron-Trivedi test rejects equidispersion, and a likelihood-ratio test rejects the Poisson model in favor of the negative binomial (alpha = 1.39). The two models give the same signs and similar magnitudes for the variables of interest, and the negative-binomial model reproduces the share of people with no visits (33% predicted, 32% observed) where the Poisson model predicts 8%.

Mistakes to avoid Using the model-based Poisson standard errors. They are far too small under overdispersion. Use robust ones. Reading a coefficient as a change in the count. It is a change in the log count; use the rate ratio or the marginal effect. Transforming the count and using OLS. The log of a count with zeros is undefined and log(y + 1) gives biased effects. Ignoring different exposure. If observation periods or populations differ, add an exposure variable. Choosing between Poisson and negative binomial only by a significance test. Compare the fit of the whole distribution, not only alpha. Treating excess zeros as overdispersion. If a separate process generates the zeros, a zero-inflated or hurdle model describes the data better.
Comparing NB2 and Poisson coefficients as if they estimated different things. Both estimate the mean function; if they differ much, check the specification.

Generalized Linear Models and Fractional Responses

How does the employer match raise the share of eligible employees who take up a 401(k) plan? The outcome prate is the proportion of eligible employees who participate, between 0 and 1. In the fractional-response model the mean is a logistic function of a linear index, so predictions stay in (0, 1) and the effect of a variable shrinks near the bounds. The model is estimated by the Bernoulli quasi-likelihood, which gives consistent estimates for any distribution of \(y\) on [0, 1], including a large mass at 1, as long as the mean is right; the standard errors are made robust to the unknown variance. prate participation rate: share of eligible employees with an account mrate employer match per dollar of employee contribution ltotemp log of the number of employees age age of the plan in years sole 1 if the 401(k) is the only pension plan offered Before you estimate anything Is the outcome a proportion, with or without exact 0s and 1s? Fractional logit allows both. A Beta regression does not allow the boundary values. Is the mean function the target? The model is about the expected share; it says nothing about the distribution unless you add assumptions. Are the observations the unit you want to weight? Each firm counts once here. If you want the share of employees, weight by firm size.
Generalized Linear Models and Fractional Responses

How to write it: model section The participation rate is a proportion with 44% of firms at exactly 1, so we model its conditional mean with a logistic function and estimate it by quasi-maximum likelihood (a generalized linear model with the binomial family and logit link; Papke and Wooldridge, 1996). Standard errors are robust to heteroskedasticity. We report average marginal effects on the participation rate and compare the logit link with the probit and complementary log-log alternatives.
Generalized Linear Models and Fractional Responses
Load the data and look at the bounded outcome

How to read it Participation is high (mean 0.87), piled up at 1 (44% of firms), and rises with the match rate: from 0.80 in the lowest quartile to 0.96 in the highest. A distribution like this, bounded and with a spike at the upper bound, is not described well by a normal linear model.
Generalized Linear Models and Fractional Responses
Step 1: OLS and what is wrong with it

How to read it OLS says a dollar more of match raises participation by 4.9 percentage points on average. It predicts a rate above 100% for 63 firms, and a constant slope cannot be right for a variable that cannot exceed one: firms near the ceiling have little room to respond. The fractional-logit model builds this into the mean function.
Generalized Linear Models and Fractional Responses

How to read it The coefficients are on the logit scale: a higher match, an older plan and the sole-plan indicator raise participation, and a larger firm lowers it. The marginal effect of the match rate is 0.097, twice the OLS slope: a dollar of match raises participation by about 9.7 points on average, and the effect of one more log point of firm size is −2.2 points. The OLS slope is smaller because it averages over the whole range, including firms near the ceiling where the logistic curve is flat. How to write it: main result A one-dollar higher employer match raises the participation rate by 9.7 percentage points (average marginal effect, robust standard error 1.4), about twice the OLS estimate of 4.9 points. Larger firms have lower participation (−2.2 points per log point of employment), and plans that have existed longer have higher participation (0.34 points per year).
Generalized Linear Models and Fractional Responses
Step 3: Does the choice of link matter?

How to read it The three links agree on the sign and significance but not exactly on the size of the marginal effect of the match rate (0.097 for the logit, 0.079 for the probit, 0.064 for the complementary log-log), and the logit has the best fit by both the squared correlation (0.182) and the sum of squared residuals (35.07). The OLS squared correlation is lower (0.147). All three link tests reject, with t statistics from −3.8 to −4.3, which says that the index is not fully captured by a linear combination of these four variables and a single link (for example, the effect of the match probably differs by firm size). The link choice is not what drives the result; the specification of the index is the issue to investigate.
Generalized Linear Models and Fractional Responses
Step 4: Fit by decile and the variance question

How to read it The fitted means follow the observed means closely across deciles. The Pearson ratio is about 0.24, far below 1, because a share is much less variable than a single yes/no outcome. This is why the robust (sandwich) standard errors matter: the model-based Bernoulli standard errors would be too large by a factor of about two, and the robust ones are valid whatever the true variance.
Generalized Linear Models and Fractional Responses
What to report in the paper

Report the share at the bounds; the family and link and why; coefficients with robust standard errors; average marginal effects on the mean; the comparison with OLS and with other links; and the fit by decile. If the outcome is a share of a total, say what the weights are. How to write it: results and robustness Table 2 reports the fractional-logit estimates. The sign and significance of the match rate are the same with probit and complementary log-log links, although the marginal effect is smaller (0.079 and 0.064 against 0.097), and the logit link fits best. The link test rejects a single-index specification for all three links, so the point estimates should be read as an approximation to the average effect, and a richer index (for example an interaction between the match and firm size) is a natural extension.

Mistakes to avoid Using OLS on a share and reading the slope as constant. It ignores the bounds and predicts impossible values. Using log(y/(1-y)) with OLS. It fails when y is exactly 0 or 1, and the transformed mean is not the mean of the share. Reading the logit coefficient as a percentage-point effect. Use the average marginal effect. Model-based standard errors. For a quasi-likelihood use robust standard errors. Treating a mass at the bound as a censoring problem. The values at 1 are real values here, not censored (use Tobit for a censored outcome). Forgetting the weights. A firm-level rate and an employee-level rate are different targets. For positive skewed amounts, using a log transform in OLS. Use a GLM with a gamma family and log link, which gives the effect on the mean without retransformation bias.
Heckman Sample-Selection Model: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

What is the return to a year of schooling for women, including those who do not work? Wages are observed only for women in the labor force. The Heckman model has two equations: with \((u_i,\varepsilon_i)\) jointly normal and correlation \(\rho\) . If \(\rho \neq 0\) , the workers are a selected sample and OLS on them is biased. The correction adds a term, the inverse Mills ratio, that measures how strongly each worker was selected. Variable in the file Definition inlf 1 if the woman worked in 1975 (selection indicator) lwage log wage (blank for women who did not work) educ , exper , expersq years of schooling, labor-market experience and its square

age age in years kidslt6 , kidsge6 children under 6 and aged 6 to 18 nwifeinc household income other than the woman's own earnings, in thousands Before you estimate anything Do you have an exclusion restriction? At least one variable should affect selection but not the outcome. Here kidslt6 , kidsge6 , age and nwifeinc affect whether a woman works but are assumed not to affect her wage given education and experience. Without such a variable the model is identified only by the shape of the normal distribution, which is fragile. Is the exclusion restriction believable? This is a judgment about the economics, and no test can settle it. State the argument in the paper.

Is the outcome truly missing for the non-selected? The model is not for outcomes that are zero (use Tobit or a hurdle model). How to write it: model section Wages are observed only for the 428 of 753 women who worked, so OLS on workers may be biased by selection. We estimate a Heckman sample-selection model in which a probit for working is estimated jointly with the log-wage equation. Age, the number of young and older children and other household income enter the selection equation only. We report the two-step estimator with corrected standard errors and the full-information maximum likelihood estimator, and we test whether the errors of the two equations are correlated.
Load the data and look at the selected sample

How to read it Women who worked are more educated, more experienced, younger, and have far fewer young children (0.14 against 0.37) than those who did not. They are not a random sample of women, and the variables that differ most are experience (13.0 against 7.5 years) and young children. Young children, age and other household income are the candidates for the exclusion restriction because they predict selection.
Step 1: OLS on the selected sample

How to read it On working women, a year of schooling raises wages by about 10.7% and experience has the usual concave profile. This is the benchmark. The question is whether it describes all women or only those who chose to work.
Step 2: The selection equation and the inverse Mills ratio

How to read it Young children lower the probability of working sharply (−0.87), as do age (−0.053 per year) and other household income (−0.012 per thousand), while education and experience raise it. The inverse Mills ratio is large for women who were unlikely to work but did, and small for women who very likely work. Because the ratio is correlated with education among workers (−0.33), omitting it would bias the education coefficient if the ratio mattered for wages.

How to read it The coefficient on the inverse Mills ratio is 0.032 with a corrected standard error of 0.134 (t = 0.24): there is no evidence that selection biases the wage equation. The education coefficient moves only from 0.107 to 0.109, and the implied correlation between the two errors is close to zero. The corrected standard errors are almost identical to the naive OLS ones (marginally smaller here), because the correction term matters little when rho is small. In this sample, then, OLS on workers is a good guide to the wage equation, a legitimate and useful finding, not a failure of the method.

How to read it Maximum likelihood estimates both equations at once and is more efficient than the two-step estimator if the normality assumption holds. It gives almost the same wage equation (education 0.108, experience 0.043) with smaller standard errors, and an estimated correlation rho of 0.03 (standard error 0.15). The likelihood-ratio test of rho = 0 gives chi-squared of 0.03 (p = 0.86), so independent equations are not rejected. Two-step and ML agree, which is reassuring.
Step 5: How fragile is the correction?

How to read it When the selection equation uses only the outcome regressors, the inverse Mills ratio is almost a linear function of them, so the coefficients become unstable: the standard error of education is 0.051 against 0.016 with the restriction, and the ratio's own coefficient has a standard error of 0.95. The R-squared of the ratio on the outcome regressors is 0.986 without the restriction and 0.539 with it. The exclusion restriction is what separates selection from the outcome equation. The R-squared of the ratio on the outcome regressors tells you how much room the correction has; report it.
What to report in the paper

Report the sample sizes (selected and total); the selection equation; the outcome equation by two-step and maximum likelihood; rho and sigma; the test of rho = 0; the argument for each exclusion restriction; and the OLS estimate for comparison. How to write it: results and robustness Table 1 reports the Heckman model for 753 women, 428 of whom worked. Young children, age and other household income strongly affect participation. The wage equation implies a return to schooling of 10.9% (two-step) and 10.8% (maximum likelihood), close to the OLS estimate of 10.7% on workers. The estimated correlation between the errors is 0.03 and a likelihood-ratio test does not reject independence (p = 0.86), so we find no evidence of selection bias in this sample. The result depends on the exclusion restrictions, which we motivate by the fact that family circumstances change the value of time at home but not market productivity.

Mistakes to avoid No exclusion restriction. Identification then rests on normality alone. Always include a variable that shifts selection but not the outcome, and defend it. A weak or invalid exclusion restriction. If the excluded variable affects the outcome directly (children and wages through hours), the correction is wrong. No test can prove validity. Using the naive OLS standard errors in the two-step. They ignore that the ratio is estimated. Use the corrected ones or maximum likelihood. Treating a rejected rho = 0 as a causal result. It says selection matters, and the corrected estimates are only as good as the normality assumption. Applying Heckman to a corner solution. Zero hours are not missing data; use Tobit or a hurdle model.

Reading the coefficients of the selection equation as effects on wages. They are effects on the probability of being in the sample. Dropping non-selected observations before estimation. The probit needs them.
The right microeconometric model depends on what your outcome looks like and on what stands in the way of a plain regression: a yes/no outcome and more.
Choose the answer that describes your outcome. Each answer lights up the decision tree and narrows the choice to one guide.

IV Probit and the Control Function (Endogenous Regressors in a Binary Model): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code and more.
IV Probit and the Control Function (Endogenous Regressors in a Binary Model)

Does schooling raise the probability that a married woman is in the labor force? Years of education educ is plausibly correlated with unobserved ability and motivation that also drive employment. With an instrument \(z\) (the parents' education) that moves education but has no direct effect on participation, the model is If \(\rho \neq 0\) , ordinary probit is inconsistent. The control function writes \(u_i = \rho v_i/\sigma_v + \text{noise}\) , so adding the first-stage residual \(\hat v_i\) to the probit "controls" for the endogeneity, and the coefficient on \(\hat v_i\) tests exogeneity ( \(H_0: \rho = 0\) ). Variable Definition inlf 1 if the woman was in the labor force in 1975
IV Probit and the Control Function (Endogenous Regressors in a Binary Model)

educ years of education (the endogenous regressor) motheduc , fatheduc years of education of the mother and father (excluded instruments) exper , expersq , age labor-market experience, its square, age kidslt6 , kidsge6 , nwifeinc children under 6 and aged 6 to 18, other household income Before you estimate anything Is there an instrument that is relevant and excluded? Relevant means it predicts education in the first stage (check the F statistic); excluded means it has no direct effect on participation. Parents' education satisfies the first condition easily; the second is a debatable assumption (educated parents may pass on other advantages). How many instruments? At least one per endogenous regressor. With more, you can test overidentification only in a linear model; for the probit, the check is informal.
IV Probit and the Control Function (Endogenous Regressors in a Binary Model)

What do you report? Coefficients depend on the scale of the error, so report average effects on the probability. How to write it: model section We estimate the effect of education on the probability of labor-force participation of 753 married women. Because education may be correlated with unobserved ability, we instrument it with the education of the woman's mother and father and estimate a probit with a control function (Rivers and Vuong, 1988), with standard errors that account for the estimated first-stage residual. We test exogeneity of education with the coefficient on the first-stage residual, check the strength of the instruments in the first stage, and compare average effects with those of an ordinary probit.
IV Probit and the Control Function (Endogenous Regressors in a Binary Model)

How to read it Each year of the mother's or father's schooling raises the woman's schooling by 0.17 and 0.16 years, and the F statistic of the two instruments is 96, far above the rule-of-thumb value of 10: the instruments are strong. The first-stage residual vhat is the part of education that the instruments and the controls do not explain, and it is the "control function".
IV Probit and the Control Function (Endogenous Regressors in a Binary Model)
Step 2: Ordinary probit, then the control-function probit

How to read it The coefficient on education rises from 0.131 in the ordinary probit to 0.150 once the first-stage residual is included, and the residual itself is small and not significant (z = −0.40, p = 0.69): there is no sign that education is endogenous for participation here, so the ordinary probit is consistent and the instrumented estimate is just less precise. The test of the residual is a valid exogeneity test with the naive standard error; the other standard errors in the second stage need a correction, because \(\hat v_i\) is estimated.
IV Probit and the Control Function (Endogenous Regressors in a Binary Model)
Step 3: Standard errors that account for the first stage (bootstrap)

How to read it The bootstrap re-estimates both stages in every sample, so it reflects the uncertainty of the first stage. For education the bootstrap standard error (about 0.05) is of the same order as the naive 0.055; for the other coefficients the two are close. The OES engine computes the correction analytically from the stacked first-stage and probit moment conditions, and it agrees with the bootstrap to within sampling error. Use one of these, not the naive second-stage standard errors, for the exogenous variables and the endogenous one.
IV Probit and the Control Function (Endogenous Regressors in a Binary Model)
Step 4: Average effects on the probability

How to read it One more year of education raises the probability of working by 4.5 percentage points with the instrument and by 3.9 points in the ordinary probit. The effects of the other variables are almost the same in the two models, as the weak evidence of endogeneity suggests (young children lower the probability by 26 points, other household income by 0.4 points per thousand dollars). The OES engine reports a standard error of 0.016 for the instrumented effect against 0.007 for the ordinary probit: more than twice as large, which is the price of the instrument. How to write it: main result An additional year of education raises the probability that a married woman works by 4.5 percentage points in the instrumented probit (standard error 1.6 points), against 3.9 points (0.7) in the ordinary probit. The coefficient on the first-stage residual is not significant (p = 0.7), so we cannot reject exogeneity of education, and the two estimates are statistically indistinguishable.
IV Probit and the Control Function (Endogenous Regressors in a Binary Model)
Step 5: Maximum likelihood for the same model

How to read it Maximum likelihood gives almost the same coefficient on education (0.150) as the control function and a correlation rho between the two errors of −0.05 (standard error 0.11), also not significant. The two estimators agree because the model is the same; maximum likelihood is more efficient if normality holds, and the control function is more robust to non-normality of the outcome error. Both rely on the normality of the first-stage error.
IV Probit and the Control Function (Endogenous Regressors in a Binary Model)
What to report in the paper

Report the first-stage coefficients of the instruments and the F statistic, the exogeneity test, the second-stage estimates with standard errors that account for the first stage, and average effects with the ordinary probit alongside. State the exclusion argument for each instrument. How to write it: results and robustness Table 4 reports the first stage (F = 96) and the instrumented probit. The coefficient on the first-stage residual is small and insignificant (z = −0.4), and a maximum-likelihood estimate of the same model gives a correlation between the errors of −0.05 (standard error 0.11). We therefore cannot reject that education is exogenous. The exclusion restriction (parents' schooling affects participation only through the woman's schooling) is an assumption: it fails if educated parents also transmit labor-market attachment, in which case both instrumented and ordinary estimates would be biased in ways the tests above cannot reveal.
IV Probit and the Control Function (Endogenous Regressors in a Binary Model)

Mistakes to avoid Plugging fitted values into a probit ("forbidden regression"). This is inconsistent in nonlinear models. Use the control function or maximum likelihood. Using the naive second-stage standard errors. The first-stage residual is estimated. Bootstrap or use the stacked-moment correction. Comparing coefficients across models. The scale of the error differs; compare average effects. A weak instrument. Check the first-stage F; with a weak instrument the estimates are unstable and biased toward the ordinary probit. A non-excluded instrument. No test confirms exclusion when the model is exactly identified; argue it on economic grounds. Using a binary endogenous regressor in a continuous first stage without caution. The control-function approach assumes a linear first stage with normal errors; with a binary endogenous variable use a bivariate probit or a different approach.

Reading an insignificant exogeneity test as proof of exogeneity. It may only reflect low power.

Does a new teaching method (PSI, the Personalized System of Instruction) raise the probability that an economics student earns an A in the next course, once we control for ability? Spector and Mazzeo (1980) observed 32 students and recorded whether the final grade improved over the grade in the previous course. In a binary-outcome model the probability of success depends on a linear index: The coefficients \(\beta\) are estimated by maximum likelihood. The data have three explanatory variables. Symbol Variable in the file Definition \(y\) GRADE 1 if the final grade was higher than in the previous course, 0 otherwise \(x_1\) GPA grade point average before the course (a measure of ability)

\(x_2\) TUCE score on a pre-test of economics knowledge \(x_3\) PSI 1 if the student was taught with the new method, 0 otherwise Before you estimate anything Is the outcome really binary and coded 0/1? A variable coded 1 and 2, or text such as "yes" and "no", must be recoded first. Are there enough observations in both classes? The rule of thumb is at least 10 observations of the rarer outcome for each parameter. Here 11 students improved and 21 did not, for four parameters: this is a small sample, and the guide shows what that means for inference. Does any regressor predict the outcome perfectly? Then the maximum-likelihood estimate does not exist (separation). The estimator will fail or return enormous coefficients.

How to write it: model section We model the probability that a student's grade improves as a function of prior ability and the teaching method with a logit model estimated by maximum likelihood. The outcome equals one if the final grade is higher than the grade in the preceding course. The explanatory variables are the grade point average (GPA), a pre-test score (TUCE) and an indicator for the personalised system of instruction (PSI). Because logit coefficients are not changes in probabilities, we report average marginal effects and odds ratios, and we check the specification by a likelihood-ratio test, the Hosmer-Lemeshow test and a link test.
Load the data and look at it first

How to read it Of the 32 students, 34% improved their grade. Among students taught with the PSI method 57% improved, against 17% under the traditional method, a large raw gap. But the students who improved also had a higher GPA (3.43 against 2.95 on average), and ability may be unevenly spread across the two methods. A model that controls for GPA and TUCE separates the teaching effect from the ability effect. The figure shows the pattern: the students who improved are concentrated at high GPA, and the orange PSI students are on the right.
Why not a linear regression? The linear probability model

How to read it The linear probability model (LPM) is easy to read, because each coefficient is directly a change in probability: here a student taught with PSI is about 0.38 more likely to improve. But the model has two known flaws. It can predict impossible probabilities (the output counts the fitted values outside the 0 to 1 range), and the variance of a binary outcome is \(p(1-p)\) , which changes with the regressors, so the errors are heteroskedastic by construction and the standard errors must be robust (the Breusch-Pagan test does not reject here, p = 0.16, but with 32 observations it has little power). The LPM is still a useful benchmark: when the logit marginal effects are close to the LPM coefficients, the choice of model is not driving your conclusion.

How to read it The logit coefficients are the change in the log odds of improving. GPA has a coefficient of 2.83 (p = 0.025) and PSI 2.38 (p = 0.025); TUCE, 0.10, is not significant. The signs and significance are the first read, and the size is easier in odds: the odds ratio for PSI is 10.8, so the odds of improving are about ten times higher under the PSI method, holding GPA and TUCE fixed. The confidence interval (1.3 to 86.9) is very wide, a reminder that 32 students, 11 of whom improved, cannot pin the size down. The likelihood-ratio test rejects that all slopes are zero (chi-squared 15.4, p = 0.0015). Do not interpret a logit coefficient as a change in probability: that is the job of the next step.
Marginal effects: the change in probability

How to read it The average marginal effects answer the question in probabilities. Averaged over the 32 students, one more grade point raises the probability of improving by 0.36, and switching a student from the traditional method to PSI raises it by 0.36 (a discrete change from 0 to 1, not a derivative). The effect of TUCE is 0.01 and not significant. The by-hand calculation reproduces the numbers, which shows that the marginal effect is the logistic density times the coefficient, averaged over the sample. The figure shows why the effect is not a single number: it is the vertical gap between the curves, which is small at low GPA, large in the middle and small again near the top, where almost everybody improves. The LPM coefficient for PSI (0.38) is close to the logit AME (0.36), but for GPA the linear model gives 0.46 against 0.36, because a straight line cannot bend where the probability flattens out. The marginal effects at the sample means (0.53 for GPA, 0.46 for PSI) are larger than the averages, because the student with mean characteristics sits on the steep middle of the curve, while many real students sit in the flat parts. Report the average marginal effect unless there is a reason to describe a typical case.
Marginal effects: the change in probability

How to write it: main result Holding GPA and the pre-test score constant, the PSI method raises the probability of an improved grade by 0.36 (average marginal effect, standard error 0.14, p = 0.012), and the odds of improving are 10.8 times those under the traditional method (95% confidence interval 1.3 to 86.9). An additional grade point raises the probability by 0.36 (standard error 0.11, p < 0.001). The pre-test score has no significant effect. The wide confidence interval for the odds ratio reflects the small sample of 32 students.
How well does the model fit? Classification and the ROC curve

How to read it At the 0.5 cut-off the model classifies 26 of 32 students correctly (81%), with a sensitivity of 73% (8 of 11 improvers) and a specificity of 86% (18 of 21). That should be compared with the benchmark of always predicting "no improvement", which is right 66% of the time: the model beats it, but not by a wide margin. The AUC of 0.88 is better than the classification rate as a summary, because it does not depend on a cut-off. It says that a randomly chosen improver has a higher predicted probability than a randomly chosen non-improver 88% of the time (0.5 is chance, 1 is perfect). McFadden's pseudo R-squared (0.37) is not comparable to an OLS R-squared: values of 0.2 to 0.4 are already considered a good fit.

How to read it The Hosmer-Lemeshow test does not reject (p = 0.54): the predicted and observed frequencies agree across groups. With 32 observations the test has very little power, so a non-rejection is weak evidence. The Pregibon link test (p = 0.81) and the likelihood-ratio test of a squared GPA term (p = 0.15) find no sign that the index is misspecified. Robust and conventional standard errors are similar, within about 20%. In the logit, unlike in OLS, heteroskedasticity is not a nuisance but a misspecification: if the variance of the latent error depends on the regressors, the coefficients themselves are inconsistent, and robust standard errors do not repair that. Treat the robust errors as a diagnostic.
Logit or probit? A robustness check

How to read it The probit coefficients are about 0.57 times the logit coefficients (the ratio is close to 1.7), because the two latent errors have different scales, the logistic having a standard deviation of 1.81 and the normal of 1. That is why coefficients cannot be compared across the two models. The marginal effects are what to compare, and they are almost the same: the probit and logit AMEs for GPA and TUCE agree to the third decimal, and for PSI they differ by 0.016 (0.374 against 0.358), far less than the standard error of 0.14. The linear probability model agrees for TUCE and PSI but not for GPA (0.46). The log-likelihoods differ by less than 0.1 and the fitted probabilities have a correlation above 0.99. In practice the choice between logit and probit almost never changes a conclusion; logit has the advantage of odds ratios, probit of a link to a normal latent variable and to the extensions with correlated errors (bivariate and ordered probit).
What to report in the paper

Report, in this order: the number of observations and the share of ones; the coefficient table with standard errors; the average marginal effects (and the odds ratios if your field reads them); the likelihood-ratio test and the pseudo R-squared; a measure of fit that does not depend on a cut-off (the AUC) with the classification table at a stated cut-off; and the specification checks. Say whether the standard errors are conventional, robust or clustered, and why. How to write it: results and robustness Table 1 reports the logit estimates. The model is jointly significant (likelihood-ratio chi-squared of 15.4 with 3 degrees of freedom, p = 0.002) and has a McFadden pseudo R-squared of 0.37. The model classifies 81% of the students correctly at a cut-off of 0.5, against 66% for always predicting no improvement, and the area under the ROC curve is 0.88. The Hosmer-Lemeshow test (p = 0.54) and the Pregibon link test (p = 0.81) do not indicate misspecification, although with 32 observations they have little power. A probit model gives average marginal effects that agree with the logit to within 0.02, and a linear probability model gives a similar effect for the teaching method, so the conclusion about the teaching method does not depend on the functional form.

Mistakes to avoid Reading a logit coefficient as a change in probability. The coefficient is a change in the log odds. The change in probability depends on where you are on the curve; report marginal effects. Comparing logit and probit coefficients. They differ by a scale factor of about 1.6 to 1.8. Compare marginal effects. Treating a dummy variable's effect as a derivative. For a 0/1 regressor report the discrete change from 0 to 1, not the slope of the curve at a point ( dummy=True in statsmodels). Judging fit by the share correctly classified alone. With a rare outcome, predicting "no" for everybody scores very high. Compare with the benchmark and report the AUC.

Ignoring separation and small samples. With few observations in the rarer class, the maximum-likelihood standard errors are unreliable. Consider a penalised (Firth) estimator or exact methods. Using robust standard errors to repair heteroskedasticity. In a nonlinear model heteroskedasticity makes the coefficients inconsistent. Robust errors only protect against other misspecification of the variance. Forgetting to cluster. If observations are grouped (students in classes, firms in industries), cluster the standard errors at the group level.

What makes a British voter in 1997 choose Labour or the Liberal Democrats rather than the Conservatives? The multinomial logit gives each of the \(J\) categories a linear index and sets the probability of category \(j\) to The coefficients \(\beta_j\) of the other \(J-1\) equations compare category \(j\) with the base. The data have one outcome and six regressors. Variable in the file Definition vote 0 = Conservative (base), 1 = Labour, 2 = Liberal Democrat age age in years econ_national , econ_household assessment of the national and the household economy, 1 (very negative) to 5 (very positive) europe Euroscepticism on an 11-point scale: high scores are Eurosceptic, low scores Europhile

political_knowledge knowledge of party positions, 0 to 3 female 1 for women Before you estimate anything Is the outcome unordered? If the categories have a meaningful order, an ordered model uses it and needs fewer parameters. Does every category have enough observations? Each category needs at least about 10 observations per regressor. Merge sparse categories. Are the categories really distinct alternatives? The multinomial logit assumes that adding or removing a category does not change the relative odds of the others (IIA, Step 7). Close substitutes violate it. How to write it: model section We model the vote as a choice among three parties with a multinomial logit estimated by maximum likelihood, with the Conservatives as the base category. The explanatory variables are age, the assessments of the national and the household economy, attitude to European integration, political knowledge and gender. Because the coefficients compare each party with the base, we report relative risk ratios and the average marginal effects on the probability of voting for each party.
Load the data and look at it first

How to read it Labour is the largest party in the sample (47%), then the Conservatives (30%) and the Liberal Democrats (22%). The pattern in the raw data is clear: voters who think the national economy is doing well are far more likely to vote Labour, the party in opposition that year, while Euroscepticism is concentrated among Conservative voters. The model asks how much of each pattern survives once the other regressors are controlled.

How to read it Three separate binary logits give probabilities that do not add up to one (the output shows the sums). The multinomial logit estimates the three probabilities jointly, so they sum to one, and it is more efficient. The binary logits remain useful as a robustness check, but not as the model.

How to read it Each block compares one party with the Conservatives. Voters who see the national economy more positively are more likely to vote Labour (0.81, z = 9.0) and, less strongly, Liberal Democrat (0.35, z = 3.6) than Conservative. Each point more Eurosceptic lowers the odds of voting Labour (−0.31, z = −12.9) and Liberal Democrat (−0.27) relative to Conservative, that is, Euroscepticism is a Conservative marker. Political knowledge lowers both (−0.53 and −0.22), and age lowers both slightly. The household economy matters for Labour (0.25, z = 3.2) but not for the Liberal Democrats (0.03), and gender matters for neither. The model is strongly better than the category frequencies (chi-squared 476.8 on 12 degrees of freedom), with a pseudo R-squared of 0.15.

How to read it A relative risk ratio is the factor by which the probability of a party relative to the base changes when the regressor rises by one unit. Each step up in the assessment of the national economy multiplies the relative probability of voting Labour rather than Conservative by 2.24 (95% interval 1.88 to 2.67), and of voting Liberal Democrat by 1.41. A ratio above one favours the party over the base, below one the base. Relative risk ratios compare two parties and say nothing about the third, so they are not changes in probability: for that use the marginal effects.

How to read it One step up in the assessment of the national economy raises the probability of a Labour vote by 0.126, lowers the Conservative probability by 0.099 and the Liberal Democrat probability by 0.027: the three effects add to zero. The figure shows what that means over the whole scale. Notice that the effect on the third party is not simply the sign of its own coefficient: the Liberal Democrat coefficient is positive against the Conservatives (0.35), yet the Liberal Democrat probability falls, because voters move even more strongly to Labour. This is why marginal effects, not coefficients, are what to report for a multinomial model. How to write it: main result

Voters who assess the national economy more favourably are markedly more likely to vote Labour: one more step on the five-point scale raises the probability of a Labour vote by 12.6 percentage points (standard error 1.4) and lowers the probability of a Conservative vote by 9.9 points (standard error 1.2), with a smaller fall for the Liberal Democrats (2.7 points). Relative to the Conservatives, the relative risk ratio of voting Labour is 2.24 (95% confidence interval 1.88 to 2.67).
Classification and the independence of irrelevant alternatives

How to read it The model classifies 60% of voters correctly against 47% for always predicting Labour, so it improves on the benchmark. But look at the pattern: 66% of Conservative and 83% of Labour voters are predicted correctly, and only 4% of Liberal Democrat voters. The model rarely predicts the smallest party, which is common: the highest probability is seldom the third party even when its probability is substantial. Judge a multinomial model by its probabilities and marginal effects, not by the classification rate alone. The Hausman-McFadden test of independence of irrelevant alternatives gives negative statistics here, a known failure of the test in finite samples, which means it cannot be used as evidence either way. The practical question is whether Labour and the Liberal Democrats are close substitutes whose relative odds would change if one of them were absent, which a multinomial probit or a nested logit allows.
Robustness: the choice of base category

How to read it Changing the base category changes the coefficients, which now compare each party with Labour, but not the fitted probabilities, the log-likelihood or the marginal effects. The coefficient of Conservative against Labour is exactly minus that of Labour against Conservative. Choose the base for convenience of interpretation, usually the largest or the natural reference category, and never conclude anything from the fact that a coefficient is significant against one base and not another.
What to report in the paper

Report the number of observations and the share in each category; the coefficient table for each equation with the base named; the relative risk ratios if your field reads them; the average marginal effects on every category; the likelihood-ratio test and pseudo R-squared; the classification table with the benchmark; and a discussion of IIA. How to write it: results and robustness Table 1 reports the multinomial logit estimates for 1,525 voters. The model is jointly significant (likelihood-ratio chi-squared of 476.8 with 12 degrees of freedom) with a McFadden pseudo R-squared of 0.15, and classifies 60% of voters correctly against 47% for always predicting Labour. The marginal effects sum to zero across parties by construction. Changing the base category does not alter the fitted probabilities.

Mistakes to avoid Reading a coefficient as an effect on that category's probability. It is an effect relative to the base category, and the probability of a category can even move opposite to its own coefficient. Report marginal effects. Concluding from significance against one base. Change the base and the table changes. Test differences between categories directly. Using multinomial logit for ordered outcomes. If the categories are ordered, use the ordered model. Ignoring IIA. If two alternatives are close substitutes (red bus and blue bus), the model overstates the effect of removing one. Consider a nested logit or a multinomial probit. Judging fit by accuracy alone. A small category is almost never the most probable one for any voter, so its accuracy is low even when the model is good. Compare the average predicted shares with the observed shares.

Too many categories for the sample. The number of parameters grows with the number of categories; merge categories with fewer than about 10 observations per regressor. Treating the Hausman IIA test as decisive. It is known to be unreliable and often negative.
Ordered Logit and Probit Regression: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

What makes tenants more satisfied with their housing: a say in how the building is managed, the type of building, or contact with neighbours? Madsen (1976) surveyed 1,681 tenants of Copenhagen housing estates and recorded satisfaction as low, medium or high. The ordered model assumes there is a latent (unobserved) satisfaction \(y^*\) that depends linearly on the regressors, and that we see only which of \(J\) ordered ranges it falls in: where \(F\) is the logistic (ordered logit) or normal (ordered probit) distribution function and \(c_1 < \dots < c_{J-1}\) are the cut-points. There is no intercept : the cut-points play that role. A positive coefficient moves the latent variable up and so raises the probability of the highest category.

Variable in the file Definition Sat satisfaction: 1 = low, 2 = medium, 3 = high InflMedium , InflHigh influence on management: medium or high (low is the base) TypeApartment , TypeAtrium , TypeTerrace type of building (tower block is the base) ContHigh 1 if the tenant has high contact with other residents Before you estimate anything Is the order meaningful? Low, medium, high is. Occupations or colours are not: use a multinomial model. Does every category have enough observations? Merge sparse categories (a category with fewer than about 5 to 10 observations makes the cut-points unstable). Will you test the proportional-odds assumption? The model gives each regressor one coefficient for all cut-points. This is a strong restriction that the data can contradict (Step 6).

How to write it: model section Satisfaction is recorded in three ordered categories, so we estimate an ordered logit by maximum likelihood. The model assumes a latent satisfaction that depends linearly on the perceived influence on management, the type of building and contact with other residents, and that tenants report the category in which this latent variable falls. We report odds ratios and average marginal effects on the probability of each category, and we test the proportional-odds assumption with the Brant test.
Load the data and look at it first

How to read it Satisfaction is spread over the three categories (34% low, 27% medium, 40% high). It rises with the tenant's influence on management: among tenants with low influence only 28% are highly satisfied, against 58% of those with high influence. The question for the model is how much of this gap survives once the building type and contact with neighbours are held fixed.
Why not OLS, and why not a multinomial model?

How to read it OLS gives a signed effect on the average code, for example about 0.55 more for high influence than for low, but that number means something only if the step from low to medium is worth the same as the step from medium to high, and the model can predict values outside 1 to 3. The multinomial logit makes no such assumption but needs twelve slopes (six regressors times two categories) and two intercepts, 14 parameters in all, against six slopes and two cut-points (8) for the ordered model, and it ignores the ordering, so it gives up power. The ordered model is the middle way: it uses the ordering, needs one slope per regressor and gives probabilities for every category.

How to read it All coefficients are significant at the 5% level. Influence on management has the strongest effect: high influence raises latent satisfaction by 1.29 relative to low influence, medium influence by 0.57. Living in an apartment, atrium house or terrace house lowers satisfaction relative to a tower block, with terraces the lowest (−1.09), and high contact with neighbours raises it by 0.36. The two cut-points (−0.50 and 0.69) are the thresholds on the latent scale: a tenant whose index is below −0.50 reports low satisfaction, between −0.50 and 0.69 medium and above 0.69 high. The model is strongly better than the category frequencies (chi-squared 170 on 6 degrees of freedom). The pseudo R-squared is low (0.05), which is normal for individual survey data: satisfaction depends on much that is not in the model.

How to read it In the ordered logit, \(e^{\beta}\) is the factor by which the odds of being in a higher category rather than in the current one or below change. High influence has an odds ratio of 3.63: the odds of being more satisfied are 3.6 times as high as for low influence, whether we compare high with medium-or-low or high-or-medium with low. This single number for both comparisons is the proportional-odds assumption, tested in Step 6. The confidence interval (2.83 to 4.66) is narrow because the sample is large.

How to read it An ordered-model coefficient does not tell the size of the effect on any one category, and the effect on the middle category can even have the opposite sign to what the coefficient suggests. The marginal effects do. Moving a tenant from low to high influence raises the probability of high satisfaction by 0.30 and lowers the probabilities of low and medium by 0.24 and 0.06. Moving from low to medium influence raises high satisfaction by 0.12 and lowers low by 0.12, while the medium category barely moves (−0.01). Each row adds to zero: what the top category gains the others lose. The figure shows the full distribution for a tenant with average characteristics: high influence shifts probability from the low category to the high one.

How to write it: main result Perceived influence on management is the strongest determinant of satisfaction. Compared with tenants with little influence, those with high influence are 29.6 percentage points more likely to report high satisfaction and 23.7 points less likely to report low satisfaction (average marginal effects; odds ratio 3.63, 95% confidence interval 2.83 to 4.66). Tenants in towers are more satisfied than those in apartments, atrium houses or terraces, and high contact with neighbours raises the probability of high satisfaction.

How to read it The proportional-odds model forces one slope per regressor. If it were wrong, the slopes from the two binary comparisons would differ. They are similar: for high influence 1.24 against 1.30 and for terrace −1.08 against −1.11, and the ordered-logit values (1.29 and −1.09) lie close to both. The largest gap is for atrium houses (−0.18 against −0.49), but the standard error of that coefficient is 0.16, so the gap is within sampling noise. The Brant test confirms it, with a p-value of about 0.20, so there is no evidence against proportional odds. If the test rejects, the usual remedies are a generalised ordered logit that lets some slopes differ across cut-points, or merging categories. A caution: with large samples the Brant test rejects for tiny differences, so look at the size of the differences as well as the p-value.
Logit or probit? A robustness check

How to read it Probit coefficients are smaller than logit coefficients by a factor of about 1.6 to 1.7, because the logistic error has a larger variance than the normal, so only marginal effects can be compared across the two models. The average marginal effects on high satisfaction agree to the second decimal, and the log-likelihoods differ by about 0.3. As in the binary case, the choice between logit and probit does not change the conclusions here; logit has the advantage of odds ratios and of the Brant test.
What to report in the paper

Report the number of observations and the share in each category; the coefficient table (without an intercept) and the cut-points; the odds ratios if your field reads them; the average marginal effects on every category, or at least on the highest and lowest; the likelihood-ratio test and the pseudo R-squared; the Brant test; and a statement of the link function and standard errors used. How to write it: results and robustness Table 1 reports the ordered logit estimates for 1,681 tenants. The model is jointly significant (likelihood-ratio chi-squared of 169.7 with 6 degrees of freedom) and the pseudo R-squared is 0.05, which is typical for individual survey data. The Brant test does not reject the proportional-odds assumption (chi-squared 8.5, p = 0.20), and the slopes from the separate binary logits are close to the ordered-logit slopes. An ordered probit gives average marginal effects that agree with the logit to the second decimal.

Mistakes to avoid Reading a coefficient as an effect on a category. The coefficient moves the latent variable. The effect on the middle category can have either sign; report marginal effects for every category. Including a constant. The cut-points replace the intercept. Dummies that add up to one cause the same problem: drop one. Forgetting the sign convention. Some programs (Stata ologit , R polr , statsmodels) define \(\Pr(y \le j) = F(c_j - x'\beta)\) , so a positive coefficient means higher categories; others report the opposite sign. State the convention. Ignoring proportional odds. If the Brant test rejects, one slope per regressor is wrong. Use a generalised ordered model, or check which regressor causes the rejection.

Merging categories to save the test. Collapsing categories until the Brant test passes is a form of specification search. Say what you did. Treating the cut-points as unimportant. They show where the categories lie on the latent scale. Very close cut-points mean that the middle category is hardly distinguishable. Using an ordered model for an unordered outcome. If the order is not meaningful, estimate a multinomial model.

Panel Logit and Probit (Pooled, Random and Fixed Effects): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
Panel Logit and Probit (Pooled, Random and Fixed Effects)

Does getting married change whether a man belongs to a union, once we allow for stable personal traits? Let \(y_{it}\) be 1 if man \(i\) is in a union in year \(t\) . The latent-variable model with a person effect \(c_i\) is Pooled logit sets \(c_i = 0\) (or treats it as part of the error) and corrects the standard errors for clustering. Random effects assumes \(c_i \sim N(0,\sigma_c^2)\) independent of \(x_{it}\) . Fixed effects leaves \(c_i\) free and removes it by conditioning on the number of years the person is a union member (Chamberlain 1980). The Mundlak version of random effects adds each person's average of the time-varying regressors, which allows \(c_i\) to be correlated with them.
Panel Logit and Probit (Pooled, Random and Fixed Effects)

Variable Definition union 1 if the man is a union member in the year married 1 if married (changes over time) educ , black , hisp years of schooling, race and ethnicity (time-invariant) exper , expersq labor-market experience and its square (change every year) Before you estimate anything How much does the outcome change within people? Fixed-effects logit uses only people whose outcome changes at least once. If few do, the estimator is imprecise. Which regressors vary within people? Time-invariant variables (education, race) are absorbed by a fixed effect and cannot be estimated. Is the person effect plausibly correlated with the regressors? If so, pooled and random-effects estimates are inconsistent for the within-person effect.
Panel Logit and Probit (Pooled, Random and Fixed Effects)

What do you want to report? Fixed-effects logit gives odds ratios but no probabilities or marginal effects; random effects and pooled give average partial effects. How to write it: model section We model the probability of union membership for 545 men observed in eight consecutive years. We estimate pooled logit with standard errors clustered by individual, a random-effects logit with a normally distributed individual effect, a correlated random-effects (Mundlak) logit that adds the individual averages of the time-varying regressors, and Chamberlain's conditional fixed-effects logit. The Mundlak test and a comparison of the within-person coefficients across estimators indicate how much unobserved heterogeneity matters.
Panel Logit and Probit (Pooled, Random and Fixed Effects)
Load the panel and check the within variation

How to read it Only 45% of men change union status at some point; the other 55% are always or never members and carry no information for the fixed-effects logit. Union status is a persistent trait: 59% of its variance is between men, and marital status is similar (58%). Experience changes every year (34% between men), while education never changes (it is entirely between-person).
Panel Logit and Probit (Pooled, Random and Fixed Effects)
Step 1: Pooled logit with clustered standard errors

How to read it The pooled estimates treat the 4,360 observations as independent. The clustered standard errors are up to twice the naive ones (for black, 0.22 against 0.10), since the eight observations of a man are strongly related. Married men are 5 percentage points more likely to be in a union, and Black men 15 points more likely. This is a population-average relation: it compares different men and makes no allowance for stable unobserved differences.
Panel Logit and Probit (Pooled, Random and Fixed Effects)

How to read it The unit effect is huge: sigma_u is 3.0, which means that 73% of the latent variance is a stable personal trait, and the likelihood-ratio test rejects its absence with overwhelming force. The random-effects coefficients are on a different scale from the pooled ones (they are conditional on the person effect, roughly 2 times larger for variables with a strong signal, such as race). They are not comparable with the pooled coefficients unless converted to average partial effects. The random-effects model assumes the person effect is unrelated to marriage and experience, which the next steps test.
Panel Logit and Probit (Pooled, Random and Fixed Effects)
Step 3: Allow the person effect to correlate with the regressors (Mundlak)

How to read it The averages of experience and its square are strongly significant, and the Mundlak test rejects the random-effects assumption (chi-squared 13.9 on 3 degrees of freedom, p = 0.003). Men with more average experience differ in unobserved ways that are associated with union membership, so the person effect is correlated with the regressors. In the correlated-random-effects model the coefficient on marriage is 0.27, close to the pooled estimate and to what the fixed-effects model will give, but the model still assumes a particular distribution for the person effect.
Panel Logit and Probit (Pooled, Random and Fixed Effects)

How to read it Only 246 men switch union status and contribute to the conditional likelihood. For them, getting married multiplies the odds of union membership by 1.31 (95% interval 0.94 to 1.83), not significantly different from 1 (z = 1.57). Experience has no significant within-man effect. The pooled coefficient on experience (0.17) is much larger than the fixed-effects one (0.02): the pooled estimate reflects the comparison between men, where those with more experience belong more often, and the fixed-effects estimate removes this. Marriage is similar in all estimators, so the "marriage premium" is not driven by stable traits. How to write it: main result Pooled logit suggests that married men are 5 percentage points more likely to be in a union (clustered standard error 1.4), but this partly compares different men. The random-effects assumption is rejected by a Mundlak test (chi-squared 13.9, p = 0.003), and the fixed-effects logit, which uses the 246 men who change union status, gives an odds ratio of 1.31 for marriage (95% confidence interval 0.94 to 1.83). The experience effect found in the pooled model disappears within men.
Panel Logit and Probit (Pooled, Random and Fixed Effects)
Step 5: Average partial effects from the random-effects model

How to read it The random-effects estimate of the average partial effect of marriage is 2.9 percentage points and the correlated random-effects estimate 2.4 points, much smaller than the pooled 5.0, which is a population-average comparison that includes the stable differences. Only the models with a distributional assumption for the person effect give probabilities; the fixed-effects model gives the odds ratio alone.
Panel Logit and Probit (Pooled, Random and Fixed Effects)
What to report in the paper

Report the number of units and periods, the share of units whose outcome changes, the four estimators for the same set of time-varying variables, the Mundlak test, sigma_u or the intraclass correlation, and what each estimate answers: the pooled and RE estimates a population-average effect, the fixed-effects odds ratio the within-person effect. How to write it: results and robustness Table 3 reports the four estimators. The unit effect is large (sigma = 3.0, intraclass correlation 0.73) and correlated with experience (Mundlak p = 0.003), so we base inference on the conditional fixed-effects logit, which relies on the 246 men whose union status changes. The effect of marriage is positive in all estimators (odds ratio 1.31 in the fixed-effects model) but imprecisely estimated in the within-man models. Average partial effects of marriage from the correlated random-effects and random-effects specifications are 2.4 and 2.9 percentage points, against 5.0 for the pooled model.
Panel Logit and Probit (Pooled, Random and Fixed Effects)

Mistakes to avoid Using plain pooled standard errors. Observations of the same unit are dependent; cluster by unit. Comparing random-effects and pooled coefficients directly. They are on different scales; compare average partial effects. Assuming random effects without a test. Run the Mundlak test or a Hausman test. Estimating a fixed-effects probit with dummy variables. With few periods this is biased (the incidental-parameters problem); use conditional logit. Wondering why time-invariant variables vanish. A fixed effect absorbs them; use correlated random effects if you need them. Ignoring the units that drop out. Fixed-effects logit uses only units whose outcome changes, so it describes switchers. Reporting marginal effects from a fixed-effects logit. They are not identified without assumptions about the effect.

Too few quadrature points. The random-effects likelihood is an integral; check that the result is stable.
