Systems of Equations: SUR and Three-Stage Least Squares

Two outcomes, one person. Sleep and paid work compete for the same 168 hours. We write one equation for each: If \(\sigma_{12} \neq 0\) and the regressors differ between the equations, generalized least squares weighted by the estimated error covariance (SUR, Zellner 1962) is more efficient than OLS. If the right-hand side of one equation contains the outcome of another, the regressor is correlated with the error, and 3SLS uses instruments for it. Variable Definition sleep , totwrk minutes of sleep and of paid work per week educ , age , male years of schooling, age, 1 for men yngkid , gdhlth 1 if a child under 3 is in the home; 1 if in good health
Systems of Equations: SUR and Three-Stage Least Squares

union , south 1 if union member; 1 if living in the South Before you estimate anything Are the errors plausibly correlated? Outcomes that share unmodelled determinants (time, budgets, a common shock) are. A Breusch-Pagan test says whether the correlation is large enough to matter. Do the equations have different regressors? With identical regressors in every equation, SUR equals equation-by-equation OLS. The gain comes from the different sets. Is any regressor an outcome of another equation? Then OLS and SUR are inconsistent. Use 3SLS with at least one excluded instrument for every endogenous regressor. How to write it: model section Weekly minutes of sleep and of paid work are determined by overlapping factors, so we estimate the two equations as a seemingly unrelated regression system with different regressors in each equation and test for correlated errors with a Breusch-Pagan Lagrange-multiplier test. For the labor-supply system, in which hours depend on the wage and the wage on hours, we estimate the two equations by three-stage least squares with experience, age, children and other household income as instruments, and test the overidentifying restrictions.
Systems of Equations: SUR and Three-Stage Least Squares
Load the data and estimate by OLS

How to read it The residuals of the two OLS equations are correlated at −0.33, and the Breusch-Pagan test rejects independence decisively (chi-squared 76 on 1 degree of freedom). A person who works unusually much, given the observed characteristics, also sleeps unusually little. This is the situation in which SUR can help, since the two equations contain different regressors (children and health in one, union membership and region in the other).
Systems of Equations: SUR and Three-Stage Least Squares

How to read it The SUR coefficients are close to the OLS ones, and the standard errors are smaller by 0 to 6%. The largest changes are for regressors that appear in only one equation: the coefficient on a young child in the sleep equation falls from 30 minutes to 1, and the coefficient on living in the South in the work equation rises from 152 to 209 minutes. This is how SUR works: it uses the information in the other equation's residual to adjust each equation's estimates. The gain in precision is modest here, as it usually is. Large gains need strongly correlated errors and very different regressors. How to write it: main result
Systems of Equations: SUR and Three-Stage Least Squares

Table 1 reports the SUR estimates. The equation errors are significantly correlated (−0.33; Breusch-Pagan chi-squared 76, p < 0.001), and SUR standard errors are up to 6% smaller than the OLS ones. Men work 729 more minutes per week than women, and people living in the South work 209 more minutes. The estimates for sleep are imprecise: no single regressor has a significant effect at the 5% level.
Systems of Equations: SUR and Three-Stage Least Squares

How to read it With the same regressors in both equations, SUR and OLS are the same estimator, to numerical precision. A system whose equations have identical right-hand sides is not a case for SUR. The gains come only from the exclusion of different variables from different equations, or from cross-equation restrictions.
Systems of Equations: SUR and Three-Stage Least Squares

How to read it OLS says that the wage has no effect on hours (−17 minutes per unit of log wage), because the wage and hours determine each other and OLS mixes the two. With instruments the labor-supply elasticity becomes large and significant: 2SLS gives 1,545 hours per unit of the log wage (standard error 477) and 3SLS 1,677 (431). The 3SLS standard error is smaller, the gain from using the correlation between the equations. In the wage equation the effect of hours turns from slightly negative with OLS to positive with instruments (0.16 and 0.20 per thousand hours), but it is small and imprecise. The residuals of the two equations are strongly negatively correlated (−0.91), which is a sign that this simultaneous structure is mechanically related by the hours-wage identity and that 3SLS should be compared with 2SLS rather than trusted alone.
Systems of Equations: SUR and Three-Stage Least Squares

How to read it Neither Sargan test rejects (p = 0.35 for the hours equation and 0.40 for the wage equation), so the extra instruments are not contradicted by the data. The excluded instruments are only moderately strong in the first stage for the wage: the F statistic is 8.3, below the rule-of-thumb value of 10, so the 2SLS and 3SLS estimates may be biased toward OLS and their standard errors understated. Experience is a valid instrument for the hours equation only if it affects hours through the wage and not directly, which is an economic assumption that no test confirms. The Sargan test checks only the consistency of the instruments among themselves.
Systems of Equations: SUR and Three-Stage Least Squares
What to report in the paper

For SUR: the equations and their regressors; the residual correlation and its test; the coefficients with standard errors; and the comparison with OLS. For 3SLS: the endogenous variables; the instruments and the argument for exclusion; first-stage strength; the Sargan test; and the 2SLS estimates next to 3SLS. How to write it: results and robustness Table 2 reports the labor-supply system. OLS suggests that the wage has no effect on hours, but with experience and family variables as instruments the labor-supply coefficient is 1,677 hours per unit of the log wage by 3SLS (standard error 431) and 1,545 by 2SLS (477). Sargan tests do not reject the overidentifying restrictions (p = 0.35 and 0.40), but the first-stage F statistic for the excluded instruments is 8.3, so we treat the magnitude with caution. The 3SLS and 2SLS estimates have the same sign and similar size, so the conclusion does not depend on the cross-equation weighting.
Systems of Equations: SUR and Three-Stage Least Squares

Mistakes to avoid Using SUR with identical regressors. It reproduces OLS exactly; the gain is zero. Expecting large gains from SUR. The gain needs strongly correlated errors and different regressors. It is usually modest. Using SUR when a regressor is endogenous. SUR does not solve simultaneity. Use instruments. Using 3SLS when an equation is not identified. Each equation needs at least as many excluded instruments as endogenous regressors. Trusting 3SLS over 2SLS without comparing. A specification error in one equation contaminates all equations in 3SLS. Treating the Sargan test as proof of validity. It tests the consistency of the instruments with one another, not their exogeneity. Ignoring weak instruments. Check the first-stage F statistic.

Tobit Regression (Censored Outcomes): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

What determines how many extramarital affairs a married person has? Fair (1978) asked 601 people how often they had an affair in the past year. Most (451) had none, so the outcome is zero for three quarters of the sample. The Tobit model says there is a latent propensity \(y^*\) that depends linearly on the regressors, and that we observe it only when it is positive: The coefficients \(\beta\) are effects on the latent propensity. The effects on the observed number of affairs are smaller, because part of any change in \(y^*\) happens below zero where it is not observed. Variable in the file Definition affairs number of affairs in the past year (0 to 12)

age age in years yearsmarried years married religiousness 1 (anti-religious) to 5 (very religious) occupation occupation index (Hollingshead), 1 to 7 rating self-rating of the marriage, 1 (very unhappy) to 5 (very happy) Before you estimate anything Is the outcome censored or simply zero? Tobit fits when the zero hides a negative or small latent value (hours a person would work at the going wage). If the zeros come from a different decision (whether to have an affair at all), a two-part model fits better (Step 6). Are the limits known? Tobit needs the censoring point (here 0) for every observation. Is normality plausible? The Tobit estimator is inconsistent if the latent error is not normal and homoskedastic, unlike OLS.

How to write it: model section The number of affairs is censored at zero for 75% of the sample, so we estimate a Tobit model by maximum likelihood, in which the observed number is the larger of zero and a latent propensity that depends linearly on age, years of marriage, religiousness, occupation and the rating of the marriage. We report the effects on the latent propensity and the average marginal effects on the observed number of affairs, and we test the Tobit restriction against a two-part alternative.
Load the data and look at it first

How to read it The distribution has a spike at zero (451 of 601 people) and a long right tail, which is why a linear regression is a poor description. People who had an affair rate their marriage lower on average and are less religious: the question for the model is how large these differences are after the regressors are held fixed.
Why not OLS, and why not drop the zeros?

How to read it OLS on all 601 observations is biased toward zero because the zeros are not the values of the latent propensity: it gives −0.05 for age and −0.71 for the marriage rating. Dropping the zeros ("OLS, positive only") is biased too, in a different way: it keeps only people with a high enough latent value, which selects on the outcome and moves the slopes in unpredictable directions (years married 0.26 against 0.16, religiousness −0.71 against −0.48). It also throws away 75% of the data, and OLS predicts a negative number of affairs for 60 people. The Tobit estimator uses both the zeros and the positive values.

How to read it The coefficients are effects on the latent propensity. A marriage rating one point higher lowers it by 2.28 (z = −5.6), one more year of marriage raises it by 0.55, one more point of religiousness lowers it by 1.69, and age lowers it by 0.18 per year; occupation has no significant effect (p = 0.20). Estimated sigma is 8.2, large compared with the observed range, which says that the latent propensity varies a great deal among people with the same characteristics. The Tobit slopes are three to three and a half times the OLS slopes, the usual attenuation of OLS on censored data. The coefficients themselves are not the answer to "how many affairs fewer", which is the next step.
Marginal effects on the observed outcome

How to read it The effect on the observed number of affairs is the latent coefficient times the average probability that a person is uncensored (0.26): one more point of marital rating lowers the expected number of affairs by 0.585, and one more year of marriage raises it by 0.14. This is the McDonald-Moffitt decomposition: the change in the expected outcome has one part that works through the probability of having an affair at all and one part that works through how many, if any. The effect on the number among those who have affairs is 0.24 of the latent coefficient. Note that these OLS-like effects are close to the OLS slopes (−0.585 against −0.71 for the rating), which explains why OLS is often a good approximation of the average effect on the observed outcome, but not of the latent one.
Marginal effects on the observed outcome

How to write it: main result A one-point higher rating of the marriage lowers the latent propensity to have affairs by 2.28 (standard error 0.41) and the expected number of affairs by 0.585 per year (average marginal effect). Each additional year of marriage raises the expected number by 0.14, and each point of religiousness lowers it by 0.43. Age and occupation have small effects. The Tobit slopes are about three times the OLS slopes on the same data, as expected when 75% of the outcome is censored.
Is the Tobit restriction credible? A two-part check

How to read it Under the Tobit model the probit for "any affair" has coefficients equal to \(\beta/\sigma\) , and the truncated regression for the positive values has coefficients \(\beta\) . Cragg's likelihood-ratio test compares the Tobit with the two-part model that lets these differ. It does not reject at the 5% level, although only just (chi-squared 11.1 on 6 degrees of freedom, p = 0.084), and the probit coefficients are close to \(\beta/\sigma\) . The data are therefore broadly consistent with a single process for whether and how many, and Tobit is an acceptable model here, with the borderline p-value worth reporting. When the test rejects, use a hurdle (two-part) model or a Heckman selection model.
What to report in the paper

Report the number of observations and of censored observations; the Tobit coefficients and sigma with standard errors, saying that they are effects on the latent outcome; the average marginal effects on the observed outcome (and, if needed, the conditional effect); the likelihood-ratio test; a comparison with OLS; and the test of the Tobit restriction. How to write it: results and robustness Table 1 reports the Tobit estimates for 601 people, 451 of whom report no affair. The model is jointly significant (likelihood-ratio chi-squared of 78.3 with 5 degrees of freedom). Cragg's likelihood-ratio test of the Tobit restriction against a probit plus truncated-regression alternative does not reject at the 5% level (chi-squared 11.1, p = 0.084), and the probit coefficients are close to the Tobit coefficients divided by sigma, so we maintain the Tobit specification and note that the evidence is borderline. The OLS estimates are about one third of the Tobit slopes, as expected for a censored outcome.

Mistakes to avoid Reading a Tobit coefficient as the effect on the observed outcome. It is the effect on the latent variable. Multiply by the probability of being uncensored, or report the marginal effects. Using Tobit for a corner solution with a different process. If the zero comes from a separate decision, use a hurdle or two-part model (Cragg test). Dropping the zeros and running OLS on the rest. It selects on the outcome and biases the slopes. Ignoring non-normality and heteroskedasticity. Tobit is inconsistent if the latent error is not normal and homoskedastic. Check with Cragg's test, with a different link, or use censored least absolute deviations. Mixing censoring and truncation. In censored data the zeros are observed; in truncated data the observations below the limit are missing. The estimators differ.

Forgetting an upper limit. If the outcome is also capped (a maximum rating), specify both limits. Comparing the sigma of a Tobit and of OLS. Sigma is the scale of the latent error, not the residual standard deviation of the observed outcome.
Zero-Inflated and Hurdle Count Models: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

What explains the number of times a young man is arrested in a year? Most men are never arrested, and the ones who are may be arrested several times. Two features of the data matter: a great many zeros, and a skewed tail. Zero-inflated model. With probability \(\pi_i\) the person is a structural zero (never arrested whatever the circumstances); otherwise the count follows a Poisson or negative binomial with mean \(\mu_i\) : Hurdle model. A logit decides whether \(y_i > 0\) , and a zero-truncated count model gives the size: Variable in the file Definition narr86 number of arrests in 1986 pcnv proportion of prior arrests that led to conviction

ptime86 months in prison in 1986 qemp86 quarters employed in 1986 (0 to 4) black , hispan race and ethnicity indicators Before you estimate anything Does the story of the zeros make sense? A zero-inflated model needs a group that is never at risk. Counting doctor visits, there may be people who never go. For arrests, "never arrested whatever happens" is a stretch; a hurdle (a first arrest, then repeat arrests) can be more natural. The data cannot decide this for you. Do the zeros really exceed the standard model's prediction? Fit the Poisson and negative binomial first. A negative binomial often absorbs excess zeros without a second equation. Which variables drive the zeros? The zero equation can use the same variables as the count equation, but identification is stronger if some variable affects only one of them.

How to write it: model section Seventy-two percent of the men have no arrest in 1986, so we compare the standard negative-binomial model with a zero-inflated negative binomial, in which a logit equation separates men who are never arrested from those who are at risk, and with a negative-binomial hurdle model, in which a logit equation determines whether any arrest occurs and a truncated count model gives the number. We compare the models by AIC and BIC, a Vuong test and the predicted share of zeros.
Load the data and check the zeros

How to read it The variance (0.74) is only about 1.8 times the mean (0.40), and the Poisson model predicts 68% zeros against the 72% in the data. The gap is moderate, not dramatic, so the question is whether the improvement from a second equation is worth its extra parameters.

How to read it The negative binomial raises the predicted share of zeros to 73%, close to the 72% observed, and its dispersion parameter alpha is 1.03. A higher conviction rate (−0.46), more prison time (−0.11) and more quarters of employment (−0.24) lower the log expected number of arrests, while the black (0.70) and Hispanic (0.55) indicators raise it. This is the benchmark that the two-equation models must beat.
Step 2: Zero-inflated and hurdle models by maximum likelihood

How to read it Adding a second equation always raises the log-likelihood, so we compare AIC and BIC, which penalize the extra parameters. The negative-binomial versions (ZINB and the NB hurdle) fit much better than the Poisson versions, because a Poisson count cannot capture the tail. Both are better than the standard negative binomial by AIC (4,304 and 4,307 against 4,385), and the ZINB also wins on BIC (4,381 against 4,426 for the standard model). The zero-inflated Poisson (AIC 4,385) does no better than the standard negative binomial, so the extra equation helps only when the count part can also handle the tail. The two zero-augmented negative binomials are close to each other, which is typical.
Step 3: Interpret the two equations of the ZINB

How to read it The two equations answer different questions. In the zero equation, a higher conviction rate (6.8) and more prison time (0.64) raise the probability of being a structural zero, and the black and Hispanic indicators lower it (−0.74 each, significant only at the 10% level). Prison time as a predictor of "never at risk" is hard to read literally (men who were in prison cannot be arrested outside), a warning that the zero equation may be a stand-in for something else. In the count equation, more employment lowers the expected number of arrests among men at risk (−0.21), and the black (0.59) and Hispanic (0.38) indicators raise it. The average probability of a structural zero is 18%. When the interpretation of the zero equation is awkward, say so and prefer the hurdle interpretation or the standard model.
Step 4: Test and compare against the standard model

How to read it The Vuong test favors the zero-inflated model (V = 4.5), but it does not reproduce the share of zeros better (73.1% against 72.9% for the standard model, 72.3% observed). The gain is in the likelihood rather than in the shape of the marginal distribution: both models are within about two percentage points of the observed shares for the counts 0 to 5 (largest gap 2.3 for the ZINB and 2.0 for the standard model). The Vuong statistic is a test of non-nested models and says which model is closer to the data, not which story is true.
What to report in the paper

Report the share of zeros and the Poisson-predicted share; both equations with standard errors; AIC, BIC and the Vuong test against the standard model; the economic reason for separating zeros; and the average marginal effects on the expected count when a variable appears in both equations. How to write it: results and robustness Table 3 compares the standard negative binomial with the zero-inflated and hurdle versions. The zero-inflated negative binomial has the lowest AIC (4,304 against 4,385) and BIC (4,381 against 4,426), and a Vuong test favors it over the standard model (V = 4.5); the negative-binomial hurdle model is close (AIC 4,307). Employment lowers the expected number of arrests among men at risk, and the black and Hispanic indicators raise it. Because the zero equation loads on prison time and prior convictions, we do not interpret it literally as a group that is never at risk, and the models do not differ in how well they reproduce the share of zeros (73.1% against 72.3% observed).

Mistakes to avoid Adding a zero equation because there are many zeros. Many zeros are normal for a low-mean count. Compare with the standard negative binomial first. Telling a story the data cannot support. "Structural zeros" must exist in the subject matter. Otherwise use a hurdle or the standard model. Reading the zero-equation sign as the effect on the count. In a zero-inflated model it refers to the structural zero; in a hurdle model, to a positive count. Interpreting the Vuong test as a test of the zero-inflation story. It compares fit only. Ignoring the effect on the expected count. A variable that enters both equations acts through both. Report the marginal effect on E[y].

Overparametrized zero equations. With the same variables in both equations the model can be weakly identified; if the likelihood is flat, use fewer variables. Local maxima. Zero-inflated likelihoods can have several maxima. Start from several points and keep the highest log-likelihood.
Causal Forest: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. Effects that differ across people, N ≥ 2,000.

The DML interactive guide found that 401(k) eligibility raises net financial assets by about 8,000 dollars on average . For policy that is only half the answer. Does eligibility mainly help households that would have saved anyway, high earners with spare income, or does it also build assets for lower-income households? The question is about the conditional average treatment effect (CATE): A causal forest (Wager and Athey 2018; Athey, Tibshirani and Wager 2019) estimates \(\tau(x)\) with trees that split the sample where the treatment effect differs most, not where the outcome differs. Two features make its confidence intervals valid: honesty : each tree uses one half of its sample to choose the splits and the other half to estimate the effect in each leaf;

orthogonalisation : as in DML, the outcome and the treatment are first residualised on the controls with machine learning, so that confounding by \(X\) does not leak into the heterogeneity estimates. The implementation used here is CausalForestDML in Microsoft's EconML package. Heterogeneity needs data and discipline Effects by subgroup are noisier than the average, so a causal forest needs thousands of observations (the selection tool requires 2,000). And a search for heterogeneity can always find something: decide in advance which dimensions matter for the question (here income, age, education), and report the variation honestly, including when it is small.
Load the data and recover the average effect

The forest's average agrees with the DML estimate from the interactive guide. That is the first check: if the average of the conditional effects did not match the doubly robust ATE, something would be wrong with the forest.
How much do the effects vary?

The estimated effects vary a great deal around the average. Part of that spread is estimation noise: individual CATEs are imprecise. The questions that can be answered reliably are about groups and about which variables drive the variation.
The forest records how often, and how early, each variable is used to split on the treatment effect.

Income is the obvious policy dimension. The group average treatment effect (GATE) for each income quintile needs a valid confidence interval. Averaging the forest's individual intervals does not give one: it treats the spread of individual effects as if it were uncertainty about the average. The clean way is to average the doubly robust (AIPW) scores within each group, which is what DoubleML's gate() does (Semenova and Chernozhukov 2021), with joint confidence bands across the five groups. The effect is modest and roughly flat across the bottom three income quintiles and then climbs steeply: the top fifth of earners gain about four times as much as the bottom fifth. The bands are joint, so they can be read together: the top-quintile band lies entirely above the second quintile’s, but the bands of neighbouring quintiles overlap, so the evidence is for a rising pattern, not for sharp differences between adjacent groups.
How does the effect change with income and age?
Hold every other variable at its observed value and vary one: the forest's predicted effect as a function of income (and, separately, age).

How to write it: heterogeneity To study who gains from 401(k) eligibility, we estimate conditional average treatment effects with a causal forest (Wager and Athey 2018), using the orthogonalised, honest implementation of EconML with 2,000 trees and random-forest first stages for the outcome and the propensity score. The forest's average effect matches the doubly robust DML estimate. Income accounts for most of the splits on the treatment effect, followed by age. Group average effects by income quintile, estimated from doubly robust scores with joint confidence bands (Semenova and Chernozhukov 2021), are small in the bottom three quintiles (between about 1,000 and 5,000 dollars) and then rise sharply, to about 10,300 dollars in the fourth quintile and 19,900 dollars in the top quintile (Table X): eligibility mainly raises the financial assets of higher-income households, although the effect is positive and significant even in the lowest quintile. Individual effects are imprecise; we therefore report group averages with confidence intervals and do not interpret individual estimates.

Checklist for the paper Start from the average effect (DML) and show that the forest reproduces it. Say in advance which dimensions of heterogeneity are of interest. Report the forest settings: number of trees, honesty, leaf size, first-stage learners. Report group effects with confidence intervals, not individual effects. Show which variables drive the heterogeneity and how the effect varies along them.
Classification: Logit, Penalised Logit, Random Forest and Boosting
Classification: Logit, Penalised Logit, Random Forest and Boosting: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code and more.
Classification: Logit, Penalised Logit, Random Forest and Boosting

How well can we predict a yes/no outcome, and is the predicted probability trustworthy? A classifier maps predictors \(x\) to a probability \(\hat p(x) = P(y=1\mid x)\) . Three properties matter: Discrimination: does a randomly chosen positive get a higher score than a randomly chosen negative? The area under the ROC curve (AUC) is that probability; 0.5 is chance and 1 is perfect. Calibration: among units with predicted probability 0.9, do about 90% have \(y=1\) ? A model can rank well and still be miscalibrated. Cut-off performance: accuracy, sensitivity and specificity depend on a threshold that should come from the costs of the two errors, and on the class balance.
Classification: Logit, Penalised Logit, Random Forest and Boosting

The Brier score \(\frac1n\sum(\hat p_i-y_i)^2\) and the log loss combine discrimination and calibration. Three checks before you report a classifier What is the share of the common class? Accuracy of a model that always predicts the common class is the benchmark, not 50%. Is the test sample untouched? Tuning on the test set overstates every number. Would a predictor be inappropriate to use? A model that predicts well using a protected characteristic is a different finding from one that does not. How to write it: the model We predict whether a mortgage application in Boston was approved, using 15 characteristics of the applicant and the loan: race, marital status, sex, dependants, years of schooling, the housing expense and total obligation ratios, the loan-to-price ratio, the unemployment rate in the industry, a co-signer, a consumer credit history score, public records, two mortgage-lateness indicators and a verification flag. We estimate a logit, an L1-penalised logit with the penalty chosen by five-fold cross-validation, a random forest and gradient boosting on 75% of the sample, and evaluate them on the remaining 25% by AUC, accuracy, Brier score, log loss and calibration (Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman 2009).
Classification: Logit, Penalised Logit, Random Forest and Boosting
Load the data and set the benchmark

How to read it Of the 1,971 applications, 87.6% were approved, so a rule that approves everything is right 87.6% of the time and any accuracy below that is worse than no model. The raw approval rate is 90.8% for white applicants and 70.3% for the others (303 applications), and that difference is part of why the sensitive predictor needs a separate check below. With 12.4% rejections, the question is whether the predictors can find them: accuracy will move little and AUC is the better yardstick.
Classification: Logit, Penalised Logit, Random Forest and Boosting

How to read it On the 493 test applications the random forest has the highest AUC (0.808), against 0.761 for the logit and the L1 logit and 0.769 for boosting. Its Brier score (0.096) and log loss (0.320) are also the lowest, so the ranking by AUC is confirmed by the probability measures. Accuracy at the 0.5 cut-off is nearly the same for all four (0.866 to 0.876), within 0.01 of the 0.868 benchmark of approving everyone in the test sample: accuracy hides the differences that AUC reveals, because most applicants are approved. The penalised logit is no better than the plain logit, as expected with 15 predictors and 1,500 training cases.
Classification: Logit, Penalised Logit, Random Forest and Boosting

How to read it At the default cut-off of 0.5 the forest approves almost everything: it catches 99.8% of the approvals (sensitivity) but only 7.7% of the rejections (specificity). Moving the cut-off to 0.871, the value that maximises sensitivity plus specificity, gives 81.8% and 70.8%: 46 of the 65 rejections are now found, at the price of refusing 78 of the 428 applications that were approved. The cut-off is a policy decision, and which error costs more (lending to a bad risk or refusing a good one) should set it. Calibration by quintile of predicted probability is good in the upper four quintiles (predicted 0.88, 0.93, 0.95 and 0.98 against observed 0.88, 0.90, 1.00 and 0.96) and over-optimistic in the lowest, where the model predicts 72% approved and 61% were.
Classification: Logit, Penalised Logit, Random Forest and Boosting
Should a sensitive predictor be in the model?

How to read it Dropping race lowers the AUC by 0.013 for the forest (0.808 to 0.795) and by 0.026 for the logit (0.761 to 0.735), so race adds some predictive content but most of it is in the other variables, and a model without race can be used where race must not enter the decision. Using only the eight credit variables the forest falls to 0.754 and the three models are within 0.01 of each other. Removing race does not make the model neutral: the remaining variables can proxy for race, and the approval gap by race in the data should be examined with a causal design (for example, a regression of approval on race with controls) before a classifier trained on these decisions is used to make new ones. A classifier trained on past decisions learns the practices that produced them.
Classification: Logit, Penalised Logit, Random Forest and Boosting

How to read it The forest is best at every test share (AUC 0.800 to 0.810), ahead of boosting (0.769 to 0.779) and the logit (0.750 to 0.761), and each AUC moves by about 0.01 with the split, which gives the size of the noise in a single hold-out comparison. Differences of 0.01 between models would not be reliable on one split; the gap of about 0.05 between the forest and the logit is.
Classification: Logit, Penalised Logit, Random Forest and Boosting

How to write it: results Approvals are 87.6% of applications, so a rule that approves all of them has accuracy of about 0.88. On a 25% hold-out sample the random forest discriminates best (AUC 0.808; Brier 0.096), ahead of boosting (0.769) and the logit and L1 logit (0.761). All four are within 0.01 of the benchmark accuracy (0.868 in the test sample) at a cut-off of 0.5, where the forest approves almost every applicant (sensitivity 0.998, specificity 0.077); at the Youden cut-off of 0.871 they are 0.818 and 0.708. Predicted probabilities are well calibrated except in the lowest quintile, where they are too high. Excluding race lowers the AUC by 0.01 to 0.03, and the ranking of the models is stable across test shares of 20% to 40%. The model describes past approval decisions and should not be used to make new ones without an assessment of the practices that generated them.
Classification: Logit, Penalised Logit, Random Forest and Boosting

Clustering: k-Means, Gaussian Mixtures and Ward, with a Test of Whether the Clusters Are Real
Clustering: k-Means, Gaussian Mixtures and Ward, with a Test of Whether the Clusters Are Real: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper and more.
Clustering: k-Means, Gaussian Mixtures and Ward, with a Test of Whether the Clusters Are Real

Is there group structure in these variables, and how many groups? The variables are first standardised (mean 0, variance 1) so that each counts equally. Three methods: k-means minimises the within-cluster sum of squares \(\sum_c\sum_{i\in c}\lVert z_i-\bar z_c\rVert^2\) for a given \(k\) ; clusters are compact and roughly spherical. Ward hierarchical clustering merges, at each step, the two clusters whose union increases the within-cluster sum of squares least. Gaussian mixture assigns each observation a probability of belonging to each of \(k\) multivariate normal components, and \(k\) can be chosen by the BIC. The silhouette of observation \(i\) is \((b_i-a_i)/\max(a_i,b_i)\) , where \(a_i\) is its average distance to its own cluster and \(b_i\) its average distance to the nearest other cluster. The average is near 1 when clusters are well separated and near 0 when they overlap; Kaufman and Rousseeuw (1990) call values above 0.5 reasonable structure and below 0.25 none. Stability is the average adjusted Rand index (ARI) between the full-sample partition and the partitions found in bootstrap resamples; 1 is perfect agreement and 0 is chance.
Clustering: k-Means, Gaussian Mixtures and Ward, with a Test of Whether the Clusters Are Real

Three checks before you report clusters Is the structure real? Look at the silhouette and the stability, not at whether the algorithm returns clusters, because it always does. Do the variables define the clusters? Redundant variables (life expectancy and child mortality) count twice. State how the result depends on the variable list. Do the methods agree? If k-means, Ward and a mixture give different groups, the data do not have a unique partition. How to write it: the model We group 90 countries by eight characteristics measured around 1965: log initial GDP per capita, years of schooling, log life expectancy, fertility, the investment share, government consumption, openness and child mortality. The variables are standardised. We run k-means with 2 to 8 clusters and choose the number with the highest average silhouette (Rousseeuw 1987), describe the clusters by their means, and assess stability by refitting on 50 bootstrap samples and computing the adjusted Rand index (Hubert and Arabie 1985) between each bootstrap partition, applied to all countries, and the full-sample partition. We repeat the analysis with Ward hierarchical clustering and a Gaussian mixture.
Clustering: k-Means, Gaussian Mixtures and Ward, with a Test of Whether the Clusters Are Real

How to read it The variables have very different scales (fertility from 1.5 to 8, the investment share from 0.03 to 0.48), which is why they are standardised. Several are strongly correlated: initial GDP and life expectancy correlate 0.89, and life expectancy and child mortality -0.96, so health and income count several times in the distance between countries. The clusters will mostly reflect one dimension, general development, and the guide shows that this is what they do.
Clustering: k-Means, Gaussian Mixtures and Ward, with a Test of Whether the Clusters Are Real

How to read it The silhouette is highest with two clusters (0.41) and falls to 0.26 with three and 0.24 to 0.27 for four to six. The Calinski-Harabasz index agrees (85 for two clusters, 57 for three) and so does the Davies-Bouldin index (0.94 for two, against 1.32 for three). The within-cluster sum of squares falls smoothly from 366 to 173 between two and eight clusters, without a clear elbow. Two clusters is therefore the choice, with a silhouette of 0.41, a moderate value: there is structure, but not sharply separated groups.
Clustering: k-Means, Gaussian Mixtures and Ward, with a Test of Whether the Clusters Are Real

How to read it The larger cluster has 50 countries (56%) with log initial GDP of 7.1 (against 8.5), 2.5 years of schooling (6.3), fertility of 6.3 (2.8), an investment share of 15% (25%) and child mortality of 0.106 (0.026). The 40 countries of the second cluster are the richer, more educated, lower-fertility group. The two clusters differ on every variable, including openness (0.19 against 0.25) and government consumption (0.117 against 0.138), but most of the distance is on the development variables. The partition is very stable: the average adjusted Rand index against the full-sample partition is 0.97 and its 10th percentile is 0.96, so bootstrap resamples reproduce the same two groups. The scatter of the first two principal components (75% of the variance) shows two overlapping groups along the first component, with a thin region between them but not an empty gap, which agrees with the moderate silhouette.
Clustering: k-Means, Gaussian Mixtures and Ward, with a Test of Whether the Clusters Are Real
Do the methods and the number of clusters agree?

How to read it k-means and Ward both choose two clusters (sizes 50 and 40 against 52 and 38), but the Ward partition is less stable (0.67 against 0.97). The Gaussian mixture chooses four components by BIC, with a silhouette of 0.24 and a stability of 0.53: its four groups are not reproducible. Forcing three clusters lowers the silhouette to 0.22 to 0.34 and the stability to 0.58 to 0.63 in all three methods. A reader should be told that two groups (richer and poorer) are supported by the data and that finer typologies are not. A finer partition could be described, but it would not be a finding.
Clustering: k-Means, Gaussian Mixtures and Ward, with a Test of Whether the Clusters Are Real

How to read it Without the two health variables the number of clusters is still two, with sizes 50 and 40, a silhouette of 0.38 and a stability of 0.93. With only the five development variables the clusters are 47 and 43 countries and the silhouette rises to 0.55, because the variables that remain are strongly correlated and one dimension dominates. The result is robust to the list, as long as the list is about development. A list of different kinds of variables (for example institutions and trade) would produce a different partition and needs its own check.
Clustering: k-Means, Gaussian Mixtures and Ward, with a Test of Whether the Clusters Are Real

How to write it: results The 90 countries fall into two groups. The silhouette is highest for two clusters (0.41, against 0.26 for three), and the same two groups appear in 97% of bootstrap resamples (adjusted Rand index 0.97). The larger group (50 countries) has lower income (log GDP 7.1 against 8.5), schooling (2.5 against 6.3 years), investment (15% against 25%) and openness, and higher fertility (6.3 against 2.8) and child mortality (0.106 against 0.026). The silhouette of 0.41 and the principal-component plot show two overlapping groups, not separated ones. Ward clustering gives similar groups (52 and 38 countries) with lower stability, a Gaussian mixture selects four components that are not stable (adjusted Rand index 0.53), and requiring three clusters produces partitions that are not reproducible (0.58 to 0.63). We therefore report a two-group typology and do not interpret finer partitions.
Clustering: k-Means, Gaussian Mixtures and Ward, with a Test of Whether the Clusters Are Real

Double Machine Learning: Interactive Model: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Does eligibility for a 401(k) pension plan raise households' net financial assets? In the early 1990s, eligibility was determined by the employer, not chosen by the worker. Poterba, Venti and Wise (1994, 1995) argued that, once income and other characteristics are held fixed, eligibility is as good as randomly assigned: people did not choose their job because of its pension plan. This is the classic application of DML (Chernozhukov et al. 2018). The treatment \(D\) (eligible or not) is binary, and its effect may differ across households. The interactive regression model (IRM) allows that: and targets the average treatment effect \(\theta = E[g_0(1, X) - g_0(0, X)]\) . DML estimates it with the doubly robust (AIPW) score, averaged over cross-fitted predictions:

The first two terms compare predicted outcomes with and without treatment; the last two correct the prediction errors, weighted by the inverse propensity score. Variable Definition net_tfa Net total financial assets, dollars (outcome) e401 1 if eligible for a 401(k) (treatment) age , age_sq Age and its square inc , inc_sq Income and its square educ , educ_sq Years of schooling and its square fsize , marr , twoearn Family size; married; two earners db , pira , hown Defined-benefit pension; IRA; home owner
Load the data and confirm the starting point

Eligible households hold far more financial assets, but they also earn more: the raw difference mixes the effect of eligibility with the effect of income. Adjusting for the controls cuts the difference roughly in half. With 12 controls (Rule B2: at least 10), DML is the method; with a binary treatment, the interactive model (Rule B3).

The AIPW score divides by \(\hat m(X)\) and \(1 - \hat m(X)\) . If some households are almost certain to be eligible, or almost certain not to be, those weights explode and the estimate becomes unstable. Before estimating anything, check overlap : the propensity scores of treated and untreated households should cover the same range, away from 0 and 1. Overlap is reasonable in the middle of the distribution, but 4.8 % of households, almost all of them not eligible (451 of the 478 below 0.05), have propensity scores outside [0.05, 0.95]: households whose characteristics almost never come with a 401(k) offer. DoubleML trims extreme scores at a threshold; the guide reports the estimate at several thresholds in Step 5.

The interactive model needs three predictions: the outcome for treated households \(\hat g(1, X)\) , for untreated households \(\hat g(0, X)\) (both from ml_g ), and the propensity score \(\hat m(X)\) (from the classifier ml_m ). Each is cross-fitted.

Both learners give an average effect of eligibility of about 8,000 dollars (8,316 with LASSO, 7,896 with random forests), close to the published DML estimates for these data, below the OLS estimate of 9,396 and less than half the raw difference. The two learners differ by a third of a standard error (Rule B4), so the result does not hinge on the choice of machine-learning method.
Robustness: trimming and the effect on the treated

Two checks belong in the paper. First, how much do the extreme propensity scores matter? Second, the average effect on the treated (ATTE), the effect for households that actually were eligible, may differ from the ATE.

How to write it: method and results We estimate the average effect of 401(k) eligibility on net financial assets with the interactive regression model of Chernozhukov et al. (2018), assuming, following Poterba, Venti and Wise, that eligibility is as good as random conditional on income, age, education, family structure and other pension and asset holdings (twelve controls including squares). The outcome regressions and the propensity score are estimated with LASSO and, alternatively, random forests, with five-fold cross-fitting repeated three times and propensity scores trimmed at 0.01. Eligibility raises net financial assets by about 8,000 dollars on average (8,316 with LASSO and 7,896 with random forests; standard errors about 1,200), less than the OLS estimate of 9,396 and far less than the raw difference of 19,559 (Table X). The estimate barely moves when propensity scores are trimmed at 0.05 or 0.10 (7,709 and 7,727). The effect on eligible households is larger, about 10,900 dollars (ATTE), consistent with larger gains for the higher-income households who are more often eligible.

Checklist for the paper Argue why treatment is as good as random given the controls. Show the propensity-score distribution and the share outside [0.05, 0.95]. Report the learners, folds, repetitions and the trimming threshold. Show DML with two learners next to OLS and the raw difference. Report the ATTE and the estimate at other trimming thresholds.
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)

What is the effect of actually participating in a 401(k) plan on a household's financial assets? Participation is a choice: households that save a lot anyway are more likely to join, so comparing participants with non-participants, even with controls, overstates the effect. Eligibility is a natural instrument. It is set by the employer, so (following Poterba, Venti and Wise) it is as good as random given income and the other controls; it strongly shifts participation, because only eligible workers can participate; and it plausibly affects assets only through participation. The partially linear IV model is with \(D\) participation, \(Z\) eligibility and \(X\) the controls. DML-IV predicts \(Y\) , \(D\) and \(Z\) from \(X\) by cross-fitted machine learning, and then runs IV on the residuals: \(\hat\theta = \sum \tilde Z_i \tilde Y_i / \sum \tilde Z_i \tilde D_i\) .
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)

Whose effect is this? With a binary instrument and heterogeneous effects, IV estimates the effect for compliers , the households who participate because they are eligible (a local average treatment effect; Imbens and Angrist 1994). Here non-eligible households cannot participate at all (one-sided non-compliance), so the compliers are all participants and \(\theta\) is the average effect of participation on the participants.
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)
Load the data and confirm the starting point
Nobody who is ineligible participates, and 70.5 % of the eligible do. OLS gives a large effect of participation, but it compares savers who chose to participate with households that did not.
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)

An instrument must move the treatment. The first-stage regression of participation on eligibility and the controls tells how strongly; the selection tool requires an F statistic of at least 10 (Rule B3). The instrument is extremely strong: eligibility raises the probability of participating by 70 percentage points (F ≈ 7,600). Weak-instrument problems do not arise here. When the F statistic is close to or below 10, report Anderson–Rubin confidence intervals, which stay valid however weak the instrument is.
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)

2SLS is the standard estimator, but it controls for \(X\) linearly. With income entering wealth and participation in a strongly nonlinear way, a linear adjustment may leave confounding behind. DML-IV relaxes that.
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)
Three nuisance functions are cross-fitted: \(\ell(X) = E[Y \mid X]\) ( ml_l ), \(m(X) = E[Z \mid X]\) ( ml_m ) and \(r(X) = E[D \mid X]\) ( ml_r ).
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)
Reading the result: the intention-to-treat and the Wald ratio

With one binary instrument, the IV estimate is the effect of eligibility on assets (the intention-to-treat , ITT) divided by the effect of eligibility on participation (the first stage). Seeing the two pieces makes the result transparent:
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)

How to write it: method and results Participation in a 401(k) is chosen by households and is therefore endogenous. We instrument it with eligibility, which is determined by employers and, following Poterba, Venti and Wise, is as good as random conditional on income, age, education and family characteristics. The first stage is very strong (eligibility raises participation by about 70 percentage points; F in the thousands). We estimate the partially linear IV model by double machine learning (Chernozhukov et al. 2018), with LASSO and random-forest learners, five-fold cross-fitting and three repetitions. Participation raises net financial assets by about 13,000 dollars among participants (13,641 with LASSO and 12,880 with random forests; standard errors about 1,900), close to linear 2SLS (13,526) and somewhat below OLS (14,159), which is biased upwards by the self-selection of savers into participation (Table X). The two learners differ by 0.4 standard errors.
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)

Checklist for the paper Argue relevance, exclusion and as-good-as-random assignment of the instrument. Report the first stage and its F statistic; use Anderson–Rubin intervals if it is weak. State whose effect IV identifies (compliers; here, participants). Show DML-IV with two learners next to OLS and 2SLS. Report folds, repetitions and the learners for all three nuisance functions.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model

Do poorer countries grow faster? The neoclassical growth model predicts conditional convergence: holding constant the determinants of a country's steady state, a lower initial income should mean faster growth. The test is the sign of \(\theta\) in where \(X_i\) are the steady-state determinants. The Barro–Lee data used by Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen (2011, 2014) have 90 countries and 60 candidate controls: schooling by level and sex, population growth, fertility, investment, government spending, openness, political instability, the black-market premium and more. With 60 controls and 90 countries, OLS is barely estimable, and choosing a handful of controls by hand is exactly the specification search that convergence studies have been criticised for.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model

This is the partially linear model : the treatment \(D\) enters linearly with one coefficient \(\theta\) , and the controls enter through an unknown function \(g\) that machine learning can estimate. DML (Chernozhukov et al. 2018) estimates \(\theta\) in three steps: predict the outcome from the controls, \(\hat\ell(X) \approx E[Y\mid X]\) , and the treatment from the controls, \(\hat m(X) \approx E[D\mid X]\) , each by machine learning; form the residuals \(\tilde Y = Y - \hat\ell(X)\) and \(\tilde D = D - \hat m(X)\) ; regress \(\tilde Y\) on \(\tilde D\) : the slope is \(\hat\theta\) . Two ingredients make the standard error valid even though the predictions are regularised: the residual-on-residual form is Neyman-orthogonal (small errors in \(\hat\ell\) and \(\hat m\) have only second-order effects on \(\hat\theta\) ), and every prediction is made by cross-fitting , on observations the learner was not trained on.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model

The identifying assumption is the same as for OLS DML assumes that, given \(X\) , the remaining variation in initial GDP is unrelated to unobserved determinants of growth. Machine learning makes the adjustment for \(X\) flexible; it does not make the assumption true. Argue it as you would for OLS, and if it fails, use an instrument (DML-IV) or a research design.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model
Load the data and confirm the starting point

Without controls, richer countries did not grow more slowly: unconditional convergence fails. With all 60 controls, OLS uses up most of the sample (29 residual degrees of freedom) and the estimate is too imprecise to say anything. That is the case for DML (Rule B2: 60 controls, far more than 10). The forest predicts growth slightly better than LASSO from the controls, and initial GDP slightly worse. Neither clearly dominates, so the guide estimates DML with both learners and checks that they agree (Rule B4).
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model
Why not just use LASSO to pick the controls?

The tempting shortcut is to run LASSO of growth on initial GDP and the 60 controls, keep what survives, and report OLS on the survivors. This single selection is biased: LASSO drops controls that predict growth only weakly, even if they are strongly related to initial GDP, and those are exactly the confounders that matter. Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen (2014) show that one must also keep controls that predict the treatment . Their double selection is the simplest valid version of the DML idea: LASSO's penalty matters here. Cross-validation chooses a penalty for prediction and, with 90 observations, keeps most of the 60 controls. For selecting controls, Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen use a theory-based plug-in penalty, \(\lambda = 2c\,\hat\sigma\sqrt{n}\,\Phi^{-1}\!\big(1 - \gamma/(2p)\big)\) with \(c = 1.1\) and \(\gamma = 0.1/\log n\) , iterated on the residual variance. It keeps only controls whose signal is clearly above noise.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model
Why not just use LASSO to pick the controls?

The result is a textbook illustration of the problem. LASSO of growth on the controls keeps none of them: no single control predicts growth strongly enough. Single selection therefore reduces to OLS without controls and finds no convergence. But several controls strongly predict initial GDP, and those are the confounders. Double selection keeps them and finds a clearly negative \(\theta\) , close to the \(-0.050\) (s.e. 0.016) that Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen (2014) report with the same data.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model

The DoubleML package (Bach et al. 2022) implements the estimator with cross-fitting and repeated sample splits. The learners are passed in as scikit-learn models: ml_l predicts the outcome and ml_m the treatment. With 90 observations, one random split into folds can matter, so the estimator is repeated over 10 different splits ( n_rep=10 ) and the median is reported, with a standard error that includes the variation across splits.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model
How much does the sample split matter?
The spread across splits is the price of a small sample. Report the median over many splits, never the result of one split chosen after the fact.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model

How to write it: method and results We estimate the effect of log initial GDP per capita on growth in the partially linear model \(\text{growth}_i = \theta \log \text{GDP}_{i,1965} + g(X_i) + \varepsilon_i\) , where \(X_i\) contains 60 country characteristics, using double machine learning (Chernozhukov et al. 2018). The nuisance functions are estimated with LASSO and, alternatively, with a random forest, using five-fold cross-fitting repeated over 10 random splits. Unconditionally there is no convergence ( \(\hat\theta = 0.001\) ), and OLS with all 60 controls is too imprecise to be informative (s.e. 0.032). Double machine learning gives \(\hat\theta \approx -0.04\) with both learners (s.e. about 0.015, p < 0.01), and the two learners agree within a fraction of a standard error. The estimate is close to post-double-selection LASSO with a plug-in penalty ( \(-0.042\) ), and to the \(-0.050\) reported by Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen (2014): conditional on their steady-state determinants, poorer countries grew faster (Table X).
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model

Checklist for the paper State the partially linear model and argue that the controls capture the confounders. Explain why OLS is not enough (many controls, or nonlinear controls). Report the learners, the number of folds and of repeated splits. Show DML with at least two learners, plus OLS and double selection as benchmarks. Report the variation across sample splits.
Double-Selection LASSO: Inference on One Variable with Many Controls
Double-Selection LASSO: Inference on One Variable with Many Controls: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code and more.
Double-Selection LASSO: Inference on One Variable with Many Controls

What is the effect of \(d\) on \(y\) when the right set of controls is unknown? The model is with \(p\) controls, possibly more than \(n\) , of which only a few matter (approximate sparsity). Double selection: LASSO of \(y\) on the controls: keep the selected set \(S_y\) . LASSO of \(d\) on the controls: keep \(S_d\) . OLS of \(y\) on \(d\) and the controls in \(S_y\cup S_d\) , with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. Step 2 is what protects the estimate. A control with a small coefficient \(\beta_j\) can be missed in step 1, but if it predicts \(d\) strongly its omission biases \(\hat\alpha\) by about \(\beta_j\gamma_j\) , and step 2 catches it. The penalty is the plug-in value of the rigorous LASSO, \(\lambda = 2c\sqrt n\,\Phi^{-1}(1-\gamma/(2p))\) with \(c=1.1\) , \(\gamma=0.1/\log n\) , and heteroskedasticity-robust loadings, which the theory covers. A cross-validated penalty is not covered by the theory and selects many more controls.
Double-Selection LASSO: Inference on One Variable with Many Controls

Three conditions for reading double selection Sparsity: a few controls (or good approximations to them) explain \(y\) and \(d\) . If the effects of the controls are dense, no selection method is reliable. Selection on observables: the controls must contain the confounders. Selection does not create variables you did not measure. A treatment that the controls do not explain completely: if \(d\) is almost a function of the controls, there is no variation left to identify \(\alpha\) . How to write it: the model We test conditional convergence: do countries with lower initial GDP grow faster, holding other characteristics fixed? The outcome is the growth rate of GDP per capita and the target is the logarithm of initial GDP (gdpsh465); there are 60 potential controls (education, institutions, trade, demographics, health) for 90 countries. We use post-double-selection (Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen 2014): the plug-in rigorous LASSO of the outcome and of initial GDP on the controls, then OLS of growth on initial GDP and the union of the selected controls, with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (the degrees-of-freedom convention of the R package hdm).
Double-Selection LASSO: Inference on One Variable with Many Controls

How to read it There are 90 countries and 60 candidate controls, so a regression with all controls has 62 coefficients to estimate from 90 observations. Growth averages 4.5% a year with a standard deviation of 5.1 points, and initial log GDP has a mean of 7.7 and a standard deviation of 0.9. With so few observations per control the OLS with all controls is imprecise, which is the case for selection.
Double-Selection LASSO: Inference on One Variable with Many Controls

How to read it Double selection gives -0.0500 (robust standard error 0.0158, 95% interval -0.081 to -0.019): holding the selected controls fixed, a country with one log point higher initial GDP grew 5 percentage points a year more slowly, which is evidence of conditional convergence. This reproduces the estimate published with the R package hdm (-0.05001, standard error 0.01579). Without controls the coefficient is 0.001 (standard error 0.005), the textbook finding of no unconditional convergence. With all 60 controls it is -0.009 with a standard error of 0.026, so the 60 controls take the precision away. Selecting controls for the outcome alone keeps one control (the black-market premium, bmp1l) and gives -0.011 (standard error 0.005, which would reject zero), while selecting for the treatment alone gives -0.044 (0.017).
Double-Selection LASSO: Inference on One Variable with Many Controls

How to read it The outcome equation selects only the black-market premium (bmp1l). The treatment equation selects six other controls: a trade-policy variable (freetar), three education variables (hm65, sf65, humanf65), life expectancy (lifee065) and a population-share variable (pop6565). The growth equation selects none of them, but each predicts initial GDP. Dropping them, as the outcome-only selection does, leaves their confounding in the coefficient: the estimate moves from -0.050 to -0.011. This is the bias that double selection removes, and it is not visible in the standard error of the single-selection estimate, which is small (0.005) and would mislead the reader about precision.
Double-Selection LASSO: Inference on One Variable with Many Controls
Sensitivity to the penalty and to the set of controls

How to read it A larger penalty keeps fewer controls: 10 at c = 0.8, 7 at 1.1 and 5 at 1.5 and 2.0. The estimate is -0.044 at 0.8, -0.050 at 1.1, -0.043 at 1.5 and -0.031 at 2.0, and the 95% interval stays below zero except at the largest penalty. The sign and rough magnitude are stable; the third decimal is not. With random subsets of 40 of the 60 controls the estimate is between -0.050 and -0.020 and the standard error between 0.0158 and 0.0168, so the conclusion does not depend on which controls were offered, but a precise value does, and a reader should be told so.
Double-Selection LASSO: Inference on One Variable with Many Controls

How to write it: results Without controls, initial GDP has no relation with subsequent growth (0.001, standard error 0.005). Controlling for country characteristics selected by post-double-selection, the coefficient is -0.050 (robust standard error 0.016, 95% confidence interval -0.081 to -0.019), which is evidence of conditional convergence: seven of 60 potential controls are selected, one for the growth equation and six for initial GDP. A regression with all 60 controls gives -0.009 (0.026) and is too imprecise to be informative with 90 countries. Choosing controls for growth alone gives -0.011, because it omits controls that predict initial GDP and that confound the relation. The point estimate varies between -0.031 and -0.050 with the penalty constant (0.8 to 2.0) and between -0.020 and -0.050 with random subsets of the candidate controls, and the interval excludes zero in most specifications. The result relies on sparsity and on the controls containing the relevant confounders.
Double-Selection LASSO: Inference on One Variable with Many Controls

Elastic Net: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. Linear, strongly correlated predictors.

Can next quarter's U.S. inflation be forecast from the recent history of inflation, unemployment, interest rates, output and money? The file holds inflation and four lags of five series (20 predictors) for 198 quarters. The lags of each series are highly correlated with one another: inflation this quarter and last quarter move together. That is the setting for the elastic net (Zou and Hastie 2005), which combines the LASSO and ridge penalties: \(\alpha = 1\) gives LASSO and \(\alpha = 0\) ridge. In between, the ridge part makes correlated predictors share their weight, and the LASSO part still sets weak groups to zero. Both \(\lambda\) and \(\alpha\) are chosen by cross-validation.

Predictor group Columns Series Inflation infl_l1 … infl_l4 CPI inflation, annualised % Unemployment unemp_l1 … unemp_l4 Unemployment rate, % Interest rate tbilrate_l1 … tbilrate_l4 3-month Treasury bill rate, % Output gdp_growth_l1 … gdp_growth_l4 Real GDP growth, annualised % Money m1_growth_l1 … m1_growth_l4 M1 growth, annualised % Every predictor is dated before the quarter being forecast, so the model uses only information that was available at the time.
Load the data and test for unit roots

Machine learning does not remove the need to check stationarity. A model trained on a trending series learns the trend's past range: a random forest can never predict a value it has not seen, and a linear model on I(1) series risks a spurious fit. So each series is tested first, exactly as in the Time-Series Guide, and I(1) series are differenced. The T-bill rate has a unit root in levels (ADF does not reject, KPSS rejects stationarity) and is stationary after one difference; inflation, unemployment, GDP growth and money growth reject the unit root at 5 %. Following the selection tool, the four T-bill lags enter in first differences.
Load the data and test for unit roots
Several pairs of lags are correlated above 0.9, far above the 0.8 threshold: the elastic net's case.
Validate forward in time, never backward

Ordinary k-fold cross-validation shuffles the observations, so a model would be trained on 2005 and tested on 1975, using the future to predict the past. For time series, every validation fold must come after the data the model was trained on. TimeSeriesSplit does this: each split trains on an expanding window of the past and validates on the next block. The elastic net has the lowest rolling-origin error, LASSO is close, and the random forest is clearly worse: a nonlinear model does not help here (Rule A3), and with lags correlated above 0.8 the tool chooses the elastic net (Rule A4).
Grouped selection: elastic net against LASSO

Fit both on the full sample and compare which lags they keep. Within a group of correlated lags, LASSO tends to keep one or two and drop the rest; the elastic net, the more so the smaller its mixing weight α, spreads the weight. To see the effect, the table also shows an elastic net with α fixed at 0.3. Cross-validation chooses a mixing weight of α = 0.9, close to LASSO, so here the two give almost the same coefficients: the data prefer a mostly-LASSO penalty with a little ridge stabilisation. The α = 0.3 column shows what a stronger ridge component does: weight is spread across correlated lags (the third lag of inflation loses weight to the fourth, which almost triples) and one more lag ( unemp_l1 ) enters. Report the cross-validated α, and show that the main conclusions do not depend on it. In every version the first three lags of inflation dominate, followed by the T-bill rate and money growth.
A real forecasting test: recursive one-step-ahead forecasts

The honest test of a forecasting model is to simulate using it in real time. From 1990 onwards, each quarter the model is re-estimated on all data up to the previous quarter (penalty re-chosen each time) and forecasts the next quarter. The benchmark every forecasting paper must beat is a simple AR(4) model of inflation on its own four lags, estimated the same way. A ratio below 1 means the model beats the AR(4) benchmark. Here it does not : both penalised models forecast about 6 % worse than the AR(4) over 1990–2009. Whether a difference is statistically significant is tested with the Diebold–Mariano test on the loss differences (with a Newey–West variance, because forecast errors are serially correlated):

The difference is not significant (p ≈ 0.2): the twenty extra predictors neither help nor clearly hurt. This is a well-known result, not a failure of the method: since the mid-1980s, inflation has been hard to forecast with anything better than its own recent history (Atkeson and Ohanian 2001; Stock and Watson 2007). A paper must report it honestly. The elastic net is still the right tool for the question which lags carry information; the forecasting test says that, out of sample, the information beyond inflation's own lags is small. How to write it: method and results We forecast quarterly CPI inflation with an elastic net on four lags of inflation, unemployment, the change in the Treasury-bill rate (the level has a unit root), real GDP growth and M1 growth. Because lags of the same series are highly correlated (|r| up to 0.97), we prefer the elastic net to LASSO, which selects arbitrarily within correlated groups. Penalty and mixing weight are chosen by rolling-origin cross-validation, so that no model is ever validated on data earlier than its training sample. Cross-validation selects a mixing weight of 0.9, close to LASSO; the first three lags of inflation, the change in the T-bill rate and lagged money growth carry most of the weight. In recursive one-step-ahead forecasts over 1990Q1–2009Q3, re-estimating the model each quarter, the elastic net does not improve on an AR(4) benchmark: its RMSE is 2.67 percentage points against 2.52, and a Diebold–Mariano test with HAC variance does not reject equal accuracy (p = 0.18). Consistent with Atkeson and Ohanian (2001), the additional macroeconomic predictors contain little information about future inflation beyond its own history.

Checklist for the paper Test every series for a unit root and difference I(1) series before any learning. Date every predictor before the forecast target; never let future information in. Use rolling-origin (expanding-window) validation, not shuffled k-fold. Report the chosen mixing weight α and penalty λ, and which lags survive. Compare recursive out-of-sample forecasts with an AR benchmark; report the RMSE ratio and a Diebold–Mariano test.
Who Gains? Heterogeneous Effects with BLP, GATES and CLAN
Who Gains? Heterogeneous Effects with BLP, GATES and CLAN: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
Who Gains? Heterogeneous Effects with BLP, GATES and CLAN
The question and the three outputs

Does the treatment effect vary, and who gains most? In a randomised experiment with treatment share \(p\) , split the sample at random into an auxiliary half and a main half. In the auxiliary half fit a machine-learning model of the outcome separately for treated and control units. For each unit in the main half this gives a baseline prediction \(B(x)\) and a proxy of the effect \(S(x)=\hat m_1(x)-\hat m_0(x)\) . Then, in the main half: BLP. Regress \(Y\) on \(1, B, S\) and \((D-p)\) and \((D-p)(S-\bar S)\) with weights \(1/(p(1-p))\) . The coefficient \(\beta_1\) on \(D-p\) is the average effect, and \(\beta_2\) says whether the proxy tracks the true effect: \(\beta_2=0\) if it carries no information, \(\beta_2=1\) if it is perfect.
Who Gains? Heterogeneous Effects with BLP, GATES and CLAN
The question and the three outputs

GATES. Sort units into groups by quantiles of \(S\) and estimate the effect \(\gamma_k\) in each group. A real heterogeneity shows as \(\gamma_K>\gamma_1\) . CLAN. Compare covariate means in the most and least affected groups: the characteristics that separate them. Repeating over many random splits and taking medians removes the dependence on any one split; the p-value is twice the median p-value, which keeps the size. Three conditions for reading the output The treatment must be randomised (or the propensity score known). The method does not correct for selection. A significant \(\beta_2\) is the test of heterogeneity. GATES and CLAN describe it. If \(\beta_2\) is not significant, the groups are not evidence of differences.
Who Gains? Heterogeneous Effects with BLP, GATES and CLAN
The question and the three outputs

Power is low in small samples. Half the sample is used for estimation, so a null result is weak evidence of homogeneity. How to write it: the model We ask whether the earnings effect of the National Supported Work job-training programme differs across participants. Assignment was random (185 of 445 participants were treated). Following Chernozhukov, Demirer, Duflo and Fernández-Val (2018), in each of 40 random half-splits we train random forests of 1978 earnings for the treated and the control separately on one half, using age, education, race, marital status, degree status and earnings in 1974 and 1975, and use their difference as a proxy of the individual effect in the other half. There we estimate the best linear predictor of the effect, the effects in four groups sorted by the proxy, and the covariate means of the most and least affected groups. We report medians over the splits and p-values equal to twice the median p-value.
Who Gains? Heterogeneous Effects with BLP, GATES and CLAN

How to read it The covariate means are close in the two arms (for example age 25.1 and 25.8, education 10.1 and 10.4), as random assignment implies. Mean earnings in 1978 are 1.79 thousand dollars higher in the trained group. The question is whether this average hides a spread: for some participants the programme may matter much more.
Who Gains? Heterogeneous Effects with BLP, GATES and CLAN

How to read it The average effect is 1.75 thousand dollars (95% interval -0.41 to 3.92, adjusted p = 0.13). It is less precise than the simple difference in means because only half of the sample is used in each split and the regression carries the machine-learning proxy. The heterogeneity loading \(\beta_2\) is 0.10 with a standard error of 0.37 (adjusted p = 1.0): the forest-based proxy has no detectable relationship with the actual effect. A value of 1 would mean a perfect proxy, and the interval of -0.72 to 0.93 includes 0 but not 1, so the data are consistent with a poor proxy and rule out a perfect one.
Who Gains? Heterogeneous Effects with BLP, GATES and CLAN

How to read it The four group effects are 1.20, 1.77, 1.45 and 2.08, with standard errors of 1.6 to 1.9, so every group has a positive point estimate and none is separated from zero or from the others. The difference between the most and the least affected group is 0.80 (standard error 2.59, adjusted p = 1.0). The ordering is not monotone, and the two extreme groups are far from distinguishable. There is no evidence in this sample that the effect of the programme differs along the dimension that the forest finds.
Who Gains? Heterogeneous Effects with BLP, GATES and CLAN
Who is in the most affected group?

How to read it The classification shows what the forest uses, not an effect. Participants in the group with the highest predicted effect are older (29.4 against 22.5 years), more educated (11.3 against 9.6 years), more often married (31% against 7%), less often without a degree (55% against 89%) and had lower earnings in 1974 (1.0 against 4.3). The differences are large, and they describe the participants that the forest predicts will gain, but because the GATES are not different, the forest's predictions did not turn out to separate real gains. The CLAN results alone would be misleading: they would be a story about older, more educated participants, and the evidence for it is not there.
Who Gains? Heterogeneous Effects with BLP, GATES and CLAN
Robustness to the number of groups and the random splits

How to read it Across three seeds and two to four groups the heterogeneity loading is between 0.04 and 0.16 with adjusted p-values of 0.995 or more, the average effect is between 1.60 and 1.75, and the top-minus-bottom difference is between 0.25 and 0.83 and never significant (the smallest adjusted p-value is 0.96). Nothing in the conclusion depends on the number of groups or the random splits. The seeds change the average effect by up to 0.15, which is the sampling variation from using half the sample, so report the number of splits and the seed.
Who Gains? Heterogeneous Effects with BLP, GATES and CLAN

How to write it: results Job training raises earnings by an estimated 1.75 thousand dollars (95% confidence interval -0.41 to 3.92; the interval is wider than for the simple difference in means because inference is based on half-samples). We find no evidence that the effect varies with the observed characteristics. The coefficient on the machine-learning proxy of the effect is 0.10 (standard error 0.37, adjusted p-value 1.0), and the effect in the group predicted to gain most exceeds that in the group predicted to gain least by 0.80 (standard error 2.59, adjusted p = 1.0). The groups differ in age, education, marital status and earlier earnings, so the forest does find variation in who the participants are, but that variation is not related to the size of the effect. The sample of 445 gives low power: the 95% interval for the difference between the most and least affected groups runs from -5.0 to 6.6 thousand dollars, so large differences cannot be ruled out. The results are medians over 40 random splits (seed 0).
