Interpreting a Machine-Learning Model: Importance, Partial Dependence and Interactions

What did the model learn? A forest or a boosted ensemble has no coefficients. Three summaries describe the fitted function \(\hat f(x)\) : Permutation importance: shuffle one predictor in the test set and record how much the test \(R^2\) falls. A variable the model relies on costs a lot when shuffled. Because it is measured on data the model has not seen, it does not reward overfitting. Partial dependence: \(\mathrm{PD}_j(v) = \frac1n\sum_i \hat f(x_{ij}=v,\, x_{i,-j})\) , the average prediction when predictor \(j\) is set to \(v\) and the others keep their observed values. It shows the shape of the effect (linear, saturating, threshold). Interaction strength: Friedman's \(H^2_{jk}\) is the share of the variance of the joint partial dependence of \(j\) and \(k\) that is not explained by the two separate partial dependences. It is 0 for an additive model.
Interpreting a Machine-Learning Model: Importance, Partial Dependence and Interactions

Three cautions before you report importance Correlated predictors split their importance. If two variables carry the same information, shuffling one leaves the other to compensate, so each looks less important than the pair is. Importance is not an effect. A variable can be important because it proxies for something omitted. A weak model has little to interpret. If the test \(R^2\) is low, the importance of a variable is small in absolute terms, so report it next to the test fit. How to write it: the model We ask which characteristics a random forest uses to predict the log wage of 663 U.S. men, and how. We train the forest (200 trees, minimum leaf size 5) on 75% of the sample and compute the permutation importance of each of 15 predictors on the other 25%, as the fall in test R-squared averaged over 30 random shuffles. We plot the partial dependence of the log wage on the three most important predictors, measure pairwise interaction strength with Friedman's H statistic (Friedman and Popescu 2008) and compare the ranking with standardised OLS coefficients (Molnar 2022).
Interpreting a Machine-Learning Model: Importance, Partial Dependence and Interactions
Load the data and look at the correlated predictors

How to read it The predictors are correlated: education correlates 0.54 with the IQ score and 0.41 with the knowledge-of-the-world-of-work score (KWW), and the two test scores correlate 0.41. Each of the three correlates 0.31 to 0.32 with the log wage. These are the variables whose importance will be shared, so the ranking among them is less firm than the ranking between them and the rest.
Interpreting a Machine-Learning Model: Importance, Partial Dependence and Interactions
Fit the model and measure importance

How to read it The forest explains 26.5% of the variance in the test sample, so there is a modest signal to interpret. The most important predictor is the KWW score: shuffling it lowers the test R-squared by 0.086 (standard deviation over shuffles 0.023), against 0.052 for education, 0.052 for IQ, 0.040 for urban residence and about 0.02 each for mother's education and age. Six predictors (region, hours, marital status, siblings, race and birth order) have importance below 0.01, and birth order is slightly negative, which means that shuffling it does not hurt the fit at all. The importance share of KWW is 26%. The rank correlation between importance and the absolute standardised OLS coefficient is 0.48: the two models agree that education and urban residence matter (OLS coefficients 0.094 and 0.093 per standard deviation) but not on KWW, which the forest ranks first and OLS gives only 0.037, or on marital status, which has the third-largest OLS coefficient (0.066) and almost no importance in the forest.
Interpreting a Machine-Learning Model: Importance, Partial Dependence and Interactions
Shape of the effects: partial dependence

How to read it Moving KWW from its 5th percentile (23) to its 95th (48) raises the predicted log wage from 6.78 to 6.95, a range of 0.17 (about 17% in wages), and the profile is not a straight line (R-squared 0.73 for a linear fit), so the gain per point of KWW differs along the range; the chart shows where. Education raises the prediction by 0.15 between 11 and 18 years, and IQ by 0.10 between 77 and 127, with a nearly straight profile (R-squared 0.96). The forest does not use the whole range of the data equally, so partial dependence shows an average pattern and not the effect for any individual.
Interpreting a Machine-Learning Model: Importance, Partial Dependence and Interactions

How to read it Friedman's H-squared is 0.060 for KWW and education, 0.031 for KWW and IQ and 0.011 for education and IQ. Between 1% and 6% of the variance of the joint partial dependence is therefore left after adding the separate effects: the interactions among the leading predictors are weak, and an additive model would capture most of what the forest has learned about them. The largest, KWW and education, is still small, so there is no evidence here that the value of education depends on the test score.
Interpreting a Machine-Learning Model: Importance, Partial Dependence and Interactions

How to read it The forest's top predictors are KWW, IQ and education in the first split and KWW, education and urban residence with a 40% test sample; boosting, which fits worse (test R-squared 0.15 against 0.26 for the forest), puts education, urban residence and KWW first. The same few variables appear at the top in all three, in a different order. The order among correlated predictors, and the importance numbers themselves, depend on the model and the split, so say which variables are important and avoid ranking them to the second decimal.
Interpreting a Machine-Learning Model: Importance, Partial Dependence and Interactions

How to write it: results The forest explains 26.5% of the variance of the log wage in a test sample of 25%. Permutation importance is largest for the KWW score (a fall in test R-squared of 0.086), followed by education (0.052), IQ (0.052) and urban residence (0.040); six of the 15 predictors have importance below 0.01. The partial dependence of the log wage on KWW, education and IQ is increasing, with ranges of 0.17, 0.15 and 0.10 between the 5th and 95th percentiles; the profile for KWW is the least linear (R-squared of a straight line 0.73). Interactions among the three leading predictors are weak (H-squared 0.01 to 0.06). Education, IQ and KWW are correlated (0.41 to 0.54), so their importances are not separable, and their order changes with the model and the test sample. These are descriptions of the fitted prediction function and not estimates of the effects of the variables on wages.

Kernel-Based Regularized Least Squares (KRLS): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

How do education, experience, tenure, ability and demographic characteristics relate to wages, without assuming that the relationships are linear or additive? The file holds the log wage and characteristics of 935 men. Ordinary regression reports one coefficient per variable. If the return to education differs between people, one number hides that. Kernel-based regularized least squares (Hainmueller and Hazlett 2014) approximates the regression function by a weighted sum of Gaussian bumps centred on the observations, where \(\lambda\) penalises roughness and is chosen by leave-one-out cross-validation. Predictors and outcome are standardised, and \(\sigma^2\) is set to the number of predictors. Because \(f\) is smooth and known in closed form, its derivative with respect to each predictor is available for every observation:

The average of these derivatives plays the role of the regression coefficient, and the spread of the derivatives shows how much the effect varies. What KRLS can and cannot do It is a description of conditional associations, not a causal estimator. For a 0/1 predictor a derivative is meaningless, so the effect is the difference between predictions with the variable set to 1 and to 0. The fitted function is fully determined by n weights, so the method becomes slow above a few thousand observations (the kernel matrix is n by n). How to write it: model section We estimate the wage equation by kernel-based regularized least squares (Hainmueller and Hazlett 2014) with a Gaussian kernel, standardised variables and the penalty chosen by leave-one-out cross-validation. We report the average pointwise marginal effect of each predictor with delta-method standard errors, and its distribution across individuals.
Load the data and build the estimator

How to read it After dropping men with missing values on the eight predictors, 663 remain (530 for training, 133 for testing). The leave-one-out search chooses lambda = 1.71, which gives 53.6 effective degrees of freedom: the fitted surface is about as flexible as a linear model with 54 parameters, against 9 for OLS. The number of effective degrees of freedom is the honest measure of complexity for a kernel method, and it also sets the degrees of freedom of the t tests below.
Fit, test and compare with OLS

How to read it Flexibility is not free. KRLS fits the training sample better than OLS (R² 0.36 against 0.28), but on the 133 held-out men it predicts no better: RMSE 0.393 for both and test R² of 0.18 for KRLS against 0.18 for OLS. In this sample a linear log-wage equation is already about as good a predictor as can be built from these eight variables. The value of KRLS here is not prediction but the effect heterogeneity it reveals, in the next steps.
Average marginal effects against OLS coefficients

How to read it The average effects are on the same scale as OLS coefficients: one more year of schooling is associated with 4.1 per cent higher wages on average (standard error 0.7 points), compared with 5.3 per cent in OLS. Experience (1.4 against 1.7), tenure (0.7 against 0.7) and IQ (0.33 against 0.35 points per point) are close to OLS. For the three binary variables the KRLS effect is a first difference, and it is smaller than the OLS coefficient: married 0.155 against 0.234, black −0.099 against −0.155, urban 0.180 against 0.206. All eight are significant at 5 per cent. The standard errors are smaller than the OLS ones because the weighting by a smooth function averages over many observations; they are conditional on the chosen lambda and so ignore the uncertainty from choosing it.

How to read it The average hides large differences. For schooling the middle half of men have effects between 2.7 and 5.6 per cent per year, and the 10th percentile is 0.8 per cent against 7.1 per cent at the 90th. The effect of experience is negative or near zero for about a tenth of the men (10th percentile −0.16 points) and 2.8 points at the 90th percentile. The effect of being black ranges from −30 per cent at the 10th percentile to +8 per cent at the 90th, with a median of −8 per cent, so the average of −10 per cent summarises a wide spread. The scatter plots show which values of the variable the effect varies with. These are descriptions of the fitted surface; a spread of effects is not proof that the effect truly varies, since the pointwise effects are themselves estimates.

How to read it The penalty matters for the effects more than for prediction. Test RMSE is almost flat across a hundredfold range of lambda (0.392 to 0.407 for the first four rows), but the average effect of education moves from 0.051 with weak regularisation to 0.023 with very strong regularisation (14 effective degrees of freedom). Strong smoothing pulls the surface towards a flat function and shrinks every effect towards zero. Report the leave-one-out choice and show at least one neighbouring value.
What to report in the paper

Item What to give Sample Number of observations (and the training/test split, if used) Specification Kernel, sigma squared, standardisation Penalty Lambda by leave-one-out and the effective degrees of freedom Fit Out-of-sample R² or RMSE next to OLS Effects Average marginal effect, standard error and p-value for every predictor, first differences for binary ones Heterogeneity Quartiles of the pointwise effects and a plot against the variable Sensitivity Average effects under a smaller and a larger lambda How to write it: results section The average marginal effect of an additional year of schooling is 4.1 per cent (standard error 0.7), somewhat below the OLS coefficient of 5.3. The effect varies across men: its interquartile range is 2.7 to 5.6 per cent. Out-of-sample, KRLS predicts about as well as OLS (RMSE 0.393 for both), so we use it to describe the heterogeneity of the associations and not to improve prediction. The estimates are conditional associations and not causal effects.

Reading a pointwise effect as a precise individual effect. Only the averages come with standard errors. Treating the standard errors as accounting for the choice of lambda. They are conditional on it. Interpreting a derivative for a 0/1 variable. Use the first difference, as the table does. Using KRLS on tens of thousands of observations. The n by n kernel matrix needs a subsample or an approximation. Expecting better predictions than a linear model. When the relationships are close to linear, KRLS reproduces OLS at a higher cost. Using KRLS to claim causation. It describes associations conditional on the included variables.
LASSO: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. Linear, few predictors matter.

The question is a practical one for any economics department: which student characteristics predict the final score in an introductory economics course? The file records fourteen candidate predictors for 814 students: study habits, grades, ACT scores, prior economics and calculus, attendance attitudes and family background. Some surely matter and many probably do not. Choosing among them by hand invites a specification search; LASSO makes the choice by a rule. LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator; Tibshirani 1996) estimates a linear model but adds a penalty on the size of the coefficients: The absolute-value penalty sets the coefficients of weak predictors to exactly zero , so LASSO selects variables while it estimates. The penalty weight \(\lambda\) controls how many survive: \(\lambda = 0\) gives OLS; a large \(\lambda\) drops everything.

Variable Definition Variable Definition score Course score, % (outcome) male 1 if male age Age in years calculus 1 if took calculus work Hours worked per week econhs 1 if took economics in high school study Hours studied per week attexc , attgood 1 if attendance rated excellent / good colgpa College GPA before the course fathcoll , mothcoll 1 if father / mother has a degree hsgpa High-school GPA acteng , actmth ACT English / maths score Prediction, not causation LASSO answers which variables help to predict the score . It does not say that studying more would raise a student's score: a selected variable may stand in for an omitted one, and a dropped variable may still have a causal effect that is small relative to the noise. If the question is causal, use double machine learning instead (see the DML guides).
Load the data and confirm the starting point

The selection tool's rules are met: there are more than 100 observations, the random forest does not beat LASSO out of sample (it is worse), so the relationship is treated as linear, and no two predictors are correlated above 0.8. The last check, sparsity, comes in Step 4. How to write it: data section The sample contains 814 students with complete records. The outcome is the course score (in per cent). Fourteen candidate predictors describe study effort, prior achievement, preparation in mathematics and economics, attitudes to attendance and family background. A random forest does not improve on a linear model in five-fold cross-validation, so we model the score as a linear function of the predictors and use LASSO to select among them.
Standardise, then choose the penalty by cross-validation

The penalty treats every coefficient alike, so the predictors must be on the same scale: a coefficient on hours per week and one on a 0/1 dummy are otherwise not comparable. Standardise first (mean 0, standard deviation 1), inside the pipeline, so that each cross-validation fold is standardised with its own training data. \(\lambda\) is chosen by five-fold cross-validation. Two choices are standard (Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman 2009): \(\lambda_{\min}\) : the penalty with the lowest cross-validated error, the best for prediction ; \(\lambda_{1se}\) : the largest penalty whose error is within one standard error of the minimum, the more conservative choice for selection , because it keeps only predictors whose contribution is clearly above noise.
Standardise, then choose the penalty by cross-validation

The error curve is flat near its minimum and rises steeply once the penalty starts to remove the strong predictors. The one-standard-error rule moves to the right along the flat part: a simpler model that predicts almost as well.

The coefficients are in units of the score per one standard deviation of each predictor, so their sizes can be compared directly. At \(\lambda_{1se}\) LASSO keeps fewer than half of the predictors: the problem is sparse, which is the condition for LASSO in the selection tool (Rule A4). College GPA and the ACT maths score carry most of the signal; high-school GPA, calculus, work hours and sex add smaller amounts. The coefficient path shows the whole story at once: as the penalty falls (to the right), predictors enter one by one.

A single LASSO fit can be fragile: with a slightly different sample a borderline predictor may enter or leave. A simple check is to refit LASSO on many bootstrap samples, with the same \(\lambda_{1se}\) , and count how often each predictor is kept (the idea behind stability selection ; Meinshausen and Bühlmann 2010). Predictors kept in nearly every bootstrap sample are robust findings. Predictors kept about half the time are borderline: report them as such and do not build an argument on them. Reading the frequencies A common rule is to call a predictor stable if it is selected in at least 80 % of the resamples (Meinshausen and Bühlmann suggest thresholds between 60 % and 90 %). Below that, the evidence that it adds predictive power is weak, even if the full-sample fit keeps it.
Accuracy on data the model has not seen

Cross-validation chose \(\lambda\) , so the cross-validated error at \(\lambda_{\min}\) is slightly optimistic. The honest test is nested cross-validation: an outer loop holds out each fold in turn, and the whole procedure, including the choice of \(\lambda\) , is run on the other four. LASSO predicts slightly better than OLS with all fourteen predictors (an RMSE of 10.18 against 10.26 points), while setting five of them to zero even at \(\lambda_{\min}\) ; both explain about 40 % of the variance out of sample, far better than predicting the mean. The forest is worse. When OLS and LASSO predict equally well, the advantage of LASSO is the interpretation : it shows which few predictors carry the signal.
Post-LASSO OLS, and why its p-values are not valid

A common next step is to re-estimate OLS on the predictors LASSO selected ( post-LASSO ; Belloni and Chernozhukov 2013). This removes the shrinkage bias in the kept coefficients and gives them their natural units. Do not report these p-values as tests The predictors were chosen because they fit well in this sample, so the usual standard errors are too small and the p-values too optimistic (the post-selection inference problem). Report post-LASSO coefficients as descriptions of the selected model. If you need a valid test of one variable's effect, use the double-selection or DML methods in the causal guides, which are designed for exactly that.

How to write it: results We select predictors of the course score with LASSO, choosing the penalty by five-fold cross-validation and using the one-standard-error rule for selection. Of the fourteen candidate predictors, LASSO keeps six (Table X): college GPA and the ACT mathematics score are the strongest, followed by high-school GPA, a calculus background, hours of paid work (negative) and sex. College GPA and the ACT mathematics score are selected in every one of 200 bootstrap resamples and calculus in 97 %; high-school GPA and work hours in about 80 %, and sex in only 55 %, so we treat sex as a borderline predictor. In nested cross-validation, LASSO predicts the score with an RMSE of 10.2 points (out-of-sample R² of 0.42), slightly better than OLS with all fourteen predictors and far better than the sample mean (13.3 points); a random forest does not improve on it. Because the predictors were chosen on the same data, we report the post-LASSO coefficients as descriptive and do not interpret their p-values as tests.

Checklist for the paper State the aim (prediction or selection) and why a penalised model is used. Report how λ was chosen (CV folds, λ min or λ 1se) and that predictors were standardised. Show the selected predictors, the coefficient path, and the selection frequencies. Report out-of-sample accuracy against OLS and a mean-only benchmark (nested CV). Do not give causal readings or post-selection p-values.
Neural Network Regression: Architecture, Early Stopping and Ensembles
Neural Network Regression: Architecture, Early Stopping and Ensembles: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code and more.
Neural Network Regression: Architecture, Early Stopping and Ensembles

Does a neural network predict better than a linear model or a forest, and by how much? A multilayer perceptron with one or two hidden layers of ReLU units fits by minimising the squared error plus an L2 penalty \(\alpha\lVert\theta\rVert^2\) with the Adam optimiser. Four choices decide whether the result can be trusted: Standardise the inputs and the outcome, otherwise the optimiser is dominated by the variables with large scales. Choose the size and penalty by cross-validation on the training sample, not by looking at the test set. Stop early: hold back 15% of the training sample and stop when its \(R^2\) has not improved for 25 epochs, which limits overfitting without choosing the number of epochs by hand.
Neural Network Regression: Architecture, Early Stopping and Ensembles

Average over random starts: training is not convex, so different seeds reach different solutions. The mean of \(S\) networks has a lower test error than the average single network (by convexity of the squared error) and removes most of the seed noise. Three cautions before you report a neural network Report the spread across seeds of a single network, or use an ensemble. One run is not a result. Small data favour simple models. With a few hundred observations, a forest or a regularised linear model is often as good, and a network has no coefficients to read. A network predicts; it does not explain. Use importance and partial-dependence tools to describe it, and do not interpret the weights.
Neural Network Regression: Architecture, Early Stopping and Ensembles

How to write it: the model We predict the log median house price in 506 census tracts from eight characteristics: log nitrogen oxide concentration, average number of rooms, distance to employment centres, access to radial highways, the property tax rate, the pupil-teacher ratio, the share of lower-status residents and the log crime rate. The network has ReLU hidden layers, is trained with Adam on standardised data, and stops when the R-squared on 15% of the training sample has not improved for 25 epochs. The architecture ((16) or (32, 16) units) and the L2 penalty (0.01 or 1) are chosen by three-fold cross-validation on the 75% training sample, and the reported prediction is the average of five networks started from different seeds. We compare it on the 25% test sample with OLS and a random forest.
Neural Network Regression: Architecture, Early Stopping and Ensembles

How to read it The log price has a standard deviation of 0.41. The strongest single correlates are the share of lower-status residents (-0.79), the number of rooms (0.63), the crime rate (-0.60) and the property tax rate (-0.56). A linear model will find these linear relations; a flexible model can gain if the relations are curved or interact, which the comparison below shows.
Neural Network Regression: Architecture, Early Stopping and Ensembles

How to read it Cross-validation chooses two hidden layers of 32 and 16 units with the small penalty (alpha = 0.01), with a cross-validated RMSE of 0.189, against 0.196 for one layer of 16 units and 0.205 to 0.207 with the large penalty: the penalty of 1 is too strong for this sample. On the test sample, the ensemble of five networks has an RMSE of 0.138 (R-squared 0.884), against 0.180 (0.804) for OLS, a reduction of 23% in the error. The random forest has 0.135 (0.889), as good as the network. A single network has a mean RMSE of 0.153 and a range of 0.141 to 0.167 across the five seeds, so a single run is between 2% and 21% worse than the ensemble depending on the seed.
Neural Network Regression: Architecture, Early Stopping and Ensembles

How to read it The first network trained for 178 epochs. The training loss falls from 0.26 to about 0.035 and is still declining slowly at the end. The validation R-squared rises from 0.61 to about 0.80 by epoch 100 and then fluctuates around 0.79 to 0.80 without a further trend, and training stops 25 epochs after its best value. Beyond that point the network would improve its fit to the training sample but not to data it has not seen, which is what early stopping is for.
Neural Network Regression: Architecture, Early Stopping and Ensembles
Sensitivity to the test sample and the number of networks

How to read it In all six runs the ensemble is better than OLS, with an RMSE of 0.132 to 0.145 against 0.180 to 0.190, and the ensemble is better than the average single network in each. The forest and the ensemble are within 0.004 of each other: the ensemble is better in two of the six runs (0.139 against 0.142 at a 20% test share and 10 networks, 0.132 against 0.135 at 25% and 10) and worse in the other four. More networks help a little: with 10 networks instead of 3 the RMSE is lower at test shares of 20% and 25% and slightly higher at 33% (0.1444 against 0.1438). The conclusion that a flexible model beats OLS by about a quarter of the error does not depend on the split. The conclusion that the network beats the forest does not hold.
Neural Network Regression: Architecture, Early Stopping and Ensembles

How to write it: results On a 25% test sample, a neural network (two hidden layers of 32 and 16 units, L2 penalty 0.01, chosen by cross-validation, average of five networks) predicts the log house price with an RMSE of 0.138 and an R-squared of 0.884, against 0.180 and 0.804 for OLS, a reduction in error of 23%. A random forest performs equally well (RMSE 0.135, R-squared 0.889). A single network has an RMSE between 0.141 and 0.167 depending on the random starting weights, which is why we report the ensemble. In six combinations of test share (20% to 33%) and ensemble size (3 or 10), the ensemble has an RMSE of 0.132 to 0.145 against 0.180 to 0.190 for OLS. We conclude that the relation between prices and tract characteristics is nonlinear and that a network, like a forest, captures this, but the network has no advantage over the forest with 506 observations.

Random Forest: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. Nonlinear, fewer than 1,000 observations.

How well can a baseball player's salary be predicted from his career record? The file holds the 1993 salaries of 353 Major League Baseball players and fifteen career statistics: years in the league, games, at-bats, runs, hits, home runs, runs batted in, batting average, walks, strikeouts, stolen bases, fielding percentage, all-star seasons and race. Salaries are not linear in performance: rookies are paid little whatever they do, salaries jump once players can bargain, and stars are paid far more than a linear model would suggest. A random forest (Breiman 2001) averages many regression trees. Each tree is grown on a bootstrap sample of the players, and at every split it may choose only from a random subset of the predictors. A single deep tree fits the sample closely but is very unstable; averaging hundreds of decorrelated trees keeps the flexibility and removes most of the instability:

What a forest can and cannot do A forest captures thresholds, curvature and interactions without being told about them. It cannot extrapolate: a forest never predicts a value outside the range of the outcomes it was trained on. And it gives no coefficients; Steps 6 and 7 show how to describe what it has learned.
Load the data and confirm the starting point

The forest's error is far below LASSO's, much more than the 5 % threshold (Rule A3): salaries are strongly nonlinear in the career record. With only 353 players, below 1,000, the selection tool chooses a random forest over gradient boosting (Rule A5). How to write it: data section The sample contains 353 Major League Baseball players with 1993 salaries and career statistics. The outcome is the log salary. In five-fold cross-validation a random forest predicts log salaries with an error about 28 % lower than LASSO, indicating strong nonlinearities and interactions between career statistics and pay; given the modest sample, we use a random forest rather than a boosted model, which has more tuning parameters to overfit.
Grow the forest: how many trees?

More trees never overfit: they only reduce the variance of the average. The question is how many are needed before the error stops falling. The out-of-bag (OOB) error answers it for free: each player is left out of about a third of the bootstrap samples, and the trees that did not see him predict his salary. The error is essentially flat beyond a few hundred trees. Use 500: cheap, and safely on the flat part.
Tune the two parameters that matter

Two parameters control how flexible each tree is: min_samples_leaf : the smallest number of players in a final leaf. Larger leaves make smoother, less variable predictions. max_features : the share of predictors each split may consider. Smaller values decorrelate the trees more. The surface is flat near the optimum: forests are forgiving, and any setting in the low-error region gives similar predictions. Report the chosen values and the grid.
Accuracy on data the model has not seen

The tuning above used the same folds that measured the error, which flatters the winner. Nested cross-validation repeats the tuning inside each outer fold. The forest explains a much larger share of the out-of-sample variance than OLS or LASSO. That gap is what justifies its loss of interpretability.

The forest has no coefficients. Permutation importance measures how much the held-out error rises when one predictor's values are shuffled, breaking its link with salary while leaving everything else intact. Compute it on a test set the forest did not see; the impurity-based importance that scikit-learn reports by default is computed on the training data and favours predictors with many distinct values. Correlated predictors share their importance At-bats, hits, runs and runs batted in are almost the same variable (correlations above 0.95). When one is shuffled, the forest still learns from the others, so each looks less important than the group is. Read the importances by group, or shuffle a correlated group together, before concluding that a statistic does not matter.
How do the key predictors affect salary? Partial dependence

A partial-dependence plot shows the average prediction as one predictor is varied over its range, with the others held at their observed values. It is the forest's answer to "what is the coefficient?", but it can bend. The curves are far from straight lines: salary rises steeply over the first years of a career and then flattens, which is the nonlinearity a linear model misses and the reason the forest predicts so much better.

How to write it: results We predict the log salary with a random forest of 500 trees, tuning the minimum leaf size and the share of predictors considered at each split by five-fold cross-validation. In nested cross-validation the forest's out-of-sample error is far below that of OLS and LASSO, and it explains a substantially larger share of the variance (Table X). Permutation importance on a held-out sample shows that years in the league and cumulative career output (at-bats, runs batted in, hits) dominate the predictions. Partial-dependence plots show that predicted salaries rise steeply over the first years of a career and then level off, a nonlinearity that linear models cannot capture.

Checklist for the paper Show why a nonlinear model is needed (forest vs LASSO, cross-validated). Report the number of trees, the tuned parameters and the tuning grid. Report nested out-of-sample accuracy against OLS, LASSO and the mean. Use permutation importance on held-out data, and read correlated predictors as a group. Show partial-dependence plots for the main predictors; do not call them causal effects.
Ridge Regression: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. Linear, many small effects.

How well can a man's wage be predicted from his ability, schooling, experience and background? The Blackburn–Neumark data, used throughout Wooldridge's textbook, record 15 candidate predictors for 663 men with complete data: two test scores (IQ and the Knowledge of the World of Work test), schooling, experience, tenure, age, marital status, race, region, urban residence, siblings, birth order and both parents' education. Unlike the exam-score example in the LASSO guide, nearly all of these plausibly matter a little. That is the setting for ridge. Ridge regression (Hoerl and Kennard 1970) adds a squared penalty to the least-squares objective: The squared penalty pulls every coefficient towards zero but, unlike the LASSO penalty, never sets one exactly to zero. It trades a little bias for a large reduction in variance, and it has a closed-form solution: \(\hat\beta = (X'X + \lambda I)^{-1}X'y\) .

Variable Definition Variable Definition lwage Log monthly wage (outcome) married 1 if married hours Average weekly hours black 1 if black IQ IQ score south , urban 1 if in the South / an SMSA KWW Knowledge of world of work score sibs Number of siblings educ Years of schooling brthord Birth order exper , tenure Years of experience / with employer meduc , feduc Mother's / father's schooling age Age in years When is ridge the right choice? When the true model is dense (many predictors with small effects), LASSO's habit of setting coefficients to zero throws away real signal, and ridge predicts better. When it is sparse (a few strong effects), LASSO wins. The selection tool decides with the share of predictors LASSO keeps at the one-standard-error penalty: half or more means dense, so ridge.
Load the data and confirm the starting point

All three conditions for ridge hold: the forest does not beat the linear model, no correlation exceeds 0.8, and LASSO keeps well over half of the predictors even at its conservative penalty. The signal is spread across many variables. How to write it: data section The sample contains 663 men with complete records from the Blackburn–Neumark extract of the National Longitudinal Survey. The outcome is the log monthly wage in 1980. Fifteen predictors describe measured ability, schooling, labour-market experience, demographics and family background. A random forest does not improve on a linear model in five-fold cross-validation, and a LASSO fit retains most predictors, indicating many small effects; we therefore use ridge regression.
Standardise, then choose the penalty by cross-validation

The penalty acts on the size of the coefficients, so the predictors must be on a common scale; standardise them inside the pipeline. Then search a grid of \(\lambda\) values. For ridge, leave-one-out cross-validation has a closed form and is almost free ( RidgeCV uses it by default), but five-fold CV is shown here to match the other guides. The error curve is shallow: moderate shrinkage helps a little, and only very large penalties (which shrink everything towards zero) hurt. That is typical of a dense, well-measured problem: ridge improves on OLS at the margin rather than dramatically.
How much does ridge shrink each coefficient?

Coefficients are per standard deviation of each predictor. Ridge keeps every predictor and shrinks the vector of coefficients as a whole; most individual estimates move towards zero (siblings by a third, experience by a fifth), but a few correlated ones grow slightly (the KWW score, age, father's education), because ridge spreads weight across predictors that carry overlapping information. The ridge path shows how all coefficients move smoothly towards zero as the penalty grows, without any of them hitting zero:

Ridge does not drop variables, so "number of predictors" no longer measures model complexity. The effective degrees of freedom do: with \(d_j\) the singular values of the standardised \(X\) , which equals \(p\) at \(\lambda = 0\) (OLS) and falls towards 0 as \(\lambda\) grows. Report this number: it tells the reader how much the penalty actually constrained the model.
Accuracy on data the model has not seen

Choosing \(\lambda\) on the same folds that measure the error flatters the model. Nested cross-validation repeats the whole procedure, including the choice of \(\lambda\) , inside each outer fold. The differences between the three linear models are small relative to their variation across folds: with 663 observations and 15 predictors, OLS is not badly overfitted, and ridge's gain is modest. That is an honest and common finding. Ridge earns its place when \(p\) is large relative to \(n\) or when predictors are noisy; report the comparison either way.

How to write it: results We predict the log wage with ridge regression on fifteen standardised predictors, choosing the penalty by five-fold cross-validation. Because LASSO retains most predictors even at its one-standard-error penalty, the signal appears to be spread across many variables, the setting in which ridge's proportional shrinkage is preferable to variable selection. The largest standardised coefficients belong to urban residence, schooling, marital status, IQ and weekly hours (negative), followed by experience and tenure (Table X); race and the South enter negatively. The chosen penalty (λ = 73) reduces the effective degrees of freedom from 15 to 13. In nested cross-validation ridge has the lowest error of the models compared (RMSE 0.357 against 0.358 for OLS and 0.359 for LASSO), although the differences are small relative to their variation across folds; all three explain about a quarter of the out-of-sample variance, and a random forest does not improve on them.

Checklist for the paper Explain why the problem is dense (LASSO keeps most predictors) and why ridge is used. State the standardisation, the λ grid and the CV scheme; report λ and the effective degrees of freedom. Show OLS and ridge coefficients side by side, and the ridge path. Report nested out-of-sample accuracy against OLS, LASSO and a mean-only benchmark. Ridge coefficients are shrunk on purpose: do not attach OLS-style standard errors to them.
Stacking: The Super Learner: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Can a weighted average of models predict better than any one of them? With \(L\) learners, each is fitted on \(K-1\) folds and used to predict the remaining fold, giving a cross-validated prediction \(\hat y_{i\ell}\) for every training observation. The weights solve a non-negative least-squares problem (van der Laan, Polley and Hubbard 2007). Every learner is then refitted on the whole training sample and the final prediction is the weighted average. Non-negativity keeps the ensemble stable when learners are highly correlated. The discrete super learner keeps only the learner with the lowest cross-validated risk; the weighted version can do no worse than it in the cross-validated sample, and in large samples it performs as well as the best weighted combination in the library.

Three things to settle before you stack Is the library diverse? An ensemble of five random forests adds nothing. Include a linear model, a regularised one and at least one flexible nonlinear learner. Is the evaluation clean? The weights are fitted on cross-validated predictions of the training set, so the test sample must stay untouched. Is the gain worth the complexity? If the weights collapse onto one learner, report that learner. How to write it: the model We predict the log salary of 353 Major League Baseball players from 15 career statistics. The library has six learners: OLS, LASSO and ridge (penalties chosen by cross-validation), a random forest, gradient boosting and k-nearest neighbours (k = 10). On 75% of the sample, we compute five-fold cross-validated predictions for each learner and obtain non-negative weights summing to one by non-negative least squares (van der Laan, Polley and Hubbard 2007). We compare the weighted ensemble, the best single learner and an equal-weight average on the remaining 25% by RMSE and R-squared.

How to read it The 353 players have a mean log salary of 13.49 (about $720,000) with a standard deviation of 1.18, so a model that predicts the mean has an RMSE of about 1.18. The sample is small, which matters twice: the cross-validated risk is noisy, and the test sample has only 89 players.

How to read it The three linear learners get weight zero. Their cross-validated RMSEs are 0.89 to 0.92, against 0.66 to 0.69 for the forest, boosting and nearest neighbours, which share the weight: boosting 0.46, nearest neighbours 0.32, forest 0.22. The relation between salary and career statistics is clearly nonlinear (the test R-squared is 0.35 for OLS and 0.71 for the ensemble). The weighted ensemble has a test RMSE of 0.632 (R-squared 0.705), against 0.626 for the forest, the best single learner on this test set, 0.683 for boosting and 0.667 for nearest neighbours, and 0.727 for an equal-weight average that includes the three linear learners. The ensemble is not better than the forest in this sample: the difference of 0.006 is far inside the noise of an 89-player test sample.
Why the weights look like this

How to read it The cross-validated predictions of OLS, LASSO and ridge correlate 0.97 with each other, and those of the forest and boosting 0.98, so within each group the learners are substitutes and the weights are shared between them rather than being meaningful one by one. The correlation between a linear learner and a tree-based one is 0.73 to 0.79. The linear learners add nothing the nonlinear ones do not already have, which is why they get zero weight. Do not read a weight of 0.22 against 0.46 as a ranking: with correlated learners it is the total weight on a family that carries information.
How much does the answer depend on the split?

How to read it The weight on the linear learners is zero in all eight runs, so that conclusion is stable. The split between the three nonlinear learners is not: the forest gets between 0.00 and 0.57, boosting between 0.16 and 0.64. The test RMSE of the ensemble is between 0.62 and 0.68 and is within 0.03 of the best single learner chosen on the test set (the best single learner is chosen after seeing the test data, so it flatters the benchmark). The ensemble is never far behind the best learner without having to know in advance which learner that is, and this is what it is for.

How to write it: results The relationship between player statistics and salary is nonlinear: in a 25% hold-out sample OLS has a test R-squared of 0.35 and the random forest 0.71. The super learner gives zero weight to OLS, LASSO and ridge and divides the weight among boosting (0.46), nearest neighbours (0.32) and the forest (0.22). Its test RMSE of 0.632 (R-squared 0.705) is close to that of the best single learner (0.626, forest), which cannot be identified in advance, and well below an equal-weight average of all six learners (0.727). The weights on individual nonlinear learners change with the split and the number of folds, while the zero weight on the linear learners does not, so we interpret the result as favouring tree-based and nearest-neighbour methods over linear ones and do not rank the three nonlinear learners.

Support Vector Regression: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

How well can a baseball player's log salary be predicted from his career record? The file holds the 1993 salaries of 353 Major League Baseball players and fifteen career statistics. Performance enters salaries smoothly but not linearly, and the statistics are highly correlated (hits, runs and at-bats move together). Support vector regression (Drucker et al. 1997) fits a function that stays within a tube of half-width \(\varepsilon\) around the data and penalises only the points that fall outside it: The penalty \(C\) controls how hard errors are punished. With the Gaussian kernel \(k(x,x')=\exp(-\gamma\lVert x-x'\rVert^2)\) the function can be curved, and \(\gamma\) controls how local that curvature is. Only observations on or outside the tube become support vectors and shape the fit.

What SVR can and cannot do SVR needs standardised predictors and a standardised outcome, because the penalty and the kernel are scale dependent. It gives no coefficients and no standard errors. It is a prediction tool, and the tuning ( \(C\) , \(\gamma\) ) must be done inside the training data. How to write it: model section We predict log salary with epsilon-insensitive support vector regression using a Gaussian kernel (Drucker et al. 1997). Predictors and outcome are standardised, the penalty C and kernel width gamma are chosen by three-fold cross-validation on the training sample, and performance is evaluated on a held-out test sample against LASSO and a random forest.
Load the data and split it

How to read it There are 264 training players and 89 test players. Log salary has a mean of 13.49 and a standard deviation of 1.18. The career statistics are almost collinear: at-bats and hits correlate at 0.99, games and at-bats at 0.99. Collinearity hurts coefficient interpretation but not prediction, and a kernel method works on distances between players, so it is not troubled by it.
Fit SVR and tune the penalty and kernel width

How to read it Cross-validation picks C = 50 and gamma = 0.01, with a three-fold RMSE of 0.616 in log points. The grid shows how the two parameters trade off: a small C underfits (RMSE 0.97 at C = 0.1, gamma = 0.003), a large gamma with a large C overfits (0.81 at C = 50, gamma = 0.1), and the good region is a diagonal valley. Several neighbouring cells (0.617, 0.620, 0.621) are almost as good, so the choice is not delicate. If the chosen cell were on the edge of the grid you would extend the grid; here C = 50 is the top row and the RMSE is flat between C = 5 and 50 at gamma = 0.01, which is acceptable.
Test it honestly against LASSO and a random forest

How to read it On the 89 held-out players the mean-only benchmark has an RMSE of 1.077. LASSO, which is linear, reaches only 1.017 (R² 0.08), and an ordinary linear regression is no better (1.016): the salary is not a linear function of the statistics. SVR reaches an RMSE of 0.695 (R² 0.57) and the random forest 0.669 (R² 0.60). So SVR captures most of the nonlinearity and is within about 0.03 log points of the forest, a difference that is small relative to the sampling noise of an 89-player test sample. 204 of 264 training players (77 per cent) are support vectors, which is normal with a narrow tube.
Does the kernel matter? Linear versus Gaussian SVR, and the width of the tube

How to read it A linear-kernel SVR has a cross-validated RMSE of 0.904, against 0.63 for the Gaussian kernel, so the curvature is what matters. The tube width has a mild effect: epsilon = 0.1 is best (0.630), epsilon = 0 is slightly worse (0.641) and a wide tube of 0.6 is worse again (0.667). Epsilon controls sparsity: the share of support vectors falls from 100 per cent at epsilon = 0 to 24 per cent at 0.6. Wider tubes give a smaller model at some cost in accuracy.
What the fitted surface looks like: partial dependence

How to read it Permutation importance measures how much the test error rises when one predictor is shuffled. Games played comes first (0.60), then runs batted in (0.34), hits (0.30) and years in the league (0.27). Because games, at-bats and hits are almost the same variable, shuffling one of them while keeping the others leaves some of the information intact, so the importance of a group of correlated variables is spread out and individual values understate it. Read the partial dependence plots as the shape of the average relationship between each predictor and predicted log salary, holding the others at their observed values; a straight line would mean that a linear model was enough.
What to report in the paper

Item What to give Sample and split Number of observations, training and test sizes, and the random seed Preprocessing Standardisation of predictors and outcome Tuning Kernel, grid for C and gamma, epsilon, and the chosen values Out-of-sample accuracy Test RMSE and R² next to a benchmark (mean, linear, LASSO, forest) Complexity Share of support vectors Interpretation Permutation importance and partial dependence, with a note on correlated predictors How to write it: results section On the held-out sample of 89 players, a Gaussian-kernel support vector regression (C = 50, gamma = 0.01, epsilon = 0.1, tuned by three-fold cross-validation) attains a test RMSE of 0.695 in log salary (R² = 0.57), compared with 1.017 for LASSO and 0.669 for a random forest. Games played, runs batted in, hits and years in the league are the most important predictors by permutation importance.

Forgetting to standardise. Without it the kernel is dominated by the variables with the largest units. Tuning on the test sample. Choose C and gamma inside the training data only. Reading permutation importance of correlated predictors as separate effects. Expecting a confidence interval. SVR has none; use the test error and, if needed, a bootstrap of the test errors. Using SVR for causal effects. It predicts; it does not identify. Using it on a very large sample. Fitting time grows quickly with n; use a forest or boosting above a few thousand observations.
Gradient Boosting (XGBoost): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

How long will an injured worker stay out of work? Workers' compensation insurers and labour economists both want to know. The file covers 6,822 workers injured in Kentucky and Michigan around benefit increases studied by Meyer, Viscusi and Durbin (1995). The outcome is the log number of weeks on temporary disability benefits; the eighteen predictors describe the worker (age, sex, marital status, previous earnings), the injury (medical costs, hospitalisation, body part, occupational disease), the industry, the state, and whether the injury happened after the benefit increase. Durations depend on these in strongly nonlinear ways: medical costs matter a great deal up to a point, and the type of injury changes how much.

Gradient boosting (Friedman 2001) builds trees one after another. Each new tree is fitted to the errors that the current model still makes and is added with a small weight \(\eta\) , the learning rate: A random forest averages many independent deep trees; boosting adds many small dependent ones, each correcting the last. XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin 2016) adds penalties on tree size and leaf weights, and is the standard implementation in applied work. Body part injured (dummies) lprewage Log weekly wage before the injury occdis 1 if occupational disease age , male , married Worker characteristics manuf , construc Industry dummies ky 1 if Kentucky (0 = Michigan)
Load the data and confirm the starting point

The forest beats LASSO by more than the 5 % threshold (Rule A3), so the relationship is nonlinear, and with almost 7,000 workers there is enough data to tune a boosted model (Rule A5). Validation must respect the structure of the data Here every row is a different worker, so ordinary shuffled folds are fine. If the same unit appears several times (a firm over years, a route in several years), keep all of its rows in the same fold ( GroupKFold ); otherwise the model memorises units and looks better than it is. With time series, validate forward in time only (see the Elastic net guide). The nonlinearity test is only as honest as its folds: on panel data, shuffled folds can make a forest look far better than it is.
Load the data and confirm the starting point

How to write it: data section The sample contains 6,822 workers injured in Kentucky and Michigan (Meyer, Viscusi and Durbin 1995). The outcome is the log number of weeks on temporary disability benefits; eighteen predictors describe the worker, the injury, the industry, the state and the timing of the injury relative to a benefit increase. In five-fold cross-validation a random forest predicts log durations with an error about 8 % lower than LASSO, so we model durations with gradient-boosted trees.
The parameters that matter, and early stopping

Boosting has more tuning parameters than a forest, and unlike a forest it can overfit if it runs too long. The ones that matter most: learning rate \(\eta\) : smaller is better but needs more trees; 0.03 to 0.1 is usual; number of trees : chosen by early stopping , i.e. stop adding trees when the error on a validation set has not improved for a while; max_depth : the depth of each tree, which sets how many variables can interact; min_child_weight , subsample , colsample_bytree : regularisation, as in a forest. The training error keeps falling as trees are added; the validation error falls, flattens and then creeps up as the model starts to fit noise. Early stopping picks the number of trees at the bottom of the validation curve.
Trees of depth 3 do best: durations depend on interactions between a few variables at a time, not on deep combinations, and depth 6 overfits. The minimum leaf weight hardly matters.
A fair comparison with the alternatives
Nested cross-validation: the boosted model is tuned inside each outer training sample, then scored on the held-out fold.
Open the black box: SHAP values

SHAP values (Lundberg and Lee 2017) split each prediction into additive contributions from each predictor, measured from the average prediction. XGBoost computes them exactly for trees ( pred_contribs=True ).

Medical costs do almost all the work: predicted durations are flat for the cheapest injuries (log costs below about 4.5, roughly $90) and then rise steeply. Age and the previous wage shift predictions far less. These are predictive patterns, not causal effects. The benefit increase ( afchnge ), for example, is the treatment in the original study; its causal effect needs a difference-in-differences design (see the Causal Inference Guide), not a prediction model.

How to write it: results We predict log benefit durations with gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost) with a learning rate of 0.03, choosing the number of trees by early stopping and the tree depth and minimum leaf weight by five-fold cross-validation. In nested cross-validation the boosted model has the lowest out-of-sample error of the models compared: it explains 44 % of the out-of-sample variance, against 43 % for a random forest and 31 % for OLS and LASSO (Table X). SHAP values show that medical costs dominate the predictions (a mean absolute contribution of 0.64 log weeks, ten times that of the next predictor, age), followed by head injuries, the previous wage, industry and hospitalisation. The partial-dependence plot for medical costs is flat for the cheapest injuries and then rises steeply and almost linearly in log costs, a threshold that a linear model misses; age and the previous wage matter much less. We interpret these patterns as predictive, not causal.

Checklist for the paper Build validation folds that respect the data's structure (groups, time). Report the learning rate, early stopping and the tuned depth and regularisation. Compare with a random forest and with linear models in nested cross-validation. Interpret with SHAP values and partial dependence, and say that the patterns are predictive.
Extreme Value Theory: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

How large can the losses be, and how often? For a high threshold \(u\) the excesses \(y = x - u\) are approximately generalised Pareto with shape \(\xi\) and scale \(\sigma\) , \(P(y > t) = (1 + \xi t/\sigma)^{-1/\xi}\) . A positive \(\xi\) means a heavy tail: moments of order above \(1/\xi\) do not exist. With \(\zeta\) the share of observations above \(u\) , the level exceeded once in \(m\) observations is \(u + (\sigma/\xi)\bigl((m\zeta)^{\xi} - 1\bigr)\) . The 99% value at risk is the 1-in-100 level and expected shortfall is the mean loss beyond it. The threshold trades bias (too low) against variance (too high). How to write it: the model

We fit a generalised Pareto distribution to the excesses of Danish fire claims over a threshold of 10 million krone by maximum likelihood. We check the stability of the shape across thresholds, compare it with the Hill estimator of the tail index, and report return levels with delta-method intervals, value at risk and expected shortfall at 99 and 99.5 per cent. We test the fit and check the estimator in a simulation from a known generalised Pareto distribution.

How to read it There are 2,167 claims with a mean of 3.39 and a median of 1.78 million krone and a maximum of 263.3, 148 times the median. The 10 largest claims make up 13% of the total: the risk is in the tail.

How to read it Above a threshold of 10 there are 109 claims (5.0% of the sample). The generalised Pareto fit gives shape xi = 0.497 (standard error 0.136) and scale sigma = 6.98 (1.11). A positive shape means a heavy power-law tail with a tail index of 2.01: the mean exists, and the variance is at the borderline, because it needs xi below 0.5 and the confidence interval for xi contains 0.5. The Hill estimator gives 0.54 to 0.72 for 20 to 250 top observations, a tail index of 1.4 to 1.8, somewhat heavier than the likelihood estimate and with no flat region. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test does not reject the fit (p = 0.98; the p-value is approximate because the parameters are estimated).
Return levels, value at risk and expected shortfall

How to read it The claim exceeded once in 100 is 27.3 (standard error 2.8, 95% interval 21.8 to 32.8): 20 claims exceed it, which matches the 21.7 expected. The 1-in-250 level is 45.4 (32.0 to 58.7, 9 observed) and the 1-in-1,000 level is 94.3 (44.8 to 143.9, 3 observed). The interval for the 1-in-10,000 level, 305, runs from -11 to 621: the delta-method interval is symmetric and is not credible so far out. The 99% value at risk is 27.3 from the tail model and 26.0 from the empirical quantile; at 99.5% the model gives 40.2 and the data 34.8. Expected shortfall at 99% is 58.2 from the model and 61.8 from the data. At 99.9% the empirical quantile (131.6) rests on two observations and differs from the model (94.3).

How to read it The shape is not stable across thresholds: 0.69 at the 85% quantile (325 exceedances), 0.58 at 90%, 0.45 at 92.5%, 0.49 at 95% (our choice), 0.63 at 97.5% and 0.86 at 99% (22 exceedances), but the standard errors grow from 0.10 to 0.42, so most of the movement is noise. For fixed thresholds from 5 to 20 the shape is between 0.41 and 0.68, while the 99% value at risk stays between 25.8 and 28.3. Quantiles inside the range of the data are robust to the threshold; the shape, and with it the far tail, is not.
Diagnostics: a simulation with a known tail

How to read it When the data are generalised Pareto with xi = 0.3, the estimate is biased and noisy with few exceedances: with 30 exceedances the mean is 0.199 (a bias of -0.10), the standard deviation is 0.270 and the 95% interval covers the truth in 88% of samples; with 100 the mean is 0.282, the standard deviation 0.143 and the coverage 94%; with 400 they are 0.298, 0.064 and 94%. With the 109 exceedances of the Danish data the precision is about 0.14, as the standard error says. Report the interval for the shape, not only the point estimate.

How to write it: results We fit a generalised Pareto distribution to the 109 Danish fire claims above 10 million krone (5.0% of 2,167 claims). The shape is 0.50 (standard error 0.14) and the scale 6.98 (1.11), so the tail is heavy, with a tail index of about 2; the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test does not reject the fit (p = 0.98). The 99% value at risk is 27.3 million (95% interval 21.8 to 32.8) and the expected shortfall 58.2 million; the 1-in-1,000 claim is 94 million, with a wide interval (45 to 144). The Hill estimator gives a somewhat heavier tail (0.54 to 0.72) and the shape estimate moves between 0.45 and 0.86 across thresholds, with large standard errors. The 99% value at risk is stable across thresholds (25.8 to 28.3), but levels beyond the data depend on the shape and are uncertain. In simulations the shape is biased downward with 30 exceedances and nearly unbiased with 100 or more.

Kernel Density Estimation: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

What does the distribution look like, and is it one hump or several? The estimate is The bandwidth \(h\) is chosen by a rule (Scott, Silverman), by least-squares cross-validation, or by the Sheather and Jones (1991) plug-in, which is close to the optimum for non-normal densities. Silverman (1981) tests the null of at most \(k\) modes through the critical bandwidth, the smallest \(h\) at which the estimate has \(k\) modes, and a smoothed bootstrap. How to write it: the model We estimate the density of waiting times between eruptions with a Gaussian kernel. We compare the Scott, Silverman, cross-validation and Sheather-Jones bandwidths, take the Sheather-Jones value, report the modes and test the null of a single mode with Silverman's (1981) smoothed bootstrap. We check the choice of bandwidth in a simulation with a known two-component mixture.

How to read it There are 272 eruptions. The waiting time averages 70.9 minutes with a standard deviation of 13.6, between 43 and 96 minutes, and 35% of the waits are shorter than 65 minutes. The median is 76.0, above the mean.

How to read it The four bandwidth selectors range from 2.61 (cross-validation) and 2.64 (Sheather-Jones) to 3.99 (Silverman) and 4.70 (Scott), and all four estimates have two modes. The normal-reference rules smooth more and give a lower peak (0.034 and 0.037 against 0.041), which is what is expected when the density is not normal. We take the Sheather-Jones bandwidth, 2.64 minutes. Silverman's test of a single mode has a critical bandwidth of 8.07 and p = 0.00: none of the 200 bootstrap samples from a single-mode density needs more than one mode at that bandwidth, so one mode is rejected.

How to read it The modes are at 53.2 and 80.1 minutes: short waits of about 53 minutes and long waits of about 80. The distribution is skewed to the left (skewness -0.42) with an excess kurtosis of -1.14, flatter than a normal distribution. A normal density with the same mean and standard deviation would peak at 70.9 minutes, between the two modes, and misses the structure entirely. The area under the estimate is 1.000.

How to read it The number of modes depends on the bandwidth in the way the test uses: 8 modes at h = 1 (noise), two modes for every bandwidth from 2 to 8, and one mode from h = 12. The critical bandwidth for a single mode (8.07) is therefore far above the selected one (2.64). The test of at most two modes gives p = 0.73, so there is no evidence of more than two modes.
Diagnostics: bandwidth selectors in a simulation

How to read it For an equal mixture of N(-1.5, 0.5) and N(1.5, 0.5) with 500 observations, the bandwidth that minimises the integrated squared error is 0.19. Sheather-Jones gives 0.186 on average and cross-validation 0.173, close to the optimum, while Scott (0.48) and Silverman (0.41) are more than twice too large. The data-driven bandwidths pay for the closeness with some spurious extra modes: exactly two modes appear in 90% of samples for Sheather-Jones and in 75% for cross-validation, against 100% for the two over-smoothing rules. A mode in a kernel estimate needs to be backed by a test, as above.

How to write it: results We estimate the density of the waiting time between eruptions of Old Faithful (272 eruptions) with a Gaussian kernel and the Sheather-Jones bandwidth of 2.64 minutes. The density has two modes, at 53.2 and 80.1 minutes, and Silverman's smoothed-bootstrap test rejects a single mode (critical bandwidth 8.07, p < 0.01) but not two (p = 0.73). The normal-reference bandwidths (Scott 4.70, Silverman 3.99) give the same two modes with lower peaks. A normal distribution fitted to the data peaks at 70.9 minutes, between the modes. In a simulation, the Sheather-Jones and cross-validation bandwidths are close to the optimal one, while the normal-reference rules are more than twice too large.

References. Silverman (1981), Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B ; Silverman (1986), Density Estimation for Statistics and Data Analysis ; Sheather and Jones (1991), Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B ; Azzalini and Bowman (1990), Journal of the Royal Statistical Society C .
Kernel Regression: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

What is the shape of E(y | x) when we do not want to assume it? The local-linear estimator at a point \(x_0\) solves a weighted least-squares problem, with weights that fall with the distance from \(x_0\) : The bandwidth \(h\) controls the trade-off: a small \(h\) follows the noise, a large \(h\) approaches a straight line. We choose it by minimising the leave-one-out prediction error, which has a closed form for a linear smoother. A wild bootstrap compares the straight-line model with the kernel fit (Härdle and Mammen 1993). How to write it: the model We estimate the relation between log wages and age by local-linear kernel regression with a Gaussian kernel. The bandwidth is chosen by leave-one-out cross-validation. We compare the cross-validated error with polynomials of degree one to four, test the linear specification with a wild bootstrap, check the sensitivity to the bandwidth and to local-constant fitting, and check the method in a simulation with a known function.

How to read it There are 205 workers aged 21 to 65. Mean log wage rises from 13.16 in the 21-30 band to 13.73 in the 31-40 band, stays near 13.6 up to age 60 and falls to 13.09 in the last band, which has only 8 workers. A straight line cannot describe this pattern: it rises, flattens and falls.

How to read it Cross-validation selects a bandwidth of h = 3.27 years (the rule of thumb 1.06 s n^(-1/5) gives 4.47, which smooths more). The smoother uses 6.8 effective parameters. Its leave-one-out error is 0.303, against 0.391 for a straight line: the straight line predicts held-out workers about 29% worse. The wild-bootstrap test rejects linearity (statistic 18.8, p = 0.005 with 199 replications). The residual standard deviation is 0.54 and the in-sample R-squared is 0.32. A quartic polynomial has a slightly lower cross-validated error (0.295), so the kernel fit is not the only flexible model that works here, and the choice among them would matter little for prediction.

How to read it The fitted log wage climbs from 12.50 at age 22 to 13.53 at age 29 and 13.72 at age 36, where the slope reaches zero. It then stays between 13.64 and 13.73 until age 53 and falls to 13.31 by age 60. Pointwise 95% bands are about ±0.23 at the ends and ±0.13 to ±0.14 in the middle, and they ignore the smoothing bias. The fall after 55 rests on few workers: only 8 are older than 60.

How to read it The cross-validation error is flat near its minimum: 0.305 at h = 2.5, 0.303 at 3.27 and 0.308 at 5, while h = 1.5 (13 effective parameters) gives 0.319 and h = 20 (2.3 parameters, almost a straight line) gives 0.361. A local-constant fit needs a smaller bandwidth (1.86) and has a higher error (0.316) than the local-linear fit (0.303). The Epanechnikov kernel gives the same error (0.302), with a larger bandwidth because its window ends at h. The shape and the conclusion are the same for all reasonable choices.
Diagnostics: a simulation with a known function

How to read it With a known sine function and noise of 0.4, the mean absolute error of the kernel fit falls with the sample: 0.092 with 100 observations, 0.053 with 300 and 0.028 with 1,000, while a straight line stays at 0.36 because its bias does not shrink. The selected bandwidth falls from 0.30 to 0.23 as the sample grows. When the true regression is a straight line, the linearity test rejects in 3 of 30 samples at the 5% level, which is consistent with the nominal rate for this number of samples.

How to write it: results We estimate the relation between log wages and age for 205 workers by local-linear kernel regression with a Gaussian kernel and a bandwidth of 3.3 years chosen by leave-one-out cross-validation. The estimated profile rises steeply from age 22 (12.50) to about age 36 (13.72), is flat until the early fifties and falls afterwards (13.31 at age 60). A straight line predicts held-out workers worse than the kernel fit (cross-validated error 0.39 against 0.30), and a wild-bootstrap test rejects linearity (p = 0.005). A quartic polynomial predicts about as well as the kernel fit, the shape is stable for bandwidths between 2.5 and 5, and the estimate at the oldest ages rests on few workers. In a simulation the kernel fit recovers a known nonlinear function, with an error that falls as the sample grows.

References. Nadaraya (1964), Theory of Probability and its Applications ; Watson (1964), Sankhya ; Fan and Gijbels (1996), Local Polynomial Modelling and its Applications ; Härdle and Mammen (1993), Annals of Statistics ; Pagan and Ullah (1999), Nonparametric Econometrics .

Multiple Testing and False Discovery Rate

With thousands of tests, how many of the rejections are false? At the 5% level, 5% of true nulls are rejected by chance, so 3,072 tests with no effect would give about 150 false rejections. Family-wise procedures (Bonferroni, Holm, Hochberg) keep the probability of any false rejection below \(\alpha\) and are strict. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (1995) keeps the expected share of false rejections among all rejections below \(\alpha\) : it sorts the p-values and rejects all up to the largest \(k\) with \(p_{(k)} \le \alpha k/m\) . The Benjamini-Yekutieli version is valid under any dependence, and Storey's q-value (2002) uses the estimated share \(\pi_0\) of true nulls to be less conservative.
Multiple Testing and False Discovery Rate

How to write it: the model We test 3,072 genes for differential expression and adjust for multiplicity. We report the number of rejections at the 5 per cent level without adjustment, with the Bonferroni, Holm and Hochberg family-wise corrections, with the Benjamini-Hochberg and Benjamini-Yekutieli false discovery rate procedures and with Storey's q-value, estimate the share of true nulls, and check in a simulation that the false discovery proportion stays below the nominal level.
Multiple Testing and False Discovery Rate

How to read it There are 3,072 genes. 42.6% of the p-values are below 0.05 and 16% are below 0.001, far more than the 5% and 0.1% expected if no gene were affected. In the histogram by deciles the first bin holds 1,552 p-values and the others between 285 and 114: a spike near zero on top of a flat floor of about 130 per bin, which is the shape of a mixture of true effects and true nulls.
Multiple Testing and False Discovery Rate

How to read it Without adjustment 1,310 genes are rejected at the 5% level. The family-wise corrections (Bonferroni, Holm and Hochberg) keep 60, because they guard against even one false rejection among 3,072. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure keeps 1,015, the Benjamini-Yekutieli version, valid under any dependence, 485, and Storey's q-value 1,315. The differences are the price of the guarantee: Bonferroni protects against any false rejection and loses 95% of the discoveries; false discovery rate control accepts a known share of false ones.
Multiple Testing and False Discovery Rate

How to read it The estimated share of true nulls is pi0 = 0.42, so about 1,290 genes are unaffected and 1,780 are affected. If all genes were null, about 154 false rejections would be expected at the 5% level without correction. For the Benjamini-Hochberg rejections, the expected number of false discoveries is at most 5% of 1,015, or about 51. The smallest p-values are of the order of 1e-6 and their adjusted values are still tiny: the top genes are not in doubt under any procedure.
Multiple Testing and False Discovery Rate

How to read it At the 1% level the numbers are 900 (unadjusted), 37 (Bonferroni), 580 (Benjamini-Hochberg), 98 (Benjamini-Yekutieli) and 786 (Storey); at 10% they are 1,552, 93, 1,235, 620 and 1,637. The upper bound on the number of false discoveries among the Benjamini-Hochberg rejections is 6 of 580 at 1%, 51 of 1,015 at 5% and 124 of 1,235 at 10%. The ranking of the procedures is the same at every level: Bonferroni and Holm are the strictest and Benjamini-Hochberg and Storey the most generous.

Diagnostics: error control in a simulation

How to read it With 500 tests, 20% of them false with an effect of 3 standard deviations, and a nominal level of 5%, the unadjusted test rejects 106 hypotheses on average, 85% of the false ones, but 19% of its rejections are false. Benjamini-Hochberg rejects 63, finds 60% of the false ones and has a false discovery proportion of 3.5%, below the 5% level (the theory gives 5% times the share of true nulls, 4%). Bonferroni rejects 19, finds 19% of the false ones and has a false discovery proportion of 0.2%. Each procedure trades power for error control and the right choice depends on the cost of a false discovery.
Multiple Testing and False Discovery Rate

How to write it: results We test 3,072 genes for differential expression. 1,310 are significant at the 5% level without adjustment, but this includes false discoveries: if all genes were null we would expect about 154. Bonferroni, Holm and Hochberg leave 60 genes, Benjamini-Yekutieli 485 and Benjamini-Hochberg 1,015, which keeps the expected share of false discoveries among them below 5% (about 51 genes at most); Storey's q-value gives 1,315. The estimated share of true nulls is 0.42. We report the Benjamini-Hochberg list as the main result and the Bonferroni list as the most conservative one. In a simulation, Benjamini-Hochberg has a false discovery proportion of 3.5% against 19% without adjustment and keeps 60% of the true effects against 19% for Bonferroni.
