Partially Linear Model: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

What is the effect of x on y when another variable z has an unknown effect? The model is with \(g\) unknown and smooth. Taking the expectation given \(z\) and subtracting gives \(y - E(y|z) = (x - E(x|z))'\beta + \varepsilon\) . Robinson (1988) replaces the two conditional means by kernel regressions and applies least squares to the residuals; \(\hat\beta\) is root-n consistent and has the usual standard errors. The function \(g\) is then estimated from the remaining variation. How to write it: the model We estimate a partially linear model of food spending on the number of kids and log wages, with log total expenditure entering through an unknown function. Following Robinson (1988) we remove the function by kernel regression with a cross-validated bandwidth and estimate the coefficients by least squares on the residuals. We plot the estimated function, compare the fit with linear and polynomial controls, check the coefficients against different bandwidths, and show in a simulation that a linear control biases the coefficient when the true function is curved.

How to read it There are 1,655 households. The food share of the budget averages 0.21 (standard deviation 0.10), the child indicator is coded 0 or 1 and 62% of households have the value 1, log wages averages 5.86 and log total expenditure averages 5.42 with a range from 3.61 to 7.43. The question is the effect of children and wages on the food share once total expenditure is allowed to enter in any smooth way.

How to read it Households with children spend 0.055 more of their budget on food (robust standard error 0.004, z = 13.6), and a higher log wage raises the share by 0.016 per log point (standard error 0.005, z = 3.3, p = 0.0009). These estimates are almost the same as those from least squares with log expenditure entered linearly (0.0548 and 0.0158), with a quadratic (0.0546 and 0.0158) or with a cubic (0.0543 and 0.0155). The residualising smooths use bandwidths of 0.42 for food, 0.19 for the child indicator and 0.08 for log wages.

How to read it The estimated function falls from 0.178 at log expenditure 4.56 to -0.018 at 6.27: the food share declines as total expenditure rises, as in Engel's law, by about 0.10 to 0.13 per log point, with the steepest part near 5.5. The residual sum of squares is 10.691 for a straight line, 10.690 for a quadratic, 10.673 for a cubic and 10.668 for the nonparametric fit, a gain of less than 0.2%. In these data the Engel curve is almost a straight line in log expenditure, which is why the linear model gives the same coefficients.

How to read it The coefficients hardly move with the bandwidth used to remove log expenditure: from 0.0545 to 0.0553 for the child indicator and from 0.0156 to 0.0158 for log wages with bandwidths between 0.1 and 3.0, and they agree with the quadratic control (0.0546 and 0.0158). A very large bandwidth turns the smooth into a straight line, so the last row is the linear model.
Diagnostics: bias from a linear control

How to read it In a simulation where the true coefficient is 2 and the function is 2 sin(2z), correlated with x through sin(z), the partially linear estimator is centred on the truth (mean 1.990, standard deviation 0.021 over 20 samples), and least squares with z entered linearly is biased downward (mean 1.851, standard deviation 0.062), a bias of more than two of its own standard deviations. The bias appears only when the control is both curved and related to x; in the Engel data the curve is nearly straight, and nothing is lost.

How to write it: results We estimate the effect of children and wages on the food budget share of 1,655 households with a partially linear model (Robinson 1988), in which log total expenditure enters through an unknown function estimated by local-linear smoothing. Households with children spend 5.5 percentage points more of the budget on food (standard error 0.4), and a higher log wage raises the share by 0.016 (standard error 0.005, p < 0.001). The estimated function falls with expenditure at about 0.10 to 0.13 per log point and is close to a straight line: the residual sum of squares is only 0.2% lower than with a linear control, and the coefficients are the same to the third decimal place for linear, quadratic and cubic controls and for bandwidths between 0.1 and 3. A simulation shows that a linear control would bias the coefficient when the true function is curved and related to the regressor, so the agreement here is a finding about these data.

References. Robinson (1988), Econometrica ; Engle, Granger, Rice and Weiss (1986), Journal of the American Statistical Association ; Yatchew (1997), Economics Letters ; Delgado and Mora (1998), Journal of Applied Econometrics (the Engel95 data).
Robust Regression: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Are the estimates driven by a few observations, and what are they without them? Least squares minimises squared residuals, so one large residual can dominate. An M estimator minimises \(\sum \rho(e_i/s)\) with a \(\rho\) that grows more slowly: Huber's is quadratic near zero and linear beyond a cut-off, and Tukey's bisquare gives zero weight to very large residuals. These are not robust to points that are far out in \(x\) (leverage). The MM estimator starts from an S estimate of scale with a 50% breakdown point and then takes an efficient M step. Observations with a robust residual above 2.5 scales are flagged. How to write it: the model We regress race time on distance and climb with ordinary least squares, a Huber M estimator, a bisquare M estimator and an MM estimator (Yohai 1987). We compare the coefficients and the residual scale, list the observations with the largest robust residuals and the highest leverage, and check the estimators against a simulation in which 20 per cent of the data are bad leverage points.

How to read it There are 35 races with record times averaging 57.9 minutes (from 16 to 204.6), distances from 2 to 28 miles (mean 7.5) and climbs from 300 to 7,500 feet (mean 1,815). The largest race is far from the others in both distance and climb.

How to read it Five of the 35 races are flagged as outliers. The residual scale is 14.7 minutes for least squares and 3.8 for the MM estimator, a ratio of almost four. The distance coefficient is 6.22 minutes per mile by least squares and 6.64 by MM; the climb coefficient is 0.0110 by least squares and 0.0064 by MM, so least squares overstates the effect of climb by 70% and the largest shift is 2.2 least-squares standard errors. The MM standard errors are about one third as large (0.199 against 0.601 for distance, 0.0007 against 0.0021 for climb). Huber, bisquare and median regressions are in between or close to MM (distance 6.55 to 6.68).

How to read it Knock Hill (time 78.65 minutes, fitted 14.1) has a robust residual of 17.2 scales, but a least-squares residual of only 4.4 standard deviations. Bens of Jura (204.6 against 146.5) has 15.5 against 2.1, and Two Breweries (170.3 against 145.0) has 6.7 against 0.7: least squares is pulled toward these races, which hides them (masking), and the robust fit reveals them. All three get zero weight. Black Hill and Goatfell are flagged more mildly (-2.9 and 2.6). Lairig Ghru has the highest leverage (0.69 against a rule of thumb of 0.17) but a small residual (0.33), so it is a good leverage point that supports the fit. Bens of Jura has a leverage of 0.42 and a large residual: it is a bad leverage point, the kind that moves least squares.

How to read it Dropping Knock Hill and Bens of Jura moves least squares a lot (distance 6.22 to 6.69, climb 0.0110 to 0.0080, residual scale 14.7 to 6.1) and the MM estimator hardly at all (distance 6.641 to 6.645, climb 0.0064 to 0.0064, scale 3.8 to 3.2). Huber, bisquare and median regressions end up within 0.05 of MM on distance after the deletion. Two Breweries remains in the sample and keeps the least-squares scale well above the robust one.

How to read it The true slope is 2. Without contamination all five estimators give 1.99. With 20% of the observations shifted vertically by 15 units the slope hardly changes for any of them (1.97 to 2.05), because the outliers are unrelated to x. With 20% bad leverage points (large x and very low y) the slope of least squares is -1.22, Huber -1.31, bisquare -1.30 and median regression -1.27: none of them is robust to this contamination. The MM estimator gives 1.99. M estimators and median regression protect against outliers in y only; protection against bad leverage needs a high-breakdown start such as MM.

How to write it: results We regress race time on distance and climb for 35 Scottish hill races. Least squares gives 6.22 minutes per mile and 0.0110 minutes per foot of climb with a residual standard deviation of 14.7; the MM estimator (Yohai 1987) gives 6.64 and 0.0064 with a scale of 3.8, and its standard errors are about one third as large. Knock Hill, Bens of Jura and Two Breweries have zero weight in the robust fit; Bens of Jura is also a high-leverage race. Removing Knock Hill and Bens of Jura moves the least-squares coefficients by 8% (distance) and 27% (climb) but leaves the MM estimates unchanged. In a simulation with 20% bad leverage points, only the MM estimator recovers the true slope. We report MM as the main estimate and least squares as the comparison.

References. Huber (1964), Annals of Mathematical Statistics ; Rousseeuw and Yohai (1984); Yohai (1987), Annals of Statistics ; Maronna, Martin and Yohai (2006), Robust Statistics ; Atkinson (1986), Journal of the Royal Statistical Society C .
Penalised Splines: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

What smooth curve describes y as a function of x? The fit minimises where \(B\) is a B-spline basis and \(D\) takes second differences of neighbouring coefficients. A large \(\lambda\) gives a straight line and \(\lambda \to 0\) interpolates the noise. The effective degrees of freedom, the trace of the smoother matrix, say how many parameters the curve is worth. We pick \(\lambda\) by generalised cross-validation and compare the straight line with the smooth curve with an approximate F test. How to write it: the model We fit head acceleration against time after impact with a penalised cubic B-spline (Eilers and Marx 1996), with 20 knots and a second-order difference penalty. The smoothing parameter is chosen by generalised cross-validation, and we report the effective degrees of freedom. We test the straight line against the smooth curve with an approximate F test, compare the fit with polynomials, and check the dependence on the number of knots and on the penalty in a simulation with a known function.

How to read it There are 133 observations of head acceleration for times from 2.4 to 57.6 milliseconds after impact. Acceleration averages -25.5 and ranges from -134 to 75: it is flat before the impact is felt, falls sharply, rebounds and decays.

How to read it Generalised cross-validation chooses lambda = 0.56, which gives 11.6 effective degrees of freedom (10.6 for the smooth part); a straight line would have 2. R-squared is 0.80 and the residual standard deviation is 22.7. The approximate F test of a straight line against the smooth curve is 44.1 on 9.6 and 121.4 degrees of freedom, with p below 0.0001: the relation is clearly not linear.
The curve and the comparison with polynomials

How to read it The cross-validated squared error is 540.7 for the spline, against 1,633 for the best polynomial (degree 3) and 2,162 for a straight line, a reduction of about two thirds. The curve is flat at about -1 to -7 until 14 ms, drops to -104 at 19 ms, climbs through -74 at 25 ms to +31.5 at 30 ms, and decays to about zero (-4.7 at 47 ms). The credible bands are about ±24 at 2.4 ms, where the process is quiet, and ±11 at 19 ms, where it is violent: the method assumes constant noise, and in these data the noise is clearly larger in the middle, so the bands are too wide at the ends and too narrow in the middle.
Robustness: knots and the smoothing parameter

How to read it The number of knots matters little once the penalty is chosen from the data: with 8, 12, 20 and 40 knots the effective degrees of freedom are 9.8, 10.4, 11.6 and 12.3 and R-squared is between 0.784 and 0.799. The penalty matters a lot when it is fixed: lambda = 0.001 gives 21.7 degrees of freedom and follows the noise, lambda = 5 gives 7.8 and R-squared falls to 0.747, lambda = 500 gives 3.3 and 0.315, and lambda = 100,000 gives 2.02 degrees of freedom, a straight line with R-squared 0.09.
Diagnostics: a simulation with a known function

How to read it With the true function sin(2x) and noise 0.4, the spline uses 11 to 13 effective degrees of freedom and its mean absolute error falls from 0.102 with 100 observations to 0.064 with 300 and 0.042 with 1,000. A cubic polynomial stays at 0.58 to 0.59, because the function is too wavy for it and more data does not remove its bias.

How to write it: results We fit head acceleration against time after impact in 133 simulated crashes with a penalised cubic B-spline (20 knots, second-difference penalty). Generalised cross-validation selects a smoothing parameter of 0.56 and 11.6 effective degrees of freedom. The fitted curve is flat until about 14 ms, falls to -104 at 19 ms, rebounds to +31 at 30 ms and settles near zero after 45 ms. A straight line is rejected (F = 44.1, p < 0.0001), and the cross-validated error is 541, against 1,633 for the best polynomial. The fit is stable to the number of knots (8 to 40), but the bands assume constant variance and are too wide where the data are quiet and too narrow where they are noisy. In simulations the spline recovers a known function with an error that falls with the sample, while a cubic polynomial does not.

References. Eilers and Marx (1996), Statistical Science ; Wood (2017), Generalized Additive Models: An Introduction with R ; Silverman (1985), Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B ; Ruppert, Wand and Carroll (2003), Semiparametric Regression .

Cluster-Robust Inference and the Wild Bootstrap

How much do we overstate precision if we ignore the grouping, and how do we test with few groups? In a regression \(y_{gi} = x_{gi}'\beta + u_{gi}\) with \(u\) correlated within group \(g\) , the variance of \(\hat\beta\) is estimated by summing the scores within each group, \(\hat V = (X'X)^{-1}\bigl(\sum_g X_g' \hat u_g \hat u_g' X_g\bigr)(X'X)^{-1}\) , with a small-sample factor (CR1). This is valid when the number of groups is large. The wild cluster bootstrap imposes the null, multiplies the residuals of each group by a random sign (or a Webb weight, which has six points and suits fewer than 12 groups) and uses the distribution of the t statistic.
Cluster-Robust Inference and the Wild Bootstrap

How to write it: the model We regress y on x in Petersen's (2009) panel of 500 firms and 10 years and report conventional, heteroskedasticity-robust and cluster-robust (CR1) standard errors and a wild cluster bootstrap-t p-value that imposes the null. We then draw a simulation with 8 clusters and no true effect to compare the rejection rates of the tests at the 5 per cent level.
Cluster-Robust Inference and the Wild Bootstrap

How to read it There are 5,000 observations on 500 firms over 10 years. Every firm is observed in 10 years, so the clusters have equal size. The outcome has a standard deviation of 2.25 and the regressor of 0.99.
Cluster-Robust Inference and the Wild Bootstrap

How to read it The slope is 1.035. The conventional standard error is 0.0286 and the heteroskedasticity-robust one 0.0284, almost the same. The cluster-robust standard error is 0.0506, 1.77 times larger, and the cluster jackknife (CR3) gives 0.0508. The t statistic falls from 36.2 to 20.5. The wild cluster bootstrap-t reports the CR1 standard error and its own p-value. All the p-values are below 0.001: with 500 clusters the inference is not in doubt, only its precision.
Cluster-Robust Inference and the Wild Bootstrap

How to read it The conventional 95% interval is 0.979 to 1.091 (width 0.112). The cluster-robust interval is 0.935 to 1.134 (width 0.199) and the wild bootstrap-t interval is 0.932 to 1.138 (width 0.206): ignoring the clusters understates the uncertainty by about 44%. The cross-products of the scores within clusters are 2.2 times as large as the squared scores themselves, which is what makes the conventional variance too small: both the regressor and the error are persistent within firm.
Cluster-Robust Inference and the Wild Bootstrap
Robustness: a different null and weights

How to read it With 500 clusters the three weight distributions (Rademacher, Webb and Mammen) agree: the p-value is below 0.0001 for each. A test of beta = 1 is not rejected (cluster-robust p = 0.491, wild bootstrap p = 0.489). Using only the first 8 firms, the coefficient is 1.164 and the methods disagree: the conventional standard error is 0.231 (p < 0.001), the cluster-robust one is 0.445 (p = 0.035), the jackknife gives 0.495 (p = 0.051) and the wild cluster bootstrap-t with Webb weights gives p = 0.141. With 8 clusters, the conclusion at the 5% level depends on the method.
Cluster-Robust Inference and the Wild Bootstrap

How to read it In 100 samples with 8 clusters of 25 and no effect of x, with errors correlated within clusters, the conventional test rejects at the 5% level in 61% of the samples, the cluster-robust test with t(G-1) critical values in 14%, and the wild cluster bootstrap-t (Webb weights) in 3%. Conventional standard errors give a test with nearly no meaning, cluster-robust standard errors are too liberal with few clusters, and the wild bootstrap is close to the nominal size (3% with 100 samples, a standard error of about 2 points).
Cluster-Robust Inference and the Wild Bootstrap

How to write it: results We regress y on x in a panel of 500 firms and 10 years. The slope is 1.035. The conventional standard error (0.029) ignores the correlation within firms; the firm-cluster-robust standard error is 0.051, 77% larger, and the 95% interval widens from 0.112 to 0.199. With 500 clusters the wild cluster bootstrap-t gives the same conclusion as the cluster-robust test (p < 0.001), and a test of a slope of 1 is not rejected (p = 0.49). With only 8 firms the cluster-robust p-value (0.035) and the bootstrap p-value (0.141) differ, and in a simulation with 8 clusters the cluster-robust test rejects a true null in 14% of samples at the 5% level against 3% for the wild bootstrap, so we report the bootstrap when the number of clusters is small.

Cross-Sectionally Augmented ARDL: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

The question is the same as in the PMG guide: what are the long-run price and income elasticities of cigarette demand? This time the data are used as they are. Cigarette consumption in every state was driven by national forces: the 1964 Surgeon General's report, advertising bans, changing social norms, federal excise taxes. These common factors affect states to different degrees, and they are correlated with prices and incomes. A model that ignores them confuses the national anti-smoking trend with the effect of price. For each state \(i\) , CS-ARDL(1,1) estimates where \(x = (p, y)\) are the log real price and log real income, and \(\bar z_t\) are the cross-sectional averages of \(c\) and \(x\) in year \(t\) , with \(p_T\) lags. Each state's long-run effect is \(\theta_i = (\beta_{0i} + \beta_{1i}) / (1 - \lambda_i)\) , and the estimate reported is the mean group average of the \(\theta_i\) .

The neighbours' price used in the PMG guide is left out here. It moves almost one-for-one with the state's own real price, and once the cross-sectional averages absorb the national component, the two can no longer be separated in 29 annual observations per state: with both included, the state-level long-run estimates become erratic. With CS-ARDL, keep the model small. Why the cross-sectional averages work If the errors contain unobserved common factors \(f_t\) with state-specific loadings, the cross-sectional averages of the observed variables are (as N grows) a linear combination of those factors. Adding them, and their lags, to each state's regression with state-specific coefficients controls for the factors without having to name or measure them. Because every state gets its own coefficients on the averages, states can respond to the common shocks to different degrees, which year dummies cannot do.

How to write it: model section We estimate state-specific ARDL(1,1) models of cigarette demand augmented with the contemporaneous and lagged cross-sectional averages of all variables, following Chudik et al. (2016). The averages proxy unobserved common factors, such as national anti-smoking campaigns and federal tax changes, to which states may respond heterogeneously. Long-run elasticities are computed for each state and averaged across states (mean group).
Load the data and run the pre-tests

How to read it Cross-sectional dependence is overwhelming: CD statistics above 100 and average absolute correlations between states of 0.7 to 0.9. The states are driven by national forces. Unit roots (CIPS). Sales and income are I(1); the real price rejects a unit root in levels and is I(0). A mix of I(0) and I(1), none I(2): the ARDL family applies. Slopes are heterogeneous. Mixed integration orders and strong cross-sectional dependence: this is the combination for which the model selection tool recommends CS-ARDL. It is the result the tool gives for this example dataset.
What goes wrong if the common factors are ignored

How to read it PMG and MG on the raw data assume independent states. The CD test on the PMG residuals shows that the assumption fails badly: the residuals are strongly correlated across states. With common factors in the errors that are also correlated with the regressors, these long-run estimates are biased. The clearest symptom is income: real incomes rose everywhere while smoking fell everywhere for reasons unrelated to income (health information, social norms), so the national trend cancels the income effect in PMG and turns it negative in MG. The PMG guide deals with this by demeaning; CS-ARDL deals with it inside the model.

How to read it Price. Once the common factors are absorbed, the long-run price elasticity is about −0.9: a 10% rise in the real price lowers sales by about 9% in the long run. The estimate is close to the PMG estimate on demeaned data (−0.77), which used a different way of dealing with the same common shocks. Two methods agreeing is strong evidence. Income. Positive and significant, about 0.6: cigarettes are a normal good once the national anti-smoking trend is no longer confounded with rising incomes. Adjustment. The error-correction coefficient is negative and significant: each state's consumption returns towards its long-run relationship. Adjustment is faster than in PMG on demeaned data, because the averages also absorb slow-moving national trends.
Standard errors are mean-group standard errors, from the dispersion of the 46 state estimates. They are valid whatever the heterogeneity across states.
Test 1: are the common factors removed?

How to read it The CD statistic falls from the very large value of the raw PMG residuals to a small one: the cross-sectional averages have absorbed the common factors. Report this test; it is the evidence that the augmentation did its job. A remaining small, insignificant or weakly significant CD statistic is normal, since the averages approximate the factors only up to an error that shrinks with N.
Robustness: the number of lags of the averages

How to read it Chudik et al. recommend about \(T^{1/3}\) lags of the averages, which is 3 here. But each state regression has only 29 observations, and every lag adds four regressors, so with this many variables the number of lags must stay small. Show that the results do not depend on the choice: here the long-run price elasticity stays between −0.73 and −0.88 and the income elasticity between 0.51 and 0.61. The results are robust to the lag length.
Build the results table for the paper

How to read it Put the estimators that ignore the common factors next to CS-ARDL, with the residual CD test in the table, so the reader sees both the bias and its correction. Column (3) is the preferred estimate. Cite the PMG-on-demeaned-data estimate as a second robustness check.

How to write it: pre-tests and estimator All variables exhibit strong cross-sectional dependence (Pesaran CD tests), reflecting national anti-smoking trends and federal policy. CIPS tests indicate a mixture of I(0) and I(1) variables, and the Pesaran–Yamagata test rejects slope homogeneity. Because estimators that assume cross-sectional independence would be biased, and because states may respond differently to common shocks, we estimate the long-run elasticities with the cross-sectionally augmented ARDL (CS-ARDL) approach of Chudik et al. (2016). How to write it: results The mean group long-run price elasticity is about −0.9 and the income elasticity about 0.6 (Table 6, column 3). The price elasticity is close to the estimate from a pooled mean group model on cross-sectionally demeaned data, and both are robust to the number of lags of the cross-sectional averages. The error-correction coefficient is negative and significant, confirming adjustment towards a long-run relationship. The CD test on the CS-ARDL residuals indicates that the cross-sectional averages successfully absorb the common factors, in contrast with PMG and MG estimates on the raw data, whose residuals remain strongly dependent.

Common mistakes Adding too many lags of the averages relative to T. Each lag costs one regressor per variable in every unit regression. Using CS-ARDL with small N. The averages approximate the common factors only as N grows; with fewer than about 15 units they are poor proxies. Reporting the long run without the residual CD test, which is the evidence that the method worked. Forgetting that the mean group long run is an average of unit-specific ratios: a few units with \(\lambda_i\) close to 1 produce extreme \(\theta_i\) . Check the distribution, and report the median as well.
Panel Model in First Differences: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

The question: how does gasoline demand respond to income and to the price of gasoline? The dataset is the one Baltagi and Griffin used to compare panel estimators of gasoline demand across OECD countries, before and during the oil shocks of the 1970s. Symbol Variable in the file Definition Expected sign \(\ln G_{it}\) lgaspcar Log gasoline consumption per car dependent variable \(\ln Y_{it}\) lincomep Log real income per capita positive: income elasticity \(\ln P_{it}\) lrpmg Log real price of gasoline negative: price elasticity \(\ln C_{it}\) lcarpcap Log cars per capita negative: more cars, each driven less In first differences, the coefficients are short-run elasticities : how much gasoline use per car changes in the year that income or the price changes.

Why differences, and what you give up If the variables are I(1) and cointegrated, a long-run relationship in levels exists and an error-correction model (the PMG or CS-ARDL guides) estimates it. If they are I(1) and not cointegrated, there is no long-run relationship to estimate: a regression in levels would be spurious, and the valid model is in differences. You give up the long-run elasticities, which is why the cointegration tests deserve care. How to write it: model section We relate the growth of gasoline consumption per car to the growth of real income per capita, the real price of gasoline and the stock of cars per capita, \(\Delta \ln G_{it} = \beta_1 \Delta \ln Y_{it} + \beta_2 \Delta \ln P_{it} + \beta_3 \Delta \ln C_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}\) . The coefficients are short-run elasticities.
Load the panel and run the pre-tests

How to read it Cross-sectional dependence is strong for every variable (the oil shocks hit every country), so CIPS is the unit-root test to use. Unit roots. CIPS does not reject a unit root in levels for any variable, and rejects it in first differences for all of them: all four are I(1) . Slopes are heterogeneous: the Δ test rejects. This will matter for the choice of cointegration test and of estimator.

How to read it In levels, fixed effects gives large, highly significant elasticities and a high within R-squared. This is exactly what a spurious regression looks like. With I(1) variables, the t-statistics do not follow the t distribution, and trending series appear related whether or not they are. These numbers are only meaningful if the variables are cointegrated, which is the next test.

How to read it The null hypothesis of both tests is no cointegration . Kao pools the fixed-effects residuals and assumes the same slopes in every country. It rejects narrowly, at the 5% level. Fisher–Engle–Granger runs an Engle–Granger test for each country, with its own slopes, and combines the p-values. Its Z version does not reject (p = 0.25); its P version comes close only at the 10% level. The tests disagree, and the pre-tests tell us which to believe: the slopes are heterogeneous , which violates Kao's assumption. A Kao test applied to heterogeneous panels can reject spuriously, because the pooled residuals mix different long-run relationships. The model selection tool therefore uses the heterogeneous test here, and concludes that there is no cointegration.

This is a close call, and the paper must say so: report both tests, and add the Westerlund (2007) error-correction tests with bootstrap critical values, which allow for both heterogeneity and cross-sectional dependence ( xtwest in Stata). With T = 19, every panel cointegration test has limited power.
Estimate the model in first differences

How to read it Differencing removes the country fixed effects (permanent differences in levels), so the pooled regression on differences needs no country dummies. Compare the elasticities with the spurious levels regression: the income and price responses are much smaller in differences , as one would expect when drivers can adjust only gradually. (The cars coefficient is similar, because the stock of cars and fuel use per car are linked almost mechanically in every year.) Price. A 10% rise in the real price of gasoline reduces consumption per car by roughly 1–3% within the year, depending on the estimator. Income. The short-run income elasticity is positive. Cars per capita. More cars means each car is driven less, so consumption per car falls.
Estimate the model in first differences

With heterogeneous slopes and cross-sectional dependence, CCE-MG is the preferred estimator : it averages the country-specific elasticities and removes the common factors (the oil shocks) through the cross-sectional averages. Its standard errors are larger, because they reflect the cross-country dispersion of the elasticities.

How to read it The pooled regression in differences leaves strong common shocks in the residuals. In the CCE-MG residuals the CD statistic is close to zero and no longer significant: the cross-sectional averages absorb the common oil-price and business-cycle shocks.
Build the results table for the paper
How to read it Including the levels regression in column (1) shows the reader the spurious result the paper avoids. Column (4) is the preferred estimate.

How to write it: pre-tests CIPS tests, which allow for the strong cross-sectional dependence indicated by the CD test, do not reject a unit root in levels for any variable but reject it in first differences. Because the Pesaran–Yamagata test rejects slope homogeneity, we test for cointegration with the Fisher-type combination of country-level Engle–Granger tests, which allows the long-run coefficients to differ across countries; it does not reject the null of no cointegration. The Kao test, which assumes homogeneous slopes, rejects at the 5 percent level. Given the heterogeneity of slopes, we treat the evidence for cointegration as weak and estimate the model in first differences. How to write it: results

Table 4 reports short-run elasticities. In the common correlated effects mean group model (column 4), gasoline consumption per car rises with income and falls with the real price and with the number of cars per capita. The short-run income and price elasticities are much smaller than the coefficients of the levels regression in column 1, which, given the absence of cointegration, should not be interpreted. Common mistakes Running a levels regression on I(1) variables without testing for cointegration, and interpreting the t-statistics. Choosing the cointegration test that gives the desired answer. Choose it from the pre-tests (homogeneous or heterogeneous slopes, dependence or not), and report the others. Calling short-run elasticities from a model in differences “long-run” effects.
Ignoring cross-sectional dependence in the differenced model. Common shocks remain after differencing.
Dynamic Panel Threshold Regression: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Does the response of working hours to the wage differ between low-wage and high-wage women? A linear model gives one elasticity. A threshold model lets the elasticity change when a variable crosses a value. Hours are persistent, so last year's hours belong in the model, and then fixed effects estimated by the within transformation are biased. Our question is: is there a wage level below which hours respond to wage changes differently, and where is it? The threshold variable is last year's log wage, so it is determined before the shock \(\varepsilon_{it}\) . First-differencing removes \(\mu_i\) ; the lagged change \(\Delta h_{i,t-1}\) is correlated with \(\Delta\varepsilon_{it}\) , so it is instrumented with the levels \(h_{i,t-2}\) and \(h_{i,t-3}\) .

Symbol Variable in the file Definition \(h_{it}\) lnhr log annual hours worked \(w_{it}\) lnwg log hourly wage \(kids_{it}\) kids number of children \(\gamma\) threshold to be estimated, in log wage Before you estimate anything Decide how you treat the regressors. Here the wage change is treated as exogenous in the differenced equation, which is a strong assumption (wages may respond to hours, and are measured with error). The last step relaxes it and shows what changes. Also decide the threshold variable on theory, and keep at least 15% of the observations in each regime. How to write it: model section We estimate a dynamic panel threshold model for annual hours. The model is differenced to remove individual effects, the lagged change in hours is instrumented with its second and third lags in levels, and the regime is defined by the lagged log wage. We choose the threshold by minimising the instrumental-variable residual sum of squares over a grid of the 15th to 85th percentiles of the threshold variable, test for its existence with a fixed-regressor wild bootstrap clustered by individual, and report cluster-robust standard errors for the slopes.
Load the data and see the Nickell bias

How to read it The panel has 532 women observed for ten years (5,320 observations), and 3,724 observations remain after differencing and losing the first lags. Log hours are persistent but the estimates of that persistence depend strongly on the estimator: the coefficient on lagged hours is 0.48 in pooled OLS, 0.12 with the within (fixed-effects) estimator and 0.15 with the first-difference IV estimator. Pooled OLS is biased upward because the individual effect is in the error and in the lag. The within estimator is biased downward in short panels (the Nickell bias), and the IV estimator removes the effect by differencing and uses lagged levels as instruments. This is why a dynamic threshold model needs the IV approach.

How to read it The grid search picks a threshold of 2.79 in log wage (a wage of about 16.3 per hour in the units of the data), with 69.5% of the observations at or below it. The IV residual sum of squares falls from 375.97 in the linear model to 367.04. The figure shows that the threshold is not sharply located. Every candidate has a smaller SSR than the linear model, but the curve is jagged, is lowest at the two ends (around 2.2–2.3 and above 2.9) and has a sharp dip at the chosen value 2.79, which a few observations can produce. Read the grid search together with the test and the interval in the next step.
Is there a threshold? A bootstrap test

How to read it The test of a threshold against a linear model gives F = 90.4. The wild bootstrap by woman, with the same search over the grid in every draw, gives a 95th percentile of 55.7 and a 99th percentile of 71.3, so the bootstrap p-value is 0.005 (one draw in 199 exceeds the statistic). We reject the linear model: the wage response differs by regime. The location is a different matter. The approximate 95% interval is 2.20 to 3.01 in log wage, which is almost the whole 15th–85th percentile range of the grid. The data say that there is a threshold effect, but not where it is. The interval comes from the likelihood-ratio rule for iid errors, and with differenced data it is approximate.

How to read it In the low-wage regime a 10% rise in the wage raises hours by about 2.0% (coefficient 0.203, cluster standard error 0.114, t = 1.78). In the high-wage regime the response is negative (−0.193, s.e. 0.090, t = −2.15), as in a backward-bending labour supply curve where the income effect dominates. The two slopes differ by 0.396 (s.e. 0.148, t = 2.67). The coefficient on lagged hours (0.136) and on children (−0.013) are not significant. The AR(2) statistic is −0.17 (p = 0.87), so there is no second-order serial correlation in the differenced residuals, as required. The Hansen J test rejects (J = 5.98, p = 0.014) with one degree of freedom, which means that the second and third lags of hours are not both valid instruments here. Report this and treat the point estimates with caution.

How to write it: results We estimate a dynamic threshold model of annual hours for 532 women over 1979–1988, with the lagged log wage as the threshold variable. A bootstrap test rejects a linear model (F = 90.4, p = 0.005). The threshold estimate is 2.79 in log wage, but the approximate 95% interval of 2.20 to 3.01 shows that its location is imprecise. Below the threshold the wage elasticity of hours is 0.20 (cluster s.e. 0.11), above it is −0.19 (s.e. 0.09), and the difference is significant (t = 2.67). The Hansen J test rejects the over-identifying restriction (p = 0.014), so we interpret the regime difference as suggestive and show robustness to trimming, to other threshold variables and to treating wages as predetermined.
Robustness: trimming, the threshold variable and the instruments

How to read it The sign pattern is stable in the first three rows, where the wage is the threshold variable and only the trimming changes: the slope is positive below the threshold and negative or near zero above it. The location is not. Trimming 10% gives a threshold of 2.07 with 10% of the sample below it, and trimming 15% or 20% gives 2.79 with 69% below, so the estimated threshold jumps between two places. With the number of children as the threshold variable the pattern reverses (−0.04 below, 0.45 above). Treating the wage as predetermined (instrumented by its second lag, last row) gives a threshold of 2.20 with 15% below and slopes of 0.30 and 0.18, and the SSR on the grid varies by a factor of three, a sign of weak instruments. The robust conclusion is that the linear model is rejected and that the effect is heterogeneous. The exact threshold and the size of the high-regime slope depend on choices that the data cannot settle, and a paper should say so.
What to report in the paper

Item What to show Transformation first differences (or forward orthogonal deviations) and why the within estimator is not used Instruments which lags, how many, and the Hansen J test Threshold variable why it is predetermined, and the trimming Test the bootstrap design, the number of draws and the p-value Threshold the estimate and an interval, and the share of observations in each regime Slopes coefficients by regime with cluster-robust standard errors and the test of equality Robustness trimming, other threshold variables, and the exogeneity assumption on the regressors Common mistakes Using a static threshold estimator with a lagged dependent variable. The within transformation is biased in short panels (Nickell), and so is the threshold search.
What to report in the paper

Using an endogenous threshold variable. The indicator must be determined before the error. Lag it. Reading the chi-square or LR interval as exact. With differenced, instrumented data the interval is approximate. Present it as a guide and check it with the bootstrap. Weak or too many instruments. With many regimes the instruments are split. Check how smooth the SSR path is and report the Hansen J test. Ignoring the exogeneity assumption on the regressors. Show a specification that treats them as predetermined, as in the last step. Interpreting the threshold as a causal tipping point. It is a statistical break in the slope, and it may move with the sample.
Fixed Effects: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. Unit effects correlated with the regressors.

The question is a classic of labour economics: do union members earn more than comparable non-members? A cross-section cannot answer it, because workers who join unions may differ in ability, motivation or occupation in ways the data do not record. A panel that follows the same workers over time can: it compares each worker with himself, in years with and without union membership. Symbol Variable in the file Definition Expected sign \(\ln w_{it}\) lwage Log hourly wage dependent variable \(union_{it}\) union 1 if wage set by a union contract positive: the union wage premium \(married_{it}\) married 1 if married positive: the marriage premium \(exper^2_{it}\) expersq Years of experience, squared negative: wage growth slows with experience

\(\alpha_i\) — Worker fixed effect: ability, motivation, occupation unobserved \(\lambda_t\) — Year effect: inflation, the business cycle common to all workers Experience itself is not in the model. Every worker gains exactly one year of experience per year, so with worker and year effects the level of experience is perfectly collinear and cannot be estimated. Its square still varies within workers. Before you estimate anything Write down what the fixed effect \(\alpha_i\) stands for in your application and why it may be correlated with the regressor of interest. Here: more able workers may be less likely to join a union and also earn more. If that is true, pooled OLS mixes the union effect with the ability effect, and only the within-worker comparison isolates it. That argument is the reason for using fixed effects, and the paper must make it.

How to write it: model section We estimate \(\ln w_{it} = \beta_1 union_{it} + \beta_2 married_{it} + \beta_3 exper^2_{it} + \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{it}\) , where \(\alpha_i\) is a worker fixed effect and \(\lambda_t\) a year effect. The worker effect absorbs all time-invariant characteristics, including unobserved ability, which may be correlated with union status. The union premium \(\beta_1\) is therefore identified from workers who change union status during the sample.
Load the panel and confirm the starting point

How to read it The panel is balanced and short : 545 workers, each observed in all 8 years. With so few periods, unit-root tests are not the issue; the question is how to treat the worker effects. The model selection tool ran that sequence on this file and recommended fixed effects (the F, LM and Mundlak tests are repeated below). The within standard deviations matter most. Union status has a within standard deviation of about 0.28: plenty of workers move in and out of union jobs, and the line below shows how many. Those switchers identify the fixed-effects estimate. Education has a within standard deviation of zero: it never changes for these men, so fixed effects cannot estimate its return.

How to read it Pooled OLS treats the 4,360 rows as if they were 4,360 different people. It puts the union premium at about 18%. This estimate uses both the comparison across workers (union members against non-members) and the comparison over time, so if union members differ in unobserved ways, the premium is biased. Even in pooled OLS, the standard errors must be clustered by worker : the same man appears eight times, and his errors are correlated across years. Unclustered standard errors would be far too small.

How to read it Union. Comparing the same worker in union and non-union years, union membership raises the wage by about 8%. That is less than half the pooled OLS premium: much of the cross-sectional premium reflects who joins unions, not what unions pay. Married. The marriage premium falls from about 15% in pooled OLS to about 5%, significant only at the 5% level. Much of the cross-sectional marriage premium is a selection effect. Experience squared. Negative and highly significant: wage growth slows with experience. Standard errors. Clustered by worker, which allows for any pattern of heteroskedasticity and serial correlation within each worker. This is the standard choice for a short panel with many units.
The constant reported by PanelOLS is the average of the fixed effects and has no economic meaning.
Test 1: do the workers differ? The F test

How to read it The null hypothesis is that every worker has the same intercept, in which case pooled OLS would be enough. The F statistic is large and the p-value is essentially zero: the worker effects are jointly significant , so ignoring them is not an option. The remaining question is whether to treat them as fixed or random.
Test 2: fixed or random? Hausman and Mundlak

How to read it Random effects is more efficient than fixed effects, but only consistent if the worker effects are uncorrelated with union status, marriage and experience. Hausman test. It compares the FE and RE coefficients. Under the null both are consistent and differ only by sampling error. Here the gap is large and the test rejects strongly. Mundlak test. It adds each worker's average union status, marriage rate and squared experience to the RE model. If the worker effect is correlated with the regressors, those averages pick it up. The test uses clustered standard errors, so unlike the conventional Hausman test it remains valid under heteroskedasticity and serial correlation. It also rejects.
Test 2: fixed or random? Hausman and Mundlak

A useful check. In the Mundlak model, the coefficient on union is identical to the fixed-effects estimate. This is an exact algebraic result, and it is why the Mundlak model is also called correlated random effects. Conclusion: random effects is rejected, and fixed effects is the estimator to report.
Diagnostic tests: serial correlation and cross-sectional dependence

How to read it Serial correlation. The Wooldridge test rejects: the errors of the same worker are correlated over time, as they almost always are in wage data. This does not bias the FE coefficients, but it invalidates conventional standard errors. Clustering by worker already corrects for it , which is why the clustered standard errors are the ones to report. Cross-sectional dependence. With T = 8, the residual correlation between any two workers rests on eight observations and is very noisy, so a mean absolute correlation of this size is what pure noise would produce. The average signed correlation is close to zero: once year effects are included, there is no common shock left. Year effects are the standard way to deal with common shocks in short micro panels.

How to read it First differences is the other estimator that removes the worker effect. It compares adjacent years only, so it is more sensitive to measurement error in union status: a misreported switch in one year looks like two genuine switches. The FD premium is smaller, which is the usual sign of measurement error in a binary regressor. Report it, and explain the difference. Correlated random effects adds the worker averages of the time-varying regressors. Its union and marriage coefficients equal the fixed-effects ones, but it can also estimate the effect of time-invariant variables such as education and race. This is the answer when a referee asks for the return to education in a fixed-effects paper.
The ranking pooled > RE > FE for the union premium is exactly what positive selection on unobserved ability predicts.
Build the results table for the paper

How to read it A panel results table shows the main estimator next to the benchmarks, so the reader can see how much the unit effects matter. Report under the table: the number of workers and years, that standard errors are clustered by worker, that all columns include year effects (except where they are differenced away), and the F, Hausman and Mundlak statistics. Column (3) is the preferred estimate.

How to write it: specification tests An F test rejects the hypothesis that the worker effects are jointly zero, so pooled OLS is inappropriate. A Hausman test rejects the consistency of random effects, and a cluster-robust Mundlak test, which remains valid under heteroskedasticity and serial correlation, leads to the same conclusion. We therefore estimate the model by fixed effects with worker and year effects, and cluster standard errors by worker; a Wooldridge test confirms serial correlation within workers. How to write it: results Table 1 reports the estimates. Pooled OLS puts the union wage premium at about 18 percent (column 1). Once time-invariant worker characteristics are controlled for, the premium falls to about 8 percent (column 3), and it remains significant at the 1 percent level. The decline is consistent with workers of higher unobserved ability being less likely to hold union jobs. The first-difference estimate is smaller (column 4), as expected if union status is measured with error.

Common mistakes Reporting unclustered standard errors. In a panel they are almost always too small. Including a regressor that moves one-for-one with time (age, experience) together with year effects. It is collinear and either drops out or gives a meaningless coefficient. Claiming the FE coefficient on a variable that never changes. It is not identified; use correlated random effects instead. Treating fixed effects as a cure for all endogeneity. It removes time-invariant confounders only. If union status responds to wage shocks in the same year, FE is still biased, and you need an instrument or a dynamic model. Using only the conventional Hausman test. Report the robust Mundlak version as well.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors

The question: in the OECD economies of 1967–1990, how was output growth related to unemployment and to changes in trade openness? Macro panels like this one, a few dozen countries over a few decades, are typical of empirical papers in international and environmental economics. Their defining feature is that the countries share the same shocks: the oil crises of 1973 and 1979 and the recessions that followed hit all of them at once. Symbol Variable in the file Definition Expected sign \(g_{it}\) gdp_growth Real GDP growth, % dependent variable \(u_{it}\) unem Unemployment rate, % negative: slack and low growth go together (Okun's law) \(\Delta open_{it}\) d_trade Change in trade (exports + imports) as % of GDP
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors

positive if openness raises growth \(\alpha_i\) — Country fixed effect permanent differences in growth Before you estimate anything In a macro panel, three properties decide the estimator, and each needs a test: cross-sectional dependence (do the countries share shocks?), stationarity (do the variables have unit roots?) and slope homogeneity (is \(\beta\) the same in every country?). The next three steps run them. Fixed effects with Driscoll–Kraay errors is the answer when the variables are stationary and the slopes are homogeneous. How to write it: model section We estimate \(g_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_1 u_{it} + \beta_2 \Delta open_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}\) for 14 OECD countries over 1967–1990, where \(g_{it}\) is real GDP growth, \(u_{it}\) the unemployment rate and \(\Delta open_{it}\) the change in trade openness, and \(\alpha_i\) are country fixed effects.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors
Load the panel and test for cross-sectional dependence

How to read it A balanced panel of 14 countries over 24 years. The Pesaran CD test rejects cross-sectional independence for every variable, decisively. The average absolute correlation between two countries' growth rates is about 0.45: the OECD economies move together . Two consequences follow. Unit-root tests must allow for this (CIPS rather than Fisher-ADF), and standard errors that treat countries as independent will be too small.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors

How to read it Stationarity. Because the variables are cross-sectionally dependent, CIPS is the test to use. It rejects a unit root in levels for all three: every variable is I(0) . Notice that for unemployment the first-generation Fisher test does not reject. It ignores the common shocks, and the two tests disagree; CIPS is the valid one here. Slope homogeneity. The adjusted Δ test does not reject: there is no evidence that the effects of unemployment and openness differ across countries. Pooling the slopes is defensible. These are the conditions under which the model selection tool recommends fixed effects with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors
Estimate fixed effects with three kinds of standard errors

How to read it The coefficients are the same in every column; only the standard errors differ. Unemployment. A one-point higher unemployment rate goes with growth about a third of a point lower. Significant under every choice of standard errors. Trade openness. With conventional or clustered standard errors, the negative coefficient looks significant. With Driscoll–Kraay standard errors it is not. Clustering by country allows for correlation over time within a country, but still treats countries as independent of each other. Driscoll–Kraay standard errors also allow for correlation across countries in the same year , which the CD test showed is strong. Openness moves together across countries (world trade booms and slumps), so its standard error is the one most affected.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors
Estimate fixed effects with three kinds of standard errors

The Driscoll–Kraay estimator needs a reasonably long T, since it averages over years rather than countries; with 24 years it is appropriate. The bandwidth (lags of the Newey–West kernel) is set to 3, roughly \(T^{1/3}\) .
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors

How to read it Residual dependence. Even after the two regressors, the residuals of different countries remain correlated: the common shocks are not explained by the model. This is exactly the case Driscoll–Kraay standard errors are built for. Serial correlation. The residuals are positively autocorrelated, as is usual for annual macro data. The Bartlett kernel in the Driscoll–Kraay estimator corrects for it. But there is a deeper question. Driscoll–Kraay fixes the standard errors . If the common shocks are also correlated with the regressors, the coefficients themselves are biased, and no standard-error correction helps. The robustness checks test this.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors
Robustness: are the coefficients driven by common shocks?

How to read it This is the most important table in a macro-panel paper. Bandwidth. A longer kernel changes the standard errors only a little. Year effects. Adding a dummy for each year removes everything common to all countries in that year. The unemployment coefficient shrinks towards zero and the openness coefficient turns positive and significant . CCE pooled removes common factors through cross-sectional averages, allowing each country to respond to them differently. It tells the same story as the year effects. The interpretation: in the baseline, both coefficients mostly reflected the common OECD cycle . In the 1970s oil shocks, growth fell everywhere while unemployment rose and the value of trade (inflated by oil prices) rose. Once the common shocks are removed, countries whose openness rose faster than the OECD average grew faster. The baseline coefficient was biased by the common shocks, not just its standard error.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors
Robustness: are the coefficients driven by common shocks?

So for this question the robustness check changes the conclusion: report the model with year effects or CCE as the main specification, and the plain FE-DK as the comparison. The model selection tool flagged the residual cross-sectional dependence; this step is how you act on it.

Build the results table for the paper

How to read it Report the pre-tests (CD, CIPS, slope homogeneity) in a separate table before this one. In this table, the progression from column (1) to columns (2) and (3) shows the reader how much of the raw correlation is due to common shocks.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors

How to write it: pre-tests and estimator Pesaran's CD test rejects cross-sectional independence for all variables, so we test for unit roots with the CIPS test, which rejects a unit root in levels for each series. The Pesaran–Yamagata test does not reject slope homogeneity (adjusted Δ, p = 0.16). We therefore estimate a fixed-effects model with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors, which are robust to heteroskedasticity, serial correlation and cross-sectional dependence. How to write it: results In the fixed-effects model, higher unemployment is associated with lower growth, and the change in trade openness has a negative but insignificant coefficient once standard errors allow for cross-sectional dependence (Table 2, column 1). Because the residuals remain cross-sectionally dependent, we also control for common shocks with year effects and with the common correlated effects estimator. In both specifications, increases in trade openness relative to the OECD average are associated with significantly higher growth (columns 2 and 3), indicating that the baseline estimate was confounded by the common business cycle.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors

Common mistakes Clustering by country in a macro panel and calling the standard errors robust. They are not robust to common shocks. Using Driscoll–Kraay with a short T. The estimator averages over time periods, so it needs many of them. Thinking Driscoll–Kraay solves cross-sectional dependence. It corrects the inference only; if the common factor is correlated with the regressors, the coefficients are biased. Always compare with year effects or CCE. Using first-generation unit-root tests (LLC, IPS, Fisher) when the CD test rejects.
Feasible GLS for Panels (Parks-Kmenta): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

The model is the same gasoline demand equation as in the PCSE guide, Feasible GLS (FGLS) assumes that the errors have a known structure up to a few parameters: a variance \(\sigma_i^2\) for each unit, a covariance \(\sigma_{ij}\) between each pair of units in the same period, and an AR(1) coefficient \(\rho\) in time. It estimates these from OLS residuals and then weights the data by the inverse of the estimated error covariance. If the structure is right and well estimated, FGLS is more efficient than OLS. The problem is the word well : the N × N cross-covariance matrix has N(N+1)/2 free elements, all estimated from T observations. Before you estimate anything

FGLS with cross-correlation needs a balanced panel and T of at least N. Beck and Katz (1995) show that Parks FGLS gives standard errors that are far too small unless T is at least about three times N. Check this rule first, then decide whether to model only the unit variances (always feasible) or the full covariance structure. How to write it: model section We estimate the gasoline demand equation by feasible generalized least squares, allowing for panel-specific heteroskedasticity, contemporaneous correlation across countries and a common AR(1) process in the errors (Parks 1967; Kmenta 1986). Because the efficiency gains of FGLS depend on a good estimate of the error covariance, we compare it with OLS with panel-corrected standard errors.
Load the data and check the sample size rule

How to read it The panel is balanced with N = 18 and T = 19, so the full covariance estimator can be computed (T is at least N). But it has 171 free covariance parameters estimated from 342 residuals, and the sample is far from the Beck-Katz threshold of T of at least 3N = 54. This is a case where FGLS runs without complaint and its output should still not be believed.
Step 1: OLS, rho and Prais-Winsten transformation

How to read it The first stage reproduces the PCSE guide: the OLS residuals have an AR(1) coefficient of 0.923, and removing it moves the income elasticity from 0.89 to 0.41 and the price elasticity from −0.89 to −0.39.
Step 2: the error covariance and GLS

How to read it Modelling more of the error structure changes the standard errors dramatically. The price standard error is 0.033 with identical weights, 0.029 with country-specific variances, and 0.004 once the full cross-covariance is used. The coefficients barely move (price −0.39, −0.34, −0.39), so nothing in the data has become ten times more informative; the estimated covariance matrix has simply been treated as known. Its condition number is about 8,000, a sign that it is nearly singular.

How to read it The Parks coefficients are almost identical to Prais-Winsten OLS, but the Parks standard errors are only 10 to 25 per cent of the PCSE (0.095 for the price). Both cannot be right. Beck and Katz show that it is the Parks errors that are too small, and the simulation below confirms it.
Why the Parks standard errors cannot be trusted here: a simulation

How to read it The simulated data have N = 10 countries, a common shock in the errors, AR(1) errors with coefficient 0.5 and a true slope of 1. A 95 per cent interval should contain the truth 95 per cent of the time. With Parks FGLS it does so only 18 per cent of the time when T = 10, 71 per cent at T = 20, 88 per cent at T = 40 and 94 per cent at T = 100. Prais-Winsten with PCSE is close to 95 per cent from T = 10 on (93, 94, 92 and 97 per cent). Here T = 19 and N = 18, so the gasoline data sit in the bad region of this table.
Why the Parks standard errors cannot be trusted here: a simulation

Do not report the Parks errors for this panel A narrow confidence interval is not evidence that FGLS is efficient. If the sample does not satisfy T of at least about 3N, report OLS or Prais-Winsten with PCSE, and at most show FGLS with only panel-specific variances as a robustness check.
What to report in the paper

Item What to give Sample N, T, balanced, and the ratio T / N Error structure Which of heteroskedasticity, cross-correlation and AR(1) was modelled, and the estimated rho Estimates FGLS next to pooled OLS and Prais-Winsten with PCSE Justification Why T is large enough for the covariance matrix, or why only the diagonal was used Robustness The same table with PCSE or clustered errors How to write it: results section With N = 18 and T = 19 the sample is far below the T of at least 3N that Beck and Katz (1995) recommend for the Parks estimator. In a simulation with N = 10 and T = 20 its 95 per cent intervals cover the true value in 71 per cent of draws, against 94 per cent for Prais-Winsten with panel-corrected standard errors. We therefore base inference on the latter (price elasticity −0.39, PCSE 0.044) and report FGLS only to show that the coefficients are similar.

Trusting FGLS because its standard errors are small. With T not much larger than N they are too small. Running full FGLS on an unbalanced panel. The cross-covariance is not defined. Forgetting serial correlation. Without the AR(1) step the GLS weights are wrong for long panels. Assuming FGLS corrects bias. If regressors are correlated with the errors, FGLS is as inconsistent as OLS. Reporting only one covariance structure. Show how much the standard errors move across the three structures.
Difference GMM for Dynamic Panels: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
The question and why the usual estimators fail

The question: how persistent is firm employment, and how does it respond to wages and capital? Employment adjusts slowly because hiring and firing are costly, so this year's employment depends on last year's. That makes the model dynamic: with all variables in logs: employment \(n\) , the real wage \(w\) , capital \(k\) (current and two lags) and industry output \(ys\) (current and two lags). \(\eta_i\) is a firm fixed effect. Estimator Problem with a lagged dependent variable Bias in \(\alpha_1\) Pooled OLS \(n_{i,t-1}\) contains \(\eta_i\) , which is in the error upwards Fixed effects demeaning makes \(n_{i,t-1}\) correlated with the demeaned error (Nickell bias, of order 1/T) downwards Difference GMM
The question and why the usual estimators fail

first-difference to remove \(\eta_i\) , then instrument \(\Delta n_{i,t-1}\) with \(n_{i,t-2}, n_{i,t-3}, \dots\) consistent as N grows, if the instruments are valid When to use this guide, and when not GMM for dynamic panels is designed for many units and few periods . Its consistency comes from N growing, not T. With 20 countries over 40 years the Nickell bias is small, the instruments multiply out of control, and fixed effects (or the macro-panel guides) are the better choice. The model selection tool sends a panel here only when T is short (below 15), N is large (at least 30 units) and you say the model is dynamic. With fewer units it recommends bias-corrected fixed effects (LSDVC) instead.
The question and why the usual estimators fail

How to write it: model section We estimate a dynamic labour-demand equation in which log employment depends on its own two lags, the current and lagged log real wage, and current and lagged log capital and industry output, together with year effects \(\lambda_t\) and firm effects \(\eta_i\) . Because the lagged dependent variable is correlated with the firm effect, pooled OLS is biased upwards, and because T is short, the within estimator is subject to the Nickell bias. We therefore use the difference GMM estimator of Arellano and Bond (1991).
Load the panel and build the lags

How to read it This is the shape GMM needs: 140 firms and 7 to 9 years each . The model selection tool ran the static tests on this file (fixed effects is preferred to random effects) and then asked whether the model is dynamic. Because employment adjusts gradually, the answer is yes, which leads here. Download the helper file and the data .
Step 1: pooled OLS and fixed effects give the bounds

How to read it The coefficient on lagged employment is above 1 by pooled OLS and about 0.73 by fixed effects. Because the first is biased upwards and the second downwards, a credible GMM estimate should lie between them, or close to the fixed-effects bound . This check (Bond 2002) costs two regressions and is the first thing to run in any dynamic panel study.

How to read it These are one-step estimates with standard errors robust to heteroskedasticity and to correlation within each firm. They reproduce the published Arellano–Bond results for this dataset (0.686 on lagged employment), which is how the helper function was checked. Persistence. About 0.69 on the first lag. Employment adjusts gradually. Wages. A 1% rise in the real wage lowers employment by about 0.6% in the same year; the long-run elasticity, which allows for the dynamics, is about −0.5. Capital. A 1% rise in capital raises employment by about 0.36% at once, and by about 0.7% in the long run. The bounds. The GMM persistence lies slightly below the fixed-effects estimate. That is a warning sign of weak instruments in the differenced equation: when employment is highly persistent, its lagged levels predict its differences poorly. Step 4 returns to this.

How to read it A dynamic panel GMM table is not complete without these. AR(1) in the differenced residuals is expected: differencing creates it. It says nothing about validity. AR(2) is the test that matters. If the errors in levels are serially uncorrelated, the differenced errors have no second-order correlation. Here it is not rejected, so levels dated \(t-2\) are valid instruments. If it were rejected, the instruments would have to start at \(t-3\) . Hansen J. The null is that all instruments are valid. It is not rejected. Be suspicious of p-values very close to 1: that is a symptom of too many instruments, not of very good ones.
Instrument count. The count must stay well below the number of firms. Too many instruments overfit the endogenous variable, pull GMM towards the biased OLS estimate and weaken the Hansen test.
Step 4: robustness to the instrument set

How to read it Referees always ask whether the results depend on the instruments. Report a table like this one. The wage and capital effects are stable across all instrument sets: they are the robust findings. The persistence coefficient is not. It moves with the lag depth, and with collapsed instruments its standard error grows. Persistence is the parameter for which difference GMM is known to be weak when the series are highly persistent. What to do. Report the baseline, show this table, and estimate system GMM (Blundell and Bond 1998), which adds the equations in levels instrumented by lagged differences and is much stronger when persistence is high. Build the results table for the paper

How to read it Columns (1) and (2) are the bounds, columns (3) and (4) the GMM estimates. Always report the AR(2) and Hansen p-values and the instrument count in the table itself, not only in the text.

How to write it: estimation strategy Because the model includes lagged employment and firm fixed effects, and T is short, both pooled OLS and the within estimator are inconsistent, with biases of opposite sign. We use the Arellano–Bond difference GMM estimator, instrumenting the differenced lags of employment with levels dated \(t-2\) and earlier and treating wages, capital and output as strictly exogenous. We report one-step estimates with standard errors robust to heteroskedasticity and within-firm correlation. How to write it: results The Arellano–Bond test does not detect second-order serial correlation in the differenced residuals, and the Hansen test does not reject the validity of the instruments (Table 1, column 3). A 1 percent increase in the real wage reduces employment by about 0.6 percent on impact and by about 0.5 percent in the long run. The wage and capital elasticities are robust to the choice of instrument lags and to collapsing the instrument matrix, whereas the estimated persistence of employment is sensitive to the instrument set, consistent with weak instruments for highly persistent series.

Common mistakes Using GMM with few units (say, 20 countries). The asymptotics need large N, and the instrument count quickly exceeds the number of units. Not reporting the instrument count, or using all available lags without collapsing in longer panels. Treating a Hansen p-value of 0.99 as reassuring. It usually means too many instruments. Ignoring the bounds check. A GMM persistence estimate above pooled OLS or well below fixed effects signals a problem. Treating endogenous regressors as exogenous. If wages respond to employment shocks, they must be instrumented with their own lags, just like the lagged dependent variable.
Hausman-Taylor Estimator: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

What is the return to schooling when ability is unobserved? In a wage panel the model is where \(X_1\) are time-varying regressors uncorrelated with the unit effect \(\mu_i\) , \(X_2\) are time-varying regressors that may be correlated with it, \(Z_1\) are time-invariant regressors uncorrelated with \(\mu_i\) and \(Z_2\) are time-invariant regressors that may be correlated with it. Schooling is the standard example of \(Z_2\) : unobserved ability raises both schooling and wages. Fixed effects cannot estimate the schooling coefficient because schooling does not change, and random effects is biased if ability is in \(\mu_i\) . Hausman and Taylor use the within deviations of all time-varying variables and the unit means of \(X_1\) as instruments. The unit means of the exogenous time-varying variables identify \(\gamma_2\) , which needs at least as many variables in \(X_1\) as in \(Z_2\) .

Three checks before you trust the estimator Is the classification defensible? Every result depends on which variables you call exogenous. State the reason for each choice, not only the choice. Is the model identified? The number of variables in \(X_1\) must be at least the number in \(Z_2\) . The engine stops with a message if it is not. Do the unit means of \(X_1\) predict \(Z_2\) ? If the exogenous time-varying variables are unrelated to the endogenous time-invariant ones, the instruments are weak and the standard errors are large. How to write it: the model We estimate a log wage equation on a panel of 595 workers observed for seven years with the Hausman-Taylor (1981) estimator. Experience, experience squared, weeks worked, marital status and union membership are treated as correlated with the worker effect; occupation, region, urban residence and industry are treated as uncorrelated with it. Sex and race are treated as uncorrelated with the worker effect, and years of schooling as correlated with it. The model is identified because four time-varying exogenous variables instrument one endogenous time-invariant variable. We follow the classification of Baltagi and Khanti-Akom (1990).
Load the data and check which variables vary within workers

How to read it The panel is balanced: 595 workers for seven years (coded 1 to 7), 4,165 observations. Schooling, sex and race do not change within a worker (between-worker share 1.0), so fixed effects cannot estimate them. Most of the variance of log wages is between workers (0.73), which is the variation that the unit effect absorbs. Experience is almost entirely between workers too (0.97), because every worker ages one year per year, so its within variation is a time trend. Only 11% of the workers are women and 7% are black, so the coefficients on sex and race rest on small groups.

How to read it The estimated return to schooling is 0.138 (standard error 0.021): one more year of schooling is associated with about 14% higher wages, after allowing schooling to be correlated with the worker effect. Experience raises wages by 0.113 per year at the start of a career, with a negative squared term. Union membership is associated with a 3.3% wage premium (p = 0.028), and living in a metropolitan area with a 4.2% discount (p = 0.027). The coefficient on race is -0.286 (p = 0.066) and on sex -0.131 (p = 0.30); both are imprecise because they are identified from a few workers and from the unit-level variation only.

The unit effect dominates the error: its standard deviation is 0.94 against 0.15 for the idiosyncratic part, so \(\rho\) = 0.975. With so much weight on the unit effect, \(\theta\) is 0.94 and the estimator is close to the within estimator for the time-varying variables.
Compare with fixed effects and random effects

How to read it For the time-varying variables the Hausman-Taylor and within estimates are nearly identical (experience 0.1131 against 0.1132, union 0.0328 in both), which is expected when most variables are treated as endogenous. They differ only for the variables treated as exogenous: the region coefficient moves from -0.002 to 0.008 and industry from 0.019 to 0.014, small changes within their standard errors. The big difference is in the time-invariant variables. Random effects gives a schooling return of 0.100 (standard error 0.008), Hausman-Taylor 0.138 (0.021). Random effects assumes schooling is uncorrelated with the worker effect. If ability sat in the worker effect and raised schooling, random effects would be biased upward, so the Hausman-Taylor estimate would be lower; here it is higher, so the data do not show that pattern. Possible reasons, which this guide does not test, are measurement error in schooling or a negative correlation between schooling and the worker effect. The instrumented estimate is also much less precise. The other contrasts are large too: the union premium falls from 0.063 to 0.033, the sex coefficient from -0.339 to -0.131 (no longer significant) and the race coefficient moves from -0.210 to -0.286.
Compare with fixed effects and random effects

The Hausman test compares the within and Hausman-Taylor estimates of the time-varying coefficients: the statistic is 5.33 with 3 degrees of freedom (p = 0.149), so the extra instruments, the unit means of the four exogenous variables, are not rejected.
How sensitive is the answer to the classification?

How to read it The schooling coefficient is between 0.132 and 0.144 in four of the five classifications, and the union premium between 0.033 and 0.038 in all of them. The exception is the classification that treats experience as exogenous: schooling jumps to 0.237. The Hausman test rejects that classification decisively (statistic 372, p < 0.001), which is what it is for: experience is a function of age and past career choices and is not plausibly uncorrelated with the worker effect. Treating weeks worked, marriage and union as exogenous also rejects (p = 0.0045). Treating schooling as exogenous is not rejected (p = 0.238) and gives a coefficient of 0.144, so the test does not distinguish between random effects and Hausman-Taylor for schooling. A test that does not reject is not proof of the classification.

How to write it: results The Hausman-Taylor estimate of the return to schooling is 0.138 (standard error 0.021), compared with 0.100 (0.008) from random effects. The estimate allows schooling, experience, weeks worked, marital status and union membership to be correlated with the worker effect. A Hausman test comparing the within and Hausman-Taylor estimates of the time-varying coefficients does not reject the classification (chi-squared with 3 degrees of freedom = 5.33, p = 0.149). The union premium is 3.3% (p = 0.028). The estimates are robust to moving union membership or schooling to the exogenous group (schooling 0.132 to 0.144), whereas classifying experience as exogenous is rejected (p < 0.001) and would raise the schooling coefficient to 0.237. Standard errors assume the random-effects error structure; the worker effect accounts for 97.5% of the variance of the error.
