What if the common shocks hit units unequally? The model is where \(f_t\) is a vector of \(r\) unobserved common factors and \(\lambda_i\) are unit-specific loadings. If \(x_{it}\) is correlated with \(\lambda_i' f_t\) , omitting the interaction biases \(\beta\) even when unit and period effects are included. Bai (2009) shows that \(\beta\) can be estimated by iterating between the slope given the factors and the factors given the slope: extract the first \(r\) principal components of the residual matrix, subtract them, re-estimate \(\beta\) , and repeat. This needs both \(N\) and \(T\) to be reasonably large. Three checks before you trust the estimates Is there cross-sectional dependence left after two-way fixed effects? The average pairwise correlation of the residuals tells you whether factors are needed.

How many factors? Information criteria help, but they often choose the largest number you allow. Look at how the coefficients move with \(r\) . Are the standard errors reliable? The engine reports the homoskedastic asymptotic standard errors without bias correction. They assume that T and N are both large. How to write it: the model We estimate the demand for cigarettes in 46 US states over 1963-92 with the interactive fixed effects estimator of Bai (2009). Log per-capita sales are regressed on log price and log income, and the model includes state and year effects and two unobserved common factors with state-specific loadings, which capture national shocks such as changing attitudes to smoking that affect states differently. The number of factors is chosen by looking at the Bai-Ng information criterion and at the sensitivity of the coefficients to the number of factors. Standard errors are the asymptotic standard errors of Bai (2009).
Load the data and look at the dependence left by two-way fixed effects

How to read it The panel is balanced: 46 states for 30 years (1963-92). Without any factors the model is the two-way fixed-effects regression, and it gives a price elasticity of -1.03 (standard error 0.040) and an income elasticity of 0.53 (0.045). The residuals are still strongly dependent across states: the average absolute pairwise correlation is 0.45, which means that a large common component remains in the errors. The Pesaran CD statistic (-1.91, p = 0.057) is a signed average and understates this, because positive and negative correlations offset each other. If this common component is correlated with price and income, the two-way estimates are biased.

How to read it With two factors the price elasticity falls from -1.03 to -0.48 (standard error 0.025) and the income elasticity from 0.53 to 0.40 (0.033). The average absolute residual correlation falls from 0.45 to 0.24, so the factors remove about half of the common structure. The CD statistic does not improve (-3.58, p = 0.0003), for the reason given above, and this is why the mean absolute correlation is the more useful column. The estimator converged in 47 iterations. The factors are identified only up to rotation, so the lines in the chart describe a two-dimensional space of national shocks, and should not be read as two separately interpretable series.

How to read it The Bai-Ng criterion falls with every added factor and is smallest at the largest number allowed (5), so it does not settle the number of factors here. The price coefficient moves most at the start: -1.03 with none, -0.64 with one, -0.48 with two, -0.39 with three, and then -0.38 and -0.37 with four and five. The income coefficient is steady at 0.40 to 0.46 for one to four factors and drops to 0.20 with five, so it is not stable at the highest number. With 46 states and 30 years the panel is small for a method designed for large N and T, so I would report the range of the price elasticity (-0.64 to -0.37) and not a single value, and not push the number of factors higher.
Robustness: which additive effects are removed first

How to read it The conclusion on price depends on the effects, not just on the factors. With unit effects only (no year effects) the estimate is -0.70 with no factors and -0.65 with one, close to each other, and then falls to -0.45 and -0.30 with two and three. The income elasticity is -0.01 with no factors, because income trends are not separated from the common trend, then 0.52, 0.25 and 0.40, so it is the less reliable of the two coefficients. All variants agree that the elasticity of demand with respect to price is negative and well below the -1.03 of two-way fixed effects in absolute value once common factors are allowed.

How to write it: results Two-way fixed effects gives a price elasticity of cigarette demand of -1.03 (standard error 0.040) and an income elasticity of 0.53 (0.045), but the residuals remain strongly correlated across states (mean absolute pairwise correlation 0.45). With two interactive fixed effects (Bai 2009) the price elasticity is -0.48 (0.025) and the income elasticity 0.40 (0.033), and the mean absolute residual correlation falls to 0.24. The price elasticity decreases in absolute value as factors are added (-0.64 with one factor, -0.39 with three, -0.37 with five), and we therefore report it as lying between -0.64 and -0.37. The Bai-Ng criterion does not select a number of factors below the maximum considered, and the income elasticity is unstable at five factors (0.20). Standard errors are asymptotic and do not correct for bias from heteroskedasticity or serial correlation, and the panel (46 states, 30 years) is small for this estimator.

Graduate lecture on cross-sectional dependence, slope heterogeneity, panel unit roots, cointegration, Mean Group, CCE, AMG, PMG and CS-ARDL.
1. Panel structure and the common-factor problem

Let \(i=1,\ldots,N\) index countries or other macro units and \(t=1,\ldots,T\) index time. A heterogeneous panel regression is where \(\alpha_i\) is a unit-specific intercept, \(\boldsymbol{\beta}_i\) is a potentially heterogeneous slope vector, \(\mathbf{f}_t\) is a vector of unobserved common factors, and \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_i\) contains unit-specific factor loadings. Global interest rates, commodity prices, financial conditions, technology and common policy shocks can induce dependence across countries even after observed controls are included. For macro panels, asymptotics often require both \(N\) and \(T\) to be sufficiently informative. A large-\(N\), short-\(T\) micro-panel design is not interchangeable with a country panel having moderate or large \(T\).

After a baseline model is estimated, let \(\widehat{\rho}_{ij}\) be the pairwise correlation between residuals for units \(i\) and \(j\). Pesaran's CD statistic is based on The null is cross-sectional independence. Rejection indicates that conventional first-generation panel procedures relying on cross-sectional independence may not be appropriate without adjustment. The test should be considered alongside the economic structure of common shocks and residual diagnostics. Implementation: Stata's xtcd2 is distributed with xtdcce2 . Run it on the variables or, more importantly, on residuals from a defensible baseline model.

In a homogeneous specification, \(\boldsymbol{\beta}_i=\boldsymbol{\beta}\) for all \(i\). The Pesaran–Yamagata delta test assesses this restriction using dispersion in unit-specific slope estimates relative to a pooled estimate. The economic question is whether a common response is credible across countries with different institutions, production structures, energy mixes and policy regimes. If homogeneity is defensible, pooled estimators may gain precision. If slopes differ, Mean Group or CCE-MG/AMG estimators allow unit-specific slopes. PMG imposes a common long-run coefficient vector but allows short-run coefficients and adjustment speeds to vary.
4. Panel unit roots: first versus second generation

Family Examples Key maintained structure First generation LLC, IPS, Fisher-ADF, Fisher-PP Cross-sectional independence, or an adjustment that makes it credible. Second generation CADF and CIPS Cross-sectional averages proxy unobserved common factors. The cross-sectionally augmented Dickey–Fuller regression includes lagged levels and cross-sectional averages. The CIPS statistic is the cross-sectional average of individual CADF statistics: In Stata, xtcips implements the Pesaran CIPS test and requires a balanced panel. Deterministic terms (intercept or trend), lag selection and sample comparability must be specified and reported. A test result should not be treated as an integration-order label independent of those choices.

Cointegration is considered when variables are appropriately established as I(1) and theory supports a long-run equilibrium relation. Residual-based tests include Pedroni and Kao. Westerlund's error-correction tests ask whether deviations from long-run equilibrium generate adjustment. The null in the Westerlund error-correction framework is no error correction (no cointegration); the alternative can allow adjustment in some or all panel members depending on the statistic. When cross-sectional dependence is material, bootstrap inference or a dependence-aware implementation is important. Cointegration tests do not by themselves establish a common long-run coefficient vector.

Estimate a separate time-series regression for each unit and average the coefficients: MG allows slope heterogeneity but does not automatically remove bias from unobserved common factors. It is a useful heterogeneous benchmark when each unit has enough time observations.

CCE augments unit-specific regressions with cross-sectional averages of the dependent and explanatory variables, and where needed their lags. These averages proxy the unobserved common factors. CCEMG averages the unit-specific CCE slope estimates. The rank condition and the number of cross-sectional averages relative to the factor structure matter.

AMG estimates a common dynamic process from a pooled first-difference model with time effects, then includes that process in unit-specific regressions. It allows heterogeneous slopes while controlling for an estimated common dynamic component.

For an error-correction representation, PMG constrains the long-run vector to be common, while allowing short-run coefficients, intercepts, variances and adjustment speeds to differ: The long-run restriction \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_i=\boldsymbol{\theta}\) is substantive. Compare PMG with MG and dependence-aware estimators; do not select PMG solely because it produces a smaller standard error.

CS-ARDL augments a dynamic heterogeneous ARDL with current and lagged cross-sectional averages. Unit-specific long-run effects can be formed from the distributed-lag coefficients and then averaged. This combines dynamic adjustment with a proxy for unobserved common factors.

Describe \(N\), \(T\), balancedness, missingness, frequency and the economic comparability of units. Estimate transparent baseline FE/RE specifications and inspect residual dependence. Test cross-sectional dependence and slope homogeneity. Choose first- or second-generation unit-root procedures accordingly; specify intercepts, trends and lags. Test cointegration only when the integration orders and theoretical relation warrant it. Compare MG, CCE-MG, AMG, PMG and CS-ARDL under explicit restrictions. Report residual dependence, serial correlation, adjustment coefficients, lag sensitivity, sample sensitivity and long-run coefficient comparisons.

Mean Group and CCE Mean Group

The question is one of the oldest in growth economics: do countries that save more grow faster? In the Solow model a higher saving rate raises the level of income and, during the transition, the growth rate. But there is no reason to expect the same relationship in Japan, Chile and Nigeria: financial systems, openness and the use of saving differ. Symbol Variable Definition Expected sign \(g_{it}\) growth Growth of real GDP per capita, % (computed below) dependent variable \(s_{it}\) sr Saving rate, % of GDP positive \(\beta_i\) — Country-specific effect of saving on growth what we want to average The model lets every country have its own slope \(\beta_i\) . The parameter of interest is the average slope \(\beta\) .
Mean Group and CCE Mean Group

Pooled or mean group? Fixed effects imposes \(\beta_i = \beta\) for all countries. If that is wrong, the FE estimate is a weighted average of the \(\beta_i\) , with weights that depend on the variance of each country's saving rate, not on anything economically meaningful, and its standard error ignores the slope heterogeneity. The mean group estimator (Pesaran and Smith 1995) estimates each \(\beta_i\) separately and averages them. Its standard error comes from the dispersion of the \(\beta_i\) across countries, so it is valid whatever the heterogeneity. It needs T large enough to estimate a regression for each country. How to write it: model section We allow the effect of saving on growth to differ across countries, \(g_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_i s_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}\) , and estimate the average effect \(\beta = E(\beta_i)\) with the mean group estimator of Pesaran and Smith (1995), and with the common correlated effects mean group estimator of Pesaran (2006), which in addition controls for unobserved common factors.

Load the data and run the pre-tests

How to read it 125 countries over 25 years : long enough to estimate a regression for each country. Cross-sectional dependence. The CD test rejects for both variables. World growth has a common cycle, so CIPS is the right unit-root test. Stationarity. CIPS rejects a unit root for both growth and the saving rate: both are I(0), and a model in levels is valid. Slope heterogeneity. The Δ test rejects decisively. The effect of saving on growth differs across countries , so pooling the slopes is not defensible. Stationary variables with heterogeneous slopes: this is where the model selection tool recommends mean-group estimation.
Mean Group and CCE Mean Group

How to read it The histogram is the reason for this guide. The country slopes are spread widely, and a substantial minority are negative. A single pooled coefficient would hide all of this. The mean group estimate is the simple average of these slopes , and its standard error is their standard deviation divided by \(\sqrt{N}\) . The extreme slopes come from small countries with volatile data and few effective observations. Because every country gets the same weight, a few of them can move the mean; the robustness step checks this.

Mean group, CCE mean group and the pooled comparison

How to read it Mean group. On average across countries, a saving rate one percentage point higher goes with growth about 0.35 points higher, and the effect is significant. CCE mean group adds the cross-sectional averages of growth and saving to each country's regression. They proxy the unobserved common factors (the world business cycle, oil prices, world interest rates), and each country can respond to them differently. The average effect is a bit larger and remains significant. Pooled fixed effects gives a smaller slope. The difference is the weighting: FE gives more weight to countries whose saving rate varies more, and those are not the countries with the largest effects. With heterogeneous slopes the FE number has no clear interpretation, which is the point of the Δ test.
Mean Group and CCE Mean Group
Diagnostic test: are the common shocks removed?

How to read it The plain mean-group residuals are still cross-sectionally dependent: country regressions with only their own saving rate leave the world cycle in the error. With the cross-sectional averages included, the CD statistic falls from about 26 to about 0.2 and is no longer significant: the common factors have been removed. This is why CCE-MG is the preferred estimator when the CD test rejects. If the common factors were correlated with saving, plain MG would be biased. (The mean absolute correlation barely changes, because with T = 25 any two countries' residuals are correlated by chance; the CD test looks at the signed correlations, which are what common shocks create.)
Mean Group and CCE Mean Group

How to read it Because the mean group gives every country equal weight, report the trimmed mean and the median alongside it. Here they matter. The distribution of country slopes is skewed to the right: a few countries have very large slopes (the largest is 6.8), and they pull the mean up. Trimming the extreme 5% at each end, or taking the median, gives an effect of about 0.23 : smaller than the baseline mean group, but still positive and, for the trimmed mean, more precisely estimated. The sign is robust; the size depends on how much weight the extreme countries get. Say so in the paper.

How to read it Report the pooled estimates for comparison, but make column (4) the main result: it allows for both heterogeneous slopes and common shocks, the two features the pre-tests found.

How to write it: pre-tests and estimator The CD test indicates strong cross-sectional dependence, and the CIPS test rejects a unit root for both growth and the saving rate. The Pesaran–Yamagata test strongly rejects slope homogeneity, so pooled estimators would average heterogeneous country effects with arbitrary weights. We therefore estimate the average effect with the mean group (MG) estimator and, to account for unobserved common factors, with the common correlated effects mean group (CCE-MG) estimator. How to write it: results The CCE-MG estimate implies that a saving rate one percentage point higher is associated with growth of GDP per capita about 0.5 percentage points higher on average (Table 3, column 4). The effect varies considerably across countries: it is negative in about a fifth of them, and the distribution is skewed by a few countries with very large effects. Excluding the most extreme 5 percent of country estimates at each end, or using the median country slope, yields a smaller but still positive effect of 0.2 to 0.3. Pooled fixed-effects estimates are smaller still, consistent with the arbitrary weighting of heterogeneous slopes.

Common mistakes Reporting a pooled FE coefficient after the slope-homogeneity test rejects, without comment. Using mean group estimators with short T. Each country regression needs enough observations; with T below about 20 the unit estimates are noisy and MG can be badly biased in dynamic models. Forgetting the common factors: MG with cross-sectionally dependent errors can be biased. Use CCE-MG and report the residual CD test. Reading the average slope as causal. Saving and growth are jointly determined; this is a conditional correlation unless you have a source of exogenous variation.

Correlated Random Effects (Mundlak) and the Robust Hausman Test

Is the unit effect correlated with the regressors? In the model \(y_{it}=x_{it}'\beta+z_i'\gamma+c_i+e_{it}\) , random effects needs \(c_i\) to be uncorrelated with \(x_{it}\) and fixed effects does not, but fixed effects cannot estimate \(\gamma\) . Mundlak models the correlation directly, where \(\bar x_i\) is the unit mean of \(x_{it}\) . The coefficient \(\beta\) is then the within (fixed-effects) estimate, \(\pi\) is the difference between the between and the within effects, and \(\gamma\) is estimated from the variation between units. The null \(\pi = 0\) is the hypothesis that random effects and fixed effects agree, so a Wald test of \(\pi=0\) with standard errors clustered by unit is a Hausman test that remains valid under heteroskedasticity and serial correlation.
Correlated Random Effects (Mundlak) and the Robust Hausman Test

Three checks before you trust the estimates Do the time-varying regressors vary within units? The within estimate for a regressor that barely changes is imprecise, and the engine rejects one that never changes. Is the unit effect really correlated with the regressors? The Mundlak test answers this. If it does not reject, random effects is more efficient. Are the time-invariant variables credible? Their coefficients are identified only from differences between units, so they carry whatever omitted unit characteristics are correlated with them. How to write it: the model We estimate a log wage equation for 545 men observed for eight years (1980-87) with the correlated random-effects approach of Mundlak (1978) and Chamberlain (1982). The model includes union membership, marital status and the square of experience as time-varying regressors, schooling and race as time-invariant regressors, period dummies, and the worker means of the three time-varying regressors. Standard errors are clustered by worker. The coefficients on the time-varying regressors are numerically the fixed-effects estimates, and a cluster-robust Wald test that the coefficients on the worker means are jointly zero is a robust Hausman test of random effects against fixed effects.
Correlated Random Effects (Mundlak) and the Robust Hausman Test
Load the data and see where the variation is

How to read it The panel is balanced: 545 workers observed for eight years, 4,360 observations. Between 42% and 59% of the variance of log wages, union status, marital status and squared experience lies between workers, so a large part of the variation is lost when the unit effect is removed; schooling, which never changes, is entirely between workers (1.00). Twenty-four percent of the worker-years are union years and 44% are married years. The within variation in union status comes from 246 workers (45%) who change status at least once, which is the group that identifies the fixed-effects union coefficient.
Correlated Random Effects (Mundlak) and the Robust Hausman Test

How to read it The coefficients on the time-varying variables are the within estimates: union membership is associated with 8.0% higher wages (standard error 0.023), marriage with 4.7% (0.021) and the square of experience has a coefficient of -0.0052 (0.0008). The coefficients on the worker means are significant for all three variables: 0.183 for union, 0.094 for marriage and 0.0072 for squared experience. Each is the between effect minus the within effect, so the between-worker association of union membership with wages is 0.263 (0.080 + 0.183), more than three times the within effect, and that of marriage is 0.141. The time-invariant coefficients are 0.094 for a year of schooling (standard error 0.011) and -0.142 for black workers (0.051); the Hispanic coefficient is 0.008 (0.038) and not significant.
Correlated Random Effects (Mundlak) and the Robust Hausman Test
Compare fixed effects, random effects and CRE, and test

How to read it Random effects gives a union coefficient of 0.110 and a marriage coefficient of 0.077, against 0.080 and 0.047 from fixed effects (the CRE column reproduces the fixed-effects estimates exactly). The coefficient on squared experience is -0.0015 under random effects and -0.0052 under fixed effects. Random effects therefore overstates the union and marriage premiums by about 0.03 each, which is what the positive coefficients on the worker means predict: workers with higher average union and marriage rates are also workers with higher unobserved wage components. The cluster-robust Wald test that the three means are jointly zero is 68.2 with 3 degrees of freedom (p < 0.001), so random effects is rejected. The variance of the worker effect (standard deviation 0.327) is about as large as that of the idiosyncratic error (0.351), which gives rho = 0.47.
Correlated Random Effects (Mundlak) and the Robust Hausman Test

How to read it Each regressor rejects on its own: the coefficient on the worker mean is 0.193 for union (p = 0.0001), 0.122 for marriage (p = 0.0085) and 0.0079 for squared experience (p < 0.001). The conclusion that random effects is inconsistent does not rest on one variable. The squared-experience means are the strongest signal, partly because average squared experience is closely related to how long a worker has been in the labour market, so it picks up worker heterogeneity mechanically. The union and marriage results are the ones with an economic interpretation.
Correlated Random Effects (Mundlak) and the Robust Hausman Test

How to write it: results A correlated random-effects specification in the sense of Mundlak (1978) rejects the random-effects assumption that the worker effect is uncorrelated with union membership, marital status and experience (cluster-robust Wald chi-squared = 68.2, 3 degrees of freedom, p < 0.001); each regressor rejects on its own. The within estimates, which the model reproduces for the time-varying variables, show a union premium of 8.0% (standard error 0.023) and a marriage premium of 4.7% (0.021), compared with 11.0% and 7.7% under random effects. Schooling raises wages by 9.4% per year (0.011) and the coefficient for black workers is -0.142 (0.051); these time-invariant coefficients are identified from differences between workers and may reflect unobserved worker characteristics. Standard errors are clustered by worker.

Panel Granger Causality (Dumitrescu-Hurlin): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Does x help predict y, in at least one unit? For each unit \(i\) the regression is and every coefficient, including \(\beta_{ik}\) , may differ by unit. The null hypothesis is homogeneous non-causality : \(\beta_{ik}=0\) for all \(k\) in all units. The alternative allows causality in some units and not in others. Dumitrescu and Hurlin average the unit Wald statistics, \(\bar W = N^{-1}\sum_i W_i\) , and standardise them. \(\bar Z\) is for large \(T\) and \(\tilde Z\) is for small \(T\) with fixed \(N\) ; with \(T\) around 25, as here, use \(\tilde Z\) . Three checks before you trust the test Are both series stationary? The test is for stationary series. A variable with a unit root must be differenced first, or the regressions are spurious.

Is T long enough for the number of lags? Each unit regression loses \(2K+1\) parameters. With \(T = 25\) , more than two or three lags leaves few degrees of freedom. Do you want a causal claim? Granger causality is about prediction. A third variable that moves both series produces it as well. How to write it: the model We test whether unemployment helps predict GDP growth, and the reverse, in a panel of 14 OECD countries over 1966-90 with the Dumitrescu-Hurlin (2012) Granger non-causality test for heterogeneous panels. Each country has its own regression with one lag of each variable, so the coefficients may differ across countries. GDP growth is already a growth rate and is used in levels; the unemployment rate is persistent and is used in first differences. Because T is short (24 observations per country), we base inference on the small-sample statistic \(\tilde Z\) .
Load the data and check stationarity

How to read it The panel is balanced: 14 countries with 25 annual observations each, 24 after first differencing. GDP growth has a mean of 3.25% and a standard deviation of 2.43. It is stationary in levels (IPS and Fisher p-values below 0.001), as a growth rate should be, so it enters in levels. The unemployment rate, with a mean of 4.99%, does not reject a unit root in levels (IPS p = 0.64, Fisher p = 0.62) and is stationary in first differences (p < 0.001), so it enters as a change. With 14 series of 25 observations these unit-root tests have limited power, which is one more reason to keep the transformation simple and state it.
Run the test in both directions

How to read it Changes in unemployment do not help predict GDP growth: W-bar is 1.29 (it is expected to be near the number of lags, 1, under the null), Z-tilde is 0.40 and the p-value is 0.69. GDP growth does help predict changes in unemployment: W-bar is 2.29, Z-tilde is 2.59 and the p-value is 0.0097. The large-T statistic Z-bar gives a p-value of 0.0006 for the second test, sixteen times smaller than the 0.0097 from Z-tilde, which shows why the small-sample statistic should be used with 24 observations per country. The predictive relationship runs from growth to unemployment, which fits an Okun-type relationship, and not the other way.

How to read it No country rejects the hypothesis that unemployment changes do not predict growth at 5%: the smallest p-value is Finland's 0.067, followed by Italy (0.100) and Canada (0.117). In the opposite direction, growth predicts changes in unemployment in Italy and the United Kingdom at 5%. With 14 countries, about 0.7 rejections would be expected by chance, so two is not many, and the panel rejection reflects modest evidence in several countries as much as strong evidence in two. The test cannot say which countries have causality, only that it is unlikely to be absent in all of them.

How to read it The result for unemployment to growth is the same for every number of lags (Z-tilde p-values of 0.69, 0.48 and 0.19). The result for growth to unemployment is not: the Z-tilde p-value is 0.010 with one lag, 0.119 with two and 0.432 with three, while the large-T statistic Z-bar gives 0.001, 0.012 and 0.059. Each added lag uses two more parameters in a regression with 24 observations, which lowers power, so the evidence that growth predicts unemployment changes is confined to the one-lag specification. Choose the lag length before looking at the test, with an information criterion or from theory, and report the others.

How to write it: results The Dumitrescu-Hurlin (2012) test does not reject the null that changes in unemployment do not Granger-cause GDP growth in any of the 14 countries (W-bar = 1.29, Z-tilde = 0.40, p = 0.69, one lag). It rejects the null that GDP growth does not Granger-cause changes in unemployment (W-bar = 2.29, Z-tilde = 2.59, p = 0.010); at the 5% level the country regressions reject for Italy and the United Kingdom. The finding is specific to the one-lag specification: with two lags the p-value is 0.12 and with three it is 0.43. Both variables are treated as stationary after taking first differences of unemployment, and inference uses the small-sample statistic because T = 24. Granger causality measures predictive content and not a causal effect.

Panel Unit-Root and Stationarity Tests: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Do the series in this panel have unit roots? Each unit has the augmented Dickey-Fuller regression and the null of a unit root is \(\rho_i = 0\) . The tests differ in the alternative. Levin-Lin-Chu assumes one common \(\rho\) for all units and pools the regressions: it is powerful if the series are alike, and says little if some are stationary and some are not. Im-Pesaran-Shin averages the individual \(t\) statistics (the \(\bar t\) statistic) and allows a different \(\rho_i\) for every unit. Fisher-type tests combine the individual \(p\) -values, \(P=-2\sum \ln p_i\) , which is chi-squared with \(2N\) degrees of freedom under the null of independence. All three have a unit root in every series as the null. Hadri reverses the null: all series are stationary.

In this engine the null distributions of the Levin-Lin-Chu type and IPS statistics are simulated for the panel's own number of units, series length and lag selection rule, rather than taken from published tables. They assume independence across units. Three checks before you trust a panel unit-root test What does the alternative say? A rejection by IPS or Fisher means that at least one unit is stationary, not that all are. Look at the unit-by-unit table. Is there a common shock? Global inflation or a world business cycle makes the series dependent, and the tests then reject too often. Re-run with cross-sectional means removed. Are the deterministic terms right? A trending variable tested with a constant only will look like a unit root, and a driftless one tested with a trend loses power.

How to write it: the model We test for unit roots in annual CPI inflation in 34 countries, 1990-2023, using four panel tests: the Levin-Lin-Chu type test with a common autoregressive coefficient, the Im-Pesaran-Shin test, the Fisher-type tests that combine the individual Dickey-Fuller p-values, and the Hadri test of the null of stationarity. Individual regressions include a constant, with up to two lagged differences chosen by the AIC. Critical values for the Levin-Lin-Chu type and Im-Pesaran-Shin tests are simulated for the length of the panel and the lag-selection rule. As a robustness check we remove the cross-sectional mean in every year, which removes a common time effect.
Load the data and look at the series

How to read it The panel is balanced: 34 countries with 34 annual observations each. The highest mean inflation rates are in Egypt (10.7%), Colombia (10.3%), Hungary (10.3%) and Mexico (9.4%), and Indonesia has the largest single value (58.5%, the 1998 crisis). The average pairwise correlation of the country series is 0.51, which is high: inflation across countries moves together with global shocks such as the commodity booms of 2008 and 2022. The tests below assume independence across units, so this is the first warning that their p-values may be too small.

How to read it Every test that has a unit root as its null rejects it at p < 0.001: the Levin-Lin-Chu type statistic is -8.32 after standardisation, the IPS t-bar is -3.19 (W = -9.64), and the Fisher statistics are P = 284.1 (68 degrees of freedom) and Z = -11.8. In 67.6% of countries (23 of 34) the individual test also rejects at 5%. The Hadri test points the other way: its null of stationarity is rejected (LM = 1.385, against 1/6 expected under the null; z = 47.7). The two sets of tests are not contradictory, but they say that inflation is neither a clean unit root nor a clean stationary process. The Hadri statistic used here has no correction for serial correlation and is known to over-reject when series are persistent or have shifts in the mean, which both apply to inflation over 1990-2023. Treat its rejection as a sign of persistence rather than as evidence of a unit root.

How to read it Eleven countries do not reject a unit root at 5%: Austria, Colombia, Germany, Egypt, France, Hungary, India, Israel, Italy, Korea and Mexico. Three of them are close to the line (India p = 0.058, Israel 0.061, Korea 0.072), and two countries that do reject are also near it (Japan 0.043, South Africa 0.047). With 34 observations an individual test has little power, so a non-rejection is not evidence that the series has a unit root, and with 34 tests about one or two rejections at 5% would occur by chance even if all series had unit roots. The lag selection picks no lagged differences for 22 countries, one for 7 and two for 5. The panel tests are informative precisely because they use all 34 series at once.

How to read it The panel conclusions survive every variant: all four unit-root tests reject at the 1% level, with the smallest margin for the constant-and-trend specification (Levin-Lin-Chu p = 0.0004, IPS p = 0.0001). What changes is how many countries reject individually: 67.6% in the baseline, 41.2% (14 countries) after the cross-sectional mean is removed, 41.2% with a trend, 70.6% with the BIC and 64.7% with no lagged differences. A large share of the individual rejections therefore depends on the common component of inflation. The Hadri test rejects stationarity in every variant.
A trending panel where the tests disagree

How to read it Log gross state product behaves as the series that it is. With a constant and trend, the Levin-Lin-Chu type test (p = 0.70), the IPS test (p = 0.90) and the inverse-normal Fisher test (p = 0.25) do not reject a unit root, and the Hadri test rejects trend stationarity (z = 28.2). The inverse chi-squared Fisher test is the exception (P = 154.1, p = 0.0002), and the note printed below the table explains why it should not be trusted here: with only 17 years, the asymptotic MacKinnon p-values that the Fisher tests combine are too small, whereas the IPS and Levin-Lin-Chu type tests use null distributions simulated for T = 17. After the cross-sectional means are removed none of the unit-root tests rejects (p between 0.92 and 1.00) and Hadri still rejects. The practical lesson is that a disagreement among panel tests is often a sign that one of them is outside its valid range, so check the sample length and the notes before choosing a test.

How to write it: results Panel unit-root tests reject a unit root in annual inflation for 34 countries over 1990-2023: the Levin-Lin-Chu type test (z = -8.3), the Im-Pesaran-Shin test (W = -9.6) and the Fisher-type tests (inverse normal Z = -11.8) all have p-values below 0.001, with simulated critical values and individual regressions that include a constant and up to two lags chosen by the AIC. The conclusions hold with a trend, with BIC lag selection and after removing cross-sectional means. The rejection means that at least some countries have stationary inflation: at the 5% level the individual tests reject a unit root for 23 of 34 countries (14 of 34 after removing cross-sectional means). The Hadri test rejects stationarity (p < 0.001), which we attribute to persistence and mean shifts, since the statistic is not corrected for serial correlation. All tests assume independence across countries, and the average pairwise correlation of the series is 0.51, so the p-values should be read as indicative. In the log-GSP panel, by contrast, no unit-root test that is valid for T = 17 rejects, and we treat that variable as non-stationary.

A long-run demand function says that fuel use per car depends on income, the real price of fuel and the stock of cars, and that deviations from that relation are temporary. Our question is: are gasoline use, income, price and the car stock cointegrated across 18 OECD countries, so that the long-run elasticities mean something? If all variables are I(1) and \(u_{it}\) is stationary, the variables are cointegrated. Residual-based tests (Kao, Pedroni) test the null of no cointegration by checking whether \(\hat u_{it}\) has a unit root. The Westerlund (2007) test looks at the error-correction term \(\alpha_i\) in and the null is \(\alpha_i=0\) for all \(i\) . Symbol Variable in the file

Definition \(\ln g_{it}\) lgaspcar log gasoline consumption per car \(\ln y_{it}\) lincomep log real per-capita income \(\ln p_{it}\) lrpmg log real gasoline price \(\ln c_{it}\) lcarpcap log stock of cars per capita Before you estimate anything Panel cointegration tests need I(1) variables, enough time periods for the unit-root and ADF steps, and an answer to two questions: are the slopes the same in all countries, and are the countries cross-sectionally dependent? Here \(N=18\) and \(T=19\) , which is short, so each test has low power and we expect them to disagree. Plan to report several tests and not to rely on one. How to write it: model section We test for cointegration between gasoline use per car, income, the real gasoline price and the car stock in 18 OECD countries for 1960–1978. We first establish the order of integration with panel unit-root tests that allow for cross-sectional dependence. We then apply the Kao residual test, a group-mean ADF test on country-specific cointegrating residuals in the spirit of Pedroni, and an error-correction test in the spirit of Westerlund. Critical values for the last two are simulated for N = 18 and T = 19. We repeat the tests after removing cross-sectional means.
Load the data and test for unit roots

How to read it The panel has 18 countries and 19 years. The CIPS test, which allows for common shocks across countries, does not reject a unit root in the levels of any of the four variables (p between 0.17 and 0.80) and rejects it in the first differences (p between 0.000 and 0.028). By this test all four are I(1). The Fisher-ADF test, which assumes independent countries, gives a different answer for gasoline use (p < 0.001), the price (0.04) and the car stock (p < 0.001) in levels. We follow CIPS because the countries are clearly not independent (see the figure, where the series move together, and the CD test below). The variables are I(1), so a cointegration test is meaningful.
Residual-based tests: Kao and a Pedroni-type group test

How to read it The Kao test, which pools the residuals and imposes common slopes, gives t = −1.69 and rejects no cointegration at 5% (p = 0.045), only just. The group-mean ADF test on country-specific residuals gives −2.97, which is not below its simulated 5% critical value (−3.14). The country statistics vary a lot: three countries have a statistic below −4 (France −5.8, Greece −4.2, Japan −4.1) and several are around −2.0 to −2.5 (Ireland, Italy, the U.K.). Residual-based tests have low power with 19 observations, and they also need the cointegrating regression to be right for every country. The tests have different nulls on slopes, so we cannot say that one is correct. The next test uses a different principle.

How to read it The Westerlund error-correction statistic is −3.00 without lags, far below the simulated 5% critical value of −2.48, and −2.44 with one lag, just below its critical value of −2.39 (p = 0.045). These tests reject no cointegration. The Pedroni-type group ADF statistic (−2.97) does not (p = 0.17). The error-correction tests use the information in the short-run dynamics and are usually more powerful than residual-based tests, which is why they reject here. With so few observations per country the lag choice matters: the evidence is weaker with one lag.
Cross-sectional dependence and the demeaned tests

How to read it The countries are cross-sectionally dependent. The Pesaran CD test on the differenced residuals is 5.68 (p < 0.001) and the mean absolute correlation between countries is 0.27. First-generation tests assume independence and over-reject when it fails. After removing the cross-sectional mean of every variable (a simple way to remove common shocks), the group ADF statistic is −3.22, below its simulated 5% critical value (−3.15, p = 0.025), and the Westerlund statistic still rejects (−3.30). Five of the six tests we ran reject at 5%, and the plain group ADF does not. The evidence points to cointegration, but it is not unanimous, and the simulated critical values assume independent random walks, so they are approximate for demeaned data.
Cross-sectional dependence and the demeaned tests

How to write it: results All four variables are I(1) according to the CIPS test, which allows for cross-sectional dependence. The Kao test rejects no cointegration at the 5% level (t = −1.69, p = 0.045). A Pedroni-type group ADF test does not (−2.97, 5% critical value −3.14), but a Westerlund-type error-correction test does (−3.00 without lags and −2.44 with one lag, against simulated 5% critical values of −2.48 and −2.39). Because the countries are cross-sectionally dependent (CD = 5.68, p < 0.001), we repeated the tests after removing cross-sectional means and both reject (group ADF p = 0.025). We read the evidence as favouring a long-run relation, with the caveat that the panel is short (T = 19) and the tests do not agree on every specification.

How to read it The fixed-effects regression in levels gives elasticities of 0.66 for income, −0.32 for the price and −0.64 for the car stock. Dynamic OLS, which adds a lead and a lag of the differenced regressors to correct for endogeneity, gives smaller numbers in the mean group: 0.36 (s.e. 0.10), −0.21 (0.06) and −0.39 (0.06). The medians (0.33, −0.17, −0.38) are close to the means, so a few countries do not drive them. Between 89% and 94% of the countries have the expected sign. The difference between the pooled static and the DOLS estimates is large, and it is a reason to trust DOLS more, although with 15 usable years per country and ten coefficients each country estimate is imprecise, so use the mean-group standard errors and not the country ones.
What to report in the paper

Item What to show Orders of integration panel unit-root tests that allow for cross-sectional dependence (CIPS), and the Fisher-ADF as a comparison Tests at least two cointegration tests with different nulls and assumptions (Kao, Pedroni, Westerlund) Critical values how they were obtained, especially in a short panel Dependence the CD test and the results after removing cross-sectional means Estimates a long-run estimator robust to endogeneity (DOLS or FMOLS) with the mean-group and pooled versions Honesty state that the tests disagree and what that means, instead of picking the one that rejects Common mistakes Testing for cointegration before checking for I(1). The tests assume integrated variables. A stationary variable in the system can produce a rejection that has nothing to do with a long-run relation.
What to report in the paper

Using one test. The tests have different nulls, different slope assumptions and different power. Show several. Ignoring cross-sectional dependence. Common shocks make the first-generation tests over-reject. Using asymptotic critical values in a short panel. With T below about 30, use simulated or bootstrap values. Taking the static levels regression as the long-run effect. Static regressions are biased in finite samples. Use DOLS or FMOLS. Treating a rejection as proof of a causal long-run effect. Cointegration shows a stable relation, not its direction.
Panel-Corrected Standard Errors (PCSE): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Comparative political economy and macroeconomics often use time-series cross-section (TSCS) data : 15 to 50 countries or states, each observed for 15 to 50 years. Our question is: how do income, the real gasoline price and the stock of cars affect gasoline consumption per car, across 18 OECD countries? The model is a pooled regression where \(g\) is gasoline use per car, \(y\) income, \(p\) the real price of gasoline and \(c\) the stock of cars per capita. Symbol Variable in the file Definition \(\ln g_{it}\) lgaspcar log gasoline consumption per car \(\ln y_{it}\) lincomep log real per-capita income \(\ln p_{it}\) lrpmg log real price of motor gasoline \(\ln c_{it}\)

lcarpcap log stock of cars per capita The coefficients are easy. The standard errors are the problem. In TSCS data the error of one country in a year is correlated with the errors of other countries in the same year (oil shocks hit everybody), the variance differs between countries, and errors are correlated over time within a country. Beck and Katz (1995) showed that the usual remedy, the Parks feasible GLS estimator, is badly overconfident unless T is much larger than N. Their alternative keeps the simple OLS coefficients and corrects only the standard errors. This is the panel-corrected standard error (PCSE) . Before you estimate anything Decide how you will handle three things: the effect of units (unit dummies or not), serial correlation (a lagged dependent variable or an AR(1) correction) and the structure of the cross-sectional covariance (full, or heteroskedasticity only). PCSE only repairs the standard errors; it does not remove omitted variables, and it needs T large enough to estimate the N × N covariance matrix, which in practice means T of at least about 15.

How to write it: model section We estimate a pooled log-linear demand equation for gasoline for 18 OECD countries over 1960–1978. Because the errors of a time-series cross-section are likely to be heteroskedastic across countries and correlated between countries in the same year, we report panel-corrected standard errors (Beck and Katz 1995) and compare them with conventional and country-clustered errors.
Load the data and see the panel

How to read it The panel is balanced: 18 countries times 19 years gives 342 observations. T = 19 clears the rule of thumb of about 15 years, but it is barely larger than N = 18, so any method that must estimate the full 18 × 18 error covariance from 19 years is on thin ice. That is exactly why Beck and Katz prefer correcting the standard errors of OLS to running Parks GLS. The mean log price (orange) rises sharply after the 1973 oil shock in every country, which is the common shock that makes cross-country errors correlated.
Pooled OLS and what is wrong with its errors

How to read it The pooled coefficients are large and very precise: income elasticity 0.89, price elasticity −0.89, car-stock elasticity −0.76. The diagnostics warn against trusting those precise errors. The Breusch-Pagan LM test rejects cross-sectional independence decisively (707 on 153 degrees of freedom), and the average absolute correlation between two countries' residuals is 0.42. The Pesaran CD test is not significant (1.22) because positive and negative correlations cancel in its sum; when the LM and CD tests disagree, the LM test is the one that detects mixed-sign dependence. The residuals are also very persistent (AR(1) coefficient 0.92) and their spread differs by a factor of five across countries, from 0.046 in Norway to 0.230 in Greece.

How to read it Compare the columns. Heteroskedasticity-only PCSE is close to the conventional errors. Full PCSE is smaller than the conventional errors (ratios 0.55 to 0.87), because the correlation between countries in this sample is partly negative. The clustered errors are four to five times larger than the conventional ones, and that gap is not about cross-sectional dependence: it comes from the residual autocorrelation of 0.92, which PCSE with no time-series correction leaves untouched. The lesson is that PCSE answers one problem only. Before reading the full PCSE column as the truth, deal with serial correlation, which is the next step.
Serial correlation: Prais-Winsten with an AR(1) coefficient

How to read it Removing the AR(1) component changes the coefficients a great deal: the income elasticity falls from 0.89 to 0.41, the price elasticity from −0.89 to −0.39, and the car-stock elasticity from −0.76 to −0.54. The standard errors double or quadruple (price: 0.026 to 0.044), and the residual AR(1) coefficient is now −0.025, so the dynamics are gone. The dynamic alternative gives a coherent story: the lagged dependent variable has a coefficient of 0.93, the short-run price elasticity is −0.08 and the implied long-run price elasticity is −1.10. A static pooled regression mixes short-run and long-run effects and is not the model to report here. Choose between Prais-Winsten and a lagged dependent variable on theory, and report both if they tell different stories.
Serial correlation: Prais-Winsten with an AR(1) coefficient

Do not skip this step PCSE alone on a series with an AR(1) coefficient of 0.92 gives confident, wrong inference. Beck and Katz (1996) recommend either a lagged dependent variable or Prais-Winsten before computing PCSE.

How to read it Country dummies move the slopes a lot: the price elasticity goes from −0.89 to −0.32, the income elasticity from 0.89 to 0.66 and the car-stock elasticity from −0.76 to −0.64, with PCSE of 0.038, 0.046 and 0.019. The pooled estimates therefore mix between-country differences with the within-country response to prices. Dummies absorb permanent differences between countries, such as fuel taxes and geography, but they also remove all between-country variation and with T = 19 they can make a lagged dependent variable biased. Treat the pooled and dummy results as a sensitivity check and say which one your argument rests on.
What to report in the paper

Item What to give Sample N, T, balanced or not, and the years Estimator OLS or Prais-Winsten, common or panel-specific rho, full or heteroskedastic-only covariance Serial correlation The estimated rho, or the lagged dependent variable, and the residual autocorrelation after the correction Cross-sectional dependence Breusch-Pagan LM (and Pesaran CD) before the correction Standard errors PCSE next to conventional and clustered errors Sensitivity With and without unit effects How to write it: results section Pooled OLS residuals reject cross-sectional independence (Breusch-Pagan LM = 707.3, p < 0.001) and are highly persistent (AR(1) = 0.92). We therefore estimate the model by Prais-Winsten with a common AR(1) coefficient of 0.92 and report panel-corrected standard errors (Beck and Katz 1995). The price elasticity of gasoline demand is −0.39 (PCSE 0.044) and the income elasticity is 0.41 (0.051). A dynamic specification with a lagged dependent variable gives a long-run price elasticity of −1.10.

Using PCSE with a short panel. With T below about 15 the covariance matrix is badly estimated. Use clustered errors or a model for the dependence instead. Ignoring serial correlation. PCSE corrects the cross-sectional part only. Treating PCSE as always larger. It can be smaller than conventional errors, as here; it is correct, not conservative. Reading PCSE as a fix for omitted variables. It changes the standard errors, not the estimates. Using it for N much larger than T. The N × N matrix is then not estimable.
Panel Local Projections: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

How does the outcome of a unit evolve after a shock to that unit? For each horizon \(h = 0, 1, \dots, H\) the panel local projection estimates where \(\alpha_{i,h}\) is a unit effect, \(\delta_{t,h}\) is an optional time effect, \(s_{i,t}\) is the shock and \(x_{i,t}\) holds the controls (lags of the outcome, of the shock and of other variables, and any variables ordered before the shock). The coefficient \(\beta_h\) is the impulse response at horizon \(h\) . Because every horizon is a separate fixed-effects regression, the method is robust to misspecification of the dynamics and does not require a balanced panel. Four checks before you trust a panel local projection

Is the shock plausibly exogenous to the unit's own outcome? The shock should be a change that is not driven by anticipated changes in the outcome (a tax change, a policy reform, an external shock). A price that responds to expected demand is not a shock. Which effects? Unit effects remove permanent differences between units. Time effects also remove everything common to all units in a period, so the response is identified from differences across units only, and the average effect of a common shock is lost. Which standard errors? The horizon- \(h\) errors overlap across horizons and are correlated within a unit, so cluster by unit. If shocks hit all units at once, errors are also correlated across units, and Driscoll-Kraay errors (which need a long time dimension) or time effects are needed.

Is T large enough? With unit effects and lagged outcomes among the controls, a short panel has Nickell bias. Check that the response is stable to the number of lags. How to write it: the model We estimate the dynamic effect of a cigarette-price increase on sales with panel local projections (Jordà 2005). For each horizon \(h = 0, \dots, 8\) years we regress log per-capita sales at \(t+h\) on the change in the log real price at \(t\) , on the contemporaneous change in log income, on two lags of the price change, of income growth and of log sales, and on state fixed effects. The price change is scaled to one standard deviation. Standard errors are clustered by state.
Load the panel and check its structure

How to read it The panel is balanced: 46 states observed for 30 years (1963-92). Log sales and log price are persistent, so the shock used is the one-year change in log price ( d_log_price , mean 0.011, s.d. 0.060). The per-state unit-root test rejects a unit root in none of the states for the levels and in only 13% for the change, but with 30 years per state and two lags the test has little power, so treat it as a warning about persistence, not proof. Because every state has all 30 years, no grid gaps need filling.

How to read it Each row is a separate regression of log sales at t+h on the price shock, with state effects, two lags and the contemporaneous income change, scaled to a one-standard-deviation shock. Sales fall by 1.9% on impact (-0.0192, s.e. 0.0015), the response deepens to a peak of -0.0369 at horizon 3, and decays to -0.0255 by horizon 8. Every horizon is significant at 1%, and the 95% band stays well away from zero. The observation count drops from 1,242 to 874 as the horizon grows because later outcomes need more future years.
Choose the effects: pooled, unit or unit and time

How to read it The effects choice matters for the shape. Pooled and unit-effects responses are almost identical (about -0.036 at horizon 4), so state-level differences in average sales do not drive the result. Adding year effects shrinks the response (-0.018 at horizon 4, -0.008 at horizon 8) because common national shocks, such as federal tax changes and health campaigns, move prices and sales together. Report which comparison you mean: unit effects give the within-state response to a price change; two-way effects give the response relative to other states in the same year.

How to read it Driscoll-Kraay errors are two to six times larger than clustered errors and grow with the horizon (0.0081 versus 0.0020 at horizon 4, 0.0185 versus 0.0028 at horizon 8). Clustering by state allows arbitrary serial correlation within a state but assumes states are independent; Driscoll-Kraay also allows common shocks across states, which matters here because the years are shared. With only 30 periods, the Driscoll-Kraay errors are the more cautious choice; the response stays significantly negative through horizon 8 under both.
Robustness: lags, outcome, controls and leave-one-state-out

How to read it The impact and peak responses barely move: -0.018 to -0.020 at horizon 0 and -0.033 to -0.039 at horizon 4 across one lag, four lags and no income control. The far horizon is less stable (-0.008 with four lags against -0.032 with one), so quote the horizon 8 value with care. The change-since-t-1 outcome matches the baseline exactly because the regression includes a lag of the outcome, as expected. Dropping any one state leaves the horizon 4 response between -0.0369 and -0.0357, and all 46 runs are negative, so no single state drives it.

How to write it: results A one-standard-deviation increase in the annual change in log cigarette price (about 6 percentage points) lowers per-capita sales by 1.9% on impact. The response grows to a peak of 3.7% after three years (95% CI -4.0% to -3.3%, state-clustered) and is still 2.6% below its starting path after eight years. The estimates use local projections with state fixed effects, two lags of sales and the price change, and a contemporaneous income control. The impact and peak responses are stable across lag length, outcome definition and leave-one-state-out checks. Driscoll-Kraay standard errors are larger but the response remains significant through horizon 8. With year effects the response is smaller (1.8% at horizon 4), so the result partly reflects national co-movement of prices and sales. With T = 30 and lagged outcomes among the regressors, fixed-effect estimates carry a small Nickell-type bias.
