Use the government budget constraint to link monetary and fiscal policy, classify policy regimes as active or passive (Leeper, 1991), and understand the fiscal theory of the price level. Analyse the inflation tax on nominal debt and apply the framework to the 2021–23 inflation.

Let \(B_{t-1}\) be nominal one-period debt maturing at \(t\) , \(s_t\) the real primary surplus and \(P_t\) the price level. In equilibrium the real value of outstanding debt equals the present value of surpluses: where \(\Lambda\) is the real stochastic discount factor. Seigniorage can be included in \(s_t\) . This valuation equation must hold in every equilibrium; the question is which variable adjusts to make it hold.

Leeper (1991) calls a policy active if it is not constrained by current budget conditions and pursues its own objective, and passive if it responds to current conditions to satisfy the other authority's constraints. With a monetary rule \(i_t=\phi_\pi\pi_t\) and a surplus rule \(s_t=\psi b_{t-1}+z_t\) (with \(b\) real debt): Passive fiscal ( \(\psi>1/\beta-1\) ) Active fiscal ( \(\psi<1/\beta-1\) ) Active monetary ( \(\phi_\pi>1\) ) Unique equilibrium: monetary policy determines inflation; surpluses adjust (Regime M) No stable equilibrium Passive monetary ( \(\phi_\pi<1\) ) Indeterminacy Unique equilibrium: fiscal policy determines the price level (Regime F) In Regime M a debt-financed transfer leads to higher future taxes; Ricardian equivalence holds and inflation does not move. In Regime F surpluses do not respond to debt, so the price level must jump to make the real value of debt equal to the present value of surpluses: unfunded transfers are inflationary.
3. The fiscal theory of the price level

The fiscal theory (Leeper, 1991; Sims, 1994; Woodford, 1995; Cochrane, 2023) reads the valuation equation as an equilibrium condition that determines the price level, like a stock price determined by the present value of dividends. Key implications: A fiscal expansion without expected future surpluses raises inflation even with an unchanged policy rate. With long-term debt, the adjustment can come through a gradual rise in inflation and a fall in bond prices rather than a price-level jump, so a fiscal shock produces persistent inflation (Cochrane, 2001). An interest-rate rise with passive fiscal policy can raise inflation in the short run in some versions (the "Neo-Fisherian" result), because higher interest costs are not backed by surpluses.
3. The fiscal theory of the price level
Critics question whether governments can credibly commit to "non-Ricardian" behaviour and whether the theory's equilibrium selection is plausible (Buiter, 2002; Niepelt, 2004).

Sargent and Wallace (1981) show that if fiscal policy is dominant and the public will only hold a limited amount of debt, tighter money today means more debt and therefore more seigniorage, and higher inflation, later. Monetary control of inflation requires fiscal backing. Many hyperinflations and the high inflation of several emerging markets fit this pattern.
5. The inflation tax on nominal debt

Surprise inflation lowers the real value of nominal debt with fixed coupons. In the debt-ratio decomposition the nominal-growth term splits into real growth and inflation. In 2021–2023 U.S. inflation lowered the federal debt ratio by roughly 17 points of GDP in gross terms (Exercise 11.2). Hall and Sargent (2011) show that inflation and growth were the main forces that reduced U.S. debt after World War II.
6. The 2021–23 inflation through a fiscal lens

Large pandemic transfers in 2020–21, with no announced future surpluses, coincided with the inflation surge. Fiscal-theory accounts (Cochrane, 2023; Bianchi, Faccini and Melosi, 2023) attribute part of the inflation to unfunded fiscal expansion; Bianchi, Faccini and Melosi distinguish funded and unfunded spending in an estimated model with regime switching. Other accounts emphasise supply-chain disruptions, energy prices and labour-market tightness with a steep Phillips curve (Bernanke and Blanchard, 2023). The episodes need not be mutually exclusive.

Lecture 12 of Monetary Economics (Part IV · Heterogeneity and estimation): full notes, problem set and coding exercises.

Understand how household heterogeneity changes the transmission of monetary policy. Decompose the consumption response into direct and indirect effects, derive the two-agent (TANK) model analytically, and see why high marginal propensities to consume (MPCs) and the distribution of liquid wealth are central to Heterogeneous-Agent New Keynesian (HANK) models.

In the representative-agent model (RANK), consumption responds to interest rates almost entirely through intertemporal substitution: \(c_t=E_tc_{t+1}-\frac1\sigma r_t\) . Kaplan, Moll and Violante (2018) decompose the aggregate consumption response to a rate cut into a direct effect — the response to the change in interest rates holding income fixed — and indirect effects that work through the general-equilibrium rise in labour income, profits and transfers. In RANK the direct effect accounts for about 95% of the response. In their two-asset HANK model it accounts for less than a third; the rest comes from households with high MPCs spending the extra income.

Bilbiie (2008, 2020) gives an analytical benchmark. A share \(\lambda\) of households are hand-to-mouth (H) and consume their income each period; the rest are savers (S) who satisfy the Euler equation. If hand-to-mouth income moves with aggregate income with elasticity \(\chi\) , \(c^H_t=\chi y_t\) , then market clearing \(y_t=\lambda c^H_t+(1-\lambda)c^S_t\) gives \(y_t=\frac{1-\lambda}{1-\lambda\chi}c^S_t\) , and the aggregate IS curve becomes If \(\chi>1\) (hand-to-mouth income is more cyclical than average, inequality is countercyclical), \(\delta>1\) : heterogeneity amplifies monetary policy. If \(\chi<1\) (for example, profits accrue to savers or transfers cushion the poor), heterogeneity dampens it. If \(\lambda\chi\to1\) the multiplier explodes; for \(\lambda\chi>1\) the IS logic is inverted and determinacy requires different policy rules.

With idiosyncratic risk and transitions between types, the Euler equation also acquires a discount factor \(M\neq1\) on expected future output, giving the "discounted" Euler equation of Lecture 10 when \(M<1\) and resolving the forward-guidance puzzle.
3. The household block of a HANK model

The core of a HANK model is an income-fluctuation problem: with idiosyncratic productivity \(z\) . It is solved efficiently by the endogenous grid method (Carroll, 2006): invert the Euler equation \(u'(c)=\beta(1+r)E[u'(c')]\) on a grid of next-period assets. The stationary distribution follows from iterating the transition of the histogram (Young, 2010). The key outputs for monetary policy are the distribution of MPCs and the sensitivity of aggregate saving to \(r\) . The MPC puzzle. Empirical quarterly MPCs out of small windfalls are around 0.15–0.25 (Johnson, Parker and Souleles, 2006; Parker et al., 2013; Fagereng, Holm and Natvik, 2021). One-asset models match this only if households are poor on average, at odds with total wealth in the data. Two-asset models distinguish a low-return liquid asset from a high-return illiquid asset with adjustment costs. Many households are "wealthy hand-to-mouth" (Kaplan, Violante and Weidner, 2014): they own housing or retirement wealth but little liquid wealth, and they have high MPCs.

Modern methods linearise the aggregate dynamics around the stationary distribution. The sequence-space Jacobian method (Auclert, Bardóczy, Rognlie and Straub, 2021) computes how aggregate household outcomes respond to sequences of prices and solves for equilibrium paths with a few linear-algebra operations. Dynare 6 includes support for heterogeneous-agent blocks, and the method underlies most current HANK work. Intertemporal MPCs — how spending responds over time to an income change — summarise the household block for fiscal and monetary analysis (Auclert, Rognlie and Straub, 2024).

Monetary policy redistributes through several channels (Auclert, 2019): the earnings heterogeneity channel — the incomes of some groups are more cyclical; the income composition channel — labour versus capital income; the Fisher channel — surprise inflation transfers wealth from nominal creditors to debtors; the interest-rate exposure channel — households with short-duration assets and long-duration liabilities gain when rates rise, and vice versa. Because MPCs are correlated with these exposures, redistribution has aggregate effects. Patterson (2023) shows that workers whose earnings are most cyclical also have high MPCs, which amplifies shocks.

Korean households hold most wealth in housing and have high levels of debt, much of it at variable rates. This raises the cash-flow effects of monetary policy on indebted households and makes the interest-rate exposure channel especially important; two-asset HANK models calibrated to Korean balance-sheet data are a natural tool for studying it.

The first-order solution of a DSGE model is a linear transition equation for the state vector, and the observables are linear combinations of states plus measurement error: The mapping from structural parameters \(\theta\) to \(P\) and \(Q\) is computed by the QZ-based solver (Lecture 5); if the Blanchard–Kahn conditions fail, \(\theta\) is assigned zero posterior probability.

With Gaussian shocks the likelihood is computed recursively. Starting from the unconditional mean and variance of \(s_0\) : and \(\log L(\theta)=-\frac12\sum_t\left[k\log2\pi+\log|F_t|+v_t'F_t^{-1}v_t\right]\) . The number of shocks plus measurement errors must be at least the number of observables to avoid stochastic singularity.

Bayes' rule gives \(p(\theta\mid Y)\propto L(Y\mid\theta)p(\theta)\) . Priors encode information from micro data and other studies and regularise weakly identified parameters. Standard choices: Beta distributions for parameters in \((0,1)\) such as autocorrelations and Calvo probabilities; Gamma for positive parameters such as the Phillips-curve slope; Normal for policy coefficients; inverse Gamma for shock standard deviations. Priors should be reported and their influence checked by comparing prior and posterior densities.

Mode. Maximise \(\log p(\theta\mid Y)\) numerically after transforming parameters to an unbounded space (logs for positive parameters, logits for probabilities). Multiple starting points guard against local maxima. Metropolis–Hastings. Draw \(\theta'=\theta^{(j)}+c\,\Sigma^{1/2}\eta\) , \(\eta\sim N(0,I)\) , with \(\Sigma\) the inverse Hessian at the mode, and accept with probability \(\min\{1,p(\theta'\mid Y)/p(\theta^{(j)}\mid Y)\}\) . When sampling in transformed parameters, add the log Jacobian of the transformation. Tune \(c\) for an acceptance rate of 20–35%. Diagnostics. Run several chains, check trace plots, the Brooks–Gelman (1998) diagnostic and effective sample sizes. Model comparison. The marginal likelihood \(p(Y)=\int L(Y\mid\theta)p(\theta)d\theta\) (computed with the modified harmonic mean, Geweke 1999) gives posterior odds between models.

A parameter is weakly identified if the likelihood is flat in its direction. Common examples in monetary models: the Taylor-rule inflation coefficient when policy has kept inflation stable (Cochrane, 2011), the Phillips-curve slope when inflation barely moves, and the separate roles of Calvo and indexation parameters. Iskrev (2010) proposes checking the rank of the Jacobian of the model's moments with respect to \(\theta\) ; Dynare's identification command implements such tests.

Smets and Wouters (2007) estimate a medium-scale model with seven shocks and seven U.S. observables; it forecasts as well as Bayesian VARs and has become a template for central-bank models (the ECB's NAWM, the Fed's EDO and FRB/US for comparison, the Bank of Korea's BOKDSGE). Estimated models attribute output fluctuations largely to demand and investment-specific shocks at business-cycle frequencies and to monetary shocks only modestly, and they imply a flat Phillips curve with large estimated price and wage rigidity. Lecture 14 of Monetary Economics (Part V · Evidence and practice): full notes, problem set and coding exercises.

Understand the identification problem in measuring the effects of monetary policy, and compare recursive VARs, narrative shocks, high-frequency identification and local projections. Interpret the price puzzle, information effects and the empirical evidence that DSGE impulse responses should match.

Policy rates respond to the state of the economy, so the correlation between interest rates and output says little about the causal effect of policy. Write policy as a rule plus a shock, \(i_t=f(\Omega_t)+\varepsilon^m_t\) , where \(\Omega_t\) is the central bank's information. The effects of policy are the responses to \(\varepsilon^m_t\) , the part of policy not explained by the systematic response. Every identification strategy is a way of isolating \(\varepsilon^m_t\) (Ramey, 2016).

Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (1999) estimate a VAR \(Y_t=c+\sum_{l=1}^pA_lY_{t-l}+u_t\) and assume that output and prices do not respond to the policy shock within the period, while policy may respond to them. With the policy rate ordered last, the shock is the last element of \(S^{-1}u_t\) , where \(S\) is the Cholesky factor of \(\Sigma_u\) . The approach produces the facts of Lecture 1 — a gradual fall in output with a trough after 1–2 years — but also the price puzzle : prices often rise after a tightening (Sims, 1992). The usual explanation is that the Fed reacts to information about future inflation not in the VAR. Adding commodity prices or Fed forecasts reduces the puzzle.

Romer and Romer (2004) construct the Fed's intended funds-rate changes at each FOMC meeting from narrative records and regress them on the Greenbook forecasts the Fed was looking at; the residual is a shock purged of the Fed's information. With these shocks, output falls substantially more than in recursive VARs, and prices fall after a delay. Updates extend the series to 2019 (Exercise 14.2 uses Acosta's update). Narrative methods depend on the quality of records and forecasts.

Monetary-policy surprises can be measured as changes in interest-rate futures in a narrow window (e.g., 30 minutes) around FOMC announcements (Kuttner, 2001; Gürkaynak, Sack and Swanson, 2005). Within the window, nothing else systematically moves rates, so the surprise is plausibly exogenous. Surprises are used as external instruments (proxies) in VARs (Stock and Watson, 2012; Mertens and Ravn, 2013; Gertler and Karadi, 2015). Two problems arise: Information effects. A surprise tightening can signal that the Fed sees a stronger economy, so stock prices may rise rather than fall (Nakamura and Steinsson, 2018). Jarociński and Karadi (2020) separate pure policy shocks from information shocks using the sign of the co-movement between interest rates and stock prices.

Predictability. Surprises are predictable from public data released before the announcement, reflecting the Fed's response to news (Bauer and Swanson, 2023); orthogonalising them yields cleaner shocks.

Jordà (2005) estimates the impulse response at horizon \(h\) directly: Local projections do not impose the dynamic restrictions of a VAR, so they are robust to misspecification at long horizons, but they have larger variance. Plagborg-Møller and Wolf (2021) show that LPs and VARs estimate the same population impulse responses with enough lags; the difference is a bias–variance trade-off (Li, Plagborg-Møller and Wolf, 2024). Residuals are serially correlated by construction, so inference uses heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-robust standard errors or lag augmentation (Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller, 2021).

Across methods, a 100 bp contractionary shock lowers industrial production by roughly 1–5% at the peak after one to two years and eventually lowers the price level, with substantial uncertainty about magnitudes and timing (Ramey, 2016). Estimates based on high-frequency instruments and on narrative shocks tend to find larger output effects than recursive VARs. Monetary shocks explain a modest share of output fluctuations — systematic policy matters more than shocks. Matching these responses is a common way to estimate DSGE models (Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans, 2005): choose structural parameters to minimise the distance between model and VAR impulse responses.

For small open economies such as Korea, identification must account for the exchange rate and foreign shocks (Kim and Roubini, 2000). Block-exogeneity assumptions for foreign variables and high-frequency surprises from government bond futures around Bank of Korea announcements have been used. For economies with monetary targeting and administered rates, such as Bangladesh before 2023, the policy instrument itself must be chosen carefully.

The CPI, however, rises for a long time instead of falling: the "price puzzle" (Sims, 1992). The usual interpretation is misidentification. The Fed raises rates when it expects inflation, using information the VAR does not contain, so the "shock" is partly a response to anticipated inflation. Adding commodity prices or Greenbook forecasts reduces the puzzle, and narrative or high-frequency identification (Exercise 14.2) removes most of it. Note also the sensitivity to the sample: the 1970s, with oil shocks and accommodative policy, drive much of the puzzle.
Exercise 14.2 — Local projections with Romer–Romer shocks

Data: mp_shocks_monthly.csv (Romer–Romer narrative shocks, updated by Acosta, 1969–2019) and us_monthly.csv . Romer and Romer (2004) purge the Fed's intended rate changes of the Greenbook forecasts the Fed reacted to. Estimate for \(y\) = 100 log IP and 100 log CPI, \(h=0,\dots,48\) , on 1970–2007, with Newey–West standard errors. Report \(\beta_h\) per 1 percentage point shock at 6, 12, 24, 36 and 48 months. Compare the shapes with the recursive VAR of Exercise 14.1. Is there a price puzzle? Why are local projections less efficient but more robust than a VAR? File ex14_2.m File ex14_2.m Output: With narrative shocks, a 1 pp tightening is followed by a large fall in industrial production of about 2% after two years, roughly twice the VAR response once both are scaled to a 1 pp rate change. Prices still rise for one to two years — a short-lived price puzzle that is statistically significant here — before falling steadily, by about 2.5% after four years. Romer and Romer (2004) also find that prices respond only after a long delay. Local projections estimate each horizon by a separate regression, so they do not impose the VAR's dynamic restrictions: they are robust to misspecification at long horizons but have larger standard errors, as the widening intervals show. Plagborg-Møller and Wolf (2021) show that VARs and LPs estimate the same impulse responses in population; the choice is a bias–variance trade-off (Li, Plagborg-Møller and Wolf, 2024).

Lecture 15 of Monetary Economics (Part V · Evidence and practice): full notes, problem set and coding exercises.

Connect the theory of the course to how central banks operate: independence and mandates, communication, inflation expectations, operating frameworks and balance sheets, and the measurement of inflation risk. Evaluate the evidence on inflation targeting and the lessons of the 2021–23 inflation.

The time-inconsistency problem (Lecture 6) motivates delegating monetary policy to an independent central bank with a clear mandate (Rogoff, 1985). Cross-country evidence shows a negative correlation between legal independence and inflation in advanced economies (Alesina and Summers, 1993), weaker evidence for emerging markets, where de facto independence (for example, governor turnover) matters more (Cukierman, Webb and Neyapti, 1992). Garriga (2016) and Romelli (2022) provide updated indices. Mandates differ: the Fed has a dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices; the ECB a primary price-stability mandate; the Bank of Korea a price-stability mandate with attention to financial stability; Bangladesh Bank broader development objectives.

Inflation targeters have had lower and more stable inflation since the 1990s. But so did non-targeters. Ball and Sheridan (2005) show that once one controls for initial inflation (regression to the mean), the advantage of inflation targeting in OECD countries largely disappears. Studies of emerging markets find larger effects (Gonçalves and Salles, 2008), but adoption is endogenous: countries tend to adopt inflation targeting at the end of a reform process — after granting independence, reducing fiscal dominance and abandoning pegs — so pre-adoption trends must be modelled. Modern staggered difference-in-differences and event-study estimators (Callaway and Sant'Anna, 2021; Sun and Abraham, 2021) address the bias of two-way fixed effects with heterogeneous adoption dates. Exercise 15.1 reproduces the Ball–Sheridan logic with World Bank data.

Because the New Keynesian model is forward-looking, expectations are the main transmission channel, and communication is a policy instrument. Central banks publish forecasts, policy-rate projections (the Fed's dot plot, the Riksbank's and Norges Bank's rate paths), minutes and press conferences. Long-term expectations in surveys and break-even inflation stayed relatively anchored in 2021–23, which helped bring inflation down without a deep recession. Households' and firms' expectations, however, are dispersed, respond to salient prices such as food and gasoline, and are often far from professional forecasts (Coibion, Gorodnichenko and Kumar, 2018). Simple communication reaches the public better than technical statements (Haldane and McMahon, 2018).

Policymakers care about the risk of very high or very low inflation, not only the mean. Inflation-at-risk estimates the conditional quantiles of future inflation, \(Q_\tau(\pi_{t+h}\mid X_t)\) , by quantile regression, analogous to growth-at-risk (Adrian, Boyarchenko and Giannone, 2019; López-Salido and Loria, 2024). Inflation persistence is typically stronger in the upper tail: when inflation is high, the risk of further increases rises disproportionately. Inflation targeting and central-bank independence compress the predictive distribution, but their additional predictive power is limited once current inflation is known, and they offered limited protection against the common 2021–23 shock. Exercise 15.2 estimates a pooled cross-country version.
5. Operating frameworks and the balance sheet

Central banks implement the policy rate either in a corridor system with scarce reserves, steering the overnight rate between a lending and a deposit facility through open-market operations, or in a floor system with abundant reserves, where the rate paid on reserves sets the floor (the Fed since 2008, ECB since 2015). Large balance sheets after QE have fiscal implications: when policy rates rise, interest paid on reserves exceeds income on long-term assets, and central banks such as the Fed and the Bank of England have reported operating losses since 2022. Quantitative tightening reduces the balance sheet gradually.

The inflation surge followed pandemic demand, supply-chain disruptions, energy price shocks after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and large fiscal transfers. Central banks initially judged it transitory, then raised rates at the fastest pace in four decades. Lessons that recur in reviews: inflation can rise quickly and nonlinearly when labour markets are tight and shocks are large (Benigno and Eggertsson, 2023); forward guidance that commits to low rates can delay the response; make-up strategies designed for the lower bound were ill-suited to an inflation surge (the Fed removed its average-inflation-targeting language in 2025); and anchored expectations and credibility made disinflation less costly. Bernanke and Blanchard (2023) decompose U.S. inflation into contributions from energy and food prices, shortages and labour-market tightness.
7. Monetary policy in emerging and developing economies

Emerging-market central banks face fiscal dominance, dollarisation, shallow financial markets and volatile capital flows. Many combine interest-rate policy with foreign-exchange intervention and macroprudential tools (Lecture 8). Bangladesh's shift from monetary targeting to an interest-rate corridor (2023), a crawling peg (2024) and a market-based exchange rate (2025) illustrates the transition towards modern frameworks under high inflation and reserve pressures. Korea's experience since 1998 shows how inflation targeting with a flexible exchange rate can lower inflation and pass-through.

The course moved from the quantity theory to the New Keynesian model, optimal policy, open economies, financial frictions, the lower bound, fiscal interactions, heterogeneity, estimation and identification. A good policy analysis combines a model for mechanisms and counterfactuals (Lectures 3–12), estimation that disciplines the model with data (Lecture 13), credible empirical evidence on transmission (Lecture 14), and institutional knowledge of how policy is made (this lecture).

Explain why central-bank independence can lower inflation without raising output volatility in the Rogoff (1985) model. Using Exercise 15.1, explain the regression-to-the-mean critique of simple comparisons between inflation targeters and non-targeters. Why might household inflation expectations differ systematically from professional forecasts? What does this imply for communication? Explain the difference between corridor and floor systems for implementing the policy rate. Write a two-page memo assessing the monetary-policy framework of Korea or Bangladesh using the tools of this course.
Exercise 15.1 — Did inflation targeting lower inflation? A Ball–Sheridan comparison

Data: cpi_inflation_wdi.csv — World Bank CPI inflation for about 190 countries, 1960–2024, with inflation-targeting adoption years ( it_year ). For each inflation-targeting country that adopted between 1990 and 2016, compute average inflation in the five years before and the five years after adoption. For non-targeters, use the same windows around 1998. Drop countries whose pre-period inflation exceeds 40%. Compare the average change in inflation for adopters and non-adopters. Following Ball and Sheridan (2005), regress the change on an IT dummy and pre-period inflation. What happens to the IT coefficient once you control for initial inflation, and why? File ex15_1.m File ex15_1.m Output: Inflation fell by about 5.5 points in adopters and 4.6 points in non-adopters over the same kind of window: adopters started from slightly higher inflation, and inflation fell almost everywhere in the 1990s. The raw difference of under one point is small and statistically insignificant. Once the change is regressed on initial inflation, the strong negative coefficient on pre-period inflation captures regression to the mean and the global disinflation, and the IT coefficient shrinks further towards zero — Ball and Sheridan's (2005) finding. This does not show that inflation targeting is useless: adoption is endogenous and often comes at the end of a reform process (central-bank independence, ending exchange-rate pegs), which is why staggered difference-in-differences and event-study designs that model the timing of adoption give more credible answers.
Exercise 15.2 — Inflation at risk: do monetary frameworks thin the upper tail?

Data: cpi_inflation_wdi.csv , 1985–2024; observations with inflation above 50% are excluded. Estimate pooled quantile regressions of next year's inflation on current inflation, an inflation-targeting indicator and their interaction, for \(\tau\in\{0.1,0.5,0.9\}\) , using qreg . Report the coefficients. Predict the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles of next year's inflation when current inflation is 3% and when it is 8%, with and without inflation targeting. Is the effect of the framework larger in the upper tail? What are the limits of this exercise? File ex15_2.m File ex15_2.m Output: Persistence rises across the distribution: the coefficient on current inflation is about 0.3 at the 10th percentile, 0.7 at the median and about 1 at the 90th, so high inflation raises the risk of even higher inflation more than it raises the median. Under inflation targeting the median is almost unchanged, but the distribution is compressed from both sides: the 90th percentile is about 2 points lower and the 10th percentile is higher, which reduces both inflation and deflation risk. The exercise is descriptive: IT countries differ in many ways (income, institutions, exchange-rate regimes), adoption is endogenous, pooling assumes common coefficients across very different economies, and the 2021–23 global surge showed that frameworks offer limited protection against large common shocks. Adding income and central-bank independence as controls, or country fixed effects, is a natural extension.

Topic Outline — Graduate course notes in monetary economics covering money demand, the classical and New Keynesian models, optimal policy and rules and more.
A condensed summary of the core results of the course.

Quantity equation: \(\pi\approx\Delta m+\Delta v-\Delta y\) ; money and inflation move together across long horizons and across countries, but velocity shocks dominate at low inflation. Welfare cost of inflation: the area under the inverse money-demand curve; small for moderate inflation. The Friedman rule \(i=0\) is optimal in flexible-price money models. Classical model: money is neutral; an interest-rate peg leaves the price level indeterminate; \(\phi_\pi>1\) restores a unique equilibrium.

Phillips curve: \(\pi_t=\beta E_t\pi_{t+1}+\kappa\tilde y_t\) , with \(\kappa\) falling steeply in the Calvo parameter \(\theta\) . Dynamic IS: \(\tilde y_t=E_t\tilde y_{t+1}-\sigma^{-1}(i_t-E_t\pi_{t+1}-r^n_t)\) . Determinacy under a Taylor rule: \(\kappa(\phi_\pi-1)+(1-\beta)\phi_y>0\) . Welfare loss: \(\tfrac12E_0\sum\beta^t(\pi_t^2+\vartheta\tilde y_t^2)\) with \(\vartheta=\kappa/\epsilon\) . Discretion: \(\kappa\pi_t=-\vartheta\tilde y_t\) . Commitment: \(\kappa\pi_t=-\vartheta(\tilde y_t-\tilde y_{t-1})\) , which makes the price level stationary; price-level targeting mimics this history dependence.

Small open economy: the model keeps its closed-economy form in domestic inflation; strict domestic-inflation targeting is optimal in the baseline, and pegs raise output volatility. Financial accelerator: net worth falls after a tightening, the external finance premium rises, and the output loss is larger and more persistent. Zero lower bound: falling inflation raises the real rate in a trap; forward guidance works through expected inflation and output, but the standard model exaggerates distant promises (forward-guidance puzzle). Monetary–fiscal interactions: a unique equilibrium needs one active and one passive authority; with passive money and active fiscal policy, the price level adjusts to make debt sustainable (fiscal theory). Heterogeneity: in TANK the IS slope is scaled by \(\delta=\frac{1-\lambda}{1-\lambda\chi}\) ; high MPCs make indirect income effects dominate transmission.

Bayesian estimation: state-space likelihood from the Kalman filter, priors, posterior mode and Metropolis–Hastings; the inflation response in the policy rule is often weakly identified. Identification: recursive VARs show a price puzzle; narrative and high-frequency shocks with local projections give larger output effects and a smaller price puzzle. Central banking: inflation targeting is associated with lower inflation risk, but much of the measured effect reflects global disinflation and reforms that came before adoption.
Assignments: Problem Sets and Solutions — Graduate course notes in monetary economics covering money demand, the classical and New Keynesian models and more.
Each problem set combines derivations with a short MATLAB/Dynare task. Show intermediate steps, state timing conventions, and submit .mod and .m files that run from a clean folder.
Problem set 1 — Money demand and the cost of inflation (Lectures 1–2)

From the quantity equation \(M_tV_t=P_tY_t\) , derive the relation between inflation, money growth, velocity growth and output growth. Under semi-log money demand \(\log(M/PY)=a-\xi i\) , derive the Bailey welfare cost of a nominal rate \(i\) . In a cash-in-advance economy where only consumption requires cash, show that money growth acts as a tax on market work. MATLAB: estimate \(\xi\) for M1 on us_quarterly.csv and compute the welfare cost of 2% versus 10% inflation. Solution guidance: The Bailey cost is the area under the inverse money-demand curve, \(w(i)=\int_0^i m(x)\,dx-i\,m(i)\) , which for the semi-log form is \(\frac{e^{a}}{\xi}\left[1-(1+\xi i)e^{-\xi i}\right]\) . In the cash-in-advance model the first-order conditions give \(u_l/u_c=w/R\) : the gross nominal rate \(R\) drives a wedge between the marginal rate of substitution and the real wage, which vanishes only at the Friedman rule.
Problem set 2 — The classical monetary model (Lecture 3)

Show that output, employment and the real interest rate do not depend on monetary policy. Under an exogenous AR(1) money-growth process, solve for inflation and the nominal rate by the method of undetermined coefficients. Show that an interest-rate peg leaves the price level indeterminate and that \(\phi_\pi>1\) restores determinacy. Dynare: write a .mod file for the model and confirm the impact response of the nominal rate. Solution guidance: The real block (labour supply, production, Euler equation) is self-contained. Combining money demand with the Fisher equation gives a forward-looking difference equation in the price level; with \(\phi_\pi>1\) the only bounded solution is the forward solution. Check Blanchard–Kahn: one forward-looking variable requires one unstable root.
Problem set 3 — Price setting and the New Keynesian Phillips curve (Lecture 4)

Derive the optimal reset price under Calvo pricing and log-linearize it. Derive \(\pi_t=\beta E_t\pi_{t+1}+\kappa\tilde y_t\) and express \(\kappa\) in terms of \(\theta,\beta,\sigma,\varphi,\alpha,\epsilon\) . Show how real rigidities (decreasing returns, strategic complementarity) flatten the Phillips curve. Add Calvo wage setting and derive the wage-inflation equation. Solution guidance: Start from the reset-price first-order condition, divide by the price level and linearize around the zero-inflation steady state. Combine with the law of motion of the aggregate price index, \(\pi_t=(1-\theta)(p^*_t-p_{t-1})\) . The slope \(\lambda=\frac{(1-\theta)(1-\beta\theta)}{\theta}\Theta\) falls steeply as \(\theta\to1\) .
Problem set 4 — The New Keynesian model and optimal policy (Lectures 5–6)

Solve the three-equation model under a Taylor rule and an AR(1) monetary shock; derive the impact output gap and inflation. Derive the determinacy condition \(\kappa(\phi_\pi-1)+(1-\beta)\phi_y>0\) . Derive the second-order welfare loss and the weight \(\vartheta=\kappa/\epsilon\) on the output gap. Derive optimal policy under discretion and under commitment after a cost-push shock. Solution guidance: Guess \(\tilde y_t=\psi_y v_t\) , \(\pi_t=\psi_\pi v_t\) and match coefficients. Under discretion the targeting rule is \(\kappa\pi_t=-\vartheta\tilde y_t\) ; under commitment it is \(\kappa\pi_t=-\vartheta(\tilde y_t-\tilde y_{t-1})\) , equivalently \(\kappa\hat p_t=-\vartheta\tilde y_t\) , which makes the price level stationary.
Problem set 5 — Policy rules and open economies (Lectures 7–8)

Estimate a Taylor rule with interest-rate smoothing before and after 1979; compute the long-run inflation response. Show how a price-level target reproduces the history dependence of commitment. In the Galí–Monacelli model, derive the open-economy IS curve and Phillips curve for domestic inflation. Dynare: compare a domestic-inflation rule, a CPI-inflation rule and an exchange-rate peg. Solution guidance: The long-run response is \(\phi_\pi/(1-\rho)\) when the rule is written as \(i_t=\rho i_{t-1}+\phi_\pi\pi_t+\dots\) ; use lagged variables as instruments to deal with simultaneity. In the small open economy, openness changes the slope coefficients through \(\sigma_\alpha\) but the model keeps the closed-economy form in terms of domestic inflation and the output gap.
Problem set 6 — Financial frictions and the zero lower bound (Lectures 9–10)

Explain how the external finance premium depends on borrower net worth in the BGG model. Solve a two-state liquidity trap with absorbing exit and derive output and inflation in the trap. Show that the effect of a promised rate cut \(T\) periods ahead on today's output does not decline with \(T\) under the standard Euler equation. Show how a discounted Euler equation resolves the forward-guidance puzzle. Solution guidance: In the trap state the system is \(x_L=\mu x_L+\sigma^{-1}(\mu\pi_L+r^n_L)\) , \(\pi_L=\kappa x_L+\beta\mu\pi_L\) ; solve the two linear equations and note that the denominator \((1-\mu)(1-\beta\mu)-\sigma^{-1}\mu\kappa\) can approach zero. Under the standard Euler equation, iterate forward: \(x_t=-\sigma^{-1}\sum_{j\ge0}E_t(i_{t+j}-\pi_{t+j+1}-r^n_{t+j})\) .
Problem set 7 — Monetary–fiscal interactions and HANK (Lectures 11–12)

Classify policy as active or passive and derive the determinacy conditions with a debt-feedback tax rule. Use the government valuation equation to explain the fiscal theory of the price level. Derive the aggregate IS curve of a two-agent model and the amplification factor \(\delta\) . Explain why high marginal propensities to consume make indirect effects of monetary policy dominate. Solution guidance: A unique equilibrium needs exactly one active authority. In the TANK model the aggregate IS curve has the slope \(\sigma^{-1}\delta\) with \(\delta=\frac{1-\lambda}{1-\lambda\chi}\) ; amplification occurs when hand-to-mouth income is more cyclical than average ( \(\chi>1\) ).

Write the state-space form of the three-equation model and the Kalman-filter log-likelihood. Set priors for \(\kappa,\phi_\pi,\phi_y\) and explain how to detect weak identification. Explain the price puzzle in a recursive VAR and how narrative or high-frequency shocks address it. Compare VAR and local-projection impulse responses; explain the bias–variance trade-off. Solution guidance: Report the acceptance rate, run several chains and compare prior and posterior densities. A posterior that barely moves from its prior signals weak identification. A recursive ordering assumes the policy rate reacts to, but does not affect within the period, the variables ordered before it; external instruments require relevance and exogeneity.

This course studies the theory and evidence of monetary policy. It begins with money demand, money in general equilibrium and the classical monetary model, then develops the New Keynesian framework in depth: price and wage setting, determinacy, optimal policy and policy rules. Extensions cover small open economies, financial frictions, the zero lower bound and unconventional policy, monetary–fiscal interactions, and heterogeneous-agent (HANK) transmission. The course closes with Bayesian estimation of DSGE models, the identification of monetary policy shocks, and central banking in practice. Models are solved and estimated in Dynare; data work uses MATLAB.

Graduate macroeconomics (or Advanced Macroeconomics, Course 04); calculus and linear algebra; probability and introductory econometrics. Basic MATLAB programming is assumed; Dynare is introduced in Lecture 3.

MATLAB (R2021a or later) and Dynare 6 only. No toolboxes are required: the course helper functions provide QZ solution, Kalman filtering, Newey–West standard errors and quantile regression. Every exercise runs from the course data files.

A probability space is \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) . The sample space \(\Omega\) contains possible outcomes, \(\mathcal F\) is a sigma-algebra of measurable events, and \(P\) is a probability measure satisfying non-negativity, normalization, and countable additivity. For pairwise disjoint events \(A_j\) , The axioms imply monotonicity, complements, and the addition rule. Conditional probability is defined by \(P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)\) when \(P(B)>0\) . Bayes' rule follows by expressing the joint probability in two ways.
Lecture 1: Probability Models, Random Variables, and Expectation

A random variable is a measurable function \(X:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) . Its cumulative distribution function is \(F_X(x)=P(X\le x)\) . For a discrete variable, probabilities are represented by a probability mass function; for an absolutely continuous variable, by a density \(f_X\) , with A density is not itself a probability at a point. The support and normalization condition must always be stated.
Lecture 1: Probability Models, Random Variables, and Expectation

For discrete \(X\) , \(E[X]=\sum_x xf_X(x)\) ; for continuous \(X\) , \(E[X]=\int xf_X(x)dx\) , when the expectation exists. For a measurable transformation \(g\) , the law of the unconscious statistician gives \(E[g(X)]=\int g(x)f_X(x)dx\) . The variance is \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2]=E[X^2]-\mu^2\) . Higher central moments describe skewness and kurtosis. Linearity, \(E[aX+bY]=aE[X]+bE[Y]\) , does not require independence. In contrast, \(E[XY]=E[X]E[Y]\) generally requires independence (or a suitable weaker condition).
Lecture 1: Probability Models, Random Variables, and Expectation

For a discrete conditioning variable, The conditional expectation \(E[Y\mid X]\) is a random variable and the best mean-square predictor of \(Y\) among functions measurable with respect to \(X\) . It satisfies the tower property: The law of total variance is The first term is average within-condition uncertainty; the second is variation explained by differences in conditional means.
Lecture 1: Probability Models, Random Variables, and Expectation

Independence means the joint distribution factors into marginal distributions. Zero covariance is weaker: it rules out linear association but not nonlinear dependence. For example, if \(X\) is symmetric around zero and \(Y=X^2\) , covariance may be zero although \(Y\) is completely determined by \(X\) . Correlation is covariance standardized by marginal standard deviations and is defined only when both variances are finite and positive.

Exercise 1.1 — Bayes' rule with real data: smoking and low birth weight

Data: bwght — 1,388 U.S. births, 1988 National Health Interview Survey ( bwght in ounces, cigs = cigarettes per day during pregnancy). Define the events \(S\) = "mother smoked during pregnancy" ( cigs > 0 ) and \(L\) = "low birth weight" (below 88 ounces, about 2.5 kg). Estimate \(P(S)\) , \(P(L)\) , \(P(L\mid S)\) and \(P(L\mid S^c)\) . Use Bayes' rule to compute \(P(S\mid L)\) , and check it against the direct sample frequency. Compute the relative risk \(P(L\mid S)/P(L\mid S^c)\) and its 95% confidence interval on the log scale. Are \(S\) and \(L\) independent? Test with a \(\chi^2\) test of independence. Output: About 15% of mothers smoked, and 6% of babies had low birth weight. Bayes' rule and the direct frequency agree exactly, as they must: \(P(S\mid L)\approx0.24\) , so a quarter of low-weight babies had smoking mothers, against 15% of all babies. The relative risk is about 1.8, with an interval from about 1.1 to 2.9, and the \(\chi^2\) test rejects independence at 5%. Only 20 smokers had low-weight babies, so the interval is wide. This is an association: smoking mothers differ in income, education and other risk factors, so a causal claim needs the tools of Econometrics Lecture 13.

Exercise 1.2 — The law of total variance in a wage distribution

Data: wage1 — 526 workers, CPS 1976. Verify numerically that \(\operatorname{Var}(wage)=E[\operatorname{Var}(wage\mid educ)]+\operatorname{Var}(E[wage\mid educ])\) , using sample moments with divisor \(n\) . What share of wage variance is "explained" by education cells? Compare with the \(R^2\) of a linear regression on educ , and explain why the cell-based share is larger. Repeat with lwage . Why does the share change? Output: The decomposition holds exactly (the "check" column reproduces the total). Education cells account for about 22% of the variance of wages, more than the linear \(R^2\) of 16.5%, because cell means capture the nonlinear CEF, while the regression line can capture only its linear part. Logs raise both shares a little, because the log transformation makes the CEF closer to linear and dampens the influence of very high wages on the total variance.

The uniform, exponential, gamma, beta, normal, lognormal, chi-square, Student-t, and F distributions appear in probability modeling and inference. For example, the exponential density is \(f(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) , \(x\ge0\) , with mean \(1/\lambda\) and variance \(1/\lambda^2\) . The normal family is closed under linear transformations; chi-square, t, and F distributions arise from independent normal and chi-square quantities.

Marginal densities integrate out other coordinates. The conditional density is \(f_{X|Y}(x|y)=f_{X,Y}(x,y)/f_Y(y)\) where the denominator is positive. Independence is equivalent to factorization of the joint distribution into its marginals. Conditional independence is a separate property.

For random vector \(X\) , \(\Sigma=E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)']\) . It is symmetric positive semidefinite because \(a'\Sigma a=Var(a'X)\ge0\) . If \(X\sim N_p(\mu,\Sigma)\) , every linear combination is normal. Within the jointly normal family, zero covariance implies independence; this implication is not generally valid outside that family.

If \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) , then \(Z=(X-\mu)/\sigma\sim N(0,1)\) . For independent standard normals, the sum of \(k\) squared values follows \(\chi_k^2\) , which underlies exact variance inference.

Exercise 2.1 — Which distribution fits wages? Lognormal versus gamma by maximum likelihood

Data: wage1 — 526 hourly wages, CPS 1976. Fit lognormal and gamma distributions to wage by maximum likelihood ( scipy.stats , location fixed at 0). Compare them by log-likelihood and AIC. Compare fitted and empirical quantiles (10th, 50th, 90th, 99th percentiles). Run a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test for each. Why are the KS p-values only approximate here? Output: The lognormal fits much better than the gamma by log-likelihood and AIC (a difference of over 60 AIC points), and it tracks the middle and upper quantiles more closely. Both understate the 99th percentile, so the right tail of wages is heavier than either model allows. Both KS tests reject — with 526 observations, even moderate misfit is detected. The KS p-values are only approximate because the parameters were estimated from the same data (a Lilliefors-type correction, or a parametric bootstrap, gives exact p-values).

Exercise 2.2 — Conditional normal distribution and the regression line

Data: econmath — 856 students in an introductory economics course: ACT math score actmth and college GPA colgpa . If \((X,Y)\) is bivariate normal, \(E[Y\mid X=x]=\mu_Y+\frac{\sigma_{XY}}{\sigma_X^2}(x-\mu_X)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)=\sigma_Y^2(1-\rho^2)\) . Estimate the mean vector and covariance matrix of (actmth, colgpa) (drop missing values). Compute the implied conditional mean and SD of GPA at ACT math scores 20, 25 and 30. Compare the conditional-mean slope with the OLS slope, and the conditional SD with the regression's residual SD. Check the normality assumption for GPA with a skewness statistic. Is a GPA above 4.0 possible under the fitted normal model? Output: The slope implied by the bivariate normal formula, \(\sigma_{XY}/\sigma_X^2\) , is identical to the OLS slope: the population regression of \(Y\) on \(X\) is the normal conditional mean. The conditional SD matches the residual SD (up to the degrees-of-freedom correction). The correlation of 0.30 means ACT math explains only 9% of GPA variance. The normal model assigns small but positive probability to a GPA above 4.0, which is impossible — GPA is bounded and slightly left-skewed, so the normal model is an approximation that fails in the tails.

Exercise 3.1 — The CLT with a heavily skewed real population: CEO salaries

Data: ceosal1 — 1990 salaries (thousands of dollars) of 209 CEOs. We treat these 209 values as a population. Describe the population: mean, median, skewness. Draw 10,000 samples with replacement of size \(n=5, 30, 200\) and record the sample mean. For each \(n\) , report the skewness of the sampling distribution and the coverage of the nominal 95% \(t\) -interval for the population mean. Relate the results to the Berry–Esseen idea that the normal approximation error shrinks like \(\text{skewness}/\sqrt n\) . Output: CEO salaries are extremely skewed (skewness 6.9, with one salary above $14 million). The sampling distribution of the mean is still visibly skewed at \(n=200\) , and the \(t\) -interval undercovers badly at every sample size — 79–89% instead of 95%. Coverage is not even monotone in \(n\) : at \(n=5\) , most samples miss the extreme salaries entirely, which produces short intervals that happen to cover the mean more often than at \(n=30\) . The Berry–Esseen bound says the error shrinks like skewness \(/\sqrt n\) : with skewness near 7, "large \(n\) " means thousands. Use logs, a bootstrap-t interval, or report the median.
Lecture 3: Sampling Distributions and Asymptotic Theory
Exercise 3.2 — Delta method and bootstrap for a ratio: the 401(k) participation rate

Data: 401k — 1,534 U.S. 401(k) plans: number of participants totpart and eligible employees totelg . The aggregate participation rate is the ratio \(R=E[totpart]/E[totelg]\) . Estimate \(R\) and its standard error by the delta method, using the gradient \((1/\mu_e,\,-\mu_p/\mu_e^2)\) and the sample covariance matrix of the means. Estimate the standard error with a nonparametric bootstrap (2,000 draws, seed 1). Compare \(R\) with the average of plan-level rates \(E[prate]/100\) . Why do they differ? Output: The delta-method and bootstrap standard errors agree closely (about 0.016), because the ratio of two means is smooth and \(n\) is large. The aggregate rate (83%) is lower than the average plan rate (87%): the aggregate weights plans by their number of eligible employees, and larger plans have slightly lower participation (negative correlation). The two numbers answer different questions — "what share of eligible workers participate?" versus "what is the typical plan's rate?".

Exercise 4.1 — Poisson maximum likelihood for arrest counts, by hand

Data: crime1 — 2,725 young men in California; narr86 = number of arrests in 1986. Write the Poisson log-likelihood for \(\lambda\) and maximize it numerically with scipy.optimize . Confirm \(\widehat\lambda=\bar X\) . Compute the standard error from (a) the observed information (numerical second derivative) and (b) the sandwich formula. Compare the sample variance with the mean. What does over-dispersion imply for the two standard errors? Compare observed and Poisson-predicted frequencies of 0, 1, 2 and 3+ arrests. Output: The numerical MLE equals the sample mean, as theory says. The variance is 1.8 times the mean, so the Poisson assumption \(\operatorname{Var}=E\) fails. The sandwich standard error is about 35% larger than the information-based one, because the information equality no longer holds. The Poisson model underpredicts zeros and, especially, three or more arrests (2.8% observed against 0.8% predicted): the classic signature of overdispersion, typically from unobserved heterogeneity in arrest risk. Lecture 9's negative binomial model addresses this.

Exercise 4.2 — Method of moments versus maximum likelihood for a gamma model

Data: wage1 — hourly wages. For a gamma distribution with shape \(k\) and scale \(\theta\) , \(E[X]=k\theta\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=k\theta^2\) . Derive and compute the method-of-moments estimators \(\widehat\theta=s^2/\bar x\) , \(\widehat k=\bar x^2/s^2\) . Compute the MLE with scipy.stats.gamma.fit . Bootstrap both estimators (1,000 draws) and compare their standard deviations. Which is more efficient, and is that what theory predicts? Output: The two estimators give quite different parameters (shape 2.5 against 3.5), which is itself a sign that the gamma model fits poorly: under correct specification both would be consistent for the same values. MLE is noticeably more precise for the scale parameter, but not for the shape. Theory says the MLE is asymptotically efficient if the model is correct ; when the model is misspecified, the two estimators target different pseudo-true values and the efficiency ranking need not hold. Compare with the previous exercise, where the gamma lost clearly to the lognormal.

Exercise 5.1 — Did job training raise earnings? Welch t-test, permutation test and a confidence interval

Data: jtrain2 — NSW randomized experiment, 445 men; re78 = 1978 earnings (thousands of dollars). Compute the difference in mean earnings between trainees and controls, with Welch and pooled-variance \(t\) -tests. Run a permutation test of the sharp null of no effect (10,000 permutations, seed 0). Report a 95% Welch confidence interval and interpret it in dollars. Earnings are highly skewed with many zeros. Which of the three procedures relies least on distributional assumptions? Output: Trainees earned about $1,800 more in 1978. All three procedures agree on significance (p < 0.01). The permutation test uses only the random assignment — no normality, no equal variances — so it is the most assumption-light, and it is the natural test for a randomized experiment. The Welch interval runs from about $470 to $3,100: the effect is clearly positive but imprecisely measured. A third of controls and a quarter of trainees had zero earnings, so the distribution is far from normal; the \(t\) -tests are rescued by the sample size of 445.
Lecture 5: Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
Exercise 5.2 — Wald, likelihood-ratio and score tests for a proportion

Data: pntsprd — 553 college basketball games; favwin = 1 if the betting favorite won. Test whether favorites win 75% of games, \(H_0:p=0.75\) . Compute the Wald, likelihood-ratio and score statistics and their p-values. Compute the Wald (normal) and Wilson (score-inverted) 95% intervals for \(p\) . Why do the three tests give similar answers here, and when would they diverge? Output: Favorites won 76.3% of games. None of the three tests rejects \(p=0.75\) , and they give nearly identical statistics, because \(n\) is large and \(\widehat p\) is close to \(p_0\) : the log-likelihood is close to quadratic over that range. They diverge when \(n\) is small or \(p\) is near 0 or 1. The Wilson interval is then much better behaved than the Wald interval, which can extend outside \([0,1]\) and undercovers.

Exercise 6.1 — Beta–binomial updating: response rates in a charity mail campaign

Data: charity — 4,268 people who received a charity's mail appeal; respond = 1 if they gave. With a uniform \(\text{Beta}(1,1)\) prior, compute the posterior for the response rate after the first 50, 500 and all 4,268 letters (in the data's order). Report posterior means and 95% credible intervals. Repeat with an informative prior \(\text{Beta}(2,18)\) (prior mean 10%, worth 20 letters). When does the prior stop mattering? Compute the posterior predictive probability that at least 400 of the next 1,000 letters get a response. Output: After 50 letters, the posterior is wide and depends on the prior: the informative prior pulls the estimate toward 10%. By 500 letters, the two posteriors differ by about one percentage point; with all 4,268, they are practically identical — the data swamp a prior worth 20 observations. The first 50 letters are not representative: only 14% responded, against 40% overall, so the data are sorted in some way. That is a warning that sequential updating assumes exchangeability. The posterior predictive probability of at least 400 responses in 1,000 is about one half, because 400 is almost exactly the expected number.

Exercise 6.2 — A random-walk Metropolis sampler for a lognormal wage model

Data: wage1 — hourly wages. Model \(\log wage_i\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with priors \(\mu\sim N(0,10^2)\) and \(\log\sigma\sim N(0,1)\) . Write the log posterior and a random-walk Metropolis sampler on \((\mu,\log\sigma)\) . Run 4 chains of 5,000 draws from dispersed starting values; discard the first 1,000 of each. Report the acceptance rate, the posterior means and 95% credible intervals, and the split- \(\widehat R\) for each parameter. Compare with the frequentist estimates. Then report the posterior for the median wage \(e^{\mu}\) and the mean wage \(e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}\) . Output: The acceptance rate of about 36% is in the efficient range for a random-walk sampler. All four chains, from very different starting points, converge to the same distribution: split- \(\widehat R\) is about 1.00. With 526 observations and weak priors, the posterior means equal the frequentist estimates to two or three decimals. The posterior of a function of parameters is immediate from the draws: the median wage is about $5.07 and the mean wage about $5.84, reflecting the right skew of a lognormal.

Exercise 7.1 — Checking a randomized experiment: balance and randomization inference

Data: jtrain2 — NSW experiment. Build a balance table of pre-treatment covariates ( age , educ , black , hisp , married , nodegree , re74 , re75 ) by treatment arm, with standardized differences. Run an omnibus test of balance: regress treatment on all covariates and test that all slopes are zero. Compute a randomization-inference p-value for the effect on re78 using the difference in means as the statistic (5,000 re-randomizations that keep 185 treated). Output: Most standardized differences are small, but nodegree differs by 0.30 SD and hisp by 0.18, and the omnibus test rejects balance at 5% (p ≈ 0.02). In a genuinely randomized experiment, imbalance on some covariate happens by chance; it is a reason to adjust for these covariates for precision, not evidence that randomization failed. The randomization inference p-value (0.004) is valid by design, with no distributional assumptions.

Exercise 7.2 — Does blocking help? A design simulation using real outcomes

Data: jtrain2 controls (260 men) — their actual 1978 earnings serve as untreated potential outcomes. Use the 260 control men as a "population" with known \(Y(0)\) . Add a constant treatment effect of 1 (thousand dollars) to get \(Y(1)\) . Simulate 5,000 completely randomized experiments (130 treated) and record the difference-in-means estimate. Simulate 5,000 blocked experiments, randomizing within blocks defined by 1975 earnings (zero vs positive) and nodegree , and estimate the effect as the block-size-weighted average of within-block differences. Compare the bias and standard deviation of the two designs. Why does blocking help only if the blocking variables predict the outcome? Output: Both designs are unbiased. Here blocking does not reduce variance — in this simulation it is even slightly worse — because the blocking variables barely predict 1978 earnings (block means range from 4.2 to 5.3, while the within-block SD is about 5.5). Blocking pays off only when blocks are homogeneous in the outcome; blocking on weak predictors costs a little precision through smaller within-block samples. In a real design, choose blocks by their predictive power for the outcome, for example from pilot data.

Inspect residuals for unequal variance, outliers, dependence, and non-normality. Welch's ANOVA accommodates unequal group variances in one-way comparisons. Robust and permutation alternatives still require a clearly specified target hypothesis.

For three teaching methods with means 70, 76, and 82, the omnibus test evaluates equality of all three means. The contrast \((-1,0,1)\) compares endpoint methods and is not the same as testing every pair.

Exercise 8.1 — One-way ANOVA and Tukey comparisons: wages by occupation

Data: wage1 — CPS 1976, with indicators profocc (professional), clerocc (clerical), servocc (service); the rest are grouped as "other". Build an occ factor with four levels and compute group means and SDs of lwage . Run a one-way ANOVA ( \(F\) test). Report the ANOVA table and \(\eta^2\) . Check equal variances (Levene). Run Welch's ANOVA as a robust alternative. Run Tukey's HSD to see which pairs differ, controlling the family-wise error rate. Output: Occupation explains about 24% of the variance of log wages ( \(\eta^2\) ), and the \(F\) test rejects equal means overwhelmingly. Levene's test rejects equal variances — professional wages are more dispersed — so the Welch ANOVA is the safer test; it gives the same conclusion. Tukey's HSD shows that every pair differs except clerical versus "other". The professional premium over service work is about 0.73 log points, roughly double.

Exercise 8.2 — Two-way ANOVA with interaction: gender, marriage and wages

Data: wage1 . Fit the two-way model lwage ~ female * married and produce a type-II ANOVA table. Interpret the interaction: compute the four cell means and the "marriage premium" for men and for women. Because the design is unbalanced, explain why type-I (sequential) and type-II sums of squares differ. Output: The interaction is highly significant: marriage is associated with a 0.43 log-point (about 53%) wage premium for men but almost none for women (0.05). Because the cells are unbalanced (86 to 188 observations), type-I sums of squares depend on the order of terms: the sum of squares for female is larger when it enters first, because it absorbs variation shared with married . Type-II sums of squares test each main effect adjusted for the other. These are associations — the male marriage premium partly reflects selection of higher earners into marriage.

Write \(Y_i=x_i'\beta+\varepsilon_i\) , with \(E(\varepsilon_i\mid x_i)=0\) . Then \(E(Y_i\mid x_i)=x_i'\beta\) . Under full column rank, OLS is \(\widehat\beta=(X'X)^{-1}X'Y\) . Regression association is not automatically causal; causal interpretation requires an identification argument.

A generalized linear model specifies a response distribution from the exponential family, linear predictor \(\eta_i=x_i'\beta\) , and link \(g(\mu_i)=\eta_i\) , where \(\mu_i=E(Y_i\mid x_i)\) . The variance function links conditional variance to the mean.

Exercise 9.1 — Logistic regression: married women's labor force participation

Data: mroz — 753 married women, PSID 1975; inlf = in the labor force. Fit a logit of inlf on nwifeinc , educ , exper , expersq , age , kidslt6 , kidsge6 . Report odds ratios with 95% intervals. Compute average marginal effects, and compare with a linear probability model. What is the predicted probability of participation for a 30-year-old woman with 12 years of education, 10 years of experience, no young children, one older child and non-wife income of 20? Output: A child under six reduces the odds of participation by about 76% (odds ratio 0.24) and the probability by about 26 percentage points on average. Logit average marginal effects and LPM coefficients are very close — typical when probabilities are not near 0 or 1. The LPM predicts probabilities outside \([0,1]\) for 4% of women, which the logit avoids. The predicted participation probability for the described woman is about 0.86.

Exercise 9.2 — Count data: Poisson, overdispersion and negative binomial for arrests

Data: crime1 — 2,725 young men; narr86 = arrests in 1986. Fit a Poisson regression of narr86 on pcnv (proportion of prior arrests leading to conviction), avgsen , tottime , ptime86 , qemp86 , inc86 , black , hispan , born60 . Test for overdispersion (Cameron–Trivedi auxiliary regression). Fit a negative binomial model and compare coefficients and standard errors. Report Poisson standard errors that are robust to overdispersion as well. Interpret the coefficient on black as an incidence-rate ratio. Output: The overdispersion test rejects strongly. The Poisson point estimates remain consistent if the conditional mean is correctly specified, but the conventional Poisson standard errors are too small; the robust (sandwich) standard errors are 15–35% larger and close to the negative binomial ones. NB coefficients are similar to Poisson. The incidence-rate ratio for black is about 1.9: black men in this sample had nearly twice the expected number of arrests, other covariates held fixed — a descriptive association that reflects policing as well as behavior.

For paired data define \(D_i=X_i-Y_i\) . The sign test uses signs of nonzero differences and targets a median-zero condition under its assumptions. The Mann–Whitney statistic compares ranks in two independent groups and is related to \(P(X>Y)+\tfrac12P(X=Y)\) . A permutation test constructs a reference distribution by reassigning labels according to exchangeability or the actual randomization design. Under a sharp null and valid assignment mechanism, randomization inference can be exact. Arbitrary permutation is not justified for dependent or selected observational data.

The nonparametric bootstrap resamples with replacement from the empirical distribution and recomputes a statistic. Percentile, basic, and studentized intervals differ. Clustered or serially dependent data require resampling schemes that preserve the dependence structure.

Nonparametric methods still require assumptions such as independence, exchangeability, or symmetry, depending on the procedure. Robustness to outliers does not imply robustness to dependence or selection.

For paired before-after data, calculate differences, rank absolute nonzero differences, and sum positive ranks. The signed-rank statistic uses both direction and rank magnitude; it is not simply a test of the arithmetic mean difference.

Exercise 10.1 — Rank tests and distributional comparisons for skewed earnings

Data: jtrain2 — NSW experiment. Compare 1978 earnings of trainees and controls with the Mann–Whitney (Wilcoxon rank-sum) test and the two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. Compare the quantiles of the two distributions at the 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles. Where is the training effect concentrated? Explain why the Mann–Whitney test is not a test of equal means or medians in general. Output: Both tests reject at 5%. The Mann–Whitney statistic estimates \(P(Y_1>Y_0)\approx0.57\) : a randomly chosen trainee out-earns a randomly chosen control 57% of the time. Exercise 10.2 — Kernel density and a bootstrap interval for a median

Data: wage1 — hourly wages by gender. Estimate kernel densities of lwage for men and women (Gaussian kernel, Silverman bandwidth) and report the modes. Compute the difference in median wages (women − men) with a percentile bootstrap 95% interval (2,000 draws, resampling within each group). Compare with a 95% interval for the difference in means. Which is more informative for a skewed variable, and why? Output: The density of log wages peaks around $5.56 for men and $3.29 for women. For rejection region \(R\) , power at parameter \(\theta\) is \(\pi(\theta)=P_\theta(T\in R)\) . At a specified alternative it equals \(1-\beta\) . For equal group sizes \(n\) , common variance \(\sigma^2\) , and difference \(\delta\) , the standard error is approximately \(\sigma\sqrt{2/n}\) . The standardized effect is \(d=\delta/\sigma\) , and the normal-approximation noncentrality parameter is \(d\sqrt{n/2}\) . Exact planning uses the noncentral t distribution and the planned sidedness.

Regression power depends on residual variance, the variance of the focal regressor after partialling out controls, and the design matrix. Collinearity reduces information even when total sample size is fixed. Proportion comparisons depend on null and alternative proportions and the selected test.

For equal cluster size \(m\) and intraclass correlation \(\rho\) , the approximate design effect is Effective sample size is approximately total sample size divided by this factor. Unequal cluster sizes and few clusters require more careful planning and small-sample corrections.

If the required analyzable sample is \(n_a\) and expected attrition is \(r\) , recruit approximately \(n_a/(1-r)\) . This inflation does not remove bias from informative attrition; the missing-data mechanism must be considered separately.

For equivalence margin \(\Delta>0\) , test \(H_0:\theta\le-\Delta\text{ or }\theta\ge\Delta\) against \(H_1:-\Delta<\theta<\Delta\) . The two-one-sided-tests procedure assesses whether the confidence interval lies inside the equivalence bounds. Failure to reject a zero-effect null is not evidence of equivalence.

If \(\sigma=10\) and the target difference is 5, then \(d=0.5\) . Use the noncentral t distribution to find the group size achieving target power at the chosen alpha, then verify sensitivity to variance and attrition assumptions.

Exercise 11.1 — Planning a job-training trial from pilot data

Data: jtrain2 — use the NSW control group as pilot data on the outcome's variability. Using the control-group SD of re78 , compute the sample size per arm needed to detect an effect of $1,000 with 80% power at \(\alpha=0.05\) (two-sided), analytically with statsmodels . Compute the minimum detectable effect (MDE) for the actual NSW design (185 treated, 260 controls). Simulate the power of the Welch \(t\) -test for a $1,800 effect in the actual design by resampling control outcomes (2,000 replications). Compare with the analytic power. Why might they differ? Output: Earnings are very noisy (SD of about $5,500), so detecting a $1,000 effect needs about 474 men per arm. The actual NSW design could detect effects of about $1,500 (0.27 SD) with 80% power, and had about 93% power for the $1,800 effect it found. The simulation reproduces the analytic power closely here. Exercise 11.2 — Power under clustering: the design effect

Data: wagepan — 545 workers observed for 8 years; outcome lwage . Suppose a wage subsidy is randomized by worker and wages are measured in all 8 years. Estimate the intra-class correlation (ICC) of lwage within workers using a one-way random-effects ANOVA. Compute the design effect \(1+(m-1)\rho\) with \(m=8\) and the effective sample size. Mixed models are commonly estimated by maximum likelihood or REML. Empirical Bayes group predictions shrink estimates toward the population mean, with greater shrinkage for groups with less information. This is partial pooling, distinct from complete pooling and separate estimation.

Inspect residuals, random-effect distributions, variance estimates, convergence, singular fits, and covariance-structure sensitivity. Exercise 12.1 — Random intercepts and slopes for wage growth

Data: wagepan — 545 men, 1980–1987. Fit a linear mixed model lwage ~ exper + educ + black + hisp + union with a random intercept for each worker (REML). Add a random slope on exper . Report the variance components and the correlation between intercepts and slopes. Compare the two models by AIC (refit with ML). Interpret the random-slope variance: how much do individual wage-growth rates differ? Compare the fixed-effect estimate of union with the FE (within) estimator. Output: Almost half of the variance is between workers (ICC 0.47). Allowing individual experience slopes improves the fit substantially (AIC falls by about 170). The SD of individual slopes (0.054) is almost as large as the mean slope (0.063): the middle 95% of workers have wage growth between about \(-4\%\) and \(+17\%\) per year of experience. The negative intercept–slope correlation means workers who start low catch up. The mixed-model union effect (0.11) lies between pooled OLS and FE (0.09), because the random-intercept model assumes worker effects uncorrelated with union status — the assumption the Mundlak test rejected in Econometrics Lecture 7.
Lecture 12: Linear Mixed Models and Hierarchical Data
Exercise 12.2 — Shrinkage: partial pooling of school means

Data: meap93 — 408 Michigan high schools; math10 = % of 10th graders passing a math test. We randomly divide the schools into 20 groups of very different sizes (4 to 78 schools) to mimic clusters with unequal information. Treat each group as a "cluster" whose mean pass rate we want to estimate. Because groups are formed at random, every group's true mean is the same — so any spread in the raw group means is pure noise. Compute the raw group means and their sizes. Fit a random-intercept model math10 ~ 1 with groups and compute the empirical Bayes (BLUP) group means. Show that small groups are shrunk more toward the grand mean, and compute each group's shrinkage factor \(\tau^2/(\tau^2+\sigma^2/n_j)\) .

Exercise 12.2 — Shrinkage: partial pooling of school means

Output: Groups were formed at random, so all true group means equal the grand mean; the spread of raw means is noise. The between-group SD is estimated at only about 1.5 points against a within-group SD of 10.4. Small groups (4 schools) are shrunk about 93% of the way to the grand mean — a raw mean of 17.5 becomes 23.8 — while the largest groups keep about 60% of their deviation. Empirical Bayes estimates are biased toward the mean but have lower mean squared error; this is the logic behind value-added models for teachers and schools.

For centered data matrix \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) , sample covariance is \(S=X'X/(n-1)\) . It is symmetric positive semidefinite. Eigenvectors identify orthogonal directions; eigenvalues measure variance along those directions. Variables on different scales can dominate covariance-based analysis.
Lecture 13: Multivariate Analysis: PCA, Covariance, and Dimension Reduction

The first component solves A Lagrange multiplier yields \(Sa=\lambda a\) ; the maximizing direction is the eigenvector associated with the largest eigenvalue. Subsequent components maximize variance subject to orthogonality. The proportion of variance explained by component \(j\) is \(\lambda_j/\sum_k\lambda_k\) .
Lecture 13: Multivariate Analysis: PCA, Covariance, and Dimension Reduction

For eigenvector matrix \(A\) , component scores are \(Z=XA\) . Loadings describe contributions of original variables, but scaling conventions differ. Eigenvector signs are arbitrary: multiplying an eigenvector by -1 leaves the component direction unchanged. Component labels require substantive interpretation.
Lecture 13: Multivariate Analysis: PCA, Covariance, and Dimension Reduction

PCA on the covariance matrix preserves original units. PCA on the correlation matrix is equivalent to standardizing variables first. Neither is universally preferable; choose based on whether scale differences are substantively meaningful.
Lecture 13: Multivariate Analysis: PCA, Covariance, and Dimension Reduction

PCA decomposes total observed variance into orthogonal linear combinations. Common factor analysis models shared covariance through latent factors and variable-specific errors. PCA is a descriptive dimension-reduction transformation, not automatically a measurement or causal model.

Use scree plots, parallel analysis, cumulative explained variance, interpretability, and out-of-sample reconstruction or prediction. When PCA is used before prediction, estimate scaling and components within each training fold to prevent information leakage.

For \(S=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}\) , solve \(|S-\lambda I|=0\) , then normalize the eigenvectors. The leading eigenvector gives the direction of maximum sample variance.

Prove covariance eigenvalues are nonnegative. Derive the first-component solution using a Lagrange multiplier. Calculate explained-variance proportions. Explain standardization before PCA. Distinguish PCA and common factor analysis.

Exercise 13.1 — Principal components of the U.S. yield curve

Data: intqrt — U.S. quarterly Treasury bill yields at 3, 6 and 12 months ( r3 , r6 , r12 ). Compute the correlation matrix of the three yields. Run PCA on the standardized yields. Report the eigenvalues, the share of variance explained, and the loadings. Interpret the first two components (the "level" and "slope" factors of the term structure). How well does the first component alone reconstruct the 12-month yield? Output: The three yields are almost perfectly correlated, and the first component explains 99.6% of their variance. Its loadings are equal across maturities: it is the level factor. The second component has opposite signs at short and long maturities: the slope factor. The third, with a hump-shaped loading, is curvature. Reconstructing the 12-month yield from the level factor alone leaves an error of only 0.22 percentage points against a standard deviation of 3.07. This is Litterman and Scheinkman's (1991) finding in miniature.
Lecture 13: Multivariate Analysis: PCA, Covariance, and Dimension Reduction
Exercise 13.2 — PCA and a crime index across U.S. states

Data: statecrime (statsmodels) — 51 U.S. states and DC: violent crime and murder rates, % high-school graduates, % below poverty, % single-parent households, % white, % urban. Run PCA on the seven standardized variables. How many components have eigenvalue above one (Kaiser rule)? Interpret PC1 using the loadings. Regress the violent crime rate on the scores of the first two components of the five non-crime variables only (principal-components regression). Compare its \(R^2\) with the regression on all five covariates, and check how collinear the covariates actually are. What does the comparison teach about PCR? Output: Two components have eigenvalues above one. PC1 loads positively on violence, murder, single-parent households and poverty and negatively on high-school graduation and the white share: a social-disadvantage index. Two components of the five covariates explain about 55% of the variation in violent crime, against 68% for the regression on all five. The covariates are only mildly collinear (condition number 4.5), so reducing dimension buys little stability here and costs some fit. More fundamentally, the leading components summarize the covariates , not the outcome : PCR can discard a low-variance direction that matters for prediction. Partial least squares and penalized regression (ridge, lasso) use the outcome when choosing directions. PCR earns its keep when the number of covariates is large relative to \(n\) or the covariates are nearly collinear, as with the yields in the previous exercise.
