Exercise 14.1 — A reproducible analysis function with data validation

Data: wage1 and wage2 . Good statistical code fails loudly on bad data and gives identical results on every run. Write a function analyze(df) that (a) validates the input — required columns present, no missing values, wages positive, education between 0 and 20 — and raises an informative error otherwise; (b) fits log(wage) ~ educ + exper + expersq with HC1 standard errors; and (c) returns a tidy table. Run it on wage1 . Then run it on wage2 (after constructing expersq ) and compare. Deliberately corrupt one value and show that validation catches it. Output: The function produces the same tidy table on both datasets, and it stops with an informative message when a single wage is corrupted, instead of silently producing a missing log or a wrong estimate. The return to education is 9.0% in the 1976 CPS and 7.8% in the 1980 NLS men; the experience profile is much flatter in wage2 , which covers men of a narrow age range. Validation checks are cheap, and they turn data errors into loud failures rather than wrong results.
Lecture 14: Statistical Modeling Workflow, Simulation, and Reproducibility
Exercise 14.2 — A simulation study with a fixed seed: which interval covers the mean of skewed data?

Data: ceosal1 CEO salaries, treated as a population. Design a small, reproducible simulation study. Using numpy.random.SeedSequence , create independent random streams for each sample size \(n\in\{10,30,100\}\) . For each \(n\) , draw 2,000 samples and compute three 95% intervals for the population mean: the \(t\) -interval, the bootstrap percentile interval and the bootstrap- \(t\) interval (199 resamples each). Report coverage with Monte Carlo standard errors, and the average interval width. Run the script twice to confirm identical output. Output: Because each sample size has its own seeded stream, the table is reproduced exactly on every run, and adding a new design would not change the existing results. With such a skewed population, all three intervals undercover. The percentile bootstrap is worst at small \(n\) , and the bootstrap- \(t\) is best, at the cost of much wider intervals. Even at \(n=100\) , none reaches 90%. The Monte Carlo standard errors (about 0.01) show that differences of 3–4 points are real, not simulation noise.

Topic Outline — Course notes in probability, estimation, testing, Bayesian inference, experimental design, ANOVA, GLMs and mixed models.

A condensed map of the core definitions and results in Statistics. Each topic is developed in full in the lecture notes . Level: Advanced undergraduate and graduate foundation. Coverage: Probability, sampling distributions, estimation, testing, Bayesian inference, experimental design, ANOVA, regression, nonparametric methods, and power.

A probability space is (Ω,F,P). For a random variable X, its CDF is F(x)=P(X≤x). Expectation E[g(X)] is a sum for discrete variables or an integral for continuous variables. Define variance, covariance, correlation, conditional density, independence, and conditional independence. Use the tower property E[Y]=E[E(Y|X)] and total variance Var(Y)=E[Var(Y|X)]+Var(E[Y|X]).

Bernoulli, Binomial, Poisson, Uniform, Exponential, Gamma, Beta, Normal, Lognormal, Chi-square, t, F, Multinomial, multivariate Normal, and Wishart. For each derive support, normalizing constant, mean, variance, and a data-generating interpretation. Example: if X~Binomial(n,p), E(X)=np and Var(X)=np(1-p), obtainable by writing X as a sum of independent Bernoulli indicators.

Joint and marginal densities, conditional distributions, transformations and Jacobians, covariance matrices, correlation matrices, conditional Gaussian distributions, and order statistics. For random vector X, Σ=E[(X-μ)(X-μ)'] is positive semidefinite because a'Σa=Var(a'X)≥0.

Random sampling, sampling distributions, LLN, CLT, Slutsky, continuous mapping, delta method, bootstrap and permutation inference. For i.i.d. observations with finite variance, sqrt(n)(Xbar-μ) converges in distribution to N(0,σ²). Explain when dependence requires different asymptotic theory.

Unbiasedness, consistency, efficiency, sufficiency, completeness, robustness, method of moments, and maximum likelihood. Likelihood L(θ)=Πf(x_i;θ); log-likelihood ℓ(θ)=Σlog f(x_i;θ). Score U=∂ℓ/∂θ and Fisher information I=E[UU']. Under regularity, sqrt(n)(θhat-θ0) is asymptotically Normal with covariance I(θ0)^(-1). Discuss boundary parameters and misspecification.

Coverage, standard errors, Type I and II error, power, p-values, z/t/chi-square/F tests, likelihood-ratio, Wald and score tests, equivalence tests, and multiple testing. A p-value is computed under the null; it is not the probability that the null is true. Distinguish statistical from practical significance.

Posterior p(θ|y) proportional to likelihood times prior. Derive Beta-Binomial and Normal-Normal conjugacy. Cover credible intervals, posterior prediction, Bayes factors, hierarchical models, prior sensitivity, MCMC, effective sample size, and convergence diagnostics. Explain the conditioning of posterior statements on model and prior assumptions.

Randomization, blocking, replication, allocation, factorial designs, nested factors, Latin squares, split plots, and power. Randomized block model Y_ij=μ+τ_i+β_j+ε_ij. Two-factor model includes main effects and interaction. Distinguish fixed and random effects and explain estimable contrasts.

One-way ANOVA partitions total sum of squares into between- and within-group components; F=MS_between/MS_within. State independence, variance, and residual distribution assumptions. Use planned contrasts or multiplicity adjustments such as Tukey, Holm, Bonferroni, and Dunnett. Avoid unadjusted multiple testing.

Linear regression, residual diagnostics, leverage, collinearity, robust covariance. GLM: g(E[Y|X])=X'β. Logistic model log[p/(1-p)]=X'β; exp(β_j) is a conditional odds ratio. Poisson log-link models, exposure offsets, overdispersion, negative binomial regression, and robust inference.

Empirical CDF, quantiles, kernel density, bootstrap, permutation tests, sign and Wilcoxon tests, Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis, and rank-based factorial procedures. Clarify that rank procedures do not universally test equality of means.

Power=1-β. Planning requires target effect, variance, alpha, desired power, design, allocation, and multiplicity. Explain standardized effect sizes, attrition, clustering/design effects, and why post-hoc observed power is not informative beyond the test result.

Derive Binomial mean and variance using indicator variables. Derive the Normal mean confidence interval with known variance and explain the t interval when variance is estimated. Derive Bernoulli MLE p_hat=Xbar by differentiating the log-likelihood. For k groups and N observations, state ANOVA degrees of freedom: k-1, N-k, N-1. Interpret logistic coefficient β_j through exp(β_j), holding other regressors fixed.

R: stats, MASS, car, emmeans, lme4, boot. Python: numpy, scipy.stats, pandas, statsmodels, scikit-learn, pymc. Every lab includes data validation, model assumptions, diagnostics, effect sizes, uncertainty intervals, and reproducible code.

Problem sets 25%; design/power report 20%; computational labs 20%; midterm 15%; final project 20%. References: Casella and Berger, Statistical Inference; Rice, Mathematical Statistics and Data Analysis; Wasserman, All of Statistics; Lehmann and Romano, Testing Statistical Hypotheses; Montgomery, Design and Analysis of Experiments; Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis.
Assignments: Problem Sets and Solutions — Course notes in probability, estimation, testing, Bayesian inference, experimental design, ANOVA and more.
Show derivations and state assumptions. Numerical answers without a probability model or inferential interpretation are incomplete.

A1. Bernoulli moments. For \(X\in\{0,1\}\) , \(P(X=1)=p\) , so \(E(X)=p\) , \(E(X^2)=p\) , and \(Var(X)=p-p^2=p(1-p)\) . A2. Total variance. Write \(Y-EY=[Y-E(Y|X)]+[E(Y|X)-EY]\) , square, take expectations, and use the zero conditional expectation of the cross term. This yields \(Var(Y)=E[Var(Y|X)]+Var(E[Y|X])\) . A3. Covariance matrix. For any vector \(a\) , \(a'\Sigma a=Var(a'X)\ge0\) ; hence \(\Sigma\) is positive semidefinite.

B1. CLT. For i.i.d. observations with finite variance, \(\sqrt n(\bar X-\mu)\to_dN(0,\sigma^2)\) . The CLT concerns the normalized sample mean, not the raw observations. B2. Delta method. If \(\sqrt n(\widehat\theta-\theta)\to_dN(0,V)\) , then for differentiable \(g\) , the transformed estimator has asymptotic variance \(g'(\theta)^2V\) . B3. Bernoulli MLE. The log likelihood is \(\ell(p)=y\log p+(n-y)\log(1-p)\) . The score equation gives \(\widehat p=y/n\) . B4. MSE. \(MSE(\widehat\theta)=Var(\widehat\theta)+Bias(\widehat\theta)^2\) .

C1. Coverage. A 95% confidence procedure covers the fixed parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions; it is not a 95% posterior probability statement. C2. Beta-Binomial. With prior \(Beta(a,b)\) and binomial data \(y\) successes in \(n\) trials, posterior is \(Beta(a+y,b+n-y)\) . C3. Multiplicity. Bonferroni controls family-wise error by testing each of \(m\) hypotheses at \(\alpha/m\) . Holm applies a sequentially less conservative step-down procedure.

D1. Randomized blocks. Blocking controls nuisance heterogeneity by comparing treatments within blocks; treatment assignment must be randomized according to the design. D2. ANOVA degrees of freedom. For \(k\) groups and \(N\) observations, between-group df is \(k-1\) , within-group df is \(N-k\) , and total df is \(N-1\) . D3. Contrast. A linear contrast \(\sum_i c_i\mu_i\) requires \(\sum_i c_i=0\) . State the contrast weights and variance.

E1. Logistic interpretation. In \(logit(p_i)=x_i'\beta\) , \(e^{\beta_j}\) is the conditional odds ratio for a one-unit increase in \(x_j\) , holding other regressors fixed. E2. Marginal effect. For continuous \(x_j\) , \(\partial p_i/\partial x_{ij}=p_i(1-p_i)\beta_j\) . Thus the probability effect varies with covariates. E3. Poisson offset. An exposure offset enters with coefficient fixed at one on the log scale, modeling a rate rather than a raw count.
F. Nonparametric, power, and mixed models

F1. Rank tests. Explain the null/estimand for the selected rank procedure; do not claim every rank test is a test of medians or means. F2. Power. Power is the probability of rejecting the null under a specified alternative. State effect size, variance, alpha, design, and sample size. F3. Intraclass correlation. In a random-intercept model, \(ICC=\tau^2/(\tau^2+\sigma^2)\) . F4. PCA. The first principal component maximizes \(a'Sa\) subject to \(a'a=1\) ; the solution is the eigenvector for the largest eigenvalue.

Stock Market Analysis — Course Home — A 15-week training course in price action analysis of stocks. Trend, key levels, pin bars, inside bars, fakeys, confluence, stop loss, risk reward, position sizing, trade management and a written trading plan.

This is a 15-week training course in price action analysis of stocks. It is not a university teaching course: there are no exams and no grades. The aim is practical. By the end you will read a daily chart on your own, mark the key levels, recognise three signals (the pin bar, the inside bar and the fakey), count the confluence, set a stop loss and a target, size the position, manage the trade and record it in a trading journal.

The method is price action: decisions come from the bars on the chart and the levels they respect. The course teaches one small set of tools and asks you to use them with discipline. Reading the chart: the daily chart, the weekly chart, the trend and the swing points. Key levels: support and resistance, and how a broken level turns into its opposite. The 21 EMA: a moving average used as dynamic support and resistance in a trend. Three signals: the pin bar, the inside bar and the fakey. Confluence: trend, key level, 21 EMA and signal agreeing at the same place. Money management: stop loss, risk reward, position sizing and the arithmetic of losing streaks.
Trade management: moving to breakeven, trailing the stop loss and taking the target. Trading plan and psychology: a written plan, a trading journal and the habits of patience and discipline.

Every week has the same shape: learning objectives, a lesson, a worked example on a chart, exercises with answers, and a chart lab. The lab is the most important part. You open your own daily charts of stocks and do the work yourself.
The charts in this course show each idea clearly. In each chart lab you repeat the exercise on real stocks using your own charting platform and your broker's demo account.

This course is general education. It is not investment advice and it is not an offer to buy or sell any security. Trading stocks involves a risk of loss, and you can lose more than you expect. Do not trade money you cannot afford to lose. Past results do not promise future results. Start on a demo account, and follow the rules of your own broker.

Week 1: How Stocks Are Traded: Brokers and Orders
Week 1 of Stock Market Analysis (Part I · Reading the market): lesson, worked example, exercises and a chart lab.
Week 1: How Stocks Are Traded: Brokers and Orders

Explain what a broker does and why every trade starts with an order. Tell a market order, a limit order and a stop order apart, and say when each is used. Place a stop loss and a target as part of the same plan as the entry. Open a demo account and place one order of each type.
Week 1: How Stocks Are Traded: Brokers and Orders

You buy and sell stocks through a broker. The broker holds your account, sends your order to the market and shows your open positions. For this course the broker also gives you a demo account : practice money that behaves like a live account, with no risk to your own savings. Use it until your trading journal says you are ready (Week 15). A stock is quoted in dollars per share. The regular trading session is 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern time. The course uses the daily chart , so one bar shows one full day, and you do not need to watch the screen all day.
Week 1: How Stocks Are Traded: Brokers and Orders

An order is an instruction to your broker. Three kinds cover almost every trade in this course. Order What it does When you use it Market order Buys or sells now, at the best price available When getting in or out matters more than the exact price Limit order Buys at your price or lower, or sells at your price or higher To enter on a retracement, or to place a target Stop order Becomes a market order once price reaches your stop price To enter on a break of a level, or as a stop loss Figure 1.1. Four orders around a stock trading at $50.00.
Week 1: How Stocks Are Traded: Brokers and Orders

Before you press the button, write three numbers: the entry , the stop loss and the target . The stop loss is the price at which the idea is wrong and you exit. The target is where you plan to take the profit. The difference between entry and stop loss is your risk . The difference between entry and target is your reward . From Week 12 you will turn those two numbers into a risk reward ratio and a position size. A stop loss is an order. It is placed with your broker when you enter the trade, not held in your head.
Week 1: How Stocks Are Traded: Brokers and Orders

A stock trades at $50.00. Your plan is to buy on a retracement to $49.20, to exit at a stop loss of $48.40 and to take profit at $50.80. Entry: limit order to buy at $49.20. Stop loss: stop order to sell at $48.40. Risk per share = $49.20 − $48.40 = $0.80 . Target: limit order to sell at $50.80. Reward per share = $50.80 − $49.20 = $1.60 , which is twice the risk (a risk reward of 1:2). If price never falls to $49.20, the limit order is not filled and you have no trade. That is a normal outcome, not a failure.
Week 1: How Stocks Are Traded: Brokers and Orders

Which order would you use to buy only if the stock breaks above $51.00? Answer A stop order to buy at $51.60. It waits until price reaches $51.60 and then becomes a market order. You buy at $20.00 with a stop loss at $19.00 and a target at $22.00. What are the risk and the reward per share, and what is the risk reward? Answer Risk = $1.00, reward = $2.00, so the risk reward is 1:2. Why is a stop loss placed as an order and not kept as a mental note? Answer Because emotion makes people move or ignore a mental stop. An order exits the trade for you at the price you chose when you were calm.
Week 1: How Stocks Are Traded: Brokers and Orders

Open a demo account with a broker. Place one market order, one limit order and one stop order on three different stocks, then cancel the two that are not filled. Write in your journal what each order did.
Week 2: Reading Price Bars and Time Frames
Week 2 of Stock Market Analysis (Part I · Reading the market): lesson, worked example, exercises and a chart lab.
Week 2: Reading Price Bars and Time Frames

Name the open, high, low and close of a bar, and its body and tail. Recognise a bullish bar, a bearish bar, a pin bar and an inside bar. Explain why the weekly chart and the daily chart do different jobs. Read a bar as a short story about who controlled the day.
Week 2: Reading Price Bars and Time Frames

On a daily candlestick chart each bar records four prices for one day: the open , the high , the low and the close . The thick part between the open and the close is the body . The thin lines above and below are the tails (some traders say wicks). A bar with a green body closed above its open and is bullish. A bar with a red body closed below its open and is bearish. The tail is the most useful part of the bar. A long tail below the body means sellers pushed price down and buyers pushed it back. A long tail above the body means buyers pushed price up and sellers pushed it back. The market tested a price and rejected it.
Week 2: Reading Price Bars and Time Frames
Figure 2.1. The price bars used in this course. The pin bar and the inside bar get their own weeks (6 and 7).
Week 2: Reading Price Bars and Time Frames

A time frame is the length of time one bar covers. In this course you use two. The weekly chart shows the big picture: the trend and the major levels. The daily chart shows the detail: the key levels, the signals and the entries. Always look at the weekly chart first, then the daily chart. A signal on the daily chart that fights the weekly trend is weaker than one that agrees with it. Figure 2.2. The same prices on two time frames. The weekly chart removes the noise and shows the trend.
Week 2: Reading Price Bars and Time Frames

A daily bar is complete once the session closes. You can study it after the close, think without pressure and place orders for the next day. Smaller time frames give more bars and more noise, and they demand your attention and your emotions all day. This course does not use them.
Week 2: Reading Price Bars and Time Frames

Take a daily bar with these prices: open $40.00, high $41.60, low $39.90, close $41.40. The close is above the open, so the bar is bullish . The body is $41.40 − $40.00 = $1.40. The upper tail is $41.60 − $41.40 = $0.20 and the lower tail is $40.00 − $39.90 = $0.10. Buyers controlled the day. They closed near the high, and sellers never pushed far below the open.
Week 2: Reading Price Bars and Time Frames

A bar opens at $25.00, trades up to $25.30, falls to $23.80 and closes at $25.10. Describe it. Answer A bullish bar with a body of $0.10 and a long lower tail of $1.20: price was pushed down to $23.80 and rejected. It is a bullish pin bar in shape, and it matters only if it appears at a key level. Why do we start on the weekly chart? Answer It shows the trend and the major levels. The daily chart then gives the timing inside that picture.
Week 2: Reading Price Bars and Time Frames
On a daily chart of any stock, label the open, high, low, close, body and tails on ten consecutive bars. Then switch to the weekly chart and write one sentence about the trend you see there.
Week 3 of Stock Market Analysis (Part I · Reading the market): lesson, worked example, exercises and a chart lab.

Define an uptrend, a downtrend and a sideways market with swing points. Mark swing highs and swing lows on a daily chart. Explain what it means when the sequence of highs and lows breaks. State why trading with the trend is the default in this course.

A swing high is a high that has lower highs on both sides. A swing low is a low that has higher lows on both sides. The swing points are the skeleton of the chart. Everything else, including the trend, is read from them.

Uptrend: each swing high is higher than the last (a higher high, HH) and each swing low is higher than the last (a higher low, HL). Downtrend: each swing high is lower (a lower high, LH) and each swing low is lower (a lower low, LL). Sideways: the swing highs and swing lows stay in a band and do not rise or fall. Figure 3.1. The trend ends in stages: first a lower high, then a lower low that breaks the last higher low.

A trend is a sequence, and the sequence can end. In the chart, the uptrend keeps printing higher highs and higher lows until a lower high appears. Then price falls through the last higher low and prints a lower low. The uptrend is over, and a downtrend has started. You do not need to predict this. You only need to notice it, and to stop buying the retracements once it happens.

Most of the time the easiest trade is the one with the trend. Momentum is on your side, retracements are shallow and the targets are often reached. A counter-trend trade can pay well, but it needs a stronger reason (Week 10) and a tighter plan. The default in this course is to trade with the trend.

A stock makes these swing points: low $100, high $108, low $103, high $118, low $111, high $130. The swing lows are $100, $103 and $111. Each is higher than the last (HL, HL). The swing highs are $108, $118 and $130. Each is higher than the last (HH, HH). Both sequences rise, so the trend is up . The last higher low is $111. A close below it would be the first warning.

The swing highs on a chart are $60, $58, $55 and the swing lows are $50, $47, $44. What is the trend? Answer A downtrend: lower highs and lower lows. In an uptrend the last higher low is $111 and price closes at $109. What does that tell you? Answer The sequence of higher lows has broken. The uptrend is in doubt, so stop buying retracements and wait for the new picture.
Pick five stocks. On the weekly chart mark the swing highs and swing lows and write uptrend, downtrend or sideways for each. Then check the daily chart: does it agree?
Week 4: Key Levels: Support and Resistance
Week 4 of Stock Market Analysis (Part II · Key levels and the 21 EMA): lesson, worked example, exercises and a chart lab.
Week 4: Key Levels: Support and Resistance
Draw support and resistance levels on a daily chart. Say what makes a level a key level. Explain why a broken resistance level can turn into support. Tell a breakout from a false break.
Week 4: Key Levels: Support and Resistance

Support is a price where buyers have repeatedly stopped a fall. Resistance is a price where sellers have repeatedly stopped a rise. A key level is a support or resistance level that is easy to see, because price has reacted at it more than once and the reaction was clear. If you have to squint to find it, it is not a key level. Draw levels as horizontal lines on the daily chart, starting from the left and looking for the places where bars turned. A level is an area more than an exact price, so do not worry if bars end a little above or below your line.
Week 4: Key Levels: Support and Resistance
Each time price reaches a level and turns, the level is rejected . Three clear rejections make a strong level. The pin bar (Week 6) is the single bar that shows rejection best.
Week 4: Key Levels: Support and Resistance

When price breaks above a resistance level and then falls back to it, the old resistance often acts as support. The same is true in reverse: a broken support often becomes resistance. This is the reason you keep old levels on your chart after they break. Figure 4.1. Price remembers key levels. The same line is resistance on the left and support on the right.
Week 4: Key Levels: Support and Resistance

A breakout is a close beyond a level. A false break is a move beyond the level that fails and closes back inside it. False breaks are common, and Week 8 builds a signal, the fakey, on top of one. Do not buy a breakout simply because price touched the level. Wait for a close.
Week 4: Key Levels: Support and Resistance

On the chart above, price tops at about $100 on days 10, 24 and 38, each time falling by 4% to 6%. That is three rejections, so $100 is a key level. On day 46 price closes above it: a breakout. On day 66, price falls back to $100 and holds. A buyer here has the trend, a key level that was proven twice and a retest. That is a trade to plan, though it still needs a signal (Weeks 6 to 8).
Week 4: Key Levels: Support and Resistance

How many rejections make a level worth drawing? Answer There is no fixed number. Two clear rejections make a level worth watching, and three or more make it strong. What matters is that the reaction is obvious on the daily chart. A stock closes above resistance, then closes back below it the next day. What is this called? Answer A false break.
Week 4: Key Levels: Support and Resistance
Draw the key levels on three daily charts of stocks. Use only levels that a friend could find without your help. Mark each as support or resistance, and write the date of each rejection.
Week 5: The 21 EMA as Dynamic Support and Resistance
Week 5 of Stock Market Analysis (Part II · Key levels and the 21 EMA): lesson, worked example, exercises and a chart lab.
Week 5: The 21 EMA as Dynamic Support and Resistance

Say what a moving average is and what the 21 EMA shows. Explain how it acts as dynamic support in an uptrend and dynamic resistance in a downtrend. Use it to judge how healthy a retracement is. Know what the 21 EMA cannot do.
Week 5: The 21 EMA as Dynamic Support and Resistance

A moving average smooths price. The 21 EMA is an exponential moving average of the last 21 closes, and it gives more weight to the most recent closes. On a daily chart it follows the trend of the last month or so.
Week 5: The 21 EMA as Dynamic Support and Resistance

The levels in Week 4 are flat. The 21 EMA is a dynamic level: it rises in an uptrend and falls in a downtrend. In a healthy uptrend, retracements often stop near the 21 EMA and the trend resumes. In a downtrend, rallies often fail near it. Figure 5.1. The 21 EMA holds twice in the uptrend. Once price is below a falling 21 EMA, the buying stops.
Week 5: The 21 EMA as Dynamic Support and Resistance

Direction of the 21 EMA: rising means uptrend, falling means downtrend, flat means sideways. Distance: a retracement to the 21 EMA is normal. A retracement far through it is a warning. A helper, not a signal: the 21 EMA never tells you to buy. It adds one more point of agreement, which Week 11 calls confluence.
Week 5: The 21 EMA as Dynamic Support and Resistance

It lags, because it is built from past prices. In a sideways market it crosses back and forth and gives nothing. Treat it as a guide to the trend and a place to look, and let the pin bar, inside bar or fakey provide the signal.
Week 5: The 21 EMA as Dynamic Support and Resistance

In Figure 5.1, price rises from $100 to about $114, retraces to the 21 EMA near $109 and turns up. It retraces again to the 21 EMA near $119 and turns up again. On the right of the chart, price closes below the 21 EMA and the 21 EMA is falling: the buyer waits and the seller looks for rallies.
Week 5: The 21 EMA as Dynamic Support and Resistance

The 21 EMA is rising and price retraces to it. What kind of market and what kind of trade? Answer An uptrend, so look for a trade with the trend: a buy signal at the 21 EMA, ideally also at a key level. Why not buy every touch of the 21 EMA? Answer It is a guide and not a signal. Without a signal and a key level there is little confluence, and in a sideways market the touches do nothing.
Week 5: The 21 EMA as Dynamic Support and Resistance
Add the 21 EMA to a daily chart. Find three retracements in an uptrend that ended at the 21 EMA and three in a downtrend. Mark any that failed, and say what the chart showed before the failure.
Week 6 of Stock Market Analysis (Part III · The three signals): lesson, worked example, exercises and a chart lab.

Recognise a pin bar (a tailed bar) by its shape. Say why a pin bar matters only at a key level. Write the entry, stop loss and target for a pin bar trade. List the cases in which a pin bar should be ignored.

A pin bar is a bar with a long tail and a small body. The tail points to a price that was tested and rejected. A bullish pin bar has a long tail below the body: sellers pushed price down and buyers took it back. A bearish pin bar has a long tail above the body. A practical rule of thumb: the tail should be at least about twice the length of the body, and the other tail should be short or absent. The bar should stand out from its neighbours. If you have to argue that it is a pin bar, it is not one.

A pin bar in the middle of nowhere is only a bar. The same bar at a key level, or at the 21 EMA in a trend, is a signal. Before you take a pin bar, ask three questions. Is the tail rejecting a key level? Does the trade go with the trend, or is there a clear reason for a reversal? Is there room for price to reach the target before the next key level? Figure 6.1. The tail rejects the key level. The entry is placed just beyond the pin bar's body side, the stop loss beyond the tail, and the target at twice the risk.

For a bullish pin bar: the entry is a stop order to buy just above the high of the pin bar. The stop loss goes just below the low of the tail. The target is at least twice the risk. For a bearish pin bar, reverse every direction. If the entry order is not triggered within a few bars, cancel it.
When to ignore a pin bar

The tail is short or the body is large. It is in the middle of a range and not at a key level. It goes against a strong trend with no reason. The next key level is too close for a target of twice the risk.

On the left of Figure 6.1, a key level (support) sits at $100.00. A bullish pin bar has open $101.00, high $101.70, low $99.10, close $101.40. Body: $0.40. Lower tail: $101.00 − $99.10 = $1.90, nearly five times the body. It passes the shape test. Entry: buy stop at $101.80, just above the high of $101.70. Stop loss: $98.90, just below the tail low of $99.10. Risk per share = $101.80 − $98.90 = $2.90 . Target: $101.80 + 2 × $2.90 = $107.60 . Reward per share = $5.80, so the risk reward is 1:2. The bearish pin bar on the right is the mirror image around a resistance level at $110.00.

A bar has open $30.00, high $30.20, low $27.50, close $30.10. Is it a bullish pin bar? Answer Yes in shape: the body is $0.10 and the lower tail is $2.50. It becomes a signal only if the tail is rejecting a key level. For that bar, set the entry above the high by $0.10, the stop loss below the low by $0.10 and a target at twice the risk. Answer Entry $30.30, stop loss $27.40, risk $2.90. Target = $30.30 + $5.80 = $36.10. Why cancel the entry order if it is not filled after a few bars? Answer The signal belongs to that moment. If price does not confirm it quickly, the reason for the trade has gone.

Find ten pin bars on daily charts of stocks. Mark them all. Then keep only those that rejected a key level, and write down what price did in the next ten bars for each. How many of the ten did you reject?
Week 7 of Stock Market Analysis (Part III · The three signals): lesson, worked example, exercises and a chart lab.

Recognise an inside bar and its mother bar. Say what an inside bar shows about the market. Write the entry, stop loss and target for an inside bar breakout. Decide when an inside bar is worth trading.

An inside bar is a bar whose high is lower than the high, and whose low is higher than the low, of the bar before it. The bar before it is the mother bar . The whole inside bar fits inside the mother bar, as a small bar in the shadow of a large one.

The inside bar is a pause. After the mother bar made a big move, the next day neither buyers nor sellers could take control, and price stayed inside the mother bar's range. Pauses end, and the end is usually a move out of the mother bar. The trade is to be there when it happens.

The method is the same in both directions. With the trend, trade the break of the mother bar in the direction of the trend. Entry: a stop order just beyond the high of the mother bar (to buy) or the low of the mother bar (to sell). Stop loss: at the other end of the mother bar. Target: at least twice the risk. Figure 7.1. The entry is above the mother bar's high, the stop loss below its low.
Choosing which inside bars to trade

Inside bars are common. Most of them are not worth trading. Take the ones where: the mother bar is not too large. A huge mother bar means a huge stop loss and a small position size; the inside bar sits at a key level or the 21 EMA, or comes after a clear move in the direction of the trend; there is room to the next key level.

In Figure 7.1 the trend is up. The mother bar has open $103.00, high $106.00, low $102.20, close $105.40. The next bar has high $105.50 and low $103.20, so it is inside. Entry: buy stop at $106.10, just above the mother bar's high. Stop loss: $102.10, just below the mother bar's low. Risk per share = $4.00 . Target: $106.10 + 2 × $4.00 = $114.10 . The next day price trades through $106.10 and the order is filled.

Mother bar: high $52.00, low $49.00. Next bar: high $51.40, low $49.60. Is it an inside bar? Answer Yes. $51.40 is below $52.00 and $49.60 is above $49.00. For that mother bar in an uptrend, set entry $0.10 above the high, stop loss $0.10 below the low, target at twice the risk. Answer Entry $52.10, stop loss $48.90, risk $3.20, target $52.10 + $6.40 = $58.50. Why does a very large mother bar make a poor trade? Answer The stop loss is far from the entry, so the position size must be small, and the target at twice the risk may be beyond the next key level.
Find five inside bars on daily charts. For each, write the entry, stop loss and target, and the next key level. Which of the five would you not take, and why?
Week 8 of Stock Market Analysis (Part III · The three signals): lesson, worked example, exercises and a chart lab.

Describe a fakey as an inside bar followed by a false break. Explain why a false break can be a stronger signal than a clean breakout. Write the entry, stop loss and target for a fakey. Tell a fakey from an inside bar that simply breaks out.

A fakey begins as an inside bar. Price then breaks out of the mother bar on one side, and the break fails: price closes back inside the mother bar's range. The break was false. The trade is in the opposite direction, because those who traded the false break are now trapped and must exit.

Many traders place orders just beyond the mother bar. When price reaches those orders and fails to continue, the traders who entered must close at a loss, and that exit adds pressure in the direction of the reversal. The fakey is a signal that comes from the failure of the obvious trade.

For a bullish fakey (a false break below the mother bar): Entry: a buy stop just above the high of the inside bar, or of the bar that made the false break, after price closes back inside the range. Stop loss: just below the low of the false break. Target: at least twice the risk. Reverse every direction for a bearish fakey. Figure 8.1. The false break below the mother bar's low fails, and price closes back inside. The trade is long, with the trend.
With the trend, or at a key level

A fakey is best with the trend, as in Figure 8.1, or at a key level. A fakey against the trend needs a clear reason, so apply the same questions as for the pin bar. If the false break pokes below a key level, the signal is stronger.

In Figure 8.1 the mother bar has high $106.00 and low $102.20. The inside bar has high $105.40 and low $103.00. The next bar trades down to $100.80, below the mother bar's low, and closes at $103.20, back inside the mother bar's range. That is a false break. Entry: buy stop at $105.50, just above the inside bar's high. Stop loss: $100.70, just below the false break's low. Risk per share = $4.80 . Target: $105.50 + 2 × $4.80 = $115.10 .

Mother bar low $49.00. The next bar trades down to $48.20 but closes at $49.30. What has happened? Answer A false break of the mother bar's low. If the bar before it was an inside bar, this is a bullish fakey. Why is the stop loss placed below the false break's low? Answer If price returns below that low, the false break was real, and the idea for the trade is wrong.

Find three fakeys and three inside bars that broke out cleanly, all in the direction of the trend. Compare the next ten bars of each. Write one paragraph on what you notice, and keep it in your journal.

Week 9: Trading with the Trend: The Retracement Entry

Explain what a retracement is and where it often ends. Combine the trend, a key level and the 21 EMA to choose a place to enter. Plan a trade with the trend from entry to target. Choose a stop loss beyond the last swing point.
Week 9: Trading with the Trend: The Retracement Entry

In an uptrend, price does not go straight up. It rises, retraces , and rises again. Each retracement is a chance to buy at a better price and with a closer stop loss than a chase of the breakout. The same is true in a downtrend, when price rallies and then falls again.
Week 9: Trading with the Trend: The Retracement Entry

Look for the retracement to stop at one of three places: a key level , especially an old resistance that has become support; the 21 EMA ; the last swing low of the trend (the higher low). The best retracements stop where two of them meet. That is confluence, and Week 11 teaches how to count it.
Week 9: Trading with the Trend: The Retracement Entry

Confirm the trend on the weekly chart and the daily chart. Wait for the retracement to reach a place from the list above. Wait for a signal: a pin bar, an inside bar or a fakey. Enter above the signal bar. Put the stop loss beyond the swing low and the target at twice the risk or more. Figure 9.1. A higher low near the 21 EMA, then an entry above the prior bar's high.
Week 9: Trading with the Trend: The Retracement Entry
The hard part is waiting. Price will often fall short of your place, or will not give a signal. Skipping those trades is part of the method. Good trades come to the trader who waits.
Week 9: Trading with the Trend: The Retracement Entry

In Figure 9.1 the trend is up with swing highs at $103 and $112.5. After the high near $103 price retraces to about $97.5, close to the 21 EMA, and a bar closes at the prior bar's high. Entry: $99.60. Stop loss: $96.40, below the swing low. Risk per share = $3.20 . Target: $99.60 + 2 × $3.20 = $106.00 . Price later reaches the target.
Week 9: Trading with the Trend: The Retracement Entry

In a downtrend, where would you look to sell? Answer On a rally that stops at a key level (an old support that has become resistance), at the falling 21 EMA, or at the last lower high, followed by a bearish signal. Entry $60.00, stop loss $57.50. What is the target for a risk reward of 1:2? Answer Risk $2.50, so the target is $60.00 + $5.00 = $65.00.

Week 10: Sideways Markets, Reversals and Counter-Trend Trades
Recognise a sideways market and trade it with care. Say what a reversal looks like and what it needs. List the extra risks of a counter-trend trade. Decide when to stay out.
Week 10: Sideways Markets, Reversals and Counter-Trend Trades

When price moves between a support level and a resistance level without making progress, the market is sideways. The key levels are the boundaries. A simple plan is to buy near support with a bullish signal and to sell near resistance with a bearish signal, with the stop loss just beyond the level. The plan stops when a breakout arrives. Figure 10.1. Buy near support and sell near resistance while the levels hold. After the close above resistance, stop selling. A sideways market has a small distance between the levels. Check that the reward is at least twice the risk before you take a trade; if the levels are too close for that, there is no trade.
Week 10: Sideways Markets, Reversals and Counter-Trend Trades

A reversal is the end of one trend and the start of the opposite one. In Week 3 you saw its stages: a failure to make a new high or low, a break of the last swing point and then a new sequence. A reversal trade tries to enter early, at a key level and with a signal such as a pin bar or a fakey.
Week 10: Sideways Markets, Reversals and Counter-Trend Trades

A trade against the trend is called counter-trend . It can pay well, because the move back to the other side of the range is large. But it carries extra risk: Momentum is against you. A key level that held three times can break on the fourth. The 21 EMA points the wrong way. If you trade counter-trend, ask for more: a very clear key level, a very clear signal and a target that is at least twice the risk. Many traders reduce the position size for these trades.
Week 10: Sideways Markets, Reversals and Counter-Trend Trades
When the weekly chart and the daily chart disagree, when no key level is close, or when the bars are messy, the correct trade is no trade. Cash is a position.
Week 10: Sideways Markets, Reversals and Counter-Trend Trades

In Figure 10.1 the support is about $100.50 and the resistance about $106.00, a range of $5.50. A sell near resistance with a stop loss $1.00 above has a risk of about $1.00 and a target at support of about $5.50 away: a risk reward better than 1:5, so the trade is worth planning. After the breakout on day 57 the sell trades have no more value, and the market is a trend again.
Week 10: Sideways Markets, Reversals and Counter-Trend Trades

A sideways market has support at $20.00 and resistance at $21.00. You want a risk reward of 1:2. Is a sell at $20.90 with a stop loss at $21.10 acceptable? Answer Risk = $0.20. The target at support is $20.90 − $20.00 = $0.90 away, which is 4.5 times the risk, so yes it passes the 1:2 test. Check that the signal and the levels are clear. Name two extra risks of a counter-trend trade. Answer Momentum is against you, and a key level can fail. The 21 EMA also points the wrong way.
Week 10: Sideways Markets, Reversals and Counter-Trend Trades

Classify five daily charts as uptrend, downtrend or sideways. For each sideways chart, mark the two key levels and measure the distance in dollars. For each trending chart, write what a counter-trend trade would risk.
Week 11 of Stock Market Analysis (Part IV · Putting the trade together): lesson, worked example, exercises and a chart lab.

Define confluence as several independent reasons agreeing at one price and time. List the four factors used in this course. Count the confluence of a setup and set a minimum count. Explain why more confluence does not make a trade certain.

Confluence means that several reasons point the same way at the same place. In this course there are four: Trend: the trade is with the trend on the weekly chart and the daily chart. Key level: the signal sits at a clear support or resistance level. 21 EMA: price is at the 21 EMA and it points with the trade. Signal: a clear pin bar, inside bar or fakey. A setup with one factor is a bar. A setup with two is worth watching. A setup with three or four is a trade to plan. Figure 11.1. Four factors in one place: the trend, the old resistance turned support, the 21 EMA and the pin bar.

Write the count in your journal before you enter. Count a factor only if it is clear, and do not count a factor you must argue for. Set a minimum in your trading plan, for example three of four. A minimum count takes the guesswork out of the choice and helps you skip weak trades.

Confluence raises the probability that a trade works. It does not make it certain, and any trade can lose. This is why every trade has a stop loss and a position size set by the risk (Week 12). Do not add factors to justify a trade you already want to take.

In Figure 11.1 the weekly trend is up and the daily chart shows higher highs and higher lows. The old resistance at about $104.40 now acts as support. The bar on day 52 has open $104.80, high $105.50, low $102.40, close $105.30 and touches the 21 EMA. Factor Clear? Count Trend Yes, up on both time frames 1 Key level Yes, old resistance now support 1 21 EMA Yes, price is at the rising 21 EMA 1 Signal Yes, a bullish pin bar (tail $2.40, body $0.50) 1 The count is 4 of 4. Entry $105.60, stop loss $102.30, risk $3.30 . Target $105.60 + 2 × $3.30 = $112.20 .

A pin bar is clear and at a key level, but the weekly trend is down and the trade is a buy. What is the count and what does it need? Answer The count is 2 of 4 at most: key level and signal. It is counter-trend, so it needs the stronger reasons of Week 10, or it should be skipped. Why write the count before entering? Answer After you enter, emotion shapes how you judge the setup. A count written before is honest and can be checked in the journal.

Count the confluence on ten setups on your own daily charts using the four factors. Keep only the setups with the count that your trading plan requires, and write the next ten bars for each. Did the higher counts work out better?

Week 12 of Stock Market Analysis (Part V · Risk and trade management): lesson, worked example, exercises and a chart lab.
Week 12: Stop Loss, Risk Reward and Position Sizing

Choose a stop loss from the chart and not from the amount you hope to lose. Calculate a risk reward ratio and the winning probability needed to break even. Calculate a position size from the risk per trade. Show why a small risk per trade makes a losing streak survivable.
Week 12: Stop Loss, Risk Reward and Position Sizing

Money management is what keeps you in the game. The signals decide when you trade. Money management decides how much you can lose when you are wrong, and you will be wrong often. It has three parts. 1. Stop loss. Place it where the idea is wrong, beyond the tail of the pin bar, the end of the mother bar or the last swing point. Never move it further away. 2. Risk reward. The reward is the distance from entry to target. The risk is the distance from entry to stop loss. A 1:2 risk reward means the reward is twice the risk. 3. Position size. Choose the risk per trade as a small percentage of the account, then set the number of shares so that a loss at the stop loss costs exactly that amount.
Week 12: Stop Loss, Risk Reward and Position Sizing
Risk per trade = account size × risk percentage Position size (shares) = risk per trade ÷ (entry − stop loss) For a short trade use (stop loss − entry). Round down to a whole number of shares.
Week 12: Stop Loss, Risk Reward and Position Sizing

With a risk reward of 1:2, you break even if you win about one trade in three. With 1:1 you need to win half of them. A higher reward for the same risk lowers the winning probability that you need. Figure 12.1. The curve shows the winning probability needed to break even. Costs such as commission and the spread push the line up a little.
Week 12: Stop Loss, Risk Reward and Position Sizing

Even a good method has losing streaks. What decides whether you survive one is the risk per trade. Figure 12.2. After 20 losses in a row, an account risking 1% per trade is at about 82. An account risking 5% is at about 36.
Week 12: Stop Loss, Risk Reward and Position Sizing

Account $10,000, risk 1% per trade, entry $50.00, stop loss $48.40, target $53.20. Risk per trade = $10,000 × 1% = $100 . Risk per share = $50.00 − $48.40 = $1.60 . Position size = $100 ÷ $1.60 = 62.5, so 62 shares . Real risk = 62 × $1.60 = $99.20. Reward = 62 × $3.20 = $198.40, so the risk reward is 1:2. A second case: account $25,000, risk 0.5% = $125, entry $99.60, stop loss $96.40. Risk per share is $3.20, so the position size is $125 ÷ $3.20 = 39.06, or 39 shares .
Week 12: Stop Loss, Risk Reward and Position Sizing

Account $8,000, risk 1%, entry $20.00, stop loss $19.00. How many shares? Answer Risk per trade $80. Risk per share $1.00. Position size = 80 shares. What winning probability breaks even at a risk reward of 1:3? Answer 25%: the average win is three times the average loss, so one win in four pays for three losses. After 10 losses in a row at 2% risk per trade, what is left of an account that started at 100? Answer 100 × 0.98^10 ≈ 81.7.

Fill in the position size table in your trading plan for your own account size and three possible risk percentages. Then pick a stock from your charts and calculate the position size for a real setup.
Week 13 of Stock Market Analysis (Part V · Risk and trade management): lesson, worked example, exercises and a chart lab.

Explain why a plan for after the entry matters as much as the entry. Move a stop loss to breakeven with a clear rule. Trail a stop loss behind the swing points of a trend. Choose between taking the target and trailing.

Once the order is filled, the trade has two possible ends: the stop loss or the target. In between, you have a decision to make every day. Trade management is the set of rules that you write before the entry, so that emotion does not make the decisions for you.

When price has moved in your favour by the amount that you risked, move the stop loss to the entry price. This is breakeven . If price returns to your entry, the trade closes at about zero, and the loss of the trade is taken out of the game. The rule in this course: move the stop loss to breakeven when the trade is one times the risk in profit.

In a trend, price makes new swing lows above the old ones. A trailing stop loss follows them: after each new swing low, move the stop loss to just below it. Never move it backwards. The trailing stop loss lets a winner run and still protects most of the profit.

A fixed target at twice the risk is simple, and it is the default. Trailing can pay more in a strong trend, and it can pay less in a choppy one. Choose one way in your trading plan before the trade and do not change it because of how you feel. Figure 13.1. Entry $100, risk $4. The stop loss moves to breakeven after price reaches $104, then trails below each swing low.
Never move a stop loss further from the entry. Never add to a losing trade. Do not take profit early because of fear, and do not hold a loser because of hope.

Figure 13.1: entry $100.00, stop loss $96.00, risk $4.00, target $108.00. Day 10: price reaches $104.00, one times the risk in profit. Move the stop loss to $100.00 (breakeven). Day 19: a swing low near $102.60 formed on day 16 and price is above it. Move the stop loss to $101.90, just below the swing low. Day 29: another swing low has formed near $108.60. Move the stop loss to $107.80. Price passes the $108.00 target around day 21 but keeps rising. A trader who took the target banked $8.00 per share, which is twice the risk. A trader who trailed still holds the trade, with a stop loss at $107.80 that locks in at least $7.80 per share. Either choice follows a rule.

Entry $40.00, stop loss $38.00. At what price do you move the stop loss to breakeven? Answer Risk is $2.00, so when price reaches $42.00 move the stop loss to $40.00. Why must a trailing stop loss never move backwards? Answer Moving it back increases the risk again and takes away the protection that the earlier move created.
Take three of your earlier trade plans. Replay each bar by bar on your chart and write the day on which you would move to breakeven and each trail. Compare the result with taking the 1:2 target.
Week 14: Gaps, News and the Daily Routine
Week 14 of Stock Market Analysis (Part VI · Plan, routine and going live): lesson, worked example, exercises and a chart lab.
Week 14: Gaps, News and the Daily Routine

Say what a gap is and how it can break a stop loss. Decide what to do when news is due. Write a daily routine that you can follow in the same order every day. Keep a trading journal as part of the routine.
Week 14: Gaps, News and the Daily Routine

A gap appears when a stock opens well above or below the previous close and no trading takes place in between. Gaps usually follow news, which arrives after the close or before the open. A gap can take price straight through your stop loss. A stop order becomes a market order once it is reached, so you can be filled well beyond your stop price, and the loss can be larger than you planned. Figure 14.1. The first bars after a gap decide whether it holds or fails.
Week 14: Gaps, News and the Daily Routine

News moves prices, and it often arrives at known times. The rule of this course is simple: if important news about the stock is due before your trade can reach its target, stay out of the trade. Do not hold a position through news hoping to be lucky, because the gap risk is not in your position size calculation.
Week 14: Gaps, News and the Daily Routine
A routine is the same steps in the same order. It saves you from deciding things in a hurry. Figure 14.2. The routine takes about thirty minutes after the close. It ends in the trading journal.
Week 14: Gaps, News and the Daily Routine

For each trade, write down the signal, the key level, the confluence count, entry, stop loss, target, position size, exit, the result in multiples of the risk and whether you followed the plan. Add the emotion you noticed. Without a journal there is no way to know what works.
Week 14: Gaps, News and the Daily Routine

On Figure 14.1 the left stock closes at $41.30 and opens the next day at $44.40, a gap of about 7%. It does not trade back into the gap, and the trend continues: the gap held. The right stock gaps up the same way, then trades down through the open and closes the gap within seven days. If you had bought the open at $44.40 with a stop loss at $43.40, the stop loss would have been hit. A buyer who waits for the first bars to show whether the gap holds will miss part of the move, and will avoid more false moves.
Week 14: Gaps, News and the Daily Routine

A stock closes at $30.00. Your stop loss is $28.50. It opens at $27.00 after bad news. Where are you likely to be filled? Answer At about $27.00 or near it, not at $28.50. The stop order becomes a market order once price reaches it, and price has already gapped through. Why stay out of a trade if news is due before the target is reached? Answer The gap risk is larger than the risk used in the position size, so one trade can lose far more than the plan allows.
Week 14: Gaps, News and the Daily Routine
Write your own daily routine on one page, using the six steps. Run it for five trading days on your demo account, even on the days when you find no trade, and record each day in the journal.

Week 15 of Stock Market Analysis (Part VI · Plan, routine and going live): lesson, worked example, exercises and a chart lab.
Week 15: The Trading Plan, Psychology and Going Live

Complete a written trading plan that covers every part of the course. Name the emotions that damage a trader and a rule for each. Review a trading journal of 20 trades. Go live in steps, with the risk per trade rising only when the rules have been followed.
Week 15: The Trading Plan, Psychology and Going Live

The trading plan on the course page is the product of the course. It records the time frames, the setups, the minimum confluence, the entry, the stop loss, the target, the position size, the trade management, the rules about news and the routine. Write it in your own words. Read it before every trade, and change it only after a review of the journal, never in the middle of a trade.
Week 15: The Trading Plan, Psychology and Going Live

The method is simple. Following it is hard. The usual enemies are: Fear: you skip a good setup after two losses, or you close a winner too early. Rule: if the setup meets the plan, take it, with the planned position size. Greed: you increase the position size after a win, or you move the target further away. Rule: the risk per trade is fixed. Impatience: you enter before the signal bar is complete. Rule: wait for the close of the bar. Hope: you move the stop loss further away. Rule: never. Revenge: you take a trade to win back a loss. Rule: after the number of losses set in the plan, stop for the day and review.
Week 15: The Trading Plan, Psychology and Going Live
You will feel each of these. Discipline means following the plan while you do. Patience means waiting for the setup.
Week 15: The Trading Plan, Psychology and Going Live

After 20 trades, count the trades, the winners and the losers, and the average result in multiples of the risk. Then count how many trades followed the plan. A trade that followed the plan and lost is a good trade. A trade that broke the plan and won is a bad one, because it teaches the wrong habit. Figure 15.1. A hypothetical journal. Most losses stay at one times the risk or less, because the stop loss was kept.
Week 15: The Trading Plan, Psychology and Going Live

Start on the demo account. When the journal shows 20 trades that followed the plan, go live with a small risk per trade. Raise it only after the rules have been followed, never after a good week. Figure 15.2. A suggested ramp. Your own plan may differ, and the broker's rules for small accounts and day trading must be checked before you go live.
Week 15: The Trading Plan, Psychology and Going Live

A trader reviews 20 demo trades. There are 9 winners and 11 losers. Four trades broke the plan, because the stop loss was moved. The trader writes: the method is not the problem, because the trades that followed the plan were fine; the problem is the stop loss that was moved, which comes from hope. The rule that is added to the plan: the stop loss order is placed at the same time as the entry, and the platform's order for moving it is not used.
Week 15: The Trading Plan, Psychology and Going Live

After a loss, you feel the urge to double the position size on the next trade. What is it, and what does the plan say? Answer It is greed combined with revenge. The plan says the risk per trade is fixed, so the position size is calculated by the same formula. A trade followed every rule and lost. Was it a good trade? Answer Yes. A loss is part of the probabilities, and the plan was followed.

A 15-week training course in price action analysis of stocks. It is written for people who can already open a chart and want a clear, rule-based way to read it. The course is a training programme, not a degree course, and the aim is a written trading plan that you can follow with discipline.

Beginners who want a method that uses the chart and little else. Self-taught traders who want rules for entries, stop loss, target and position size. Students of finance who want to see how price behaves on a daily chart.
