ARDL Bounds-Testing Model: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. A mix of I(0) and I(1) variables.

The question is: what determines the 10-year Treasury yield in the long run? The Fisher relation says nominal yields should rise with inflation; the business cycle, measured by GDP growth and unemployment, may also matter. The model selection tool found a mix : the yield and inflation are I(1), while GDP growth and unemployment are I(0). This rules out the Johansen approach, which needs every variable to be I(1), and it rules out OLS in levels. The autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) model of Pesaran, Shin and Smith (2001) is built for exactly this case. Its bounds test for a long-run relationship is valid whether the regressors are I(0), I(1) or a mixture.

The ARDL( \(p, q_1, q_2, q_3\) ) model includes lags of the dependent variable and of each regressor: It can be rewritten in error-correction form, which separates the long run from the short run: The one condition you must check ARDL allows I(0) and I(1) variables, but no variable may be I(2) . With an I(2) variable the critical values of the bounds test are not valid. The model selection tool checks this for you; in a paper, report unit-root tests on first differences to prove it. How to write it: model section Unit-root tests indicate that the 10-year yield and inflation are I(1) while GDP growth and the unemployment rate are I(0), and that no variable is I(2). Since the variables are integrated of different orders, we use the ARDL bounds-testing approach of Pesaran, Shin and Smith (2001), which remains valid for any mixture of I(0) and I(1) regressors. The model is estimated in its unrestricted error-correction form, \(\Delta y_t = c + \rho y_{t-1} + \sum_j \delta_j x_{j,t-1} + \sum_i \gamma_i \Delta y_{t-i} + \sum_j \sum_i \lambda_{j,i} \Delta x_{j,t-i} + \varepsilon_t\) , where the long-run effect of \(x_j\) on the yield is \(-\delta_j/\rho\) .
Load the data and confirm the orders of integration

How to read it Two variables are I(1) and two are I(0). No first difference has a unit root, so nothing is I(2) and ARDL can be used. The unemployment rate has a p-value of 0.045, right at the border. With Johansen you would have to decide whether it is I(0) or I(1), and the decision would change the model. With ARDL the answer does not matter. That robustness to borderline cases is the main practical reason the method is so widely used.

ARDL lets every variable have its own lag length. The search tries all combinations up to a maximum and keeps the one with the lowest information criterion. How to read it AIC picks 3 lags of the yield, lags 0–2 of inflation and 0–3 of unemployment. BIC picks a smaller model, as usual. Use 4 as the maximum for quarterly data and 12 for monthly data unless your sample is short. Notice that GDP growth does not appear at all : the search found that the model fits better without it. This is itself a result. Whether to keep such a variable is a judgement: if it is part of your research question, keep it with one lag and report that it is insignificant; if it was only a control, you may drop it. Here it is part of the question, so we keep it.

How to read it This is the model in levels, ARDL(3, 2, 1, 3). The coefficients on individual lags alternate in sign and have no direct interpretation. For example, unemployment has coefficients of −0.58, +1.13, −0.85 and +0.28. What matters is their sum relative to the persistence of the yield, which the next steps compute. Never interpret single lag coefficients from this table in a paper.
The bounds test: is there a long-run relationship?

The bounds test is an F-test of the null hypothesis that the level terms in the error-correction form are jointly zero, which means no long-run relationship . It has two critical values instead of one. F-statistic is… Conclusion above the upper bound Reject the null: a long-run relationship exists below the lower bound Do not reject: no long-run relationship between the bounds Inconclusive How to read it The F-statistic of 8.18 is above the upper bound at every significance level, including 6.40 at the 0.1% level. The null of no long-run relationship is rejected: the yield, inflation, growth and unemployment are tied together in the long run. case=3 means an unrestricted constant and no trend, the usual choice when the dependent variable has no deterministic trend. Always state the case in the paper, because the critical values depend on it. If the statistic had fallen below the lower bound, you would stop here and estimate the model in first differences only.

How to read it statsmodels reports the long-run relation as a vector with the dependent variable normalised to 1, so the signs must be reversed to write it as an equation. The code above does this. The result is yield = 0.37 + 1.98 × inflation + 0.42 × GDP growth − 0.36 × unemployment Inflation is the only significant long-run determinant. A permanent 1-point rise in inflation raises the 10-year yield by about 2 points in the long run. The Fisher relation predicts at least 1; values above 1 are common because investors also require compensation for taxes and inflation risk. GDP growth and unemployment have the expected signs but are not significant: the business cycle does not shift the yield permanently.
The error-correction form: short-run dynamics and speed of adjustment

How to read it The error-correction coefficient is the one on yield_10y.L1 : −0.045. It must be negative and significant for the long-run relationship to pull the yield back. It is, but it is small: only 4.5% of a deviation is corrected per quarter, so half of a gap remains after about 15 quarters. Long-term yields adjust slowly. Short-run coefficients are the ones starting with D. . A rise in inflation raises the yield immediately ( D.inflation.L0 = 0.11), and a rise in unemployment lowers it sharply within the quarter ( D.unemployment.L0 = −0.57), consistent with yields falling in recessions. So unemployment matters in the short run even though it has no long-run effect. That distinction is what the error-correction form is for.
The error-correction form: short-run dynamics and speed of adjustment

The t-statistic on the error-correction coefficient does not follow the standard t distribution. Use the bounds test for the existence of the relationship, and report the coefficient for its sign and size. How to write it: long-run and short-run results The bounds F-statistic of 8.18 exceeds the upper critical bound at the 1% level (5.05), so the null hypothesis of no long-run relationship is rejected. The estimated long-run coefficients (Table 3) show that inflation is the dominant long-run determinant of the 10-year yield: a one-percentage-point increase in inflation raises the yield by 1.98 percentage points (s.e. 0.45). The long-run effects of GDP growth and unemployment are statistically insignificant. The error-correction coefficient is −0.045 and significant at the 1% level, which implies that 4.5% of any deviation from the long-run relationship is corrected each quarter, a half-life of about 15 quarters. In the short run, a one-point rise in the unemployment rate lowers the yield by 0.57 points within the quarter. The long-run relationship is identified from the full sample; in the 1990–2019 subsample, when inflation was low and stable, the bounds test does not reject the null of no long-run relationship.

The bounds test assumes serially uncorrelated errors, so that test matters most. The error-correction model is a linear regression, so it can be refitted by OLS to use the standard tests. How to read it Serial correlation. Breusch–Godfrey does not reject (p = 0.20). The condition the bounds test needs is met. If it had rejected, the fix is to add lags. Heteroskedasticity. The White and ARCH tests reject. The coefficients are unaffected, but standard errors should be robust; the robustness table below re-estimates with HAC standard errors. Normality. Rejected, because of the large yield movements around 1980. With 237 observations, inference rests on large-sample results. CUSUM. The line stays well inside its 5% bounds and the test does not reject (p = 0.57): the coefficients are stable.

CUSUM of squares. This one leaves the bounds, falling below them around observations 60–78 and rising above them around 100–150. The break is at about observation 80, which is 1980: the Volcker disinflation, when the volatility of yields jumped. CUSUM of squares detects instability in the variance , and that agrees with the heteroskedasticity tests. So the mean relationship is stable but the error variance is not. Report both plots, name the episode responsible, and use robust standard errors. Do not show only the plot that passes.

How to read it Lag choice and standard errors do not matter. The BIC specification and HAC standard errors leave the long-run inflation coefficient at about 2 and strongly significant. The pre-crisis sample agrees. Ending in 2007 gives a slightly larger coefficient (2.17) and a higher bounds F-statistic. The relationship is not found after 1990. In 1990–2019 the bounds F-statistic is 2.25, which is below even the lower bound, so the null of no long-run relationship cannot be rejected in that period. Inflation was low and stable after 1990, so there is little variation left to identify its long-run effect on yields. The long-run link between inflation and the yield is identified mainly from the high-inflation decades before 1990. That is a limitation of the result and it belongs in the paper, in the robustness section and in the conclusion.

Section What goes in it From which step Data Sources, sample, unit-root tests on levels and first differences Step 2 Method Why ARDL, the equation, lag selection, the case for deterministic terms Steps 1 and 3 Cointegration Bounds F-statistic with lower and upper critical values Step 4 Long-run results Long-run coefficients as a table and as an equation Step 5 Short-run results Error-correction coefficient, half-life, short-run coefficients Step 6 Robustness Diagnostics, CUSUM plots, lag choice, subsamples Steps 7 and 8 What a referee will ask Did you rule out I(2)? Show unit-root tests on first differences. Which case for the deterministic terms, and which critical values? State both. For samples under about 80 observations, use the small-sample critical values of Narayan (2005).

Is the error-correction coefficient negative and significant? If it is positive or below −1, something is wrong with the specification. Are the residuals serially uncorrelated? The bounds test is not valid otherwise. Is the long-run relationship stable? Show CUSUM plots and subsamples. Are the regressors exogenous? ARDL assumes the dependent variable does not drive the regressors in the long run. If the yield could affect inflation, say so, or use a system method.
ARIMA and Seasonal ARIMA (SARIMA): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Many papers need a good univariate model: a forecast of inflation, a benchmark for a larger model, or a measure of how long a shock lasts. Our question is: how persistent is U.S. inflation, and can an ARIMA model forecast it better than a simple benchmark? We use monthly PCE inflation, \(\pi_t = 1200\,\Delta \ln P_t\) , the annualised monthly change in the PCE price index. An ARIMA( \(p,d,q\) ) model says that the series, differenced \(d\) times, follows an ARMA process: where \(L\) is the lag operator and \(\varepsilon_t\) is white noise. A seasonal ARIMA adds the same kind of polynomial at the seasonal lag \(s\) (12 for monthly data), written \((P,D,Q)_s\) .

Symbol Meaning How you choose it \(d\) number of times the series is differenced unit-root and stationarity tests, then forecast performance \(p\) number of autoregressive lags PACF, then information criteria \(q\) number of moving-average lags ACF, then information criteria \((P,D,Q)_{12}\) seasonal orders test for seasonality in the residuals Before you estimate anything Decide what the model is for. If the goal is to forecast, judge it by out-of-sample errors. If the goal is to describe persistence, judge it by the diagnostics and the autoregressive roots. The same model is not always best for both, and your paper should say which goal it serves. How to write it: model section We model monthly U.S. inflation, \(\pi_t = 1200\,\Delta\ln P_t\) , where \(P_t\) is the PCE price index, with an ARIMA( \(p,d,q\) ) model. The orders are chosen by the Bayesian information criterion over \(p,q \le 3\) , after the differencing order is set by unit-root and stationarity tests. We check the residuals for autocorrelation, conditional heteroskedasticity and seasonality, and we compare out-of-sample forecasts with a historical-mean benchmark using the Diebold–Mariano test.
Load the data and look at the series

How to read it The sample has 420 months from 1985-01 to 2019-12. Annualised inflation averages 2.15% with a standard deviation of 2.25. The extremes are the surge after Hurricane Katrina in September 2005 (11.53) and the fall in energy prices in November 2008 (−14.25), so the series has a few large outliers. The first autocorrelation is 0.44 and the later ones fall slowly but stay positive (0.15, 0.10, 0.12 at lags 2 to 4). The PACF has one clear spike at lag 1 and is small afterwards. That pattern points to a first-order autoregression, with the slow tail of the ACF hinting at a mean that moves over time.

How to read it The two tests disagree. The ADF test rejects a unit root (statistic −3.56, p = 0.007) and the KPSS test rejects stationarity (statistic 1.28, p below 0.01). This is the usual sign of a mean that shifts: average inflation was 2.62% in 1985–1999 and 1.80% in 2000–2019, and the volatility rose from 1.84 to 2.46. The first-order autocorrelation of 0.44 is far from one, so we take \(d=0\) with a constant as the baseline. Because the mean moved, we also keep \(d=1\) as a competitor and judge it by forecasts, not by information criteria. If a break in the mean is the main issue in your paper, see the Bai–Perron guide.

How to read it BIC picks \(p=1, q=0\) (BIC 1713.4). The next-best model, ARMA(1,2), lowers the AIC by 3.3 points but raises the BIC by 4.6. AIC alone would choose a larger model, ARMA(1,3), because it penalises extra parameters less. When the two criteria disagree, report both and prefer the smaller model unless the diagnostics demand more. Here we take the AR(1) and check the diagnostics next.
Estimate the model and check its roots

How to read it The autoregressive coefficient is 0.445 with a standard error of 0.031 (z = 14.2). The constant, 2.19, is the mean of the process in percent per year, because statsmodels parameterises the constant as the mean. The AR root has modulus 2.25, outside the unit circle, so the process is stationary. A shock to annualised inflation loses half of its effect in 0.9 months. In other words, month-to-month noise dominates and the persistence in monthly PCE inflation is low. How to write it: results The AR(1) model gives \(\hat\phi = 0.445\) (s.e. 0.031) and a mean inflation rate of 2.19% per year. The autoregressive root lies outside the unit circle, and a shock loses half of its effect in less than one month. Month-to-month PCE inflation is therefore only weakly persistent in our sample.

How to read it There is no sign of remaining autocorrelation up to 12 lags (Ljung–Box p = 0.55 at lag 6 and 0.09 at lag 12), although a little remains at lag 24 (p = 0.019). Three other tests reject. The Jarque–Bera statistic is 327.9 (p below 0.001), because of the fat tails produced by the 2005 and 2008 outliers. The ARCH-LM statistic is 52.6 (p below 0.001), so volatility clusters in time. A joint test of month dummies in the residuals gives F = 2.48 (p = 0.005), so some seasonality remains in this seasonally adjusted series. The practical meaning is that the point forecasts are reasonable, but confidence bands built on normal, constant-variance errors are not reliable. The GARCH guide shows the remedy for the volatility.
Does a seasonal term help? SARIMA

How to read it The seasonal autoregressive term at lag 12 is small and insignificant (−0.059, p = 0.21), and the SARIMA model has higher information criteria than the AR(1) (BIC 1718.0 against 1713.4). The 11 month dummies are jointly significant (χ² = 31.5, p = 0.0009) and lower the AIC from 1701.4 to 1695.1, but they raise the BIC from 1713.4 to 1750.8 because they add 11 parameters. The conclusion is that a small residual seasonality exists even after seasonal adjustment, but it is too weak to justify a seasonal model under BIC. The next step checks whether it helps forecasts.

How to read it We re-estimate each model every month from 2012-12 to 2018-12 and forecast 1, 3 and 12 months ahead, which gives 73 forecasts per horizon. At one month, the AR(1), ARMA(1,1) and SARIMA models have an RMSE of about 1.70 against 1.94 for the historical mean, a gain of roughly 12%, but the Diebold–Mariano tests are only marginal (p = 0.08 to 0.09). At 12 months the stationary models are no better than the mean, and slightly worse (AR(1) 1.87 against 1.86, DM p = 0.01 because the loss is consistently a little higher). The ARIMA(1,1,1) with \(d=1\) has the lowest error at every horizon (1.61, 1.70 and 1.69) and beats the mean at the 5% level for one and three months (p = 0.05 and 0.03) and at the 10% level for 12 months (p = 0.10). This fits the mean shift found in step 3: a model with \(d=1\) follows the local level of inflation, which fell during the sample. The seasonal term does not help (SARIMA is no better than the AR(1) at any horizon). Treat the result with care: it comes from one sample, the forecasts overlap, and we compared several models.

How to write it: forecast comparison We evaluate forecasts one, three and twelve months ahead with an expanding window from December 2012 to December 2018, re-estimating every model each month (73 forecasts per horizon). The ARIMA(1,1,1) has the lowest root mean squared error at every horizon, 1.61, 1.70 and 1.69 percentage points, against 1.94, 1.93 and 1.86 for the historical mean. The Diebold–Mariano test rejects equal accuracy at the 5% level for one and three months (p = 0.05 and 0.03). The stationary ARMA models improve on the historical mean only at the one-month horizon, and the seasonal term adds no accuracy.

How to read it The forecast from the AR(1) returns to the mean of 2.19% within a few months, which is what a stationary model should do: it has no information about the level beyond the near future. The 80% band is wide and contains all 24 observations of 2018–2019 (100%, against the nominal 80%). The band is too wide because the error variance was estimated from 1985–2017, a period that includes the 2005 and 2008 outliers, while 2018–2019 was calm. This is the volatility clustering that the ARCH test found. A GARCH model would give a band that narrows in calm periods and widens in turbulent ones.
What to report in the paper

Item What to show Data source, sample, transformation, and the unit-root and stationarity tests with both p-values Orders the grid of AIC and BIC, and a sentence saying which criterion was used Estimates coefficients with standard errors, the AR root, and the half-life of a shock Diagnostics Ljung–Box at three lags, ARCH-LM, and the test for residual seasonality Forecasts RMSE by horizon, the benchmark, the Diebold–Mariano test, and the forecast window Common mistakes Comparing AIC across different \(d\) . A model with \(d=1\) is fitted to a different series, so its information criteria cannot be compared with those of a model with \(d=0\) . Choose \(d\) by tests and forecasts.
What to report in the paper

Reporting in-sample fit as forecasting ability. Always hold out data or use an expanding window. Ignoring conditional heteroskedasticity. Point forecasts can be fine while the confidence bands are wrong. If the ARCH test rejects, see the GARCH guide. Forcing a seasonal term on seasonally adjusted data. Test for it first. Keep it only if it improves forecasts.
Structural Breaks at Unknown Dates (Bai–Perron): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

How many times did the parameters shift, and when? With \(m\) breaks at dates \(T_1 < \dots < T_m\) the model is where \(x_t\) always contains a constant, so the simplest case is a model of shifting means. For each \(m\) the break dates are the least-squares minimisers over all partitions in which every regime has at least a fraction \(\varepsilon\) of the sample (the trimming). A dynamic-programming algorithm finds them exactly. The number of breaks is chosen by the \(\sup F(\ell)\) tests of no break against \(\ell\) breaks, the UDmax test against an unknown number, the sequential tests of \(\ell\) against \(\ell+1\) breaks, or an information criterion. Three checks before you trust break dates

Are the errors close to uncorrelated? The tests assume serially uncorrelated errors. For a persistent series, shifts in the mean can be mistaken for persistence, and the reverse. Re-estimate with a lagged dependent variable among the regressors. Does the number of breaks depend on the rule? BIC, LWZ and the sequential test can disagree. Report all of them, and show that the dates you discuss are stable. Are the break dates precise? A small shift gives a wide confidence interval for the date. Say so, and do not present a date as exact when its interval spans years. How to write it: the model We test for structural change in the mean of U.S. inflation with the procedure of Bai and Perron (1998, 2003). The model allows the mean to shift at up to five unknown dates, with each regime containing at least 15% of the 240 quarterly observations (36 quarters). Break dates are the global least-squares minimisers, and the number of breaks is chosen by the BIC and checked against the sequential supF( \(\ell+1\,|\,\ell\) ) test at the 5% level. Critical values are asymptotic and were simulated for this engine. Confidence intervals for the dates follow Bai (1997).
Load the data and look at the series

How to read it The sample runs from 1960Q1 to 2019Q4 (240 quarters). Inflation averages 3.19% with a standard deviation of 2.31; GDP growth averages 3.01% with a standard deviation of 3.25. Inflation is highly persistent (first autocorrelation 0.90, ADF p = 0.19) and the KPSS test rejects stationarity (p = 0.01), the pattern a series with shifting means produces. GDP growth is stationary with a first autocorrelation of 0.30. Persistence matters because the break tests assume uncorrelated errors: for inflation, a shift in the mean and a high autoregressive coefficient are hard to tell apart, which the AR(1) check below makes visible.
Test for breaks and choose their number

How to read it Every test of no break against \(\ell\) breaks rejects at 5%: the supF(1) statistic is 106.9 against a critical value of 8.6, and the UDmax statistic is 226.8 against 8.9. The sequential tests reject zero, one and two breaks against one more (statistics 106.9, 174.8 and 29.7 against critical values of 8.6, 10.3 and 11.3) and stop at the fourth: the statistic for three against four breaks is 6.7, below the 5% critical value of 11.9. BIC and LWZ also choose three breaks, and the sum of squared residuals falls from 1,274 with no break to 437 with two and 388 with three, then barely at all. All four rules therefore agree on three breaks.
Break dates, regimes and the fitted path

How to read it The three breaks fall in 1973Q2, 1982Q4 and 1991Q4. The mean of inflation is 2.95% before 1973 (standard error 0.42), 7.44% from 1973Q2 to 1982Q3 (0.48), 3.21% from 1982Q4 to 1991Q3 (0.21) and 1.87% from 1991Q4 onwards (0.13). These are the great inflation, the Volcker disinflation and the lower-inflation period that followed. The 95% intervals for the first two dates are tight (1971Q4 to 1974Q4 and 1981Q4 to 1983Q4), because the shifts are large; the third date is much less precise (1988Q4 to 1994Q4), because the drop from 3.21% to 1.87% is small relative to the noise.
Does the answer depend on the selection rule and on the trimming?

How to read it The three breaks (1973Q2, 1982Q4, 1991Q4) are the same under BIC, LWZ, the sequential test and UDmax followed by the sequential test. The trimming fraction matters more. With 10% trimming the procedure adds an earlier break (1967Q3) and finds four; with 20% trimming it finds three breaks at 1972Q1, 1984Q1 and 1996Q1, because a break must leave at least 48 quarters in each regime, which rules out the 1973 and 1982 dates; with 25% it finds two. A larger trimming fraction restricts where the breaks can fall, so it moves the dates, and 15% is the usual choice because it balances precision and flexibility.
Serial correlation: add a lag of the dependent variable

How to read it Adding a lagged dependent variable changes the story: one break is found, in 2006Q4 (95% interval 2005Q2 to 2008Q2), and the sequential tests stop after the first. Before 2006Q4 inflation is very persistent (autoregressive coefficient 0.91, standard error 0.04); after 2006Q4 persistence drops to 0.27 and the intercept rises. The earlier breaks in the mean are absorbed because a high autoregressive coefficient already explains the long swings. The two models answer different questions: the mean model asks when the average level shifted, the AR(1) model asks when the dynamics changed. Report both, and be explicit about which one your argument needs.
A second series: real GDP growth

How to read it For real GDP growth the tests find one break, in 1969Q2: the mean falls from 4.64% (standard error 0.62) to 2.72% (0.30). The sequential test does not reject one break against two (6.2 against a critical value of 10.3). The 95% interval for the date is very wide (1960Q1 to 1982Q4) because the shift is small relative to the volatility of growth, so the break is detected but not dated. Do not present 1969Q2 as an exact date.

How to write it: results The mean of U.S. inflation shifted three times between 1960 and 2019. The supF, UDmax and sequential tests all reject the null of no break at 5% (supF(1) = 106.9, critical value 8.6), and the BIC, LWZ and sequential procedures all select three breaks, dated 1973Q2 (95% interval 1971Q4 to 1974Q4), 1982Q4 (1981Q4 to 1983Q4) and 1991Q4 (1988Q4 to 1994Q4). The mean inflation rate is 2.95% before 1973, 7.44% from 1973Q2 to 1982Q3, 3.21% from 1982Q4 to 1991Q3 and 1.87% from 1991Q4. The number of breaks is robust to the selection rule but the dates depend on the trimming fraction: with 20% trimming the breaks move to 1972Q1, 1984Q1 and 1996Q1. When a lagged dependent variable is added the tests find a single break in 2006Q4 in which persistence falls from 0.91 to 0.27, which shows that the mean shifts and the persistence of inflation cannot be separated by these tests alone. The critical values are asymptotic and simulated for the pure structural change model.

Cointegration Tests: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

The Fisher relation says the nominal interest rate moves one-for-one with expected inflation in the long run. Our question is: are the U.S. federal funds rate and inflation cointegrated, and is the long-run relation stable over 1960–2019? Two series are cointegrated if each has a unit root but a linear combination is stationary: Engle–Granger and Phillips–Ouliaris test the null of no cointegration using the residual \(\hat u_t\) . The Johansen test works on the VAR and tests the rank of the long-run matrix. Gregory–Hansen (1996) allows the intercept and slope to shift once, at an unknown date \(\tau\) , and takes the most negative ADF statistic over all dates: Symbol

Variable Definition \(i_t\) fedfunds federal funds rate, percent \(\pi_t\) inflation annualised inflation, percent Before you estimate anything Cointegration needs economic theory first. Say which relation you expect, with which sign and size, and whether you expect it to hold for the whole sample. The null of every test below is no cointegration, so failing to reject is weak evidence for "no long-run relation", especially in a sample of 60 years with a policy regime change. How to write it: model section We test for a long-run relation between the federal funds rate and inflation, as implied by the Fisher relation. We first check that both series are I(1). We then apply the Engle–Granger and Phillips–Ouliaris residual tests and the Johansen trace test, and the Gregory–Hansen test, which allows a single break in the intercept and slope at an unknown date. Critical values for the Gregory–Hansen test are simulated for our sample size.
Load the data and check the order of integration

How to read it The sample has 240 quarters, 1960Q1 to 2019Q4. Both series trend and move together in the figure: they rise through the 1970s, peak around 1980–81 and fall afterwards. The ADF test does not reject a unit root in either level (p = 0.33 for the funds rate, 0.41 for inflation), and KPSS, whose null is stationarity, rejects at 5% for both (p = 0.010 and 0.011). In first differences ADF rejects (p < 0.001) and KPSS does not (p = 0.10). Both series are therefore treated as I(1), and a cointegration test is meaningful.

How to read it Engle–Granger does not find cointegration: the statistic is −2.05 against a 5% critical value of −3.37 (p = 0.50), and swapping the dependent variable gives the same answer (−2.03, p = 0.51). The static long-run slope is 1.25, close to the Fisher value of one, but a slope from a residual that is not stationary is not reliable. Phillips–Ouliaris is closer to the line but does not reject at 5% in any of its four versions (p between 0.07 and 0.11). The Johansen trace test is not stable: it rejects r = 0 with one and three lagged differences (17.7 and 16.8 against 15.5) and does not reject with two and four (14.8 and 14.0). When the result depends on the lag, report all of them and say the evidence is mixed. The next step asks whether one fixed relation is the wrong model.
Allow a structural break: the Gregory–Hansen test

How to read it The Gregory–Hansen statistic is −2.89 for the intercept-shift model (C), −5.66 for the model with a shift and trend (C/T) and −4.05 for the model with a shift in intercept and slope (C/S). The simulated 5% critical values for our sample size are −4.52, −5.01 and −4.84. Only C/T rejects, at both 5% and 10%; it does not reject at 1% (critical value −5.79). Both C/T and C/S select a break at 1980Q1, which is the start of the Volcker disinflation. The C model picks 2005Q1 and finds nothing. In the figure the C/T line dips far below its dotted critical value around 1980 and nowhere else. The evidence for cointegration with a break is therefore specific to one specification, so we call it suggestive, not settled. One caveat: the simulated critical values use an ADF regression with no lagged differences, while the statistics use AIC-chosen lags, so the comparison is approximate. With 300 replications the 5% values have some simulation error.
Allow a structural break: the Gregory–Hansen test

How to write it: results The Engle–Granger and Phillips–Ouliaris tests do not reject the null of no cointegration between the federal funds rate and inflation (Engle–Granger statistic −2.05, p = 0.50), and the Johansen trace test is sensitive to the lag length. The Gregory–Hansen test with a break in the intercept and trend finds a statistic of −5.66 at 1980Q1, below the simulated 5% critical value of −5.01, while the intercept-only and regime-shift versions do not reject at 5% (−2.89 and −4.05). We read this as evidence that a long-run Fisher relation exists only after allowing for the change in monetary regime around 1980, and we treat it as suggestive because it depends on the specification.
The long-run relation before and after the break

How to read it The break model splits the long-run slope in two. Before 1980Q1 the slope on inflation is 0.81 (HAC standard error 0.15); afterwards it is 1.91 (0.19). The intercept falls from 2.16 to −0.38. DOLS, which corrects for endogeneity of inflation and for serial correlation, gives 0.77 (0.06) before the break and 2.20 (0.24) after, and 1.31 (0.23) for the whole sample. The whole-sample value is an average of two regimes and describes neither. After 1980 the funds rate moves by about two points for each point of inflation, which is the pattern of a central bank that raises the real rate when inflation rises (the Taylor principle). Before 1980 the response was below one-for-one. This is a description of the long-run association, not a causal effect, and the post-1980 sample has a long stretch of near-zero rates after 2008 that pulls the slope in a way the linear model cannot capture.
What to report in the paper

Item What to show Orders of integration ADF and KPSS for levels and first differences Residual tests Engle–Granger (both normalisations) and Phillips–Ouliaris, with the lag rule System test Johansen trace test with several lag lengths Break Gregory–Hansen statistic, break date, model, and how critical values were obtained Long-run estimate DOLS or FMOLS coefficient with robust standard errors, by regime if there is a break Common mistakes Skipping the unit-root step. Cointegration tests make sense only for I(1) series. Report ADF and KPSS together. Treating "no rejection" as "no relation". These tests have low power against a relation that shifted. Run the break test before you conclude. Using Engle–Granger critical values for Gregory–Hansen. The minimum over break dates is more negative. Use the Gregory–Hansen values.
What to report in the paper

Reading t-statistics of a static long-run regression. The OLS standard errors are not valid. Use DOLS or FMOLS. Choosing the break date and then telling a story only about it. Check that the date makes economic sense, such as the 1979–1982 monetary regime change. Reporting one lag length for Johansen. The result can change with the lag, as the table shows.
Factor Models: Principal Components and the Number of Factors
Factor Models: Principal Components and the Number of Factors: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code and more.
Factor Models: Principal Components and the Number of Factors

How much of the movement of inflation in 34 countries is a common, global movement? The approximate factor model writes each standardised series \(i\) as where \(F_t\) are \(r\) common factors, \(\lambda_i\) are the loadings and \(e_{it}\) is a country-specific component. The factors are estimated by principal components: \(\hat F\) are the first \(r\) principal components of the standardised data, scaled so that \(\hat F'\hat F/T = I\) . They are consistent for the space spanned by the true factors when both \(N\) and \(T\) are large (Bai and Ng, 2002). The factors are identified only up to rotation, so their sign and scale are arbitrary, and a factor means what its loadings say.
Factor Models: Principal Components and the Number of Factors

The number of factors \(r\) is chosen by the criteria of Bai and Ng, where \(V(k)\) is the average squared residual with \(k\) factors and \(g\) is a penalty; the three versions ( \(IC_{p1}, IC_{p2}, IC_{p3}\) ) differ in \(g\) . Choose the \(k\) with the smallest value. The Kaiser rule (keep factors with an eigenvalue above one for standardised data) is a rough check. Before you estimate anything Use stationary series. Growth rates, inflation or changes; factors of trending series pick up the trends. Standardise. Otherwise the series with the largest variance dominates. Check the size of the panel. The criteria work well when \(N\) and \(T\) are both large (above about 30 here); with a small \(N\) they are unreliable.
Factor Models: Principal Components and the Number of Factors

How to write it: methods sentence We extract common factors from the standardised inflation rates of 34 countries by principal components (Stock and Watson, 2002), and choose the number of factors with the information criteria of Bai and Ng (2002).
Factor Models: Principal Components and the Number of Factors

How to read it The panel has 34 years and 34 countries, from the large advanced economies to emerging markets. Average inflation differs a lot across countries, which is why we standardise: otherwise countries with the highest and most volatile inflation would dominate the factors.
Factor Models: Principal Components and the Number of Factors

How to read it The first factor explains 55% of the variance and the second 17%, and then the eigenvalues fall quickly: 2.1, 1.4, 1.0 for the third to fifth. The criteria do not agree. IC_p2, the most conservative, chooses 3 factors; IC_p1 and IC_p3 choose 6, the largest number allowed, which means that they do not find a minimum and should not be trusted with a panel of this size; the Kaiser rule gives 4. The scree plot shows the main break after the first factor and a smaller one after the second. We use one global factor for the interpretation and check results with 3.
Factor Models: Principal Components and the Number of Factors
Step 2: The factors and what they mean

How to read it The first factor loads positively on all 34 countries (average loading 0.72), which is the mark of a global inflation factor. It loads most on Italy (0.96), the United Kingdom (0.92), Spain and Portugal (0.91 and 0.90), and least on Indonesia (0.03), India (0.36), Egypt (0.41) and Mexico (0.49), where domestic factors dominate. The three factors explain most of the variance of each country: the median R-squared is 0.85, from 0.48 (Malaysia) to 0.93. The second and third factors have loadings of both signs and are rotation-dependent: do not give them a name without looking at the loadings.
Factor Models: Principal Components and the Number of Factors
Step 3: Is the factor structure stable?

How to read it The first factor explains 60% of the variance in the first half and 69% in the second, so the global component becomes more important. But the pattern of loadings is not very stable: the loadings of each half correlate only 0.43 and 0.52 with the full-sample loadings. The existence of a common component is robust, but which countries load on it most changes, so avoid strong statements about individual countries from the full-sample loadings.
Factor Models: Principal Components and the Number of Factors
What to report in the paper

Report the standardisation, the number of factors and the criteria used, the share of variance explained, the loadings (or a figure of them), the factor over time, and the stability across subsamples. State that the factors are defined up to rotation. How to write it: results The first principal component of inflation in 34 countries explains 55% of the variance, and the first three explain 78%. The Bai-Ng criterion IC_p2 selects three factors. The first loads positively on almost all countries, so we interpret it as a global inflation factor; its share of the variance rises from 60% in 1990–2006 to 69% in 2007–2023, although the pattern of country loadings differs between the two periods (correlation 0.43 and 0.52 with the full-sample loadings).
Factor Models: Principal Components and the Number of Factors

Mistakes to avoid Extracting factors from trending series. The first factor is then a common trend. No standardisation. The most volatile series dominate. Naming the factors without looking at the loadings. The rotation is arbitrary. Trusting the information criteria with a small panel. Check against the scree plot. Using estimated factors as if they were observed in a regression. For inference use a method that accounts for the estimation error, or bootstrap. Ignoring the sample split. A factor structure that changes needs a different model. Using all the variables regardless of quality. Series with many missing values or breaks distort the factors. Confusing the number of factors with the number of shocks. They can differ.
Forecast Comparison and the Diebold-Mariano Test
Forecast Comparison and the Diebold-Mariano Test: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
Forecast Comparison and the Diebold-Mariano Test

Does a model forecast inflation better than a random walk, and is the difference more than luck? Forecasts are produced at each date \(t\) using only the data up to \(t\) (an expanding window), \(h\) periods ahead. If \(e^{A}_{t+h}\) and \(e^{B}_{t+h}\) are the errors of two models and \(L\) is the loss (squared or absolute error), the loss differential is \(d_t = L(e^{A}_t) - L(e^{B}_t)\) . The Diebold-Mariano test checks \(H_0: E[d_t]=0\) : where the long-run variance uses \(h-1\) autocovariances, because forecast errors \(h\) steps ahead are correlated up to lag \(h-1\) . We use the small-sample correction of Harvey, Leybourne and Newbold and the \(t\) distribution. Model Forecast Random walk
Forecast Comparison and the Diebold-Mariano Test

the last observed value Historical mean the average of all data so far AR (BIC) an autoregression whose lag length is chosen by BIC at each date Damped exponential smoothing a damped-trend exponential smoothing model Before you test anything Use a benchmark that is hard to beat. For a persistent series a random walk is the usual benchmark; for a noisy series the historical mean may be better. Never use future data. Models must be estimated, and their lags selected, with data up to the forecast date only. Keep a long evaluation sample. With few forecasts the test has little power; the sample used here has about 100. How to write it: methods sentence
Forecast Comparison and the Diebold-Mariano Test

We evaluate forecasts out of sample with an expanding window that starts with 100 quarters, and compare squared forecast errors with the Diebold-Mariano test, using the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold correction. The benchmark is a random walk.
Forecast Comparison and the Diebold-Mariano Test

How to read it Inflation is persistent but noisy: the first-order autocorrelation is about 0.65. That is why a random walk is a poor forecaster for a noisy series (it passes all the noise into the forecast) and why a model that averages over the past can do better.
Forecast Comparison and the Diebold-Mariano Test

How to read it The random-walk forecast is the actual series delayed by one quarter, so it is as noisy as the data; the AR forecast is smoother and tracks the level without chasing every spike. The forecasts for the 102 quarters after 100 quarters of estimation are never based on data from the future.
Forecast Comparison and the Diebold-Mariano Test
Step 2: Accuracy and the Diebold-Mariano test

How to read it All three models have a lower root mean squared error than the random walk (2.88): 2.70 for the historical mean, 2.43 for the AR and 2.41 for the smoothing model, which is a gain of about 16% for the last two. But none of the differences is significant at 5% (p-values 0.63, 0.21 and 0.11). With about 100 forecasts and noisy errors, a gain of this size cannot be told from chance. The finding to report is that the data are consistent with an improvement, and not that the AR model is better.
Forecast Comparison and the Diebold-Mariano Test
Step 3: The answer depends on the horizon

How to read it Four quarters ahead the random walk does worse (RMSE 3.16) and the AR and smoothing models are significantly better (relative RMSE 0.80, p = 0.015 and 0.014). The gain from averaging over the past grows with the horizon, since the noise in the last observation matters more. The historical mean does not beat the random walk significantly (p = 0.21). A paper that reports one horizon only can give a misleading picture, so report several.
Forecast Comparison and the Diebold-Mariano Test

How to read it A model that is good on average can be good only in some periods. If the lines separate in a few quarters (for example during the 2008 crisis) and run parallel for the rest, the gain comes from those episodes. Here, 66% of the random walk's total squared error falls in the last third of the forecasts, which includes the 2008 crisis, so the large errors are concentrated in a short period. Plot the cumulative error, and check that the gain does not come from a few observations.
Forecast Comparison and the Diebold-Mariano Test
What to report in the paper

Report the benchmark, the estimation scheme (expanding or rolling window and its starting size), the number of forecasts, the loss function, the RMSE of each model relative to the benchmark, the test, and the horizons. Say if the data are revised values or real-time vintages. How to write it: results Table 4 reports out-of-sample forecasts of inflation. One quarter ahead, an autoregression and a damped exponential-smoothing model reduce the root mean squared error by about 16% relative to a random walk, but the differences are not significant (Diebold-Mariano p = 0.21 and 0.11). Four quarters ahead, the reduction is 20% and is significant at the 5% level (p = 0.015 and 0.014).

Mistakes to avoid Using in-sample fit as evidence of forecasting. A model with more parameters always fits better in sample. Look-ahead. Estimating the model or choosing the lags on the full sample before forecasting. No benchmark. An RMSE without a benchmark has no meaning. Not correcting for the horizon. For \(h>1\) the errors are autocorrelated; use \(h-1\) autocovariances in the long-run variance. Using Diebold-Mariano for nested models. The distribution is not standard; use the Clark-West test. Too few forecasts. The test has little power below about 50 forecasts. Reporting one horizon. The ranking of the models changes with the horizon. Ignoring data revisions. Forecast comparisons with revised data can differ from real-time ones.
GARCH, EGARCH, GJR-GARCH and DCC: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Large moves tend to follow large moves, and calm periods follow calm periods. A regression with a constant variance ignores this, so its standard errors, its forecast intervals and any risk number built on it can be wrong. Our question is: does the volatility of U.S. stock returns change over time, do falling markets raise it more than rising markets, and does the correlation between U.S. stocks and the Korean won move too? The returns are \(r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t\) with \(\varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t\) , where \(z_t\) is an independent standardised shock and the conditional variance \(\sigma_t^2\) follows one of these processes: Symbol Meaning What to expect \(\alpha\)

reaction to last period's shock larger means volatility jumps after big shocks \(\beta\) persistence of volatility close to one means volatility decays slowly \(\gamma\) asymmetry for stocks, bad news raises volatility more than good news (the leverage effect) \(\nu\) degrees of freedom of the Student- \(t\) shock small values mean fat tails For two series, the DCC model of Engle (2002) first fits a GARCH model to each series, then lets the correlation of the standardised shocks follow \(Q_t = (1-a-b)\bar Q + a\, z_{t-1}z_{t-1}' + b\, Q_{t-1}\) , with the correlation matrix \(R_t\) obtained by rescaling \(Q_t\) . Before you estimate anything State what the volatility model is for: a better standard error for a regression, a risk measure, a forecast, or a result in itself, such as the leverage effect. The first needs only a correct variance model, the second needs a good tail distribution, and the third needs an asymmetric model. Say which one your paper needs.

How to write it: model section We model monthly returns as \(r_t = \mu + \sigma_t z_t\) , where the conditional variance follows a GARCH(1,1), GJR-GARCH(1,1) or EGARCH(1,1) process and \(z_t\) has a Student- \(t\) or skewed Student- \(t\) distribution. The specification is chosen by the Bayesian information criterion, estimated by quasi-maximum likelihood, and checked with tests on the standardised residuals. To study co-movement with the Korean won we estimate the dynamic conditional correlation model of Engle (2002) in two steps.
Load the data and look at the returns

How to read it The sample has 527 months, from 1981-06 to 2025-04. U.S. stock returns average 0.70% a month with a standard deviation of 3.65%. They are skewed to the left (skewness −1.43) and have fat tails (excess kurtosis 6.47). The three largest falls are 2008-10 (−22.8%), 2020-03 (−21.2%) and 1987-11 (−13.4%), and the squared deviations on the right cluster around these episodes. The won is even more extreme: its excess kurtosis is 78 because of one month, the Asian crisis of December 1997, when the won lost 36.9% against the dollar. Both patterns, clusters and fat tails, are what a volatility model should capture.

How to read it For the won, constant variance is rejected at every lag (p below 0.001 at 1, 3 and 6 lags and 0.016 at 12 lags). For U.S. stocks the evidence is weaker: p = 0.003, 0.022 and 0.019 at 1, 3 and 6 lags, but 0.165 at 12 lags, and the Ljung–Box test on the squares gives 0.082. The test loses power when it uses many lags, and monthly aggregation weakens volatility clustering. Do not stop here. A likelihood-based comparison, in the next step, is more powerful. Report the tests at several lags, not at one chosen after the fact.

How to read it Three things stand out. First, the error distribution matters most: moving from normal to Student- \(t\) errors in the GARCH model raises the log-likelihood by 43 points (−1408.2 to −1365.1) for one extra parameter. Second, volatility clustering is present beyond fat tails: a GARCH(1,1) raises the log-likelihood by 15.3 points over a constant variance with the same \(t\) errors, a likelihood-ratio statistic of 30.4. Its asymptotic distribution is not the usual \(\chi^2\) , because the parameters lie at the edge of the parameter space under the null, but the statistic is far above any reasonable critical value. Third, asymmetry and skewness both help: GJR and EGARCH improve on the symmetric GARCH- \(t\) , and skewed- \(t\) errors improve on \(t\) errors. The EGARCH with skewed- \(t\) errors has the lowest AIC (2713.0) and the lowest BIC (2742.8), so we use it.

How to read it The persistence is \(\hat\beta = 0.882\) (standard error 0.054), so a shock to volatility loses half of its effect in 5.5 months, and \(\hat\alpha = 0.224\) (s.e. 0.055) says that large shocks, of either sign, raise volatility. The leverage term is \(\hat\gamma = -0.117\) (s.e. 0.059, p = 0.048), significant at 5% but with a confidence interval that nearly reaches zero. In EGARCH a negative \(\gamma\) means that bad news raises volatility more than good news. A \(-2\) shock raises next month's log variance by 0.52, which multiplies the variance by 1.68. A \(+2\) shock raises it by 0.05, a factor of 1.05. The distribution table shows fat tails (the degrees-of-freedom parameter \(\eta\) is about 5.4) and a negative skewness parameter \(\lambda\) .

How to write it: results The EGARCH(1,1) model with skewed Student- \(t\) errors has a persistence parameter \(\hat\beta = 0.882\) (s.e. 0.054), so a volatility shock has a half-life of 5.5 months. The coefficient on the size of the shock is \(\hat\alpha = 0.224\) (s.e. 0.055). The leverage term is \(\hat\gamma = -0.117\) (s.e. 0.059): a standardised shock of \(-2\) raises next month's variance by 68%, while a shock of \(+2\) raises it by 5%. The shocks have fat tails ( \(\hat\eta = 5.4\) degrees of freedom) and are skewed to the left.
Asymmetry: the effect of good and bad news

How to read it The left panel shows the response implied by the EGARCH estimates: it is steep for negative shocks and much flatter for positive ones. The evidence on asymmetry is real but moderate. The EGARCH leverage term has p = 0.048 and the GJR leverage term has a p-value of 0.016, but the Engle–Ng sign-bias test on the symmetric GARCH- \(t\) has a joint p-value of 0.071, and none of its three terms is individually significant at 5%. The information criteria favour the asymmetric models. Report the leverage effect as present but not precisely estimated, which is also what the wide confidence interval of \(\gamma\) says.

How to read it The model removes the volatility clustering: the Ljung–Box test on the squared standardised residuals gives p = 1.000 and the ARCH-LM test p = 1.000, because the autocorrelations of the squares are all within 0.03 of zero. There is no leftover autocorrelation in the residuals themselves (p = 0.103). The standardised residuals are still left-skewed (−1.41) with excess kurtosis of 6.8, because a handful of months remain extreme, above all March 2020, when the standardised shock was −7.6. The conditional volatility ranges from 7.5% a year in December 2017 to 34.3% in April 2020, against a constant-variance estimate of 12.6%. The figure shows the volatility rising in 1987, 2008 and 2020 and falling in the calm years that follow.
Do the forecasts and the risk numbers improve?

How to read it The result is mixed, and it is worth reporting as it is. Over all 183 months the constant variance has the lowest QLIKE loss (3.466 against 3.518 to 3.542), because March 2020 dominates the comparison: the GARCH models had forecast a calm month and then faced a fall of 21%. Excluding 2020 the ranking reverses and the GARCH models are better (3.129 to 3.162 against 3.250). The Diebold–Mariano tests do not reject equal accuracy in either direction (p between 0.65 and 0.75 over the full sample). The value-at-risk backtest tells a similar story. The constant-variance VaR is violated in 9 months of 183 (4.9%), exactly the nominal rate. The GARCH VaRs are narrower on average (−4.2% to −4.9% against −5.4%) and are violated 12 to 14 times (6.6% to 7.7%). None of the Kupiec tests rejects the 5% rate, but the GARCH-t is the closest to doing so (p = 0.126). The lesson is that at the monthly frequency the in-sample gain is clear and the out-of-sample gain is not. Volatility models usually earn more at daily or weekly frequency, where clustering is stronger.
Do the forecasts and the risk numbers improve?

How to write it: forecast evaluation We evaluate one-month-ahead variance forecasts with an expanding window from April 2010 to April 2025 (183 forecasts), re-estimating each model every month. Using the QLIKE loss, the GARCH-family models improve on a constant variance once March 2020 is excluded (3.13 to 3.16 against 3.25), but not over the full sample (3.52 to 3.54 against 3.47), and the Diebold–Mariano tests do not reject equal accuracy (p between 0.65 and 0.75). The 5% value-at-risk of every model passes the Kupiec test, although the GARCH models have more violations (12 to 14 of 183) than the 9 expected.
Time-varying correlation with the Korean won (DCC)

How to read it The won has strong volatility clustering ( \(\hat\alpha = 0.65\) , \(\hat\beta = 0.94\) in its EGARCH). The DCC parameters are \(\hat a = 0.157\) and \(\hat b = 0.606\) . Their sum, 0.764, is well below one, so the correlation returns to its long-run level within a few months (a half-life of about 2.6 months). The likelihood-ratio test of a constant correlation gives 15.7 (p = 0.0004). As in the GARCH test, the usual \(\chi^2\) distribution is only an approximation because the parameters are on the boundary under the null, but the value is large. The correlation is negative on average (−0.27): the won weakens against the dollar when U.S. stocks fall. It was strongest in the global financial crisis (−0.71 in 2008-11) and turned positive in 2002. If you use the DCC, report the constant correlation next to it, as the dashed line does, so that a reader can see how much the dynamics add.
Time-varying correlation with the Korean won (DCC)

How to write it: correlation The dynamic conditional correlation between U.S. stock returns and the change in the won per dollar has parameters \(\hat a = 0.157\) and \(\hat b = 0.606\) , and a likelihood-ratio test rejects a constant correlation (statistic 15.7, p = 0.0004). The correlation averages −0.27: when U.S. stocks fall, the won tends to weaken. It reached −0.71 in November 2008, and it was positive at times, up to 0.33 in August 2002.
What to report in the paper

Item What to show Evidence of ARCH effects ARCH-LM at several lags, and the likelihood-ratio test against a constant variance Specification the table of AIC and BIC across variance models and error distributions Estimates \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) , the distribution parameters, the persistence and the half-life Diagnostics Ljung–Box and ARCH-LM on the standardised residuals, and the sign-bias test Forecasts and risk QLIKE with a Diebold–Mariano test, value-at-risk violations and the Kupiec test Correlation the DCC parameters, the test against a constant correlation, and the correlation path Common mistakes Assuming normal errors. Returns have fat tails. A GARCH model with normal errors can fit the clustering and still understate risk, and it changes the estimates of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) .
What to report in the paper

Reading \(\alpha+\beta\) close to one as a unit root in variance. Check for a structural break in the variance level before concluding that shocks last forever. Skipping the standardised-residual tests. A GARCH model is adequate only if the standardised residuals show no leftover autocorrelation or clustering. Using monthly data and expecting the daily result. Aggregation weakens volatility clustering. If you can, use daily or weekly data for volatility work. Comparing log-likelihoods across different distributions without a penalty. Use AIC or BIC.
2SLS and GMM: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. Endogenous regressors that need instruments.
The question and why OLS fails

The question is: how strongly does the Federal Reserve raise its interest rate when inflation rises? The standard description of policy is a Taylor rule with interest-rate smoothing: where \(i_t\) is the federal funds rate, \(\pi_t\) is inflation over the past four quarters and \(x_t\) is the output gap. The long-run response to inflation is \(\beta/(1-\rho)\) . The Taylor principle says it must exceed 1, so that the real interest rate rises when inflation rises. OLS cannot estimate this equation consistently, for two reasons. Simultaneity. The interest rate affects inflation and output within the same quarter, so the regressors respond to the dependent variable. Policy shocks. The error term \(\varepsilon_t\) is the unexpected part of policy. Because a policy surprise moves inflation and output, the regressors are correlated with the error.
The question and why OLS fails

A regressor that is correlated with the error term is endogenous . OLS is then biased, and more data does not fix it. The solution is instrumental variables. What an instrument must do An instrument \(z\) is a variable that satisfies two conditions. Relevance: \(z\) is correlated with the endogenous regressor. This can be tested (Step 5). Exogeneity: \(z\) is uncorrelated with the error term. This cannot be tested directly; it must be argued. With more instruments than endogenous regressors, it can be partly tested (Step 6). Here the instruments are lagged values of inflation, the output gap and the interest rate. They are relevant because these series are persistent. They are plausibly exogenous because a policy surprise in quarter \(t\) cannot have influenced what happened in earlier quarters. This is the approach of Clarida, Galí and Gertler (2000).
The question and why OLS fails

How to write it: identification Estimating the policy rule by OLS would be inconsistent because inflation and the output gap respond contemporaneously to the interest rate and are therefore correlated with the policy shock \(\varepsilon_t\) . Following Clarida, Galí and Gertler (2000), we treat current inflation and the output gap as endogenous and instrument them with their own first four lags and the second lag of the federal funds rate. These variables are predetermined with respect to the period- \(t\) policy shock and, given the persistence of inflation and output, are strongly correlated with the endogenous regressors.
Load the data and build the instruments

This guide uses the linearmodels package for instrumental-variable estimation. Install it once with pip install linearmodels . How to read it There are 114 quarters. The model has 2 endogenous regressors and 9 instruments. It is overidentified : there are 7 more instruments than needed. Overidentification is useful, because the extra instruments make it possible to test instrument validity in Step 6. With exactly as many instruments as endogenous regressors the model is just identified and that test is not available. The lagged interest rate is treated as exogenous because it was set before the current shock. That requires the errors to be serially uncorrelated, which is one reason the second lag is also added as an instrument.
Always estimate OLS first. It is the benchmark that shows how much the instruments change the answer.

2SLS works in two steps. First stage: regress each endogenous regressor on all the instruments and exogenous variables, and keep the fitted values. Second stage: regress the dependent variable on those fitted values. The fitted values contain only the variation that the instruments explain, which is unrelated to the error. Never run the two stages by hand: the standard errors from a manual second stage are wrong. Use a routine that does both. How to read it Compare with OLS. The coefficient on inflation is similar (0.28 against 0.32), but the coefficient on the output gap falls from 0.26 to 0.16. OLS overstated the response to the output gap, as expected if a strong economy and a tight policy stance move together within the quarter for reasons the rule does not capture.

The smoothing coefficient of 0.83 means the Fed moves the rate gradually: only about 17% of the desired adjustment happens in a quarter. This is why the long-run responses are much larger than the impact coefficients. cov_type="kernel" requests standard errors that are robust to heteroskedasticity and serial correlation, the IV equivalent of Newey–West.

Weak instruments, only loosely related to the endogenous regressors, are worse than no instruments: 2SLS becomes biased towards OLS and its standard errors are unreliable. How to read it Partial R-squared is the share of each endogenous regressor explained by the instruments after removing the exogenous variables. Here it is 0.96 for inflation and 0.83 for the output gap. First-stage F tests whether the instruments are jointly zero in the first stage. The rule of thumb of Staiger and Stock (1997) is that an F below 10 signals weak instruments. Both statistics are far above 10. These instruments are very strong, which is no surprise: four-quarter inflation and the output gap are highly persistent, so their own lags predict them well. In cross-section work you will rarely see values like these; an F of 15 to 30 is typical of a good instrument there. With several endogenous regressors, also report a joint statistic such as Cragg–Donald or Kleibergen–Paap.
Test 2: are the instruments valid? The overidentification test

How to read it The Sargan test (called the Hansen J test in GMM) has the null hypothesis that all instruments are valid , meaning uncorrelated with the error. A large p-value is what you want. Here p = 0.35, so the null is not rejected: the data give no evidence against the instruments. Three cautions. A rejection tells you that at least one instrument is invalid but not which one. A non-rejection is not proof of validity: the test assumes that at least enough instruments are valid to identify the model, and it has low power when all instruments share the same flaw. And with a very large number of instruments the test almost never rejects. Keep the instrument set small and justify each instrument in words.
Test 3: is the regressor really endogenous?

How to read it The Wu–Hausman and Durbin tests have the null that the regressors are exogenous , in which case OLS and 2SLS estimate the same thing and OLS, being more precise, should be preferred. Both reject strongly (p below 0.001). Inflation and the output gap are endogenous, and the IV estimates are needed. If this test does not reject, report OLS as the main result and 2SLS as a robustness check. Instrumenting a regressor that is not endogenous only makes the estimates noisier.

The generalised method of moments (GMM) uses the same instruments but weights them optimally. With heteroskedastic or serially correlated errors, 2SLS is no longer the most efficient estimator; two-step GMM is. How to read it Coefficients. GMM and 2SLS give similar estimates, as they should when the instruments are valid; large differences between them would be a warning. The GMM standard error on inflation is smaller (0.079 against 0.109), which is the efficiency gain. Hansen J test. p = 0.34, so the overidentifying restrictions are not rejected. Long-run responses. The long-run response to inflation is 1.79: in the long run the Fed raised the funds rate by about 1.8 points for each point of inflation. Its standard error, 0.49, comes from the delta method, because the long-run response is a nonlinear function of two coefficients.

The Taylor principle. The estimate is above 1, but the one-sided test of "at most 1" has a p-value of 0.054. The point estimate supports the Taylor principle; the statistical evidence is borderline at the 5% level. Report the test even when it is borderline. Writing that the Taylor principle "is satisfied" on the strength of a point estimate alone would overstate the result.

How to read it Instrument set. With two lags, or with instruments dated from lag 2 only, the long-run inflation response stays between 1.6 and 1.8 and the J test never rejects. The result does not depend on the particular instruments. Before Volcker. For 1961–1979 the long-run response is 0.52, well below 1. Policy did not satisfy the Taylor principle in the 1970s. This contrast with the later period is the central finding of Clarida, Galí and Gertler (2000), and the data reproduce it. Within the later period the result is fragile. Dropping the 1979–82 disinflation lowers the response to 0.99, and for the Greenspan years alone it is 0.35. The strong response in the baseline comes largely from the Volcker disinflation.

Why would the estimate collapse after 1983? Inflation was low and stable, so there is little variation to identify the response from, and the smoothing coefficient above 0.9 makes the long-run ratio very sensitive. The measurement of the variables matters too: studies that use real-time data and forecasts, rather than the revised data and HP-filtered gap used here, find stronger responses in this period. A careful paper reports this sensitivity and does not claim more than the 1979–2007 result supports.
Part 2. Dynamic panels: why OLS and fixed effects both fail

The second half of this guide applies the same idea to panel data with a lagged dependent variable , the setting of growth regressions across countries and of investment, leverage or employment equations across firms: Here \(\eta_i\) is a fixed effect for each unit and \(\lambda_t\) a year effect. The lagged dependent variable is endogenous by construction, and the two usual estimators are biased in opposite directions. Estimator Problem Direction of bias in \(\alpha\) Pooled OLS \(y_{i,t-1}\) contains \(\eta_i\) , which is in the error upwards Fixed effects demeaning makes \(y_{i,t-1}\) correlated with the demeaned error when T is small (Nickell bias) downwards Difference GMM (Arellano–Bond) first-difference to remove \(\eta_i\) , then instrument \(\Delta y_{i,t-1}\) with levels dated \(t-2\) and earlier
Part 2. Dynamic panels: why OLS and fixed effects both fail

consistent if the instruments are valid and strong The example is the one the method was developed on: employment in 140 UK manufacturing firms, 1976–1984, from Arellano and Bond (1991). The question is how persistent is firm employment, and how does it respond to wages and capital? How to read it This is the typical shape for dynamic panel GMM: many units (140) and few periods (7 to 9) . The method relies on the number of units being large. With a long panel of few units, such as 20 countries over 40 years, fixed effects is the better choice and the Nickell bias is small. The variables are in logs: employment n , the real wage w , capital k and industry output ys . The model has two lags of employment, current and lagged wages, and current and two lags of capital and output, as in the original paper. Download the helper file and the data into your working folder.
Panel step 1: pooled OLS and fixed effects give the bounds

How to read it The coefficient on lagged employment is 1.05 by pooled OLS and 0.73 by fixed effects. Because the first is biased upwards and the second downwards, a credible estimate should lie between them . This bounds check, suggested by Bond (2002), costs two regressions and is the first thing to run in any dynamic panel study.
gmm_lags=(2, None) uses all available lags from \(t-2\) back as instruments, which gives 41 instruments for 140 firms.
Panel step 3: the three specification tests

How to read it A dynamic panel GMM table is not complete without these. AR(1) is significant, which is expected: first-differencing creates first-order correlation by construction. It tells you nothing about validity. AR(2) is the test that matters. Its null is no second-order serial correlation in the differenced residuals. If it is rejected, the errors in levels are serially correlated and levels dated \(t-2\) are not valid instruments. Here p = 0.61, so the instruments pass. If it had rejected, you would start the instruments at \(t-3\) . Hansen J has the null that the instruments are valid as a group. Here p = 0.18, which does not reject. Be suspicious of p-values very close to 1: that is a sign of too many instruments, not of very good ones.
Panel step 3: the three specification tests
Instrument count. 41 instruments for 140 firms. The count must stay well below the number of units, because too many instruments overfit the endogenous variable and weaken the Hansen test.
Panel step 4: robustness to the instrument set

How to read it The table separates what this dataset can tell you from what it cannot. The wage and capital effects are robust. Across all five instrument sets the wage coefficient stays between −0.60 and −0.71 and the capital coefficient between 0.31 and 0.37. Neither the AR(2) test nor the Hansen test rejects at the 5% level in any row, although two rows come close (p = 0.07 and 0.08). The persistence coefficient is not. It ranges from 0.39 to 1.36 depending on the instruments, with large standard errors, and in four of the five rows it falls outside the bounds of 0.73 and 1.05. This is a known weakness of difference GMM, not a mistake in the code. When a series is highly persistent, its past levels are weak instruments for its current changes , and the estimate of \(\alpha\) becomes imprecise and biased towards the fixed-effects value. Blundell and Bond (1998) proposed system GMM for exactly this case: it adds the equation in levels, instrumented with lagged differences, and is now the standard estimator for persistent series such as output, capital or employment. In Stata it is xtabond2 without the noleveleq option; in R, plm::pgmm with transformation = "ld" .
Panel step 4: robustness to the instrument set
So the paper can report the wage and capital elasticities with confidence, and should say plainly that the degree of persistence is not well identified by difference GMM in this sample.
