The instruments are strong, with first-stage F-statistics of 301 for inflation and 58 for the output gap, and the Hansen J test does not reject the overidentifying restrictions (p = 0.34). A Wu–Hausman test rejects the exogeneity of inflation and the output gap (p < 0.01), confirming the need for instrumental-variable estimation. The GMM estimates imply a smoothing coefficient of 0.87 and long-run responses of 1.79 to inflation (s.e. 0.49) and 1.50 to the output gap (s.e. 0.86). The point estimate of the inflation response exceeds one, consistent with the Taylor principle, although the hypothesis that it is at most one is rejected only at the 10% level (p = 0.054). For 1961–1979 the corresponding estimate is 0.52. The post-1979 estimate is sensitive to the sample: it falls to about one when the 1979–82 disinflation is excluded.

How to write it: dynamic panel results Table 4 reports one-step difference GMM estimates of the employment equation for 140 firms over 1976–1984, with standard errors robust to heteroskedasticity and within-firm correlation. Lagged employment is instrumented with its levels dated \(t-2\) and earlier, giving 41 instruments. The Arellano–Bond test does not reject the absence of second-order serial correlation in the differenced residuals (z = −0.52, p = 0.61), and the Hansen test does not reject the overidentifying restrictions ( \(\chi^2(25)\) = 31.4, p = 0.18). The short-run wage elasticity of employment is −0.61 (s.e. 0.18) and the short-run capital elasticity is 0.36 (s.e. 0.06); both are stable across alternative instrument sets. The coefficient on lagged employment is 0.69, slightly below the fixed-effects estimate of 0.73, and it is sensitive to the choice of instruments. This pattern is characteristic of weak instruments in difference GMM for persistent series, so the degree of employment persistence should be interpreted with caution.

What a referee will ask Why are your instruments exogenous? This is the central question, and no test answers it. Give an economic argument for each instrument. Are they strong? Report the first-stage F for every endogenous regressor. Do the results depend on the instrument set? Show at least one alternative set. How many instruments? Report the count. In panels it must be below the number of units. Does the estimate lie between fixed effects and pooled OLS? If not, as in the panel example here, suspect weak instruments and consider system GMM. Did AR(2) pass? If it is rejected, lag-2 instruments are invalid. Is IV needed at all? Report the endogeneity test and the OLS estimates.
How was the output gap measured? The gap here uses a two-sided HP filter, which uses future data; a real-time measure would be a useful check, and the paper should say so.
Granger Causality in Levels (Toda-Yamamoto): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Does money growth help predict inflation, once we use the past of prices and output too? Variable \(x\) Granger-causes \(y\) if past values of \(x\) improve the forecast of \(y\) given the past of \(y\) and of the other variables. In a VAR in levels with \(p\) lags, the null that \(x\) does not cause \(y\) is that the coefficients of \(x\) in the equation of \(y\) are zero for all \(p\) lags. With I(1) variables the Wald statistic does not have a chi-squared distribution. Toda and Yamamoto (1995) estimate a VAR with \(p + d_{max}\) lags, where \(d_{max}\) is the highest order of integration, and test only the first \(p\) lags of \(x\) . The Wald statistic is then asymptotically chi-squared with \(p\) degrees of freedom.

Before you test anything Find \(d_{max}\) . Run the unit-root tests (see the unit-root guide) and take the highest order of integration; for log prices, money and GDP it is usually 1. Choose \(p\) by an information criterion on the VAR in levels. The result must not depend on that choice; check it. Do not difference or detrend the data first. The method is designed for levels. How to write it: methods sentence Because the variables may be integrated, we test Granger non-causality with the procedure of Toda and Yamamoto (1995): a VAR in levels with \(p\) lags chosen by AIC plus one extra lag (the maximum order of integration), and a Wald test on the first \(p\) lags of the causing variable.

How to read it M2 and GDP are I(1): a unit root is not rejected in levels and is rejected in first differences. The price level is the awkward case: its first difference also fails to reject a unit root (p = 0.196), because inflation is very persistent in this sample, so the price level may be I(2). The method only needs an upper bound on the order of integration, so a safe choice is \(d_{max}=2\) . We use \(d_{max}=1\) in the main test, as is usual, and show in Step 4 which conclusions survive \(d_{max}=2\) .

How to read it The criteria do not agree: AIC and FPE choose 4 lags, HQIC 3 and BIC 2. We use 4 and show in Step 3 what happens with other lengths. Too few lags leave serial correlation and invalidate the test; too many reduce its power.

How to read it Money does not help to predict prices (p = 0.27), and prices do not help to predict money (p = 0.20). GDP predicts prices at the 5% level (p = 0.041), and prices (p = 0.002) and money (p = 0.020) predict GDP. GDP does not significantly predict money (p = 0.069). The evidence for money leading prices, a classic hypothesis, is therefore weak in this sample, once output is controlled for.
Step 3: Is the conclusion sensitive to the lag length?

How to read it Money to prices is not significant at 5% for 1 to 5 lags (p between 0.26 and 0.83) and is significant with 6 lags (p = 0.016): an isolated rejection at one lag length is weak evidence. Prices to output and money to output are significant at 5% for every lag length from 1 to 6, so these two results are robust. GDP to prices is significant only with 4 lags (p = 0.041), which makes it fragile.

How to read it Adding a second extra lag costs some power, and it matters here. Money still does not predict prices (p = 0.28), and money still predicts GDP (p = 0.023), so these two results are robust. But the effect of prices on GDP, which had p = 0.002 with \(d_{max}=1\) , is no longer significant (p = 0.12), and GDP to prices moves from 0.041 to 0.056. These two conclusions depend on treating the price level as I(1) and should be reported as such.
What to report in the paper

Report \(d_{max}\) and how you found it, the lag length and the criterion, the Wald statistics and p-values for every direction, and the p-values for other lag lengths. Use the word "predicts" or "Granger-causes", not "causes". How to write it: results Table 6 gives Toda-Yamamoto tests from a VAR in levels with four lags plus one extra lag. Past money growth does not help to predict the price level (p = 0.27), and the result holds for most lag lengths. Money helps to predict GDP (p = 0.020), and this is significant at 5% for every lag length from one to six and with one more extra lag (p = 0.023). The predictive content of prices for GDP (p = 0.002) depends on treating the price level as I(1): with two extra lags it is not significant (p = 0.12). We interpret these as evidence of predictive content, not of structural causation.

Mistakes to avoid Running an ordinary Granger test on levels with unit roots. The p-values are wrong. Testing all \(p + d_{max}\) lags. The extra lags are for the distribution and must not be tested. Differencing the series to avoid the problem. If the variables are cointegrated, differencing loses the long-run information. Choosing the lag to get a significant result. Report the sensitivity. Reading Granger causality as causation. An omitted variable that moves both can produce it. Leaving out an important variable. The result changes with the other variables in the VAR. Ignoring serial correlation in the residuals. Check the residuals of the VAR. Too many variables for the sample. The number of parameters grows with \(k^2 p\) .

Long Memory and Fractional Integration (GPH and Local Whittle)
Long Memory and Fractional Integration (GPH and Local Whittle): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code and more.
Long Memory and Fractional Integration (GPH and Local Whittle)

Is U.S. inflation a stationary series, a unit root, or something in between? A series is fractionally integrated of order \(d\) if \((1-L)^d y_t\) is stationary with short memory. The operator is with weights that fall slowly (hyperbolically), so the autocorrelations of the series also fall slowly: \(d\) Behaviour \(d = 0\) short memory: autocorrelations decay geometrically \(0 < d < 0.5\) stationary, long memory: shocks last, but the series reverts to its mean \(0.5 \le d < 1\) not stationary, but reverts to its mean: shocks die out, very slowly \(d = 1\) unit root Two semiparametric estimators use only the \(m\) lowest Fourier frequencies, so they do not require a model for the short-run dynamics. The GPH estimator of Geweke and Porter-Hudak regresses the log periodogram on \(-2\ln(2\sin(\lambda_j/2))\) ; the local Whittle estimator of Robinson maximises an approximate likelihood on the same frequencies. The bandwidth is \(m = n^{\alpha}\) , with \(\alpha\) between 0.5 and 0.8.
Long Memory and Fractional Integration (GPH and Local Whittle)

Before you estimate anything Look for breaks first. A shift in the mean or in the variance produces spurious long memory. Test for breaks, and estimate d on the sample that is homogeneous. Plot the autocorrelations. Slow, steady decay is the sign. Choose the bandwidth in advance. Report a range, since the estimate changes with \(m\) . How to write it: methods sentence We measure persistence with the fractional order of integration \(d\) , estimated by the log-periodogram regression of Geweke and Porter-Hudak (1983) and the local Whittle estimator of Robinson (1995), with bandwidths \(m = n^{\alpha}\) for \(\alpha\) between 0.5 and 0.8.
Long Memory and Fractional Integration (GPH and Local Whittle)
Load the data and look at the autocorrelations

How to read it The autocorrelations are 0.64 at one quarter, 0.24 at three years (lag 12) and 0.26 at five years (lag 20), and fall to 0.03 only at ten years: large and slowly decaying. The ADF test rejects a unit root (p = 0.027), but the KPSS test rejects stationarity (0.67 against a critical value of 0.46). When the two tests with opposite nulls both reject, a fractional order between 0 and 1 is a natural description.
Long Memory and Fractional Integration (GPH and Local Whittle)

How to read it The estimates of d are between 0.47 and 0.76 across the bandwidths, so inflation is at the border between stationary and non-stationary long memory. The two estimators agree on the range, and at the central bandwidth (m = 31) they give 0.76 (s.e. 0.14) and 0.67 (s.e. 0.09). The estimates fall as the bandwidth grows, because higher frequencies contain the short-run dynamics, which biases the estimate toward zero. Report the whole range, not the value that suits the argument. All the estimates are significantly above 0. The lowest (0.47, s.e. 0.06) is clearly below 1, while at the central bandwidth the GPH estimate (0.76, s.e. 0.14) is within two standard errors of 1.
Long Memory and Fractional Integration (GPH and Local Whittle)
Step 2: Does fractional differencing remove the dependence?

How to read it Fractional differencing with d = 0.67 reduces the Ljung-Box statistic from 618 to 44, but the p-value is 0.002, and the first-order autocorrelation changes from 0.64 to −0.26: the filter removes the slow decay but over-corrects the first lag, so some short-run dependence is left. A real model would combine the fractional difference with a short-memory ARMA part (an ARFIMA model), which this semiparametric approach does not estimate.
Long Memory and Fractional Integration (GPH and Local Whittle)
Step 3: A check on the estimator with simulated data

How to read it The estimator recovers the true d on average (the mean estimates are close to 0, 0.3 and 0.6) with a standard deviation of about 0.06 for 1,000 observations. With our 202 observations the uncertainty is larger, which explains why the interval for inflation is wide.
Long Memory and Fractional Integration (GPH and Local Whittle)
What to report in the paper

Report d with its standard error for a range of bandwidths, the autocorrelation plot, and the unit-root and stationarity tests. Say that breaks were checked. Interpret d, not only its significance: with d about 0.7, a shock to inflation fades, but over many years. How to write it: results Inflation is highly persistent: its first-order autocorrelation is 0.64 and the autocorrelations remain positive for five years. The ADF test rejects a unit root, and the KPSS test rejects stationarity. The local Whittle estimate of the order of fractional integration is 0.67 (standard error 0.09) at bandwidth \(m = n^{0.65}\) , and the estimates lie between 0.47 and 0.68 for other bandwidths, so inflation is neither stationary with short memory nor a unit root.
Long Memory and Fractional Integration (GPH and Local Whittle)

Mistakes to avoid Mistaking a break for long memory. A change of mean produces a high d. A single bandwidth. The estimate depends on \(m\) ; show a range. Estimating d on a series with a trend. Remove it first, or the estimate is biased. Using the asymptotic standard error with a small sample. It is approximate. Reading d = 0.4 as a unit root. The series reverts to the mean. Differencing fully when d is below one. It over-differences the series. Applying it to very short series. Under 100 observations the estimates are unreliable. Treating the fractional difference as the final model. The short-run dynamics still have to be modelled.
Local Projections (Impulse Responses): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

What is the path of \(y\) after a shock \(s\) ? A local projection estimates the impulse response at each horizon \(h = 0, 1, \dots, H\) with a separate regression: where \(x_t\) holds the controls dated \(t\) or earlier (lags of \(y\) , of the shock and of other variables, and any variables ordered before the shock). The coefficient \(\beta_h\) is the response of \(y_{t+h}\) to the shock, and the sequence \(\beta_0, \dots, \beta_H\) is the impulse response function. A VAR gets the same object by iterating one estimated system forward; a local projection estimates each horizon directly. That makes it less efficient but more robust: a misspecified lag length or a nonlinear dynamic does not propagate from short to long horizons.

Three checks before you trust a local projection Is the shock identified? The coefficient is a causal response only if \(s_t\) is unrelated to the other things that move \(y\) . Either the shock is exogenous by construction (a narrative or high-frequency measure, an instrument), or you control for what the shock responds to within the period (the recursive, or Cholesky, assumption). Is the transformation right? Local projections work in levels, in differences and in growth rates, but the outcome must match the question. A response of a level needs the level (or a cumulative sum of growth rates) on the left-hand side. Are the standard errors right? The horizon- \(h\) errors are a moving average of order \(h\) , so ordinary standard errors are wrong. Use Newey-West errors (with bandwidth \(h+1\) ) or lag augmentation with robust errors.

How to write it: the model We estimate the dynamic effect of a credit-spread shock on industrial production with local projections (Jordà 2005). For each horizon \(h = 0, \dots, 24\) months we regress the cumulative growth of industrial production from \(t\) to \(t+h\) on the change in the credit spread at \(t\) , on the contemporaneous stock return, and on six lags of every variable. Identification is recursive: the stock market reacts to news about credit conditions within the month, whereas industrial production and the policy rate respond with a lag. Standard errors are Newey-West with bandwidth \(h+1\) , and the shock is scaled to one standard deviation.
Load the data and check the transformation

How to read it All four series are stationary: the ADF tests reject a unit root (p ≤ 0.001) and the KPSS tests do not reject stationarity (p = 0.10 is the top of the table of available p-values). Stock returns, industrial-production growth and the changes in the fed funds rate and the credit spread are already in the form a local projection needs, so no further transformation is required. The sample has 420 months (1985–2019), and the credit-spread change has a standard deviation of 0.17 percentage points, so a "one-standard-deviation shock" is a 17 basis-point widening. If your shock or outcome were a trending level, use a change or a growth rate; local projections in levels are also valid (see lag augmentation in Step 6), but the interpretation changes.
Identify the shock and choose the controls

The choice of controls is the identification. Compare the response with and without the stock return as a contemporaneous control. How to read it The controls change the answer. If the stock return enters only through its lags, a one-standard-deviation spread shock lowers industrial production by 0.88% after 12 months; if the contemporaneous stock return is held fixed, the fall is 0.64%. The two estimates differ because stock prices and credit spreads react to the same news within the month. Holding the stock return fixed treats that news as already priced in by the stock market and attributes only the part of the spread movement that is not contemporaneously reflected in stock returns to the credit shock. Neither choice is "correct" without an argument. State the ordering you assume and report the other as a robustness check (Step 6). The baseline in the rest of the guide holds the stock return fixed, which is the more conservative of the two.

How to read it A one-standard-deviation widening of the credit spread lowers the level of industrial production by 0.06% in the month of the shock (not significant, p = 0.14), by 0.32% after three months, and by 0.64% after twelve months (95% band −1.04 to −0.23). The response keeps deepening to a maximum of −0.74% at 19 months and is significant at 5% from month 1 to month 19. After 20 months the band includes zero. Each row is a separate regression with 390 to 414 observations; the bands widen with the horizon (standard error 0.04 at h = 0, 0.21 at h = 12 and 0.40 at h = 24), which is the main cost of the method. In the output, "Peak response" is the largest absolute response and "Peak horizon" is the horizon at which it occurs.

A VAR with the same variables and the same ordering gives the same object by a different route. Agreement is reassuring; a large gap means that the VAR dynamics are misspecified or that the local projection is imprecise. How to read it The VAR and the local projection agree closely for the first year: −0.32 against −0.32 at three months, −0.64 against −0.63 at twelve months. They separate at long horizons. At 18 months the figures are −0.73 and −0.67, and at 24 months the local projection shows a recovery (−0.55) while the VAR continues to deepen (−0.69). That is the usual pattern: a VAR imposes a smooth, geometrically decaying response because it extends the short-run dynamics to every horizon, whereas a local projection lets each horizon speak for itself. The difference at 24 months (0.13) is small relative to the local-projection standard error (0.40), so the two are not statistically distinguishable. Report the local projection as the main result and the VAR as a cross-check, or the other way round, but state which.
Robustness: lags, lag augmentation, standard errors and the shock size

How to read it The sign and the timing are robust, the size is not. With three lags the response at twelve months is −0.54, with six lags −0.64 and with twelve lags −0.78; the lag-augmented specification with heteroskedasticity-robust errors gives −0.62 with a larger standard error (0.28 against 0.21). Widening the Newey-West bandwidth to 24 leaves the estimate unchanged and lowers the standard error slightly (0.19), so the significance does not depend on the bandwidth rule. The largest fall is at 19 months in every specification that holds the stock return fixed (18 months without it). The identification choice matters most: leaving the stock return out of the contemporaneous controls gives −0.88 at twelve months. In the paper, say that the response at one year is between 0.5% and 0.9% depending on lags and identification, and that all specifications agree on the shape.
A level or a growth rate? The outcome option

Industrial-production growth is a monthly growth rate. With the level outcome the response at horizon \(h\) is the effect on growth in month \(t+h\) ; with the cumulative-sum outcome it is the effect on the level of production, which is usually the question. How to read it The monthly growth effects are small (−0.06 to −0.11 percentage points per month for the first six months) and fade by the end of the first year (−0.03 at twelve months, +0.06 at 24). Read on their own, the late-horizon figures suggest that the shock has no lasting effect. The cumulative-sum outcome shows what they add up to: a level of industrial production that is 0.64% lower after twelve months and still 0.55% lower after 24. Choose the outcome to match the question, and say in the text whether the response is of a growth rate or of a level.
A level or a growth rate? The outcome option

When the shock is not observed: LP-IV If you have an external instrument for the shock (a high-frequency surprise, a narrative series), add it with the instrument option. The shock is then estimated by two-stage least squares at every horizon (LP-IV; Stock and Watson 2018), and the first-stage F statistic is reported. Check that the F statistic is well above 10 before you read the response.

How to write it: results A one-standard-deviation (17 basis-point) widening of the credit spread lowers the level of industrial production by 0.32% after three months (standard error 0.08) and by 0.64% after twelve months (standard error 0.21). The response reaches its maximum of −0.74% after 19 months, and is statistically significant at the 5% level from month 1 to month 19. The local-projection response is close to that of a VAR(6) with the same ordering for the first year; at 24 months the local projection shows a partial recovery (−0.55) while the VAR does not (−0.69). The size of the response at twelve months ranges from −0.54 to −0.88 across lag lengths and identifying assumptions; its sign and timing are the same in all of them.
