Time-Varying-Parameter Regression (Kalman Filter): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Did the persistence of inflation, or its sensitivity to unemployment, change between 1959 and 2009? The regression is with a diagonal \(Q\) whose elements are the variances of the shocks to each coefficient. The Kalman filter computes the likelihood, which is maximised over \(\sigma^2_\varepsilon\) and the diagonal of \(Q\) ; the Kalman smoother then gives the path of each coefficient using the whole sample. A variance of zero for a coefficient means that it is constant. The model is a Phillips curve: With a time-varying intercept \(\alpha_t\) , the quantity \(\alpha_t/(1-\rho_t)\) is a moving long-run level of inflation, so the intercept absorbs a trend in inflation that persistence would otherwise have to explain.

Before you estimate anything Estimate the constant model first. It is the benchmark, and its coefficients are the averages of the paths. Know what the model can and cannot find. Random-walk coefficients find slow drift, not a sudden break. Watch the error variance. If \(\sigma^2_\varepsilon\) goes to zero, the moving coefficients absorb everything and the paths mean little. How to write it: methods sentence We allow the coefficients to vary over time by modelling each as a random walk, and estimate the variances of the coefficient innovations and of the regression error by maximum likelihood with the Kalman filter. We report the smoothed paths of the coefficients with 95% bands.
Load the data and the constant benchmark

How to read it The constant model says that inflation is persistent (0.64 on its own lag) and that unemployment has no effect at all (0.009, standard error 0.09). This is the average over fifty years, and it is a hard result to believe for a Phillips curve. The next step shows whether the average hides coefficients that move.

How to read it The error variance is 3.7 and positive, so the moving coefficients do not absorb everything. The variance of the shocks to the intercept is 0.13 (s.e. 0.08) and to the persistence coefficient 0.005 (s.e. 0.002), and the variance of the shocks to the unemployment coefficient is zero. The data support a moving intercept and a moving persistence, and a constant slope on unemployment. Because the variances are on the boundary, the standard errors of the small ones are not reliable.
Step 2: The paths of the coefficients

How to read it The intercept moves between 5.8 and 11.3 (at the selected dates it is 5.8 in 1962, 9.3 in 1984 and 6.8 in 2009), and the persistence coefficient moves between −0.34 and 0.44 (smoothed standard deviation 0.17 in the middle of the sample), so it is much lower than the 0.64 of the constant model. The two moving paths are linked: when the intercept captures a slowly moving level of inflation, the persistence of the deviations from it is low. This is the usual finding of trend-cycle models of inflation (inflation is a moving trend plus noise), not a statement that inflation is not persistent. The unemployment coefficient is constant at −0.71, with a smoothed standard deviation of 0.19, so it is clearly negative, while the constant model found no effect (0.009). A plausible reading is that, in the constant model, the slow movement of trend inflation, which is correlated with unemployment over the sample, contaminated the slope; once the intercept is free to move, the Phillips-curve slope appears. This is an interpretation, and other specifications could give another answer. The first values of the paths are poorly determined, since the filter starts without information.
Step 3: Does time variation improve the fit?

How to read it The log-likelihood rises from −474.8 to −447.7 and the AIC falls from 951.5 to 903.4, which supports time variation in at least some coefficients. The likelihood-ratio statistic of 54 cannot be compared with a chi-squared distribution, because the null of zero variances is on the boundary of the parameter space; use the AIC, the paths and the estimated variances. The test says that the coefficients are not constant, but not when or why they changed.
What to report in the paper

Report the constant model as a benchmark, the estimated variances and their reliability, the smoothed paths with bands, and a comparison of the fit. Say that the paths are smoothed, which use future data, so they describe what the data say in hindsight. If a coefficient has a variance of zero, report it as constant. How to write it: results The Phillips curve with constant coefficients gives a persistence of 0.64 and no effect of unemployment on inflation. Allowing the intercept and the persistence coefficient to follow random walks improves the log-likelihood by 27 points (AIC 903 against 952). The estimated persistence is much lower than in the constant model, because the intercept absorbs a slow-moving level of inflation, and the unemployment coefficient is constant and clearly negative (−0.71, smoothed standard deviation 0.19), while the constant model finds no effect (0.009).

Mistakes to avoid Reading the smoothed path as real-time. It uses the future; use the filtered estimates for real-time claims. A zero error variance. The paths then fit anything; treat them with caution. Comparing likelihoods of models with different initial conditions. Use the same state-space basis for both, as above. Testing zero variances with a chi-squared. The null is on the boundary. Interpreting an intercept and a slope that move together separately. They are not separately identified in short samples. Applying the random-walk model to a sudden break. Use a break test. Time-varying coefficients on non-stationary variables. The paths can be spurious. Too many moving coefficients for the data. Let only the coefficients of interest move.

Trend-Cycle Decomposition: Unobserved Components, HP and Hamilton Filters

How much of the movement in GDP is a lasting change in the trend, and how much is a temporary cycle? The unobserved-components model writes the series as where \(\mu_t\) is the trend, \(\psi_t\) is a cycle and \(\varepsilon_t\) is noise. The trend is smooth: \(\mu_t = \mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1}\) and \(\beta_t = \beta_{t-1} + \zeta_t\) , so the growth rate changes slowly. The cycle is a damped stochastic cycle with a period \(2\pi/\lambda\) and a damping factor \(\rho<1\) : The model is estimated by maximum likelihood with the Kalman filter, and the trend and cycle come from the Kalman smoother. The two filters it is compared with do not use a model:
Trend-Cycle Decomposition: Unobserved Components, HP and Hamilton Filters

Method Idea Weak point Hodrick-Prescott a smooth curve that trades fit against smoothness ( \(\lambda = 1600\) for quarterly data) creates spurious cycles in a random walk; the end of the sample is unreliable Hamilton regression the cycle is the forecast error of the series two years ahead from its four latest values a different concept of the cycle; no value for the first years Unobserved components a model with a trend and a cycle the answer depends on the model and on the bounds on the cycle period Variable Definition gdp_level real GDP, 100 times the log, built by cumulating the annualised quarterly growth rates divided by four (the level is relative to 1959Q1, which is all the decomposition needs)
Trend-Cycle Decomposition: Unobserved Components, HP and Hamilton Filters

Before you estimate anything Plot the series in logs. Decomposition applies to a level, not to a growth rate. Decide what you mean by the cycle. The deviation from a smooth trend (HP, UC) and the unpredictable part of the series (Hamilton) are different things. Set the plausible cycle length. Business cycles in the U.S. last roughly 1.5 to 10 years; the bounds you set limit what the model can find. How to write it: methods sentence We decompose log real GDP into a trend and a cycle with an unobserved-components model with a smooth trend and a damped stochastic cycle with a period between 6 and 40 quarters, estimated by maximum likelihood with the Kalman filter. For robustness we compare the cycle with those from the Hodrick-Prescott filter (smoothing parameter 1600) and the Hamilton (2018) regression filter.
Trend-Cycle Decomposition: Unobserved Components, HP and Hamilton Filters
Load the data and plot the series

How to read it GDP grows at about 3% a year on average, with recessions as dips below the line of the trend (1974, 1980–82, 2008–09). The level of the series is a smooth line with small deviations, which is why the trend and the cycle are hard to separate: the answer depends on the model you use.
Trend-Cycle Decomposition: Unobserved Components, HP and Hamilton Filters
Step 1: Unobserved-components model with a stochastic cycle

How to read it The cycle has a period of 26.8 quarters, or 6.7 years, and a damping factor of 0.93, so a shock to the cycle loses about 7% of its size every quarter. The variance of the shocks to the cycle (0.49) is large relative to the variance of the shocks to the slope of the trend (0.004), so the model assigns most of the movement to the cycle and keeps the trend smooth. The standard deviation of the estimated cycle is 1.8 percentage points. The variance of the irregular is zero at the boundary.
Trend-Cycle Decomposition: Unobserved Components, HP and Hamilton Filters
Step 2: Is the cycle needed? Compare specifications

How to read it The smooth trend with a cycle has the lowest AIC (508.8), but BIC, which penalises parameters more, prefers the simple random walk with drift and no cycle (524.1 against 525.2 for the model with the cycle). So the data do not give strong support to the existence of a regular cycle: a series that is close to a random walk with drift produces a cycle estimate that is mostly the assumption of the model. Report this, and avoid presenting the cycle as a measured quantity.
Trend-Cycle Decomposition: Unobserved Components, HP and Hamilton Filters
Step 3: Compare with the HP and Hamilton filters

How to read it The unobserved-components and HP cycles are almost the same (correlation 0.98), with a standard deviation of 1.8 and 1.55; the model-based cycle is slightly larger because its trend is less flexible. The Hamilton cycle is quite different: it has a correlation of 0.71 and 0.74 with the other two and its standard deviation is about 1.7 times as large (3.2), because it measures the error of a two-year-ahead forecast, which contains the growth shocks of the next two years, not the gap to a smooth trend. The three are not interchangeable: if your result changes with the filter, it depends on how you define the cycle.
Trend-Cycle Decomposition: Unobserved Components, HP and Hamilton Filters

How to read it The estimated trend growth is close to 3 to 3.7% a year from the 1970s to the 1990s and falls to about 1% at the end of the sample, after the 2008–09 recession (the 5% at the very start is an edge effect of the smoother). The value at the end of the sample is the least reliable, since the smoother has no data after it; adding a few quarters can change it.
Trend-Cycle Decomposition: Unobserved Components, HP and Hamilton Filters
What to report in the paper

Report the model (trend and cycle), the estimated period and damping of the cycle with standard errors, a comparison with at least one other filter, and the sensitivity of your main result to the choice. Say that the cycle is an estimate, and that end-of-sample values are revised when data are added. How to write it: results and robustness The estimated cycle has a period of 6.7 years and a damping factor of 0.93, and a standard deviation of 1.8 percentage points. It is almost the same as the Hodrick-Prescott cycle (correlation 0.98). The Hamilton-filter cycle, which measures forecast errors, is correlated 0.71 with ours and has a larger variance, and we report our main results with all three measures. The information criteria give mixed support for a cycle in the model: AIC prefers it and BIC does not.
Trend-Cycle Decomposition: Unobserved Components, HP and Hamilton Filters

Mistakes to avoid Treating the cycle as data. It is an estimate that depends on the filter. Using HP with a wrong smoothing parameter. 1600 is for quarterly data; use 129600 for monthly and 100 for annual data (or 6.25 as Ravn and Uhlig suggest). Applying a filter to growth rates. Use the level, in logs. Ignoring the end of the sample. The last values change when data arrive; policy gaps in real time are different from those that use the full sample. Estimating the HP cycle and then regressing on it as if it were observed. The filter creates dynamics that can produce spurious results. Choosing the filter by its results. Decide on the filter before you see the main result and report the others as robustness.

Setting no bounds on the cycle period. The model can pick a cycle at a frequency that has no economic meaning. Reading a zero variance as a finding. A variance on the boundary means the component is deterministic in this specification, and the standard error is not meaningful there.
Unit-Root and Stationarity Tests: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Is the series stationary, or does a shock to it never die out? Write the series as \(y_t = \rho\, y_{t-1} + u_t\) . If \(|\rho| < 1\) , shocks fade and the series is stationary, I(0). If \(\rho = 1\) , shocks last forever and the series is a random walk, I(1). The augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) regression tests this by adding lagged differences to absorb serial correlation: Test Null hypothesis What it adds ADF unit root the standard test; sensitive to the number of lags Phillips-Perron unit root corrects the statistic for serial correlation without extra lags DF-GLS unit root removes the constant and trend by GLS first; more powerful when the root is near one

KPSS stationary reverses the null, so the two kinds of test can be compared Zivot-Andrews unit root without a break allows one structural break under the alternative Because a unit-root test has low power against a root close to one, rely on several tests with both kinds of null, and never on one p-value. Before you test anything Plot the series. A trend, a break or a change of mean tells you which deterministic terms to include. Choose the deterministic terms. A constant for a series that fluctuates around a mean; a constant and trend for a series that grows. A wrong choice distorts the test. Decide on the lag length. Too few lags leave serial correlation, too many lose power. Choose it with BIC or AIC and show that the conclusion does not depend on it.

How to write it: methods sentence We test for unit roots with the augmented Dickey-Fuller, Phillips-Perron and DF-GLS tests, whose null is a unit root, and the KPSS test, whose null is stationarity. Lag lengths are chosen by the Bayesian information criterion. Because these tests have low power against persistent stationary alternatives, we also report the Zivot-Andrews test, which allows one structural break.
Load the data and look at the series

How to read it The Treasury-bill rate drifts up through the 1970s, peaks at the start of the 1980s and falls afterwards, with long swings and no clear mean to return to. These are the signs of a unit root or of a very persistent series. The first difference looks like noise with larger swings at the end of the 1970s and the start of the 1980s. The tests below put numbers on this impression.

How to read it In levels the statistic does not pass the 5% critical value with a constant or with a constant and trend, so we cannot reject a unit root. In first differences the unit root is rejected at any level. The second table shows what happens if you fix the lag length by hand: the p-value moves a good deal (from 0.09 with 6 lags to 0.50 with 2 lags) but never falls below 5%. A conclusion that changed with the lag would not be one you could rely on; here the failure to reject a unit root in levels holds for every lag length.

How to read it Phillips-Perron gives the same answer as the ADF: no rejection in levels (p = 0.26 and 0.45). DF-GLS, which has more power when the root is close to one, comes closest to rejecting: with a constant its p-value is 0.041, but the statistic (−2.04) is almost equal to the critical value (−2.05), so this is a borderline result, and with a trend it does not reject (p = 0.22). When the specifications differ like this, report both and say that the evidence is not clear-cut instead of choosing the one that agrees with your model.
Step 3: KPSS test with the opposite null

How to read it The two kinds of test agree when ADF does not reject a unit root and KPSS rejects stationarity (a unit root), or when ADF rejects and KPSS does not (stationary). When both fail to reject, the data do not have enough information; when both reject, suspect a break or a fractional root. Here, KPSS rejects stationarity of the level around a constant (0.81 against a critical value of 0.46) and around a trend (0.65 against 0.15), and does not reject for the differences, in line with an I(1) series; the p-values of KPSS are interpolated and bounded between 0.01 and 0.10.
Step 4: Allowing for a structural break

How to read it A unit-root test can fail to reject because the series has a break (a regime change such as the monetary-policy change at the end of the 1970s), not because it has a root. The Zivot-Andrews test searches for the break date that gives the strongest evidence against the unit root. With a break in the level only, the unit root is not rejected (statistic −3.75 against a critical value of −4.81). With a break in the level and trend, the test rejects at 5% but only marginally (−5.19 against −5.07, p = 0.038), at 1978Q2, close to the change in U.S. monetary policy at the end of the 1970s. That is weak evidence for stationarity around a broken trend, and not enough to override the other tests; it shows that the break matters and should be reported.
Step 5: Put the evidence together for several series

How to read it A series is classified as I(1) when most tests point to a unit root in levels and the first difference is stationary, and as I(0) when none do. GDP growth is stationary by every test, as expected for a growth rate. The interest rate is I(1) by all three tests. For inflation (ADF and Phillips-Perron reject a unit root, KPSS rejects stationarity) and unemployment (ADF rejects, Phillips-Perron does not, KPSS does not reject) the tests are split, which is typical for persistent macro series: do not force a label, report the split and show that your main results hold when the series is treated either way.
What to report in the paper

Report the order of integration of every series in a table with the test statistics and the lag lengths; say which deterministic terms were used; present both the ADF-type and the KPSS-type tests; and state what you decided when the tests disagree and why. If a break is likely, report Zivot-Andrews with the break date. How to write it: data section Table 2 reports unit-root tests for the series in the model. The augmented Dickey-Fuller and Phillips-Perron tests do not reject a unit root in the level of the Treasury-bill rate (p = 0.16 and 0.26), DF-GLS is borderline (p = 0.04 with a constant, 0.22 with a trend), and the KPSS test rejects stationarity, while the first difference is stationary by all tests; we therefore treat the rate as I(1). GDP growth is stationary in levels. The tests are split for inflation and unemployment, which are highly persistent; we report results with these variables in levels and in first differences.

Mistakes to avoid Relying on one test. A unit-root test has low power; use tests with both kinds of null. The wrong deterministic terms. Leaving out a trend that is there, or adding one that is not, changes the answer. Choosing the lag length to get the result you want. Choose by BIC or AIC and show sensitivity. Ignoring structural breaks. A break can mimic a unit root; run Zivot-Andrews or a break test. Testing only levels. Test the first difference too, to rule out I(2). Differencing a stationary series. Over-differencing creates a moving-average unit root and lowers the information in the data. Treating "do not reject" as "has a unit root". It means the data cannot tell the two apart.
Forgetting that a regression on I(1) series can be spurious. Test for cointegration before you regress levels on levels.
VAR in First Differences: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

The question is: do stock prices and real activity help to predict each other? Finance theory says stock prices are forward-looking and should lead output; a feedback from output to prices is also possible. A vector autoregression (VAR) treats every variable as endogenous. Each variable is regressed on its own lags and the lags of the others, so you do not have to decide in advance which one is "the" dependent variable. The model selection tool found that the log S&P 500 and log industrial production are both I(1) and are not cointegrated . With no long-run relationship to preserve, the correct model is a VAR in first differences: The first difference of a log, multiplied by 100, is a percentage growth rate, so the VAR is in monthly stock returns and monthly industrial production growth.

Why not estimate the VAR in levels? With unit roots and no cointegration, a regression in levels is a spurious regression: the usual t- and F-tests are not valid. If the series were cointegrated, differencing would throw away the long-run relationship, and you would need the VECM guide instead. This is why the cointegration test comes before the model. How to write it: model section Augmented Dickey–Fuller tests indicate that the log S&P 500 index and log industrial production are integrated of order one, and the Johansen trace test finds no cointegrating relationship between them (trace statistic 4.74 against a 5% critical value of 15.49). We therefore model the joint dynamics of the two series with a vector autoregression in first differences, \(\Delta y_t = c + \sum_{i=1}^{p} A_i \Delta y_{t-i} + u_t\) , where \(\Delta y_t\) contains the monthly stock return and the monthly growth rate of industrial production, both in percent.
Load the data and take first differences

How to read it In levels the ADF p-values are far above 0.05: both series have a unit root. After differencing they are 0.000: the growth rates are stationary. The plots show the same thing. The levels trend and wander; the differences move around a constant mean. One observation is lost by differencing, leaving 419 months.

The lag order \(p\) is chosen with information criteria. Each one trades off fit against the number of parameters; the lowest value wins. How to read it The star marks the minimum of each column. AIC and FPE choose 4 lags; BIC and HQIC choose 3. The criteria often disagree, because BIC penalises extra parameters more heavily. A sound rule: start from the AIC choice, check that the residuals are free of serial correlation (Step 5), and use the BIC choice as a robustness check. Too few lags leave autocorrelation in the residuals, which invalidates the tests. A few too many lags only costs some precision.

How to read it There is one equation per variable. In the ipg equation, the second and third lags of the stock return are positive and highly significant: a rise in stock prices is followed by faster industrial production growth two to three months later. In the ret equation, the first two lags of industrial production growth are also significant. Individual VAR coefficients are hard to interpret because the lags interact. Do not build your results section on them. Papers report three summaries instead: Granger causality tests, impulse responses and variance decompositions, which follow below. Most papers put the coefficient table in an appendix. The correlation of the residuals (−0.08) is small. That will matter in Step 7.

A VAR is only usable if it is stable and its residuals are free of serial correlation. How to read it Stability. All eigenvalues of the companion matrix have modulus below 1 (the largest is 0.83), so the VAR is stable: shocks die out, and impulse responses are meaningful. A modulus at or above 1 would mean the system is not stationary, and you should check the differencing and the lag order. Serial correlation. The portmanteau test has the null of no residual autocorrelation. The p-values of 0.66 and 0.85 do not reject it, so four lags are enough. If this test rejected, you would add lags. Normality. Rejected, as is usual with financial data and extreme months such as October 2008. Estimates stay consistent; with over 400 observations the asymptotic tests remain usable. Report the result.

ARCH. Both equations show volatility clustering. This does not bias the coefficients but affects standard errors, which is a reason to treat borderline p-values with caution. How to write it: specification and diagnostics The lag length is set to four months, as selected by the Akaike information criterion; the Schwarz criterion selects three, and results with three lags are reported as a robustness check. The estimated VAR is stable, with all eigenvalues of the companion matrix inside the unit circle (largest modulus 0.83). A portmanteau test does not reject the null of no residual autocorrelation up to 12 lags (p = 0.66). Multivariate normality of the residuals is rejected, reflecting a small number of extreme observations, and the residuals show ARCH effects, as is common for monthly financial data.

Variable \(x\) Granger-causes \(y\) if past values of \(x\) improve the forecast of \(y\) beyond what the past of \(y\) alone provides. The null hypothesis is no Granger causality : all coefficients on the lags of \(x\) in the equation for \(y\) are zero. How to read it Both nulls are rejected at the 1% level, so predictability runs in both directions. The evidence is much stronger from stock returns to industrial production (the larger F-statistic), which fits the view that stock prices look ahead. "Granger causality" is about prediction, not cause . Stock prices may rise because investors expect output to grow; that does not mean higher prices cause the growth. Use the phrase "Granger-causes" or "helps to predict", never "causes".

An impulse response shows how each variable reacts over time to a one-time shock in one of them. Because the residuals of the two equations are correlated, the shocks must be separated first. The standard method is the Cholesky decomposition, which requires an ordering : the first variable can affect the second within the same month, but not the reverse. We order stock returns first. The justification is practical: the S&P 500 series is an average over the month, while industrial production for a month is published only in the middle of the next month, so stock prices cannot react to it within the month. How to read it Each panel shows the response of one variable (named second in the panel title) to a shock in another. The dashed lines are 95% confidence bands: a response is statistically different from zero only where the band excludes zero.

A stock-return shock of one standard deviation (3.4%) is followed by significantly higher industrial production growth two to three months later. The cumulative effect, which is the effect on the level of industrial production because the VAR is in growth rates, builds to about 0.6% after two years. An industrial-production shock (0.5%) raises stock returns over the next two months, with a cumulative effect of about 1.7%. All responses return to zero, as they must in a stable VAR. Because the model is in first differences, always say whether you are describing the response of the growth rate or the cumulative response of the level. Readers usually care about the level.

The forecast error variance decomposition (FEVD) answers a different question: of the unpredictable movements in each variable, what share is due to each shock? How to read it At a two-year horizon, stock-return shocks account for about 12% of the forecast error variance of industrial production growth, up from under 1% at one month. Industrial production shocks account for about 5% of the variance of stock returns. Each variable is mostly driven by its own shocks, which is normal; what matters is that the cross shares are not zero and that the share of stock shocks in output grows with the horizon. Statistically significant Granger causality can go with a small variance share. Report both: one says whether the link exists, the other how much it matters.

The three choices a referee will question are the ordering, the lag length and the sample. How to read it This table changes the conclusions, which is exactly what a robustness table is for. Ordering and lag length do not matter. Reversing the ordering, or using 3 or 8 lags, leaves the tests and the size of the responses almost unchanged. The ordering is harmless here because the residual correlation is only −0.08. The sample matters a great deal. Before 2008, stock returns still Granger-cause industrial production (p = 0.002), but the cumulative response is less than half as large (0.26% against 0.61%). The reverse channel, from industrial production to stock returns, disappears completely (p = 0.63).

After 2010 neither test rejects. With only 120 months the tests have low power, so this is weak evidence of no relationship, but it is certainly not evidence for one. The honest summary: stock returns lead industrial production, with an effect that the 2008–09 crisis roughly doubles; the feedback from production to returns is a crisis-period result only. A paper that reported only the full-sample numbers would overstate both findings. Always run the subsample check before you write the results section.

Section What goes in it From which step Data Sources, sample, transformations, unit-root and cointegration tests Step 2 and the selection tool Method The VAR equation, why first differences, lag selection, identification (ordering) Steps 1, 3 and 7 Results Granger causality table, impulse-response figure, variance decomposition table Steps 6 to 8 Robustness Diagnostics, alternative ordering, lag length, subsamples Steps 5 and 9 Appendix Full coefficient estimates Step 4 How to write it: results Table 3 reports Granger causality tests. In the full sample, the null that stock returns do not Granger-cause industrial production growth is rejected at the 1% level (F = 13.06, p < 0.01), as is the reverse null (F = 4.58, p < 0.01). Figure 2 shows the orthogonalised impulse responses. A one-standard-deviation shock to stock returns (3.4%) is followed by a statistically significant rise in industrial production growth two to three months later, and raises the level of industrial production by 0.6% after two years. Stock-return shocks account for 12% of the forecast error variance of industrial production growth at the 24-month horizon.

These full-sample results are influenced by the 2008–09 financial crisis. In the 1985–2007 subsample, stock returns continue to Granger-cause industrial production growth (p < 0.01), but the cumulative response falls to 0.3%, and there is no evidence of predictability running from industrial production to stock returns (p = 0.63). We conclude that stock prices are a leading indicator of real activity, while the apparent feedback from activity to stock prices reflects the crisis period. What a referee will ask Why this ordering? Give an economic or institutional reason, and show the reverse ordering. Why differences and not levels? Cite your unit-root and cointegration tests. Is the lag length arbitrary? Report the criteria and a different lag length.

Is this causal? Granger causality is predictive. Structural claims need identifying restrictions that you must defend. Is it stable over time? Show subsamples, especially around 2008. Only two variables? Omitted variables, such as interest rates, can create or hide Granger causality. Say so, or add them.
Vector Error-Correction Model: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

The question is: are short and long interest rates tied together in the long run, and which one adjusts when they drift apart? The expectations hypothesis of the term structure says the long rate is an average of expected future short rates plus a premium, so the two should not move apart permanently. The model selection tool found that both yields are I(1) and cointegrated . A vector error-correction model (VECM) is a VAR in first differences with one extra term, the deviation from the long-run relationship in the previous period: Part Name What it tells you \(\beta' y_{t-1} + \rho\) error-correction term how far the system was from its long-run relationship last period

\(\beta\) cointegrating vector the long-run relationship between the variables \(\alpha\) adjustment (loading) coefficients how fast each variable moves to close the gap \(\Gamma_i\) short-run coefficients the short-run dynamics Why a VECM and not a VAR in differences? A VAR in differences uses only changes, so it ignores the information that the two rates are currently far apart or close together. When the variables are cointegrated, that gap predicts future changes, and leaving it out is a misspecification. The VECM is the model that keeps both the long-run relationship and the short-run dynamics. How to write it: model section Both yields are integrated of order one, and the Johansen procedure indicates one cointegrating relationship between them. We therefore estimate the vector error-correction model \(\Delta y_t = \alpha(\beta' y_{t-1} + \rho) + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \Gamma_i \Delta y_{t-i} + u_t\) , where \(y_t\) contains the 10-year and 1-year Treasury yields, \(\beta\) is the cointegrating vector describing their long-run relationship, and \(\alpha\) contains the adjustment coefficients that measure how quickly each yield responds to deviations from that relationship.
Load the data and look at the long-run relationship

How to read it Each yield has a unit root in levels (p-values of 0.81 and 0.53) and is stationary in first differences: both are I(1). But the difference between them is stationary (p below 0.01). That is cointegration in its simplest form: two series that wander, but wander together. The plot makes this visible. Both yields rose until the early 1980s and fell for decades afterwards; the spread kept returning to its mean of about 1 percentage point. Always plot your candidate long-run relationship before testing it formally.
Choose the lag order and the deterministic terms

Two specification choices come before the cointegration test. Lag order. k_ar_diff is the number of lagged differences in the VECM. It equals the lag order of the VAR in levels minus one. Deterministic terms. This choice matters more than students expect, because the critical values of the Johansen test depend on it. Option in statsmodels Meaning Use when "n" no constant almost never "ci" constant inside the cointegrating relation the series have no trend; the long-run relation has a non-zero mean. Interest rates, spreads, ratios. "co" constant outside the relation the series have linear trends (log GDP, log prices) "cili" trend inside the relation the long-run relation itself trends Interest rates have no deterministic trend, and their spread has a positive mean, so "ci" is the right choice here.
Choose the lag order and the deterministic terms

How to read it AIC chooses 7 lagged differences, HQIC 5 and BIC only 1. As in any VAR, the choice is settled by the residuals: Step 8 shows that with 1 lag the residuals are strongly autocorrelated, so the BIC choice is too short. We use 7 and check 5 as robustness.

The rank \(r\) is the number of independent long-run relationships. With two variables it can be 0 (no cointegration: use a VAR in differences), 1 (one long-run relation: use a VECM), or 2 (both series are actually stationary: use a VAR in levels). How to read it Read each test from the top. "Rank ≤ 0" is rejected (29.39 is above 15.49), so there is at least one cointegrating relation. "Rank ≤ 1" is not rejected (1.07 is below 3.84), so there is exactly one. The trace test and the maximum-eigenvalue test agree, which makes the conclusion solid. When they disagree, most authors follow the trace test and say so.

How to read the long-run relation The software reports the vector as \(\beta' y + \rho = 0\) . Moving everything except the first variable to the right-hand side changes the signs : a coefficient of −0.936 on the 1-year yield means the long-run relation is yield_10y = 1.31 + 0.936 × yield_1y In the long run, a 1-point rise in the 1-year yield goes with a 0.94-point rise in the 10-year yield, and the constant of 1.31 is the average term premium. Forgetting the sign change is the most common mistake in student papers that use a VECM.
Test restrictions on the long-run relation

Theory often predicts a specific value. The expectations hypothesis implies that the long-run coefficient is exactly 1, which would make the simple spread stationary. How to read it The estimate of 0.936 is not significantly different from 1 (p = 0.12). The data are consistent with a one-for-one long-run relationship, which agrees with the stationary spread found in Step 2. Testing the value that theory predicts turns a statistical result into an economic one.

The adjustment coefficients show which variable does the correcting . How to read it Sign. For the variable the vector is normalised on, the adjustment coefficient should be negative : when the 10-year yield is above its long-run value, it falls. Here it is −0.111 and significant, so the error-correction mechanism works. A positive or insignificant coefficient on every variable would mean there is no adjustment, which contradicts cointegration. Speed. The 10-year yield closes about 11% of any gap per quarter, so half of a deviation is gone after roughly 6 quarters. Weak exogeneity. The coefficient for the 1-year yield is small and insignificant (p = 0.65). The short rate does not respond to the gap: it is weakly exogenous . In economic terms, the short rate, which follows monetary policy, leads, and the long rate adjusts to it.

How to write it: long-run results The estimated cointegrating relationship is \(y^{10}_t = 1.31 + 0.936\, y^{1}_t\) , with a standard error of 0.041 on the slope. The hypothesis of a unit long-run coefficient cannot be rejected in the system estimate (p = 0.12), consistent with the expectations hypothesis and a stationary term spread, although dynamic OLS yields a smaller coefficient of 0.84. The adjustment coefficient in the 10-year yield equation is −0.111 (t = −2.78), implying that about 11% of a deviation from the long-run relationship is corrected each quarter, with a half-life of roughly six quarters. The adjustment coefficient in the 1-year yield equation is statistically insignificant (p = 0.65), so the short rate is weakly exogenous: the long rate adjusts to the short rate rather than the reverse.

How to read it Causality. In a VECM there are two channels. Long-run causality runs through the error-correction term (Step 7). Short-run Granger causality runs through the lagged differences, tested here. The 1-year yield Granger-causes the 10-year yield (p below 0.01); the reverse is not significant at 5%. Both channels point the same way: from the short rate to the long rate. Serial correlation. The portmanteau test does not reject (p = 0.67): 7 lags are enough. With the single lag that BIC preferred, the same test rejects strongly, which is why we did not use it. Normality. Rejected, because of the extreme interest-rate movements of 1979–82. The Johansen procedure is robust to non-normality, in particular to excess kurtosis, so this does not overturn the results. Report it.

How to read it VECM impulse responses differ from those of a stationary VAR in one important way: they do not return to zero . The variables are I(1), so a shock moves their levels permanently. What cointegration guarantees is that the two responses settle at levels that respect the long-run relationship, so the gap between them closes even though each yield ends up at a new level.

How to read it The long-run coefficient is stable in the Johansen estimates. It lies between 0.87 and 1.02 across lag lengths and subsamples, always within about two standard errors of 1. The adjustment is less stable. With 5 lags the 10-year adjustment coefficient is smaller and only significant at 10%, and weak exogeneity of the 1-year yield becomes borderline (p = 0.06). In 1990–2019 the adjustment coefficient is not significant at all (p = 0.18). Error correction was fast and clear before 1990 and is hard to detect afterwards, a period that includes seven years of short rates held near zero. Dynamic OLS disagrees on the size. It gives a long-run coefficient of 0.835 with a small standard error, which is significantly below 1. Single-equation and system estimators can differ in finite samples, and when they do the paper must say so.

What can be claimed: the two yields are cointegrated, the long-run coefficient is close to one, and the long rate does the adjusting. What cannot be claimed without qualification: that the coefficient is exactly one, or that the adjustment speed is constant over time.

The trace statistic rejects the null of no cointegration (29.39 against a 5% critical value of 15.49) but not the null of at most one cointegrating vector (1.07 against 3.84). The maximum-eigenvalue test gives the same conclusion. We therefore proceed with a cointegration rank of one.

What a referee will ask Why these deterministic terms? Justify the choice from the behaviour of the data; do not leave the software default unexplained. Is the rank robust to the lag length? Show the test for at least two lag lengths. Did you read the signs correctly? Write the long-run relation as an equation in the text. Is the adjustment coefficient negative and significant? If not, the error-correction story does not hold. Is the long-run relation stable? Report subsamples; long samples of interest rates span very different monetary regimes. Does a different estimator agree? Report DOLS or FMOLS next to the Johansen estimate.
Wavelet Coherence: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Do money growth and inflation move together, and does the answer depend on the horizon and on the decade? A single correlation averages over all horizons and all dates. Wavelet analysis keeps both: it measures the relation at each period (in months) and at each point in time. Our question is: at which horizons and in which decades are U.S. M2 growth and CPI inflation related, and do they move together or in opposite directions? The Morlet wavelet transform of a series \(x_t\) at scale \(s\) and time \(\tau\) is \(W_x(\tau,s)\) . The wavelet coherence of two series is where \(S\) is a smoothing operator over time and scale, and the phase \(\phi_{xy}=\arg S(W_{xy})\) tells us whether the series move together (near 0), in opposite directions (near \(\pm\pi\) ) or one behind the other. \(R^2\) lies between 0 and 1 and behaves like a local squared correlation. Without the smoothing the ratio would be exactly one everywhere.

Symbol Variable Definition \(x_t\) infl CPI inflation, 12-month log change, percent \(y_t\) m2 M2 growth, 12-month log change, percent period cycle length in months, 16 to 512 Before you estimate anything Wavelet coherence describes association by horizon. It does not test a causal claim or a long-run relation. Decide the range of periods you care about before you look (here 16 to 128 months, so cycles of about one to ten years), and decide what you will call significant. With overlapping 12-month changes the series are very smooth, so do not read the shortest periods. How to write it: model section We compute the squared wavelet coherence between 12-month M2 growth and 12-month CPI inflation, using a Morlet wavelet with central frequency six. The coherence is smoothed over time and scale. We assess significance by Monte Carlo against 300 pairs of independent AR(1) series with the same persistence as the data, and we mark the cone of influence where edge effects matter. Phase differences show whether the two series move together or in opposite directions.
Load the data and look at the series

How to read it The sample has 720 months, 1960-01 to 2019-12. Inflation averages 3.62% and M2 growth 6.54%, and both are smooth because they are 12-month changes. The correlation over the whole sample is only 0.18, and it is not stable: 0.06 in 1960–79, 0.29 in 1980–99 and −0.18 in 2000–19. A single correlation therefore hides a relation that changes sign across periods. The wavelet analysis asks whether it also changes with the horizon.

How to read it The coherence is computed for 41 periods from 16 to 512 months. Only 53% of the time-period plane lies inside the cone of influence, because long periods need a lot of data on both sides of each date. In the check, a series delayed by six months at period 48 gives a phase of +0.79 radians, which is six months. So a positive phase means the second series (M2) lags the first (inflation), and a phase near ±π means the two move in opposite directions.

How to read it The series are very persistent (AR(1) coefficients 0.991 and 0.985), so high coherence arises easily by chance. Against 300 pairs of independent AR(1) series with the same persistence, 12.6% of the plane inside the cone is above the 95% critical value. Five percent is expected under the null, and the null simulations themselves exceed 9.9% in only 5% of draws, so the excess is real but modest. In the figure, the white contour encloses a few islands: short periods (about 16 to 25 months) in the 1960s, 1970s, mid-1980s, around 2000 and 2008, and longer periods (about 40 to 80 months) in the late 1960s and 1970s and in the 2000s. Most of the map is below the critical value, even where the coherence looks high (yellow-green). The critical value is about 0.9, so colour alone says little.
Turn the picture into numbers: by period, by decade and by phase

How to read it By period, the mean coherence is 0.77 at 16 months, 0.50 at 32, 0.80 at 64 and 0.53 at 128, but the mean 95% critical value is about 0.9 at all of them, and the share of significant points is 26%, 0%, 28% and 0%. The mean phase is close to ±π at 16 and 32 months (−3.06 and 3.12 radians) and about 2.1 to −2.3 radians at 64 and 128 months, so where the series are related they move in opposite directions. By decade, the mean coherence in the 32–128 month band is 0.73 in the 1960s, 0.70 in the 1970s, 0.57 in the 1980s, 0.52 in the 1990s and about 0.70 after 2000. The 1980s and 1990s have almost no significant points (4% and 1%) against 27% in the 1970s. The first and last decades have few points outside the cone, so be careful with them. Of the 1,043 significant points in the 32–128 month band, 99% are in anti-phase, with a circular mean phase of 144 degrees. This fits the signs of the sub-sample correlations: where co-movement exists at these horizons, faster M2 growth goes with slower inflation, not faster.
Turn the picture into numbers: by period, by decade and by phase

How to write it: results The correlation between 12-month M2 growth and CPI inflation is 0.18 over 1960–2019 but changes from 0.06 to 0.29 to −0.18 across the three twenty-year sub-periods. Wavelet coherence shows that the relation is concentrated at specific horizons and dates: 12.6% of the time-period plane inside the cone of influence is significant at 5%, against 5% expected from 300 independent AR(1) simulations, at short periods (16 to 25 months) and at 40 to 80 months, the latter in the late 1960s, the 1970s and the 2000s. Almost none is significant in the 1980s and 1990s (4% and 1% of the points in the 32–128 month band). Where coherence is significant, the series are mostly in anti-phase (99% of significant points in the 32–128 month band). We therefore find no stable positive co-movement between money growth and inflation at these horizons.
What to report in the paper

Item What to show Wavelet and smoothing Morlet, central frequency, smoothing windows, the range of periods Figure coherence map with the cone of influence and the 95% contour Significance Monte Carlo design: the null model, the number of replications and the share of the plane that is significant, compared with 5% Numbers average coherence by period and by sub-period, not only a picture Phase the phase, with the sign convention checked on a test signal Next step a regression or VAR at the horizon the map points to, since coherence is not an effect size Common mistakes Reading colour outside the cone of influence. Edge effects make coherence unreliable there. Mask it or shade it.
What to report in the paper

Reading pointwise significance as a finding. With thousands of points, some are significant by chance. Compare the share of the plane that is significant with what the null series give. Using persistent series without a persistent null. Smooth series produce high coherence by chance. Use AR(1) surrogates that match the persistence, as here. Getting the phase sign wrong. Conventions differ between packages. Test it on a signal with a known lead. Treating coherence as a regression coefficient. It says nothing about size or direction of an effect, only about co-movement at a horizon. Using overlapping changes at the shortest periods. Twelve-month changes are smooth by construction, so start at periods longer than 12 months.

Open Econometric Systems is a free tool on this site that runs 173 models in 17 method groups in your browser (time series, panel data, causal inference, machine learning, Bayesian, Markov switching, microeconometrics, nonparametric and robust, finance, productivity and spatial, and statistics): you upload a CSV, choose the model and read the results, and nothing leaves your computer. Every model has a tutorial guide with real output and the Python code behind it.
Which model should I use for time series that are not stationary?

It depends on the unit-root tests. All variables stationary: OLS or local projections. All I(1) and not cointegrated: a VAR in first differences. All I(1) and cointegrated: a VECM. A mix of I(0) and I(1): ARDL, or NARDL if increases and decreases may differ. The Time-Series Guide has a decision tree and a questionnaire that picks the model from your answers.
When should I use a threshold regression and when a smooth-transition regression?

Use a threshold regression (TAR or SETAR) when behaviour changes abruptly once a variable crosses a level, and you want to estimate the level with a bootstrap test and confidence interval. Use a smooth-transition regression (LSTAR or ESTAR) when the change is gradual as a state variable moves through a range. With a very fast transition the two give nearly the same fit, which the smooth-transition guide shows on a Taylor rule.
How is a threshold different from a structural break?

A structural break is tied to a date: the parameters change at some point in time and stay changed. A threshold is tied to the level of a variable: the same regime can occur at several dates whenever the variable is above or below the threshold. The Bai-Perron guide covers breaks and the threshold guide covers thresholds. If the high regime sits in one period, as high inflation does in the 1970s, the two readings can look alike.
How do I estimate the effect of a monetary policy shock?

Use a structural VAR or local projections. The SVAR guide identifies shocks by a Cholesky ordering, long-run restrictions (Blanchard-Quah) or an external instrument (proxy-SVAR). The local-projections guide gives impulse responses horizon by horizon without a full system. For Bayesian versions see the Bayesian guide.

The Panel Data Guide covers pooled OLS, random and fixed effects, GMM, Driscoll-Kraay errors, mean-group and CCE estimators, first differences, pooled mean group, CS-ARDL, panel local projections and Hansen's panel threshold regression, with a decision tree to choose among them.
How do I estimate causal effects?
The Causal Inference Guide covers difference-in-differences and event studies, regression discontinuity, instrumental variables and related designs, each with code and real output.
Is there a guide for Bayesian estimation or Markov-switching models?

Yes. The Bayesian Guide covers Bayesian VARs, factor-augmented and time-varying parameter VARs, stochastic volatility and more. The Markov-Switching Guide covers Markov-switching autoregressions, regressions and VARs.
Can I run the models on my own data?

Yes. Open Econometric Systems runs in your browser: choose a model, upload a CSV, map the columns and run it. The data stay on your computer. Each result can be reproduced with the Python code shown in the model's guide.
The site is by Tuhin G. M. Al Mamun, an economist working on macroeconomics, Bayesian and time-series econometrics and policy. See the home page and the working-papers page for research and teaching.
Does OES clean my data before estimation?

Yes. When you upload a CSV or Excel file on the OES page, it is checked and prepared for estimation in your browser: numbers and dates written as text, missing-value codes, column names and sort order are fixed, the unit and time columns are found, and problems such as an unbalanced panel or duplicate rows per unit and period are listed. Missing values are not filled in and no observation is deleted unless you choose to: an optional step can fill missing values with the median or by interpolation, or cap extreme values. You can download the prepared file and a cleaning log. The Data Cleaning Lab offers manual control.
